Back to 2005, Indigo Prophecy (or Fahrenheit as uncensored version) developed by Quantic Dream. It's first game that introduces new combination between adventure game and interactive cutscene. The idea is to provide the movie-like experience and let audiences participate on each event rather than watch the whole scene.
The story introduces supernatural drama thriller where all the things begin in one of New York's Diner as very strong intro. You take control the character perspectives for both murderer and investigators. Each character is intriguing and has their own personality where you learn from story and your interaction. Whats make Fahrenheit unique is storytelling and choices, most in-game interactions and dialogues have consequences in term of moral and ethics. It could impact on your character mental state or change the pace of story or both along with well-executed and connection between characters.
The gameplay involves environmental and dialogue interaction that required mouse swiping as it gives strong feelings of control. Some scenes allow you to explore small section and interact at you own will or switch between characters to observe and progress the story. The game also contain heavy QTE in most physical action sequences. Require player's reflex action which might distract player from whole cinematic scenes.
Remastered version offers sharpen textures, new UI, and some typographical changes which are slightly different from original. It's also uncensored version which contain some nudity contents I used to play on retailed version.
On the other hand, mouse interaction are quite unnecessary in some parts. Transition between two types of QTE might get annoying and bit over usage. The story pacing also heavily change in final. It's bit letdown and less interaction compare where the first act is so interesting.
Fahrenheit might have some gameplay flaws and story itself left some unexplained answers. But it first brings fully interactive movie into video games. It's classic, unique, and intriguing in direction. Set the new standard of video game as we see nowadays.
Plus, I personally did love songs and ambient soundtracks

For a game that is f2p and in alpha im quite impressed by the result.
DD2 is a very casual Tower Def game that suits players of all age.
Theres a decent amount of dif maps to be played with each of them having a few tricks to make them easier.
The game includes 4 dif heroes to choose from - pets - equipment (not only +stat) and a lot of grind. My only real problem with the game is that it's way too easy to reach the highest difficulty nm4. And progressing through the difficulties is based on getting new gear from harder maps - which drives people to join games that are too difficult for them, so that they can be carried by the others a few times to up their gear. Progressing from nm3 to nm4 and from nm4 900 to 1000 just requires getting carried once through a map to get usable gear.
After a player has reached the highest possible difficulty, thats when the real grind starts. Getting the optimal gear will take a lot of time and you end up running the same map over and over. The real issue with the game is the fact that progressing doesn't feel very rewarding. You can easily grind a lvl 1 hero to 50 in 2 hours if you know what you are doing and reach the top difficulty in a day.
Theres no real character customisation in the game. Sure theres stat points that lead to certain builds, but the builds are so obvious and 1 way streets that everyone ends up with the same builds. Until nm4 you can defeat the maps with a big variety of strategies, but after you reach the highest difficulty, theres 1 strategy that you might have to tweak a bit depending on the map.
The game also has some weird fps drop problems for me during the first 15-20 minutes, after which they completely disappear.
Over all the game is a good time sink and decently fun - but the game feels too simple and easily beaten that I wouldn't for that reason invest any money on this. After playing 34 hours I can already say that im bored of running nm4 incursion  and nm4 necro and that theres no real replay value here. The game is just very repeatative and doesn't give me the feel of real progression or uniqueness to my character.
My suggestion would be to take a look at the stat point system really well and ask if theres something to be changed there. I would also want to see some type of real customisation on your hero - skill points + skill tree (for towers etc.) to choose from?
I understand there ideas would make balancing difficult and would require the devs to create a lot new skills with real variety, but something needs to be done to make the game more interesting.
I up voted this game, but if there was a neutral option I would have gone for that.

I have taken sometime to play this game myself and I decided that I should write a review here so that it would be helpful for those who read it and decide whether to purchase this game or not.
Get to the point, right now the game is in 'Early Access' so it is not really complete. However, personally, only what the Early Access has offered now worths the money.
The very first thing that can be accounted as pros is the the game's very own concept. It is a new dimension of 'survival game', unlike many mainstream survival game lists which involve zombies and mutants to horrify you, this game is another story: just you against the 'Mother Nature'. You are on your own, among the cold, hunger, thirst, tiredness, or even danger from wolves. All you need to do is 'survive'. It sounds simple and uninteresting, but believe me this game is well enough even with this simplicity in this game genre. No safe place with lots of supplies (unless you choose 'Pilgrim' mode). You need to take risks with your own actions. Everything is by yourself.
The gameplay ... I don't know if I should classify it as a pro or con, but it is mixed. You can never expect anything from each playthrough; when you restart, everything except the regions will be resetted. This gives you the survival experience to some extends. For example, you might find a rifle, the only 'real' weapon in the game, without any bullets before you find one bullet miles away, or you need a can opener but still yet to be found; what will you do? which way? where is it going to be? Everything which other survival games may overlook matters in this game. You need clothes to keep you warm, raw food, if not cooked well, can be a threat when eaten, or you can even hurt your legs if you do not watch your steps (which happens to me a lot lol). These are some of the situations that I found and I need to give the 'thumb up' for the developer's careful planning so as to make this game as realistc as possible.
However, there is something that still bugs me; the wolves. They still lack realistic movements: too repetitive and can be easy to deal with as you get get used to the game. Even though the developer has mentioned something about the wolves, their movements and some behaviors, such as how slow or fast it should be in different situations, are needed for consideration *for developers*. I hope if the wolves are readjusted in the right way it would gives me more exciting experience. Nevertheless, even with this comment I still find dealing with wolves sometimes hard anyway. (I heard that more wildlife will be added, so it might be the solution for this problem as well.)
If you are fans of survival game and need a new dimension on survival experience, I suggest you that you buy this and try it once or wait for sometime until the full release comes (Story Mode, I'm really looking forward to that!).
My last warning ..
"Beware of the wolves, the cold, or even yourself as you play this game".

Farm Frenzy: Heave Ho is the sequel to Farm Frenzy: Hurricane Season and is a casual game from Buka Entertainment/Alawar. The game bears the Buka trademark cute childrens story book graphics. As is characteristic of nearly all games from this publisher the game is family friendly and well suited for younger children, but will appeal to casual game fans of all ages.
The graphics are full HD and are both cute and well animated. The artstyle is colourful and pleasing to look at.  The game has been given a pirate themed make-over this time with all the animals wearing pirate themed attire or sporting pirate themed tattoo's.
The sound is contextual with pleasant samples. Music is sequenced sound loops in a pseudo country style arangement which is pleasing to listen to. There appears to be a single in-game track repeated during game play stages which gets a bit repetitive. The repetition is broken to an extent by different tracks for the menu and pre-game instructions.
The player is tasked with purchasing chickens, collecting eggs, processing the eggs to make powder eggs, processing the powder eggs to make pasta and also accumulating funds. Storage facilities can be upgraded as can manufacturing facilities. Dogs can be hired to help capture ferrets and bears which can be sold at the market. Cats can be hired to collect goods and place them in storage.  As storage becomes full goods need to be transported to the market for sale.  There are additional facilities and more stages to complete than in earlier games in the series.
The style of play is arcade action with puzzle solving and resource management aspects. There are rewards for completing level completion criteria within certain time constraints.
The game is fun to play and it can be quite challenging completing stages within the required time.
The game size is small which should be a relief to those with limited storage capacity on their compter or laptop.
To summarise, a fun family friendly game with really cute graphics and good re-play value for those who like casual games.

Farm Frenzy: Heave Ho is the sequel to Farm Frenzy: Hurricane Season, and if you enjoyed the previous one you will definitely have a good time playing this game.
Essentially, you will have to complete all tasks per level within a specific time to achieve the golden chest. Upon your success you will receive a token which you can use in the slot machine to get well-needed booster which you will be able to use on the next level. Of course you will also gather money which will can be used to purchase upgrades.
The pirate theme does give this game a plus and the cartoon style graphics are always fun. One thing I noticed is the levels are considerably more challenging than the previous title. In terms of the audio, not much change; I would personally prefer something a little bit exotic, Flamenco perhaps?
In-game achievements but no Steam achievements, however you will still be getting trading cards.

I got this game for free from Gira through my friend Viviflare. It is a simple arcade reaction-based action game which involves timing a ball launch towards a spinning paddle to send the ball towards any of two green/blue coloured sides. Sending the ball towards a green/blue coloured side will award the player one point, while sending the ball towards a red/yellow coloured side will reduce 1 life for the player. Sending the ball to touch a constantly moving +1 or life icon will award an additional point or a life point. Losing all life points will immediately end the game. For every 10 points the player has scored, the paddle will spin progressively faster, making it more difficult to score points. Scoring 50 points to get all achievements will be somewhere between normal and hard in difficulty. As the game is quick and easy to restart upon losing all life points and has more or less reasonable achievements which can be obtained in less than 10 hours, I am recommending this game when at discount of less than 1 dollar as it has relatively inexpensive trading cards and versatile English/Latin alphabet emoticons.

I'm not remotely close to be a programmer (not a clue about scripting)... and just in a couple hours, managed to understand the basics.
Everything is labeled and tagged; you just click on a button, hover the cursor on the options, and you'll get how and what to do. And if you can't find "your" option, there are more than enough to get what you want in some other way.

In-game graphics are simple, but pretty and well done. And they can be edited easily as they're just a bunch of images in a folder, no compressed weird files or bulls#it like that.
The portraits are beautiful. There's a TON of them, and you also have a character generator to make more (which can also be edited easily). You also have backgrounds, main title screens, items, animations... and again, everything easily editable.
All in all, it's actually entertaining in itself, aside of being a software program.
Totally recommended.

- difficulty options (difficulty scales well)
- calming music

- re-playability

Over all it's a good game but the glitches can really ruin the experience.

It is hard to state something like this when you're talking about one of the most famous indie game ever released, but here we go: I hate LIMBO. The whole game is just a repetitive exercise of attempt->death->retry->death->solution found->new death. The death in LIMBO is not a punishment for the player's mistake, but the only possibility to find the solution to a puzzle. Frustration above satisfaction, you'll never solve a puzzle because you're good, but because you died enough to understand the only way to pass a section of the level. Praises go to the art style and to the atmosphere, and to the decision to have merciful checkpoints. Not enough for me.

Poor Scarlett has been dragged into more farming mayhem in this new addition to the Farm Frenzy series. After having a bit of misfortune during her trip, she ends up on an island where the local animals need her help with farming. It's a game filled with talking animals, making steaks and so much more.

A Hat in Time is a long awaited yet marvelous success. Gears for Breakfast have really outdone themselves to not only deliver on their promises but go further than we could have expected. While many kickstarter games are full of obtrusive bugs, issues and critical design flaws. This game will remind you why we loved 3D platforming. Teadious moments of the genre have been reworked and fixed to create a streamlined experience. The controls feel so responsive and make it fun just to move around each world. Plus sound design is fantastic, befitting the time manipulation vibe of the story.
While there are only 5 worlds each one is different. The way you go about objectives and how you are asked to explore them means you'll never feel like you're doing the same set of tasks twice; And for once each collectable is important and feels meaningful. You will want to obtain 100%, which is so important for this type of game.
It's also impossible not to mention the charm. Hat Kid is goofy and adorable, which really allows you to connect to the character even if the story is a little unimportant. Moods can change quickly though, with a rather shocking mansion level that might make you rethink the cutsey atmosphere. The only big issue? It's a little too short. I want more and can't wait for the dlc chapters down the line as well as workshop support.
Fans of Mario and other platformers will be glad to know: It's fluid, fast, well-designed and an absolute joy to play. A few minor bugs here and there but nothing that could hurt the experience. Get it now, especially if you've been tarnished by recent kickstarter projects. This one proves it can be done.

Pros:
-Very interesting story and plot
-Well done QTEs
-Multiple endings
-Interesting characters
Cons:
-Terrible controls and camera
-SPOILER (see the end of the recommendation)
Actually, as I am writing this, I still don't know whether I should recommend this game or not, I'll probably make my choice when the post will be over. On the one hand, it's a Quantic Dreams game, I love them, I love QTEs, and I love the way they create stories and put you at the center of it. Fahrenheit, Indigo Prophecy is one of these stories that you want to be told again and again, because you're part of it and it's really great. Those who don't like QTEs shouldn't even think about buying the game, but hey, that's Quantic Dreams, that's the purpose of a game, those who don't like strategy games won't buy a Total War, that's nonsense.
The story is again, really interesting and so are the characters, I had a lot of fun switching between one and the other, seeing the game through different points of view instead of only one. Sadly, it breaks some of the element of surprise sometimes, as you already know things your characters don't, so you can orientate their search rather than have to find out with them. That's a double edged sword.
However, the game is stained by terrible controls, you basically can't play the game without a controller, or the camera will be your worst enemy, and even with one, the camera will always tend to do shoit, and your movements will be accordingly troubled. And if you intend to do the game in hard mode as I did, that could be a real gamebreaker sometimes.
Alright, so, I appreciated the game, and QTE lovers will appreciate it as well, should at least, because it's really a good game in the end, despite its controls, you can still beat it...I'd say I'll recommend it then. Because although there are some scenaristic troubles in the game (one major one will follow in the spoiler) it's still a game I finished 100%, so I can't really say I don't recommend it to people, just be aware, controls are really bad, and...well...
SPOILER
However, the ending is really a piece of junk. It's sad, because it leaves me with the same disgust the first Mass Effect 3 ending left me with. The game was fine, honestly, with its very bad controls, I still enjoyed it personally, but the end was so lame...actually, there are three endings, the "normal" one, the "good" one, and the "bad" one, and guess what ? The only ending I liked was the bad one, because it's actually the only one that...well, that works as an ending. The others are just terrible ways to end a story such as Fahrenheit's.

Farm Frenzy: Heave Ho is next in the series of the very popular time management game series, and it maintains the same standard of quality of its predecessors.  If anything, it may be a little too similar to the previous entry with few gameplay changes, although if you enjoyed Hurricane Season, this one will certainly appeal to you.
The game is your standard genre fair; each level gives you a set of objectives in the area of collecting a number of items and creating food dishes. You're only given so much time and money to purchase livestock and tend to your land, so figuring out a strategy on what to buy and sell while keeping critters out of the barnyard and picking up produce before it disappears is the gist of the gameplay. Things can get hectic, especially if you're trying for gold, but can be rather laid back if you're not worried about challenging yourself.
As you complete levels, you'll earn stars (in-game currency) that can be used to upgrade your farm equipment which will then churn out more product or give more storage space. You can also level up your trusty companions to better help fend off pesky intruders, and even buy tokens to use on the slot machine, making an overabundance of currency actually useful.  Completing in-game achievements also awards slot machine tokens which can be used to win more tokens, stars, and power-ups useable in the game levels. The power-ups aren’t required, but are beneficial if you’re aiming for gold trophies.
All of the artwork has a cartoony aesthetic to it that compliments the casual game play elements quite well. This is clearly the same artist as the previous game; all the characters look the same save for wearing pirate-ey apparel, but it’s pleasant on the eyes and fits the overall humor of the game.
Once again, the absence of Steam Achievements is a sore spot.  At least the in-game achievements award tokens which are much more valuable now since they are no longer awarded from gold trophies.   But full Steam integration is a must for casual games, as it adds so much value to the overall package.  Trading cards are indeed nice, but not enough.
That said, Heave Ho is another great casual title, especially if you're looking for lighter fair to relax with in-between more serious gaming sessions. Despite my misgivings with the lack of Steam integration, it’s still a solid time management game that will appeal to those who enjoy the genre.

Bottom Line: Recommended for those looking for a relaxing casual title with lots of polish and character.

My first game went something like this:
-Spawned into the cold, harsh land of... Canada.
-Found some sort of bunker in the woods and entered (<-Penumbra Overture logic, yet oddly agreeable in this situation).
-Stole an absurd amount of water bottles from the bunker.
-Walked a couple feet and found the Trapper's house.
-Grabbed his rifle and a box of bullets.
-Attempted to hunt deer, wasted most of my bullets.
-Attracted wolves, shot at them (still missed) and ran out of bullets.
-Obtained three can openers.
-Drank water and contracted dysentery
-Ran around in the cold looking for bullets to hunt for food.
-Died of hypothermia.
The average game:
-Find absurd amounts of individual bullets, but not a single rifle.
-Eat some granola bars.
-Drink from toilet water.
-Fail to start a fire indoors 4 times in a row, wasting all your tinder plugs.
-Smash open your only can of food because you don't have a can opener.
Then you have two options:
a) Freeze to death because the only nearby shelter was the dam.
b) Enter the dam and die from shock and blood loss.
While playing this game you may find yourself
a) having strange sudden food cravings (such as but not limited to sardines, granola bars, and tomato soup).
b) having an extreme urge to drink bottled water.
c) slowly developing a hatred towards dams.
d) realizing that in the end, nothing really mattered.
e) noticing how terrible your aim actually is.
f) contemplating in-game suicide.
g) being stunned by the beauty this game can show you if you actually notice.

Tales of Zestiria is a fantastic game that’s totally worth playing — especially for fans of the Tales series. So far I’ve spent about one hundred hours playing and I still have not completed the game.
There are tons of side quests to do along with the main quest, many dungeons to explore, and optional bosses. This game is just chock-full of content as you’d expect for a Tales game.
While there are some unfortunate issues that I have with the game, they aren’t enough to really affect my enjoyment (no crashing, freezes, or glitches). Sure, the battle system, fusion system, and minor graphical issues leave some things to be desired, but I think the story and the overall fun of this game makes up for any of those issues.
Since each of the games are totally different stories and don’t depend on previous entries, you don’t have to worry at all about playing previous titles. New players can feel free to begin with this game, as well as go back to play previous titles in any order, and it won’t matter at all.
The bottom line is that Tales of Zestiria is a fantastic entry in the series and I highly recommend it for newcomers and fans alike.

I would describe the pace of this game as "glacial" it is methodical and long, there is no end goal, only to survive as long as you can.
The best technique I have found is to keep moving until you find a cabin that has a stove/fireplace a bed a work bench and is semi centralized on the map. From there you can have a place to store the goods you find everywhere else.
Your immediate goals upon entering the game should be to find shelter especially if you spawn in a blizzard or if it is close to night fall, or in the night.
Save your flares because they are the only thing that is going to save you from wolves, wait until a wolf runs at you and then pop the flare and wave it around some, the wolf will back off but will continue to follow you. Use the time to get inside somewhere and hope to hell you have enough food/water/warmth to wait out the wolf it will eventually leave.
The game is still in development and as such it is a pretty bare bones system, although there are alot of things to do and goals to aim for. Finding a rifle and ammunition as well as renewable sources of food are basically your "end game" goals. Once you do that its simply a matter of trying to keep them going.
A story mode is coming for the game eventually but right now its just the sand box.
Also stay the ♥♥♥♥ away from the hydroelectic dam, otherwise you will be introduced to fluffy. You don't want to meet fluffy. Fluffy is the thing that can take a 50+ day survival run and end it in seconds even if you go in there fully armed and with the best stats you can muster. If you can kill fluffy though you can reap the rewards of the dam.  Good luck with that though.
The art style for the game isnt extremely indepth or hyper detailed but it has its own beauty and pretty much everything is very well done. If you enjoyed the art style for games such as "the walking dead" by telltale games you will enjoy this because its the same sort of approach.
Do I recommend it? I enjoy survival games alot, they are in their own way very relaxing to play but also equally as frustrating sometimes as sometimes the game just deals you a bad hand and it costs you a good run. I would say if you are looking for a new one to play and want one that veers a bit more towards the realistic then the fantastical you should try it.

Just to get it out of the way, yes, I am a HUGE fan of the Tales of Namco games and have played more of them than I'd care to share here.
As a long time fan of the Tales of Namco games: No. I don't recommend this. At first I was concerned that maybe I was just not giving it enough time. The truth is, I'd given it much more time than it deserved.
The beginning of the game starts off strong, with you (Sorey) exploring some ruins with your childhood friend (Mikleo) who happens to be some sort of spirit and you're pretty much the only human that can see him. However, it quickly falls flat on its face after the 10 hour mark. I didn't care about ANY of the characters, they all just seemed like the same cookie-cutter party members from previous tales games. But, since you and another party member (who is replaced later on to sell DLC about her abscence, I got it for free however so I can't really complain too much.) are the only ones that can see the spirits that make up the rest of your party, making most dialogue feel somewhat awkward. This is also a huge negative towards character development, in my opinion.
What the hell is that Skill System? I think I got PTSD from trying to figure it out.
The combat is the second worst I've ever experienced in a Tales game, my least favorite being Tales of Graces f, who (unsurprisingly) is the team behind Zestiria as well. I'll take mana and having to munch on Orange/Peach Gels over whatever the hell this crap is, any day. However, on the bright side...
The music in the game is phenomenal. I went into the Earth Trial area and was blown away by how good the music was. I sat there for a good half hour, absolutely baked, just enjoying the wonderful music, kinda like everyone who owns Hotline Miami. The opening video is my favorite too, especially if you replace it with the Japanese version with vocals.
"GONNA BE A BRIGHT, BRIGHT LIGHT. NA NA NANANANA NA NA NA NANA" (I even made sure I put enough NA's in there. Accuracy and stuff, y'know?)
The animation both in-game and during the amazingly detailed animated cutscenes are top notch as well. Considering these games tend to get a bit of flack for having somewhat cheesy animations (Some scenes in Symphonia are downright cringy by todays standards.) I'd say they did quite well, all things considered. Even in some of the newer titles you can see where they got lazy, and instead of making an all new animation for something, they just re-use animations and it can become quite jarring.
I've yet to encounter a single bug or glitch, big or small. If there are any game-breaking glitches any of you have encountered, I'd love to hear about it.
The game certainly has some redeeming factors, but as a whole I really just can't recommend it. Maybe I'm an idiot and the game picks up after all of the trials, or maybe I'm just an idiot for pre-ordering it?
If you're a newcomer to the Tales series and are looking for something to get you into the series, I'd suggest playing Tales of Xillia, or Abyss, not Symphonia. (Yeah sure it's great and everything but has it really aged that well? The combat is a bit too clunky and I'm not too big on the character design, those big heads bug me.) Xillia, along with Symphonia are some of the few games in the franchise to get a direct sequel, and I loved them both. The sequel introduced choice/consequence (or to be honest, the illusion of choice and consequence for a lot of it) and some of the things that could happen were just... Wow. The bad ending was one of the most messed up things I've seen in an anime, and I watched Berserk. If you can ignore the padding in the sequel (you get a 20 million gald debt at one point, and the story locks until you pay enough of it off.) it's really quite enjoyable. Paying off the debt get's you a VERY interesting cutscene...
This is by no means a bad game, it's just not a good Tales game. It's definitely not a good starting point for people wanting to get into the series, either. And unfortunately, the next Tales of game (Berseria) will be a prequel to this. I guess I'll hafta pass, as I'm not a fan of prequels, or this game.
If this review is a disjointed mess, I apologize, but this game was one of the biggest disappointments I've ever pre-ordered, and I was one of the fools that pre-ordered No Man's Sky.

I don't particularly like to ragequit a game, but this is the first one that's driven me to do so in a while.
The Howler has a lot of things a good game should have. There's the unique concept of using your voice (or noise in general) to move your hot air balloon around the map. The artwork is beautiful and really worth taking a good time to enjoy. That's where it stops. Right there is where The Howler ceases and I find myself completely irritated with the game.
There is simplicity in the game. You are delivering parcels and you don't want your balloon oblierated on the ornate and breath-taking buildings. That's great and that would appeal to a wide audience there. That's perfect. Yet here's what flubs it up. The wind and weather direction should be something that gives you a slight challenge, not forces you to constantly restart the level because the angle wasn't just perfect so your balloon didn't pop or you didn't fly too high into the heavens. I've played similar games to this before and especially when you're starting out, they're a lot more forgiving with their wind merchanics. The Howler punishes you mercilessly on level 3 and continues to kick you in the stomach with that mechanic until you've had enough and switch the game off.
There's also the fact that the voice control, even when your microphone is on the most sensitivity possible, will not be enough to keep your balloon afloat. Now I'm aware that the game suggested I scream, but not everyone using Steam is living in a house where we have enough privacy to scream. If I have to make my voice raw to get that thing off the ground, why am I playing the game at all? That's entirely too much work and I'm not getting a sore throat just to play it.
The screens betwen levels are charming and give me the option to turn off the microphone (your mouse will be easier to play with at this rate, I suppose!) but little exposition except a bit of real life history of the city. There's no actual substansial story here and I was expecting a tiny bit more, given I felt teased with the artwork and fairly let down by game play.
It's like a really pretty flappy bird with a harder obstacle course you're supposed to scream at. I just didn't feel the need to open my big trap since it doesn't actually help!
Accessibility warnings? Transition screens are bright and have a white light. May cause migraines or seizures if you're sensitive. It certainly brought me a migraine. The repetitive motion of clicking upward gets sore (and pretty old!) fast as well.

Dungeon Defenders II is an online 4 players co-op tower defence game. It is still in its Alpha stages. It'd be recommended if you like the Dungeon Defenders series, especially there isn't much change towards is predeccessors. There's four playable classes, the Magician, Warrior, Monk and Archer. Basically it's just spilt into melee and ranged attacks, both either with a easy and advanced play mode. But generally all the classes goes through the same motion.
What's good is that you can actually use your high-tier classes to farm for lower level items to be equipped to your new classes. Each account is allowed to play all four classes, I don't think there's an intention to create other new classes. The inventory is shared among all four classes, each with four bags of inventory by default and a pet bag. Levelling up in this game is fairly easy, compared to now after the Carnival update. Where now players hunt for higher-tier items and ending up you have to play solo through the early stages of your levels. I'd recommend you play Magician first, followed by Warrior, Archer, Monk. For item hunting, the drop rates for this game is pretty high! You can get roughly around 2-3 Legendary items per dungeon map. However do note that the drops are in accordance to the character you have selected to fight during the rounds. The good thing is that you get to mix-match different classes skill towers to be deployed during the Building stage, before the wave starts. So a complementary of both offensive and defensive methods is needed for this game. There are some maps that are good for earning good experience, and drops. For example the The Throne Room, The Sewers. These maps are highly lane-constructed maps and can be 'afk-able' or rather less maintenance to lookout for.
For networking wise, there's an Asia server as well as Europe and North America servers! Though the Asia server is connected through Australia. The ping for this game is fairly manageable, not much latency issues for this game. Although it may be hard to get players to co-op with you during specific time regions.

A Neat Challenge against the Environment, a Cool art style, and replayability of the design make this a refreshing Singleplayer title with a Lot to explore.
With the recent "Deep Forest" update - there are many changes that all add up to a very rewarding player experience. Wolf attacks are much more nuanced, having many various effects - more than just critical injuries. Harvestable wood from both interior and exterior environments, and the removal of the old "Time exchange" harvesting mechanic make the struggle to stay warm a much more involved process.

The torches give you one more chance against the wolves, and the craftable clothes, items, and even a Bow - you'll always have some reason to keep a keen eye out for supplies, or a place to call home until the task is completed. There are hidden bunkers as well, which spawn in random locations during each playthrough - those have been in for quite some time but they still add to the chance of a big payoff for explorers. This game is EASILY the BEST use of the Early Access system here on Steam, with dedicated devs doing very thoughtful things with the design - you get a LOT for your investment!
Nothing like wandering through a blizzard at night, freezing, starving, getting lost with only a storm lantern to light your way - as you TRY to remember where you need to go... this game is worth every second of it.

I'd say this is a must play for every shooter fan and that one should pick it up at any price, but seeing as how the game's been on sale several times for $5, wait for the next sale.

This game is a masterpiece.
Just Cause 2 is like playing a B-grade action movie: It couldn't care less about realism and just goes all-out on the explosions and badassery.
The game throws normal physics, any remotely serious storyline, and common sense of all kinds out the window in favour of pure, uninhibited fun. You are almost never limited by such annoyances present in other games as dying, getting from point A to point B, invisible walls, cutscenes, or morality. You're handed 400 square miles of awesome on a plate, given a toybox of recklessness and let off the leash.
You play as Rico Rodriguez, a secret agent/demigod equipped with a grappling hook, a bottomless bag of parachutes and the ability to turn any gun he picks up into a WMD. As Rico, you can grapple people to cars, grapple cars to people, parachute onto military bases while shooting everyone, steal helicopters in mid-air and then go on a rampage, and cause many, many explosions. Like, wow. I'm pretty sure it rains gasoline in Panau. Just shooting at cars for a few seconds causes a satisfying Hollywood fireball to blossom forth, and most military bases are practically layered with fuel containers and interestingly volatile SAM sites and communications equipment. Even moving around is fun, grappling the ground with your parachute out to propel yourself forward at sportscar-like speeds.
You can steal jets, take down armies single-handed, run rickshaw bike thingies off cliffs, and go on an entertaining variety of explosion-packed missions. This game offers you an incredible degree of freedom that other games just don't have. Not to mention there's a community-made multiplayer mod, where you can embark on epic explosive adventures with your friends, use boost plugins to propel your car to lightspeed, and have derbies with fire engines on top of airborne strip clubs.
I can't reccomend this game enough. It's just beautiful to play. I mean, how can you go wrong with a game about a demigod secret agent with a grappling hook using dictator statue heads as wrecking balls?

This game is awesome, and has a lot of potential. I enjoy survival games, but was sick and tired of zombies in every game. So this game was just right for me. There's a lot to keep you busy in game. It is challenging enough and there is a lot to explore.
I made it 14 days, but then the same thing that happened to another reviewer ('Jesus'), happened to me.
This was my best game so far. i had accumulated many items at my 'house'. I was going out and exploring all shelters on the map. I finally made it to the 'abandoned lookout'. I found the rifle and was ready to leave but wolves were nearby. After fighting a couple wolves and having to run back into the lookout; I licked my wounds and was ready to set back out again. When I would walk back down the stairs, there was another wolf; and it would not go away. This lasted for a couple days. (I tried saving and exiting game also of course) I was running out of food and water so I knew I had to face him. I waited for a good break in the weather and went down to fight him. I was in pretty good condition; no fatigue or anything. For whatever reason this wolf seemed to kill my quicker. I barely got one hit in and that was it, I was like 'wtf'. I was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at first and I still don't understand why it killed me quicker; felt like I barely had a chance. (unless there is a setting/mechanic that allows the wolf a chance to kill you quickly) That might be something that needs to be looked into. (and of course the way the wolves waited for me at bottom of stairs)

Played this game blind on launch to 100% completion. Heres some bullet points because I could gush for hours about what I just witnessed.
The Surprising:
-Control is fluid and allows for a lot of variability for completing objectives. Very similar to Mario 64 and Sunshine.
-All of the level missions feel like completely unique tasks, rather than 'do platforming challenge and recieve reward'
-Every single mission has its own beautiful title card and some missions even change the whole level on some way.
-The bosses are surprisingly high energy compared to the usual 3d platformer. Makes the most of Hat Kid's movement kit.
-Camera is very good for a 3d platformer and rarely gets in the way. Has various quality of life settings for the camera too.
-Soundtrack is baller and changes dynamically like banjo kazooie
-A lot of graphical settings to fine tune the game to run even on toasters.
-My horrible direct input gamepad worked immediately with it, though that might be because of steam big picture. Still cool.
-Ability hats can be changed on the fly (even mid-platforming) and all stay useful through the whole game.
-A lot of TECHNOLOGY. Hat Kid wears a raincoat when its raining, she blows raspberries at close by enemies, she lays belly down on the floor after landing from a dive, she kicks cans when you walk over them.
-Low/medium difficulty, but with a very very very high skill ceiling. Custom workshop levels will be insane.
-Tricks like jumping right as you land from a dive for a speed boost and chaining jumps into wall climbing and jumping into dives are treated as something the player learns naturally through playing rather than something that requires a tutorial to teach.
-Loads of secret areas and things to find in each level.
-Dangerously cute and charming. Hat Kid and the various NPCs you meet are oozing with character.
The Disappointing:
-Maybe one or two of the bosses use the same or very similar attacks to other bosses.
-Visually noisy at times. It doesn't really hurt knowing what you can and cant jump on, however.
-Too Shoooooort. 40 hourglasses aren't nearly enough, even if the levels are very big.
-Yarn becomes useless after getting all of the hats. I'm sitting on 20 extra balls of yarn at end game and still finding more.
-Would be nice to keep the mission specific cosmetic hats as a reward for fully clearing areas
-The last two worlds are veeeery large and hard to keep track of progress in. A map item might help.
-Rift tokens and yarn balls aren't trackable, making it a little sad for completionists.
-Not many badges to play with and one is absolutely required to have on at all times.
-The inventory is largely unused
-There is a weapon slot but only one weapon in the game (Two, if you count when you're holding a key)
-A lot of content from alpha footage is missing. Understandable that the developers would want to put out something that feels like a complete package rather than an incomplete forever early access type thing but it would be very cool to see these things return as official dlc or free updates.
Considering the dev team listens quite closely to their fanbase, I wouldn't be surprised if some of these things were fixed or added to in the not too distant future. Its obvious to me that A Hat in Time is a passion project with a lot of heart poured into it and I wish I backed it when the kickstarter was running. Would absolutely recommend for fans and veterans of the genre.

At a glance, one would rejoice at the idea that it's a Tales game on Steam. However, it isn't all sunshines and rainbows, as veterans of the franchise are likely to disagree with some of the gameplay changes moving on from previous games. When looking at the game at its own, Zestiria proves to be a solid entry point for those new to the franchise, which is especially important when considering that this is
first Tales game on the PC platform.
With the game in its current state, I would argue that even without the Tales of Zestiria fix, the PC version is the best one out there. While it is far more stable than the initial PS3 version, the game was developed with no cross-gen support in mind. As a result, the game is locked at 30 FPS when played as is (IMHO, this could've been a 60FPS game on the PS4). Additionally, the graphics menu is pretty barebones as you can see in this below screenshot. On the bright side though,
Due to the nature of the Tales series, I haven't even bothered to look at keyboard and mouse due to the series being designed with the DualShock controller in mind. (Can someone confirm if DirectInput controllers work with this game?)
And finally, performance. This part of the PC Specifics section requires the ToZFix for me to look at properly, and I would go as to say that when locked to 60, the game is lightweight enough for mid-range gamers to run this game at 1440p with little issue. However, I cannot confirm what it takes to play it on 2160p60 due to the limitations of AMD's VSR (Virtual Super Resolution).
This section of the review is a (possibly indefinite) work in progress, as I will be doing a second playthrough to refresh my memory of Zestiria. Additionally, I will also be playing Xillia in short bursts to get a better comparison of how ToZ holds up.

Given the nature of the Tales franchise, it is nigh impossible to explain the premise of the story in a spoiler free manner, though what I will say is that prior to Tales of Zestiria, the franchise itself would almost always avoid the classic "good vs evil" story when it comes to storytelling. The best example I can think of would be the intentions behind Tales of Symphonia's world regeneration prophecy. In Zestiria's case, players familiar with other games in the franchise will be left disappointed,
However, it wouldn't be fair to say that the game doesn't have its moments, as some of characters you see will spice up an otherwise familiar narrative.
As for the main character, a complaint I would often hear about Sorey is his apparent lack of flaws, seeing that he has an intimate familiarity with ancient ruins, is often held in high regard by the world around him and from what I remember, that definitely seems like the case (Currently playing the game a second time to jog my memory)
Being a Japanese RPG, the meat of the game will often come from the battle system. While the world map acts more like a traditional Japanese RPG where monster encounters are dotted on the map, the actual battles will play out more like an action RPG, using Bandai Namco's Linear Motion Battle System. In regards to this, your movement tied to the enemy you are targeting, often moving either towards or away from the enemy (since 2005, you are also able to move freely when holding down a dedicated button). In Zestiria's case, Sorey will also be able fuse with the seraphim party members to gain access to stronger, albeit more costly abilities. In general, the action-oriented battles is why I would often view the Tales series on a higher pedestal than the far better known Final Fantasy franchise, though I will admit that in Zestiria's case, the combat is not without flaws.
Personally, I don't quite get the rationale of the the rear-facing camera, as previous Tales games would often go for a side-to-side view even with a 3D plane. While this will likely not affect newer players, veterans might get thrown off. However, this is the most inconsequential problem when you later realize how stupid the AI can be, with your party members often getting themselves killed in several opportunities (especially so when you fight bosses). Another thing that I personally dislike on a more subjective note is the Spirit Chain system. While I understand that the devs don't want you to spam the default attack button, previous games didn't need such a mechanic to better vary your attack patterns.
Another problem I have is the game's usage of the world map for its battle system. Because a lot of the attacks in the Tales series were made with a flat plane in mind, the world map can hinder the attacks of both you and your enemy. Additionally, the camera will sometimes collide with the world and cause additional problems. Regarding my experience during my first playthrough however, these moments were few and far enough for these problems to not detract from the overall experience. With that said however, I think i would've preferred a battle system more like Xillia's (so as for those problems to not even happen in the first place)
Outside of the battle system, you will also stumble upon a large amount of content outside the main story that will encourage the player to backtrack around the game. I know not how long the main story is, but there are enough distractions in between to give the player something to provide the 72 hours of gameplay it took me to actually beat the game. Speaking of backtracking, one nitpick I have is that discovered treasure chests are not marked on your map upon discovery. The alternative would be to purchase the
, but I should not need to resort to this option if the "dee ell see" is something i can actually get through normal gameplay. I would prefer if the game had tools to make backtracking much less of an annoyance.
Yes, I can see where fans of the series are going at when they call Tales of Zestiria the worst game in the series, though I will admit that this doesn't stop the game from being fun as all hell and I would go as far as to say that it's worth my pre-order at the time of its release. On its own, it's a good entry point for PC gamers to enjoy what the the Tales franchise has to offer and I feel that as a history piece in the grander scheme of things, we can thank Bandai Namco Studios for when Japanese game developers hold themselves accountable on the PC side of things.

Start of the game is a bit slow, takes a little while to get into and combat is limited until you assemble your "team". Deep combat system seems simplistic at first, but opens up the longer you play. Clearing dungeons can get a bit tedious near the end of the game if you're powering through, but there are ways to avoid combat and that can speed you along the story quickly. There is a good mix of "simple" bosses and "frustratingly hard" bosses, as well a several different levels of difficulty that allows you to adjust your experience to suit your needs.
Some people have noted the large amount of DLCs. There is only one that has gameplay, the rest are costume packs. The game comes with the God Eater costume pack and TONS of costume items as gameplay rewards, so there's no "need" to purchase most of the DLCs. If you like a set of the DLC costumes, grab them, but don't let the amount of DLCs detract you from the game.

The most outstanding feature of The Howler is the art style for sure. Hand drawn art for both background and foreground objects. The later actually appear like paper cut-outs attached to the former.
Gameplay is simple and straight forward! You are only required to click the left mouse button to control your balloon (click = balloon will rise, no-lick = balloon will drop). Movement to the left/right is controlled by flowing air currents; e.g. if you want to move to the right, just let the balloon rise or drop to the corresponding current, but beware of sharp objects that will let it burst by touching.
The object in each level varies from simply getting to the landing spot to picking up packes, dropping them off and land.
As much as I enjoy my time with The Howler, there is one important thing to mention, which might be shortcoming for some people: There is NO REAL FULLSCREEN support, that is, even if you go fullscreen, the game itself takes place in a realtively small window!

Banished is an average city building engine. I use the word "engine" because it is not a game- it doesnt really have a point other than creating a large city. "But that is the point of the genre" i hear you say. Well yes and no. Look at the classics- Ceaser, Children of the Nile etc - you build the cities- but you have to meet objectives along the way, be it appeasing gods, fulfilling the requests of other cities on a global map- or meeting the ever demanding needs of a popualtion who aspire for a more luxurious life.
Banished has none of these- a balancing trick between population growth, and food production easily masterd and applied before a population reaches 100. The only need to increase the population beyond this is if you want to- and the game becomes boring.
The saving grace wo9uld be the fact the game is moddable- however the mod tools/ support is atrocious- text editor modding! This locks out all but the most apt modders and as such mod content is limited.
Some random gripes:
- No way to micromanage resources with resource specific storage or priortised storage space.
-trade being underdeveloped- with no "global stage" to mange trade relations or diverse trade deals- its mostly like for like- so if you have a  surplus of food- you can trade it away for....more food of a differnet type?
-beyond construction, clothing and food- there are no commodities to add complexity for established settlments.
- "disasters"act more like setbacks than a challange to be circumnavigated.
- Populouce demands- they really dont demand much- they dont demand commodities or luxuries, nor do they show their wealth in their house- heck there isnt even a class system!
Summary: This engine could be used to build some great games- but it appears to have fallen short of excellence. If you enjoy city builders- go play Children of the Nile, Ceaser, Pharoah, Anno etc all of which have a lot more depth.

The game is obviously for people who loved this game back in 2005 in the first place.
Back then Fahrenheit delivered very unique performance which was completely new at that time. Outstanding motion capture, staging direction, music and fun gameplay did their best for keeping the player interested.
Surely Fahrenheit has flaws in its plot which is fairly silly overall but still very entertaining.
Aspyr did a good job with the Remaster. Textures and resolution are much better than in 2005 and look fine for someone who loved the original version.
However it's unlikely the new players will enjoy the game as unfortunately Fahrenheit itself has become quite outdated in its technical implementation.
Dated graphics, bulky characters animation (by the 2017 standards), ancient manual facial animation and direction that was great 12 years ago. Video games have evolved since then in every aspect Fahrenheit represents. Modern AAA titles leave Fahrenheit no chance and even the next David Cage game Heavy Rain released in 2010 made a huge step forward as an interactive movie making Fahrenheit just an interesting step in history.
Still for those who spent countless delightful hours with the original this version will certainly provide some fun once again with the help of the refreshed textures, high resolution and perfect Xbox 360 controller support.

A game plagued by a terrible launch has recovered nicely, mostly due to the Rising Storm expansion and the huge amount of great patches Tripwire has deployed for RO2.
One of the best shooter games in terms of realism(at least in terms of gunplay,how fast you die and how you can't rambo), using systems like cover right, suppression and support in the form of Arty etc.
The balance of the game is revolving around thinking before running in because in this game doing that is going to get you killed by either the MG's, snipers or the riflemen in the bushes. Now this can be both a postive as negative point if you like more serious games(less HP, headshot almost instakills) or if you like more casual shooters(more health).
And it has one of the best lag compenstation systems I've ever seen, I could play on a 300 ping server and not notice a difference with a 100 ping server so that makes up for the relative low population of servers(64 players for a full server though!). Games about WWII are more than enough I'd say, especially shooters. But these shooters deform the reality of war were thousands died by adding health, or invulnerability, or a number of times you must be shot to die, like in Call of Duty, the newer ones. In RO 2 there's no such HP, at least not visible. In here, a bullet shot in the right part of the body means death. Arttilery barages are hell, and  carelessly moving around the map with your head high, as you'd do in other games, means death.
Truly on of the hardest and most realistic WWII/war/shooter games out there, and most (hopefully) the closest you'll ever get to a real war. If you're ever tired of going Rambo in CoD, then try this on for size.
Granted, as the game pushes for realism, the key roles ( sniper/squad leader/commander/tank commander) must be filled by people with some clue of the game, and new recruits filling up those spots can lead to your team's defeat, some vissible weapon advantages are also causing unbalance, and the morale system isn't that easy to figure out and fails sometimes. The game also doesn't provide much for game modes, seeing as territory is the only mode (but there are enough maps to keep you busy, and anyway, a deathmatch mode were people die by one bullet wouldn't last that long anyway, so this mode is more than enough).
All in all you can't really call yourself a FPS or action guy if you don't play this game. 8.5/10

Play this game!  Its not perfect, but its ridiculously fun.  I've been itching for a proper 3d platformer for a while, and this is right up there with my favorite ever.  Its absolutely adorable and one of the most cheerful games I've ever played.  There are 40 total time pieces to collect(Think Mario stars) spread across 4.5 worlds.  That's 81 less than Mario 64, so this isn't going to be as long a game.  If you don't go for 100% (in-game, not achievements) then you can get out much sooner.  I was having so much fun I went for everything.  I'd say my playtime is at the upper-end of what you could expect, because I tooled around with the camera and just explored a bunch.
The level design is spectacular, with a ton of variety.  The first and third world feel the most like your classic Mario/Banjo game, while the second plays more like a series of challenges and the fourth is more like an open-world game.  Likewise, the control feels just right.  They've opted for a smaller number of normal moves, pretty much only a double jump, lungs, and wall jumps/slides, but they combine in interesting ways.  Example: You get an extra jump after a lunge.  Also, if you jump up a half-second or so after landing in a slide from a lunge, you get a speed boost.
Outside of the core move set, you have hats which do different things.  Most aren't that novel outside presentation, but they are put to good use.  There's also badges, which further mix up gameplay.  I found myself using the grappling hook one with a treasure hunting map and one that kept me from taking damage from falls.
This game also features reasonable to good voice acting in a lot of roles.  If you don't like that, you can muffle them with a badge.
You really should play this game.  There's a ton of content in it, and its all extremely unique.  The  game camera isn't perfect, but its a major step up from the games of yore.  The platforming is tighter too, and I actually felt like I had good control over my character.  If you're looking for a cheerful game about an adorable alien becoming a movie star and kicking mafia off ledge, please buy this game.

Played this game blind on launch to 100% completion. Heres some bullet points because I could gush for hours about what I just witnessed.
The Surprising:
-Control is fluid and allows for a lot of variability for completing objectives. Very similar to Mario 64 and Sunshine.
-All of the level missions feel like completely unique tasks, rather than 'do platforming challenge and recieve reward'
-Every single mission has its own beautiful title card and some missions even change the whole level on some way.
-The bosses are surprisingly high energy compared to the usual 3d platformer. Makes the most of Hat Kid's movement kit.
-Camera is very good for a 3d platformer and rarely gets in the way. Has various quality of life settings for the camera too.
-Soundtrack is baller and changes dynamically like banjo kazooie
-A lot of graphical settings to fine tune the game to run even on toasters.
-My horrible direct input gamepad worked immediately with it, though that might be because of steam big picture. Still cool.
-Ability hats can be changed on the fly (even mid-platforming) and all stay useful through the whole game.
-A lot of TECHNOLOGY. Hat Kid wears a raincoat when its raining, she blows raspberries at close by enemies, she lays belly down on the floor after landing from a dive, she kicks cans when you walk over them.
-Low/medium difficulty, but with a very very very high skill ceiling. Custom workshop levels will be insane.
-Tricks like jumping right as you land from a dive for a speed boost and chaining jumps into wall climbing and jumping into dives are treated as something the player learns naturally through playing rather than something that requires a tutorial to teach.
-Loads of secret areas and things to find in each level.
-Dangerously cute and charming. Hat Kid and the various NPCs you meet are oozing with character.
The Disappointing:
-Maybe one or two of the bosses use the same or very similar attacks to other bosses.
-Visually noisy at times. It doesn't really hurt knowing what you can and cant jump on, however.
-Too Shoooooort. 40 hourglasses aren't nearly enough, even if the levels are very big.
-Yarn becomes useless after getting all of the hats. I'm sitting on 20 extra balls of yarn at end game and still finding more.
-Would be nice to keep the mission specific cosmetic hats as a reward for fully clearing areas
-The last two worlds are veeeery large and hard to keep track of progress in. A map item might help.
-Rift tokens and yarn balls aren't trackable, making it a little sad for completionists.
-Not many badges to play with and one is absolutely required to have on at all times.
-The inventory is largely unused
-There is a weapon slot but only one weapon in the game (Two, if you count when you're holding a key)
-A lot of content from alpha footage is missing. Understandable that the developers would want to put out something that feels like a complete package rather than an incomplete forever early access type thing but it would be very cool to see these things return as official dlc or free updates.
Considering the dev team listens quite closely to their fanbase, I wouldn't be surprised if some of these things were fixed or added to in the not too distant future. Its obvious to me that A Hat in Time is a passion project with a lot of heart poured into it and I wish I backed it when the kickstarter was running. Would absolutely recommend for fans and veterans of the genre.

Rarely do I review a product on Steam but I wanted to leave a recommendation to purchase this game, especially now that it's on sale.
The main reason I want everyone to play it because I don't own a PS4 or Xbox One and I REALLY want to see more PC ports for the Tales game series.
I know I am only 20 hours into the game but here are the pros and cons so far as I see it...
Pros:
1. A general enjoyable plot. (Yeah sure I don't nitpick but I really just want it to feel like a fun engaging story)
2. Entertaining and enjoyable characters.
3. I ALWAYS love Tales graphics. It NEVER gets old.
4. Cool Music all throughout the game even when it's atmosphere based!
5. NO bugs that I have noticed and it works RIGHT away with my Xbox 360 wireless controller adapter. Great Job!
Cons:
1. I actually poke my head around the corner a bit to make sure games don't have a CRAPPY ending. Like a real stinker waiting for me. I heard this has MULTIPLE endings. Now that's ok and all. BUT I am paranoid that if i mess up, something will suck later and nothing pisses me off more than a sad ending. This is a con for me because.... wait I can't give away spoilers. Sorry.
2. The learning curve is a little more than the other tales (to me at least) BUT. BUT. I have to justify and say that I LOVE THE improvements so far to the entire fighting system and grade integration. Wait. this is a pro in a con area?
3. I have to admit that the gameplay on this game VS Tales of Berseria, now that I am playing them right next to each other, is a little sloppy.
4. This is a slight step back vs a game like Tales of Vesperia. Why is it SO hard to make such an amazing game like that? Where's the magic touch they had?
TL;DR
This is a great game but the series is walking down a path that is hard to return from. After playing Tales of Berseria I have found the gameplay to be slightly better there and I have stalled on this game now that ToB is out. This game is not as great as Tales of Vesperia. That game was pure epic. I don't know how to help them get back their magic. But Tales of Berseria was a good SMALL turnaround.. This game? It's good, but not amazing. I recommend it but wait for a REAL GOOD SALE.

LIMBO is a sidescrolling platformer with physics- and gravity-based puzzles and an unique visual art style.
'Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters LIMBO' is the only thing that the store page says about the game. This single line is basically the whole story of the game and your one and only reason to go on.
The puzzles are decent but not extraordinary brilliant or innovative. After all, it's the visual art style of the game that raised the interest among players.
With roughly 2 hours of playtime, the game is extremely short for a game of this genre. On the other hand, it doesn't try to stretch the playtime by repeating the same puzzles over and over again.
LIMBO certainly isn't a bad game, but if you are expecting a brilliant platformer with loads of playtime and replayability, then you might want to look somewhere else as this game most likely isn't for you.
I'm not sure I would recommed it at its full price, but at 75% off during the major sales, it's certainly worth it.

So I was in an internship where my team thought it would be a brilliant idea to make a videogame where you have players play a game where your voice is the game, and the key goal is that at certain points in the game, you scream as
as you can. And the the louder you scream, the more points you get.
Everyone's all for that idea.
Except for me.
I thought it was a stupid idea from the start, because not only does that just sound stupid on its own, but that encourages players to be annoying.
It's already bad enough you have CoD kids screaming at you online, why the hell are we making a game that promotes being obnoxious?
I honestly hope it doesn't fly out of production. Because if it does fly, they'll probably get something like "The Howler."
This game uses the gimmick of using your voice to help elevate your hot air balloon and get from point A to point B, C and so on. And the louder you are, the faster you go up. That's basically your goal in this game.
Yeah, I could use the mouse instead, but that already sounded lame, so lets go use my voice.
I couldn't stand the idea I had to talk/scream louder than I should be, and it's really unfortunate too with this kind of art style. Whoever's the artist deserves better than this. And if the artist is one of the Game Devs themselves: shame on him for thinking this concept was even a good idea.
Eventually after 5~10 minutes of screaming, I got tired and stopped.
And you know what I did?
No, I didn't start using my mouse.
I got a paper towel, wrapped it around my mic, and started stroking it to raise my hot air balloon across the field.
...yeah. If that ain't innuendo enough for you, I don't know what is.
This game blows.
Literally.
Please don't make anything atrocious like this ever again, game developers.
It encourages people to be stupid, and you should feel bad for it.

I recommend this game, but not for the reason most people would.
I'm just gonna say, right off the bat, that Indigo Prophecy is one of the dumbest, most insane games I have ever experienced. The characters are all cut-out stereotypes, the action sequences are laughable, and the game's attempts at trying to be emotional and dramatic are equally as laughable. Gameplay is functional (for the most part), but nothing to really write home about. Judging this as a video game, Indigo Prophecy ranges from mediocre to awful, with a bevy of questionable design decision. As an experience, however, it is absolutely something that I recommend everybody look into.
This game's biggest claim to fame, as is the case with most David Cage games, is its emphasis on story and player choice. These are two things that this game fails to achieve. The story feels like David Cage went on a movie binge one night, putting on everything from The Matrix (especially The Matrix) to Silence of the Lambs to even a blaxploitation film for good measure, decides to take as many of the cool or memorable parts of those movies and attempts to replicate them and make something awesome and inspiring. Unfortunately, in doing so, he forgot how to make a story that was cohesive and give us characters that we could give a damn about. David is far more focused on delivering "spectacle" than an engaging narrative. The story starts promising enough, but quickly devolves into just trying to copy other movie scenes and throw together this ridiculous prophecy story. Entire sequences of the game are literally ripped straight out of those more popular films, with one sequence late in the game showing off some of the goofiest motion-captured fight choreography I have ever seen. I have never laughed so hard during a game. Oh, and not to mention there are two laughable sex scenes in the game that have no reason to be there (one of which is accompanied by incredibly unfitting music from Theory of a Dedman, the one band David could afford for this game).
As for the characters we end up playing with? Well, we have Lucas, a boring wannabe Neo; Carla, a straight-edge independent female cop; and Tyler, the token black guy that seems to have gotten lost in the 1970s (he even has '70s funk and R&B playing just about everywhere he goes). And really, there's not much to these people beyond those basic characterizations. Lucas is dull and boring the whole way through, Carla eventually devolves into just another (incredibly forced) love interest, and Tyler is mostly put on screen to be the "hip" character rather than be all that good at his job...or even relevant to the story as a whole.
You can also expect to come across other colorful characters, like the token angry police commissioner, the token girlfriend, an incredibly offensive Chinese stereotype, the prototypical gay best friend, a discount Hannibal Lecter. This game has every token cliche and stereotype under the sun.
Those who have played any other David Cage game (specifically Heavy Rain) should find the gameplay familiar. The game is divided up into a few main gameplay styles. The most common of which is exploring your environment, interacting with stuff to either just faff about or actually use to advance the story. There are a few scenes in the game that do slightly change depending on how you approach certain objectives, but a lot of them make me question why on Earth they would even offer multiple ways of doing things if the outcome is going to be the same regardless. In the beginning of the game, I'm expected to clean up the crime scene. I do so, pay my bill, go outside and get away just as soon as the cop discovers the body. I go back to that same sequence again, only this time just washing my hands and leaving the corpse as is. I do everything else, and the game plays out exactly the same. Another annoying thing to note is that I'm expected to help Lucas dodge the police, only to be switching over to the police and trying to make them do their job and try to capture him. Do you want me to help Lucas or not?
Then there are moments where you get to interact with other characters picking dialog choices. Most of the dialog is merely there to add some extra context to a situation. There are points in the game where you can potentially make "game-changing" decisions, but more often than not it does not matter what choice you make as the story will continue on in a linear fashion. Say for example Lucas's girlfriend calls you asking to come over to his apartment, I can tell her no if I want to, but she is still going to come to my apartment later anyway regardless of me telling her to leave him alone. Either David Cage didn't think a lot of these choices through, or he only wanted to provide the vein illusion of choice to make his game seem deeper than it actually is. The only major change that occured from that exchange is that I got more depressed, in-game that is.
Speaking of which, that's one of biggest parts of the game. Each character you play has this "Distress Meter" of sorts. It more or less acts like a glorified health bar. If it goes down completely, your character can get so depressed to the point of committing suicide, or simply moving away to Florida. Basically, it's a game over (Yes, David. No matter how many times you say game overs are the failure of the game designer, this is in fact a game over). Your depression goes down by either making specific choices, interacting with certain things in your environment or simply taking too long to complete an objective. This is very poorly implemented as there are moments in the game (especially for newcomers) where losing points is all but unavoidable. How was I supposed to know before hand that looking at my family photo would make me more depressed, or looking in the mirror and seeing the illusion of a ghost?
The other main gameplay section in the game are these glorified SImon Says QTEs. Follow the direction of the colors and you'll succeed. Fail too many times, and your story ends. It can be finnicky with reading your movements at points, but for the most part its functional. The biggest problem I have with this gameplay style is that I can't pay attention to the ridicuous action sequences. This Simon Says gameplay also gets incorporated into regular cutscenes as well, but aside from making you more depressed if you fail they don't offer much.
Other little scraps of gameplay are thrown in for the sake of adding variety, like during action scenes you where you multi-tap buttons to do streneous tasks. There are also sections of the game where you have to carefully tap back and forth to help with breathing or balancing. And then there two of some of the most phoned in, most poorly implemented Metal Gear-esque stealth sections that occur during flashbacks. These sections are easily the worst parts of the game.
So for as negative as I have been about this game, why do I still recommend it? It has to be seen to believe. Indigo Prophecy is an experience. It is an interesting, mind-boggling exploration into the mind of David Cage. It offers some of the most hilarious, ridiculous moments I have witnessed in a video game. It's story and characters are so easy to riff on. This is a game that is at its best when you bring over some unsuspecting friends of yours that have never heard of this game, and watching their reactions to the madness. It is absolutely great in that regard. Get Indigo Prophecy if you just want to have a good laugh.
Thank you, David, for being so pretentious and unintentionally hilarious.

The Cat and the Coup is a simple Flash game where you play the cat of a Mohammed Mossadegh, the first democratically elected leader of Iran and the head of Nationalist Party of Iran. You will play Iran's history in reverse from the 1960s to the 1950s. You will realise that the heart of all this conflict is for energy, mainly Iran's oil. You will learn of characters such as Kermit Roosevelt, the main CIA agent that engineered the fall of Mossadegh. You will learn that the bribe budget to oust Mossadegh was approximately around $1,000,000 USD. You will learn of the Iran's Shah,  Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and how he temporarily got his throne back due to Kermit Roosevelt's aid. As for the rest of history, I will let you play the game to learn more about Iran's history.
Gameplay-wise, there is nothing special. You simply move the cat using WASD into special little cat cutouts and press the Spacebar. There is a little balancing beam act but it's childish.
Conclusion, do try the game. It is slightly less informative than Wikipedia and not properly organised by timeline but you will figure the game out.

Games about WWII are more than enough I'd say, especially shooters. But these shooters deform the reality of war were thousands died by adding health, or invulnerability, or a number of times you must be shot to die, like in Call of Duty, the newer ones. In RO 2 there's no such HP, at least not visible. In here, a bullet shot in the right part of the body means death. Arttilery barages are hell, and  carelessly moving around the map with your head high, as you'd do in other games, means death.
Truly on of the hardest and most realistic WWII/war/shooter games out there, and most (hopefully) the closest you'll ever get to a real war. If you're ever tired of going Rambo in CoD, then try this on for size.
Granted, as the game pushes for realism, the key roles ( sniper/squad leader/commander/tank commander) must be filled by people with some clue of the game, and new recruits filling up those spots can lead to your team's defeat, some vissible weapon advantages are also causing unbalance, and the morale system isn't that easy to figure out and fails sometimes. The game also doesn't provide much for game modes, seeing as territory is the only mode (but there are enough maps to keep you busy, and anyway, a deathmatch mode were people die by one bullet wouldn't last that long anyway, so this mode is more than enough).
All in all you can't really call yourself a FPS or action guy if you don't play this game. 8.5/10

Red orchestra 2 is a refreshing attempt to bring realistic FPS games to wider audience. I didn't play original Red Orchestra (except once during a free weekend) so I can't say how this differs from it or if the gameplay has been dumbed down in the attempt to cater slightly larger audience. But now to the review.
Singleplayer:
Red orchestra 2 is clearly a multiplayer game. Singleplayer is basically playing multiplayer maps with bots and at least in the case of this game, the result is not worth it. When I played trough the singleplayer campaing (I think about a year ago) it also had a huge amount of bugs. To summarise. DO NOT buy this game if you are not going to play multiplayer.
Multiplayer:
I have mainly played multiplayer in territory game mode with "hardcore" settings so my review mainly covers this side of the multiplayer. The multiplayer was good, but not amazing. i was hoping for more.
Anyways the gameplay is solid and it differes much from mainstream FPS games. The gameplay is slower and there are tanks in most maps which I like. I also liked a lot the way how weapons worked in the game. For example instead of often used artifical spread caused by cone of fire, the bullets will go out of the gun parallel to barrel. Player just need to be really good at controlling extensive recoil to aim well.
The thing that I didn't like in Red Orchestra 2 was that the game favours camping a bit too much. Of course in a game like Red Orchestra there is going to be some camping but on my opinion a better map design would have kept camping in smaller levels.
I recommend this game to those who want to play relatively realistic multiplayer FPS games and who are also able to tolerate camping.
