Would you criticise chess for being feature poor because the boards are always an eight by eight grid? No, because that's not the point. Superhot is so original and well crafted that it doesn't need any extra padding to be worth your time and money.The devs focused on what really mattered. But as if to make sure nobody could accuse their game of being feature poor, the devs have snuck in loads of goodies. There are a lot of smaller mini-features which add immensely to the character of the game. So much creativity and love has been put into superhot, as evidenced by loads of extra goodies that I don't want to spoil for you - for a start, just explore the options below the primary buttons in the main menu.

This is a very small (20 minute) puzzle game. The premise is an allegory about British and US foreign policy toward Iran in the 20th century. It's free and short, and it's good.
Mohammad Mosaddegh was Prime Minister of Iran from 1951 until 1953. He was a champion of secular, democratic values, and sought to modernise Iran by nationalising its oil industry. Having been democratically elected by the people of Iran, he was overthrown in a coup organised by the CIA and British intelligence services.
Why was nationalisation of oil so contentious? In the early 1950s, many key industries in Western states were nationalised, or part-owned by the state. The UK had itself just nationalised its coal and steel industries. But as the Cold War developed, the US became more hawkish about any states showing socialist tendencies. As the UK's might withered and its postwar ration economy continued to struggle, the British state attempted desperately to assert its interests in the Middle East.
This revanchiste British foreign policy, upheld by a Conservative administration but instigated by a Labour Prime Minister, would eventually culminate in the disastrous attempt to hold the Suez Canal of 1956. It also meant protecting British supplies of cheap oil. If the Iranian government were to control the nation's oil reserves, then it could set its own prices. When Mossaddegh sought to limit the influence of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC), the AIOC refused to cooperate. Iran responded by nationalising their assets. The UK initiated a worldwide boycott of Iranian oil, and began an extensive programme of bribery and co-ercion to protect its interests in Iran. The situation escalated into a coup signed off by the British and US governments at the highest levels. A democratically-elected government had been overthrown by a foreign power for trying to take a local resource into the people's hands.
The Cat and the Coup briefly tells this story using a few headlines, photographs, mockups, and collage art. The game is a sequence of about six vignette puzzles, each of which takes about two minutes to complete. Mossaddegh's ghost enters a room symbolising a moment in his own memory, and the player, his cat, forces him to leave or encourages him to follow a falling object. It's all rather strange, and not overly polished, but it's intuitive enough, and not difficult enough to be frustrating. The animations are lovely. I think you should play this game.

I will admit, I only bothered to look at this game due to its very cool graphical style. Though, on watching the gameplay video and reading the main synopsis present on the store page, I became fearful of a very real possibility. Namely, that hiding behind an excellent artistic direction is a shallow, and probably irritating, gimmick driven “game”. Not unexpectedly, I’m obliged to report that my suspicions proved accurate, but also that my discoveries come with several reservations.
First, the gameplay itself (and this should be obvious from the accompanying trailers), is minimal. The goal is to slowly raise and lower your balloon in tune with the weather patterns, which push you left and right, to varying degrees, and land at some designated point. As the game goes on, you’ll have to contend with the added complexity of doing this several times per level, and occasionally even drop things down holes or bombs on unsuspecting flying spiky balls. Playing with a standard mouse, this gets boring, and at times irritating, though mostly due to the slow nature of your balloon and having to
for your chance to fail again. Chances are, you will have to reset levels several times due to popping or floating too far off-screen. This is where the gimmick comes in, and the developers clearly hope that people haven’t learned from every other throwaway peripheral and gimmick that console makers try to push down our throats. By using your mic, you can control the balloon with your voice. Or any manner of sound, I suppose, so long as you can easily fluctuate it. This is also where my first aforementioned reservation comes in. If you can entertain yourself for hours on end by making stupid noises in the dark, than by all means, play and thoroughly enjoy The Howler. If you’re considering this as a fun diversion for you and your drunk friends, ask yourself this – when was the last time you were able to keep a group of drunks quiet for more than 5 seconds? If you can’t answer that question, than you’re better dusting off the ol’ Kinect for another go around of drunk digital soccer.
Now here’s my second reservation: the art design. It is superb, often ranging from the melancholy to the downright foreboding. And of course, the Wolf. It really bothers me that such a fantastic art style is wasted on a game like this. Given that this mediocre excursion could be beaten in little more than hour (provided you’re forced to reset as often as I had to), than I would seriously consider recommending this title given you have a fondness for such things. If you can forgive, or at the very least tolerate the gameplay, than you may have a better time than I did, if only for the joy of viewing the set pieces. Know, though, that for some reason the game is limited to a small window (surrounded by a large black border in fullscreen), and cannot appear to be changed. While this keeps the art crisp and clean, I am disappointed that I couldn’t have a closer look at some of the better murals.
The Howler is based off of a book, and you’ll see a direct link to it on
in the game’s menu. It’s a shame that there is absolutely no exposition or plot to the game’s events, offering only a quick phrase explaining your mission for whatever group and
. Perhaps it might have alleviated the boredom of the actual gameplay mechanic to have given it all a more defined purpose. In any case, The Howler is something you probably shouldn’t even bother playing in the first place. Unless you really think you’re going to enjoy making stupid noises into your mic for an hour, or absolutely refuse to use google to find the game’s sublime artwork, I’d recommend you at least find a better mobile port to spend your time on.

Hi, I played The Howler for like 25 minutes and it's really cool.
The game looks great. It's very peaceful, there not a lot of sound or music aside from your own voice. Only problem I had was that I coudln't put the game into fullscreen. So the footage I made of the game is essentially in letterbox format (I should have lowered the desktop resolution).
You control the altitude of a hot air baloon with a the mouse or by the making sound into a microphone. Lateral movement depends on the strength and direction of the air current you are in. So you have to navigate the air currents. Each level has a different objective e.g. to start you just have to fly to the landing pad and later you need to pick up and deliver parcels.
It's a lot of fun to use voice to control the hot air Baloon. I lost control several times when I spoke or burst into laughter which would seen the baloon rising out of the boundaries of the level. So I had to make myself shut sometimes lol. The game gets pretty tricky fast. It will make you navigate through currents pushing against you. The only way to do so is by gaining momentum in a current moving in the correct direction. I had back track a lot and it can be pretty slow using the air currents. But you need to concentrate to create just the right amount of sound. You are supposed to be able to drop objects by using your voice. But I couldn't get this to work so I used the space bar.
So it is a really cool game and $2.99 is an awesome price.

TL;DR: If you loved the first one, you'll at least like this one. If you haven't played the first one, I'd recommend you to do that. But if you don't have the money, this is a great alternative.
Let me start off by saying DD1 is one of my favorite games of all time. Therefore this review may be a bit biased.
For a game in alpha stage it's definitely not bad, there is a decent amount of content and more is being developed all the time. I bought the game more or less as soon as it was available and I don't regret that decision. You could get it for free, and here's why you should:
Even if you've played DD1, it feels like a new game. It's different enough, but at the same time it's similar enough to be called a Dungeon Defenders game.
Leveling feels somewhat rewarding, though the early levels go by really fast while the later levels are a grind. However, it's rather satisfying to hit that level you needed for a new weapon or piece of armor.
Extremely fun with friends. If you're playing this alone or with randoms, you're missing out.
The graphics are beautiful. A definite upgrade from DD1
The map designs are great, the only complaint here is that some maps in DD1 felt bigger.
Trendy communicates with the playerbase, frequent devstreams and posts. This is something you don't see very often, especially this early in development.
Some of the weapons have really cool passive effects. There's a lot of variety in weapons, especially bows. You could find 4 of the same bow and they could all have a different shot types, making them better for different situations.
One of my biggest complaints is a bit of an odd one. I really don't like the fact that it's f2p. Maybe it's the fear of it becoming p2w, but I highly doubt that will happen. Another thing is the amount of paid DLC's. DD1 had a TON of them, and the game wasn't free. Now that this one is free, it feels like there will be even more DLC's. I don't mind throwing a bit of cash at the game however, but I really hope the amount won't be excessive.
Most of the negative things I have to say about the game will (probably) be fixed by the time the game fully releases, so I won't get too much into them but:
Upgrading weapons isn't that rewarding. There aren't as many upgrade levels on weapons, probably partly due to how they changed the upgrading system as a whole. You can only have so many items to upgrade with.
The amount of legendary drops you get. In DD1 this wasn't as much of a problem. Now it's rare to go even one map without getting a legendary. It doesn't feel satisfying at all, and most of the time they're worse than the equipment you're already using anyway. They are nice for upgrading other gear though.
The towers feel a bit more.. bland? compared to DD1. Though I do really like how you can change certain towers (or abilities) with uber spheres.
The lack of challenge mode. I can't remember exactly what it was called but if you've played DD1 you probably know what I'm talking about.
I enjoyed showing off my achievements in DD1 inside my tavern, especially with the eternia crystal. There aren't that many achievements in the game yet, but when they do add them I hope we'll get something like that.
I find it kind of silly how they're already about to release an additional hero, when in DD1 it took them almost 2 years. I don't mind a new hero to play around with, but I'd prefer some other content instead.
This review probably wasn't very coherent at all, but the point I'm trying to make is that the game is worth a try, especially with the $0 price tag. I have faith in Trendy, the game will improve by heaps by the time of release.

The game really runs like an inefficiency simulator, and you need to carefully minimize sources of inefficiency.  You are either into this kind of game or you're not.  It is about resource management and optimization of resource acquisition.
You'll love this game if:
...you get a thrill out of having more food than your population could use in a year.
...you are excited that your population did not zero out after a disaster, disease, or food shortage nearly eliminated your entire population.
...you feel satisfaction having enough of every resource.
...you are interested in figuring out why your town failed.
...you like dealing with imperfect circumstances, and are happy to just make it through.
You'll hate this game if:
...you want something exciting to happen.
...you want your people to go to war.
...you think it's boring waiting for buildings to build and populations to grow.
...you get frustrated when you "did what you were supposed to do" and you fail anyway.
...you read a review that said this game was amazing or groundbreaking, and you realize it's really straightforward, predictable, and focused on micromanaging in a macromanagment situation.
I enjoyed the game.  I only ever pay for games on big sales, and I felt the $5 I paid for it was a good price, but not a great price.  It was half the game I was hoping for.  Still a good game for the OCD side of me.

I played this game when it first came out on the PS2, then picked up this re-release (HD remake is a bit of a stretch) on sale. This fun little murder-mystery-turned-superhero-origin is a WILD ride from the folks at Quantic Dream. There's a term I kept repeating while playing this game and that is "Tone". This game doesn't seem to know what that is. One minute, I'm trying to hide a body of a man I killed while possesed, the next I'm playing basketball to get my 5 dollars back, and then I'm jumping over cars and helicopters evading the police. The game starts out SO GOOD, but just devolves into these ridiculously over the top action sequences by the end. It starts out legitmately enjoyable, but around the halfway mark, it becomes enjoyable for its B-movie aesthetic, which is a shame.
I replayed this through with my girlfriend (she likes the Quantic Dream, Telltale type games), and she said that it was actually her favorite one that we played because it gets absolutely insane by the end, and you have NO idea what is going to happen next.

Didn't love it, didn't hate it. For a brief moment I almost thought I felt something and that maybe the character was relatable but the more I thought about it it just seemed like a ploy. Maybe the point of all this is to feel hollow after playing.  Maybe I should go outdoors and not expect a seven dollar purchase to give me fulfillment. Perhaps the takeaway is don't always expect games to meet your demands of them. I'd almost like to get my money back but would not want to hinder anyone's ability to create titles in their future. Based more on Stanley Parable than on this I will gladly hand you my money.

Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered is a cinematic interactive drama written and directed by David Cage.
The game takes 10h to finish, however, there are some choices you have to make which lead to a few different endings. You get to play as multiple protagonists: Lucas Kane, Carla Valenti and Tyler Miles.
The story starts on a cold New York City night in January 2009, Lucas Kane is caught in a trance and stabs a man to death in the restroom of a diner and then flees the scene. Lucas attempts to uncover the reason behind the murder. Soon after that, you get to play as both Carla Valenti and Tyler Miles in this investigation.
Each of the characters has a sanity meter that is affected by choices the player makes and interactions with the environment.
There are a lot of QTEs here...like a lot, recent Telltale Games have less QTEs and those games are just QTEs and dialog. There were times where I would've loved to just sit back and watch the action without an 8 button input on the middle of the screen.
The
is brilliant and it was composed by Angelo Badalamenti, best known for his work scoring films for director David Lynch.
I enjoyed this game for its story, however, gameplay wise the QTEs can get annoying from time to time.

I've had this game for over a year now, but was never able to really play it until now (I had horrible framerate issues back then).
It's a realistic World War II FPS game.
-Weapons never stay centered on the screen
-You die in 1 to 2 hits (or you bleed out from non fatal injuries)
-Magazines are actually preserved (you don't regain unspent bullets from a changed mag; instead, the partially used mag is saved for later)
-There is no ammo counter. You check the number of bullets by feeling the weight of the magazine, or by pulling back the bolt of a rifle to count the bullets inside (done by holding the reload button). Even then, you won't know the exact number. It'll tell you if it's empty/near-empty/half-full/more than half/full.
-Suppression is a thing. If there's too much gunfire around you, your screen will turn black and white. Your character will start shaking, and you can't steady your aim down your iron sights.
-Bullet drop is a thing. When aiming down your sights, you can compensate for bullet drop by adjusting your view down the iron sights (done by scrolling up/down with the mouse scroll). The further a target, the more you'll have to lower your sights to get an accurate shot.
-There's a cover system. I don't use it much, but it's still there. You can also lean left/right.
-Roles are limited so as to prevent the Battlefield problem. Depending on the number of players, there can only be 1-2 snipers, 1-4 machinegunners, 1-2 elite assaults, 1-5 squad leaders, etc.
-There is a commander role. The commander is responsible for calling in aerial recon (to reveal enemy locations), force respawning (to support a large push against a capture point), and various types of artillery. Artillery coordinates must be requested from squad leaders, which further illustrates the team aspect of this game.

The story is what you'd expect from a 3D Platformer, plain and simple. You play as a girl named Hat Girl who is trying to get home but when she passes over a planet, a Mafia man stops her and causes all her fuel (time pieces) to fly out and it's your job to get them back.
The gameplay is extremely fun. Hat girl is fun to control and extremely responsive. She can do the dive from Super Mario Sunshine which is very fun to do. Throughout the game you can collect hats with different abilities that help you with certain platforming challenges. You can collect tokens to spin a wheel to get items to customize Hat Girl. It can be from music remixes to color palette swaps to different hat variations.
The music is absolutely amazing. It's so catchy you'll find yourself humming the tune of some of them. Every track in this game is phenomenal and I can't stop listening to it.
Overall this game is a must buy if you like 3D platformers. I highly recommend you buy this and show the devs some love. :)

Really loved this game. I love to play games that have an in-depth story and this definitely had that. I haven't played any of the other tales games so I cannot compare them to each other but as a rpg itself i loved it. The characters were endearing and their personalities made sense and didn't feel forced. Some people may argue that Sorey may have been whiney and a goody two shoes but he stayed true to his character till the end which is to always to look for the good in people and will always try his best to avoid killing. All of the characters felt real and they had good interactions with each other if you were to watch all their side stories. Their actions were understandable and even the villians had a good reason for their actions which you may sympathize with.
If you played above the normal difficulty the gameplay could be a little tricky. Heck even normal can be hard sometimes but you'll get used to it in time. The grades for each battle with normal mobs was heavily dependent on time so if you want a good grade you have to kill them fast. The gameplay was also quite flexible and different types of combos and moves could be used to counter a certain type of enemy. Martial artes, hidden artes and seraphic artes had a type of rock paper scissors affinity which was cool. Armatization, where a human and a seraph becomes one, may seem quite op at first but you will come to realise that its not all powerful and sometimes its better not to armatize.
One thing i didn't like was that when the mobs detect you (and they probably always will unless you approach behind them with rose's silent step support action) they will chase you like hell and unless you have windstepping from your wind or water seraph, you won't be able to outrun them and you will engage in battle which is bad because your SC bar drops when you engange in battle. So resting in inns are actually quite frequent unless you saved some of your herbs.
If you love open world rpg you will love this.
All in all 8/10

Do you absolutely love the colour green? Do you find yourself never quite able to see enough of the colour in your day to day life? Do you long to play a video game where the only colour you will see for a vast majority is green? This game is for you! Read on for my full review:
THE GOOD:
The game really feels like a true survival horror game. You aren't an expert Special Ops paratrooper or even a normal person who knows how to use a gun. In fact, you get no weapons at all. You get your camera and your legs. You can run and you can hide. It's a really unique spin on the genre. The game is really pretty for an indie title, and the atmostphere is fantastic, however the jump scares can quickly become boring.
THE BAD:
The game is played in a first-person perspective, and you're basically supposed to have your camera up the entire time (which can get really annoying later) in order to get all of your "notes" recorded. Your camera has a night-vision feature, which the game tells you to "manage well," but what it doesn't tell you is that you will have to use the night-vision for about 90% of the game (presumably because Red Barrels was too lazy to implement any sort of real colour palette to the game) and having the night-vision turned on will drain your camera's battery faster than Charlie Sheen can snort a line of coke. Batteries aren't too difficult to come by though, so there are only a small handful of times where that can really become a problem. The constant use of night-vision can seriously hurt your eyes though.

While I am a fan of the Tales games... This one... is quite iffy...
On a scale of 0-100, with 0-50 being thumbs down and 51-100 being thumbs up, this game gets a 60.
Let me start with the positives.
The graphics are pretty good, no complaints here.
The music is good, I actually have a few songs modded into my Sm4sh cause they're catchy.
The animations are... well, you know, Tales-y. It's pretty much always been this clunky, so it's bearable.
The game actually looks pretty fluid (if you unlocked the 30-fps frame cap, cause seriously, f*** that sh*t).
The combat isn't TOO horrendous, other than relying on the weakness' and what not, but Xillia 2 did that too, so w/e.
Negatives, oh boy.
The story, oh boy.
One of the characters, oh boy. (One of the main characters pretty much gets ditched/forgotten about)
The combat... I know I said it isn't too bad, but it can become a 50/50 if you don't understand (or I should say 'abuse') the weakness/element system. You will actually do almost no damage if you don't hit weakness'.
Mind you, I have 60 hours on Zestria at this moment, but most of the time is spent on grinding, which actually doesn't actually strengthen your characters that much. Most of the time I spent grinding was actually just learning techniques, certain combo's that strung well, learning the characters I didn't like to play as (sorry, Mikleo, you're just... not fun to play as), and most of all, eventually learning to make you CPU allies useful, cause holy crap, are they pretty stupid. It is CRITICAL that you use the setting that tells them to 'hit the opponents weakness'' because that way, they can actually start doing damage on their own without having you needing to babysit them.
Very weak thumbs up. I still do play it from time to time, but I'd much rather go back to Xillia/Xillia 2 (Rip PS3). Hopefully, Tales of Berseria keeps me interested for far longer.

I'm not saying its a terrible game, but it's sad to see games which think, "I have a cool gimmick, so I'll ignore content, plot, and everything else a normal game has." It's lacking in everything. Weapon selection is low, and monster variety is tied to weapons. Plot is shaky: another game riding the rails of vague hints with no actual substance. "Who? Where? One quirk, bullet speed is slow. Ever play Max Payne? You'd hav'ta lead the bullets a bit. This game takes that to the next level . Even when a few steps away from a baddie, you'll be aiming nowhere near them to connect a shot.
Another quirk is the AI having omniscience, which I'm sure made it easy to program. I'm not saying the game should have a stealth element... but actually, that's exactly what I'm saying. When the biggest threat is an enemy sneaking up behind you, it's strange you can never sneak up on anyone.
I picked it up in a moment of weakness. I hope you don't do the same.

Gonna go back to RC. At least the 12 year olds aren't a bunch of seal clubbers killing this game in it's early stages. It is rife with gunbrella and gunbricks, as in literal "borg cubes" which the devs have sworn up and down they will "reward better ship design" constantly, the majority of dev blogs and updates mention this. But in half a year, this hasn't changed, guns still serve properly as armor, without even a hotfix. However the game is bound to literally only space ships (which should be cool) but they designed it as more moba-esque experience and you'll spend your time using blinks, stuns, shields and slows.... ruining your awesome ship-to-ship combat with gimmicky effects for readability. The concept of using different ship classes I thought was at first cool, but it became novel and then jarring when I realized they interpreted "class" in this sense to be the RPG context and not the nautical.
However, there are some things done right, if they are sort of just the cherry on top, so it doesn't save this. The ships explode well and look nice while being destroyed. The class system is a good attempt at adding diversity between builds. The ability to upgrade parts is nice, it allows for a real feeling of progression. The music is MAF, which I appreciate greatly. The different tiers of the same weapon behave differently and allows it to feel like a group of different weapons and not just versions of the same one.
So in the end I must give this a not reccomend. There are too many errors on behalf of the developer which they could have avoided by researching the development history of the biggest competitor in this genre. And the pros are generally the fluff of the game and not the meat, which is spoilt. It's like a really good looking burger, with the best toppings that actually are good and a professional presentation. But the reason you came, the meat.... just wasn't done right.

I'm not sure what I can contribute here that the other reviews haven't already said a thousand times over. The game is very short, though not necessarily to its detriment. If you like peaceful games, jumping puzzles, or speedrunning you will like Refunct. And despite the game's brevity, it is absolutely worth its asking price.

Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered is a cinematic interactive drama written and directed by David Cage.
The game takes 10h to finish, however, there are some choices you have to make which lead to a few different endings. You get to play as multiple protagonists: Lucas Kane, Carla Valenti and Tyler Miles.
The story starts on a cold New York City night in January 2009, Lucas Kane is caught in a trance and stabs a man to death in the restroom of a diner and then flees the scene. Lucas attempts to uncover the reason behind the murder. Soon after that, you get to play as both Carla Valenti and Tyler Miles in this investigation.
Each of the characters has a sanity meter that is affected by choices the player makes and interactions with the environment.
There are a lot of QTEs here...like a lot, recent Telltale Games have less QTEs and those games are just QTEs and dialog. There were times where I would've loved to just sit back and watch the action without an 8 button input on the middle of the screen.
The
is brilliant and it was composed by Angelo Badalamenti, best known for his work scoring films for director David Lynch.
I enjoyed this game for its story, however, gameplay wise the QTEs can get annoying from time to time.

Oh boy... I finished the game and I really thought a long time about whether to refund the game or not. In the end I did not but chose to write this review and share my thoughts on why this game doesn't work for me.
The game was an instant buy for me. From the creator of "The Stanley Parable" (which I enjoyed much and would always recommend someone to buy and play. Just so much to discover about yourself as a player, so well designed and so much attention for detail... but that's another review), a fair price connected with a nice release discount, many reviews and most of them positive,.... what could go wrong?
Well, my first reason for buying this one was already the one which tricked me the most. Just because someones first game is awesome doesn’t make the next game automatically awesome, too. It’s more that the next game
also be great and that the chances are very high, but it’s not a direct dependency.
On the other hand,... maybe that thought is already wrong, since this game is not really made by the guy from TSP. It’s more a compilation of several small projects by a friend who is called Coda by the narrator (It’s of course up for interpretation whether this person could be the same person as the narrator and therefore the creator of TSP, but that’s irrelevant for the reason why the game didn’t worked for me)
My biggest problem with the game is that it disappointed me on that parts which TSP made overwhelmingly well. When there was a choice given to the player, even not an obvious one, there was also a new way the story of the game would proceed,…in TSP. That's not the case in this game. When you're trying to trick the game by making something not intended by the narrator, or even when accidentally having the right solution to one of the many crazy puzzles you're just being pushed back on the “correct” way of the story. The narrator not even reacts on your behavior. Believe me, I tried hard to break the game in order to find the hidden clue or some alternative solutions. But nothing… Not even a filthy steam achievement “for trying”.
And then there are these “mini games”, which you can also argue about whether or not they can be considered as games. In combination with the narrator some of them were quite interesting and I was like: “ok, cool. These first ones are crap but hey, it's getting better and better. The designer learns his stuff… The last game must be mindblowing and I will understand and see the path the designers took to get there.” And then the game suddenly ended…with the shoot out to Coda to please get back in contact.
That alone is not a problem for me. It's even a nice move to show your admiration for someone's work by doing a narrated tribute version of his work. The game lost me because in the end I had the feeling I just watched a movie. There was not a single moment when my choices or how I behaved had any influence on the story and its outcome. The game didn't even try to give me the feeling I could've had any influence on it at all. All of the time I felt like I have been put in a baby buggy and been pushed through the game. When I tried to break out of it, I have been pulled back “dudududududu, you're not old enough to walk around alone! Just sit down and let me show you the world. Here, take your teddy and be quiet!”
That's not what I expect from a game or what a good game should provide. I want to make my own experiences in a game or at least the illusion about this freedom should be kept up. Finally, there is just the disappointment because in my opinion the game wasted a lot potential and it could have been easy to become as big and meaningful as TSP.

The characters are kind of annoying and they don't experience much character development over the course of the game. It takes quite a while for things to actually "happen" so you're going to spend a lot of time just running around and killing things.
I have some issues with the gameplay as well. The battle camera is extremely annoying, especially when playing with a 2nd player. They got rid of the battle "arenas" and instead encounters occur in the actual maps, so you wind up with a lot of very awkward battles. This is especially bad if they happen near doorways or in smaller spaces, the camera gets stuck on the environment and then you can't really see what's going on. There are other problems like the 30 FPS cap, but some of those are fixed in a community patch.
I don't really like the "fusion" mechanic or the layout of the artes. My favourite thing about the Tales games is being able to play through the story with friends controlling members of the party ... in Zestiria, you're really limited to only having one other player. That player also can't really play when there is only one human on the team.
I'm enjoying the game but I'm a huge fan of the Tales series. This is among my least favourite.

Having spent over 100 hours on this game on my first playthrough, and more than happy to spend the same amount (if not more) on a second, I have to say this: this is a very good game, but Your Mileage May Vary.  This game is a lot less direct about guiding you on where to go (especially early on), and you won't get a lot out of the game unless you do the optional side quest content.  That's where a lot of the characterization will come in.  If anything, this is unlike a lot of the other Tales games in that you get the bare bones minimum experience if you just do a straight playthrough without the side quests.  Earlier entries into the series gives you a good experience if you skip the optional content.
But before you go running off for the nearest FAQ for the game, let me just say I managed to get a good experience even without consulting a FAQ, because the game is really good about giving you prompts regarding available side quests.  Talk to your other human party member (who trails behind you as you travel in the overworld) and you will get little hints and tips on where to go next to follow up on a side quest.  And with the save point warp travel system, it's really easy to hop from place to place to get where you need to for a quest.
Also, the OST for this game is amazing, 10/10 would totally buy if it was available as a DLC or iTunes.

HOSTING/SEARCHING FOR ONLINE MATCHES IS OFTEN FRUITLESS
There are NO official servers. Games are hosted by players. So don't buy this if you want to host but can't do port forwarding. Only open NATters can host online games.
Don't buy it either if you don't have any friends willing to play. You'll rarely ever find random people to play with. I CAN host games and even so I spend several 5-minute waits on the lobby and NOT A PERSON shows up.
GAME MODES/BOARDS SPLIT THE PLAYERBASE
There are several game modes and boards. I wish the game would list all open servers so you could choose the one that best suited you (I prefer the fast dice rule + dynamic board). But it forces you to choose all the options before searching for a game, effectively splitting the (already small) player base into 24 different groups that can't see each other. That means EVEN LESS PEOPLE TO PLAY WITH.
NO SAVE STATES ON ONLINE MATCHES
If someone loses his Internet connection, ever so briefly, he's not allowed to return to the game and a bot takes his place. I bet you can imagine how it feels to be disconnected from a match after playing for over an hour. It also sucks for the remaining players, because the challenge is suddenly gone. Who cares about beating bots?
Local matches have save states, though. And by "local" I mean all players on the same PC (who does that?). There's no LAN multiplayer.
CUMBERSOME INTERFACE MIGHT TAKE SOME TIME TO GET USED TO
This is most certainly a console port. I recommend playing with a controller instead of your keyboard. You can't play with your mouse. People will struggle at first, specially when doing negotiations.
The user interface is also unnecessarily sluggish on a game that already takes too much of your time. Matches usually go for more than 1 hour if the players are quick.
LESSER ANNOYING SIHT
- you have to choose your language EVERY TIME the game is launched;
- you're forced to listen to the overly loud music & voice when the game launches. It doesn't matter if you disabled them in the options menu;
- it's such a simple game but it takes a LOONG TIME to get to the title screen;
- Ubisoft's Uplay is required;
- you CAN'T TYPE THE NUMBERS ON AN OFFER. You have to hold -right arrow- and wait for the game to count from zero to whatever;
- not all animations are skippable. They look good but take too long and are a test of patience;
- there are unnecessary delays for everything, even for throwing your dice.
TL;DR:
I gifted this to several friends and not a single one liked it (and I don't blame them - the game takes too damn long). It should be way faster, specially on the first rounds where there are still unowned properties. People get bored and quit way before the exciting part of buildings and negotiations begins. Controls are not responsive enough, too many delays, too many unskippable animations. You'll rarely find someone online to play with. If someone disconnects, that's it, they're out, replaced by a bot, and can't come back - all the time the player invested until that point gets wasted.
My advice is: STAY AWAY.

We did planning beginning of every round, and made sure to use the best of our gems to get the defenses top notch :D. Sadly, after defeating the final boss on the airship battle we decided to take a break (Not before we ran a few hundred other non-story missions XD).
After the break I saw an update on my steam activity list (Tbh I'm probably one of the few people who actually checks that...) I noticed they had the "Chaos update" And of course I was like: Huh. Sounds cool!. First thing I did was head to the store page to reinstall the game (As my laptop only had like 200gb of space :T ). I instantly noticed the reviews of the game and how it suddenly went downhill. I began reading many of them and watched a few videos about it at the time. Apparently from what I saw they tore down the old loot system (No more magic fireball weapon staffs of doom? QAQ), and added some sort of, gem thing, that you fuse to weapons, they also messed with the inventory setup which made me want to vomit all over my horrible laptop, and many more issues I strongly agreed with. I have been keeping in tact with all the updates ive seen on the activity page lately, and it finally turned my view.
I noticed the reviews started going back to positive, and I read the comments and reviews them selves. And, surprisingly, as I write this review I am actually installing Dungeon Defenders II on my new PC. The beloved game of my high school childhood I played that kept me entertained because I loved the art style, I loved how the old loot system worked. And for being a vetran DD2 player its hard to switch off something like that. I completely understand. Thats why I am not going to give this a thumbs down. Because doing so is totally prejudice as I havent even visited the game myself here... Now. I am not sure if this review will stay positive or negative, but for now its positive because back then I loved the game, and Im willing to face whatever is different or new. I do hope they bring some version of the loot drop system back because apparently I've heard the new system is complicated and item level based and something about the term: "ilvl". Anyways. In conclusion I'd honestly say, for any new player, definitely give it a shot. You really dont have anything to lose coz its a free game ^^;. But in my honest opinion. I wouldnt spend a dime on this game until I know for sure its something I'll enjoy for a while. Till then... in about, hmm, probably..3 minutes ill be loading it up and taking a step back into the cartoonistic world of DD2 :) Anyways uhm, see ya I guess. Thank bloody christ for game that invovles a catastrophe but not zombies. For that matter, I'm glad the catastrophe isn't another god damned virus outbreak or nuclear war. Granted, I'm sure we'll just end up killing each other with Mother Nature sitting back and eating her cous-cous or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ a metaphorical mound of dirt would eat, but while we still have our imaginations and aren't♥♥♥♥♥♥♥leashed by another corporation, I like the idea that a massive snowstorm has rendered a little Canadian town absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing useless.
Long story short, a super massive sun spot appeared causing a huge geomagnetic storm. This one is so strong that it eliminates all life forms (except rabbits, foxes, deer, wolves, fourteen types of fish, and you) leaving the land barren and hopeless (except for the dozens of intact homes, perfectly fine flora, and a mostly intact railroad system that probably just needs some good elbow grease). You must survive by scrounging the land for food and water. Yet, you know what else you have survive against, which probably makes this game one of the best I've seen? The ♥♥♥♥ing cold. (Sidenote: I refuse to a believe a Canadian can't handle some snow).
I'll get into the cold later, but let's examine the food and water. You have a very standard hunger and thirst meter. You have a fatigue meter, too, but at the moment, I think sprinting and scripted-event foraging are the only things that really drain your fatigue in any significant degree. Anyway, so you gather food to stuff your face with, and you drink plenty of water found conveniently in toilets all over the abandoned - yet oddly undisturbed - homes (Yum yum!). Run of the mill. It's nothing new, but it's done rather well.
The cold: every time you step out of any structure you are stricken with the winter winds and will continuously suffer - for a lack of better terms - damage. You find ways of warming yourself either by ducking into homes, foraging for extra thick coats and gloves, or by starting a fire somewhere (I think). However, as simple as this sounds, the cold feature is what makes me god damn ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the most. It's one thing to have simple enemies (Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ those wolves), and it's another thing to have basic survival needs (technically, Minecraft had a food meter). However, it's another thing to have the entire world be against. Why? Because it gives you a sense of urgency.
Taking Minecraft for example, there's no real threat once you've armed yourself well enough; get enough enchants and weapons and you can make the Wither your freakin' butler. In The Long Dark, you can better prepare yourself, but in the end, you're still suffering the cold. It's like holding your breath now versus when you were a kid; you can probably hold your breath longer now because you've better control over you body, but in the end, you still need to breathe. No matter how well you prepare yourself, there's always a threat. There's a sense of urgency and need when you're outside in the harsh cold. You have to complete an objective, or you're just wasting energy in the cold.
"But Jay, you can just catch more food, yeah?"
Well, yes, but oddly, there's seems to be a finite amount of resources available. While food may infinitely spawn thanks to deer and rabbits, means to make fire or bullets or such seem to be limited. Clothes, too, aren't entirely infinite. So, there's a vague idea present that may suggest your death is inevitable, and yet, the idea is obscured enough that it gives you hope; that just because one person died on day 15 doesn't mean you will. What does all this mean?
The Long Dark doesn't give you a chance to just wander around and waggle your♥♥♥♥♥♥at everything. You have to find shelter; you have to find food; you have to find tinder; and you have to conserve your resources or the last bit of bait you'll have for fishing will be your very own♥♥♥♥♥♥sicle slathered with O'Canada maple syrup.

You spend the majority of your time sitting in a disgusting ditch filled with the shattered corpses of your fallen comrades, as well as those still unfortunate to be "alive", if you can even use that term to describe what is left of those wretches. As you crawl through soggy trenches, you can hear the shouts of orders being given and soldiers being slain, either blown to torn meat by mortar explosions or cut in half from machine gun fire. You are not a man, you are a frightened rabbit that dashes from cover to cover, whispering wishes of survival for but a few more seconds while pieces of concrete are chipped away around you by enemy sharp shooters. In the worst of times, you are a worm that crawls in the mud, lest a rifleman spots your shape in the distance. There is no salvation from a tank. Death can come from nowhere at all.
Stay away fom windows.
Also, you can't drop more than five feet without breaking a leg. It's fine though, since your small pack of two bandages offers you a second chance at life. Try not too die to quickly, and remember to check your magazine. You can also modify your sights and give out commands. There are a variety of classes to choose from. Choose wisely, and don't be afraid to loot corpses; they don't need anything anymore anyway.
Stay away from windows.
There is also a morale system, where you slowly lose your mind if you are under a barrage of enemy rounds, or if you see an ally get half of their face blown off and fall to the ground screaming in agony for a good minute or so before bleeding out. The result is blurred and discolored sight. I think I got this when I saw a guy get his legs shot off and watched him crawl about an inch away from cover before getting taken out by a sniper.
Stay away from windows.
In all seriousness, this game has a great deal of work put into detail and animations, but there remain some optimization issues. They're not bad, and a someone with an excellent PC might never even notice them.
Rising Storm and Red Orchestra 2 have different dynamics, although the mechanics are exactly the same, if that makes any sense.
If there is one thing I have to ABSOLUTELY give this game credit for, is that it has a personality. A very grim personality, but it's better than the typical "♥♥♥♥ yeah" jingoism many games go for.
There is nothing more satisfying than watching an enemy tank blow to bits.
The singleplayer is good practice, but the AI is really ditzy. The soldiers do not show a lot of initiative and tanks commanders seem to forget that tanks can't climb walls.
Also, about the window thing: I was waiting for my squad to move up and about seven of them decided march right in front of a window in a factory. A machine gunner across the chasm opened up on them and killed them all. It was really unpleasant to watch them panic and stumble and run into each other while being shot to pieces.
The game is good until it crashes every 30 seconds...
Trapped inside of a car, with a hungry wolf on the other side of the window. Cujo, anyone?  Can't wait to see where this game goes. Definitely recommended.

An enticing visual story of the imperial West's role in Iran during the 1950s.
In The Cat and the Coup, you play as the cat of Mohammad Mosaddegh, the first democratically elected Prime Minister of Iran, and go through back in time his story as Prime Minister, starting with his death under house arrest, and ending with his defense of the nationalization of the oil in Iran. The Cat and the Coup is a must for anyone interested in Iranian history, and especially for anyone who hasn't heard of Anglo-American intelligence operations that led to Operation Ajax, and the outing of Dr.Mosaddegh.
A short visual novel, the few minutes you'll spend in The Cat and the Coup will detail to you the events that led up to Operation Ajax, and will, with subtle jabs, the imperialist ambitions of the West whose espionage led to Mossadegh's overthrow.
Great storyline, great music, excellent dialogue, and a beautiful and intricate world. What isn't to love?

Los MiniDrivers boasted itself as the craziest arcade racing game, but admittedly, I have seen more crazy games back in Playstation 2 with in fact more traditional grandprix elements than this game. Despite that, the game has several features, charms, and cutenesses that keep the fans of Adaco, the mastermind behind the original flash web video series, to enjoy themselves.
MiniDrivers is, at a glance, a top-down, auto pilot racing game with superdeformed racing cars very similar to Table Top Racing and Mini Motors Racing. but the game is actually more adjustable than it appears. The options are rather simple yet effective. You can choose a different camera, steering sensitivity, and whether or not you control the pedels to fit your driving style. The control is simple and very easy, to the point it can be a hit or miss. Your car tends to have very responsive steering, so there's no real need to brake other than tricky tracks like Monaco and Japan where you'll spin like mad when overthrottling into uphill and downhill curves. especially when your car has become faster. Still, it's a decent control, and with over 20 track in over 500 events each with its own racing conditions, lap numbers, regulations, and surprisingly increasing difficulty, you can jump right into F1 with no experience, and drive for fun and challenge.
The races themselves are also "okay" in that it stimulates the F1 feel enough to enjoy. The game is on a fair balance between realism and fantasy, and the powerups are better balanced and easier to understand than F1 Race Stars, but comparing MiniDrivers to that, the game can be very lackluster.  First of all, the graphic is very, very bad. The lack of fantasy and bright color makes this game not very eye-catcing and in fact makes the game harder to play in the depressingly dark and rainy races.  The pace of the game can also be hurting, since you start very sluggish, and build you way up slowly due to how expensive the cars and upgrades are despite you having multiple ways to gain coins. The tracks can also become boring and repetitive after a while. which doesn't help in that there's variety in music at all except the flash series's main theme jingle, which is downright disappointing for this type of racing game. In most arcade racing games, each track tends to have its unique personality, in MiniDrivers, every track feels almost the same.
On the track, the powerup can be very helpful or annoying. In your hands, you can upgrades several weapons like boomerang, oil, Safety Car barrier, turbo boost, and streamroller boost to make it very effective to your races. In the hands of AIs, however, the race can be disasterious as they suddenly use them to annoy you, then crash themselves into you like idiots. Speaking of AI, they can be very frustrating. The opponents tend to run a racing line, yet go mad into corners, resulting them crashing into barriers, each other and, worst of all, into you and ruin your race. On the other hand, there's no rubberband, so AI will be left in the dust when you have an overpowered car, something which can be good or bad depend on your preference.
Despite the gameplay problems, the selling point of this game is a fanservice, and they nail it correctly with the fanservice. Fans of the flash series will not be disappoint with the adorable sounds that the drivers make, and while there's only one real theme, it's catchy and enjoyable for fans. The delivery of the game is also superb, as it cutely parody all the inside F1 jokes and drivers' personalities in the ways you feel heartwarming and not offended at all. The selection of F1 cars are also very incredible. Included in the game are larger number of racers from the iOS game, mockoff F1 cars way back from the 50s to the 2000s as well as classic tracks and constantly updated car skins, tracks, and events. The problem, however, is that not everything is nice and dandy. For whatever reason, the game couldn't license the fictional catchy names like "Mini Rosso" or "Minicedes" like they used to do, and the beautiful stickers have been replaced with child's doddles. Buying a car is also rather difficult because the showroom constantly changes the selection and the cars are all very expensive despite that they're really just skin swaps with slightly different performances: a Manor can easily win against a Mercedes when fully upgraded.
"Craziest races" are far from what MiniDrivers convey. The game is disappointingly lacking in graphic and sounds. Other than fanservice, there's not really anything new to add to the likes of tabletop racers, and the game simply isn't cute enough like its competitors. The gameplay, however, is rather decent and flexible, the fanservice and the delivery are very appealing, and it's in fact a rather cheap game. If you're F1 or Los MiniDrivers fan, this game should be enough to entertain you. If you're not either, then consider looking for something else.

Having spent over 100 hours on this game on my first playthrough, and more than happy to spend the same amount (if not more) on a second, I have to say this: this is a very good game, but Your Mileage May Vary.  This game is a lot less direct about guiding you on where to go (especially early on), and you won't get a lot out of the game unless you do the optional side quest content.  That's where a lot of the characterization will come in.  If anything, this is unlike a lot of the other Tales games in that you get the bare bones minimum experience if you just do a straight playthrough without the side quests.  Earlier entries into the series gives you a good experience if you skip the optional content.
But before you go running off for the nearest FAQ for the game, let me just say I managed to get a good experience even without consulting a FAQ, because the game is really good about giving you prompts regarding available side quests.  Talk to your other human party member (who trails behind you as you travel in the overworld) and you will get little hints and tips on where to go next to follow up on a side quest.  And with the save point warp travel system, it's really easy to hop from place to place to get where you need to for a quest.
Also, the OST for this game is amazing, 10/10 would totally buy if it was available as a DLC or iTunes.

My current opinion on this game is : "interesting ideas, but tries too hard to be cool just for the sake of being cool, and as such, lacks depth"
Now, I'll admit that i didn't get past the first town, and as such have not a full picture of the game. But that start had me cringe in several ways. Maybe I'll revisit this game and push past that point, and it may or may not change my opinion, but here are my observations so far :
- the world has interesting ideas and concepts, but they're not developped, and I was often left wondering how exactly even the most basics things were working (like, where do the Seraphs come from? How does the Malevolence works on people, is it irreversible? Where does the Purification Ritual come from?) Now, don't get me wrong, I love fantasy settings, and I can afford a high supension of disbelief. But you've got to give me an origin story, as in "where does this world/universe come from?", especially when you throw so many concepts at me. And even if the characters know about it, I, as a gamer, want to know about it asap.
- the characters start interesting, but some of their actions don't make any sense and feel forced. Also, you sometimes can't really picture what is their place into the world, because they lack support casts. That may change after the point where I stopped, but...the characters parents/friends are rarely mentionned, which is really wierd and make them artificial. Of course, you don't need to have every family fully developped, but you have only 1 support character (the grandfather) for 4 playable characters after the 10 hours mark...that's really really few. And no amount of in-party interaction can make up for the lack of support cast.
- the plot is simple, and it's ok in my book, you don't need to have a revolutionary story. But the events need to make sense! And, again, I was left several times thinking "hey, that was cool, heroes did their thing, some other characters show up and shine, and all, but...WHAT WAS THE POINT? We already won! We didn't need you, and you really didn't help at all! So why are you here looking cool for NO reason?" Or "but...you could have done that ages ago! You had the time, the opportunity, there was nothing preventing you from doing it earlier, then why didn't it happen earlier! You know, when you were actually WITH the person! Now I'll have to backtrack to said person for no reason!" Overall, it's not the plot itself but the very narration, the logic (or lack thereof) that the events were following that made me cringe so much.
- if there is one thing that the Tales of games are famous for, it's for their gameplay, and, yes, I enjoyed playing Tales of Zestiria...after having digested some unecessarily complex notions (you have three different words for side-steps : one for forward side-steps, one for side side-steps, and one for backward side-steps, with one full paragraph explaining what it is each time. One general paragraph presenting the whole "side-step" mechanic and the three different keywords would have make it soooo much easier to understand) Also, there is a seemingly complex combo system with each hit having its special properties, but maybe I wasn't playing in a high enough difficulty, because I found it quite inconsequential. Overall, I found the management of the "energy bar" much much more important than choosing the good combo. I also found your companions AI quite slow to act as you programmed them to in the menu, especially regarding to healing, which required some heavy micromanagement, breaking the flow of combat.
- and then there is the game system out of combat, aka, the equipment...Again, interesting concept, flawed execution that leads to uselessness. Every piece of gear gains exp as you battle, and you can fuse two of the same piece of gear to, hopefully, combine them into one better piece of gear with the properties of both of its components, and sometimes another, more powerfull, property. But here is the flaw : those properties are not interesting enough to justify keeping an old piece of gear when a new one, with better base stats, is available. Which makes grinding for several hours for powerfull multi-properties gear pointless, as you'll have to replace them anyway in a couple hours, max.
I could go on and on, but you get the idea : in every aspect, Tales of Zestiria has interesting ideas, things that could have been great, and that can be enjoyed...if you don't look too deeply into them.
From the world to the characters, from the combat to the gear, to the titles to the cooking, it looks great and cool, with flashy "badass" events, but as soon as you try to stop and think, and go out of your way to find something a little more complex...it just falls apart.
Hence why I don't recommand it. Now, I can get why people like it, I kinda enjoyed the combat system, and the world looks interesting enough, it looks good and I like the character design. But it just made me too frustrated with all the holes, be it in the writing or the designs, to keep playing.

A lot of modern "horror" games nowadays rely on the idea of putting players in a dark atmosphere and occasionally popping them ewith a jumpscare before the player is put into your standard-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t action movie style shooting scene (resident not-so-evil). this is identical to the process of a magician playing the exact same trick over and over again. Its wrong, boring, and doesn't define the genre at all.
even the amnesia games are guilty of not being able to produce enough of an atmosphere, and frequently relied on the hope that the player was still actually scared of the whole two enemies in the entire game.
And thats what good horror comes from: atmosphere. tension. the idea of knowing that something bad is going to happen and you don't know exactly how much poop is going to dribble out of your pants leg when it does.
In my opinion the best things are often made unconventionally. Conventional horror nowadays consists of dim lighting (which is reversed by tuning up your gamma) lots of blood and monsters or some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t jumping around a corner to chase you.
Five Nights at Freddy's has none of this:
the premise of the game is so cripplingly simple, the resources used are equally artificial, and yet the game locks you into the seat that your character is in and straps you for a ride through real horror.
where most games place jumpscares, FNaF simply sits there, like the animals themselves, and stands idly in the middle of a dimly lit security light, you're there, waching them as they stand there, eyeing off the camera or the doors to your room, and you experience terror that rattles the very fabric of your being when you switch back and notice another one is gone or god forbid
is open. and as the game ticks on, so will your sanity as you find it harder and harder to cope with the onslaught and torment of those five possessed animatronics.
Yes. There are
of them. And the fifth is the worst of the lot.
in summary, FNaF does something in horror that is not frequently done due to its atmospheric risk: it dangles the object of horror right in your face, and lets it sit there. There's jumpscares. but those don't even hold a candle to when you watch that purple rabbit disappear from the stage for the first time.

When I first played this game in Early Access, I thought this was the great game that would definitely become the next Robocraft. Popular, fun, and now in 3-dimensional space battles. Now, I pray the devs would get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together. I played 3 games before writing this review because I wanted to see how much it progressed in the few months I haven't played, and I'll explain how each of those reveal a major issue with this game.
The first game was good enough, I noticed some improvements to promote making cool ships over just functionally broken ships. I was doing pretty good as far as I could tell, because my score was decent, but I had no clue whether or not I was shooting or not. You see, the sound of my gattling guns, which I remember as that satisfying noise during battle, was almost silent entirely. I tried to change the audio settings and volume settings on my computer, but there was no way to even hear the damn things without making explosive noises and other sound effects blow out my eardrums. And near the end of the game it just crashed, and showed me a pop-up window asking me to send the crash log to the developers. After a short facepalm I tried to launch the game again and I was pleased to see that I at least got some amount of reward from the game I had lost anyway.
Then after returning to queue, I got matched against an enemy who tore through my big armored battleship like it was butter. After the game I found out, he is the bloody #1 player of the game. I, who had barely a floating heap of garbage with a few gattling guns and some armor plating to hide the fact that I didn't even have the money or level for good abilities, got matched against the #1 player of all time. After looking into it, I found out I was but one of the 77 players active in the game. Even so the queue time was short, but I was matched against people waaaaaaaay out of my league. And it showed, the guy got 16 kills and 1 death that game. In an arena shooter where all that matters is kills. That's insane.
Then, the third game I played, I noticed the new abilities. I've had one or two used against me in the previous 2 games. But now I was constantly "Hacked". "Stunned". "Pulled". The enemy had more control over my ships than I did, and my weapons didn't even fire the entire game. If they had a splitsecond in which one bullet slipped out of the barrel I wouldn't know because there was no sound coming from my gattling gun.
So in short. The game is awful if you're new, or if you're coming back into the game. I understand low queue times are a priority. Then maybe work on making people stay rather than shoving the newbies with the top of the leaderboards, because if people like me get tired of getting matched with people so far beyond my skill level then the entire playerbase will drop and queue times will be longer eitherway. It's Early Access. I see that. I understand the terms of this. But this game already had a period in which it shined and that period is over. Release won't fix this. This game is dead, and the devs won't be able to fix it unless they fix the matchmaking and do some major publicity stunt to attract more players. Unless you like getting spawn-killed by the top of the game, don't even bother with this game.

Galactic Junk League has a similar building system to other popular games that give it a fun creative element when constructing spaceships. The game is a competitive player vs player style arena game with different classes each with their own abilities and attributes which provides an unique experience when combined with each player's unique creations.
Everyone in the game starts with a Rookie ship and begins relatively weak compared to other players. As one levels up upgrades become available to improve parts and attributes of the spaceships making the player more powerful. To provide you with some realistic expectations: New players will likely die and lose many matches when they first begin playing however those who stick with the game and work to level up will find the game more fun and rewarding as they grow and create bigger and more powerful ships. The community is relatively small but very good and it's easy to team up with other players and get some matches. Matchmaking can take up to a couple of minutes to get but games are fun and worth waiting for. Player have the chance to rate each other's creations while the match loads giving artistic builders a chance to make extra income when the match ends. The game does have an option to pay for cosmetics (skins) but Galactic Junk League is not a pay to win game.
I recommend this game and I like many of the mechanics of this game better than titles like Robocraft. It's a shame that many players, like some in these reviews, get frustrated when they get into Galactic Junk League because it isn't as easy and inviting as some similar titles when first starting out. For those who stick it out (get beyond level 10 in all the classes) the game becomes much more rewarding and fun to play. There is no cookie cutter meta builds dominating every match like in other similar titles because everyone builds their own creations in this game unless you choose to purchase a ship from the developers to help support the game.
If anyone ever doubts, that Games are not art, then show them this game.

DayZ indoctrinated me to the realistic shooters out there. Red Orchestra 2, while not as robust as the ArmA series, has nailed so many aspects of the gritty, unprejudiced realities of war that these soldiers had gone through. Machine guns prey on on potentially dozens of enemies if caught unaware. The sheer imbalance of close quarters and the impractibility of being in the open for even short amounts of time prove how fragile your life is. Squad tactics become important and smoke grenades, explosives, and covering fire become essential when taking objectives. Artillery can wipe out nearly all the members of a team in just once strike and seeminly good cover can prove fatal when a stray bullet pierces your helmet. When one life is so meaningless you cherish it for some reason, nobody wants to be the one to cross the machine gun nest's field of vision, or the sniper that is watching for your slightest mistake. Your life becomes valuable despite it seemingly not being so. Your participation in capturing objectives can make or break a game, however. Teamwork and leadership wins the majority of games through good squad leaders and a good team leader. Red Orchestra 2 is a realism shooter for the hardcore, but is accessible to anyone just looking for an intense, but good time.
Its not perfect. Certain angles with the prone system are abused, but this is very, very rare. Sometimes the cover system in the game messes with your ability to bandage yourself (they share a key) and you die a needless death. This is slightly less rare, but it doesn't happen often. Also against players the cover system is rarely worth it. Exiting cover in the system to shoot is often a sure way to die quickly as you expose an awful lot of your body while doing so. Melee combat is often not perfect and for some reason servers that display 50 ping in the browser sometimes gives everyone 200 ping in game. These are all very minor, however, and do not affect the game much. Its certainly less annoying than certain things in Call of Duty, Battlefield, and ArmA. Counter Strike Source (or GO) is much more polished but that is a very different game so I wouldn't compare the two.
Rising Storm, the standalone expansion (you dont need the base game to play) is like a whole new game. The large, open areas and bombed out ruins of the Eastern Front are replaced with the dense jungle of the Pacific Isles and despite some similar sized maps, the battles are closer and even more intense. It becomes even more brutal despite the absence of tanks as it becomes very clear, very quickly, the Japanese forces are at a disadvantage. The force multiplier the Allies rely on are provided by larger machine gun belts, semi-automatic rifles, powerful sub-machine guns and support weapons, and flamethrowers that can take out entire squads with a bursting swath of fiery death. This forces Japanese to abuse their mechanics of knee-mortars and banzai charges or overwhelmingly lose any given match. Often, banzai charges make the difference between a win and a loss in a match and melee combat is a much more common occurance than in RO2:HoS, further amplifying the brutality of the close quarters, unfair, Pacific Front.
Together you have two amazing takes on war that doesn't feed on its own ridiculousness or cheesy one-off matches of quick entertainment. The campaign system gives some meaning to playing on your favorite servers with your favorite communities and following the lead of a good squad leader (while contributing) is a sure way to make some fast friends. The community is very mature as kids tend to avoid the difficult learning curve of the game but once you get into it, learn the maps, the guns, and the basics of realism, it will really grow on you. Listen to the veterans and you'll stay alive.

How you come to this game will determine your experience in it.  I came into this game with a feeling of melancholy and hoping for something light to bring me back out of the depths Soma took me to.  This game was like reading a tragic novel.  It was made all the more powerful by my already riled emotions and so I think:
If you come into this looking for a 'game,' something to enjoy and walk away from, you will be disappointed.
If you come into this game ready to feel, you will feel.  However, you will not feel joy or amusement.  You will feel sadness, guilt, and futility.  You had better be ready for it.  This journey might end poorly for you.

Worth buying simply because a Tales game easily beats most of the JRPGs out there.
The story is quite neat. Each character is well-developed, but not overdone (looking at you Symphonia DoNW). Side quests have story elements which are coherent with the overarching main theme of the game.
Since combat is the main draw of the series, I would rate it good. It's better than Tales of Symphonia, but worse than Tales of Graces f.
To get it out of the way, the camera sucks. It sucks real bad when you're against a wall or in an area with trees.
However, the armatization mechanics add an interesting dimension to combat strategy. For example, you can increase the combo count or save your seraphim from KO by armatizing at the correct time.
The weaknesses mechanism is generally more straightforward than ToG. Since every seraphim represents one major element, you can simply use the correct seraphim to hit the corresponding weakness. If you also want to hit the enemy type weakness, then you'll need a bit more referencing, but no big deal. I don't think they have additional bonuses for hitting consecutive weaknesses ala ToG, but I might be wrong.
It's also less flashy as there seems to be less hi ougi available than other games in the series. Also, I find myself using less hi ougi because most of the blast gauges get used on armatization instead. It's a matter of taste, so don't take this as an entirely bad comment.
The equipment fusion mechanics has potential but is confusing and costly to optimize. It's probably easier to fuse indiscriminately with whatever you find (what I did), or ignore it altogether until the end.
If I sound too critical, it's because I'm harsh with the review. The game is good. Get it.

"Zestiria" is a mixed bag. Ultimately, it's a fine piece of work - yet it's very much a "Your Mileage May Vary" sort of experience.
In terms of the macro game (the way the whole experience builds to the conclusion), this title works beautifully. The difficulty curve is a steady slope that leads to the final, epic encounters in an entirely natural way. Getting around in the world and unlocking new areas makes perfect sense in-game. Every place you visit has some sort of recognizable, unique flavor. To be brutally frank, if the overall experience had been married to Square-Enix art, "Zestiria" would have been a great "Final Fantasy XIII."
The individual bits are where the good/ not as good balance comes in.
The combat system is basically fun, but only in smallish doses. There's supposed to be a lot of "finagly" stuff you can do, but in the end, you'll probably just find one particular, repetitive, button-mashing routine that works 95% of the time. It actually can get rather dull, and in my case, I went through a bout of falling asleep during fights. I'd nod off for a few seconds, and then reawaken to Sorey (the main character) running at nothing in particular.
The "grade" system is particularly odd. It does indeed offer an explanation of itself, yet it still remains opaque. There were battles that felt like they went very smoothly, yet awarded very little grade, and encounters that seemed a bit more fraught, but yielded high grade.
The equipment skill-sheet...thing is a nifty idea, but it ends up being overwrought, fiddly, unnecessary, and ultimately ignorable. Much is made of the equipment-fusing system, especially in light of skills, whereas the reality is that actually optimizing your results appears to mostly be a waste of time.
There's a pretty darn good story, along with lots of excellent worldbuilding, yet the pacing seems to bog down in spots. The endgame is a major example of this, where there are 2 - 3 times where you think the whole thing is going to conclude, and - nope! More walking! Here's another puzzle-dungeon! (It would have been better if, at that point, the battles were more interesting and you still had a chance for some real character progression, but that wasn't the case.) There's a point where fighting legendary creatures for high-level equipment actually manages to become completely pointless.
And the ending is a bit of a weak payoff for a 60+ hour project that encompasses world-shattering events and truly interesting characters. The dramatis personae in this game are THE strongest point, and I was disappointed in not getting a better sense of how they ended up.
But please don't get me wrong if you're seeing this as a negative review! "Zestiria" is worth the price of admission. The flaws can be easily forgiven, because the gestalt experience is very strong. The basics were gotten right; Everything else is commentary on details.

But, then I saw a blurred construct, quickly coming into sight as I moved forward. Could it be? It was, a trapper's house! I rushed in, and I was blessed with a cornucopia of supplies! Wood, food, drink and even my own gun. I quickly made a fire, ate and drank everything that I had collected and decided to have a little sleep while the fire was going in the wood stove right next to me. I woke an hour later and took a look at myself, reflecting the early moments of my life here and I realised I was going to be okay. I was still alive.
