Out of all the makers before MV hit steam it was my default engine, There is loads of content for the community to use and lots of DLC of different qualities in the store for you to enrich your game, But as expected of a niche program designed for a niche audience there are some problems or points you need to keep in mind when purchasing this product:
Making games:
+ It's fun and you get to learn to make complex systems as you keep using the engine
+ Plethora of resources made by the RPG maker community all around the internet
+ Complex systems achieved via scripts
+ Freedom of doing anything you want
- Complex systems demand you know ruby language in order to create scripts
- Only one default battle mode which is classic turn based combat as seen in the screens
- Not enough "Conditions" when you want to create specific types of events
Now onto the part you might have been interested... Selling your games:
+ Anyone can sell a RPG Maker on steam
+ You can use resources found anywhere on the internet so long as credit is given (depends sometimes)
- Default assets are a huge turn off for potential customers
- Minimal amount of scripts make you game very unlikely to sell
- 99% of people expect you to use custom made assets and sprites that no one else has
- You actually might need to dump money if you want to sell your game (sprite artist and the like)
- "RPG Maker" is generally a bad label to your product as most people tend to avoid these games
- Lots of "Shovelware" games made on store with "RPG Maker" make it hard to sell your game
Now that you know what to expect of this engine it's best advised to use it as a hobby rather than a way to earn extra coin, Sadly if you plan on selling a game you will need an artist to create custom assets for you as the community practically hates games made with official DLC or the default assets that come with the engine.
I'll be honest, I always avoid RPG Maker games in steam too except for very exceptional cases like "To the moon" and some others like "space pilgrim", If you use the default battle system prepare to be bashed as well as it has been labeled over time as "Generic" and "Boring" by the community.
The situation is the same with the official DLC, Nothing else will give you a remote chance of selling like having custom made assets no one else has... Then again any retard can RIP and use your assets without your conset with asset rippers for this engine like "RGSS decrypt" so there is that problem too...
Now the final and most important issue... The games on steam made with this engine seem to be just quick cash grab attempts leaving customers with an unfinished product and a lame game (maybe), It's just sad to see how some porn games on DLSite (also made with this engine) manage to be leagues better than what steam devs for this engine have ever done...
Now with that said you now know what you're getting into when you want to purchase this and good luck!

TL:DR If you like simulation style games and/or have ever crewed a tank: BUY THIS GAME!
It's the game I always wanted but never thought would be developed! Definitely a niche game, but if you want a realistic armor game look no further! I was a driver and gunner on the Abrams tank, so I do not have firsthand knowledge of the tanks in this game. What I do know is that the interiors are VERY well designed, and while the graphics might not be flashy they convey everything you need to shoot, move, and communicate with a tank company.
So far I've only just finished the USSR campaign in Afghanistan. This campaign has you supporting Soviet motor rifle platoons as they move to flush the Mujahadeen out of a rural area with several villages. This is made difficult due to the technology of the era, these tanks have no FLIR and more importantly no stabalization. Making this a truly challenging and rewarding endeavor, even when facing a poorly equipped enemy. I've played around with the other campaigns too, and I have to say the penetration mechanics are second to none when firing on enemy armor.
To digress this is a rich game with many well implemented systems, on the operational map you'll basically be acting as company commander for your tanks. Maneuvering them on a turn based map, which does an excellent job of painting the picture in relation to the battlefield; and also obscuring enemy units and forcing you to rely on intel and orders from (presumably) the battalion commander to execute a well coordinated attack and keep your frontline troops supplied and vehicles repaired. However, if you really wanted, you could move your units wherever you want. If you are familiar with Graviteam's other strategy games the operation portion is virtually identical, with the key difference being you will be playing the tactical portion from the perspective of the tank instead of a bird's eye view.
PROS:
-Rich and rewarding dynamic campaigns
-Thorough tutorials (which you may very well need!)

Tales of Zestiria is the first attempt at a full 3D combat system by the Tales series and it largely falls flat. The story is what you expect in a typical series, but there\'s numerous problems with the game and you\'d think that a company that has been making these types of RPGs for nearly 20 years would be learning from their mistakes. First and foremost are the controls. They haven\'t been adopted to fit the 3D style. Holding down now often means holding back, and your character runs backwards when you try to use down + attack or down + arte. Another problem with the game is that you only have 2 human characters to use at a time. One human character can only be partnered up with one of the Seraphs, spirit like beings that only some people can see. The result is that even though you have four characters in your party, you can only use two. I also hope you don't get too attached to the heroine of the game because she gets replaced halfway through.
A serious issue I had with the game is the fact that Lailah is somehow bound to not speak about the past. The emphasis of learning your own answer through a journey is important, but the fact that she withholds crucial information throughout the game makes me feel like everyone is an idiot.
Another problem with the game is that the enemies have huge amounts of super armor and invincibility frames. Super armor is when the enemy breaks your combo and become immune to stun and knockbacks for a period of time. Invincibility is when they are immune to all damage while they are performing their attack. This occurs far too frequently in the game and many enemies activate it after a fixed number of hits, automatically ending your combo, even if they are airborne at the moment. Ironically, many of your character\'s powered up transformations hit very rapidly and very quickly, allowing you to make high hit combos. The problem is that this automatically triggers the enemy\'s auto response that makes them invincibile, largely making this feature useless.
There are some massive changes in this game compared to the other ones. Levels mean nothing in this game as it only gives you additional HP and the ability to equip more Skills (you can get more of those points from finding stupid monuments in the game than leveling up though). Stats are acquired from new equipment and killing bosses, not from leveling up. They also changed Grades and Skills to be unlocked by acquiring achievements. There are hints as to what you need to do to unlock them, but it quickly becomes something tedious. For the first time there is also no dedicated healer. Instead, everyone has a bunch of small heals, nothing that is meant for the entire party. Compared to the previous installments of Tales of Xillia and Tales of Xillia 2, this game has a worse story and worse gameplay.
The only good thing about buying this game was that I received Tales of Symphonia for free because I pre-ordered a terrible game. Hopefully Tales of Bestiria will improve on the combat and the story.

Possibly the scariest game I've EVER played. Outlast, which is a journey through an insane asylum that has become a true hell on earth, is Red Barrels' pride and joy, if you want my opinion on it. If you haven't played the game, allow me to explain how its scare factor is significantly high.
Similar to games like Amnesia and SCP: Containment Breach, Outlast is a survival-horror game where you only have three options, which (as stated in the intro of the game) are as follows: run, hide, or die. While this may make Outlast seem like a sort of ripoff, there are a few major differences, the greatest being the camcorder and how it is implemented into the gameplay. Not only is the camcorder your only means of navigating the dark via infrared vision, it also gives you the ability to get info on what happened in the story by recording certain events as they happen before you. This, to me, makes Outlast stand out to the other horror games I have played.
While the game does tend to get rather repetitive at some points, what with a find a few things while avoiding homicidal enemies in the process, this is only a minor flaw that can be overlooked if you try hard enough. Story, setting, ambience, and quite a few other things make this game feel like what a found footage film should aspire to be.
What really sells this game to me are the enemies themselves. Known as the "Variants," the enemies of this game come in all shapes and sizes, quite literally. The unique Variants are the most effective means of terrifying the player, and their backstories (explained via documents found as you go through the asylum) make them even more monstrous.
If you're into scaring the pants off of yourself this Halloween (or any time of the year, really), I suggest you get Outlast. And if you have a little extra coin, put it into the Whistleblower DLC, which adds in a completely new story that ties in to the main game almost perfectly! This game is the scariest I've ever played, and I'm certain it will scare the pants off of you as well.

There isn't much out there in the way of tank sims right now, and even less if you want post-WWII tanks. Really, the only choice for that is Steel Beasts Pro, which carries a hefty price tag and has very little in the way of singleplayer content.
In walks Steel Armor: Blaze of War. SABOW is an armor sim (you aren't required to memorize startup sequences, but everything relevant to combat is simulated as accurately as it needs to be) set primarily during the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s. Iraq is equipped with the Soviet T-62, Iran has the US-produced M60A1. There are other scenarios in different periods, but they always use one of those two tanks as their player-controlled units. The game is really broken into two components: A turn based strategy segment, where the player moves around groups of men and vehicles around a large battlespace, and then a real time segment which plays out the engagements set up on the turn based map. The player is responsible, in this real time segment, for controlling units under their command to fight whatever enemy they've encountered, all while usually also commanding their own tank and tank platoon.
In the real time segment, the player can choose to occupy any position within their tank and assume the responsibilities of that crew position. Usually, though, you'll be playing as the tank commander, giving orders to your driver to move to different positions, searching for targets and then ranging them for your gunner to engage (there are no laser rangefinders in SABOW- the M60A1 has a optical coincidence rangefinder where a lens on either side of the tanks turret is focused on the target, determining its range, the T-62 has a simple stadiameter), then searching for more targets. SABOW gets across very well how difficult armored combat is without high magnification independently-traversable optics, thermal imaging systems, and precision fire control and stabilization hardware. Often times, in a tank versus tank engagement, whoever sees the other first is the one who wins, and the greatest danger to your tank are anti-tank infantry hiding in bushes with RPGs, or recoilless rifle emplacements which are only visible from range when they fire. Likewise, SABOW does a good job of conveying how horrifying it is to be in a tank under fire, hearing rounds thud off your armor plate while you desperately search for their source. Even being on the winning side is pretty horrific, watching the tank you just perforated with a sabot round creep forward for a few meters as gouts of flame pour out of its hatches, the crew climbing out while burning alive, put down by a merciful salvo from your tank's coaxial MG.
SABOW has a lot of content, if you're into this sort of thing. Dynamic campaigns, an easy to use mission generator, as well as fixed single mission scenarios. You can even try your hand at night fighting in a tank, using your horrible gen 1 night vision to try and spot targets that are within arms length of you. If you're at all a fan of semi-modern armored warfare, especially if you enjoy either of the two player tanks modeled (keep in mind the M60A1 is a base model A1- no AOS, No TIS, maybe a RISE kit but that's mostly non-combat stuff), SABOW is worth the asking price. Please buy this game to convince the devs to make more like it.

*Early Access Review*
Imagine Star Wars Battles between Frigates and Cruisers, and Destroyers, now Imagine Star trek Battles between the EnterPrise and any ship that was About its size... That is Galactic Junk League, done between groups of 4, 5 or 6 Ships that do Battle to the Death.
What Options Do you have? well, you can build a Ship from Scratch, or from Pre-existing Ship Designs, outfitting it with Lasers, Gauss guns, or Missile Launchers, adding Abilities, such as Short Hyperspace bursts, Engine Boost, and other stuff.
Oh, there is no limit as to what Shape you can build the ship in, be it starting from the other ships designs, or starting from scratch, you can even build a Flying Empire State Building, or a Guitar if you like, as long as you slap the necessary Engine thrusters, Gyroscopes, and Weapons for Attack and Defense.
So, whats the catch? yeah, theres always a catch, isnt there? well, you have a limited amount of blocks, thrusters, weapons, etc. that you can slap on, you can unlock that amount, as well as research for better parts, as you level up and earn Junk, yeah, junk (lol). So the Junk lets you research for better parts, and buy some other more advanced parts, as well as cosmetic add ons, also, from the store. Theres also some even better parts and Special Kits, and Special SHips that you can also buy with space credits, these credits are only obtainable with, you know, cash.
Keep in mind that whatever you do, whether you start from scratch, or start from another Ship you bought, you can do Whatever Shape you like, as long as you dont get to the Block Limit, haha, there is almost no limit to what you can do. You do, However, have to stick to some principles. You have a central "energy" core, that you should build around of course, as just a few shots on that thing and your ship will explode, so you should cover it as best as you can. You can leave it unprotected from one side if you like, and you are feeling insane, and want to get blown up real fast. You also have to place gyroscopes, these let the ship move in the different ways you can move it, using mouse and keyboard, just like a shooter, but in space. You also have to place Engine Thrusters, to let the ship move forward, haha. You have parts that grant abilities to your ship, if you want to add them, like a Short Hyperspace Burst, Energy Burst, or Engine Boost. Of course you have the weapons, which are of 3 types: gauss guns, lasers and missiles. With the Gauss guns, you will have to lead the target if it is moving, the lasers, just point at want you want to destroy, and missiles, point like the lasers, although, you will have to keep aiming at your opponents ship to let the missiles get there. you can also add these armor parts, or better said, you should, but you will always have this limit that you have to play with, cause you have the Hull Blocks, that make the principal body of the ship, and are used for attaching everything (weapons, abilities, thrusters, gyroscopes, etc.) so armor blocks and hull blocks are in the same group that come with a placement limit, which is called "cpu" for some reason, so you will have to see how you go there.
When you have enough Junk, and have advanced some levels, you will be able to buy more ships, ya know, to build different ones, like some wacky design you wanna try, or a really well strategically planned design, as you do have to buy ship slots if you want to build more than 4 ships, I think is the initial amount allowed. So after you selected your ship, be it anything that can fly and shoot, you will press the green play button and wait for a match. Then you will be in a team of 4, 5, or 6 ships at one side of  a map, going against the same amount of ships, that will have spawned at the other side, kind of like a deathmatch. If a ship is "killed" it will spawn after 3 seconds on the starting area and go at it again. The match lasts 5 minutes, It can be a bit short, but the maps are not that big either, but sometimes I have found myself racing to kill one last ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, when the clock reaches zero, and yeah, im screwed, so the kill count isnt too high, unless you have got to the higher levels, and have this Super Star Destroyer Type Thingy that kills anyone in sight. (grrrrrrrrrrrrr)
The maps have these different layouts, some are like over some alien terrain, others are around some SpaceSport encrusted on an asteroid or something like that, so there is this Terrain, or amount of Space Objects, where you can Hide, in a way, when shooting at the other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
So whats it like? well, the action can get quite intense, with all these lasers, bullets, missiles, and Spaceship parts flying around, and the enemy can be at some times above and below you, cause it is a totally 3D moving shooter, so at some point you could have guys shooting at you from any point imaginable.
The movement is quite decent, as long as the connection is good, you can move your spaceship forwards, backwards, turn, hover up, down, and strafe to the sides, adding more gyroscopes makes your ship turn faster or something like that, although I still dont feel like its that noticeable, maybe a bit. I still dont know how there are these guys that zoom around you as if they were on Fighters, maybe because they got to build smaller ships or something like that. Well you can, but I havent done it, haha, and the parts do have a weight characteristic, measured in tons, so it could be that... (sigh)
There are also different kinds of ships, as you have these predetermined designs, or classes, and from there you biuld or modify whatever you like or want to do with it, encouraging you to try different battling styles if you choose.
This game is a LOT of fun, But the Matchmaking definitely HAS to be improved, cause sometimes, not always, I end up in battles against these lumbering behemoths, with upgraded weapons, and special abilities i dont even know about, and I cant even get close to them before Dying after 2 or 3 blasts max. I have been able, however, to get around them, using the terrain, and shoot them from the back, making them lose their thrusters or whatever parts they chose to stick on the back, which is Hilarious.
So, the matches can definitely be improved, make more diverse maps, better matchmaking, more obstacles to get around these Super Star Destroyer Types, maybe Some Matches where you have more time, and are not racing to get that last kill, just to get counted out by that clock, dammit.
I really hope this game keeps advancing, evolving, as it is obviously an Early Access game, and Free Also! which is great, but I really hope they get to that sweet spot when it is officially released as finished and all the bugs are squatted and it is really polished, cause It can be so much fun to Build these Wacky Spaceships, to Fight against these other Wacky Spaceship designs, Its been a blast.

Wow. This is the most unique game I've ever played. Granted, I've yet to play Heavy Rain (I still have it sealed and unplayed for my PS3, which I rarely touch nowadays) and only played the demo for Beyond: Two Souls. Now that I've played Fahrenheit, I look forward to playing Heavy Rain, at the very least.
What makes it unique? For one, it's an adult game with adult situations and interactions between characters. And, no, I'm not specifically referring to the sex scenes and nudity; rather, it's how the characters behave and go about their lives within the constructs of the game. As the player, you get to control three distinct characters: Lucas Kane, the primary protagonist and unwilling participant in a ritual murder which begins the game, and two NYPD detectives on his trail. Each playable character comes alive, via both their personalities and the outstanding voice acting from the talented cast. There are numerous choices throughout, adding to a degree of branching, outcomes and replayability (either the entire game or select chapters).
The game mechanics add to the uniqueness. I recommend a controller because of the innovative implementation of interacting with the game world. For example, to open a door, you push up or down on the right stick, depending on the door and the onscreen prompts; to climb a fence, you rotate the right stick in a sort of semi-circle. In addition, much negativity has been written about the plethora of Quick Time Events (QTEs) throughout the game. However, in the context of the game, I found them to be quite acceptable, despite the fact that they broke immersion to an extent and sometimes made it difficult to focus on the action instead of the Simon-like color wheels. Initially I started on Normal difficulty, but I soon I changed to Easy to reduce the QTE difficulty in order to cut down on the frustration and be able to focus more on the story. On Easy, the QTEs were beatable on the first try 95% of the time.
The game has a very cinematic feel; in fact, the menu lists "New Movie" as opposed to "New Game." The screen is letterboxed on 16:9 displays, so you will have black bars at the top and bottom, akin to movies in the 2.35:1 aspect ratio. Also, the game utilizes split-screens to a novel effect, oftentimes showing the currently-controlled character and some impending danger. The camera angles (switchable) add to the feel of watching a primitive movie.
In terms of other elements to recommend, the excellent soundtrack features a number of well-known funk and lesser-known rock/pop tunes. The bonus section allows you to unlock the aforementioned songs as well as gallery images, movies, and sequences from both the game and extra content. One of the coolest things I've ever seen in a bonus/unlock section is the ice skating rink; it doesn't feature in the game, but had me grinning from ear-to-ear, watching the two NYPD detectives showing their respective skills on the ice.
So, very cool game and i highly recommend it -- with one important caveat: a rather large negative from my perspective is that the story goes off the rails into bizarre territory in the final act, with elements being introduced out of left field, the feel changing from supernatural suspense to something else entirely, and characters behaving completely different from their established personalities. It's not a showstopper, but it does drag the overall impression of the game down considerably. After completing the game and the achievements, I found myself replaying earlier chapters to relive the feel of the first three quarters of the game and wishing that the end lived up to what had come before.
TL; DR: Highly recommended for fans of interactive storytelling and cinematic games, but be aware of the numerous QTEs throughout (play on Easy) and that the story falters greatly in the final act.

I'm surprised by the reviews saying the game offends them by daring to suggest that gaming is futile (it doesn't, by the way) and then going on to say that most people don't understand it, and that's why they're saying it's a great game.
As both an artist and an academic, I understand this game. I'm not a game designer so I don't understand that aspect but I do play a lot of games, and always have. Based on things the author has said once you go through his personal blog it's pretty obvious what the game is about (just go to the Steam forums for this game and people have pointed it out).
From a purely narrative perspective, the over-arching story itself is crafted exceptionally well. Once you've completed the 'game', the story is framed differently in your mind and completely changes it on a second playthrough, if you feel a second playthrough is warranted. Personally, I ended up just thinking about the game, my own artistic endeavours, my need for validation and my novel I'm meant to be editing for a publisher which I put off for a long break to play this instead and then woke up to more thoughts about the game.
The game is genuinely complex and, if your life experience matches in some way the emotional path it takes you through, you'll be thinking about it for a long time. Even if it doesn't, it may strike a chord in you. Quite likely, it'll pop up in your thoughts years down the track.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. You might hate it or see it as pointless but it genuinely deserves to be bought, seen and experienced. I genuinely feel that this is the game that, if presented to Roger Ebert were he still alive, he would concede that games can indeed be Art.

I am not much into bullet hell shooters, but this one is pretty fun when you just want to unwind and play something real quick for a few minutes.
Very nice, slick controls and an excellent presentation. Visuals are very colourful and some special attacks even provide nice eye candy. The gameplay is pretty simple. You move forward, shooting down minions and then take down a boss. After 5 or so bosses, you face Chuck Norris. After that you go on fighting a new sequence of bosses but at a higher difficulty. The bosses are all based on celebrities, internet personas, and various memes. Each one has their own unique attack pattern, but that pattern doesn't change, so once you've figured out how to tackle it, you should have an easy time.
Throughout each run, you get various drops from enemies. It's either health, armour, or it can be one of the superfoods or new special moves. Superfoods provide passive bonuses such as stronger firepower, higher crit rate, or various stray shots that fire automatically at the enemies after every few seconds. The special moves take role of a powerful secondary fire that has a cooldown and you can only carry one at a time. It's well worth checking out all of them before you decide which ones suit your playing style the most.
In general, this game is not something that's likely to last you hours upon hours, but it's a pretty neat little bullet hell shooter to pass the time. Definitely worth getting on sale.

I wasted 1.5 hours of my life on this game.
Like The Stanley's Parable, this "game" is a narrative. It is designed to make you think about yourself and, for lack of a better phrase, the human condition. What made the Stanley's Parable great was a combination of factors. First off, a great narrator and dialogue. It kept you interested in the game, and the humor he offered kept you engaged during those long, empty hallways you went through. It made you forget about the boring parts of the game like that. Secondly, the options. When you chose a path, you chose it, and when you would ultimately learn what that told you about yourself, it made sense, because YOU chose it.
Now to this mess. It is completely linear. Not inherently a bad thing. You follow the narrative of the creator, also the narrator, a very uninteresting man (I think the goal was for it to be more relatable that way), through his friend's games. The problem is, with all of this, through the 90 minutes you play it, you play through EXTREMELY uninteresting landscapes, with nothing but the narrator's boring, dreary voice the whole time. The whole game I was just thinking, "Okay I'll make it through this part THEN it will be interesting." It never did.
I made it to the end of the game. But WAIT! It could be worth it if the message is just strong enough! It could tie it all together! No. Literally, (without spoiling anything), it does not share a message, but rather just tells you everything you saw in the game was wrong just for the sake of putting a spin, and then it's over. Nothing learned. Nothing gained. I just played through the game for a twist at the end so I can say, "MAN I DIDN'T SEE THAT COMING BECAUSE IT WOULD BE COMPLETELY UNINTERESTING AND CONTRIBUTE NOTHING TO MY LIFE."
In the end, the message I took from the game was "Don't judge a book by it's cover. Or it's contents. It's all wrong. Ask the author what it really means." Obviously someone's work would convey something about them or the meaning, but this tells you to do the opposite and just, not think.

The Long Dark is a newish take on the survival/horror genre; it eliminates the fantasy aspect and instead pits you against the forces of nature. You no longer have to fight off the undead or any of that gaff. No, rather than that, you are simply plopped into the most godless, inhospitable place in the known natural world...
Canada.
Below is a recalling of my first few days in the game. If you can't be bothered listening to me prattle on about that, skip to the next part and i'll go over what I thought of the game in some detail.
---
On my first playthrough, I noticed one thing right away. The game is appealingly good looking even on medium graphics, seeing as my s****y laptop strained a little too much on the high and highest graphics settings. It has that rustic sort of pencil drawn look, although that may not be your cup of tea. Second thing I noticed is that there is very little in the way of a tutorial, which I am personally okay with. No real hints are dropped on you other than you character giving off the occasional DayZ-esque winge about how cold they are, hungry they are, how dark it is, how little time they have left to live, waah waah waah. Other than your character's bellyaching, it very much just sends you into the Long Dark with a firm slap on the bottom and worryingly few words of encouragement.
I survived 1 hour and 9 seconds. Saw a wolf munching on a rabbit, thought i'd get in on the action. Lit my flare, confronted the wolf, and quickly found myself a jugular vein and a lot of blood down. Wolf 1, Khan 0.
On my second playthrough, I did a bit better. Survived for just under two days. This time dodging any and all wolves, I found my way to a railway line while lead me to a collapsed train tunnel first of all, where I got some food. Then, it led me to a little station just outside the titular subject of the map, Mystery Lake. I got comfy, lit a few fires, brewed some tea and messed about with a work bench in the downstairs area (which you can currently only do a handful of things on). The next day, I quickly discovered that I had almost nothing left in the way of food, wood or drink. So I set out across the lake - very, very slowly, as the frozen lake sounded like it was going to give in under me every step of the way - to some cabins on the other side. Looted them, then on the way back I decided i'd try my luck at ice fishing in one of the fishing huts. I fished for so long, I almost froze to death, stupidly. And while trying to tiptoe my way back to the station, some wolves must have picked up the scent of fish or the looming essence of imminent death around me, and they took me down.
Third playthrough was the best yet. Similar strategy, only this time I looted a hill-top logging outpost, made my base in a trappers camp and survived for a good few days on a frozen deer carcass and what I could catch in some snares. Eventually, I set off to explore the map and find more wood. I came to a dam, and immediately went inside, frozen and tired, only to be blindsided by a wolf. I seemed to win our little skirmish, and he ran off bleeding down the stairs. I patched myself up, and spent the rest of the night looting the upstairs area while the injured wolf occasionally attempted to creep up on me, only to be scared away by my lantern. I slept for a while in my bedroll, then found the wolf had expired during the night from it's wounds. Of course, I skinned, gutted and butchered him then ate his liver with some dog food and a nice granola bar (fff-fff-fff-fff). I even found a hunting rifle down there, which made me and my 30 something useless bullets very happy. In the morning, I ventured outside, encumbered and eager to try out my new rifle. Lucky me, a wolf was happy enough to help me with the latter. I shot him, but he just kept coming. After wrestling him off of me, he tried to run off but bled out. Now even more injured, I carried on homewards, only to be jumped again. I got a shot off, but he did me some major damage and got away. I was able to stop the bleeding when I was at just 1% condition. My vision was now hazy, shaking and disoriented, but I knew if I just kept to the tracks i'd get home in time before the cold got me. Needless to say, I lost the tracks in the snow thanks to the muddled vision, and I froze to death in the middle of the woods.
---
I should state that the recommendation for the game at this point was a narrowly earned one. Not due to any fault in the game, instead owing to the fact the game is rather barebones at this time in the way of features or shiny bells and whistles to keep you coming back to it after one good, long run. That being said, the game does well with what little it has. If cash is a deciding factor in this for you, then you want to keep your wallet in your pocket until the game makes some more progress.
The map has a real feeling of emptiness and I feel the survival mechanics hit what the developers were going for right on the head, giving everything a more real, desperate feel. There are a few things which keep you scared and on your toes despite the absence of much substance. Wolves, for one, and the occasional corpse you find hidden away in a corner. You'll even become scared of the wind after a while, once you feel the cold for the first time.
The lack of help may put some players off. It took me until late on in my third attempt to discover the tab menu - a pretty important aspect of the game. Other than that, the game is pretty easy to figure out.
I'd definitely say give the game a go. I have no doubt that once the story mode is complete and the maps are either expanded on or more features are added to the game (i'd like to say basebuilding and more creatures for a start) then the game will have a definite replay factor. Until then, we're singing the early-alpha blues.
tl;dr - Captures the atmosphere really well, throws you in at the deep end, easy to learn, although barebones at the current time.
(And for those keeping score, that's Wolves 3 - Khan 2)

As someone with over 600 hours in Tales of the Abyss and 800 on Vesperia, I like to think of myself as a "Tales of" fan. I've seen playthroughs of Xillia/2 & Graces. I really like most of the characters the Tales of series has presented throughout its many stories.
Some of those games do have "cliche" stories, but the saving grace for them all are the characters, the many side quests get you involved with them and their quirks, as you see them develop their individual personalities. By the end of the game, these characters feel fully fleshed out and you care for them. This, did not happen in Zestiria for me, at all.
Now when it comes to Zestiria, the story is so boring an uninspiring I could just not care less about it. But I kept playing because I know "Tales of" and I kept thinking something big is bound to happen, some character is likely to be hiding a big twist for the story..well, that never happened.
The characters, oh boy, I can't believe it myself but there is literally only one character I like in this game and that is simply because she's my "type" (Edna) as I love sarcastic/ironic characters. I could not care less about any of the rest of the cast, they are so boring and bland, lacking that special something that all other Tales Of characters have.
The camera during combat is awful, yes you can work around this problem by "luring" enemies into open room before engaging in combat, however, most of the dungeons have long thin corridors where monsters spawn randomly, making them hard to avoid.
The gear, what where they thinking? I know they tried to innovate by trying something different, well, it did not work, gearing the characters is so annoying, having to take into accound all the special effects in each piece of gear instead of going the tradition way. Hell, they even made it so that character levels mean pretty much nothing at all.
Another change they were super eager about was the new "Open world". That was such a bad idea, open world doesnt automatically make a game "better", this is clearly seen in Zestiria, the maps are huge, literally huge, the problem is, theres nothing on them at all save for a few monsters and some random chests.
I bought this game the day it came out, and I havent finished it yet, thats how much I care about this cast and this story. The game felt like a chore, I was not having fun while playing as I did in pretty much every previous Tales of games.
Edit: I finally finished the game, however, my opinion did not change at all, boring, bland and uninspiring story and cast of characters.

Summary:
It's a fun game. However, I wouldn't say there's anything special about it. As a Tales game, it's probably one of the weaker ones. What I liked was that it was surprisingly dark. Children die, often the only redemption possible for people is through death, light doesn't triumph over dark, and humanity is generally awful. It makes for a really nice change. So, if you like JRPGs and the Tales series you will probably like this. It also has puns. The sheer amount they manage to fit in should be commended.
Detailed:
The overarching plot is very simple, a village boy leaves home for the first time and is later tasked with defeating the Big Bad, which is done through trials to get the power necessary. Where this game shines is in its characters. Maybe due to the game's battle mechanics, but every character feels necessary. They also have unique personalities and their personal stories are explored throughout the game. The voice acting is decent and you really learn to love the characters. However if you play with English audio you'll frequently notice the character will stop talking but their sprite's mouth keeps moving for a good five seconds, which can be annoying.
The battle system can be pretty complicated at first, but it's very smooth once you get used to it. The new enemies are called 'hellions' and your job is to purify them (which gameplay-wise is just defeat them). There's the usual fire, water, earth, wind strong/weak system, but the hellions also have their own categories to consider. For example, a hellion might be a beast type, and you can get equipment which is more effective against beasts. The unique battle system here is 'Armatisation', where you combine with another person to get more HP and special powers. Combat can be challenging as often you can't just hack and slash your way through battles. but the amazing invention of the quick step (back step, front step and side step) make them feel fun.
The worst part of combat is the camera. Sometimes, it's a real ♥♥♥♥♥.
If you're not smart, like me, the equipment system is very complicated. The basics are given to you, but its only through skits a lot of the information explained. To put it simply, one piece of equipment can have a maximum of 4 skills on it. You fuse equipment together to make it stronger and get better/different skills. By doing so, you can comfortably take on enemies which are 5-10 levels higher than you. There's also another dynamic, all about bonus skills which comes from E-Unions and links and other nonsense, but you don't need to know it well to play the game. Just randomly fusing everything together works well enough.
If you like skits, this game does have them, but they're only viewable in certain places and it's quite easy to miss some. My advice is to frequently stay at inns.
Regarding the New Game+, the best thing to do to is to make sure your Lords of the Lands are at the highest level you can be bothered to get them to. Their level affects how many points you get at the end of the game, which affects what bonus things you get in New Game+. However, there is a lot of replayability in this game, like all Tales, as you get bonus dungeons and bosses.
As this game isn't as popular as the others, if you encounter any problems you will often struggle to find a solution and wind up having to work it out yourself. For example, I accidentally activated local co-op (which is only in battle) but I had no idea how I'd done it and there was no support anywhere which told me how to turn it on, let alone turn it off (FYI, you have to change whether their moves are auto, semi-auto or manual in the artes menu).
Otherwise, it's okay.

Wow, just wow. Man, seriously. Wow. That is pretty much all I can say about this games. If you've ever played the Graviteam games, you know these guys are Ukranians, and you know that they are all about tanks. People are saying these days that devs really don't have a heart for what they do and that devs aren't very Ukranian, but those people are stupid and this game is great.
When I was growing up my dad used to read me field manuals to put me to sleep after I had a big poop, and I have got to say that those experiences really primed me for this game. Everything tanks do is modeled in this game. A lot of people say that other games have tanks and that those tanks can get shot in the transmission and jack up their wheel houses and that's a bunch of crap. Wow. This is the most unique game I've ever played. Granted, I've yet to play Heavy Rain (I still have it sealed and unplayed for my PS3, which I rarely touch nowadays) and only played the demo for Beyond: Two Souls. Now that I've played Fahrenheit, I look forward to playing Heavy Rain, at the very least.
What makes it unique? For one, it's an adult game with adult situations and interactions between characters. And, no, I'm not specifically referring to the sex scenes and nudity; rather, it's how the characters behave and go about their lives within the constructs of the game. As the player, you get to control three distinct characters: Lucas Kane, the primary protagonist and unwilling participant in a ritual murder which begins the game, and two NYPD detectives on his trail. Each playable character comes alive, via both their personalities and the outstanding voice acting from the talented cast. There are numerous choices throughout, adding to a degree of branching, outcomes and replayability (either the entire game or select chapters).
The game mechanics add to the uniqueness. I recommend a controller because of the innovative implementation of interacting with the game world. For example, to open a door, you push up or down on the right stick, depending on the door and the onscreen prompts; to climb a fence, you rotate the right stick in a sort of semi-circle. In addition, much negativity has been written about the plethora of Quick Time Events (QTEs) throughout the game. However, in the context of the game, I found them to be quite acceptable, despite the fact that they broke immersion to an extent and sometimes made it difficult to focus on the action instead of the Simon-like color wheels. Initially I started on Normal difficulty, but I soon I changed to Easy to reduce the QTE difficulty in order to cut down on the frustration and be able to focus more on the story. On Easy, the QTEs were beatable on the first try 95% of the time.
The game has a very cinematic feel; in fact, the menu lists "New Movie" as opposed to "New Game." The screen is letterboxed on 16:9 displays, so you will have black bars at the top and bottom, akin to movies in the 2.35:1 aspect ratio. Also, the game utilizes split-screens to a novel effect, oftentimes showing the currently-controlled character and some impending danger. The camera angles (switchable) add to the feel of watching a primitive movie.
In terms of other elements to recommend, the excellent soundtrack features a number of well-known funk and lesser-known rock/pop tunes. The bonus section allows you to unlock the aforementioned songs as well as gallery images, movies, and sequences from both the game and extra content. One of the coolest things I've ever seen in a bonus/unlock section is the ice skating rink; it doesn't feature in the game, but had me grinning from ear-to-ear, watching the two NYPD detectives showing their respective skills on the ice.
So, very cool game and i highly recommend it -- with one important caveat: a rather large negative from my perspective is that the story goes off the rails into bizarre territory in the final act, with elements being introduced out of left field, the feel changing from supernatural suspense to something else entirely, and characters behaving completely different from their established personalities. It's not a showstopper, but it does drag the overall impression of the game down considerably. After completing the game and the achievements, I found myself replaying earlier chapters to relive the feel of the first three quarters of the game and wishing that the end lived up to what had come before.
TL; DR: Highly recommended for fans of interactive storytelling and cinematic games, but be aware of the numerous QTEs throughout (play on Easy) and that the story falters greatly in the final act.

Subjectively:

Okay, so I have mixed feelings about this game.
On one hand, it's old and it's still QuanticDream, so you can forgive many things. But not the controls and not the camera! Man! No swear words are enough for those. I saw that the game supported a controller, but hey, I'm just a regular PC gamer with my keys & mouse for playing. Playing this game was really a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Good thing that there are almost no episodes where you have to run somewhere and do stuff super quick, otherwise you'd be screwed. The fighting & mini-games keyboard sequences weren't as bad as I thought at first, I even started enjoying them because I always won, but of course they'd be a lot better with a joystick. Then, the episodes with breathing/balancing exercises... UGH, when you have to  be constantly watching and pressing the arrows, looking around and walking at the same time! I mean, really, ugh.
As for the story: I see now why so many people talk about the great beginning and a so-so end. I liked the first chapters, especially the ability to switch between characters. The characters were nice, too, until by the end of the game they started behaving in a really weird manner. *Spoiler alert* I mean, detective Carla spent all her time aggressively hunting a violent murderer, then suddenly she's shaking hands with the now-dead figutive and the next thing you know she's confessing her love to him, having sex and carrying his Indigo baby. I mean... *End of spoiler alert* I also think the developers just tried to squeeze too much into one story, and it didn't fit in smoothly. But hey, it was still fun.
So yeah, the game wasn't always logical. But I think it's worth playing just as we watch old movies. The music is nice, too. Fahrenheit has many features Quantic developed in their further games, and there are lots of references, which I liked. Nothing beats Heavy Rain, though - which is basically Fahrenheit without any things paranormal (but with weird things AI),  some scenes there basically copy Fahrenheit. But it's much better written and made - and runs only on consoles, alas...

Quick review -> imagine robocraft, but instead of "vehicle types" defined by the blocks you use, there are "ship-classes" that you pre-select.  Each class effects the communal block stats differently, in addition to providing class-specific blocks.
So, like if robocraft and team-fortress had a baby.
It's fun, addictive, and due to the class system, requires some teamwork, which I appreciate (beware though, there's still people that play lone-wolf style, diving headlong into a full team)
Cons -
- purchasing system is whack currently, very little that can be purchased with in-game earned currency, but, on the other hand, most of the stuff thats available for purchase with real-cash is just aesthetic so its not pay2win (although, you Can drop $11 for a 30-day xp/junk booster, which is a great deal, and the only thing i'd spend money on if you were the type to do so)
- you start out with a "rookie ship" (a fifth class) which is junk, i don't know why you have to earn access to the main classes, except maybe to teach new kids that its "dangerous to go alone".   It's a little bit of a hassle to get to lvl 10 to unlock the full classes, personally should be lvl 5 access.  (this rookie ship is responsible for most of the negative reviews, new kids getting junked in every match, rage-quiting, not realizing that the real game unlocks at lvl 10)
Pros-
-balance is better than it was, and the player-base is learning how to properly counter some of the slightly less balanced tactics (teamwork).
-game play is fun, addictive, and rewarding (if you dont go lonewolf)
-not pay2win, as skill/teamwork/tactis is the name of the game here, though ten bucks does get you a long♥♥♥♥♥xp booster pass.
summary -> for a free game, its the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I think it could be better than robocraft in time.  beware the rookie ship, hunker down and get to lvl 10 before reviewing

This really and truly does belong to the "Walking Simulator" genre in spite of whatever praise it may receive. I'm not saying that it does not deserve most of the praise it receives, but you really ought to know that this is an entirely linear narrative experience where the player's choices are irrelevant except as a means to fully explore the idea of each of the game's levels.
You can't not compare this game to the Stanley Parable, so let me make the differences between the two distinct. Despite obstinately declaring itself a game where choices do not matter across its narrative, the Stanley Parable is recognizable as a type of puzzle game where the player's choices lead to new explorations and discoveries of new branches in the narrative's path.
The Beginner's Guide is not a different type of game masquerading as a narrative game. It's thoroughly a narrative game. It is an entirely self-indulgent narrative, totally aware of its self-indulgence. Whereas lesser "walking simulators" can feel as though they may as well just have been entirely cinematic, however, this is one of those narratives which could not be told in any other format. I did feel a little brow-beaten by the message of the narrative at a couple of points, and frankly any sophistry about this being a game for intelligent people is lusciously ironic. The message is simple. That's why it works. It's not a narrative to appeal to some kind of intellectual elite. It's a narrative to appeal to people who find some deeply compelling meaning in thinking about themselves and others.
It's worth the price of admission for anyone who fits that description. If you are looking for something like a fun way to pass time, this would not be my first choice of a game.

received this game as a gift, although I already had an interest in it. The Long Dark is beautiful in its presentation of the beauty and deadliness of winter/snow hell. I liked this game because it is very brutal to the player in its medium difficulty (I haven't mustered the courage to go for hard), and it is extremely intense when death is near or wildlife is chasing you. The usual lack of basic necessity such as warmth, food, drink and protection from the cold/wildlife will usually always get you killed. This is not the only thing that will get you killed though, lack of thought and calculation will lead you off of cliffs and onto thin ice. The learning curve on this is not so difficult for those who are familiar with slower game play and having to calculate moves like a chess game, since most things require sacrifice and trade.
I would recommend this to someone who is ready to invest a considerable amount of time into actually learning how to be good at this game. If you prefer to point and shoot at things in a very fast paced style, I would not recommend this game to you.
That being said: the more support behind this game there is, the better the finished product (I hope) will be. Do not sleep on this one.

Wow. Now I see why I dropped this game so many years ago.
Don't expect your controller to work. As far as I can tell, there's no real way to rebind your keys properly, even with the config hidden in the game's files rather than in the game's in-game menus.
That aside, the actual controls are abysmal. The jumping, the backdash, the dash, the attacking. Almost every control is halfway designed to do things beyond your actual control. Jumping maintains its velocity if you let go, instead of stopping you, so you're going to unintentially jump into many things. Attacking stops you in place, which feels terrible against fast moving bosses. You can perform a backwards dash by crouching and pressing jump, which feels extremely out of place and also useless. The actual dash you unlock feels super slippery upon activation. You are able to shoot in 8 directions, but if you want to actually turn around to shoot behind you, you have to stop shooting, and then turn around, as you can only really move between half of those directions in the direction you are facing.
The first boss you come across, which you come across fairly quickly only a few steps outside of the start of the game, definitely doesn't feel like one you're really prepared to fight at all - that is if you end up going their without the sword. With the basic projectile weapon you start with, it's a much harder battle as you'll have a tough time hitting the boss at all, and you can't destroy her projectiles to avoid them. With the sword, those projectiles are destroyed in one hit, and the boss is plain easier to hit by the sword.
This is why I initially quit the game from the start, because that boss seemed way too difficult. I randomly decided to go back to this game after years, and randomly found out that I can obtain new weapon drops randomly, and managed to get a sword to fight her with.
After trying to fight her with the starting weapon, I thought that maybe I wasn't supposed to fight her yet, and that I was actually intended to go explore and find other stuff and power up. But as far as I can tell, there was nothing else I could get to in the surrounding area and this boss was it.
In any case, after being frustrated by yet another game that doesn't even allow proper binding of its basic controls, frustrated by very poor control physics, and a very poorly orchestrated lead into the first boss, I can't say I recommend this game.

Sandbox Mode Review
Ok, so I've only ever written one review before this. That was for a CD on Amazon. (Lindsey Stirling if you must know).
I've been playing this game for some time now and it never fails to amaze me how much effort Hinterland Studios have put into this game, especially considering it's still in Alpha!
As stated on the store page, this is early access. So there is still content missing that will be in final release. There is another region to be added as well as story mode which I am thorougly excited for! Because of this, this review is of Sandbox mode only.
On to the review!
The Menu System
This for me has always been very accessible. After seeing some very early menus from watching older videos on YouTube they have definitely made some good changes. As it is now, it's brilliant! The first aid screen in particular is pretty cool.
I find it very handy that you can sort each section of the inventory by condition, name or weight. Very handy when you want to get rid of something weighing you down or checking on condition of food.
The Graphics
While not to everyones taste, I find the graphics stunning. Very refreshing art style. Not cel shaded but not "photo realistic" either. Catching a glimpse of the sky when it's sunset is always amazing. The wild life is also very well designed and implemented. Even if wolves are the bane of my existence. *Shakes fist*
The Gameplay
My god, this game is incredible. There is rarely a moment where you can relax. There is always something. Lack of food, lack of warmth, no weapons or tools, wolves prowling and out for blood... it just doesn't stop. My best run I managed 12 days. Each time I kick the bucket I just want to start again. The atmosphere of this game is amazing.
The Sound
The sounds in The Long Dark are spot on. Great wind sound effects, wolves when howling sound perfect and even the sound of checking through a cupboard or draw sound realistic. Great job all round from the sound department.
Overall
HIGHLY recommended. Something a little different from the usual survival games. After watching a couple friends playing this game on their YouTube channels (RentAHero & Dzaran), I just had to get it. I don't normally invest in early access games but this one I am glad to of made an exception for. One of the best survival experiences I've had in my 20+ years of gaming. Even though there is only Sandbox mode available at the moment, that's still enough to keep you playing and coming back for more especially with the number of updates Hinterland Studios makes! Bring on the story!

In a Nutshell: Excellent game engine that's easy-to-learn and easy-to-use, you'll make your first game in no time at all.
Pros:
- It really is simple enough for a kid to learn, no really, I made an experimental game in about 30 minutes, I'd say you will probably take a good 2 hours to figure out enough to make something good but it absolutely is easier to make a game in this than say, Unreal Engine (which I would not recommend unless you've already made a couple games already).
- Runs on just about any computer, I'm easily making games on a cheap Lenovo G580 with bare-bones specs, if my laptop can run this, any computer can (ok, a Commodore 64 won't be able to... but still)
- If 2D RPG games like on the NES or SNES is your thing, this engine will most certainly be worth every penny.
Cons:
- You are limited to only RPG games, that said, if that's what you want to make this isn't really a con.
- Limited graphical capabilities, I think just about anyone is able to read the description but this engine is pretty bare-bones, this engine is DESIGNED for beginners, thus, if you're already experienced and you're looking for something that won't limit your game design skills compared to whatever you had before, don't buy this, buy something like Unreal Engine which is made for more experienced developers.
Overall this is well worth the money, because it's perfect for a beginner or someone who has no skill of any kind in developing a game, sure it might take 1-2 hours of tutorials on youtube to figure stuff out, but it's most certainly easy to use after that.

I started writing this as a response to someone who said "Do not buy this software" and it got really long so I wanted to use it as my review of RPG Maker VX Ace. Keep in mind the way I wrote and worded this was intended to be directed at someone telling people not to buy this software, so if you're wondering if you should and have seen some negative reviews I hope this changed your mind. Keep in mind, RPG Maker is for people who are willing to put a solid effort into what it is they are creating.
You know, the beauty of RPG maker is you can create your own sprites and tilesets free of charge! What rpg maker does is provides you with DLCs with various community made resources that you can use in your commercial games! That literally means people put hard work and effort into creating images that you can then use and profit off of! It's pretty great, and to have so many to choose from at reasonable prices (when on sale) you can't really go wrong. So in the aspect assets, tilesets etc. the world is really endless as long as you have the creative power. That being said not all of us are super talented digital artists and just want to piece together a game but not draw out every little thing, well those DLCs are just perfect for that. The base game comes with very limited tilesets (a free dlc has a few more good stuff) and honestly a little re colour or touch up of the free tilesets and you can create new ones quite easily. I'm doing a modern story and was having trouble with how retro and final fantasy every tileset looked, a quick little touch up in an art program and i've recreated my own tileset.
The making of the game and the time that goes into it is A LOT, but it's also quite enjoyable along the way. I am brand new to the game development world, but grasping how RPG maker works isn't too much of an effort. The menus and stuff are very simplistic and thankfully when you want to create more elaborate scenarios there's a huge group of people on the internet to help each step of the way. RPG maker makes creating games easier and more accessible for people who don't have degrees and is all in all an amazing experience. Plus, VX ACE being on sale for $7, that's a down right steal.

Updated review 1/14/17:
I would like to take a moment to update my review that was really close-minded.  I would like to say that I DO recommned this software if you want to get a start to developing games, as it is very good at giving you the basics, just look up some tutorials if you are lost, yes, I just said that, even though I criticizied the idea of having to spend hours of my time doing so in my old review.  Let me make myself clear, as I am now more attuned to how video game development works, yes, it is difficult, yes, it is time consuming, which is why we see independent game developers take years upon years to finish games that we want to see.  Some things that I didn't realize are how much time it takes to do the simplest of things when developing games or even more basic programs.  The assets that you are given to start out may be basic, but they took time and effort for someone to create, you didn't make these things, someone else had to give them to you for you to be able to even start.  While I have only made part of a very simple text-based game as of writing this review update, I can definitely see that I was wrong to say a lot of things that I did in my previous review.  Making even basic visuals and sound take time and effort, something I thought was easier done than it really was.  While I still am not an RPG guy, please, take a chance, get this when it goes on sale, get some experience, do something I didn't do.  Make games to the best of your ability with what you are given, and if that doesn't satisfy you, create something new to use.  The true power of making games comes from the amount of effort you are willing to put into them.
Old review (don't even bother, it's just a lot of complaining):
I got this game on sale at the very beginning of this year, when I wanted to experiment with making games and thought it would be a good idea, however, the base software comes with the most minimalistic assets and MAKES you pay for everything else.  I would definately not recommend purchasing any of the RPG Makers if you don't have a great interest in RPGs or want to become a profressional RPG developer, and especially don't buy these pieces of software at full price, it's not at all worth it.  I wouldn't even recommend buying it on sale either, unless you are what I mentioned above, not unless you have over one thousand dollars to pay for every single asset.  I realized my calling was not to make RPGs until it was too late, so please, really consider this purchase, if you are not a fan of RPGs or making games in general, DO NOT buy this software or any other software in the lineup and really don't buy any of the expansions.  These softwares are for people who have at least some experience in how programming works, because if you don't understand how games work internally then you are going to have a massively large time being confused or looking at tutorials.  I am going to school to learn how to program and trust me, it is very a long, complicated and precise process.  The tagline of there being no programming required may be true to an extent, but there are still many instances you'll be confused because your game isn't working right.  Games take time to make, and I learned that the hard way.  So please, really think about what you want to do with your time in game creation and with your money.

I think it's important to keep in mind two things.  1. it's an Early access game, and 2. It's FTP.  The FTP aspect (in the way it tries to get you to buy premium Currency) is actually pretty good.  Prices for the the stuff that helps you level is fine, though the price for the visual stuff is kinda high.  And there tends to be a code or two floating around that gives out some of the level boosting stuff.
The ship building is relaxing and figuring out how to put things together to cover all your important bits, and have your weapons be effective.  Doing it all to cater to how you play is pretty fun and having a good ship design is rewarding.
The gameplay is pretty wonky though, there's a meta that's hevily used and tends to be annoying.  There's also matches where you'll get steam rolled no matter what (whether you're a low level rookie just doing what you can, or a high level player doing your very best).  The steam rolling tends to be connected to who has the side with the most meta abusers on it.  Though such games are in a minority.  But it feels great when you do wipe them out, even if it took 5 deaths to do it.
By and large the people tend to be polite (people ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the meta like I'm to do and random trolls do crop up though.  It's an online game after all).
Starting out might be rough, and starting entails getting the Rookie ship to Level 10 and another ship class to level 10.  But by then you'll either have a good enough grasp on it and be able to enjoy it, or burn out.  Still takes a bit for that to all happen though.  And again, it's free.

Dungeon Defenders II is pretty fun. It has a lot of the features of the old game with soem improvements, and it as some that are downgrades.
Keep in mind that this is supposed to be "Early Access" as it is still in Alpha. It is up to us to take to the forums at
in order to suggest improvements to the game, report bugs, and ultimately to help them make the game one small bit of influence at a time.
Simply walking into an early access game like this and then leaving because you did not like it is a huge waste if you can help to make it better.
Some of the worst I can think of though mainly have to do with the cosmetic system which was poorly executed. It is presented as if there are many cosmetic slots, but you cannot mix and match pieces between the various costumes you can buy in the game, so there is very little point in getting more than one per character (except in the likely F2P even they release.
One of the best things so far is that completing levels of the campaign and doing Onslaught mode or Boss fights really feels like a Dungeon Defenders game. You build. You fight. You protect objectives that are more different and interactive than the crystal that was a very simple binary win condition. Sometimes you need to stop alternate lanes from opening. Sometimes you need to protect the giant hermit crab with a shell-moutned cannon who is protecting your defenses while you protect the "core" of the level. It starts off a lot like how you started off in Dungeon Defenders 1 with a progression system that is nearly 1:1 like the old game, but with new features. Like the old game I keep wanting to go back in and do "one more level".
Every aspect of the game feels rough around the edges, but that is why I am recommending it. It needs improvement so paly it a bit and tell the developers what you think could make it better.

Brought the game yesterday and have played 7 hours of it. I'll give you all the pros and cons based on ratings out of 10 Note: I'm writing on my mobile.
- Art: the art style on the characters are on point. I believe that some textures on walls could be updated though. 6/10
- Combat: this is a hard one, the combat is extremely confusing as there's so many different buttons to press. It's also good that you have to learn combos as most of the time button mashing deals little to no damage. The main problems is the awful camera controls. You have to keep pressing the RB (if using 360 controller) to lock onto the nearest target otherwise it looks a mess. 6/10
Cosmetics: they're pretty funny. You're allowed a suit and a hat as your main outfit then you can have accessories to go on top of the outfit such as wings etc. There's a lot of cosmetics from DLCs and by looting from chests. 8/10
Armour: this is probably the most disappointing part, the armour doesn't display on your character. Bummer. All armour is basically the same name with a different prefix. 'Old' to 'Amber' etc. The armour at beginning game doesn't do a lot, I haven't progressed far enough to see if it's better at late game. 4/10
World: The world is extremely large but this games world reminds me of a game called last revenant where it's all instanced, the instances are very large though. The world's can be very bland with a few scattered chests and trees but sometimes they can be very beautiful with castles etc. The dungeons are all different but are still all extremely empty. 6/10
Enemies: There's a massive variety of enemies, from large bosses to small animals. All have their own attack patterns, weaknesses, strengths. 8.5/10
Cutscenes: there's two different types of cutscenes, one of them is from in-game and the other is the classic anime style. I can tell you now there's LOADS of cutscenes, almost around every corner, they are all skip panel though. They don't bother me too much as its a story game. The cutscenes art is glorious, sometimes the in-game cutscenes can be buggy. 6/10
FPS: it's at 30, a very noticeable 30, there's already a fix for this. -/10
Professions: there's not really any professions in the game, you can choose a small selection of what you can do but it does everything automatically. 2/10
Exploration: Not a whole lot of exploring, the lands are very similar. 4/10
Replay value: this depends, if you enjoy these games it can have an extremely high replay value. I can't see myself making more than one character. 7/10
Saving: strange, there's saving points scattered on the map yet you can go in the menu and select quick save. The save is also not done by characters but by overall, so if you made s new game it would overwrite the previous save. 5/10
Story: It's very generic and here's the rundown 'guy takes sword from the stone, finds then kills a guy'. There's a lot of background story and lots of elements so I make sure I watch every cutscenes. It might be generic but it's very manipulative. 6/10.
Upgrading: to upgrade you have to either play with your equipment and it upgrades overtime or you can take it to a blacksmith and combine it with the same type of clothing. No weapon customisation. 4/10.

This game was on my wishlist for a while due to the good reviews so when the Summer Sale came it was on a very good discount and I snatched it, praise our Lord Gaben!
Now, I haven't fully explored the game. On the contrary, I have just 10 hours of it on easy mode, but I get why people wrote so much nice stuff about it.
Unlike other town-simulation games where you just reach a point when you can build tons of houses or whatever and massively grow your town till you die of boredom, this game is a bit different.
You have to always worry about food production, clothes, tools and pretty much managing everything else. If you increase too much the production of a certain item you can disrupt the production balance and find yourself with a lack of something else in the next winter. If you grow too much your population, be careful because it isn't that simple (the Hapiness/Health indicators and the "what is he doing" are a good start to a Sim-like panel!^^)
And as I mentioned I played only on easymode so the worst I faced was some dude with Influenza (luckily I had a "hospital" and the dude just went there and got cured), but reading through some reviews I realize that there are many more disasters that can threaten your small town at any given moment, this makes the game more interesting and challenging
Managing who does what job is also interesting: you literally have to decrease the number of workers in certains jobs to be able to make others be sucessful, and you ALWAYS have to do this there will be people dieing and having kids is not THAT fast. I guess that there isn't much realism, at least nowadays constantly reassigning workers is frowned upon, but back then it was necessary. However, there is no drawback, maybe there should be like an expertise system (in-game, a school makes someone an expert at everything :P)
The trading mechanism is also interesting, you have to buy seeds to be able to grow certain things in your lands (even chickens!), obviously at a high price, although there's not THAT much variety and once you unlock everything the trading post becomes a bit irrelevant unless you are a greedy dude (oh, there's no money, so everything is by direct exchanges). The trader only comes from time to time (and there are different traders), so that's even more interesting
Oh, and roads are not really necessary (except for speed), people can walk in the wilderness, neat
The minor faults are imo:
- There's no upgrading system, you can only upgrade roads into stone roads, and wooden houses must be destroyed to make rooms for stone houses (realistic, so no complaints here)
- Knowing if your workers have a gathering mission on an inacessible place (like across a river) and are therefore stuck on that task (I've caught guys "Idling" when there was work to be done -.-) is not easy so you can cancel that pointless task
For the future, as some said a night cycle would be interesting, but I would really like other ages (not like the medieval mod, ALL of them in the same game), although that would be hard to implement (not because of the game engine - that seems to be very flexible as proven by all the SteamWorkshop contributions - but because time passing is not like in the Total War titles, reaching 50 years is already an acomplishment), maybe it could work with Tecnologies?

An exercise in futility regarding the existential crises of humanity and ones deeply personal want for purpose within a given system.
At first I wanted to ignore this game until I saw Ken Levine and Peter Molyneux speaking to each other over twitter about it. Two of my favorite game developers.
I wish there were an option for giving this a sideways thumb as I can't easily recommend my experience with this game and it is a game. I'm not about to have that argument. But its.. lacking. I feel personally, that these things have been said before.
Now, is this game art? Are games art? I don't care, I'm not here to tell you that. What I can tell you is that this is an interactive guide though some builds of games that “coda” made while a narrator explains what the build is, what it was and what his own interpretations of why design choice “X” was made over design choice “Y”
Its hard to explain; and despite what you've likely heard. While it does not make sense on its face, around the 1 hour mark I felt I had an understanding of what the narrator was trying to convey. At least, to my satisfaction. In short, being creative... as well as existing derives its meaning from those who give it meaning. There is no external force pushing you forward, there is only you and your decisions living in the now, the present.
Why is that there? Ask 10 different people and its likely you'll get 10 different responses.
Its a reflection piece summed up best in a quote from BioShock 2 (which I know Ken Levine had nothing if very little to do with BioShock 2 forgive me) made by the character Eleanor Lamb
“Love is just a chemical, we give it meaning by choice”

On my way home, I became exhausted due to the distance, overencumbered by my basic load, continued starving and suffered a sprained ankle while climbing a small hill in order to dodge a rabid wolf. BUT LO, I had arrived and all would be well. I quickly cooked up my meat, ate it and settled in for a well deserved nap.
I wake up. It's 1 am. I have 5 calories remaining and my hunger and thirst are through the roof. I decide I need to forage in the night. I take my flares out, hoping the wolves will stay at bay as I fitfully wander the forest, praying for a frozen deer to pop up in the darkness. Barking... barking in the deep. I spin around - 3 pairs of green eyes surround me. I quickly charge them one by one, chasing them away with my light. I breathe a sigh of relief and decide to sprint back to the safety of the tower. Suddenly, one of the ballsier ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s attacks me from the front again, unafraid of my flare's light. We battle in the snow, but I come out victorious, although wounded. As I limp up the hill, I hear the wolves' barks receding. I WILL MAKE IT. I WILL SURVIVE. As I near the top of the hill, barking suddenly comes out of nowhere once again and a wolf mauls me to death on my doorstep.
TLDR: 10/10 Would get all my hopes and dreams destroyed by a single wolf again.
