Freebie is an arcade game where you have to release a ball from the top left or bottom right corner of a square to bounce it from a rotating paddle to the green light.
The game uses no bgm by default. You can enable the bgm by pressing Track 01, Track 02, or Track 03 in the main menu to bring up some retro bgms. The game itself has some sfxs when you're releasing a ball, when the ball hit a green light, and when the ball hit a red light.
The main menu confuses me a lot with tons of information in it. Although there are a lot of informations in the main menu, the mouse instruction isn't clear enough. It's written that you can launch a ball with a left click, although you can only launch it by clicking the top left and bottom left box (you can't click it on random spot). Sadly, clicking the top left and bottom right box can break your concentration and waste more time rather than using keyboard because you need to move the mouse.
After opening the confusing main menu and finding the play button, the game shows a screen containing a rotating paddle, a score, 3 hearts, and a square with 2 green lights and 2 red lights. I don't even know what to do which make me have to return to the store page to read the game description: "you have to launch a ball against a paddle and hit a green surface".
The game itself offers you a maximum of 3 hearts which will be reduced when your ball hit a red light. There will be either a heart or +1 score floating in the square which will give the said effect when it's touched by the ball. You'll earn +1 score if the ball hit a green light and -1 heart when the ball hit a red light. The paddle will move faster after the score reach a multiple of 10.
You'll basically have to figure out how to make sure that the ball launches to the green lights. After you figure out how to do it, the game become quite easy and repetitive (aside from the fast spinning paddle). There is also a high score in the main menu to compete your score.
There are also two themes in this game: classic and epilepsy. The classic theme will give you the standard game screen although the epilepsy theme will make the game more difficult by giving a rotating background inside the square.
After you start the game, you can't return to the main menu or pause the game. The only way you can return to the main menu after you start the game is to die in game.
Pros:
- High score.
- Two themes.
Cons:
- No tutorial.
- Wrong control description in the main menu.
- Unable to return to main menu and pause in game.
This is an arcade game where you have to release a ball from the top left or bottom right corner to hit a paddle and reach a green light. There's nothing else to do in this game except by going for high scores.

This game is like the platonic ideal in my head of everything a doujin game should be. A parody of several different mainstream series at once, and a pastiche of the gameplay of those and other, completley unrelated games that should by all rights fall apart entirely, but somehow manages to coalesce into a neat little package of fun. This is a metroidvania in the strictest sense, in that it is a fusion of both Metroid and Castlevania elements -- but on top of this, it adds bullet hell gameplay softened up to playability with Street Fighter III-style parries.
Skrubs be warned; this is a HARD game. The controls are weird and take a lot of getting used to, and the level design pulls no punches whatsoever with its difficulty curve. This is not a game that you can just brute-force your way through with sloppy tactics, nor is it a game that you can cheese your way through with outside-the-box thinking. It demands clever planning and skillful execution. It's hard.
But it's fun. You're in for a good time.

if you are looking for a fast paced 'shoot 'em up' style game, then this is
for you, this game is a simulator, not Call of Duty. If, however you are looking for a good armoured warfare simulator, Steel Armor Blaze of War is a sim you must have.
SABOW offers a large variety of gameplay, from intense close in battles in the bushes of Angola, to the mountainous regions of Afghanistan or long distance battles across the sprawling deserts of Iraq. There are two playable tanks in the game, the T-62 and the M60A1, both have fully 3D modeled  interiors and most if not all systems in the tanks are operational.
There are three campaigns in the base game, each with two sub-campaigns for each faction as well as a fourth campaign avaliable as a DLC. The included factions that you can play as are Angola, Iran, Iraq and the USSR, I think you can also play as a Cuban tank crew. The large & numerous maps are incredibly fun to play on, and they all offer a unique experience and require different tactics for the different types of terrain.
The phsyics of the game are also incredibly realistic, firing your gun over long distances will cause bullet drop which you need to account if you are to hit your desired target.
Some people have complained about the lack of tanks, while I would have liked to see some legends such as the T-72, T-55, Chieften etc. I beleive that the quality of the playable tanks in the game easily makes up for the quantity of them.
While this game is incredibly fun and realistic, it does have some minor problems, but these are certainly not game breaking,
- Occasional but minor audio glitches
- Driver AI is sometimes quite frustrating (Probably just my poor commanding skills to be honest)
- Mission editor had a lot of potential, fully customisable scenarios and a 3D editor would be great.
Steel Armor: Blaze of War is incredibly fun and realistic tank simulator with a good variety of maps and vehicles, all in all I would highly recommend this game.

Its the most innovative shooter Ive seen in years.
Now that we have that out of the way, lets actually get to it. SUPERHOT is a shooter/puzzle game. Its very short story tasks you with shooting red dudes. Its not a very interesting story, but they do with it what they can to make it an enjoyable hour and a half to 2 hours. The game is pretty stylish, and its simple look actually underplays how cool the action can be sometimes. The red dudes shatter in an almost glasslike way, making it pretty satifying to kill them in all sorts of ways.
While that doesnt sound to interesting its the games "puzzle" elements that make it enjoyable. When you are not moving time moves at a snails pace. Giving you time to enjoy the mayhem around you. As glass shatters and bullets wiz by your head, you do a dance between machine gun fire to smack a dude in the face with a bat, before throwing it at another guy, and grabbing the machine gun from out of the air to riddle their friends with bullets.
While the story is rather uninteresting and doesnt offer much replayability, it does have an Endless Mode and a Challenge Mode. These are honestly where you are going to spend most of your game time, with Endless Mode having several maps to hone your skills and even a type of challenge mode on those as well, tasking you with killing everyone in a timely fasion as one example. Challenge Mode will also take away some time while you plink away at the story mode with such things as Katanaonly Challange, which in my opinion is a standout among the other challenges.
Other then the actually rather amazing ability to switch bodies with people there isnt much more to the game. But take it from me thats more then enough. I got through the story pretty fast, introducing me to the abilities I would need to master. And then I ran through the Katanaonly Challenge in about an hour, having already ran through the story. Now Endless Mode seems to be the thing for now.
I completely recommend it, and think the $25 price tag is more then justifiable. Its has already given me 4-5 hours of enjoyment and can totally see Endless Mode sucking up quite a bit more time. Just dont expect the story mode to carry the game.

I really like this software.
For starters, my personal favorite part is that if you feel like playing an RPG, but not any of the ones you own, you can just play this game and make an RPG. The amount you like the game depends on what you put into it. Kind of like working to play!
It's kind of confusing at the beginning but as you continue to make a game, the details will mostly be found by you messing around or whatnot. Or just look at a guide.
There is a diverse amount of tiles and songs, but if you need more songs or something, you can just add more.
RPG Maker VX Ace is easy to use and the scripting isn't too hard either (it has its own programming language called "RGSS3"). If it's too hard or you don't want to waste a lot of time, you can simply get some scripts off the internet.
There are a lot of games on Workshop, so you don't even need to make a game. You could just play a workshop item.
If you're going to make a short game, you won't take too long or even need to use all the tilesets. If you're going to make a REALLY short game you might not even need the full game. You might just need the Demo of RPG Maker VX Ace. If you're going to make a big game, however, don't expect to finish it quickly, or even finish it at all.
But there are a few cons.
1: Scripting is kind of hard and time consuming, so if you can't find what you want you might not be able to finish your game.
2: It's is a little pricey, but for the amount of content you get, I don't really care. Especially since the people who gifted it to me got it off of Humble Bundle, where it was 10$.
3: You usually need to pay extra to change the battle system, which sucks if you want to make a F2P game or something.
But I can put the cons behind me, and I am making a large game right now with a few unique concepts.
If you like to make RPGs and see what else people have made, this game is for you.
If you don't know what you're doing here, then this game is for you.
If you hate RPGs and you just want to see what people have to say about this, then you found what you were looking for.
Seriously though, get this game.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it in my Backloggery.
Gameplay: Horror and I have always had a rather difficult time. I have a hard time with it, since I'm so susceptible to immediately taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of games that are try-hard scary and they typically have a hard time doing anything to me, since ever since age six when I played the N64 version of Quake 2 (proactically a first-person horror game in and of itself), I've been rather cauterized to horror. In fact, the only horror game to consistently get to me is Silent Hill 2, and that's because of one thing: atmosphere. Dread is a much more powerful emotion than fear. Fear just incites a reaction; dread stifles reactions. Five Nights at Freddy's does dread fantastically.
Five Nights at Freddy's core gameplay is essentially a resource management game in which you keep an eye on four murderous mechanical mother-humpers so that they don't kill you. Beyond this, you've got controls for the blind spot outside your two (!) doors and a button to close said doors. Having just one door would make it easy. Having two makes it absolutely terrifying, since looking at one camera leaves the other unsupervised. One of the things that Freddy's does differently from other horror games is that the game is essentially unscripted. Rather than predictable pop-scares that happen in games like Amnesia that are great for the first or second time through until you memorize where all the spooky stuff happens, Freddy's works through an essentially unpredictable -if simplistic- AI. This helps keep the aforementioned dread at peak levels. Will you have an easy night where everyone pretty much stays to themselves, or will they be at your throat for the entire six hours? You can't know until you're through.
Going back to the controls, the incredibly restrictive nature of them is really what sets this game over the top IMO. The structure of the building is such that the security office is flanked by two narrow hallways, giving credence to the fact that you're stuck there. In other horror games, you always have the option to turn tail and run. Here? You can't, in both gameplay and story. All of these factors make a horror game that truly is timeless. It's a game that remains scary even after playing through it once, due to its inherent unpredictability. Excellent stuff. 10/10.
Story: Y'know, I really wasn't expecting to see so much lore around this game. Although, I suppose much like the Slenderman Mythos, these things tend to arise out of horror things. I've gotta say, some of this stuff is pretty interesting. However, just what's presented in game isn't exactly the most interesting. It's all very vague, and the brunt of the story presented is through phone calls to... some guy who was apparently working at Freddy's in the past. It's kinda hard to review, since there is plot there, but the fan theories are also really interesting. It's definitely worth reading into after you're through with the game. 9/10 for the combination of both fan theories and actual material.
Graphics: I'll just say this right out the bat: the fact that this game does not have resolution scaling is inherently harmful to the game experience. What I usually end up doing is Alt+Enter-ing once the game loads and then maximizing once more so that there aren't any hideous stretching of images. Apart from that, this game really is quite good from a visual perspective. The art style is superb for the style of game this is, there's loads of small touches (like handprints on Freddy's face; don't belive me? Look on the wiki. ;)), and it does the great thing of being realistic enough to not look a Lego construction, but still obscure enough in detail to let your mind conjure up the rest. That's why high-fidelity horror games don't work as well as some of the lower-fidelity ones: there's no space for your mind to work against you and add in all the details you really don't wanna see. Again, the only complaint is resolution, which can be easily fixed. 4.5/5.
Sound: Unlike in a lot of games, a masterful audio design is absolutely imperative to the horror game experience. This game... this game has a masterful audio design. The ambiance, the sound effects, the hallucinations... it's all fantastic. A game that absolutely must be played with headphones. I don't have much else to talk about here, but just know that this game's audio direction is one of the best I've ever seen in a horror game (and that's stacking up against Amnesia, Slender, Fatal Frame 1-3; in fact, the only thing comparable in sound direction is Silent Hill, and that's just for the Yamaoka headed ones). 5/5.
Overall scores are: 10/9/4.5/5; cumulative score of: 9.5/10. I can sincerely see this game being one of my top five games of the year, and for five dollars, you really can't go wrong if you're a fan of horror but not so much a fan of just jumpscares. This game isn't about jumpscares. It's about the aforementioned sense of dread; something that most horror titles just don't get.

I bought this game quite some time ago and didn't have many chances to actually finish it up until now. Having 9 to 5 jobs, a kid who needs attention and household chores tend to do that to you, heh.
Anyway, this would be my fifth Tales of - games since I entirely skipped PS3 Tales games library. I do tend to have Vesperia and Abyss standard concerning this franchise, and it ends up undermining (imho) other Tales games since Vesperia did almost everything so well with its stories, characters, and overall gameplay.
Now, Tales of Zestiria is not bad, per se. But it somehow lacks in some areas. Don't get me wrong, the combat is great, that has been the highlights of Tales series RPGs, and it is, in my opinion, the best aspect of the game. I like the Normin system, weapon crafting (or fusion), how the world is presented in the game, and the graphics is quite good. The game runs flawlessly on my GTX 950M, where I played it mostly (my GTX 970 rig is not actually portable). The main flaw of this game, maybe the for most of the Tales of - games is the story and how it is told. Zestiria somehow has this problem. The characters are quite likable, but I can't help feeling that there should be more character development. And some EXPLICIT romance would be nice. But that's just me.
I have to mention that the music in this game is superb. Especially on the Trial shrines and opening Japanese movie. There are numerous tracks, and battle musics somehow just pump up the already hectic battle system. Some would argue that it's all about button mashing, but without proper strategy and just pushing buttons haphazardly one would not get the best out of its intricate battles system. Oh, and be careful when fighting in tight spaces. The camera angle just goes bonkers in those cases.
Lastly, I cannot overlook how the game initially delivered. I'm talking about stuttering, choppy frame rate and audio problems. I have no problem with 30 fps, really, although I do prefer it to be in the sixties. It has all been fixed as of this review, but the bulk of the fix comes in the form of a third party patch. I REALLY think Bandai Namco can do better. I hope Berseria will not have these problems.
All in all, a good game, but I would say that it comes up short in some of the key aspects. I do recommend this for all Tales fans and Action JRPG fans. For newcomers to the series this would not be a bad start, but I do think they should start with the other games in the series.
Final score: 7.5/10

LORE
Ok, so there's a race of invisible people who live all around humans, angels basically, known as seraphim in the game. They're literally everywhere and according to the game they even eat food, yet somehow most people don't acknowledge or believe in them despite what I assume has to be a extremely high number of floating and disappearing food reports. The whole thing is a completely unnecessay plot device in my opinion.
The other part of the lore is that whenever a human, seraphim and even animals gets mad or hateful enough they become powerful monsters, who then apparently live forever unless the chosen one kills them, which turns them back, unless they're still angry or get angry again in which case they'll apparenly turn back into a monster. So instead of being a badass warrior of justice the game makes you feel more like an anger management counselor.
PLOT
Everything is pointless. There's several times where you will get to choose one of two seemingly important options in dialogue, but you get the same result no matter what you pick. The only difference is that you occasionally get a slightly different cutscene on some of them. And speaking of dialogue, the word "malevolence" literally shows up in almost every sentence from every character.
Another example is a character doing something in a cutscene just to show how cool you're supposed to think they are, such as one character trying to fight an enemy on their own because they're immune to it's special ability, only for you to have to fight the boss with the rest of the party like normal anyway with absolutely no changes to the fighting mechanics. So the entire cutscene was basically just that one character saying "Look how cool I am.".
There's also several times in the story where the party does something completely pointless and unsatisfying, such as confronting a major and extremely dangerous villain who intends to kill a lot of people, and then letting them calmly walk away as if they were just players on different football teams or something. Literally every time that there's a confrontation, the solution that's forced onto you is to go somewhere and do something to get stronger first regardless of what might happen in the meantime.
Despite the MC supposedly being the "chosen one", there's multiple other people that can do everything he does, only with less whining. Also, near the start of the game he pulls a legendary sword from a stone (super original) to become the chosen one, though immediately after the sword isn't shown anywhere and is inexplicably never mentioned again. Yet another completely unnecessay plot device.
CHARACTERS
Completely uninteresting and generic anime archtypal characters. There's no character developement or flaws to speak of, the MC is your standard naive good guy type who generally has about as much to add to the situation as a Buzz Lightyear pull string doll. And the bad guys are equally one dimensional, they're all just flatly evil and want to do evil things because they're evil for no reason other than because they're evil. And just in case them being evil is too much for you to keep track of they all have dark colors, clothes, and auras to make things simple for you.
GRAPHICS
Standard anime style characters and medieval fantasy style world, the lack of imagination isn't that big of a deal on it's own, however the graphics are late Xbox or early 360 quality at best. Before I played this I recently played Tales of the Abyss on PS2 and the change is pretty minimal, which is inexcusable considering they're a decade apart. Aside from the quality the lack of originality and overuse of immersion breaking anime cutscenes make looking at the screen more of a chore than it needs to be. The game sports a little bit of character customization, though extremely limited, however they're all shown as their default setups in any of the numerous anime cutscenes. So it's pretty bad for the immersion.
COMBAT
The combat is bad, it's extremely awkward, boring, and one-sided. There is zero strategy involved, you can't assign any roles to your party members such as healing or tanking, and they have no problem repeatedly walking into a lingering attack that is killing them. You'd think that would make it more of a hack and slash style game, however any time you get a few good hits in on an enemy they inexplicably become invincible for a random amount of time. Which is especially annoying when you finally get one of the super moves to work, only to have it completely wasted on a basic monster who decided to turn on god mode. The whole thing could be compared to playing rock, paper, scissors but everytime you throw the right one your opponent ignores it and says that they win anyway.
So combat generally consists of you running around in circles, hitting an enemy a few times, and then running away while your party members get murdered and then automatically revived via the ridiculous super saiyan mechanic.
Aside from all that, the camera is really bad, it's more focused on following the enemy than your character and there's no way to not be locked onto something. Actions such as dodging will leave your camera where it was, leaving your character to end up off-screen while the invincible enemies curb stomp your super saiyan brains in.

Hot damn. Admittedly I haven't finished the game yet
but I'm an impatient ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and what I have played so far is well worth the recommendation.
Gameplay is refined, controls are fine tuned, and I truly appreciate the hat system that was implemented. You can switch from several hats you stitch from yarn pickups, each with their own special abilities. While the abilities aren't jaw-dropping unique, their presentation is, and each one has their use (though honestly, if you're like me, you'll find yourself with Sprint the vast majority of the time). There's also 'skins' for each hat you get through a slot machine (no microtransactions, just in gameplay) as well as remixes of the music and colors. Adds a bit more character to the game, and its fun.
Complementing these abilities and hats are badges sold by a mysterious vendor. These are very varied, from badges that give you a 'hookshot' to sling around, to giving you a scooter, to making everyone 'mumble' during their dialogue (in the same vein as Banjo) to even giving you a 1-hit-death challenge. They're very fun to play with, and definitely do spruce up the game.
But above all in the gameplay is the
. Holy ♥♥♥♥, the variety. You are virtually never doing the same thing. Granted, all of the stages revolve around platforming, but the devs
gave it their all into you never being bored, and you never are. A murder mystery? A parade? A stealth/horror mission that actually makes me♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants a bit because I'm that much a puss? All are in there, and each one is really enjoyable. The game does such a swell job at keeping varied, but don't worry, there's still some free roam in there too. Debatably the best looking area in the game is completely free roam, and even then it's large and is varied enough in and of itself. It hits all its marks, and does so with a straight As.
Not only is this game an excellent throwback to collectathons and platformers of yore (SM Sunshine, SM Galaxy, and Banjo in particular) in terms of the flawless controls and platforming in general, but it has the atmosphere to boot. Excellent music to each stage and level, and the soundtrack in its entirety is swell and nostalgic of previously mentioned upbeat platformer/collectathons. Along with games like Hotline Miami, Redout, and Undertale this has to be one of my favorite soundtracks in a game to date.
Aesthetically it keeps a beautifully styled, colorful world on each of its areas, and all of them are chock full of stuff to see and collect. Atmosphere on each world, and even parts of them, are unique and blissfully pretty to look at. The world doesn't feel empty in the slightest, as there's a multitude of secrets and jokes to find, as well as bonus worlds that are very reminiscent of Super Mario Sunshine's bonus levels. The jokes in this game, atleast for me, really land their mark. I really enjoy the wit and comedy of this game.
I'm no comedian, but for whatever reason this game really tickles my funnybone.
Lastly I'd like to talk about the characters. They are
. Bosses and side characters, while many are tropes youve seen before, are very memorable and loveable. Especially the Snatcher, who gives such a hilarious performance I can't stand but to not love him. Certainly the fully voice acted dialogue is a huge part of that, and it really helps the characters shine. The voice acting is very well done, which is why I personally would abstain from the previously mentioned 'mumble' badge. The game is drenched in the witty dialogue and the voices only help to add to it.
So yeah, my one flaw I could even begin to fathom mentioning is that it's probably a bit on the shorter side, but it is still well worth 30. This game is a blast to play and I hope it gets the attention it deserves. There's so much heart and charm put into this thing it'd be a shame to not buy it if you're even the slightest fan of 3D platformers or collectathons. Good humor, amazing variety, and a beautiful, nostalgic presentation.
tl;dr
Buy this thing.

An exercise in futility regarding the existential crises of humanity and ones deeply personal want for purpose within a given system.
At first I wanted to ignore this game until I saw Ken Levine and Peter Molyneux speaking to each other over twitter about it. Two of my favorite game developers.
I wish there were an option for giving this a sideways thumb as I can't easily recommend my experience with this game and it is a game. I'm not about to have that argument. But its.. lacking. I feel personally, that these things have been said before.
Now, is this game art? Are games art? I don't care, I'm not here to tell you that. What I can tell you is that this is an interactive guide though some builds of games that “coda” made while a narrator explains what the build is, what it was and what his own interpretations of why design choice “X” was made over design choice “Y”
Its hard to explain; and despite what you've likely heard. While it does not make sense on its face, around the 1 hour mark I felt I had an understanding of what the narrator was trying to convey. At least, to my satisfaction. In short, being creative... as well as existing derives its meaning from those who give it meaning. There is no external force pushing you forward, there is only you and your decisions living in the now, the present.
Why is that there? Ask 10 different people and its likely you'll get 10 different responses.
Its a reflection piece summed up best in a quote from BioShock 2 (which I know Ken Levine had nothing if very little to do with BioShock 2 forgive me) made by the character Eleanor Lamb
“Love is just a chemical, we give it meaning by choice”

The Menu System
This for me has always been very accessible. After seeing some very early menus from watching older videos on YouTube they have definitely made some good changes. As it is now, it's brilliant! The first aid screen in particular is pretty cool.
I find it very handy that you can sort each section of the inventory by condition, name or weight. Very handy when you want to get rid of something weighing you down or checking on condition of food.
The Graphics
While not to everyones taste, I find the graphics stunning. Very refreshing art style. Not cel shaded but not "photo realistic" either. Catching a glimpse of the sky when it's sunset is always amazing. The wild life is also very well designed and implemented. Even if wolves are the bane of my existence. *Shakes fist*
The Gameplay
My god, this game is incredible. There is rarely a moment where you can relax. There is always something. Lack of food, lack of warmth, no weapons or tools, wolves prowling and out for blood... it just doesn't stop. My best run I managed 12 days. Each time I kick the bucket I just want to start again. The atmosphere of this game is amazing.
The Sound
The sounds in The Long Dark are spot on. Great wind sound effects, wolves when howling sound perfect and even the sound of checking through a cupboard or draw sound realistic. Great job all round from the sound department.
Overall
HIGHLY recommended. Something a little different from the usual survival games. After watching a couple friends playing this game on their YouTube channels (RentAHero & Dzaran), I just had to get it. I don't normally invest in early access games but this one I am glad to of made an exception for. One of the best survival experiences I've had in my 20+ years of gaming. Even though there is only Sandbox mode available at the moment, that's still enough to keep you playing and coming back for more especially with the number of updates Hinterland Studios makes! Bring on the story!

The only "That's cool!" bits from the replays were when I would purposefully do a turn or unnecessary jump to see it played back, but even then it was underwhelming.

I'll go into this review by category first, then personal thoughts.
Gameplay: difficult to convey on my end, as I went keyboard and mouse the whole way (still not computer savvy enough to know how to set up a controller), which is decidely not ideal, as maneuvering in the air is really stiff without a control stick, among other things. That said, was pleasantly surprised at how creative and challenging the game was overall, as while some sections would undoubtedly be pretty easy with said controller, there are things like diving under a glass wall and jumping immediately upon getting under it, or you fall. How a 3D game managed to accurately convey the type of jump normally seen in a Mega Man game, I don't know, but kudos.
Music: varied and always fitting of the settings, from the chill Mafia Town to the epic *spoiler final level*, but special mention goes to boss music, which leads into:
Bosses: Honestly my favorite aspect of the game, there is all of one boss that could be considered average, that being the first against some mooks and an elite mook throwing barrels. Likely intentional, as it is the first boss. Every single subsequent boss is honestly the best selection I have ever seen in a "collectathon" platformer, each with something unique to them, and amazing music that really captures the nature of the fight, particularly the fever-pitch MIDI number used in the super frantic final boss fight.
Graphics: cute, cel-shaded look ensures this game's appearance won't likely age anytime soon, and as a special note really emphasizes the stark contrast the absolutely terrifying manor mission has with the rest of the game. Adorable, cartoony protagonist alone with a psychotist demon-ghost...thing... in a less-cartoony-than-normal location, complete with "music" that won't let you calm down. Props for that one, guys.
Personal thoughts: I notice people attempting to compare this game and Yooka-Laylee quite a bit lately. Honestly, having played and finished both, I don't see a lot of similarities between the two. YL was trying to continue the Banjo-Kazooie legacy, and only really did that. Whether that's good or bad is up to you. A Hat in Time, on the other hand, has far more in common with Super Mario Sunshine, while having Wind Waker-esque cel-shading and movement options reminiscent of Psychonauts, and still managed to develop an identity separate from its inspirations. Honestly, I feel if you liked these games, you'll love this one. I know I did (and am kinda sad it had to end, wouldn't mind seeing further adventures with Hat Kid somewhere down the line, DLC notwithstanding.)

A Hat in Time is a really good game that's worth every dime of its $30 price tag but it has some flaws that needs to be work on.
-For instance the game only has 4 worlds + 1 stage. This makes the game very short, a good ride that ends up with you wanting more.
-A lot of stages have great ideas to them and how you can use your hats to complete the level but most of the good ideas aren't used throughout the game and are only on little bits.
-The enemy variety is very poor and I can see it isn't because of lack of ideas, they have everything they want and they've proven it. Unfortunately, the game falls short on this.
-Towards the end of the act 3, right on the final seconds of the boss, the game shows a laziness it didn't show on all of the other stages. Almost if they decided to cut short the game from there on out. The chapter 4 is underwhelming and easily one of the worst chapters on the game and then they give you the chapter 5 which is actually only one level so I don't count it as a world.
-The game doesn't reward or at least it doesn't have enough incentive for you to explore the world. I did it so it's why I've played 53hours of it and I can say the game doesn't reward you to explore it on its entirely. Because of this the game feels like a linear level almost every time.
-I think there's not enough hats for you to enjoy. For a game called A Hat in Time, this could've been fixed. Also having only so many tries on the slot machine was a mistake.
Despite all of its flaws, the game still stands up but I think it'd be better to talk about his flaws more than why it is so good, everyone is talking about how good it is but they don't find any flaws.
As for the pros for this game, it has too much to count so I'll simply make a tiny list.
+Charming atmosphere.
+Level design.
+Boss battles and their difficulty. Not too easy and not too hard.
+The music is outstanding.
+Sounds effects are well done and every one is satisfying.
+Our control over the character is over the top, the best platformer controllers I've had the pleasure to play on the last couple of years.
+The writing of the characters are so good, the jokes are on point and they don't use memes every five seconds. They have their own identity and raise it proud.
+Full voice acting to inject more life to the game. While it can't be good for every character, it's worth to mention for a couple of them.
With everything and all I think this game stands out against the huge behemoths of the genre but it needs to work on its flaws if there's a sequel. Then it'd be a master piece.

-The possibility of defense layout is endless, but due to some unbalanced perks of a certain traps, the current layout is pretty much plain and similar. However, there's a undescribable joy when you and your friends discovered a new layout that actually work.
-The diversity in each heroes is wonderfully rich. Each and every characters have their own fun and perks so think twice before you choose your heroes.
-The only one thing that can really bore you is the grind. Much like every games, you must farm to be stronger, to be able to climb higher; but this game is weighted heavily on the farm and the endless grind, which is fun at first but will quickly turn into a chore rather than a game. So my advice is to not focusing too much on your stats. Looking for a piece of gear that has 1% higher in passives won't bring you any good, only frustuating and miserable; just enjoy the victory with your comrades after an epic match.
> To DD1 players, this game is designed with the co-op in mind, so it's probably a lot harder to solo; try to find some friends to play with.
**tl;dr: A good co-op strategy tower defense with a mix of RPG, game requires you to be quick on your feet, not just afk and let the defenses do all the jobs. Despite the name it's completely different from DD1 so don't compare it too much with its former self.

- use free & free under battle options so you can move around any direction during a fight.

the glorious boons for your second playthrough. It's a huge difference.

This review will be in 2 portions.
For review itself, I will keep it short and simple:
"Do not watch someone else play this. Get this for yourself; I beg of those who are interested or are content creators to play this for themselves."
The second part of this review is a personal story of mine.
The whole game reminded me of said friend whom I have known for quite a while, but not really for decades, so to say. He creates artwork that I always enjoyed experiencing and interacting with in some way, and he would interact with me in return when it came to said artwork; it would always brighten up my day/week whenever I felt bad or good and made me know him little more every time. It felt amazing and I would just forget everything terrible that was happening around me every time. It was what got me started on creating and sharing artwork with him (And others) as well, with photography, drawings and such. I kept going in hopes that I would get to share my creations as well and hear his thoughts. In a way he broke down barriers that I put up; I can't thank him enough for that.
But then, as time went on, it slowly happened less and less; I witnessed him do the same thing he did with me, but it was happening with others. Even though he is a dear friend, I was (And I am still) afraid to reach out to him, yet I would be filled with such joy when he would reach out to me and have fun chewing the fat, sharing our work, or whatever.
I am afraid to speak out, not because I believe that my work is "bad" or "dumb".
It's because I am afraid that I would be intentionally ignored/left out; I am afraid that because I admire his work, him sharing with me on such a level or at all won't happen anymore because I always want to know in one way or another what he thinks when he finishes them and I kept having that desire.
I feel as though I have failed him, as well as myself...
And it's all my fault.
But have I really failed to connect with him because I don't know him as much as he wanted? Or that I know too much and want more? I want to say: "No, that can't be true, there has to be something else that isn't my fault", but the writing might be on the wall.
I want to share my perceptions with him when it comes to my work/experiences, however silly or serious they might be. I can't stop myself from doing it; I physically can't. And I want him to do the same.
But I don't want to unintentionally burn bridges that have held up for so long when I'm trying to keep them up.
In my head, I've created this "echo-chamber" with messages bouncing around inside that say things like: "Oh, it's only just a phase, both of you will get over it," or "Just keep going at it with your work, you'll find common ground soon enough."
So...what's the solution? If I try to connect, I'll most likely frustrate him to the point where he might just "go somewhere else" with him resenting me.
If I don't say anything at all on the other hand, nothing will get done and things will simply fall apart because nothing would be holding anything up.
I only want him to see the big picture here, but maybe it's asking too much out of him. Or maybe I'm not seeing something at a certain angle, even though I felt like I have exhausted every viewpoint possible.
It's like an entirely new prison that has locked me inside and I can't get out of, all while something is beating up me inside over and over again no matter what I do.
I create things to share, and not just artwork.
But if I do, I might just alienate others in the process...
But I want that feeling to go away and never come back...
More than anything else in the world.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

Overall, I find The Beginners Guide as a shallow title. Watch the trailer and pass. It has everything the game has, and more. You won't find more inside.

I didn't know what this game was.  I bought it on a whim.  It's not my first narritive game, but it's my first in this particular style.  To tell you any more, indeed, anything at all, about this game would do you a disservice.
Instead let me tell you about a movie I watched on Cowboy Cinema at 3 AM.
Cowboy Cinema was the name of an in house movie channel that played nonstop in the dormitories at Oklahoma State University when I was living and studying there in the early 2000's.  It was a movie channel that mostly played indie films, or failed blockbusters... whatever they could get the rights to on the cheap, because it wasn't a proper channel, you see.  It was just a local channel, organized in house, probably by broadcasting students or something right there on the university grounds, and there were no commercials or announcements or anything of the like, just movies 24/7.
It was on this channel that I saw a movie called "The Shape of Things", starring Paul Rudd and Rachel Weisz.  I'm not surprised if you've never heard of the movie.  It was indie to begin with, and didn't do especially well (or, to be fair, especially bad).  But this movie had an impact on me that has left a peculiar emotional memory after all these years.
I reccomend you watch the movie.  Much like the game, to tell you too much about it would be to do you a disservice.  But it scratched a particular itch that I didn't even know I had because that movie wasn't just a movie, it was ART.  And not in a highbrow, shot in black and white with pure violin score and spoken language only in a particularly obscure local village itallian dialect kind of art.  But flashy, yet solemn modern, sexy, you came here for A list hollywood entertainment but we're gonna sneak in a sucker punch of symbollic, deep, meaningfull, thought provoking and poignant yet somehow fresh and immediate in your face ART right before we roll credits.
This game made me feel like that movie felt.
This game is art.

This game is the answer to one of the most important questions in life: If you slather a mediocre shmup in internet meme aesthetics and shallow, dated pop culture references, will it sell more copies?
Gameplay is essentially classic space invader-style shmup fare, clearing waves of enemies between boss fights. You've got 3 hearts, which you can restore with pickups. You can also get temporary extra hitpoints with armor pickups.
Your right-click attack can be switched out by collecting another type of item. Most of these attacks don't seem very powerful to me, but at least they recharge pretty quickly.
The last type of pickup is "superfood", which are randomly-dropping passive upgrades that you keep until you die, like items in some types of roguelike games. (I like this mechanic, to be honest. I've never seen it in a shmup before, so points for that.)
Bosses sometimes drop 'cards' also, but there doesn't appear to be a point to them other than filling up the collection screen on the main menu.
All the bosses are randomly selected celebrities or internet personalities, usually with some letters switched around to make things legal. Each one you encounter will babble some nonsense in broken english that may at one point have been intended to be funny(?), send out a few waves of enemies, then attack by running around the screen and shooting his or her unique bullet pattern at you. Some are way harder than others, with bullet patterns that are so constant that they are near impossible to get in front of and shoot. This is further exacerbated by the tendency of bosses to get in really close to the bottom of the screen, where the player usually is.
There's apparently a story of some kind involving aliens and kidnapped celebrities, but it's not explained to you at all other than in some vague dialogue with "Nuck Chorris", who appears as every sixth boss fight. He's the only one with multiple attacks. Every time you beat him in a single game, the enemies get stronger.
Controls are alright- they'd be difficult to mess up in a game like this. Mouse controls don't allow you to move around without holding down the shoot button for some reason, though. That peeved me.

A well-detailed tank simulation of Cold War era's M60A1 and T62 tanks with almost non-existent tutorial and a steep learning curve that is well worth it.
Since it is based on Graviteam Tactics engine apart from directly controlling tanks you are also able to give orders to other troops under your command (or give the control away to AI if you want to concentrate on a pure tanking).
Tank cockpits are nicely detailed, crew members are animated - however the actual interactivity is at the minimum, mostly done via shortcuts and interface buttons. Nonetheless cockpits provide some good immersion.
Campaigns in the game are about capturing victory points on a large map, where combat encounters are being generated on the fly depending on the situation. Both you and the enemy have limited pool of units and reinforcements, attrition, fuel and ammo running out play a large role in the ultimate outcome. Altogether this means that no playthrough is ever the same. Plus as a nice touch every destroyed vehicle and killed infantry stays on the map permanently, across every encounter in that area.
There is also a Quick Battle generator, where it is fast and easy to set up whatever combat encounter you want, with any mix of forces, on any map area, controlled by you or an AI ally.
In Cold War era depicted in the game tank crews are not as blind as they were during WW2, while still not having all the tools that make tanks such an effective weapon platforms they are today. Night vision devices are passive, low res, and have to be supported by IR spotlights, otherwise there's little you can see at night. Coincidence rangefinders require constant manual control and thus the shot requires a lot more time to be perfectly lined up. Gun stabilization is only in its infancy so a lot more skill is required from gunners to land a hit. As a result all of this provides for some tight combat, not present in other, more modern tank simulations.
The game has some downsides of course. Interface is quite bad and does not feature even half the commands that keyboard shortcuts let you access. Tutorials do not exist, apart from pop ups describing what a given button does. There are still minor bugs and pathfinding in cluttered areas is wonky.
Despite all of these issues - it is one of the best tank sims out there.

While that is all our hero ever says, sometimes a simple silence makes up for an entire novel's worth of speaking. LIMBO is a simple game, a classic Mario-styled platformer with an emphasis on physics-based puzzles, set in a black and white world both cold and extremely hostile, with everything from giant spiders to fellow children out to get you. But combine its simple, silent, monochrome atmosphere with genius level-design and physics puzzles, and you've got one of the most enjoyable games since Portal. It's also on par with Portal for length, about three hours long, but never fear, as just like with Portal, it's so enjoyable it will pull you back in again and again for more. Truly a unique modern classic.

I may not be experienced with this game all that much, I haven't unlocked all the content as I play the game with an extremely slow pace, this is a review from somebody who values creativity, and the business practises Galatic Junk League's Developers are partaking in.
Other games of this genre have styles that feel intrusive, you may feel like your vision of the machine that personally, you want to sink your effort into is being ruined by having to plaster all the functional modules all over it, and it's a tightrope of a fine-line to walk between style and stubstance when building, whereas here, it feels as if the developers have taken time and considerate effort in allowing you to build what you'd like, blocks are multi-faced and can be manipulated to achieve any number of looks and modules can easily be hidden away if their look doesn't satisfy you.
The latest update has made the "Addon" parts even better, but that's not to say they weren't already good, you can do almost whatever you want with these parts and they won't hurt the resulting build, you can clip them through blocks, no problem! Even the ships you can purchase for a small amount of in-game currency use part-clipping to enhance the craft's appearance. In the lastest update, the addon parts have a pool of "free" parts, meaning they don't cost anything to build to a point.
The game doesn't try to suck you dry of your hard earnt junk, a lot of the options are free to try, and so you can experiment with different classes and different configurations of ship if what you're working with isn't adequate, parts don't cost anything, only an initially high research cost.
Galatic Junk League plays rather slowly, you must coordinate with your team, this is especially important when you're of a lower level, the developers have announced they're planning to create deeper strategic gameplay in future updates.
Something that has me very exited for this title, has been the developers cooperating with community members from other similar titles, people like ROSEFALL, who was previously been in direct development of Galatic Junk League, this is an amazing sign, and my thanks go out to GJL's developers, for making such a great decision, as for the future? Who knows, all I'm able to say is, don't make the mistakes of your predecessors, listen to the quiet majority, not the loud minority, there's those who'll always be unhappy.

TLDR this game outshines Mario Sunshine at its own game (see what I did there?)
I've played a handful of Indie 3D Kickstarter platformers but this one is hands-down the best. Yooka Laylee stole the spotlight with regard to that market but here comes A Hat in Time to show us all how it's done. This game is a delight from start to finish and polished to a perfect sheen. This is really astonishing given this game raised about a tenth of the money that Yooka Laylee did.
I've seen the game labelled as a "Collect-a-thon" game but I don't think that's quite accurate so don't get scared off if you're not a fan of those games. I think a better comparison would be the more evolved platformers we got during the Gamecube/PS2 days like the Jak Trilogy, Sly Cooper, and Mario Sunshine more than anything else. I've never felt the 3D Mario titles (64, Sunshine, Galaxy) were true collect-a-thons, as they emphasized missions rather than collecting trinkets and a Hat in Time follows suit with this. Each star (they're hourglasses in this one...) has a lot of story packed in and most of them wildly change the nature of the level.
Like in the Mario games, you have a couple different missions you can pick from that will task you with a fun challenge in the level. Most of it is platforming but there's a ton of variety as well: stealth missions, surprisingly good boss fights, a detective mission, etc. This game achieves better variety than Mario Sunshine with only half the levels! Each and every star feels worthwhile here and the game never asks you to scour a level looking for every last shiny object. There are other collectibles but most of them serve as currency to buy upgrades. There are also a couple abilities you acquire during certain missions so there's some "come back later when you get this power-up" but it's never too bad. The game also yoinks Mario Sunshine's secret stars and actually does them far better than Sunshine (that music, OMG!).
If I had a complaint, it would be that I wish the game encouraged exploration more. I wrongfully assumed the game would be a collect-a-thon based on the previews that showed the very open Mafia town level. Though I quickly grew to like the more mission-based approach, I still wished the game had encouraged me to explore these beautiful worlds more. Aside from locking you into the mission you select, the second level has almost no exploration with 3 disconnected linear maps. The 3rd and 4th levels allow you to explore and do things out of order but it's still fairly limited. The 4th proudly touts itself as a "free-roam" level but I found that aspect underwhelming. You start at the center of the level and just choose one of four paths that quickly become linear platforming levels. That, to me, is not free-roam. Thankfully, the secret stars pick up the slack quite a bit with giving the game some more exploration.
Aside from that, I really have no complaints with this game, it is polished to a sheen. The visuals are always slick and stylish, I encountered no bugs at all, the game controls like a dream and has more depth than I thought, and even the camera works really well. It's just a delight from start to finish, and I relished every single star. If you love platformers, and even if you hate collect-a-thons, you should absolutely check this out.

Outlast is an amazing horror game. What makes it scary? You can't fight back! Instead, you have to be clever and hide/sneak past. In my opinion the game is made really well, I didn't run into any bugs and I thought the game had a good level of difficulty. It constantly kept me on edge with hiding, chase scenes and jump scares. The game flows really nicely giving you objectives to complete. Playing this game when it is dark and with headphones on loud really makes it a scary experience! 9.5/10.
As for the DLC I was a little dissapointed at the start; I felt like I had no chance to hide and it was all just chase scenes which got a little repetative, and in the end lost its scare factor. I also had a moment where there was supposed to be a "jump scare" but I was facing completly the wrong way lol. However, once you get to the 2nd half of the DLC it really starts to pick up again and you once again see signs of the brilliance from the main game. 8/10.
£14.99 for the main game, I think this is a fair price, it has quality content and great graphics as well. But you can pick it up in the sale 66% off.
£6.00 for the DLC. In my opinion not worth that money, but when it goes on sale I highly recommend it.
Overall, Outlast is an amazing horror experience, just make sure to play when its dark and with headphones on loud so you get the full experience!

This is my 4th Tales game. I thought Symphonia was excellent. I remember Destiny and Vesperia being pretty good. Sadly, Zestiria was a disappointment for me. I didn't start to enjoy it until about 20 hours in when I decided to change the difficulty setting, as I felt the fights were too easy. I would have quit were it not for the combat, as everything else was severely lacking. I wanted to like the game because I have faith in the Tales series, but I found myself pushing for the end just to see what would happen with the story. My feelings after completion of the game can be summed up as "oh" and "that's it?"
PROS:
• Abilties that look and sound cool when executing; you feel strong in battle.
• Various difficulty settings that can be changed at any time and make defeating bosses feel sufficiently challenging.
• Good music.
• The Japanese voiceovers are good.
CONS:
• Very weak and predictable story with no twists. It had potential but felt like an idea rather than a fully developed plot. You are left with many questions and no answers.
• Characters are flat and don't feel genuine. You are told insead of shown who they are.
• The villains are a joke and have little to no backstory or motivation.
• Cringy, forced, repetitive dialogue.
• Camera issues while in combat.
• Copy and paste dungeons with little to no puzzles.
• Constantly shown the same tutorial messages even when you are halfway through the game.
• Repetitive actions, such as reading monolith stones, which give you the same tutorials previously mentioned.
• Convoluted equipment/crafting system.
• Optional content/side quests can be completed very quickly and don't add much to the story. You still don't know who the characters are or learn anything compelling about the world. It feels rushed and insincere, just as the main story does.
• No incentive to play the NG+ Just more grinding through a vast but lifeless realm.
Tales of Berseria looks promising, though it is a prequel to Zestiria. Let's hope it is a better game than this was.

I really like Quantic Dreams' games and its "interactive drama" style.
I think Fahrenheit is considerated the first game with the interactive drama style by Q.D. And I believe because of that + the lack of a good logic (like on "Heavy Rain") made the game a little frustrating.
For example: On Heavy Rain, your choices affect other chapters, while on Fahrenheit, your choices barely affect something on the future. It affects more your mood instead of consequences.
The story is really great, it's really creative, but I heard that David Cage (director of Q.D.) had to rush the game I guess, and that's why from the middle until the end, the story ♥♥♥♥s logic and it's full of plot holes.
For example: Why would a catholic priest not believe on supernatural stuff??? If you ask a catholic priest for help because of "supernatural stuff" happened to you, this priest would at least offer himself to pray you or your house. (jeez, wake up, David Cage!)
There are so many plot holes that even a SECOND villian appears. This second villain is so USELESS to the story that I have no idea why David Cage invented it in the first place.
And there's something that really frustrated me. There are two moments in this game that it's up to you the "future" of two characters. But it doesn't matter of what you choose! If you keep them alive, safe or with you, these two characters DISAPPEAR from the story. And you have no idea where they are even if you save their lives. This is a HUGE mistake commited by David Cage.
Another weird thing in this game it's the MAIN COUPLE. It makes NO SENSE.
Jeez, David Cage... Again, where were your mind when you choose the main couple?
You see, there are two couples that totally match each other. And then David just put two different characters that have no reason to stay together to have chemistry with each other OUT OF THE BLUE.
But then again, on Heavy Rain, David Cage committed the same mistake by making two different people stay together in a horrible moment to have romance.
Although you can be frustrated with so many plot holes or the lack of "consequences" in this game, it's really nice. It has a creative story that makes you want to know more.
I guess Fahrenheit could be the "sketch" Quantic Dream had to make so they could get it right on their next interactive drama game.
It has some weird primitive QTEs too.
But the soundtrack is really awesome and totally fits with each character.
I hope Quantic Dream could REMAKE this game and remove some useless crap I mentioned above and fill the plot holes, because this story is worthy!

The following review is pretty lengthy. It's up to you whether or not to read it.
The world is fairly saturated with color, from the lush green trees of the jungle, to the rich brown jungle trails, to the tan and orange deserts, to the pure blue water. It is by no means the most gorgeous game out there, but personally, I have respect for the art-like, cartoonish style.
I would say that JC2 doesn't try to take itself seriously, but that wouldn't be the complete truth. The story, while not the greatest ever, does take itself seriously, with a few generic characters such as:
-The Patriotic, bacon-eating American
-The super attractive, blonde, American Bad-A** soldier
-The skin-tight suit-wearing, heavy-accented, incredibly intelligent Asian operative
And a few more! The story itself is... Well, It's no "The Last of Us", that's for sure. However, that's okay! The objectives and goals you actually get in the Agency Missions are a ton of fun for most of the time! There are also multiple "gangs" or "crime lords" you can do work for, in order to expand their influence over the country of Panau. The missions these gang leaders give out can also be very fun at times, however, the stronghold takeovers can get a little old. They essentially go like this:
-Escort a squad of gang members through a military compound. Use a grapple hook to get over the gate, in order to open it from the other side, thus letting your allies in.
-Keep the hacker alive at all costs
-Defend the hacker while he hacks some sort of system
-And finally, kill the stronghold commander to complete the stronghold takeover.
As gamers, we all know that escort missions can be a huge pain in the rear, however, I've had no trouble whatsoever with these missions.
Well, if you are killed in action in free roam, you will respawn back at the nearest stronghold, ready to get right back into the action!
Back on the subject of missions, the way in which you actually gain access to these Agency Missions and Stronghold Takeovers is simple:
Chaos is what fuels missions! By weakening the military government in free roam by assaulting bases, destroying fuel lines, destroying military vehicles, killing military personelle, overloading nuclear reactors, (etc.) you are not only having a blast by playing the game, but you're also progressing the story! I personally have not seen this replicated in any other game, and I find it to be an effective and fun way of progressing the storyline.
To keep it pretty simple, you're equipped with a grappling hook. An incredibly useful tool, the grappling hook can be used to climb buildings and mountains, attach to vehicles, link two objects together [and more, if you download the mod that lets you tether multiple things together], pull enemies off of high areas, gain momentum while parachuting, and even more. Have fun experimenting with the possibilities! I sure have!
As you cause more Chaos, you gain more items to purchase in the black market. You can call the black market dealer using a beacon, and when he arrives, you have three options:
-Buy a certain weapon / grenade
-Buy a vehicle
-Extract to any previously discovered location on the map
The more Chaos you cause, the more options you will have available to you. You can also call the black market dealer during missions should you ever find yourself low on ammunition, or just needing a new toy.
You can also find vehicle parts, weapon parts, and armor parts. Vehicle and weapon parts can be used in the black market screen to upgrade weapons and vehicles, to do things such as increase damage or increase top speed. As for armor parts, for every five you collect, you gain a health increase.
-Almost cringey voice acting among the natives. Incredibly exaggerated accents, and once I caught a female NPC misreading a line and then correcting herself. If bad voice acting is a dealbreaker, watch some gameplay on YouTube to see if you can bear it
+Vehicles, helicopters most notably, being destroyed are much more realistic than in other games. (Minor detail)
+Explosions have a satisfying sound (Minor detail)
+Rico's animation for detonating C4, followed by the sight and sound of explosion, makes you feel like a total bad-a**
+World size is MASSIVE, and I hear one of the islands is similar to the island from the TV Program "Lost".
-Some key bindings are better off in different areas. I always change my key bindings in games as soon as I play them to make sure I'm comfortable, but I recommend anyone should change the defaults to what they see fit.
-Weapon damage model for SOME weapons is a bit low. Unrealistically low. An M4 could take someone down in one bullet in reality of course, and this game is not reality, and frankly, this game is basically telling you "I'm NOT realistic AT ALL, and that's the point of the game!" However, if it was a bit quicker to kill an enemy, it would be welcomed. (MIGHT be fixed by upgrading weapons)
-No indication of a kill on an enemy. Occasionally, a bullet will knock an enemy to the ground. Thinking they were dead, you turn to deal with a new target, only for the previous enemy to get right back up. A good way to make sure you've secured the kill is to watch and see if the enemy has dropped their weapon when they fell. While this works just fine, some kind of hitmarker would be welcomed.
Just Cause 2, while being a slightly older game, is an absolute blast to play. This game just literally lets you do whatever the hell you want. If you play Grand Theft Auto 5 in single player to have fun in the sandbox world, but dislike being killed so easily and want to just feel like a bad-a**, this game is your answer. (Note: Not once did I mention Grand Theft Auto 5 being a bad game, please do not get upset over nothing)
SOME bad voice acting and story, but incredibly fun gameplay and world design to make up for it.

When I wake up in the morning I like to have a breakfast of crispy bacon and a nice glass of blood. Sometimes I wonder, however, where does my blood and bacon come from? When I asked my local bacon farmer where bacon actually comes from he simply stated, "From the shop, of course!"
As you can imagine, I wasn't particularly satisfied with the answer so I decided it was time to consult Steam. That was when I happened upon a [great co-operative, massively fun and totally entertaining] game known as Blood and Bacon. Within the game I learned where it was that the blood and bacon that adorns my table every morning at breakfast actually comes from. I also learned of the methods used to acquire said blood and bacon as the game allows you to play as one of the skeletons or undead vikings who go out onto their ranches every day for 101 days after getting their briefing from their wall mounted ranch owner. Such methods include, but are not limited to:
• Assault Rifles
• Paintball Gun
• Uzi
• Silenced Pistol
I highly recommend that you purchase this highly educational game and help yourself better understand where it is that we get our ever loved Blood and Bacon.

It's been a good year for fans of the "less zombies - more survival" theme, and this game is a nice addition to that theme.
This is inherently a game about managing your resources and your condition and keeping yourself fed, warm, healthy and decently equipped. This specific iteration of the Canadian wilderness is empty of people but not of houses, cabins and other locations you can loot from, making this a game more about loot and less about base building or crafting. In fact crafting is minimal (at least at this stage of development), though repairing your equipment is an important aspect of the gameplay. The maps (both of which are relatively small) sport houses/lootable locations at regular, easily walkable distances and they are persistent. The loot however (the type and quantity of which also seems to be more or less persistent) is randomly distributed, offering at least some amount of replayability. The rest of the replayability comes from permadeath: Basically, you die often enough that it will take you a while to explore both maps, small though they may be. Hunting (or at least looting half frozen corpses the wolfs have killed for you) becomes necessary only in later game, when you have unearthed most of the loot and are slowly running low on food. There are at the moment three animals in the game: deer, the wolfs that hunt the deer (and you) and rabbits. You can use traps for the rabbits, and you can attack the wolfs and deer with your fists, a rifle or a hunting knife (both of which you have to find first, and both of which will degrade, so you need to be conservative about your hunting). You can apparently also fish, though I have yet to succeed in ever finding a hook, so there is little I can tell you about that.
You've heard about the wolves, and they deserve their own paragraph. Fighting them melee (when for example they attack you) is very much a twitchy experience of button mashing, one that feels equally "realistic" and annoying to me. Avoiding them (by using fire, flares or decoys, or by giving them a wide berth) is possible, but not always feasible/practical. Frankly, being stuck inside a house for two days because there's two wolves parked right outside and you have no weapons whatsoever isn't my idea of fun, yet it seems to keep happening to me. But I can see where the devs are coming from, and I have heard other players who enjoy that (and are apparently better than me in the twitchy button mashing), so ymmv.
However, there is an easy mode of the game, which makes the wolves basically not an issue. Sadly, it also makes the rest of survival aspects a bit easier. I am still hoping better balance/alternative solution to this design choice will crop up before full release, but you shouldn't count on it. For now just know that if you are coming to this game for the snow and the exploration, you can feel free to play on easy mode and the wolves will ignore you.
This is a promised feature that will apparently get added pre-release, but it isn't here yet. Since this game feels somewhat limited as a sandbox, I am looking forward to the story mode. Theoretically, The Long Dark could be absolutely lifted to the next level with good story mode implementation, it's absolutely a great world to tell stories in. But at this point we have no clue what that's gonna look like, so for now buy it for the sandbox, or wait it out.
There is very little to say here, I absolutely love the art design. The screenshots you see are very representative of the real thing, so if that works for you, you won't be disappointed. The slightly stylized, less-than-realistic but incredibly evocative art style is gorgeous, atmospheric and immersive. The sound design also brilliantly contributes to the atmosphere. This is a beautiful game, even with lowered graphics.
For an early access game, this has been very much a bug free experience for me so far. And while playing this on a laptop not much above min specs, lowering the graphics from ultra to high was enough for a smooth experience, with no lag, small (hardly noticeable during play) fps drops and still stunning visuals.
Finally, here's a
to keep in mind before you make your decision:
: Walking around in the snow, listening to the howling wind is much of the appeal of this game.
: No way around it. Either you're okay with that, or you'll be very frustrated.
: The game doesn't stop while you're staring at your inventory trying to decide which socks to put on. When planning for a two hour tree cutting session, keep in mind the weather may have changed to howling winds and you may be dying of hypothermia when you emerge on the other side of it. (Not being able to break what you're doing in reaction to what's happening is one of my pet peeves with the game, btw.)
: This initially feels, but distinctly is NOT an open world survival game. There are two maps, and they are both small and persistent. You can basically learn where everything is in a couple of successful playthroughs. Also, some of the houses are too shame-y inside, which I find a pity for such small maps.
: There is a more or less set number of items you can find, spread randomly around the map in every new game. What you find when can easily make or break an early game.
: This is not an FPS and it isn't Deer Hunter. You have a rifle with very limited ammo and a knife, and that's about it. And even those degrade btw.
: There are three difficulty modes to pick and choose from. It is a bit unfortunate imo that wanting to avoid the button mashing that constitutes fighting the wolves means also having to play in a mode that seriously nerfs the rest of the survival difficulty, but at least the option is there.
: The Long Dark is a decent, if rather limited, take on the "loot, craft (minimally), repair, manage your resources, manage your condition" type of gameplay. Because of the limited crafting and the reliance on findable loot, there is less flexibility of strategy here than in other games of the genre.
And that inflexibility of viable strategies is for me this is the major negative of the game, the aspect that limits its sandbox mode the most. However, this could theoretically be completely offset with a decent story mode, effectively changing the whole feel of things. As a world to tell stories in, let me reiterate, this could potentially be an absolutely brilliant one. We'll have to wait and see.
EDIT: Please add modding support! This game is screaming for it. :)

This game looked appealing from the store page, but the controls are frustrating to the point of making the game almost unplayable to me. For a game with a similar premise where the controls are actually responsive, check out Rabi-Ribi instead.
EDIT To expand on the problems a bit after spending a bit longer with the game:
The problem is the mechanics of the controls.  In particular:
First, when in an attack animation, including after releasing the attack button for most of a second, the character can't turn around, and the game ignores any attempt to do so.  This means that attempts to attack, stop attacking, and turn around, and then attack again often result in the second attack going the wrong direction because the directional input wasn't accepted.
Second, the character doesn't stop moving in the air when you release the directional input.  You can turn them around by pressing the opposite direction, but the only way to jump off a platform and fall straight down onto one directly below is to do an incredibly awkward zig-zag, pressing left and right repeatedly all the way down.  This mechanic alone makes the platforming sections of the game way harder than they need to be.
Either of these flaws taken alone would seriously reduce the enjoyability of the game, but taken together they are a total deal-breaker.  They're both awful design choices for a platformer, and they go directly against the expectations set by nearly every other game in the genre.
Beyond the controls themselves, the game has a few other more forgivable flaws.  For example, it lacks any "continue" or "reload from checkpoint" facility.  In a game where death is frequent and expected, going through the extra two or three screens to load your save game from the title screen every time gets annoying quickly.  Also, as other reviews have noted, the weapon-switching system is based on random pick-ups that essentially erase your current weapon, many of them in central areas.  This often creates annoying avoid-the-powerup puzzles when you are simply trying to explore but don't want to lose your current weapon.
