The beginning of Ken Levine's console driven spiritual sucessor to one of the greatest games ever created for the PC. Irrational played it safe and decided that since almost nobody in the console crowd at the time would have ever heard of System Shock 2 that they could simply lift nearly every single plot element and gameplay mechanic from that game while simplifying it for consoles and then import it into their new game and nobody would be the wiser. Foor all intents and purposes it seems to have worked. When a game is a "spiritual sucessor" you can just jack everything and repaint it a new color.
In place of Shock2's psionics are the plasmids, in place of hybrids are splicers, in place of SHODAN is Fontane, and in place of cyber modules it's ADAM.
Bioshock was a highly regarded game inspite of being almost completely unoriginal. Which isn't to say it isn't a playable game, yet it's clear that it was built more with the consoles in mind rather than a PC, mouse controls are never quite right and between each save load or level transition one must wait for whatever personal sensitvity settings you've placed the mouse at to "kick back in" if you've adjusted them from the defaults at all and I most certainly did.
The psionics/plasmids are not too terrible a trade off since half of Shock2's psi abilites end up being skipped over by veterans while most of the plasmids in Bioshock serve some function for the various playstyles a person may choose to adopt in Bioshock. However gunplay and firearms are rather weak and almost entirely propped up by the research, weapon upgrades, and the tonic system.
One must research the various monsters roaming the city of Rapture to gain advantage of them, often not a big deal as you simply snap photos while being shot at. The real problem comes from needing to keep the very best tonics for your methods of dealing damage and finding all the upgrade machines located in the city while accepting the fact that some weapons are simply more efficent at dealing damage than others. The ability to craft addtional special ammo also helps make up some of the difference at the health and damage of enemies continues to upscale throughout the game and while you can buy newer versions of plasmids it's often better to wait until the third and last version is available before spending any precious adam (an exploit fixed in Bioshock 2).
So at best the gameplay in Bioshock is often just average with the occasional fight against a Big Daddy in order to get a Little Sister for more ADAM breaking up the monotony and even those are trivialized by the Vita Chambers that can bring you back again and again for no penality unless you shut them off (added in a later patch).
Little Sisters are also where the much touted big moral choice comes into the game, a simple yes or no choice to rescue what's suppose to be a little girl. The problem with Bioshock is that all the human chracters look like cheap melted wax figures and not even close to human. So any attempt to dredge up empathy for me failed abysmally and I happily harvested every Little Sister on my first playthorugh. I later found out that the big moral choice leads to three endings, if you so much as harvest one sister you get the bad ending with a sad voice, if you harvest them all you get the bad ending with an angry voice and if you save them all you get the good ending, those deep moral choices I tell ya.
The plot fares no better since it's just literally System Shock 2's plotline all over again, running around Rapture doing chores for a guy you start to trust who turns out to be the actual big bad of the whole game who then tries to kill you once he has everything he wants. At the same time someone looked at the cover of Atlus Shrugged and decided it would help make the game deep and philisophical and I think the cover is about as far as they got.
Bioshock is just a pale immitation of System Shock 2, but for a lot of people it's their first exposure to the "Shock" series even though it doesn't belong to it at all.

I'll go into this review by category first, then personal thoughts.
Gameplay: difficult to convey on my end, as I went keyboard and mouse the whole way (still not computer savvy enough to know how to set up a controller), which is decidely not ideal, as maneuvering in the air is really stiff without a control stick, among other things. That said, was pleasantly surprised at how creative and challenging the game was overall, as while some sections would undoubtedly be pretty easy with said controller, there are things like diving under a glass wall and jumping immediately upon getting under it, or you fall. How a 3D game managed to accurately convey the type of jump normally seen in a Mega Man game, I don't know, but kudos.
Music: varied and always fitting of the settings, from the chill Mafia Town to the epic *spoiler final level*, but special mention goes to boss music, which leads into:
Bosses: Honestly my favorite aspect of the game, there is all of one boss that could be considered average, that being the first against some mooks and an elite mook throwing barrels. Likely intentional, as it is the first boss. Every single subsequent boss is honestly the best selection I have ever seen in a "collectathon" platformer, each with something unique to them, and amazing music that really captures the nature of the fight, particularly the fever-pitch MIDI number used in the super frantic final boss fight.
Graphics: cute, cel-shaded look ensures this game's appearance won't likely age anytime soon, and as a special note really emphasizes the stark contrast the absolutely terrifying manor mission has with the rest of the game. Adorable, cartoony protagonist alone with a psychotist demon-ghost...thing... in a less-cartoony-than-normal location, complete with "music" that won't let you calm down. Props for that one, guys.
Personal thoughts: I notice people attempting to compare this game and Yooka-Laylee quite a bit lately. Honestly, having played and finished both, I don't see a lot of similarities between the two. YL was trying to continue the Banjo-Kazooie legacy, and only really did that. Whether that's good or bad is up to you. A Hat in Time, on the other hand, has far more in common with Super Mario Sunshine, while having Wind Waker-esque cel-shading and movement options reminiscent of Psychonauts, and still managed to develop an identity separate from its inspirations. Honestly, I feel if you liked these games, you'll love this one. I know I did (and am kinda sad it had to end, wouldn't mind seeing further adventures with Hat Kid somewhere down the line, DLC notwithstanding.)

A Hat in Time is a really good game that's worth every dime of its $30 price tag but it has some flaws that needs to be work on.
-For instance the game only has 4 worlds + 1 stage. This makes the game very short, a good ride that ends up with you wanting more.
-A lot of stages have great ideas to them and how you can use your hats to complete the level but most of the good ideas aren't used throughout the game and are only on little bits.
-The enemy variety is very poor and I can see it isn't because of lack of ideas, they have everything they want and they've proven it. Unfortunately, the game falls short on this.
-Towards the end of the act 3, right on the final seconds of the boss, the game shows a laziness it didn't show on all of the other stages. Almost if they decided to cut short the game from there on out. The chapter 4 is underwhelming and easily one of the worst chapters on the game and then they give you the chapter 5 which is actually only one level so I don't count it as a world.
-The game doesn't reward or at least it doesn't have enough incentive for you to explore the world. I did it so it's why I've played 53hours of it and I can say the game doesn't reward you to explore it on its entirely. Because of this the game feels like a linear level almost every time.
-I think there's not enough hats for you to enjoy. For a game called A Hat in Time, this could've been fixed. Also having only so many tries on the slot machine was a mistake.
Despite all of its flaws, the game still stands up but I think it'd be better to talk about his flaws more than why it is so good, everyone is talking about how good it is but they don't find any flaws.
As for the pros for this game, it has too much to count so I'll simply make a tiny list.
+Charming atmosphere.
+Level design.
+Boss battles and their difficulty. Not too easy and not too hard.
+The music is outstanding.
+Sounds effects are well done and every one is satisfying.
+Our control over the character is over the top, the best platformer controllers I've had the pleasure to play on the last couple of years.
+The writing of the characters are so good, the jokes are on point and they don't use memes every five seconds. They have their own identity and raise it proud.
+Full voice acting to inject more life to the game. While it can't be good for every character, it's worth to mention for a couple of them.
With everything and all I think this game stands out against the huge behemoths of the genre but it needs to work on its flaws if there's a sequel. Then it'd be a master piece.

- Armatization(fusing with another character) simplifies your moveset so much that it takes all skill away from the game.

- Side characters don't get almost any screen time and antagonists are easily the worst in the series.
Verdict: It's still better than Dawn of the New World and Xillia 2. If you're a Tales fan, get it. If you're new to the series, it's better to start with one of the other games.

At first, I assumed this game was a shovelware left 4 dead rip-off, but in time, after playing 31 in-game days, I've learned that this game in fact stands very well on its own. It's a comedic survival shooter with well timed horror elements and gross-out visual puns. Most of the comedic moments are due to the (somehow alive) farmer pinned to the wall with a pitchfork. He's very deadpan and sardonic, and has a voiceline for each day (at least as far as I've played). The shooter elements work very well. You have a primary weapon with ammo management and a secondary with infinite bullets. At the start of each game, you pick your two weapons and head out to the farm.
The main antagonists (and only antagonists) of this game are pigs. Boars to be exact. It's hard to tell why they're rampaging, since the plot is very light, but they seem to at least have eaten steroid-laced grain that the farmer kept in his silo (which he tells you for some reason). They can be dismembered and keep going, but ultimately you can gib them completely. This adds another gameplay elements. The gibs have physics and can be kicked, shot or melee'd around, and if you get them into a meat grinder, you can turn them into useful items like ammo, grenades and various buffs for your character. There are a variety of different pigs to kill with different variables and weaknesses.
Now, for the strangely well timed horror elements. Every now and then, you have a night mission. An entertaining enough little time-waster, which is what I installed it for. while a few more parts and skins for us free players would be nice, all-in-all it's pretty solid.
the pay prices, however, REALLY need adjusting. either the cost of things in the store, or the currency ratio. as it stands, a player would have to invest $100+ to acquire
a modest amount of cosmetics, to say nothing of the premium, so honestly buying power needs to be re-examined.
I have been thoroughly enjoying my free play, and while I
wish there was a little more variety in the free skins (for example, while the 'standard' block has something like six different skins, some of the other shapes are decidedly lacking,) I haven't really felt like the freely available content is bad or somehow restricting my creativity.
other users have expressed some gripes about 'snipe-fests' and such, but my experience has been that the various weapon/class combinations are fairly well balanced. I'll admit that I, personally, tend to use a gun-platform artillery piece- effectively a self-propelled gun IN SPAAAAACE- however my experience with the starter ship and since has been that everything is tradeoffs. my artillery platform, for example, tends to fare poorly in close-range slugging matches or duals with small, fast attack craft.
further, you have three weapons:
first you have beams, which are shorter-ranged but powerful due to their precision- a laser-armed ship can often drill down to a ship's core and destroy it in seconds, particularly Frigates equipped with the stun power. needless to say,  these fare best on ships that can rapidly close with an enemy- fast ships like frigates.... or heavier ships equipped with the warp power.
second, you have cannons- cannons are your 'middle-road' option- high damage potential and the best range, but you'd better learn to aim and lead your targets, since their relatively slow projectiles can be dodged, particularity at extreme range by smaller craft like frigates or most starter ships.
last, you have missiles. missiles to the least DPS 'on paper,' and have middling range, HOWEVER, their homing projectiles make them very attractive since aim can be much less precise. I've noticed that 'in practice' missiles have some of the best DPS simply because most of the time
while cannons often miss.
the building system is fairly intuitive- and the pre-battle viewer lets you look at other people's ships, which I strongly recommend, as it can give you a general idea of 'what works and what doesn't' by examining common building techniques.
in general: there isn't a lot here (yet, I'd assume, as the game is still in active development) but what
there is very solid.

I have been playing The Long Dark for several hours now daily for the last several days. I think it is fair to call this game a "singleplayer survival experience." Here's what I find relevant to share with the Steam Community as of now:
The paralleling concept of this game is based on the premise of you, a plane crash victim, surviving in a number of environments abandoned by humanity. With the object of survival /obviously/ in mind, you spawn in a random place on the map and must scavenge for food, water, shelter, and other assets of survival for as many days as possible.
When I first dropped into the game world, I died within 17 hours. I was really edgy and tense playing this game for the first time, expecting wolves at every corner. I played with the lights out, and sure enough, I got a jumpscare when a wolf tackled me and tore my character apart (yay for wolves tearing characters apart!) My second game has been a lot better and I have survived just over a week so far.
Time in the game passes slowly, a day in gameplay is almost a full hour. So with this game, you are guaranteed a great deal of hours that you can spend in the action.
The graphics, as far as indie games go, are pretty good. Textures are occasionally just "O.K." But what is to yell about is the art direction. This said, the overall scenery and ambience that makes up this game is stunning. The sunrise and sunset is beautiful, the snow is pretty, the lighting of user-usable items is realistic and alludes well to the general game world.
It is relevant to acknowledge that unlike some games in the "Survival-Adventure" genre title, this game is not procedurally generated. Meaning: it's not a new map everytime like games such as Minecraft. Despite this being so the case, the game has felt seemingly infinite. After playing a rather decent number of hours, I know I have only scratched the surface of the exploration on the map.
Though it IS an early access title, I think many people will be very pleased by the definite unique style the game brings. It is a nice break from the generic multiplayer gameplay introduced and obviously found in games like DayZ and Unturned. Though it is a neccesity to acknowledge that these games are both fine titles, it is equally fair to acknowledge that their gameplays involve a number of crude dynamics turning other individuals, the environment, zombies, and other things against you in a constantly regenerating world. In the universe of "The Long Dark", once things are gone: they are gone, they will not come back. The realistic experience of limited resources and materials can only be broken by a number of actual renewable resources in the wild. The differences are fair and don't really subtract anything from the gameplay. If anything, they add a great deal of intensity and action to your experience.
It's very fair to say that your only enemy in this game is how slow you move. Failure to keep moving means definite death. You will either certainly starve, freeze, or be torn to shreds by the wild wolves of the wilderness.
Overall, you will like this game, but only if you're up for taking long treks across big chunks of open world, exploring, potentially being attacked by wild animals, and playing with many basic survival game dynamics. At this point, as the game lies as an EAG,
They've done a great deal of work to make this game a wonderful experience so far for myself and hundreds of others, however, there are certain things that could definitely be added, changed, edited, or completely removed.
I look forward to seeing the future development of this game. I will refer back to this review as development progresses to update users here of the changes (game-wise, personally/opinion-wise, etc.) Shouts to Hinterland Studio, and best of luck!
Thank you, hopefully this review has served you well.

After 75 hours of play, I guess I can say that it is a really good one. At first, you have to understand how to survive: the first few tries are extremely hard and seems like it's impossible to survive a week in this environnment. But when you undrstand some basics rules, you can make it to a 100 days without problem. And it's at that moment that the game become boring. At that point, the only interest is to know how many days you can survive doing exactly the same thing over and over again.
So, the pros:
- You have at least 20 hours of play trying to figure out what to do to survive. The anxiety that comes from it is really awesome. And that is the main reason I recommend this game.
- The map is really good and fun to explore.
- The developpers listen to the fans to improve this game and every updates are made in the right direction so far.
- Really good immersive environment.
Cons:
- You can survive way to long if you know how to avoid the wolves. So it's not that much a battle against nature, but a battle to avoid wolves, you should not die from anything except that.
- For now, every ways to get food (trapping, hunting and fishing) gets repetitive and boring quickly.
- Alpha stage... it can change a lot in the next few months.
- Most of the time, you sleep or walk and nothing is happening.
- Lack of ressources diversity for now and not many things to craft.
Overall, good games, that should continue to improve. I recommend it mostly for the first 15 to 20 first hours of play, after that, it depends on how much you like to do the same thing over and over again.

I played this game a couple years ago, so when I saw it greenlit on steam it was an instant buy. It's a classic for me, and so far I've had a blast revisiting it. With that said, let's get to the review.
The story is very basic - Bunny got cursed with cat ears, get's lost, and now it's revenge time! The entire game is very silly in a good way, one boss in particular if you play classic. Speaking of, you can chose between classic and updated graphics and soundtrack. Personally I prefer the classic, but the updated version isn't bad either. Just make sure you play through the thermeowclear plant on classic.
As for the gameplay...
The controls definitely take some getting used to. You can't turn when attacking, there's no ducking, there's at least three different jumps, the dash triggers extremely easy and apparently ledges have a gravity of their own. For some people this completely ruins the game, while others see the unusual controls as part of the challenge. Personally I like how I'm forced to think differently compared to many other platformers.
Speaking of challenge, this game is hard. Some of the secrets are devilishly hard to find, the weapon system requires you consider your choices, the controls force you to think differently, and overall this game was designed specifically to make bunny die. A lot. Collecting upgrades is also incredibly rewarding - there isn't a single one that won't be worth it.
One major feature is the ability to control time, which I love. It creates a nice contrast to the normally chaotic gameplay. It's utilized very well and creates quite a few interesting puzzles. The only thing to keep in mind is that your time ability will be very lackluster until you've collected enough upgrades to unlock the eternal stop.
Other than that, the only thing to keep in mind is that when starting the game, DON'T pick fullscreen. A lot of players have had problems with that, and fixing it, while not too complicated, can still be very annoying.
Some personal tips:
- You can wall jump up a single wall. Exploit this to save time
- Save your Bunny Dolls for the final boss
- There's three different jumps: standing jump, walking jump, and dashing jump.
- Try to find as many items as you can. You're missing out on half the game if you don't.
- There's lots of objects that can be destroyed or even walked through, and there's usually no hint as to where they are. Have fun!

is a colourful* bullet-hell shoot 'em up centred around a hoverboard hipster and his ability to destroy.... Memes?
As
certainly isn't the type of game that would warrant the need for an in-depth story/plot, the lack of one does not make me feel the need to talk about it. Therefore, I will skip this aspect as it does not prove to be a positive or a negative.
For those who are uncertain where to place their palms,
offers three control options consisting of keyboard, controller and mouse. This was a convenient idea that proved to be, well, convenient.
After these controls have appeared to you, the real gameplay commences. The style of which this gameplay identifies to have is quite common in bullet-hell games; nothing new or innovative. Each enemy follows a particular pattern in a hoard filled with the same enemies. Even though there is a small variety of these enemies, their attack style is relatively similar and a lot of the time they do the same attack, just as a different enemy. By far the most enjoyable enemies to face were found in the boss battles. Each boss has a unique pattern and attack style. With 20 of them, they don't exactly get repetitive.
Powerups are dropped throughout your time playing, some of which are simple, ranging from laser enhancements to health upgrades. The others, however, cause total destruction and annihilation of your enemies. In other words: they are a variety special abilities that have a cool down on them, but when you do activate them they produce some very interesting attacks. Despite how satisfying it is to fire a giant rainbow laser beam, they can be quite a disruption to the gameplay. When you pick up these certain powerups, giant text is thrown across the screen blocking your vision. It gets much worse when you actually activate the abilities and you have no idea what is actually going on due to the giant flashing lasers worthy of causing an epileptic seizure.

After your seizure has passed you will find yourself in the situation of having just completed the 6th level (the anticlimactic ending) and getting instructions on how the levels will get harder from here, etc. I believe that the levels then go into an endless mode but I am unsure as, well, the levels get harder from there.
As far as SHMUPs go, this game's gameplay certainly doesn't stand out. But is it enjoyable? Yes, I would say so.
Visually, this game is quite colourful and vibrant as I am sure you would have gathered from the screenshots. The pixel art looks nice, so overall: visually pleasing.
The music is another aspect that was pleasing. It's something simple to listen to as you go about shooting up some celebrities. Regarding sounds, pretty standard.
Now, we have finally reached talking about the strongest selling point for this game: memes. Unfortunately, this is by far the weakest point of the game. You see, memes are easy to make people laugh. Not genuinely laugh, they only laugh because they have been told they should laugh because it's a meme-reference to pop culture. As
pops up on the screen, you're meant to let out a giggle because it's actually
. See how it's funny? Yeah, me neither. The way you have to sit through reading what the celebrities say as you wait to go to the next level is also quite annoying. It's just an annoyance and distraction from the gameplay. I think all I really need to say is that the comedy aspect of the game falls flat, and not on a soft surface**.
✔ 3 ways to control the game
✔ Great bosses
✔ Interesting powerups
✔ Relatively enjoyable gameplay
✔ Visually pleasing
✔ Good music
✘ Uninteresting enemies
✘ Nothing innovative
✘ Picking up and using powerups blocks your vision
✘ Comedy aspect fails
Shooting Stars! is a relatively enjoyable yet surprisingly mediocre entry into a large collection of SHMUPs. It doesn't have anything that stands out (apart from the meme aspect which falls flat) but this is not enough to make it a bad game. I recommend this game to people heavily interested in the genre, otherwise catch it on sale.

Edit: Having delved deeper into this product, I can safely say that it is simply a pathetic excuse for an arcade game, let alone a simulator. For everything that generates a positive experience, there will be a dozen equally large factors that results in nothing else than an unrealistic, buggy, badly designed awful gameplay experience. The devs have demonstrated lacking a fundamental understanding of how SABOT ammunition works, of how to produce an acceptable AI pathfinding, a realistic campaign, crew/unit management, etc. Add to this your average Eastern block "nationalistic" take on Soviet tanks, and the recipe is complete. T-55s on the lowest skill setting will literally speaking return fire, hit and destroy M60s at the highest skill setting with the first round.
If you consider buying this, then keep this in mind: This game is from a developer that doesn't think that you should be able to expect MP in the 21st century simulator. Yes, MP as in multiplayer. Let that stand as an indication to how fundamentally twisted this mess is.
If you're looking for an armour sim, then this is not for you. Just bite the pillow and get Steel Beasts instead and save yourself wasting money on this. It is neither realistic, nor playable.

tells the true story of the Western-backed overthrow of Mohammed Mossadegh, the first democratically-elected Prime Minister of Iran.
As history, it may be a bit confusing for those unfamiliar with the subject, because it's mostly told in reverse (though it sticks to basic facts rather than inundating the player wth obscure details). A perusal of the Wikipedia page regarding the coup might be a good idea before playing.
Gameplay-wise, it's a bit like walking through a picture book, with a few simple environmental puzzles to solve along the way. The game is very short (I finished it in 15 minutes without rushing) and boasts a unique art style: a mash-up of Persian motifs and Western surrealism, with a few agitprop touches along the way. I've never seen anything like it in a game before.
Is it fun to play? I guess so. Given how short it is, it definitely doesn't outstay its welcome. And seeing as it's free-to-play, there's no risk of suffering buyer's remorse. Unless you have a pathological aversion to anything that could even remotely be construed as an "art" game, I would recommend giving it a whirl.
On a personal level, I was very struck by the opening image of Mossadegh as an old man, lying on his deathbed more than a decade after his overthrow. A sound recording of one of Mossadegh's speeches (announcing the nationalization of Iran's oil industry -- an act that galvanized the West to plot his downfall) also struck a nerve. Before playing this game, I was already familiar with the history of the coup and its awful aftermath (the reign of the Shah and his secret police), but I had never given much thought to Mossadegh the
before. It was also the first time I had ever heard his voice, despite having read much about him. In other words,
not only succeeds in bringing to life an essential piece of 20th-century history, but it also humanizes the individual at the center of that story. In so doing, it conveys the sadness and cynicism of the coup in a visceral and memorable way.

If you know me, then you know that I like the 3D platforming genre. Describing games like Rayman 2, Banjo Tooie, and Mario Sunshine as “My childhood” is an understatement. What luck then do I find a kickstarter for a game that claims to take inspiration from not only that genre, but the mentality and spirit from the Golden days of my youth. Naturally, I backed it and began to patiently wait. Come about half a decade later and it’s finally here, a bit after the other large kickstarter 3D collectathon revival game Yooka Laylee. If you’ve read my review on that then you’ll know that while not terrible or anything, that game failed to really hook me and I left it quite disappointed. I then began to fear that the game I kickstarted before was going to end up as a similar flop.
Thankfully my fears were averted as I booted the game up for the first time and began to play. Exploring the controls was a bit of a challenge at first, and figuring out the quirks of our protagonist’s moves took some getting used to. But once I got the hang of it I found myself dashing, double jumping, sprinting and animation canceling my way all around a quirky and playful word that enticed me to find all of its secrets. The game’s music and world is what really sells it, I found myself simply standing or sitting around and appreciating the game’s atmosphere, something I rarely do in any game.
What I like most about the game is how much it loves it’s inspiration. You might scoff at that and think “But Yooka Laylee did the same thing and you didn’t like THAT game!”. Not to sound elitist, but no it did not. Between the constant fourth wall jokes and taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of itself, YL felt more like a parody of its contemporaries rather than a revival. It felt insulting and disrespectful: while at the same time blatantly pandering to the nostalgia blinded fanboys who claim Banjo Kazooie was flawless and any evolution is heresy.
But I digress; Hat in time shows it’s love for those games not by simply parroting them; flaws and all; but instead finding the best in them and figuring out what worked, while also taking a critical eye to what didn’t, or might not anymore. It isn’t lost in the past while making fun of itself, it trusts that the player will meet it halfway and give it a chance, and deliver it does. I haven’t felt this way playing a game since… well those games from my childhood actually.
The missions are varied, the progression is relatively open ended while also being quite simple, the moves you earn as the game goes on are always useful at any time in the game (With MAYBE one exception that feels a little contrived), the characters are sometimes funny, often sympathetic, and almost alway charming in their own way. The voice acting was an interesting touch, but I’m not confident in saying that it was essential, and frankly sometimes it can be a bit trite. Thankfully if you don’t like it or just don’t care you can turn it off, or even replace it with something a bit more nostalgic if you find the right secret.
Don’t mistake it as nothing but a saccharine romp all the way through. The various places you go all offer up different kinds of experiences and challenges. A surprising amount of levels involve a rudimentary stealth mechanic, some will test your ability to explore and traverse, while others offer straightforward platforming challenges. There’s plenty of skipping around being happy to be sure, but there’s also some real laughs, offbeat silliness, heartfelt sincerity, and even a few actual scares along the way. Against all odds, by the ending I felt myself genuinely touched by the game, and that’s high praise coming from someone like me.
What I can’t say however is that it’s perfect. The sectioned off design ala Mario 64/Sunshine is the kind of structure that I feel was a bit dated, though it’s much less egregious than those examples. Even once you get used to the controls there are a few quirks about them that I feel could have used ironing out. (Ex. Can’t move after you slide, you have to JUMP out?) The camera also sometimes clips through walls or spazzes out if it moves at the wrong angle. Some parts of the game seem like they have a notable lack of polish. The main story seems to be a bit short and not as demanding on players, and overall it might be a bit too much on the easy side, especially if you’ve played the games that it aspires to. Then again, it’s less challenging difficulty suits its overall feel-good atmosphere and childlike tone. It’s not really meant to push your limits unless you seek those challenges out yourself.
All in all, A Hat in Time succeeds where Yooka Laylee fails: Giving that spark of wonder and joy. Short and flawed as it may be, Hat in Time delivers on the promise of what it means to run, jump, and fly through a world worth exploring. The game is overflowing with charm, heart and soul, a passion and love for games matched only by us, the player.

Yep, this is it. No doubt about it. This is the modernized 3D platformer you've been waiting for.
This game has amazingly fluid controls that demonstrate a masterful understanding of how a 3D platformer should feel. You can tell they've put a lot of effort into making this game fun to play. After much thought, I can even say that this is a new standard for 3D platformers. This game is at the top of its genre.
In fact, let me just go ahead and talk about the controls for a minute or ten. This game has Mario Sunshine's most fun moves, without the somewhat weird and occasionally tedious water mechanics of the FLUDD. You can dive on your belly and then do a front flip right after landing to gain momentum. Also, you can cancel a dive mid-air, so you can quickly clear small gaps without having to wait for your character to land on the ground.
Speaking of ground, there is a sprint ability (the only one I'll spoil, cause you get it early and it's a core part of the gameplay), which allows you to long-jump. You can also double-jump, but you can't double-jump after doing a long-jump, so it adds this fun little mindgame of "okay, long-jumping is faster and I can go farther, but am I gonna have enough verticality to clear the gap without a double-jump?" Of course, once you've mastered the controls and the heights and lengths of your jumps, this will all happen naturally.
All these things mean that you have much more air control in this game than you ever had in Mario 64 or even Sunshine with its slow jetpack. This is great because it feels more tactile, like you're always controlling the character, and it makes it possible to recover from some mistakes if you're quick enough.
Note: I realize that air control being a good thing is subjective. You may very well prefer Mario 64's movement and how you really gotta commit to every jump. But, personally, no air control just means you get to control your character less frequently, which isn't as fun. But one isn't inherently better designed than the other.
Anyway, here's the best part: No transformations. No underwater levels. Basically, nothing that would slow down the gameplay to a floaty halt and make you lose half your moveset and kill the fun. That's right, no more walking back to some pad with Mumbo's face on it just so you can activate a thing for Banjo.
This is just pure, distilled, 3D platforming perfection, without any boring filler. Thank you.
I'm not done. Now it's time to talk about the fantastic soundtrack. ♫
It's just really great. It has some of that good Leitmotif stuff which we all love in gaming, where a melody re-occurs at multiple points throughout the game but in different styles and instruments. And it's got some legit groovy tracks that I'm going to listen to outside of the game, and some really majestic and wonderful tunes as well, always fitting with the theme of the level.
Speaking of levels. They are overflowing with memorable moments and charming characters. It's very much a Nintendo game at heart, and they certainly did not have Nintendo's budget or decades of experience to pull it off. And yet they did.
The game may not be very long, but it's still a decent length if you don't rush through it. Take screenshots, try different outfits. Chill in your favorite world for a bit, jump around and have fun. But if you want the game to move along fast, it will certainly respect your time and keep you entertained from start to finish.
So, who would I recommend this game to? Well, everyone, of course. But if I had to be more specific, I'd say this game scratches the following itches very well: Mario Sunshine. Wind Waker. Paper Mario. It perfectly emulates those GameCube vibes and it has a bit of N64 love sprinkled in there too. If the GameCube was your favorite console, or if you like good 3D platformers, or y'know, good games in general,
then you've gotta give this game a peck.
9.5 / 10

A lot of crap gets given to Steel Armor - Blaze of War because there are only two operational tank models to use.  That is a bit of a misconception.  Yes there are only the T-62 and M60A1 to be driven and operated... BUT in most battles you are a part of a tank squad, platoon, company or all three, therefore you are able to interchange between multiple numbers of M60A1s and T-62s.  You are also able to give orders to Infantry, APCs, other tank variations like the T-55, Chieftain, and Olifant, Aircraft and other units via the Tactical Map. I am an avid "Tales of" fan. My favorites include Symphonia, The Abyss, and I enjoyed Vesperia for the most part.
Key aspects of enjoyable "Tales of" gameplay include immersive environments and narrative, unique and tasteful dungeons, and rewarding combat. I will discuss each of these in comparison to past Tales games in order to evaluate Zestiria.
Tales of Zestiria has already shown me that the dungeons and environments are both an eyesore and mindless. Even the massive towns and cities don't have the graceful and fantastic architecture and layout we've come to love. The heights of Baticul in The Abyss come to mind. Zestiria features Ladylake, the spiritual successor to Baticul, and besides sharing a similar sillhouette, Ladylake comes off as an empty shell of a town. The wide expanses of town are over-textured in order to hide bland and recycled geometry. All pathways are marked by walls and posts. Nothing but knee high walls to dictate where you walk and what qualifies as "town". The shops and inns dont even have signage or unique features. They are just a door you are allowed to go through amidst dozens of fake doors. In comparison, Tales of the Abyss featured obviously marked inns and shops. Looking at my minimap for a tiny icon indicating the door is an inn breaks immersion hard.
I am just reaching the first moment in the first dungeon, and I cannot recommend this one. At this point in the story in Symphonia, we were in the holy tower which featured unique architecture and a two-level block puzzle. The puzzles were unique, and we even got to fight big stone golems, the first large/tough enemies that weren't bosses. In contrast, Zestiria has me walking through greebled hallways with no unique architectural features fighting nothing but bats and slimes. Rectangle hallways into square rooms into more hallways. I have not encountered a single puzzle.
In terms of story, Zestiria was promising to me in that it directly draws from Arthurian Legend. I am a big fan of the legends of king arthur and his holy knights. You are a king-arthur like character with a galahad agenda, and it seems the world is based on medieval times. I was even intrigued by the inclusion of story-changing choices. For example, I had the opportunity to give away a personal prized posession, or the prized posession of a friend in order to get into a forbidden area. I really weighed my morals before choosing, but in less than an hour the item I gave away came back to me. It was senseless. Why did I care at all?
The combat is Zestiria's only saving grace. It is tactile, wieldly, and pretty. It's complexity must really shine in the late game, but I won't find out because I don't want to play the game anymore. What do I care about quality combat if the world and story I do it in are bland and poorly designed? As much as I want to give Zestiria a second chance, I cannot stomach the obviously uninspired world anymore.

As I write this, the number one "Most Helpful" review is negative.  It says that this is only for developers, that this is Davey Wreden's response to negative reviews, that it only exists to show that making games is difficult.
That is wrong.
This is the most moving game I have played in a long time, and it represents many things.  To some, this game may represent hope, to others it may be freedom of expression, to others it may be the fear of being the same as everyone else, etc.  This game may not be for everyone, but I guarantee that it will be an extremely moving experience for anyone.
Davey Wreden - You probably won't read this, but I hope you reconcile with Coda.  He must understand that you were only trying to help (but publishing all of his games may push him further away).  I loved the Stanley Parable and hope to see more games.
Coda - It's even less likely that you'll read this, but your games are genuinely interesting and made me think about life in ways that I haven't before.  I don't care if you never release a single game again, even to close friends or family, but please don't stop making games.  They are too unique, and even if no one other than you sees them, their very existence will be enough.
To both of you: thank you.

Are you looking for a hard metroidvania with time-controlling abilities? Then this is for you! Just keep in mind that the controls can be clunky. Personally I like the extra layer of challenge it brings, but for some players this has dragged down (or even outright ruined) their experience. The story is very silly (but fun!) so this is a game you play mainly for the gameplay/challenge.
Unless you really, really love bunny girls or have a strong craving for a metroidvania, I'd recommend you wait with this one until it's on sale.
I played this game a couple years ago, so when I saw it greenlit on steam it was an instant buy. It's a classic for me, and so far I've had a blast revisiting it. With that said, let's get to the review.
The story is very basic - Bunny got cursed with cat ears, get's lost, and now it's revenge time! The entire game is very silly in a good way, one boss in particular if you play classic. Speaking of, you can chose between classic and updated graphics and soundtrack. Personally I prefer the classic, but the updated version isn't bad either. Just make sure you play through the thermeowclear plant on classic.
As for the gameplay...
The controls definitely take some getting used to. You can't turn when attacking, there's no ducking, there's at least three different jumps, the dash triggers extremely easy and apparently ledges have a gravity of their own. For some people this completely ruins the game, while others see the unusual controls as part of the challenge. Personally I like how I'm forced to think differently compared to many other platformers.
Speaking of challenge, this game is hard. Some of the secrets are devilishly hard to find, the weapon system requires you consider your choices, the controls force you to think differently, and overall this game was designed specifically to make bunny die. A lot. Collecting upgrades is also incredibly rewarding - there isn't a single one that won't be worth it.
One major feature is the ability to control time, which I love. It creates a nice contrast to the normally chaotic gameplay. It's utilized very well and creates quite a few interesting puzzles. The only thing to keep in mind is that your time ability will be very lackluster until you've collected enough upgrades to unlock the eternal stop.
Other than that, the only thing to keep in mind is that when starting the game, DON'T pick fullscreen. A lot of players have had problems with that, and fixing it, while not too complicated, can still be very annoying.
Some personal tips:
- You can wall jump up a single wall. Exploit this to save time
- Save your Bunny Dolls for the final boss
- There's three different jumps: standing jump, walking jump, and dashing jump.
- Try to find as many items as you can. You're missing out on half the game if you don't.
- There's lots of objects that can be destroyed or even walked through, and there's usually no hint as to where they are. Have fun!

With nearly any creative software there is a major advantage and a major flaw. The major flaw is that once you've got your hands on the software, it can be a little overwhelming and slightly complicated trying to figure out how to make this, that and the other. The major advantage is that when you've figured out HOW to make this, that and the other, the only two limits are your imagination and your willingness to spend hours on end constructing your little world.
My advice for this software? It can be narrowed down to three major points:
1: Strike while the iron's hot in the sales.
I got this for just over £5 in a sale, where it would normally be £90 or so. My immediate discovery upon this was: BUY BUY BUY!! I'm happy to have had this golden opportunity.
2: Learn the system as best you can.
If you're too lazy to figure it out yourself, you can always check online: there are plenty of tutorials and Q&A posts to help you out with making this, that and the other a virtual reality.
3: Get creative, make it original.
You can import music and graphics and you're still fighting slimes with Eric the Axe Master? There's no need for that. And besides, RPG Maker games don't earn internet popularity through giving players the same old stuff.
This is probably the part where your willingness is tested: if you are happy to take a bite out of your time playing other games to create the music and sprites for your world, then it will be worth it. If you decide to change the gameplay about by importing some new scripts as well, then your efforts will be rewared with praise and possibly some money to add to your Steam wallet.
If not, then you should just be happy like I am that you waited for the sales to buy this software, and when you can find the time, you have said software. Seriously though, you pay £90 for something you could get for £5 in the sales and you WILL kick yourself when you realise the massive mistake you've made. You know you will.

Date: 2/24/16
Review Number: 26
Game: Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 devils.
From (Creator Publisher): Platine Dispositif
Played On: Steambox w/Controller
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 30 Minutes
Review:
The next game to come up on the randomizer, another indie platformer, this time a game called Bunny Must Die long subtitle goes here by Platine Dispositif.  Now, indie platformers haven't necessarily been kind to me for the last several reviews, and when I initially had a couple of controller issues, I was concerned that that trend was going to continue.  However, after about five minutes of tweaking the default controller settings and I was surprised to find myself correcting... myself.  Behind the slightly subpar graphics and slightly off controls is a surprisingly snappy metroidvania clone.  As this is an indie game created by a smaller developer, the game seems significantly smaller than most other clones of the kings of platformers, however the gameplay is interesting, and the unique ability of the main character to both slow and reverse time is a refreshing new take on the old weapon/missile pattern.  Both the voices and the soundtrack are nothing necessarily special but fit the game very well in both tone and style, though the lack of voiceovers during the cutscenes seems like a miss.  The gameplay in general is delightfully metroid, with only a few minor flaws.  The control scheme is simple enough, with three main buttons to handle everything, though the controls are not always the most precise, and I would often find myself jumping in the opposite direction I was moving, which can become frustrating in precision platforming.
All in all, I feel like this game is certainly worthy of the genre, even if it's nothing special within it.  A decent buy if it's on sale, especially if you're not currently playing one.
Game’s Fate: Kept.  The last metroidvania I actually played actively was the trope namer, so until a better one comes up on the randomizer, this one will do nicely.
Buy/No Buy:  It's pretty good.  I know there are better ones out there, but if you see this on sale, it's totally worth the money.  Buy.

I have been playing The Long Dark for several hours now daily for the last several days. I think it is fair to call this game a "singleplayer survival experience." Here's what I find relevant to share with the Steam Community as of now:
The paralleling concept of this game is based on the premise of you, a plane crash victim, surviving in a number of environments abandoned by humanity. With the object of survival /obviously/ in mind, you spawn in a random place on the map and must scavenge for food, water, shelter, and other assets of survival for as many days as possible.
When I first dropped into the game world, I died within 17 hours. I was really edgy and tense playing this game for the first time, expecting wolves at every corner. I played with the lights out, and sure enough, I got a jumpscare when a wolf tackled me and tore my character apart (yay for wolves tearing characters apart!) My second game has been a lot better and I have survived just over a week so far.
Time in the game passes slowly, a day in gameplay is almost a full hour. So with this game, you are guaranteed a great deal of hours that you can spend in the action.
The graphics, as far as indie games go, are pretty good. Textures are occasionally just "O.K." But what is to yell about is the art direction. This said, the overall scenery and ambience that makes up this game is stunning. The sunrise and sunset is beautiful, the snow is pretty, the lighting of user-usable items is realistic and alludes well to the general game world.
It is relevant to acknowledge that unlike some games in the "Survival-Adventure" genre title, this game is not procedurally generated. Meaning: it's not a new map everytime like games such as Minecraft. Despite this being so the case, the game has felt seemingly infinite. After playing a rather decent number of hours, I know I have only scratched the surface of the exploration on the map.
Though it IS an early access title, I think many people will be very pleased by the definite unique style the game brings. It is a nice break from the generic multiplayer gameplay introduced and obviously found in games like DayZ and Unturned. Though it is a neccesity to acknowledge that these games are both fine titles, it is equally fair to acknowledge that their gameplays involve a number of crude dynamics turning other individuals, the environment, zombies, and other things against you in a constantly regenerating world. In the universe of "The Long Dark", once things are gone: they are gone, they will not come back. The realistic experience of limited resources and materials can only be broken by a number of actual renewable resources in the wild. The differences are fair and don't really subtract anything from the gameplay. If anything, they add a great deal of intensity and action to your experience.
It's very fair to say that your only enemy in this game is how slow you move. Failure to keep moving means definite death. You will either certainly starve, freeze, or be torn to shreds by the wild wolves of the wilderness.
Overall, you will like this game, but only if you're up for taking long treks across big chunks of open world, exploring, potentially being attacked by wild animals, and playing with many basic survival game dynamics. At this point, as the game lies as an EAG,
They've done a great deal of work to make this game a wonderful experience so far for myself and hundreds of others, however, there are certain things that could definitely be added, changed, edited, or completely removed.
I look forward to seeing the future development of this game. I will refer back to this review as development progresses to update users here of the changes (game-wise, personally/opinion-wise, etc.) Shouts to Hinterland Studio, and best of luck!
Thank you, hopefully this review has served you well.

After 75 hours of play, I guess I can say that it is a really good one. At first, you have to understand how to survive: the first few tries are extremely hard and seems like it's impossible to survive a week in this environnment. But when you undrstand some basics rules, you can make it to a 100 days without problem. And it's at that moment that the game become boring. At that point, the only interest is to know how many days you can survive doing exactly the same thing over and over again.
So, the pros:
- You have at least 20 hours of play trying to figure out what to do to survive. The anxiety that comes from it is really awesome. And that is the main reason I recommend this game.
- The map is really good and fun to explore.
- The developpers listen to the fans to improve this game and every updates are made in the right direction so far.
- Really good immersive environment.
Cons:
- You can survive way to long if you know how to avoid the wolves. So it's not that much a battle against nature, but a battle to avoid wolves, you should not die from anything except that.
- For now, every ways to get food (trapping, hunting and fishing) gets repetitive and boring quickly.
- Alpha stage... it can change a lot in the next few months.
- Most of the time, you sleep or walk and nothing is happening.
- Lack of ressources diversity for now and not many things to craft.
Overall, good games, that should continue to improve. I recommend it mostly for the first 15 to 20 first hours of play, after that, it depends on how much you like to do the same thing over and over again.

This was kind of a "so bad it's good" game for a while, but then it got frustrating enough to wrap back around into "so bad it's terrible" territory.
Like. The main problem comes down to the stiff, archaic controls. For one, stuff just flat out doesn't work sometimes, and random stuff just happens at other times. Double tapping to dash is always a bad mechanic, but here it doesn't even work half the time, and the other times you'll arbitrarily dash without meaning to. There's two different main jumps, a straight up jump that's taller and a lower spinning jump, and naturally the lower jump is useless in platforming and basically pointless to have at all. There's a dash kick you can use by attacking while dashing, which will sometimes arbitrarily stop for no reason and get you stuck not moving. TURNING AROUND in this game is a busted mechanic, even, you won't face the direction you're holding unless you perform the specific turning around animation first, and yes, this means you'll attack the wrong way quite often.  There's also three kinds of wall jump (though the game only tells you about one) which is great when wall jumping by itself is already super finnicky (seriously, worse than Super Metroid's wall jump... geez), and then sometimes a different wall jump than the one you want will activate (the low kicking jump is utterly useless and likes to trigger quite often). Basically, as you can see, nothing works. Outright. Nothing. It's basically one of the worst controlling games I've ever played; at least La-Mulana is consistent with its weird mechanics.
So yeah, the controls alone make the game a failure, but then it's not like the rest of the game is great design-wise; it's generally pretty awful. Most of the boss designs are just spamfests; the first boss and the fourth boss are basically the only exceptions, the only bosses that feel actually skill-based instead of luck-based. The final boss especially is a seven phase monstrosity that boils down to just a battle of attrition more than anything else. And naturally the controls make the platforming pretty bad, though even then there's a lot of one-block jumps and weird wall jumps and with how arbitrary damage output of various things is it's just not fun. Spikes do a ton of damage and there are a few enemies who randomly do a ton of damage too, while everything else does relatively little in comparison. There's also a few attacks that stunlock you, even though other times you have decently long invincibility frames... who needs consistency? The puzzle designs are mixed, there's a few clever ones but a lot of them are just "do section fast, if not, rewind time if you can". And exploring in this game... is not fun at all, because of how awkward the game is to play. On top of that, secrets are hidden in pretty universally mean places, random blocks in the wall, fake walls guarded by breakable spikes (not all spikes are breakable, notably), switches hidden behind foreground objects, just, all sorts of stupid stuff, I didn't bother exploring without consulting a guide to make sure I wouldn't miss anything.
So basically... the controls are garbage and the game design is garbage. It's... not a fun game in the slightest. It was a little fun in the earlier areas I guess, before all the game's problems really showed up in spades, but any part of the back half of the game was just filled with frustration and bitterness, it does not feel like this game likes players in the slightest.
The graphics are okay though and the soundtrack is quite good, but that's not, like, going to save a fundamentally unfun game in the slightest :P

A cautious recommendation on this one. A colourful game with good shoot em up style but I believe the games main focus, the comedy, is where it really falls down on.
Let's start with the gameplay. Shooting stars is a rather standard SHMUP as it goes. You control a character with your mouse, and can only shoot up using the left click. Enemies have standard bullet hell style patterns. Nothing out of the ordinary exists here in the simple mechanics of the game.
Power ups also exist in shooting stars. You have the simple ones, usually food of some kind, that upgrade your laser ability. They add extra beams, missiles or stronger beams and more. You can get health and armour upgrades. These are all nice but once again nothing much out of the ordinary yet. The real pleasure comes from the ultimate ability. Pressing right click on your mouse will activate this. You don't start with any but find them in powerup boxes throughout levels, There are tonnes of different abilities you can get and each are very satisfying to use.
Enemy design is a mixed bag. Some are way too simple in terms of their bullet patterns or assemblisation of enemies. It would be ok if there were just a few of these simple enemies but too many exist which can make it boring at times. There are few other more creative enemies that have unique patterns but not enough I feel. Most are just reskins using exactly the same bullet patterns which can make gameplay feel stale quickly.
The real effort has been put into the design of the bosses. These have very creative attacks and bullet patterns associated with them. Bosses are very satisfying to fight. Each are unique and I found none that were reskins. They become very difficult to fight while avoiding all the fury of bullets your presented with.
The biggest issue I found with gameplay is that i'm not positive if theres an actual end to the game. There are 5 levels in each gameplay session which each exist with there own boss. Once I completed the final boss on the 5th level I expected there to be a big ending. Instead I was presented with continued gameplay that just increased in difficulty. Needless to say I was very disappointed after all the effort I put in. So i'm not positive if an actual end exists or if it just continues increasing in difficulty.
Another small issue I found was with certain effects obscuring gameplay vision. Some powerups had overly large areas of attack that when used would leave the almost the entirety of the gameplay area not visible. Also after certain achievements in kills you would get a large message on the screen titled "rampage" which also obscured the area for a few seconds. These effects often caused me to loose health due to being unable to see enemies or bullets. This was a minor annoyance but could definitely do with being changed.
Now that i've got all the gameplay aspects out the way i'll move onto to the comedy aspect. The way in which the developers chose to do comedy is through the bosses. Each boss of a level is a famous celebrity/ video game character. There are people such as Miley Cyrus, Gabe Newell, Chuck Norris, Daft Punk and tonnes more. They speak quotes before each level. This is the part that's meant to be funny. The issue I have is that the references are often so obscure that I don't actually find it funny. In very few of the bosses did I actually get a little giggle out of it.
The only other comedy aspects present was sometimes through pickups. These were sometimes references to internet memes. They had short quotes on them which were also meant to be funny. These two things were the only comedy aspects present. Usually the fact that a game isn't really funny wouldn't be a problem for me. But the problem I have with this game is that the steam page seems to show the game being very focused on being funny. I just found the comedy to be way too obscure and mostly just immature and unfunny.
The graphics themselves is something I found particularly satisfying. An intriging pixel design with colour thrown about everywhere. Seriously this game is one of the most colourful I have seen. It's the first thing that caught my attention towards this game. But I know it's standard of the SHMUP genre usually but a minor annoyance is the fact of the bars either side instead of being a full screen game. Although it is also clear from some other aspects that this game is a mobile port. A wonderful soundtrack is also present to go along great with the graphic choice. A nice selection of dance/ techno tracks to make fighting enemies particularly satisfying.
Overall shooting stars is a rather standard SHMUP for the most part. It's definitely not a bad game, but it really doesn't do much to build upon the already well established genre. The developers attempts at comedy didn't go down well with me but it may appeal more to other audiences. I'm also not sure on the amount of replayability. I've played 1 hour and feel like i've played enough of it now. As I said it's a very cautious recommendation but it's probably worth a try if your a big fan of shoot em up games.

Steel Armor is a challenging, detailed game that combines turn-based strategy with real-time tactical battles.  You play the role of a battallion commander using a tank as a command vehicle.  As a result, there is no floating camera to move around the battlefield and you only directly participate in a battle if you can actually enter a tank in that battle.
During battle, you can take the position of any member of a tank crew while communicating with the rest of the crew as each member performs his functions.  You will have to command your troops from the commander's station of your tank, with not much more than your map, binoculars, tank optics and radio.
Each battle happens organically throughout each historically accurate campaign and can involve anywhere from a couple of sqauds to hundreds of units.  Combined arms plays an important role.  There are heavy and light armored vehicles, air units, anti-armor and anti-air units, heavy and light machine guns, artillery, mortars and various kinds of infantry.
If you enjoy GTOS, this game uses many of the same mechanics.  It's a great buy for GTOS fans because it brings you to the first-person level for battles, creating new challenges and a different kind of immersion.
Like other Graviteam titles, this game is dificult to learn but rewarding.  The included training missions are a big help.
Buy this if you are a fan of historical war simulations that emphasize meticulously realistic mechanics, especially if you enjoy GTOS.

The missions are exactly the same as they were in the prototype, while this is not nessecearily a bad thing, I do think there could be much more to it, such as breaking into places or actually trying to acomplish a task with the help of your ability, it would be very fun to delve deeper into it rather than just "killing red guys".
Overall I would like to reccomend this game however the price is way too high for such a little amount of play time and content, save your money and wait until this goes on a proper sale to buy it.

I've been playing a (I have to admit) cracked version and waiting for this game to come to Steam for years, and I bought the game the moment I saw it on Steam. I think it deserves every single cent, and is probably the most detailed post WWII tank simulator that everyone can reach and afford (who manages to get their hands on a copy of Steel Beasts anyway.)
The attention to detail in this game is great, both in the tactics phase and in the real battle phase. Supply, fuel, ammo and fatigue levels, weapon and armor characteristics are simulated quite nicely in the tactics phase. But even if you don't care for commanding platoons and you're just playing the game to simply hang out in a tank, the fact that this game has 3d interiors is enough of a reason to buy it for armor enthusiasts.
Attention to detail results in a quite unforgiving game especially in terms of vision and damage; more often than not, battles consist of scanning for enemies than actually shooting at them. This may feel underwhelming for Rambo wannabes seeking to crash tanks into helos and stuff. When things get hot, though, the sound of rounds ricocheting off your armor alone is enough to force you into a fetal position, covering your ears.
The 3 campaigns that are in game do a good job of representing the common types of warfare: Inf vs Armor, Armor vs Armor, Combined Arms vs Combined Arms. Note that the attention to detail is true for the campaigns, too. They aren't story driven, so they aren't necessarily supposed to be won if you follow a path or something. Sometimes you seal your fate in the 3rd turn with a less-than-optimal move, and you don't realize it until the 6th turn when the enemy crushes you utterly.
That might be just me, but the graphics look better than it did on the non-Steam version. Yes, it shows age, but it is still on par with ArmA 2 which should be more than enough if it is a simulation you're looking for.
It should be noted that the game does leave some things to be desired.
First of all, the game doesn't make a serious attempt to, I don't know, be learned? And I'm not talking about the difficulty or complexity level here. The tutorials (which AFAIK simply didn't exist as separate levels in the non-Steam version), while nice additions, are far from adequately polished. Failure to read one sentence of essential info when it appears on screen can force you to restart the whole tutorial level, as the game offers you no easy way of going back to previous messages.
Optimization seems to be a slight issue. I have no problem getting a constant 55-60 FPS like 90% of the time. But especially when moving in a column with other tanks, the dust kicked up by their treads cause the FPS to dip all the way down to 20-25. This is not a game-breaking performance failure though; you simply can't see and shoot through that dust and smoke anyway, so the lowered FPS doesn't impair your aiming, it just slightly annoys you for a few seconds until the dust settles.
The menus kind of feel more clunky than the actual gameplay, and you would have thought that driving a 40-ton tank would feel clunky. Sometimes pressing the buttons doesn't really do anything; you have to go for that sweet spot that's like, not in the middle of the button and also not on the edge of it or something. You will figure it out.
Also, currently it seems like you can't assign more than one button for an action. And I haven't yet managed to get this game to change the control scheme or detect my gamepad, but that might just be the inability on my part. (I appreciate all suggestions)
Long story short, SABOW is an essential part of any simulation collection. As in any military sim, it is an acquired taste. Learn to enjoy its strong points and ignore its weak ones, and you have a game you will keep coming back for more. Also, just look at that abbreviation.
SABOW! I BROKE YOUR ♥♥♥♥♥♥ TANK AND YOU ARE DEAD!

I wholeheartedly recommend this simulator. The immersion factor is 10/10, from the rain, to the vegetation, to the light and people around you. To how they act and how the war is waged in this simulator.
Very few games or simulators can make me feel like I'm there, this did. The African vegetation is spot on, and the lighting coupled with the trees and grass immerses you to no end. It makes you feel like you are a tiny battalion of tanks lost in nowhere, and the sight of a village is both a great thing and bad, as it may mean more fighting. May mean fighting? Yes, because the missions are dynamic, based on a dynamic campaign. So no mission is alike, and giving you a replayability like no other!
The dynamic campaign is really deep and interesting, and you can also choose to ignore it if you so like. The controls are intuitive and it has a nice UI in case you feel lost with buttons.
Everything is nicely explained, and including the training missions. Which is what I suggest you do before you venture any deeper. Even the campaign has tooltips and explaining what you can do.
I would also like to make a special mention to the incredible engine they have here. The mud, terrain deformation, and even small rivers and banks. For example, if a tank crosses a small creek, and with it lowering the terrain further, which will cause the tank behind you to be unable to cross. This is because the small crossing ended up damaged by your tanks track.
Amazing details like that make one hell of a difference in anything!
I also would like to mention how interesting it is the repairing mechanic, watching your crew repair your tank, to the ballistics simulation and how even small details are modelled. Like when it rains, your tank gets shiny and wet.
The developers are very friendly, and they answer all questions, especially on their own forums. They are still updating this gem, and there is a patch almost every month.

I'm not sure where to begin at the moment. Part of me loves this game and wants it to succeed so very much, and part of me is very bitter at the moment.
I'll try my best to explain why, and you can make the call based on that, whether or not it's worth your time.
Leveling, and getting to max level is not bad at all and in fact if that's all you intend to do, I say play it, you have nothing to lose really and things are quite fun especially if you have multiple friends to play with. The art is well done, the gameplay is quite smooth and it's a fun casual relaxed experience which I think anyone can enjoy really.
Here's where it starts to get gritty, and you'll either hate it or love it for the most part. Once you're maxed level, and you want to start to improve your gear, there's really not much left to be desired. You'll play the same maps you were playing, only with higher HP monsters and higher damage. And you'll not see any variation from that at all. Allow me to reiterate:
Onslaught, previously Survival in Dungeon Defenders, is ♥♥♥♥. Literally. I'm not going to sugar coat it, it's a big steaming pile of ♥♥♥♥. Literally the only reason people run it, is on a super low difficulty, so they can farm gold. Rewards suck. The time it takes to do sucks. Nothing special about it at all. Don't even waste your time, IMO.
Incursion, a slightly different variation from maps, but really nothing different other than throwing mass quantities of mobs at you in each lane. Yeah I guess it's harder but it really doesn't bring anything new to the table. Nothing new, just more mobs, more HP and more damage. Sounds so fun right?
Nightmare 1-4 is my gripe with the game, I suppose. In DD1, we had one nightmare mode and that was it. This game tried to change that and it's pretty much fell flat on its face. There is no difference between Nightmare 1-4 outside of damage numbers. So much engaging gameplay. So you farm the same enemies while you're leveling, to continue farming the same enemies through nightmare 1-4 only scaled higher. Absolutely nothing different, you'll run the same maps until your eyes bleed, and then more.
Pets are bland. Seriously if you played DD1, you're going to be very disappointed here. Liked that mega chicken and it's badass DPS from DD1? Well sorry to say you're going to laugh when you see the pets here.
Overall, this game lacks the fun that Dungeon Defenders 1 had in all aspects. No goofy weapons, no goofy pets, nothing fun at all. Defense speed and range are not a thing here, and I hope you like watching a tower fire slow as hell. Gear is boring in every since of the word, and you'll see what I mean if you play this in comparison to DD1. The same stats, and you'll be looking for 1% upgrades which is laughable to me.
Don't even get me started on the ♥♥♥♥ they've pulled with the latest update they had in which they threw a carnival at us when the game has been needing core changes for months, and what do we get along with it? A 40$ costume that's a reskin. Yes, you read that right. A frickin costume that's 40 bucks. I believe in supporting a game if you enjoy it, but they seriously overstepped their bounds on this. Every patch seems to roll out costume after costume and core gameplay changes that need to be made, have yet to make it into the game.
Take a look at steamcharts and you can see what I mean.
TL;DR: If you enjoy casual relaxed play and just shooting the ♥♥♥♥ with friends and trying out a tower defense game to level to max level and not expect much more than that, check it out.
If you want fun, laughs, and was hoping to see a sequal to the dungeon defenders name, and are expecting a hell of a fun time, avoid it.
My two cents, take it or leave it. Obviously I can't cover every major gripe/perk of the game, and if you want a good view on what players think, check the forums out for yourself and you'll get an idea for how negative they are, especially after last patch.
Obviously I want better changes to come, and I hope they do, I'd really like to recommend this game, but sadly in its current state, I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 Devils is a metroidvania platformer made by Platine Dispostif, who are known mainly thanks to their bullet hell games Gundemonium and Hitogata Happa. How did the developers manage the genre change?
The level design is in metroidvania style, with semi-open world where you are unlocking rooms of previous zones to progress further. What stands out with the game is definitely the sweet visual anime pixelart style that looks great, considering also the well-made animations. Chelsea and her moves look great!
The unique gameplay mechanics the game offers, is the option to control time. You can stop or rewind the time, and you'll have to use it for few puzzles; in other cases it's a great utility skill for combat. But don't expect spamming those skills, you have very limited resources to slow time, so you can't affect the time for more than few seconds.
Weapon system in the game feels weird, as you are finding weapons through the levels, but you can have only one weapon at time and you can't swap to the previous weapon. You have to hope you'll find your favourite sword or boomerang soon again.
What ruins the whole impression from the game is the controls. They are terribly clunky, you'll miss jumps pretty often. To dash, you have to quickly double tap the movement key which usually badly reacts in shorter ranges to jump. Blocking is made, as it feels like a tradition for Japanese platformers, by tapping the specific movement direction in the moment of impact.
Bunny must die, and she will die a lot. Sometimes because of higher difficulty, sometimes because you couldn't get her movement fully in control. Ability to control the time is nice but it doesn't change the fact that this is mediocre platformer with bad impression because of clunky controls.
