While I want to really like it, and I sort of do, this game is just too frustrating for me to really want to continue it to the end.
Now I know that I'm really just supposed to Git Gud, because it's not that the game is really bad or anything... It's just that the controls and the way the character handles are just so much of a puzzle to keep up with.
The game is almost literally Metroid Castlevania, and I do like these types of games. You start underpowered, unable to even walk to the right until you get a powerup... Wall candles that break to give you stuff and weapons, and upgrades that give you health, new abilities, etc.
The "story" of Bunny Devil Sin: Stacies First Day Out, is obviously purposely half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as a kind of joke. Much of the intro and cutscenes and other dialogue boxes show a somewhat cheesy comedic aspect, probably designed to make fun of how ridiculous situations and universes are that a lot of video game characters live in. It's dumb, but it's meant to be dumb, and that's fine.
The graphics are very well done, nice animation and sprite work. The sound effects are OK, if a little annoying and cheesy, but the music is nice and well done.
Of course though, my biggest gripe with the game is the archaic controls and movement for the player character. You can't change direction in mid-air or during a spinning jump, which means no turning around to change direction or shoot. That would normally be ok, but there are like 3 or four different kinds of jumping, with the most useful one being jumping from standing still. The sprinting/dash jump goes far but isn't tall. OK, that's understandable, but when you are walking left or right your jump will be just too short to get onto ledges for some reason, meaning you will have to run up to walls, and then stand still against them, jump, AND THEN press left or right. You can't really press any other buttons before you jump if you wanna get up, you have to jump THEN move... Which is the kind of stuff that games like Action 52 taught us was bullhonkey.
There's so many things I was irked about in just an hour of play I could probably write a million more paragraphs just about the awkward movement, but I'll at least try to wrap my qualms with the movement up. Walking to the edge of a ledge will give you a little push-back so that you don't fall off. That's cool in a lot of platformers, but there's such a large area it considers you will fall off of that it just seems more restrictive and janky than anything else. Most games would at least let one of the characters feet dangle off the ledge, but not here. You can't just start shooting to the left if you have already started shooting to the right. Once you start shooting you can hold down and aim in a couple of angles up and down. But if an enemy gets behind you as you were trying to spray at them, you have to stop shooting, finish the animation, get up, and move five feet in the other direction to turn the character around so you can shoot the other way. By that time the boss has usually done another swoop over your head back to where you were aiming before... And lastly, the multiple weapons in the game, and how you obtain them.
The variety of weapons is cool, and a lot of them have various uses... but... The way that you get them is so obtuse that you will go out of your way to try NOT to get the next new weapon since you don't even know when you will get it, or how useful it will be. Weapons drop out of a certain few candles mixed into the environment along with ones that recharge time meter stuff, but they don't look any different than the normal ones, and once you pick up that weapon you are stuck with it until you either find a new one or go back to a candle you've memorized has a weapon, and get it back there. I understand that this mechanic is basically just Castlevania, but it seems like a decent idea from Castlevania that was just taken and poorly implemented. This game isn't arcade-y at all really, and the weapon you pick up is your ONLY weapon, not a secondary one. If the candles looked different than the others, or you could keep and switch through them, or something... It's just such a weird choice to have certain weapons only hidden in certain candles in certain places and once you pick one up you can't even change it unless you backtrack.
I think my last gripe along with all of that, is just that every time you die it kicks you back to the main menu. Why. Having to do everything again from your last save-point is fine... But why do I have to go back to the main menu to load them? Why not just respawn at them right after you die...
Overall, it IS a good game, just... uh... not for me I guess... The controls and movement physics are just too puzzling and confusing to really get a hang of for me, and it's almost like every mechanic of this game was designed to stop the flow of combat and platforming that would normally be in a game like Metroid. It's expected to go fast a lot of the time, but you are made to stop every five seconds to correct a jump, or kill an annoying enemy, or to just try to figure out one simple thing that shouldn't be so complicated when plenty of other games did the same stuff so fluently... Ah well.
Oh yeah, and theres this time stopping/reversing mechanism, but it's just not too... enticing or incentivizing to use. Stopping time runs out very quickly, controls are still as clunky as before, you can't attack, and you can still be damaged. Reversing time doesn't seem to have much of a use outside of a few puzzles that have doors close too quickly to run through. You can't even rewind time to revive yourself.
Just too clunky of an action platformer for me. I'm sure the mechanics and controls can be memorized and perfected through time, but I'm an easily confused individual and even if I did memorize them I would constantly be miss-pressing and messing up things. Though even memorization of the controls still wouldn't rectify some of the other questionable issues that this game has.

With one of the longest titles in video game history, Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 Devils is a 2D platforming action adventure with rigid and terrible controls that get in the way of any fun there could be. On the surface its a good looking game and I think that's all there needs to be. You fight a giant cat, you wear a bunny girl costume while platforming a labyrinth and there's a button to take a selfie screenshot. Does a game need more than that to sell it? There is plenty of old school charm with the visuals, a few items to collect like running shoes and the game's time mechanic that lets you freeze time around Bunny and halt traps. Other games have done it better, but the genre itself is popular enough where any game in it becomes a must own.
When you start the game for the first time, you're given a choice what type of game window you'd like and you had better make the right choice because you're only asked once. Making the wrong choice gives you a black screen with music. You can sometimes remedy this by pressing Right, Right, Z and then Right, Right, Right, Up, Z. Otherwise just go digging through the game's .ini file to solve the problem. Perhaps that's a Windows 10 issue, but its still a giant issue.
The real problem is that its tough to control Bunny. Movement feels stiff and you're either attacking or moving, never both at once. There is no duck attack, but rather Bunny will attack down at an angle. She can also attack up and up at an angle. Another limitation is when you're attacking, there is no way to turn around. You need to stop attacking, move the other way and risk bumping into an enemy if they are close enough.
If you try to nudge your way off of a platform, if you do it too slight, she will correct herself back on the platform. This feels like a glitch to just disappear and move ten pixels over to safety. On the other hand, there are plenty of blind jumps with the potential for death spikes below. To compensate, you can halt all movement and push down and after a moment the screen with scroll down to show you spikes. Plus, the item icons can obscure what's below even if they're a bit transparent. The list of items seems unnecessary since you never have to switch between them.
Oh but then there are other blind challenges, such as flying enemies that shoot and gravity takes their projectiles downward to you. They can fire at you from off screen and it adds to the challenge, but only because movement is so stiff.
Once you earn the running shoes, you can dash with a double tap in one direction. The dash is quick and you can jump kick enemies with it, but the issue is that its easy to run by accident. Perhaps using a keyboard makes it less prone to issues, but I was using a 360 controller.
Bunny is a game with several weapons and she can only hold one at a time. Some are interesting, others are basic like throwing swords. Rather than a gun they are swords. She can get a slashing sword that is borderline useless since its easier to kill enemies from a distance with anything else. There are boomerangs which are always cool to have in any game and even a giant mace that will come back at you. Using the mace almost turns into an orbiting shield. The only downside is you need to catch the mace again to use it.
To get these weapons you need to break candles, which is fine because other games have done it before. The issue is if you are close enough to a candle and a weapon drops, that weapon is yours. The old weapon should be dropped so you have a choice. While weapons only pop out of specific candles I found myself getting a weapon by accident and I'd need to backtrack to get the weapon I did want.
One of the interesting facets of the game is the jump mechanic. Its just as rigid as movement, but when you just jump, its a tall jump, but when you leap in a direction, Bunny spins around. When you spin and attack she will throw weapons in a spiral. Well except the mace. The mace can destroy red projectiles, while other weapons can only take out blue ones. This is helpful for boss fights.
As for the bosses, the early fights feel laughable and easy. Just stand and spam your projectile. One boss managed to never hit me, despite standing in front of it and never moving. Perhaps that was just a boss rather than one of the 7 devils. Major bosses incorporate a cut scene, but I was never invested in the story. The title says more than what you need to know.
The time mechanic feels underutilized. Time will stop everything but Bunny and her mace. It stops your projectiles, that is except for the mace, but the catch is the mace cannot damage enemies when time is stopped. The game attempts to make more use of the time mechanic by letting you hold the button to reverse time, yet I was never able to get it to work except for a few occasions. Even then it only respawns candles and enemies I had destroyed. If there's anything that needs explaining, there are several signs with hints. Things like freeze time to jump on a platform, freeze time to disable a trap and double tap a direction to run and jump a gap.
Death in the game is a true annoyance, because its game over and you're kicked out into the main menu where you must continue from your last save. This is a ridiculous punishment for a tough to control game. I would think that a mechanic that lets you reverse time would spare you from death, but no; Bunny needs to be alive to reverse time. That feels like a missed opportunity and the entire game feels like missed opportunities. You have a time stopping mechanic yet there are no puzzles beyond find an orb to open a door. You collect items so fast and furious it makes me feel like the game is devoid of content.
Saving will restore health and your time powers. When you save it adds time to your run, so for experts, there is reason to run through the game with minimal saves. Collecting purple triangles that spray out of defeated foes and candles will refill your time meter. There are a few collectibles that will increase your time meter as well.
Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 Devils is a game that needed more time on the fun and less time on the graphics. The art and style help sell it, but its a tough game to play or enjoy for that matter. At the price tag, a night with this bunny feels like a risky proposition.

Note: I am coming primarily from a speedrunner's perspective.
This game delivers loads in a small package. Refunct costs $2.99 and I wholeheartedly reccomend paying that small fee for the treat that awaits you inside.  Refunct is a short, bright and smooth 3D Platformer with some stellar movement, a simple premise, and a soundtrack that fits the game like a tailor-made glove.
The premise is simple, you run around a world that builds itself around you to stand on red switches. Once a switch is stood on a new part of the island you are on will rise up from the sea, where your next goal will be. Despite it's simplicity, the game uses it to great effect, modelling the whole game around the concept of keeping everything simple, to create an experience you can relax yourself in.
A must-have for any platformer is fun, fluid movement, which is something that this game does better than any other game at a comparable price point that I have ever seen. A direct result of this fun traversal is that this game has an active speedrunning community which enjoys trying to push the game to its limits and beat it as fast as possible. This is also where the majority of my time in the game has come from. The simplistic nature of the game lends itself to be played over and over again, without ever feeling old.
Another area in which the game excels in is the soundtrack, which is both mesmerising, and undoubtedly the best accompaniment to your journey as can be. I must commend the composer, Kristofferson on what he has done with this game. This game is ambient music done right, which never intrudes the gameplay, and only heightens the experience.
To summarise, I really recommend giving this game a shot as I had a really good time playing it and would like to see others hopefully enjoying it as much as I did. Also to speedrunners, or hopeful speedrunners looking for a short game with a few funs tricks to run, I completely recommend it.

"The Cat and the Coup" tells the story of the former Iranian Prime Minister, Mohammed Mossadegh, and... I really liked it. I wasn't sure what to think when I saw the advertising and also that this was on the "Video Games as Art" article on Wikipedia (which they also included "Tempest 2000" and "Vib Ribbon"... for some reason), but needless to say I was very impressed.
I really like the storybook aesthetics of the game, like you're seeing this history unfold across tapestries, old photographs, and pictures cut out of magazines. Along with this, the animations on Mossadegh and the Cat look very blocky but still well-animated, like they belong with the rest of the scattered images in the game. And the game mechanics and story are influenced by you as a little, black cat pushing around the unfortunate Mossadegh, which is incredibly symbolic.
See, throughout the game, a lot of the puzzles involve balance, almost as if saying that the Prime Minister was trying to find a balance between his people and the other countries looking to get that oil, but because of bad fortune in his path, he just happened to be a stepping stone for the U.S. to grind their feet into, and a door for the Iranian people to knock down, and move onto a better life. He's constantly falling and being messed with by the cat, which really makes you feel sorry for the poor chum. He was just trying to do what any man would do in his position, and he keeps getting sh** on.
I can't think of any issues I had with the game, personally. The over-realiance on text here and there bothered me a little (but that's more of a personal gripe). Beyond that though, it uses intuitive puzzles to tell a story in a unique and intriguing manner. I can see some people throwing a fit for the game being 15 minutes, but it tells the story it aims to tell in that amount of time, and does it damn well.
I'm gonna give "The Cat and the Coup" a 9/10. If you like what video games can do as an artform, and how they can effect people emotionally in their own unique manner, this game is definitely the game for you.

This is an excellent tank simulation game, easily among the best available. It is not to be mistaken with any tank action game of any sort, so don't expect arcade gameplay. This game is about learning how to operate (either as commander, driver, gunner or loader) an American M60A1 and  a Russian T-62 main battle tank, both cold war era machinery. The developers practically crawled into both of these I've been told, this in order to create the cockpit and internal layout as accurate as possible, this is the real deal.
The cockpit or inside experience of these tanks are no small part in this game. Every little detail is present and the crew is fully represented and accurately animated. When firing a short you can witness the loader to pickup another around of ammunition and load it up the cannon. You can easily switch roles are you see fit, playing the gunner for example and receiving orders from the A.I. commander on your targets, distance and whatnot. Very impressive.
As an interesting addition the developers decided to also implement an operational part to the game, elements they carried over from their excellent Graviteam Operation Star strategy game. Here you can command platoons of tanks, infantry and motorized vehicles. So while operating your tank commanding your, excellent graphically represented, crew to battle victory, you can also issue orders and command an entire tank platoon. This by way of communicating orders and/or tactical map of the entire battlefield.
The Ukrainian developers have pored a lot of love into this one and it does show. Like I said earlier, this is really for the simulation loving crowd, not the 'World of Tank' player seeking instant action. This game requires thought, learning and researching, but offers a virtual dive into how it must have felt to operate these metal beasts...

A good _original_ 3D platformer for PC? You better believe it!
The game plays a bit like a mix between Super Mario Sunshine with it's world design and Galaxy with it's mission system, but the game goes well beyond being a Mario 64-wannabe. Each world feels very distinct from one another. Not only because of the different themes, but because each world is structured different just enough in it's narrative to keep it fresh. Exploring these worlds is made better with the buttery smooth controls. Hat Girl's air dive technique feels incredibly fluid and is an absolute joy to use and works as a great reward to skip certain platforming challenges with well timed execution. Her hat gimmick is also pretty easy to understand as well, with one button being used to control the actions of each hat. Combine that with two methods to quickly access your hats during gameplay, and the action is pretty much constant.
Not only does the game have a pretty solid core, but it's oozing with charm and has a surprisingly good soundtrack from a composer I haven't really heard of before (most of the boss tracks and 'Mafia Town Is Asleep' being my personal favorites). My only real negatives are the game's somewhat short length and a slightly odd-feeling ending.
For the asking price, you really can't go wrong here.

The bosses are challenging enough to keep you on your toes, yet as you die they do make the phases you've completed more forgiving. It is all around a fantastic collectathon that can stand on its own and thrive, and I adore it for doing pretty much everything right when it could have easily played on nostalgia and gone the route of Yooka Laylee, the devs knew what made a good game and they implemented it rather then half assing it. That's not to say that there aren't problems- certain collectables can go into floors, walls, and lava and never respawn, for example, but honestly that's the only negative bug I've found in my run, and I'm roughly 80% through the game right now. Thank you Gears for Breakfast, for making such an amazing game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a horror game fans of the genre waited for for so long. The game is unique in a way from most modern horror games. Insead of running around collecting items or finding keys to go to the next area, you stay in a small office trying to keep the animitronics out. That is the scare factor in this game: jumpscares. Like Amnesia : The Dark Desent, it focuses on build up and the "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ where did he go?!" felling. I garantee this game will not bore you.
As far as recommendations and enjoyment are concerned, I had fun with the game and creeped myself out in the process. 2005’s “Fahrenheit” or “Indigo Prophecy” (the latter was the name given to the censored version released in the USA and other countries) was marketed as the first interactive film. At a time where few games dared to be like movies, David Cage (who was lead director and writer) aimed to bridge the gap and show that video games can also tell deep and meaningful stories. Whether Fahrenheit actually did this successfully is up for debate, but what’s known for certain is that David Cage changed the landscape of video games in a huge way.
The idea that this game is indeed a movie or movie-like experience is reinforced several times. As soon as you launch the game you’re greeted with a main menu with several options. One of them happens to be “New movie”, and when you hover your cursor over the option, a billboard with the game’s title appears on your screen. When you decide to start a new game: your screen becomes permanently letterboxed (which once again gives you the impression that you are watching a movie). This game desperately wants for you to think it’s a movie but thanks to the intuitive controls and surprising amount of gameplay, you’re greatly immersed in this adventure.
Controls are a pretty simple affair. The WASD keys move your character around whilst left-clicking and swiping your mouse is needed to interact with objects and other people. This all feels very natural and you can even just hold right-click and left-click at the same time and use your mouse to move the character instead. In-between regular cutscenes are action scenes which are essentially long QTE sequences. There is a hell of a lot of QTEs in this game, which some have likened to a game of “Simon Says”, and they can be quite annoying unless you stick with them. It’s arguably Fahrenheit’s biggest flaw and I had to warn you all in case someone comes to my house and kills me for recommending this game. There are also lots of choices to make, which directly ties in with the game's mood mechanic (certain options or a combination of them will either make your character happy or send them into a depression), but the game is ultimately a linear experience in the end and this mechanic is not as irritating as it sounds.
Fahrenheit’s story on the other hand, is harder to judge fairly. Fahrenheit has arguably one of the best intros in all of video games - and there’s so much potential - but by the time you’ve reached the end of the game: the tone, pacing and story has changed so dramatically and so quickly too. This is sadly due to the fact that this game was meant to be part 1 of a trilogy, but at the last minute this plan was ditched… and the developers tried their best to conclude the game with what they had. It’s not a terrible ending, but most players will definitely be left confused after thinking that this was a crime-thriller title. I guess this is why Fahrenheit has become a cult classic.
Even as a huge fan of this game I have to admit the writing from French developers “Quantic Dream” is pretty hit and miss. One character named Tyler (who is African American) is treated in such a stereotypical fashion which undermines the serious tone of the game and David Cage’s intent to honestly tell a deep and meaningful story. Tyler has become something of a running joke in the Fahrenheit fan community but I guess it’s just another one of those things that led to this title becoming a cult classic. All of this aside, Fahrenheit’s story is still decent for me and there’s some truly epic moments sprinkled throughout. I really felt what the characters were going through at certain times (this can be attributed to some of the great tracks in this game) and most of them were relatable to me because their situations often had them doing mundane tasks.
As for the remaster done by Aspyr: most of the texture work is subtle. There’s a minor facelift throughout but in some areas the original textures might be preferred. Thankfully there’s an option to change from remastered textures to original at any given time (via a single button press) which is pretty cool. The QTE buttons that appear on your screen have also been slightly changed in both appearance and size (they’re much larger now). It's worth noting that Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy, which is the name for this remaster, is also the uncensored version of the game which very few countries ever got. Another plus in my book. The game hasn’t aged really well but apart from some minor screen tearing, which I only noticed on my last playthrough and may not have been the game's fault, it worked just fine on my PC. I wish Aspyr did get to change the models in Fahrenheit but apparently they didn’t have access to much of the original game’s art pipeline.
Obviously I’m a bit biased when it comes to Fahrenheit but I’d still recommend it to anyone who is in the least bit curious about the title. It’s a quirky, unique game and for the price of $10 you really haven’t got much to lose. I’ll give it a 7.5/10.

This aged terribly.
Back in the day, I remember enjoying playing this, because it felt kind of innovative and refreshing. I always liked story-driven games, so I was feeling right at home with this. Since then, I've experienced so many games with much more engrossing stories and intriguing universes that I really find it hard to see the appeal of this game anymore.
Everything feels subpar and cliché. The writing, the acting, the atmosphere and, of course, the gameplay. It's really obvious in this one that David Cage lacked talent to actually come up with moving ideas and just borrowed instead a lot from mainstream movies. Over the years, he got somewhat better, but you can see that many of the weaknesses in Indigo Prophecy got still carried along the way, making Quantic Dreams games rather average for seasoned gamers or cinephiles, compared to so many games out there, especially indie ones.
Anyway, I thought I'd still managed to pull through despite all these flaws, but the horrendous controls/camera and terrible gameplay really broke the deal for me. Immersion is often broken, because any action or movement can feel like a struggle and I'm not even talking about the beyond ridiculous action sequences base on a double "Simon Says" game, which, as many have reported, distracts you from what is actually going on on the screen.
Oh yeah, and that "remastered" tag is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. All that was added was 1080p support and a bunch of achievements.

There aren't many games like this one for good reason, most gamers tend to lean more towards a more active gameplay factor when it comes to their experiences and QTE (quick time events) are generally frowned upon, virtually my only hang up with this game is the length of some of the QTE scenes in the game and the lack of checkpoints within them, as you can figure it gets incredibly tedious to replay the same QTE over and over from the beginning each time you screw up so it does become discouraging.
QTE events aside the story is a well crafted piece guaranteed to keep you guessing to the very end and with three different endings dependant on your choices through the game there is plenty of different paths to take, the characters not just relatable are well rounded and have their own agenda's and idiosyncrasies to which you will find yourself either loving or hating them.
The control scheme though simple can be maddening if you are slow on the draw or using a controller without analog sticks but here are always work arounds and as for problem solving you won't wonder why you aren't slamming your head against a wall in frustration as most problems provide the solution by use of handy comic book style picture slide assuming the timer doesn't run out first.
With music tracks supplied by Theory Of A Deadman among other well placed scores will bring the whole experience together and with bonus points earned by finding hidden and not so hidden floating cards you can use them to purchase extra content by the way of Making of videos, Mocap, art design and extra minigames, ingame music and other videos.
All in all for the price you pay you get a thrilling adventure through a bizarre setting of the occult and science fiction if you can withstand the monotony of grinding QTE'.

What happened to the horror genre? Did it die? Was it replaced with mindless mass appeal action with a horror theme yet no actual fear factor? Yes... and no. The horror genre has been placed in the hands of indie developers and in those hands it still thrives with games like this. The indie gaming industry proves it can continue to add new ideas to the genre while still providing that heart-attack inducing fear we felt the first time we played Silent Hill, Resident Evil or Eternal Darkness. Amnesia showed us first person games don't always need guns and weapons, it also proved that if you've already evacuated your bowels while playing the next scare will bring out unprocessed food.
Five Nights at Freddy's shows us that heart attacks are can happen to people of any age.... okay all jokes aside this game really does stand out in the horror genre. You don't actually do anything, you aren't walking around or looking for clues. No instead you just sit there... knowing something will happen and you don't know when it will come or what will come at you but you know. It's a feeling of dread and fear that I... honestly havent experienced in a horror game before. Something about these ungodly abominations just toying with you, gives you the sense of helplessness as if you're at the mercy of these things. Usually these types of indie games don't appeal to me. Like all those knock versions of Slenderman.... actually I didn't even like Slenderman. But this, this is not some indie horror game from the quick and easy production line up of such games like Spongebob Slendypants... no this is a stand out title. Almost like a point and click adventure but without the adventure.
The person/people who made this game knew what scared people and they utilized that with game mechanics that require you to think clearly and react to what you see and hear. Which is extremely hard to do when your having a bowel evacuating heart-attack. Nonetheless I love this game and it's something I hope to see more of.

Ok, Tales of Zestiria, I've basically beaten the game, so now i feel qualified to talk about it.
Gameplay: Everything works like it should, plays nice, even with the 30FPS cap (with the modded fix I get around 60, but movement is delayed and looks like it's in slomo). The problem comes in with how the gameplay is explained, a lot of problems with this game, I'm sure are non-exsistant on the ps3 version, tutorials are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and there is no way to see your currently mapped controls in battles and unlike berseria, it just throws the control options in your face and tells you "figure it out yourself" if you have a generic USB gamepad like I do. Happily, I'm the kind of person that doesn't really listen to tutorials and I just kinda figure it out on my own, you kinda need to be to really enjoy this game(still don't know what stacking, rows and lines do when it comes to equipment skills, but I know they are good, for something.) . BTW LOOK AT YOUR ACHIVEMENTS! They are more helpful than any tutorial or monolith in the game.
Story: Pretty standard stuff, boy and his friend leave home, the boy gets some kind of mystical powers, petty fight between boy and his friend for the friend feeling left out/ left behind, more people tag along that help deal with whatever problem that you are currently facing, all trying to solve the problems of the countries and stop the big bad. Things start to feel rushed 3/4ths in no major plot holes, but it feels like it's very easy to miss a plot-point so some things can feel like they come out of left field.
Overall: It's fun, it's something different, but don't buy it full price, and don't expect it to hold your hand in ANY way shape or form you are on your own save for achivements, they are helpful as I mentioned before, don't expect anything amazing, aside from the opening song (that electric guitar though <3). You will easily get over an hour of play per $ and don't let all the things on screen scare you, just play the game, things will make sense as you go on, including the battle system.

This game is by far the most perfect survival game. I've always loved the survival aspects of other games and wished there was a game that focused just on survival. Well, here is it. The atmosphere that consumes you as soon as you enter the game captivates the sheer panic of a survival situation. You're alone and you have the whole world to yourself, do you really think you can survive?
I love the whole idea of the Sandbox mode. It gives you a chance to do a little better each time. Items seem to appear randomly after each new turn so each new game differs. My only problem with this is I'm afraid it will eventually be too repetitive after so many play-throughs. This happened for me playing Don't Starve, a game that has a similar style of gameplay.
However, unlike Don't Starve, The Long Dark is beautiful and the atmosphere that completely engulfs you cannot be praised enough. When you first enter the game you have no idea what's going on, but you see the snow surrounding you and the wind blowing against you and it almost makes you feel cold. It puts you in a state of mind of survival. The soundtrack is morose and melancholic, appearing almost randomly at intervals, furthering pulling you into thought of your inevitable demise.
My biggest hope is that the developers listen to suggestions of what Alpha fans think can improve the game, with only a few minor tweaks this game could easily become one of the greatest survival games of all time, if not #1. The only issues I have with the game are minor glitches and lack of content, nothing that couldn't be fixed with the future developement of this game. I really hope the developers are smart about this game, look through a fan's perspective and create content that truly matters to us. I'm extremely excited to see what the future of this game has to offer.
The Long Dark is challenging and fun. If you're a fan of survival games or just survival in general, you need to check this game out. The graphics are pretty good, but the well place audio really takes center stage. However still in the early stages of development, it has extreme potential to become something extraordinary.

I would not recommend this game. Especially as a veteran [Tales of] fan. TL;DR at the bottom.
(Fans of this game on STEAM are probably going to vote me down. Ok look. This might be the only Tales of game aside from Symphonia you've played. I understand. But I've played more than 10 titles in the franchise so I'm just speaking from that perspective. You can love the game, I just can't despite how much I want to.)
Tales of Zestiria is an alright game. It's worth about 45 hours of content on one playthrough. The game pans out like an action RPG, the plot is alright (some girls might like it a lot though), the graphics are pretty, and the gameplay is...
Well, that's what I really don't like. About 10 hours in I was only onboard for the story and acheivements. There is nothing else I think is worthwhile about this game past that. I'm sure this is highly rated on Steam, but I found the gameplay to be terrible. The story is pretty entertaining, but a couple horus of cutscenes cannot hold up the entire game for me.
The writing ToZ is just not quite up there either. It's fujoshi bait. I'm a fujoshi. But I'd rather watch someone else play this game, really.
The game tells you about this amazing world, and how there's such a rich history behind it, but we don't ever get much of a glimpse at it past the main plot. There are monuments in ancient writing scattered throughout the world, and they use it for tutorial, not world building. For 30 hours.
There are stretches of dungeons that is too big, too empty, and brain dead. The Great Camelot Bridge takes you a full 3 minutes to go through, and that's a straight line.  Tutorials are constantly telling you how to play the game even 30 hours in.
The dungeon design in this game is absolutely asinine. Since the battle system takes place EXACTLY where you run into the monsters and the battlefield is huge, the map in turn has to be obscenely huge. All you get is huge rooms and boring corridors just because they wanted to shoehorn that poorly thought out feature in. This is even worse in the Alisha DLC. $15 and two hours worse. You run through a dungeon for TWO DAMN HOURS. (Look up youtube.)
The battle itself is aggravating as well. But some people like it. I found myself fighting against the camera most of the time. The battlefield is usually so huge that you can't see enemies to your left or right. Which is trouble since the battle plays out like a game of rocket tag. If you don't defend on the higher levels, you will die. You want a messy challenge where your party members get KO'd 26 times in a single boss fight because of that? Try this, then. Of course, there's AI stupidity at play too.
The balancing here has some pretty strong MMO grinding feel to it. The padding I felt from this game is incredibly bad.
Once again, I found this to be an ok game. Playing through this made me so angry and disappointed I wish I was playing Tales of Vesperia on the console which is exponentially better than this garbage of a Tales game.
TL;DR: I consider this to be the worst Tales of title aside from Tempest due to all the poor design that went into this, and I think people should give the other Tales of a try to see what I really mean.

A summary and list of Pros and Cons (previous Gamersgate player since 2012), review status March 2015:
Summary:
A hardcore tank simulator with many options, variety in maps, settings and assets, not much variety in controllable vehicles and a very steep learning curve. I suggest it for people that want a hardcore game and that do not shy away from spending some hours into getting used to the game and its interface. I do not recommend it for people that just want to drive around blowing stuff up, because the realistic engagement ranges and punishing difficulty make this kind of playstyle very hard to achieve.
Pro:
-Detailed simulation of vehicular warfare
-Detailed and realistic maps, vehicles, driving and damage physics
-Lots of control over your AI squad or own tanks crew in either direct commander mode or through the map interface
-Dynamic campaign, giving plenty of replayability
-Customizable difficulty and realism levels
-Detailed Encyclopedia of the game content and its properties
Mids:
-Decent messagebox tutorial that can be turned on or off with an interface button
-Graphics are aged, but still detailled. Texture quality has suffered somewhat though
-Slow paced gameplay is rewarded, because your tank is quite fragile when hit with anti tank weaponry
-After Action Reports give a detailed view what hit a tank, from where and what damage has been done, allowing for improving ones playstyle in the future
Cons:
-Very hard to learn controls, due to somewhat unintuitive keyboard shortcuts/layout
-Interface is a bit cluttered to allow every action to be done with the mouse
-Hard to learn game, steep learning curve and very punishing in case of strategic or tactical failure
-Texture quality is considered low now and makes some assets unpleasant to look at
-Eyestrain might be caused by using the rangefinder that overlays two images to the player. You have to find the non-blurry version of the object you want to shoot at to dial in the correct range (gunning/rangefinding can be done by the AI though)
Some more detailed comments:

Now that these things have been moved to the past, the developer has aquired the rights back to his own game and implemented all the fixes that they have been released so far inofficially as the official new version of the game in hope to be able to support and release more content, now that they own their IP.

Yeah, you die a lot, so I guess the title's accurate.
--------------------------------------------------------------
is a metroidvania game in which you play as Bunny, a bunny girl who is cursed with cat ears from a thermomeowclear explosion for some reason. The story isn't incredibly important, and the writing seems to be self-referential to the point were the game knows this too. It's funny, but ultimately you're there to murder everything you see.
As for gameplay itself, it has the standard jumping, moving, attacking actions of any metroidvania, as well as some added techniques. In total, there are 6 weapons, each which different effects and powers that distinguish them from each other. No two weapons feel the same, which is good. The most interesting mechanic
has is its time warping functionality : Bunny is capable of stopping time, allowing her to move past enemies, do specific platforming things, and as she collects more Yellow Powder, rewind time, heal herself, and more.
True to any Metroidvania, Bunny encounters a variety of power-ups along her adveture, ranging from the ability to turn Right to wall-jumping, and even a suit that increases her bust size, giving her added offensive capabilities and slower movement. Not going to lie, it's pretty funny.
As hinted at from above the line,
is hard. Hellaciously hard, even. This is in part due to its steep difficult in platforming and overall difficult boss fights [which are equally as absurd as Bunny herself], but also to the game's most fatal flaw : the movement controls. Jumping is a feat in of itself. The entire system feels very clunky, and oftentimes, you might perform a somersault when you meant to do a straight jump, end up falling down a long tower shaft, and being forced to climb up again. Enemies also inflict a knockback when you're hurt, lending to frustrating moments [in particular, the Jade Tower comes to mind.] However, the controls aren't terrible, and can be surmounted with enough practice.
The game's art and soundtrack are delightful. Environments and enemies look nice and distinct, and each musical score, while nothing particularly catchy or memorable, is nice to listen to. Bunny's voice acting is also pretty solid, but it should be noted that it is in Japanese. The game runs phenomenally well. In my experience, I encountered no graphical slow down, even with dozens of fireballs on the screen at once.
A minor issue is that, should you play this game on Windows 10, you have to edit the game's configuration files to fix the window, otherwise it's just a black screen. It's annoying, but once it's fixed, it's gone.
--------------------------------------------------------------
7.3/10
is an overall enjoyable experience. Aside from its wonky controls, the gameplay is simple and fun, offering fast action and hair-trigger timing. The game is rather short, and can be beaten in as little as an hour [the game even has an achievement for doing so!], but that detail is offset by the fact it has an additional mode in which you play as a different character, who plays almost entirely differently. It is, at times, frustrating, but in the end,
is a game worth playing, and I feel as if it isn't talked about enough.
+Excellent weapon variety and smooth combat.
+Humorous story and characters
+Wide variety of power-ups and gameplay options.
+Second story mode adds replayability, in addition to speed-run possibilities.
+Good art and music.
+Excellent technical performance.
+A worthy challenge.
+You get to play as a Bunny Girl. That's a new one.

I've played a lot of Metroidvanias, and out of all of them, this one adheres closer to the original Metroid than most.  Don't be fooled by the cutesy art; this gaming is filled with tough platforming puzzles and hard bosses.  It doesn't hold your hand, and there are a lot of situations that look impossible at first but are very satisfying after you figure out how to get past them.  The game has a lot of secrets; not just in the sense of hidden rooms and items, but even aspects of the controls are not explained in depth, and the game expects you to experiment to figure out how everything works.
Then, after you think you've almost completed the game, it turns out that you're only halfway done.  It's actually got a surprising length for a Metroidvania; it's taken me about 20 hours to get the real ending and collect most (but not all) of the items.
While the gameplay is the real reason to play the game, it's got a lot of other strengths, too.  The soundtrack is fantastic, the graphics are cute, and the plot has some absurd humor.  I wholeheartedly recommend Bunny Must Die, if you're not afraid of death.

First off..  I am biased.   But I am going to give a bit O brutal review.  Not really that brutal.
1st off.  This is a "remastered" SABOW that was released back in 2011.  It had a borked release with publishers that where borderline stupid.  The game was released in a state with game braking bugs.  This had nothing to do with the dev.  In fact they released a series of unofficial patches to fix the issues.  They however, where not allowed to officially fix the game.   However, the rights just returned to the dev's.  Where all that unofficial content was made official and many fixes and improvements where added in.
There are 2 choices for realistic tank games out there that are newish.  This being one and the other being Steel Beasts Pro.  Both have their ups and downs.  But this one is a lot cheaper.  And frankly its campaign  system is better than SBpro.  Both are most certainly worth owning for a tread head.
The vehicle models have always been a strong point in this game.  And they have aged quite well.  They looked good 4 years ago and still look pretty darn good.  The textures for the interiors of models have been improved and are ok.  But they do not look as good as they could be by 2015 standards.  But they are better than they where on the 2011 release.
Some aspects have not aged super well.  Buildings and some trees/bushes are showing their age.  Not going to suger coat that.  But they do the job.   I guess as a side bonus it means it will run well enough on older vid cards =)
The campaign's are pretty dynamic.  they never play out the same way twice.  In them you have the option usually (campaign depending) of letting the ai control none playable tanks or taking that on yourself and ordering every friendly unit around on the map.  Which I totally LOVE.  Boss guys around, call in arty strikes, air strikes, and fight your tank.
You have realistic ballistics.  Realistic damage model.  Realistic shell types with realistic effects.  the more important components of the tank you can interact with the mouse.  Set angle for the gun when on slopes with the level gauge.  On the M60a1 use the realistically modeled coincidence range finder and mechanical ballistic computer.  However, for some reason you do not have player control over lights, the near infrared search lights, and unlike a previous game from Graviteam, you can not stall out your tank if in the wrong gear as driver.  I miss that.  =(
If your a tanker at heart...or in my case a Cav Scout out to pasture I do recommend.
I like this game to much....  It like being on some sort of retro FTX without the bad cold bad food, little sleep, being filthy, and endless maintance issues.
Edit... Oct. 2015
Since this review things have changed for the better.  Now you have training missions to ease into your tank commander role.  You now do have control over lights, a choice of manual gear shifting and engine throttlle settings.  This last means you can drive stupid and stall the tank, throw a track, or over heat the engine.  Which is a nifty optional feature.  Tank interior has been greatly improved since I wrote this review.  And it looks like some bushes look better now.  The T62 can now lay smoke screens!  I was, ya that's nice.  After using such I use it quite alot to stay alive now.
The Basra 86 DLC is pretty excellant as well.  Great map!  Looks sort of like places I have been too in the mid east.  While I of course never went to where this battle took place, I did get to around out skirts of Basra.  What more can I say about that?
Last thought.  This sim is pretty much what it always should have been now.   There are some rough edges and there is larger than normal learning curve, but crap, its a legit tank sim in the old school sence.  You want real without taking a heat round and having your clothes set on fire with massive flashburns, this is for you.

This is a good game!! Reminded me of the old times when I use to play Monopoly with my friends and family! I cherish those moments and somehow this game allows me to relive it again. I played this game with my 6 old friends and the experience was fantastic. (My friend gifted this game to me.)
However there are few complaints about not being able to play Online Multiplayer and Routers getting reset. So i decided to break this review in two sections as even I faced those issues.
About Complaints:
Here is what i found,
Router getting reset: (This also happened with me at start but i managed to fix this.)
In one of the post it was informed that I have to disable UPnP setting. Trying this actually helped me to resolve this issue.
- People facing this issue should google about how to disable UPnP settings and follow the steps. It is very easy.
Issues with Online Multiplayer: (Here is how me and my friends managed to find and resolve this issue)
- To play this game online with my 6 best buddies, we created a private lobby where I invited everyone.
- At the start of the game the roll dice was getting stuck, so it was not possible to play the game with having 6 of us playing together.
- We split the group and created 2 private lobbies. (First Private Lobby: 3 friends | Second Private Lobby: remaining 3 friends)
Note: I was playing in First Private Lobby.
- My friends in second private lobby were able to play this game smoothly. Without any lag or disconnection.
- However my first private lobby still had some issues with roll dice getting stuck at the start.
- We decided to find a root cause and soon we got to know that the lobby in which I join is creating a problem. This is where we realized that my network had some issues and it was generating spikes. I raised a complain to my service provider and they indeed managed to fix my network problem! \O/
- NOW I CAN PLAY THIS GAME WITH MY FRIENDS WITHOUT ANY ISSUES!! :D
About Game:
Pros:
- Visuals
- 3 different type of boards (I prefer living board cause of visuals)
- Multiple choices of rules that you can apply. (to be really honest, i haven't played them all but will be interesting to try)
- Multiplayer private lobby helps you to play with your close friends and family.
- If a player leaves the game then he gets replaced by an AI. (Difficulty unknown :| )
Cons:
- Multiplayer quick match requires players with good network connection. (Having even 1 player with bad network can ruin the game)
- Chat system is not available. (me and my friends were using Skype to communicate)
- Lobby timer for host in private session. (This feature was introduced in Patch. As it is a private session, i believe the timer is not required.)
- You cannot rejoin the game once you quit or get disconnected.
I hope you will find this review helpful.

If you would like to get a first impression of this game, I have done a Let's Play:
Prelude:
Five Nights at Freddy’s is a very simple game at its core components. You are a Security Guard at a Chuck E. Cheese styled restaurant. Simple enough, except that at night the animatronic animals wander around and make sure everyone is following the rules.
The Story:
There isn’t one that is very overt. All you get in the way of an exposition is a few pre-recorded messages from your predecessor. However, if you look at the newspaper clippings around the building, you get some interesting story. Some children were murdered by a man wearing a Freddy Fazbear suit. However if you pay attention, a human cannot fit in the costumes. The story is small but it really lets you choose how you want to see everything.
The Gameplay:
It’s simple. You move the cursor down to look at your monitors, you click on the light or door switch to activate both. Early on this is very simple, however later on it gets very very stressful. If you have the gall to attempt night 7 on all 20’s, you might go crazy.
Overall:
For a $5 USD game, I got near 20 hours of gameplay from this. Keep in mind I went for all 20’s on night 7. If you only go for night 5 or night 6 you might spend near 5 to 10 hours of gameplay on it which is well worth the price.  If you like horror games or are just looking for an insane challenge, I would definitely recommend this game.

There aren't many games like this one for good reason, most gamers tend to lean more towards a more active gameplay factor when it comes to their experiences and QTE (quick time events) are generally frowned upon, virtually my only hang up with this game is the length of some of the QTE scenes in the game and the lack of checkpoints within them, as you can figure it gets incredibly tedious to replay the same QTE over and over from the beginning each time you screw up so it does become discouraging.
QTE events aside the story is a well crafted piece guaranteed to keep you guessing to the very end and with three different endings dependant on your choices through the game there is plenty of different paths to take, the characters not just relatable are well rounded and have their own agenda's and idiosyncrasies to which you will find yourself either loving or hating them.
The control scheme though simple can be maddening if you are slow on the draw or using a controller without analog sticks but here are always work arounds and as for problem solving you won't wonder why you aren't slamming your head against a wall in frustration as most problems provide the solution by use of handy comic book style picture slide assuming the timer doesn't run out first.
With music tracks supplied by Theory Of A Deadman among other well placed scores will bring the whole experience together and with bonus points earned by finding hidden and not so hidden floating cards you can use them to purchase extra content by the way of Making of videos, Mocap, art design and extra minigames, ingame music and other videos.
All in all for the price you pay you get a thrilling adventure through a bizarre setting of the occult and science fiction if you can withstand the monotony of grinding QTE'.

Fahrenheit (or Indigo Prophecy in the USA) was originally developed by Quantic Dream for the PC before the company seemed to have a love for Sony's Playstation console and developed all its games on there. Now, Fahrenheit: Indigo Propechy has been remastered for modern day systems by Aspyr Media with help from Quantic Dream
The story follows an ordinary man named Lucas Kane living in cold New York City and it seems as if Lucas has an unknown force within him that makes him kill a man in a diner. The story then progresses from there but I am not going to spoil it
The gameplay is like that of what Telltale games uses today. You move around in the third person perspective, interact with people and objects. Make dialogue options and have loads of quick time events. Too many quick time events. There are some "stealth" sections which are really annyoing and look out of place
The remaster improves the graphical fidelity of the game, makes the game run on modern day systems and modern day resolutions and includes the cut scenes that were orignally cut in the original version due to classification restrictions which of course include nudity and sex scenes. Because where is Quanitc Dream nowadays without a good sex scene or two?
Overall, Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered is a good remastered version of a good Quantic Dream game, it runs smoothly and I encountered no crashes at all whilst playing the game. Although the game is not for everyone as it is heavily linear and heavily story driven, if you like that type of game, then give Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered a shot!

Excellent foundation for a game, with a lot of potential!
Overview: Essentially it's an arena deathmatch in a space-ish environment. Right now some maps have land, some don't, but all maps have some degree of cover one way or another.  Where this differs from usual arena DM rigamarole is in the crafting of your own vehicle to take to the fight (a la Robocraft(Grrr) or Crossout). The building is done by placing a number of different kinds of blocks (hulls, armor, weapons, engines, abilities, energy generation & storage, etc.) around a central core, then take it to battle after which you will recieve XP for the vehicle as well as some "junk"(in-game currency) to upgrade with. There are currently 4 different types of ship you can build, plus a sort of "starter" ship to learn & earn on. Each different class has it's own total block limits, it's own strengths and weaknesses and it's own set of abilities you can equip it with.  The matches are short and sweet (avoids any tedium) and accompanied by a pretty nifty little rock track throughout.
Some finer points: Game IS early access, so expect changes. Also, as such, it's continuously being tweaked in almost all aspects; balance, abilities, limitations, everything. The developers on this one seem genuinely interested in making a good game, and the changes reflect that. As you would expect with an E.A. game lots of it needs work, like balance, for instance, but things are continuously being tweaked to improve the experience as well as new features being added to same effect.
The game DOES support an in-game market (for skins, and premium time) and DOES support a real cash currency.  Some (me included) find some of the prices outrageous, but developers have already stated that they are working to make them more realistic (some proof of dev. involvement).
Great game, great potential, hope it goes far, hope they don't go the Robocraft route and drill it into the ground with money-grubbing and forum pandering and screwing their own playerbase.
Plus, it's free. Give it a shot!
-EDIT-APR27- EXTREME grind. To the point of turning the game entirely monotonous. Even with "premium" which is obscenely expensive (still), level gains are so slow and hold SO little advantage that there is almost NO sense of progression. Major turn-off.

I actually liked the game and it almost offered the type of game I wanted it to be, but for me the save game system is game breaking.
It's a nice shooter. Open world and lots of enemies makes for quite a ride. There are only two things that set it back a bit for me (except for the save system, which I will adress further):
* I don't care for cut scenes in open world games, for me they break the immersion. I don't want the controls to be taken from me;
* I hate it when you encounter masses of enemies, all with weapons and you still are low on ammo half the time. You should be swimming in the stuff. I installed a mod, but then I had unlimited ammo, which isn't nice either. Balancing should have been better.
But the save game system really destroys the game for me. A checkpoint system in an open world game is just horrible. I started exploring the game a number of times. Each time after a while I died. Tales of Zestiria (ToZ) is the 15th mothership title in the long running Tales of franchise and was released in 2015. The best way to sum up this game is an ambitious game that didn't have enough time, money, or talent to fully realize what the developers were going for.
In the past, battles that the player encountered would take you away into an instanced battle map (think of the Final Fantasy series). ToZ decided to make the battles take place where you encounter them which in theory sounds great but design decisions behind this choice influenced the maps of the world so much so that the open fields became at times 10x bigger than past games with nothing interesting populating these desolate fields. This is not mentioning how the camera fights you in combat to the point where you are unable to fully survey the battle. The camera will get caught on just about everything making battles just the pits sometimes.
Grinding in ToZ isn't for exp but for gear. While you receive exp for killing monsters on the field the exp gains are designed to give the player very little exp but instead you need to kill monsters for the gear that they drop so you can fuse it into other similar gear to level them up to make your characters stronger. This wouldn't be so bad if the AI partners in the game weren't some of the worst programmed in the modern series.
AI partners are brain dead and at higher difficulty settings severely limit the player because of how awful they are. This is because the game is designed around the two human characters to fuse with the four elemental "seraphs" and to balance this if you are not fused you have a smaller hp pool and your attacks don't do as much damage but you have 4 characters on the field as opposed to 2 in your fused forms. Because HP is so low and enemy boss encounters will always be about 15+ levels higher than you your AI partners will get beat down very fast because they lack the ability to defend themselves.
The story has many plot holes, plot lines that are picked up and dropped off whenever, and pacing that is downright bad. The game never ups the ante because of the initial premise of the story which makes it very hard for the tension to escalate which is your classic "demon lord going to destroy the world scenario". This wouldn't have been so bad if you cared anything for the characters but it is so hard to care for these characters when they offer very little.
The point in the story which I literally yelled at my screen because of how stupid it was is when a villain who is introduced very early in the game and then vanishes for 50% of the game only to reappear because the writers forgot about him and they needed someone to do something to make character development happen. Mind you, in the time of this villain's disappearance nobody has mentioned him even though the main character, Sorey, would have every reason to ask the other human partner because of the relationship between the villain and her. I can not reiterate it enough this character was completely dropped and picked up because a bad person needed to do a bad thing.
Character development in ToZ is baffling there is no other way to put it. Instead of slowly building up characters they either give a huge character dump all at once, let the character keep hitting the same one note, or very small character development which doesn't get furthered. I cared nothing for these characters save maybe 2, 3 if you really push it.
Dungeon designs save for the four elemental trials are very repetitive and force the player to fight in confined spaces because they are a dungeon. This means that the aforementioned bad camera does the player no favors.
The reasons why I can not recommend this game comes from both a long time fan of the series having played over 10+ of their titles and as a gamer. The fan in me says it a difficult sell to other fans of the series but to them I still wouldn’t recommend it. The gamer in me says that if you took away the “Tales of” and if this was just some random game I would honestly say that it is bad.
After playing the other games in the franchise I can say that this is the only game in which I put down my control got cheat engine and turned on super speed because the nonsensical story, characters, grinding, and battles broke me.
Edit: 5/4/2016
After beating this game I can safely say that the story is plagued with plotholes and pacing problems.
I understand what they were trying to go for but ultimately the story was poorly told. There is a decent story hidden here but it never fully came out. The story for the first 8 hours is great but after that it starts going downhill.
I wouldn't recommend this game at a 50$ price tag wait till it goes down to 20$ or lower. As for the DLC I wouldn't recommend paying for it at all. Watch it on youtube if you are curious.

After giving a full 24 hours to this software, I think its high time I offered an opinion on it.
I have been impressed.
Users of previous versions of RPG Maker may not have quite the same initial experience, but I discovered a certain amount of reading around was needed to actually get the hang of the assorted tools on offer.  A very quick internet search brought me to the home site for this software, and from then on, it was more or less all systems go.  The tutorial I found very quickly had me getting to grips with mapping, zoning, and events logic.
Discovering the best way to use the different triggers and outputs was actually very good fun - although I think this is something that appeals to the puzzle-solving part of my brain.  Occasional frustrations had me combing back through my logic to discover that one fatal flaw I had made when I failed to trigger a step properly, but I didn't have to refer to any outside help once i had climbed that first curve.
The only thing I haven't explored (and this is due to my own lack of experience - I will be working to overcome this!) is the use of Ruby scripts.  I know from a few fast searches that there is a vast amount of well-written scripting already available for RPG Maker, but not being a programmer on any level, I have some difficulty understanding the functionality.  Again, this is not a criticism, merely my own lack of knowledge.  If you aren't planning to do anything super fancy (and there is a lot that can be achieved without the need for scripts) then you may not need Ruby knowledge at all.
I have still to sit down and make a real attempt at a full game from this software, but I can see all the things I would want to do in a game readily available, either with the basic package or from the community which has grown around it.  A fine piece of work.

This game is by far the most perfect survival game. I've always loved the survival aspects of other games and wished there was a game that focused just on survival. Well, here is it. The atmosphere that consumes you as soon as you enter the game captivates the sheer panic of a survival situation. You're alone and you have the whole world to yourself, do you really think you can survive?
I love the whole idea of the Sandbox mode. It gives you a chance to do a little better each time. Items seem to appear randomly after each new turn so each new game differs. My only problem with this is I'm afraid it will eventually be too repetitive after so many play-throughs. This happened for me playing Don't Starve, a game that has a similar style of gameplay.
However, unlike Don't Starve, The Long Dark is beautiful and the atmosphere that completely engulfs you cannot be praised enough. When you first enter the game you have no idea what's going on, but you see the snow surrounding you and the wind blowing against you and it almost makes you feel cold. It puts you in a state of mind of survival. The soundtrack is morose and melancholic, appearing almost randomly at intervals, furthering pulling you into thought of your inevitable demise.
My biggest hope is that the developers listen to suggestions of what Alpha fans think can improve the game, with only a few minor tweaks this game could easily become one of the greatest survival games of all time, if not #1. The only issues I have with the game are minor glitches and lack of content, nothing that couldn't be fixed with the future developement of this game. I really hope the developers are smart about this game, look through a fan's perspective and create content that truly matters to us. I'm extremely excited to see what the future of this game has to offer.
The Long Dark is challenging and fun. If you're a fan of survival games or just survival in general, you need to check this game out. The graphics are pretty good, but the well place audio really takes center stage. However still in the early stages of development, it has extreme potential to become something extraordinary.

"SUPERHOT IS THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS!"
So, I bought Superhot after watching a couple of videos and was instantly sold on the premise.
The overall idea and gameplay are great + the game has a rather interesting story.
I am going to list the pros and cons of the game now, the game is great, but it does have a few issues that are worth talking about.
The good
- The game runs great, haven't had a single crash or bug since I started playing.
- Looks pretty. The overall aesthetic is quite eye catching, the minimalistic art style actually helps with the gameplay.
- The weapons feel really nice and lethal, each one is unique in it's own way.
- YOU CAN SLICE BULLETS IN MID AIR WITH A SWORD!
- Check out the Games folder, I wont spoil it :D
The Bad
- The story while interesting only took about 2 hours (it's all challenges afterwards) and it feels like there should have been more (future DLC perhaps?), the world seems to be very interesting, so I'd love to see more of it.
- The hitboxes can be imprecise, there were numerous times when I was sure that the bullet would fly past, only to see it smash on an invisible wall.
- The price is a bit steep. If the story was longer, I'd have no issues paying 23 euros for the game, but as it stands I am a bit disappointed.
Overall I feel like the game is great, especially if you don't care about the story and just want to kill the red guys, the endless mode is great and offers a lot of neat challenges.

It limits your options for attacking enemies while on the go, and enemies in this game will be guaranteed to get a few hits off on you before you can kill them. The environments you fight in are also tightly cramped, a little too much for comfort. As for bosses, the game doesn't really offer much there. Some are pretty tough, but I was able to cheese several bosses in by just getting up tot hem and shooting, and their AI couldn't make heads or tails regarding how to attack me.  Poorly coded if you ask me.
Overall, big disappointment in my eyes. I see alot of other people in these comments enjoy the game, which is a-okay by me. I just can't personally invest too much time into it, which is why I requested a refund.  It's so puzzling too, since I like the rest of the games from this developer. Guess platforming metroidvanias aren't their strong suit.

It's a simple 5-minute game. The objective is to launch a ball towards a rotating paddle and have it hit a specific side of the boundary. There's no customization, and no settings.
The 8-bit-like soundtrack is well composed, but somewhat a little too distracting on higher levels. It's a good challenge (for the love of god, I can't reach 30 points even after 1 hour of game-time) and simple as it is.
I do have a couple suggestions:
1. Allow the user to change the music volume. Priceless.
2. Rather than have the paddle spin on one of its ends, have the paddle spin about a tenth of its lenght. It still keeps the game a good challenge, but allows the player to effectively attempt a launch while the bigger side of the paddle is away from the best launcher. This reduces the time the player has to spend waiting for the paddle to rotate back to a better position, and also provides a higher challenge. Maybe an achievement of correctly launching 20 balls using the shorter side of the paddle?
3. Replenish lives at checkpoints. Although I do understand this is a challenge 5-minute game, it should also make the player believe it wants to be played. By replenishing lives during gameplay, it reduces the grief the player has to face when losing and having to start all over again.
Also, why not have a link to the musician's website, so people can either buy the soundtrack or maybe even hire Gumbel for their own projects?

This game was originally released in 2005 and well known amongst gamers. If you had not played it, you would have at least heard about it. The main reason being because of the controversial interactive sex scene.
It wasn't until 2006/2007 when I got gifted a DVD copy of the game that I decided I wanted to play it. Unfortunately the controversial scene was removed, the second sex scene was watered down and all this had become widespread on a global scale. Forgive my fuzzy memory after all these years, but I think there was a way to identify whether the game was a cut down version or not. I think it had something to do with the title. It was either Fahrenheit or Indigo Prophecy. Unfortunately the front cover on mine said "Fahrenheit a.k.a Indigo Prophecy" which was a strong indicator that it was the watered down version.
I decided not to play it. Being a bit annoyed, I tried downloading it via a torrent site ... but then realised by filename it was the cut down version and that the torrent file was improperly named on purpose. There wasn't many torrents for this game by this time, let alone seeds. When it was available on Steam prior to 2010, there was talk in the forums that it was clearly the edited version as well. Oh sad ... sad panda face. The phoenix gave up until Nobember 2015. Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered had promised to contain everything!
I didn't know too much about this game other than it was supposed to be a story-driven movie-like narrative experience. The quintessence of plot and character development. lol, the quintessence ... the crap I write sometimes. I don't even know what that means. Just thought it'd make me sound cool.
In the begining it's quite challenging. You are faced with a lot of "Think quick!" moments. To which you will fail a few times as you have to find the right linear actions to take. Once you learn them, nothing changes. And I prefer it that way...
The controls are somewhat unique to me. I don't believe I've played a game with asyncronous QTE button presses. What this means is, on a keyboard layout you have WASD for your left hand and the arrow keys for your right hand. As indicated by two colour palettes, each with Red, Yellow, Green and Blue. No more than two colours will illuminate at one time and can be on any pallete. As silly and disjointed as this may seem, somehow, I don't know how ... but the interaction not only makes sense, but tremendously enhances the cinematic or gameplay you are viewing.
There is also another interaction where you basically press the buttons A or D. There are two variations of this. The more interesting out of the two and once again as silly and disjointed as it may seem, it somehow enhances the gameplay. Basically you have to tap A or D and keep this bar in the middle of this X-axis and away from complete left or right. For example controlling breathing. On two occasions this is combined with the W key so you can move forward and use the mouse to look around. It's supposed to simulate claustrophobia, which one character in the game has. This interaction works very well.
It takes a while for the story to get good. About 50-60% of the way through it starts to get interesting. Character development was lacking imho but the story was quite good. It was definately inspired by films like Dark City and The Matrix.
As you may have guessed, there are alternative scenes in this game. Time and again I've said this in some of my previous reviews... I'm not a big fan of this. Because what ends up happening is I'll go back and replay whatever chapter and take the alternative to see what's different. Often the change is unimportant/pointless! The sensation begins to feel programmatic which then makes a game loose its immersiveness and atmosphere. There are only two big exceptions: The Walking Dead Season One which customises the gameplay on the spot for each scene for the entire game! It was the whole point of the gameplay! You wern't missing anything so long as you selected your lines truthfully. And second exception: Vampires: The Masquerade - Bloodlines which cleverly sneaks in high replayability with the point of wanting to really be different with each character you choose and which lines you select as a response ... in the end ... there were something like 5 different endings which was based on your attitude throughout the entire game. If you were a solo person, you'd see a solo ending ... etc. Fahrenheit was neither of these. In fact I was really dissapointed with the inaccurate police sketch alternative. I thought the main character would have said something like, "What a joke! That doesn't even look anything like me!" when watching the news on TV. Instead ... nothing is said and the main character turns the TV off! Your mental health state doesn't even increase! Nothing! Null! zero response!
The dialogue choices are weird. They are presented sort of like Mass Effect in which you can select a choice with a mouse movement in some direction based on a gist and before a bar timer runs out. To be honest I hate the bar timer and dislike the gist idea for dialogues in RPG's. IMHO it's lazy and feels unpoetic. Most of the time it's there only to fill in knowledge gaps for the sake of the plot. But there are some scenes where it'll lead to alternatives.
So final word, what do I think? I reckon that this game is good, it could have been a timeless classic if there was more character development, deeper atmosphere/immersiveness and no pointless alternative choices to be made. As much as I want to say it, I don't think this game can be called overrated as it probably never hit mainstream popularity as much as some other games did for its time. Look, I'm pretty harsh when I rate games. I've played a few and not many have gone beyond my 90% mark. In respect to all other games I've played (and hoping I'm not disrespecting any fans), I'd rate Fahrenheit something like a 78%, which is a pretty damn well deserved score in my books. This score includes viewing the bonus unlockable content, to which some bonus cinematics made me laugh.

Pleasantly silly (though not afraid to get a little spooky), with excellent variety that made me actually eager to see what was coming up next. The controls were pretty dang great, and the only actual hiccup I found was when using the aerial homing attack. Sometimes the window in which you can trigger it is iffy, but there are very few parts in the game where such a thing was required, and it's not like it failed every time.
My biggest complaint is that one of the achievements needs you to think like a 5th grader. I'm not going to say which achievement or what it needs you to do, but if you go through the game, you should know which one I'm talking about.
The length of the game was pretty good. 13 hours for 100% is not bad at all for a platformer.
If you like N64-esque platformers, I strongly recommend you get this game. Unlike the other one that came out recently (you know who you are) I didn't regret buying it.
