in the past, so the nostalgic aspect is lost on me personally.  But I really enjoyed playing it and the unique identity that it offered.  Even though it is an older game, I found it to be a refreshing experience.
Whether or not you’ve played this in the past, I would imagine most fans of story-driven games with QTE action will enjoy the experience. The core gameplay involves moving around your characters and interacting with the environment to unravel a mystery.  There is a lot of freedom to discover or ignore certain things, but the core arc of the story can’t be affected.  The narrative is pretty interesting and the atmosphere is well developed.  It felt like the mid-late game is a bit rushed, but I suppose too much filler would have caused it to grow boring anyway.  Regardless, the best part of the narrative is the characters.  They have some actual depth, which many game developers still overlook this many years later. And the voice acting is mostly pretty good with very few cringe-worthy parts. If I was going to nitpick then I would point out that a few lines bothered me as a New Yorker because they weren’t natural (like how the cops say “New York Police” all the time and never say “NYPD”). But who likes a nitpicker? Not me.
The “action” boils down to QTE segments that are actually fast paced and can be challenging on the high difficulties.  Obviously, it can only be as exciting as QTEs can be (not very); but I would say it’s some of the most exciting QTE action I’ve experienced.  No worries though, it is a breeze on easy if you just want to enjoy the story and exploration/investigation aspects.  Furthermore, you’ll probably want to play with a controller if you can; I found it significantly more comfortable to execute the QTEs.
My main, and basically only, gripe with the game is the ridiculous camera action.  It has one of those weird camera situations where sometimes “right” becomes “left” and “up” becomes “♥♥♥♥ you.”  I never understood what value this adds to a game, and I remember hating the old
games as a kid for this very reason.  Luckily, in
, you can quickly reset the camera with one button to make all directions make sense again, but I really wish it wasn’t necessary.
But the real reason to play this game is the sex-scene. Not because “HAHA SEX,” or even because “HAHA VIDEO GAME SEX,” but because they turned the scene into a QTE minigame where you flick the joystick up in rhythm to your pelvic thrusts.  And it feels preposterously (and splendidly) out of place in an otherwise serious game.  Everyone should experience it.

This game is both one of the best and one of the worst I have played.
Think of it as robocraft is space.  Except with an even less clear power ranking system (other games might call them teirs).
There are few things more satisfying than to murder scores of opponents in your one masterfully designed ship (only to be brought down by the combined efforts of 7 enemies / half their team); to know that you are a better at designing and using your ships than nearly all others.  And there are virtually limitless possibility's in the skeleton, if not armament, of one's design - this allows for producing some incredibly exotic shapes.
At the same time, this game is basically one continuous grind.  The truely best independent (not guide based) player designs only can be actually completed once you get your ship ranking up to a sufficiently high level due to CPU restrictions... and that sufficiently high level is often 10 to 15 levels above your current one.  It is highly like a itch to have (atleast) one garage slot dedicated to an incomplete, even unplayable in its current stage, design.
This game is highly addictive, but also lacks any real way to keep the player interested for any extended length of time.  I reccomend this game for people who want to religiously kill 20 hours of their life over the course of 4-5 days and then move on to something else.

Then again, the series is slowly changing anyway and at least they kept a lot of the important things, like the Katz!

I'm so glad the "Tales of" franchise has been finally hitting Steam, starting off with what may now be my favorite entry in the series.
There's a lot of good game design nuance found in Zestiria, with a lot of game mechanics flowing into each other nicely. A lot of these elements aren't throwaway; utilizing every tool you're given leads to a lot of success and satisfaction, unlike a lot of things that I didn't see the need to bother with in past Tales games. There aren't any forced tutorials that are long-winded; any in the game are quickly handled, with a lengthy record and lexicon for players who really wish to sink their teeth in. The armatization ability does get pretty overpowered, sadly. There's also a handful of slipups outside of battle like the obnoxious Water Trial.
With some fixes, the game runs at a groovy 60FPS, always welcome for a high action game like this. I enjoyed a lot of the nice, fairly open environments compared to past games as well. The way hopping into battle works, directly from where you are in the world, lends to occasional camera problems in combat (and even worse when playing with multiple players). I've found that Zesteria packs the best soundtrack the series has had in quite a while. The story is okayish, par enough with recent Tales games, but like those, the party's interactions is where the series shines.
Overall, Zestiria has my recommendation and I hope for future successes from this series on Steam. Too bad how Symphonia turned out, but that's a different story.

I tried giving this game a chance. At first glance, it appears to be a Metroid-inspired platformer/exploration game. You move around, explore a 2D labyrinth, collect powerups, and fight monsters. However, this game just doesn't give me the satisfaction that you'd get from your typical metroid game. First off, you can't fire your weapon while moving, unless you're pulling off an aerial maneuver, and that gets old fast. It limits your options for attacking enemies while on the go, and enemies in this game will be guaranteed to get a few hits off on you before you can kill them. The environments you fight in are also tightly cramped, a little too much for comfort. As for bosses, the game doesn't really offer much there. Some are pretty tough, but I was able to cheese several bosses in by just getting up tot hem and shooting, and their AI couldn't make heads or tails regarding how to attack me.  Poorly coded if you ask me.
Overall, big disappointment in my eyes. I see alot of other people in these comments enjoy the game, which is a-okay by me. I just can't personally invest too much time into it, which is why I requested a refund.  It's so puzzling too, since I like the rest of the games from this developer. Guess platforming metroidvanias aren't their strong suit.

"SUPERHOT IS THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS!"
So, I bought Superhot after watching a couple of videos and was instantly sold on the premise.
The overall idea and gameplay are great + the game has a rather interesting story.
I am going to list the pros and cons of the game now, the game is great, but it does have a few issues that are worth talking about.
The good
- The game runs great, haven't had a single crash or bug since I started playing.
- Looks pretty. The overall aesthetic is quite eye catching, the minimalistic art style actually helps with the gameplay.
- The weapons feel really nice and lethal, each one is unique in it's own way.
- YOU CAN SLICE BULLETS IN MID AIR WITH A SWORD!
- Check out the Games folder, I wont spoil it :D
The Bad
- The story while interesting only took about 2 hours (it's all challenges afterwards) and it feels like there should have been more (future DLC perhaps?), the world seems to be very interesting, so I'd love to see more of it.
- The hitboxes can be imprecise, there were numerous times when I was sure that the bullet would fly past, only to see it smash on an invisible wall.
- The price is a bit steep. If the story was longer, I'd have no issues paying 23 euros for the game, but as it stands I am a bit disappointed.
Overall I feel like the game is great, especially if you don't care about the story and just want to kill the red guys, the endless mode is great and offers a lot of neat challenges.

username: A Certain Boss Who Is Big
text:
An expertly made 2D platformer, old school players will adore the metroid/castlevania feel this game has.}
The gameplay is genius, the silly humor is enjoyable and Bunny is a lovable character; there is alot in here for the completionist that likes spending hours in a single room, trying to find a hidden passage or item.
Controls could be better, true, but they are accurate enough.
Music and art are both perfect, except for some places where the designers got obviously bored.
Which brings me to my next point... Level design...
As good as it is, there are parts where the designers are just exploiting the low accuracy of the controls to give the game difficulty, something I greatly disliked. The game makes broad use of geniously planned, challenging situations without having the need of pulling the "Yeah good luck making this movement with the D-pad/Arrow Keys", and sadly, it does, and it does it a lot.
The aqua colored area is an example of this, while the Yellow Area with the purple bubbly floor is entertaining and challenging, the aqua area is just tedious.
Then we have Chelsea...
I'd have to make a separate entry to tell how badly written this character is; regardless of the "unserious" nature of this game, Chelsea just seems like something out of a DeviantArt webcomic, her personality, voice and powers are just plain stupid. While Bunny has a similar, bratty attitude, there is something in her that lets you enjoy the game... While Chelsea... She just makes everything SO boring and tedious, she is a totally flat character, and her "Game" feels just forced, as if the creator of the character had made a tantrum just to have their character in the game.
Her gameplay is, while boring and unentertaining, marvelously achieved, Chelsea feels slow and clumsy, yes, but her skills do work and challenge you to find the correct use for them... Most of the time... And this is because the designers tried to play the "Easy boss before, hard boss now" card and they failed horribly. Some Lesser bosses are a big threat for Chelsea due to her rock slow combat and this just makes the fights long and boring, this feels extremely forced and unnecesary.
Chelsea's final Bosses are cleverly designed, and whoever created those things has a reserved place in the Hall of A$$shole Designers (that is a compliment). This last part is the only thing I've enjoyed in Chelsea's Run... And that is dissapointing.

Fantastic city builder that while more simple then most, has it's own complexities. What really grabs me is while in most city builders the population increase works for you, it generally means faster building, more expansion, more resources, and better technology, but in this game population works against you as it should for the time it's based in. By encouraging population growth or accepting new people into your settlement without having the proper food, shelter, fuel, clothing, tools, so forth to actually sustain them you will quickly find yourself hemorrhaging resources. Also this game enforces working with nature to sustain your people, farming while an option is situational as it is with real life, certain crops only grow better in certain climates, and yield on them maybe less if your not in an ideal environment, and with the option to trade for those harder to grow items, it creates a nice balance of growth and trade for the items you want/need. And with the ability to mod the game (I would recommend Colonial Chapters, the team has done some outstanding overhauls that breathe new complexity, realism, and content into an already great game.) whats not to love, certainly way more bang for your buck then say some other city builders with mile long paid DLC list *Cough suck it sim city*.

One of the most elegant games I've ever played.
The graphics are gorgeous: I'm not going to apologize, atmosphere and aesthetics are very important to me.  And that includes music. They keep me playing.
I remember watching a zero punctuation short?  I think it was zero punctuation.  Describing the not-semantic difference between depth and complexity.
You want a simple game with great depth.  Adding 20 kinds of food sources which require 4 links in the manufacturing would be complexity.  If at the end of the day they're just all identical roadblocks on the path to feeding your digital people, then, zero depth would have been added.
Well, this is a simple game with great depth.  The town hall keeps track of demographics and other material statistics, and is your best friend.  There's zero complexity: no tutorial is needed to show you how to read a graph that food stores are dropping.
I learned so much about demographics.  My first town grew too rapidly and starved to death.  My second town grew too slowly and died out of old age (by the time the issue was discovered, no one was left who could have kids).  My third town stumbled in its third growing phase: again I expanded too rapidly.  This game teaches you steady, stable, disciplined growth.  A giant leap in population will create an oscillating population harmonic that echoes down the centuries, like the baby boom lead to an outsized generation every 30 years.
It actually taught me an important lesson in city management that I'd never have really internalized through reading about it in a book.
Now after 60 hours this game is exhausted and has nothing left to teach me, and I'll never play it again.  There are too many other games to try now.  And that's fine.  I paid $20 and got it back.  Would I really prefer that they pump 300 hours of inane filler material, like so many MMO's?  Of course not.

Freebie is a small, simple game wherein you launch a ball from one of two corners of the square into the center where there is a spinning paddle which is long and thin, and has a pointed tip on one end. The goal is to hit the ball into one of the four sides that is green. Hitting it into a red side will make you lose a life- you have three in total. Each time you hit it into a green side, you gain a point and the sides reset their colors. The two red sides are always touching, as well as the two green sides. This can help you dictate which of the two corners you want to launch the ball from. The paddle will start to spin faster as you gain more points.
That's pretty much all there is to it. The game does have multiple music settings, though I did opt out of those and listened to Spotify instead. There doesn't seem to be a way to turn off sound effects, though, and the ball bouncing sound is rather cheap/annoying sounding, and a tad loud. There are no graphical settings to choose from besides fullscreen or windowed, sadly.
The game also includes Steam Trading Cards and a few Steam Achievements, so all things considered, not a bad game to relax and play every once in awhile. Not something you'll get 300 hours out of, probably, but a decent time-sink, especially if you love chasing a better and better highscore.

It only takes a few minutes to confirm that this is not a very good game.
Beat'em-ups can be very simple games, but various physical and audio touches can carry titles that lack in complex gameplay.  Fighters Unleashed is not only a very simple game, it lacks any of those physical or audio touches.  Beat'em-ups are about physical violence, but attacks here have no impact.  Audio is weak, enemies barely flinch, attack animations have little "omph" and no follow-through. Animations are also used awkwardly at times, with the player just standing in the air for air combos or using a weird attack when landing.  Even the beat'em-up staple of punching a vending machine for an item is weak, with the stage object taking no damage and the recovery item simply appearing on the ground next to it.
The same lack of attention and polish is evident in the game's UI.  Menus do little to draw attention to the currently selected option, just slightly increasing its size.  The default Unity start-up config screen is used to handle most settings. There is nothing like a "how to play" screen (nor of course a button config option) in-game, you just have to figure everything out through trial and error (not that there is much to figure out.)  The game even lacks an "Exit Game" option, either as a menu option or a key command, you have to Alt-F4 to exit the game.

One of the absolute worst commercial beat’em ups I’ve ever played, and I’ve waded through quite a lot of the trash available for MAME and domestic systems.
Have you played Guardians of the Hood? Fighters Unleashed makes that game look like it had solid fighting mechanics.
You’ll start noticing the terrible hit detection and sometimes iffy controls, but what will wreck your head is the fact that your hits DO NOT STOP your enemies’ attacks. See that guy walking to you? Even if you hit him first he’ll be able to start his attack and hit you! That alone completely changes the whole logic of the fight. The only way to play the game is to make the enemies whiff their attacks (by jumping like a monkey every time an enemy comes close) and then hit them freely because most of the enemies are programmed to only attack like, once every ten seconds. In a fight against several enemies you will find yourself just mashing jumping attacks because staying on the ground is suicidal. Trying to play the game sensibly will just get yourself killed as every enemy will be able to walk through your attacks and land a hit on you.
Boss fights have a similarly stupid approach. Bosses are pretty much invincible most of the time, but every once in a while they will stay idle for several seconds so that you can hit them as much as you want, keeping in mind that hitting a static target is often difficult because of the poor hitboxes.
I feel that I’m describing it in much more detail that it deserves. The gameplay is just a trainwreck. On top of that it’s glitchy: often times, just after being hit and when no enemy is longer around, you will receive hits repeatedly and the only solution is to jump around until the game apparently refreshes your status from “hit” to “not-hit” or something.
I would like to know the story behind the game, because it’s not often that you run into a game with such a terrible gameplay, and some of the assets look decent, even if coming from cheap 3D models, few in quantity and often misused and in the wrong scale, so I would assume there’s some effort behind the game.

After hearing the news that Indigo Prophecy was coming out on PS4 next week for some reason, I decided to boot this up and see how this game aged. Going back to it after all these years wasn't as bad as I anticipated. I loved this game when it first came out, I was one of the apologists who easily overlooked the nosedive the plot takes in the later chapters, but playing it in 2016 was enjoyable for more than just nostalgia. It has aged fairly well. The controls were worse than I remembered and the frequency of the QTEs can get a bit annoying. Also, I didn’t recall this game being so short, I feel like I played this for weeks way back when. However, I think the story was much better this time around, most likely because I knew when things were about to go completely off the rails, so I wasn’t caught off guard like I was 10 years ago. I fully understand why people don’t like Cage’s games, but I just happen to operate on the same wavelength as his crazy brain full of plotholes and terrible twists.
Also worth noting, this release is the “Director’s Cut” which means I finally got to see the polygonal boobs that teenage me desperately wanted to see a decade ago when this first came out.

As a big Heavy Rain fan, and having also enjoyed Beyond Two Souls partly too, I'd been looking forward to playing this game for awhile. I'd actually bought the game a few years back intending to use it with a HD mod that was being worked on. Well the remaster came out first so I ended up getting that instead.
The remaster offers controller support which I found essential as I failed the opening of the game repeatedly whilst trying to figure out how the keyboard/mouse controls worked, the answer by the way is: they don't.
The original controller mappings aren't much better. At times you're expected to furiously mash left bumper, right bumper alternately to carry out menial tasks in the form of quick time events. These include breathing, climbing a fence, exercising, and many more.
Even worse are the simon says minigame QTEs, prepare to think with all sides of your brain as you play two side by side games of Simon says at the same time using the analogue sticks.
One area where the game should be improved on PC are first person shooting sections, right? Wrong. The mouse isn't mapped to aim, instead you can use the analogue sticks or whatever the default keyboard keys are.
This is the only story focused game on steam that I've retired and the controls have a large hand in that.
Facial textures looks generally decent and sharp when you consider their age, outfits on NPCs can look pretty poor though. The homeless man outside Agatha's House comes to mind. Most background textures look accceptable if a little stretched and blurred. The lighting looks nice if outdated. One thing that puts the remaster above the original is Anti-aliasing - I can't recall seeing jagged edges at all really.
I'll be vague here to avoid spoilers. The game starts out with one of the main characters murdering a man in a bathroom. There are supernatural elements involved and afterwards the character cannot remember how they arrived there, or why they would kill this stranger. After this act you take control and have to help them escape the scene unnoticed. Throughout the rest of the game you'll be trying to uncover the truth abouth this incident, both from their perspective and from other characters who are looking for them.
Initially the story starts off relatively intriguing, however after the opening, the pace slows down immediately while we deal with the emotional toll this event has on our character as well as being introduced to others. Levels in the game can involve mandatory sections such as getting out of bed, getting dressed, eating food, working out, playing a guitar, searching a massive bookstore for a single book etc. etc.
This style of long drawn out gameplay for mostly meaningless tasks is a large drawback for me. I understand the game is supposed to be cinematic, imitating a movie, and in someways tries to be lifelike but this just makes boredom come sooner. All this becomes tedious when you make these tasks mandatory and frustratingly difficult to complete with poor controls.
The game generally maintains a dark atmosphere. In fact, one mechanic has your characters' mood go up and down depending on whether you complete tasks successfully or not and this actually affects your chances of completing other tasks successfully too. However there are some moments of levity, such as Takeo and also some of Tyler's dialogue which actually had me laughing out loud on occasion.
Ultimately the game is old, and it feels it. This is combined with really whacky and difficult game mechanics and a rather slowly unfolding story. Nothing here really grabs you enough to make you think "I cannot wait to get home and continue playing Fahrenheit."
The moment when I decided to retired the game was wheeling Agatha around her house, I'd just fed her birds and now had to fetch matches and some other random stuff. I stopped and thought to myself "Why am I even playing this game. I don't care about the characters, or the gameplay or even the story really." So I just quit, and immediately uninstalled the game. I would not waste your money, or your time.
Thanks for reading. (my first steam review)

Not a bad game so far, very inspired by Robocraft and obvious where it borrowed from its progenitor. But that does not make it a bad game by any means.
The building is decent, but not hugely important. There is simply not enough depth to the building -yet- to make it matter much. The combat is very engaging and the ground work for a solid damage system are there, but as the building doesnt matter much yet so doesn't careful targeting. On the flip side, you can make a really cool looking ship without sacrificing much in the way of power/toughness.
The weapons need a lot of work though... the game is currently a snipe fest. Everyone uses the big cannons and stays back at max range just pinging at each other. Few ships are well enough designed and piloted by skilled enough people to zip in and fight up close/mid range but they are still inferior to the large cannon cruiser/battleships in general. They have a tough uphill journey to balancing their weapons and creating better counter play.
Over-all.... the game is worth giving a try. If you like it, throw a little $$ the developers way to keep growing the game. This is very much in the same boat Robocraft is, what they are trying to do is truly epic, very hard to balance, and requires  strong community support to pull off. These guys are not 3xA developers and with no major Publishers backing them. They are making a great product and need a dedicated communities help to not only fund it but also test and balance it.
This, as with Robocraft, has the potential to be one of the best multiplayer online games out there and far far exceed the 3xA big money games. So give it a try!

I've used RPG Maker VX for about 7 hours so far and have been delighted by how easy it is to use. I have to admit at this point, that I do have some experience in programming languages, so I do have an understanding of variables, events and functions that beginners may not, but I don't think a huge knowledge of programming is essential for using RPG Maker (but it helps).
Creating maps/levels is as simple as 'painting' textures onto the map grid, a large number of textures are available by default with more available through DLC (or import your own). Same goes for sound effects, character sprites, etc. The events interface is where you will be spending most of your time once you've designed your maps, the deceptively simple interface allows you to build interactions with objects and characters; buy/sell objects, trigger events, unlock secrets, change NPC behaviour to the player and control the flow of quests and objectives.
Well recommended for budding game developers out there, you probably won't make millions with your games, but with RPG Maker, you can export your work to show off to friends and family or even sell to the public (if it's good enough!).

Awesome program! I love RPG games like Final Fantasy pretty much since I started playing video games... This allows me to easily and quickly make an RPG game for me and my friends in pretty much 20 minutes without struggle.
Pros:
-NO programming required! I mean, yeah you can program stuff in RPG Maker VX Ace, but it's not a required thing like game engines such as Unity or Unreal.
-Character generator. This comes with a built in character generator that allows you to create characters in pretty much seconds. It has many different things you can put onto a character such as a suit, hats, bandages for your characters, glasses, wings, tails, you name it!
-Easy to use. Pretty much any game engine that comes with no programming required is easy to use, but this has an event system that is VERY simple to get the hang of...
-Workshop support. This comes with support for Steam Workshop which allows you to easily share your games with other RPG Maker VX Ace users. You can also get game templates, scripts, and "resource packs" which are basically the ground, water, buildings, etc.
-Export tool with file compacter. This allows you to create a game with no way to get into the files and change the game. The export tool is self explanatory but it pretty much takes the game file and turns it into a standalone game that any computer can add to play, even without RPG Maker installed!
-Games are optimized well. When you run a game made in this version of the program, it runs really well, unlike RPG Maker MV which I've played games on and even have tried...
Cons:
-Can be confusing for certain things. It's not really all that confusing, but it does have its moments when you're using the switches system. I can't really explain why but sometimes you get lost trying to make these work...
-Adding textures (resources) is hard. I've never really gotten hold of using the import tool to create textures... I know it's not all that hard but you have to create so many tiles. Once again, I can't really explain how this works, so if you're new like me, just stick with exporting the default textures and importing your version of it.
-Export of games can only be done on Windows. This isn't much of an issue for me as I have a Windows 10 laptop, but for people that want to play games you make on Macintosh computers or phones, you can't really do that unless you figure out how to emulate Windows on another system. This is pretty much the only good thing about RPG Maker MV to me...
-There are carts and rail resources accessable, but they can't be used together. Here's what I mean, if you want to create a railroad system sort of similar to Minecraft using mine carts which are in RPG Maker, you can't unless you change the texture of the boat to a mine cart and change the rail collisions to water... It's weird I know.
-Resolution of screen. This really doesn't annoy me at all but to some people, a 640*480 resolution screen is too small. I find it just fine for playing an RPG game as it fits the game's style well. If you want to create a game with higher resolutions, you may want to pay the extra $10 to get RPG Maker MV which has high resolutions...

I'm so glad the "Tales of" franchise has been finally hitting Steam, starting off with what may now be my favorite entry in the series.
There's a lot of good game design nuance found in Zestiria, with a lot of game mechanics flowing into each other nicely. A lot of these elements aren't throwaway; utilizing every tool you're given leads to a lot of success and satisfaction, unlike a lot of things that I didn't see the need to bother with in past Tales games. There aren't any forced tutorials that are long-winded; any in the game are quickly handled, with a lengthy record and lexicon for players who really wish to sink their teeth in. The armatization ability does get pretty overpowered, sadly. There's also a handful of slipups outside of battle like the obnoxious Water Trial.
With some fixes, the game runs at a groovy 60FPS, always welcome for a high action game like this. I enjoyed a lot of the nice, fairly open environments compared to past games as well. The way hopping into battle works, directly from where you are in the world, lends to occasional camera problems in combat (and even worse when playing with multiple players). I've found that Zesteria packs the best soundtrack the series has had in quite a while. The story is okayish, par enough with recent Tales games, but like those, the party's interactions is where the series shines.
Overall, Zestiria has my recommendation and I hope for future successes from this series on Steam. Too bad how Symphonia turned out, but that's a different story.

Game Score: 8.0/10
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summery:
Tales of Zestiria's new openworld approach and battle system additions does help make the game worthy of celebrating the franchise's 20th anniversary.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
It's amazing that the very first instalment in the Tales franchise Tales of Phantasia got released 20 years ago on the Super Famicom console in Japan. Since then the Tales of Series has had their fair share of great titles, somewhat good games and then bad games that thankfully for company reasons didn't want those games to be released in the West. Whatever the case these games are known for their entertaining skit sequences, great storylines and characters and enjoyable battle systems which are well loved in the hearts of RPG fans alike. Here we are now with the next new instalment with Tales of Zestiria which was announced and eventually released to celebrate 20 years of the long running franchise. It now aims for an open world landscape design, fusions Dragon Ball Z style as well as brining the best ideas from old tales instalments. Sure it's earned a bit of controversy in Japan for the game's handing of the main characters and has earned some rather unfair reviews over in the West. So what does this new Tales instalment fell in the eyes of a long running Tales player like myself? well I am so glad that I get to answer that question.
The setting of Tales of Zestiria takes place in a medieval fantasy world where the land is corrupted by a dark source called malevolence which are caused by the negative emotions caused between the people. Humanity's only chance of purifying the land is the power of the Shepherd and the main character Sorey being your every day standard J-RPG protagonist takes on that sacred duty of becoming a Shepherd and gains the power to fight the hellions. The characters of Tales of Zestiria are very likeable and their character development during the course of the game are great to watch. Sorey is the usual kind of J-RPG protagonist who wants to know about the world as well as exploring the various ruins, he also wants to believe that humans should be able to coexist with spiritual beings known as Seraphim which cannot be seen by the human eyes. Mikleo voiced by Scott Manville who also did Lloyd from Tales of Symphonia also tends to enjoy exploring ruins as much as Sorey but also ends up being the cautious type but their brotherly relationship is a cool sight to behold. Lailah is a pun artist who will use them as a way out of telling out her oath but acts a real support for Sorey. Edna tends to make fun of the party and other people's situations and also loves to insult Mikleo by calling him Meebo which is very funny. Later on in the game there is Dezel who vows revenge for the death of his friend and lastly there are Alisha and Rose. Alisha is a princess of Hyland who takes her role as a knight who will do what she can to help out her kingdom but she holds conflictions between understanding what it takes to keep the peace as a princess as well as upholding her status as a knight. Rose a character who fills Alisha's role for Sorey offers support for him but also acts as a boss for the Sparrowfeathers and a merchant who believes what she thinks is right for Sorey and his friends and her members. The writing is really good and the english dub acting is very strong showing the emotions of each of the characters very well, plus there is also the option for the Japanese audio tracks if the players so desire.
Tales of Zestiria's new gameplay change is that it goes for an openworld exploration which allows you to explore the vast reaches of the world as you see fit, it uses the same field controls like in the Tales of Xillia games so that you'll feel more familiar. The openworld design allows you to explore the environments freely both without the penalty of having tough enemies that can destroy the player instantly (aside from optional boss encounters) and also unlocking new areas at a reasonable pace as you go through the storyline. Compared to Final Fantasy XII which did use the openworld design before this game Tales of Zestiria has a well executed openworld design that makes you feel like an explorer without the game having to punish you for going of the main path which is a great thing. You'll explore grassy field areas, mountains and plenty of cavern and ruin areas which each have treasure and herbs to pick up and returning from Tales of Graces there are hidden discovery points that can be unearthed.
Some areas will have a puzzle to solve which will involve either lighting up pedestal with fire, making your way through areas without being seen using the water, breaking blocks with earth and jumping past gaps using the wind. The earth and wind puzzles are quite good and can be done without any stress but the fire and water puzzles are the worst the game throws at you. The fire puzzles require you to light up a pedestal in order but the twist is that you need to light one of those from a direction that it wants you to light it up from which can be confusing unless you look underneath the pedestal indicating the direction and in what order you need to light them in. The worst puzzles come from the water trial where you need to use the water power to get past the eyes without being noticed, if you happen to get spotted by the eyes you get warped back to the start of the entire dungeon. It doesn't help that sometimes you'll walk into a room and then BAM! the eyes instantly see you without any warning. This actually forces the player to take it slow and examine where the eyes are and then use the water power to make it past it, however even when you do manage to unlock warp points you still end up back at the dungeon entrance if you get spotted which will force you redo some areas which afterwards it just becomes annoying. There was a sequence where I got stuck after defeating a boss fight in Marlind and I had no idea what to do next and it wasn't until I looked online that I found out that you had to burn those dark cloud hellion things using a fire spell that were placed all over the town. I had no idea that I was meant to do so because I didn't think there was possibly any indication at all during any dialogue at all at that point unless I skipped something.
You can take a stop in exploration to visit a town in order to rest up and heal up, purchase equipment and items and also get information from NPC's to your next objective or side quests you know like in other J-RPGs of the last decade or so. Sidequests and shopping have undergone a change, for sidequests they are much easier to track down thanks to a new conversation that you have with the character following you, you can talk to the character following you to have him/her remind you of your current objective or for a side quest's destination. Sidequests will range from fighting optional encounters that are hidden all through each of the maps, collecting gems or just for cutscenes and skits to unlock hidden items. Each of the ingame shops returning the levelling up system from Tales of Xillia only that each store has their own set of items and gears and buying each item increases that shops experience, if at maximum they start doing discount sales and also sell out their best item for sale if you have the gald for it.

This game is a metroidvania, in the spirit of the handheld console Castlevania games. Its major differences lie in the art style of the main characters, which more closely resemble popular Japanese doujinshi characters, and the movement mechanics of the character.
I liked the style of the MC, Bunny, the aesthetics of the areas, and the cat boss, which led me to buy this game.
The primary difference between the handheld Castlevanias' and this game's movement mechanics seems to be that this game is noticeably more rigid in where the character model is allowed to stand or land. Moving to the very edge of a platform in this game will cause the character to snap back away from the edge of the platform tile. The jumping physics also more resemble Cave Story's than Castlevania's, since more emphasis is placed on acceleration. Castlevania games allow more crisp turning/jumping commands and have less acceleration in their normal jumping physics, which is probably because characters don't jump as high in Castlevania games.
Platforming in Bunny's storyline with the 360 controller was difficult because dashing is activated with two clicks left or right, but when using the controller's analog stick, I would cause Bunny to dash inadvertently, or not dash at all, making her fall to her spikey death many times (and causing me much frustration). Other mechanics, like short wall hops and time-reversal courses, added to the difficulty.
The bosses are much more do-able than the platforming, provided one has the right weapons, which are found by breaking lamps. Bunny's interactions with bosses were amusing, though she's quite the crass lass for indiscriminately defeating them (among other reasons, including her speech mannerisms). In the end, however, she redeems herself (though you have to beat Chelsea's story for that, which I haven't).
I've read that Chelsea's playstyle is very different (and probably mitigates the hard platforming parts seen in Bunny's mode), so I'm gonna get started on that right away.
Update: Chelsea's playstyle is indeed very different. I had an faster time completing her mode; her ladder and floaty jumps made areas more accessible, and normal bosses are not as difficult as Chelsea, though this could just be due to my experience gained playing Bunny's mode. Chelsea's final boss fights are harder than Bunny's,
With Chelsea,

With that said, this game was pretty satisfying to beat, and I would rank it among my favorite metroidvanias/2d platformers.

The Tales game have always been JRPGs with a capital J.
So I went into this game, fully expecting motivational platitudes, every fight doing double duty as a metaphor for some metaphysical struggle, and unneccessary romantic tension. You know... the good stuff.
What I got instead, was a 40 hour ride of word barf, vaguelly directed at the viewer.
One of the characters defining trait is, quite literally, that she can't talk about anything relevant to the plot if it could serve to minimize unneccessary drama. And why is that? MAGIC!
Indeed, for as many times as MAGIC has to rescue the plot from whatever corner it has currently driven itself into, it's a miracle that the main character isn't named Copperfield.
I stopped playing the game, after having to sit through a half hour cut-scene which, if the music and cinematography was anything to go by, was supposed to be a the big climatic pre-final battle recap of whatever the heroes learned on their journey. For 30 minutes the characters talked non-stop, delievering one non-sequitur after the other, as long as it sounded even mildly philosophical. And having said absolutely nothing at all, the game then proceeded to show fireworks, like a child who thinks it won an argument by saying "Nuhu, you're stupid!".
That is the big theme of the game: The Creators obviously wanted to raise some big questions about sacrifice, and duty, and what is neccessary to gain peace, but never stopped to consider that at some point they also would have to present answers to those questions.
A must buy, it's the most innovative shooter I've played in years.

The port is amazing. On high end rigs, and with the mod, it runs at 2160p supersampling 60fps on fairly high powered systems without a hitch. The keyboard controls are never ideal for this type of game but god damn they tried and it shows. No advanced rendering options, but Tales games are always about the art style graphically, not the BLEEDING EDGE GRAFIX!!!1one, it's mostly just LOD options.
The gameplay is pretty well put together. It's not standard Tales fare, it's a janky beast of its own. Skill won't win the day here, you'll have to overprepare due to the amount of jank and lack of polish. Armitization, dualizing with the spirit characters, eliminates all but the highest levels of difficulty, then the game throws the party systems to the wind at interspersed spots through the game taking the crap from under you.
The story, oh god the story. Don't even bother. A strong start belies a rampant case of Author Tract. Rose goes from being a mild annoyance to an actual main character. I'm not kidding. Hideo Baby, it's reported, trainwrecked his own story because he got a raging katana over Rose's voice actor, turning the once actually-well-nuanced stories of Tales games into Rose's Mary Sue Adventures featuring Sorey the ♥♥♥♥boy (Who the ♥♥♥♥ Is Alisha Edition). The localization gets amazingly bad and disjointed later on, having people sound like they're having two halves of a conversiation and hinting at things that aren't even relevant concepts.
Go Shiina and Motoi Sakuraba put their heads together for standard Tales over-orchestration for the battle themes, sounding entirely more grand than the next batch of mooks to fight. It's a welcome return to form.
If you're a Tales fan, prepare to cringe hard. If you're here for the PC port, there's a lot to love with its flaws. Tentatively recommended.

I've finished the game and I can say that the story is impressive, but somewhat rushed
since the story focused more on Sorey alone
. However, I will admit that it's immersive in a way, especially when you start sleeping in inns and discover significant places that trigger skits known as Discovery Points. That's where this game redeems itself in terms of skits through character development.
Characters are well developed, yet needs more room for improvement as stated above. The good part of this game is that there is a companion that you can talk to, to aid you in doing your side quest (known as Sub Episodes) as well as your main quest (known as Main Episodes) which is a feature I love so I know where I left off in the event I stopped playing for some time.
Aside from that, the characters are immersive as well so I do not see that as a problem as a whole, except that, characters needs more emphasis
. Comical relief for the characters as a whole has exceeded my expectations in a Japanese Role-Playing Game.
The equipment fusion system is somewhat confusing because of the learning curve. The learning curve is so high to the point that it will be hard for you to get at first glance. You can do that by activating a skit by sleeping in the inn and by progression. Aside from that, some of the equipments in the shops are expensive from the start, but it will be alleviated as you immerse yourself to the game by encountering more enemies as you play. The summary is this: as you discover more weapons, more properties will be included in the equipment that you find during your playthrough. At the end of the day, discovering possible combinations to further synergize your passive skills to take advantage of the battle will help, especially in dire situations like optional bosses. If you're also planning to increase your stat as you level up, that's another strategy as well if you are planning to focus on a specific stat. Examples are the following: Increasing of Blast Gauge and Increasing of a certain stat as you level up. Some equipments that you obtain provide immunities, and when stacked up, you will be resistant to ailments by half, if not fully resistant. However, Fusion System will break the stack that you created, so it's all about the strategy right there.
It's good and it really feels like an action game for me because of how I control my character. The learning curve is easy and as you progress, strategies must be made to further take advantage of your enemy/ies's weaknesses and resistance. Aside from that, taking advantage of the power hits and juggling the enemy/ies is the way to go. This is better with multiplayer because the AI in Zestiria is half-baked and they tend to waste more Blast Gauge than usual
, this is noticeable in the final parts of the game, especially after tinkering the Strategy menu. But don't get me wrong. The AI is also intelligent and adapts accordingly, this is applicable before the final parts of the game, but it's not as perfect as what you think. Aiming for a no-KO for this game is something you will work hard on, especially when you are under leveled when dealing with high-tier bosses. High-tier bosses are those bosses that roam around the field with the dark smoke at the center of the enemy. Most high-tier bosses will not offer a retry but it's a gamble. However, I believe that issuing AI presets such as Prioritize Defense, Spread Out and Focus Attacks. For the Prioritize Defense, the AI tends to spam restorative and buffs all the way when they could better guard themselves from the enemy/ies's attacks as well as Spreading Out doesn't do its job either because some AIs tend to attack even though the first player ordered the AIs to Spread Out (Taken the consideration of utilizing the Strategy menu). Focusing attacks to the enemy is a lackluster for me, as it's vague whether a) the AI has to focus on the enemy attack or b) the AI has to focus on what the enemy/ies attack will come to further counter-attack the artes of the enemy/ies casted to a specific character. Don't forget the camera issues as well, it will kill your momentum in battle! Battle actions are also a plus to further customize your needs during a battle. I do recommend that you check your battle actions from time to time as you progress the game. You might discover a new battle action that will benefit you.
They are useful especially in emergency situations where Save Points aren't accessible. This is the feature that I am impressed as how Tales implemented it. However, the issue that I find in this game is that, when the player starts loading from the last save data, and the player started to quick save before the boss battle, it will load to the LAST SAVED DATA (where the player saves in the save point) rather than loading from the quick save. The player has to go to menu and will need to load the quick save by themselves.
Of course, some minor but commendable system that needs to be mentioned is that, the encounters are somewhat realistic, such as this one:
But of course, Sorey didn't fall. There was just a major re-positioning of the characters and of the battlefield.
It's somewhat half-baked as well, but tolerable (thanks to the community fix by Kaldaien, I was able to hit 60FPS with this game but it's almost perfect for a port) because Bamco just ported the game in Playstation 3 up to Playstation 4, that can only hit up to 30 FPS. I hope that they will improve on that more in their future games.
I love the soundtrack of this game. You will love it once you progress through the game.
So far, I recommend this game for those who are planning to buy Tales of Zestiria, however, it's better if it's on sale and includes discounts.

Now that I've gotten that obligation out of the way, SUPERHOT is a short but sweet game centered around the premise of time manipulation in a first-person shooter. If you haven't played the free demo that's been floating around online for the last couple years, you should probably play it, as that will determine whether or not you'll like this game.
There's an overall narrative similar to Pony Island, if you've played it. Basically, you're thrown from stage to stage with the objective of killing all the red guys. They'll be equipped with their fists, pistols, shotguns, machine guns, etc... And you'll be using time manipulation to deal with all of them. They take one hit (3 with fists or thrown objects) to kill, and so do you. If you die at any point during one of the many brief stages, you'll be thrown back to the beginning of that stage to learn from your mistakes, and try again, eventually defeating all of your foes, and moving onto the next stage.
The main story mission takes about 90 minutes to complete, give or take a little based on your ability to grasp the time manipulation concept.
Once you're finished with the main story mission, you'll be provided with access to all 32 missions you previously completed, endless mode, and some challenges.
Endless mode is a whole bunch of levels from the story mode where the overall goal in each level is to kill as many enemies as you possibly can, allowing you to unlock even more levels in this mode. This is probably the mode that most of your money is going toward, as it seems to provide the most content out of anything in the game. So before somebody tries to persuade you that the game is too expensive for a 2 hour (or 90 minute in my case) campaign, they probably didn't try out endless mode.
Challenges are unlocked by accomplishing certain tasks throughout the story mode's missions, and once a challenge is unlocked, it will unlock a new mode for all of the main story missions, such as a speed run mode, or a speed run mode with a timer that counts down even when you're not moving. Not quite sure what all the other modes are, as I haven't unlocked them yet. There's 13 in total. Besides the two speedrun ones I have, there's also one where you only have a katana.
Beyond the main time manipulation game, you can also navigate the game's unique main menu to find some other various mini-games and fun bonus content.
I've seen the pricing for this game compared to something like Firewatch, but in the end, both games are around the same length, except Firewatch doesn't have any endgame content, and frankly SUPERHOT's story is more interesting.

Extremely poor controls ruin what could be a great platformer. The dashing relies on a double tap which works 50% of the time you NEED it to, and 50% when you need it to NOT dash.
Jumping is also painful, as the game relies on several different jumps: jumping from a standstill, jumping while moving, jumping while dashing, and an attack kick which is an attack while dashing. Again, the dash jumps are painful because dashing barely works but jumping also sometimes doesn't react well when you need it. Also, jumping from a standstill has just a little more height than jumping while moving, and the game WILL require this. It makes trying to move through some parts really frustrating as you need to stop moving (and dodging!) to get a fraction more of an inch in your height to get to where you need to go.
You'll stick to ledges of platforms your standing on, which works out okay when you want to stay on a platform, but it will magnetically pull you when you want to jump down past it, or throw you off small platforms when you attempt to land on them. Just.. infuriating when this part goes wrong.
The fighting is fine, there are different weapons which feel great, the art is light-hearted and whimscle, and the game has clever time-manipulation puzzles, but I just can't recommend it due to the fact I want to break my controller in half when the game doesn't recognize my input to do a sequence of very precise moves, which is 90% of this game. 6/10

This game is a rage game, as many others have said, but what many others haven't said is some of the rage comes from some very poor coding when it comes to movement - specifically turning back and forth and jumping.  If you haven't completed all animation sequences down to the pixel, you are NOT allowed to jump or turn.  That means you can't let go of the left button and immediately hold down right and expect to turn.  You won't.  In fact, if you immediately press right after holding left, the game may sometimes glitch and keep making you walk left.
Same thing with jumping.  If your character is, for any reason, in the middle of standard movement - you will NOT be able to jump.  Yes, that does mean that if you are being pushed forward by an enemy, you CANNOT JUMP.  In certain situations this very much seems to be a bug.  Now, I admit, I'm not the best player, but 1 to 2 out of every 5 deaths feels like I was cheated.
This is a cute game, though, and if you are able to drop a gamepad and walk away from a cheated death, then you can deal with this game.

I wanted to like this game. It really blew up and got popular, but it falls flat in a few areas.
First off, the game does a good job of building tension. The puppets are creepy to watch through the cameras. The audio clues and grainy cameras really add to the creepy atmosphere.
However, this is all ruined when you actually are killed. Upon dying, whatever puppet kills you shows up in a "jumpscare" which is more annoying than scary. It is here you can see just how goofy the puppets actually look. Do not be fooled by the "scare cam" videos that everyone and their brother put out over this game. People are hamming it up for the camera and this game only has one "scare" for you which is a speaker-cracking "scream" when you die.
Puppet movement is random. This mean some levels, you are doomed to lose through no fault of your own. For example, the Fox puppet shows up (he shows up if you view him too much or not enough on the
and to stop him, you close the door. He pounds on the door and saps energy, increasing with each subsequent visit. One game, the Fox was sent at me three times within a minute (the game resets him after each attack but sometimes resets him to his "going to attack you soon" phase). There was nothing I could do to stop it.
I do like the premise and it is very creative. However, it all boils down to whether the game allows you to win rather than player skill and for that, I cannot recommend it.

This game, while rather simple and basic, offers a fair amount of entertainment for the price.  I personally picked this up half off, and it was definitely worth my two quarters.  The premise is simple. You shoot balls at a spinning weiner in the center of the screen, which bounces the ball in some direction.  Now here is where the game gets tricky; the square containing the weiner has 4 walls, 2 of which are green, two are red.  The colors are always connected, so you will never find two greens across from eachother.  If standard gaming conventions haven't taught you anything, or you just prefer to reside under rocks, red is bad, it makes you sad; green is good, it gives you wood.  The game has 3 different selections for background music, all of which are unique and pretty fun to listen to, my favorite for being the third option.  Your options for gameplay are "play" and something the devs decided to call "epilepsy mode."  The difference between the two is simply the background.  A static background for standard mode, with a spinning background with a brightness that constantly bounces up and down for the epilepsy mode.  While it is rather disorienting, the strobe light setting actually helped me to perfect the game: I will attribute this to pure goodness darn luck rather than skill.  There are 5 acheivements in Freebie, all of which are obtained by reaching the next tier of how fast gumby plays helicopter.  Every 10 points increases the speed, unlocks an acheivement, and gives you a really good overall feeling of accomplishment.  It makes you feel like you have earned your perfect game.  Something that I think is pretty rare.  This game probably won't quite make any top 10 lists, but for the price it offers a fun experience, nice challenge, and good feeling.  The game isn't spectacular, it is incredibly simple with basic geometric graphics, but it doesn't pretend to be anything it's not.  It sticks to its simple idea and works as a concept.  I rate this game 6/10.

I bought this on sale, thinking there was probably no way I'd lose my money. Wow...I was completely surprised by how this game sucked me in and became one of my favorites.
I like city builders, but usually I get to a certain point and discover that my strategy thus far isn't aplicable in the later stages of the game, or I hit disasters of some sort that I just can't deal with and I get beaten on by the game mechanics. The other thing that usually turns me off is getting to the point where you're just waiting for the things you've put into motion to bear fruit...and you just watch time go by, waiting for the chance to get involved in the game again. This game manages to solve both issues in a very nice fashion. I did not enocounter any problems (at the standard play level) that I could not recover from with a little effort, and the micromanaging on this game is presented in such a way that you're constantly optimizing your resources, but it's not a burden.
It really impresses me that the game is not complete at the time of this review. It's 100% playable and a lot of fun. Challenging, but not overkill for the casual gamer. If you have any love for city builders, I highly recommend giving this game a try. Go through the tutorials, and pay special attention to the part where assigning your workers is discussed....this will make or break the game for you. Remember to plan ahead. Things take time to happen, but you will get enough warning to make effective changes to your resource strategy if you're watching carefully.
TL;DR : Great city builder game with easy to understand mechanics that solve many of this issues that can make city builders boring or discouraging.

I remember playing the first level on a PS2 demo disc years ago, where you had to hide your murdered vicitm in a bathroom stall of a diner before the cop entered. When I bought the game on sale, I was excited at first, but sadly the first level is the high point; the game starts itself on top of quality hill, and slowly decends from there. Compared to future Quantic Dream games, Farenheit has the most supernatural elements, the most bizarre story, and the least compelling gameplay. Even Heavy Rain's QTE fest was more engaging, since there wasn't nearly as much micromanagement. Here you'll have to input a QTE for every rung of a ladder you climb, every bite of a meal, hilariously even every individual thrust in the bedroom during one scene. This gets insanely repetitive, especially with the games moderately lengthed story (for the genre) at about 12 hours (Mine is 20 because I left the game on overnight one time, I'll explain why in a sec).
The story starts pretty grounded, but the more that is revealed, the more I found myself losing interest. By the end, the story makes no sense, and I feel like David Cage was just smashing his action figures together to mimic a fight scene in front of his dev team to convey his vision for the 'epic' conclusion. I did find myself having fun for the first half of the game, playing multiple characters with different motivations was interesting, but pretty much ditched by the final quarter.  One of the main design problems with the game is that it is rushed. For example, most of the game takes place during a 5 day period, then suddenly months go by at a time, a ton of strange supernatural plotholes are introduced, and characters that were conflicted drop any resemblence of a coherant arc to form a good guys vs bad guys ending.
Technically, the game runs fine. It obviously doesn't look incredible, being more than a decade old, but atleast that means anything can run it fine. You can switch between SD and HD visuals with F9. but I rarely used it, and when I did, there wasn't much of a difference. Launching the game was another story. I was afflicted (like many), with the 'call stack error', essentially when booting up the game would freeze and a massive text box would pop up. With no exit button, you were forced to close the game through task manager. I tried deleting a ton of different files then validating and a few other workarounds I read, but nothing ever worked. I realised that if I set the monitor display to portrait, then I could see the entirety of the call stack error box, with before-hidden buttons right at the bottom. Since you can't resize this box and I don't know of any other way, this was how I launched it.
From here, after changing the default French language options, I could play. After a 4 hour session, I launched the game the same way the following night, only for the game to crash everytime loading my save. To fix this, I ended up deleting my .INI file again and validating. I ultimately left the game open overnight here, as I didn't want to go through all these workarounds just to launch and play a game. So if you can't deal with those technical issues, I definitely wouldn't recommend. If you want a more coherant and engaging crime drama-esque game, try out Quantic Dream's follow up title, Heavy Rain. It fixes many of Farenheits gripes, although it is a Playstation exclusive. Other than that, you could try Telltale's excellent The Wolf Among Us.

PROS:
-Physics obeying marble - marble has momentum and you cannot perform an instantaneous stop, therefore, the gameplay takes on a more realistic mechanism and you have a learning curve - a game with no challenge is boring!
-The game allows you to unlock other levels if you have accumulated a reasonable number of orbs, which is handy if you are stuck on one level and you would like to progress and return another time.
-Cool ingame quirks such as hidden orbs and special abilities (such as a jetpack, to reach high value orbs in otherwise inaccessible places.
-Lower skills tiered levels effectively teach you how to more around and use the basic and special features of the game, so you learn through playing and there is guidance.
-The imagery is consistently retro and is really pleasing to the eye
-The soundtrack is also super cool and fits the retro theme
-No two game designed levels look similar, so there are always new things to discover
-Custom creation levels!
-Customize your own marble
CONS:
-Whilst the soundtrack is cool, it seems that it is only a few tracks on repart throughout the entire gameplay, which may become annoying if you are playing for a long session.
-Special features, such as moving platforms, move too slowly, so if you are trying to reacha time record, it leaves you with less "actual game time" towards achieving this.
-The game awards time trophies for beating records, even if you do not find all orbs on a level
Overall, this is a highly addictive and quality game which is well worth the low cost in the Steam store.

This is the sort of game I'm looking for when I play a 3D platformer, and it's an excellent example of one to boot. Pleasantly silly (though not afraid to get a little spooky), with excellent variety that made me actually eager to see what was coming up next. The boss fights were fantastic, and while long and full of moves I had to watch out for, I didn't think any of them were particularly unfair, or that the game mechanics themselves were working against me.
The controls were pretty dang great, and the only actual hiccup I found was when using the aerial homing attack. Sometimes the window in which you can trigger it is iffy, but there are very few parts in the game where such a thing was required, and it's not like it failed every time.
My biggest complaint is that one of the achievements needs you to think like a 5th grader. I'm not going to say which achievement or what it needs you to do, but if you go through the game, you should know which one I'm talking about.
The length of the game was pretty good. 13 hours for 100% is not bad at all for a platformer.
If you like N64-esque platformers, I strongly recommend you get this game. Unlike the other one that came out recently (you know who you are) I didn't regret buying it.

Where to begin?
This game is a metroidvania in the way that Bubsy is a platformer. Not nescissarily broken but just poorly executed. Unlike defining games of the genre, Super Metroid ans Super Castlevania 4, which ease you into the game and are more or less well scaled difficulty that challenges what you've learned in previous areas, this game gives you two or three screens to aquire the skills you need to face the first boss. After the aforementioned screens it basically turns into a Super Meat Boy/Touhou/Kaizo hybrid without any of the awesome game mechanics in any of the games mentioned.
The shooting is cumbersome, at least on keyboard, And kinda hard to get used to in the SIX FIRGGIN SCREENS YOU HAVE TO DO SO!!! Super Metroid did have a similar 8 direction shooting mechanic, but at no point did you have to fight Flandre Scarlet with only one HP upgrade. This wouldn't be such a big deal if there was auto-fire like in, I don't know, most bullet hell shmups that let you fight back. To bring back metroid, the first major fight, Ridley, can be challenging but nothing you can't deal with because they hid the tutorial in the opening level and you are competent in basic combat  because of that.
Keep in mind, I don't hate rediculously difficult games. In fact, Super Meat Boy is probably my favorite platformer. But what do all good insanely difficult games have in common? The answer, make death painless (Super Meat Boy), Funny (AVGN Adventures), or preface the game with the prospect of thousands of deaths (Dark Souls). Maybe it's because I grew up with games where death was an actual setback, but I kind of expect one of those three things in games where I can't expect not to die multiple times in the first 20 minutes of the game on a first playthrough. Deaths are supposed to tell you that you did something at least a little more stupid than not memorizing attacks, in this sense if you could take more than about 4 hits from the first boss, this might be more tolerable as you could get some bearing. Harking back to Super Meat Boy, technically, only the boss of chapter 4 is trial and error, everything else, with good reaction and recognising what does what, you could get through 99% of the levels in one life... if you're good enough.
I also by no means hate anime esq art styles. what with skullgirls being my favorite head to head fighter. In fact in games that have them, they're often done remarkably well, including here. But the difference between SkullGirls and this atrocity  is that SkullGirls actually has good gameplay to back it up
Two last complaints: Soundtrack is lackluster and Chelsea is sounds about as grating as just about any character in any game I have played.

A fairly fun little metrovania, heavy on the action and with an emphasis on hardcore difficulty.
The game is setup to encourage carefully thought out movement (see notes on controls below), but it is also targeted at speed-runners.
The way the power-ups work has a very arcadey feel; eg. you can only have 1 weapon at a time, and get them from pickups.
There is also a time stop/rewind mechanic, similar to things like Braid.
The controls need an especial mention; if you look at many of the negative reviews here they will call them things like impercise or unresponsive. This is both a bit accurate and inaccurate.
The controls are NOT impercise, they are high high percision;
You can also easily make your character do many things: 'bunny' jump up, foward, and backwards, spin jump, attack up, foward, & diagonally, duck, dash, dash attack.
The problem is a number of those manuvers require very percise button presses, and the controls are also setup so that the character will 'commit' to some actions, so you can't quickly cancel it to do another action.
This can make the contols feel *unresponsive*, if you do things by refex and get a button press wrong.
For those of you who remember, it is similar to the problems in Super Metroid in making a spin vs. regular jump, or in Symphony of the Night and accidentally doing Alucards reverse mini-dash thingy, except a bit more unforgiving.
I'm pretty sure it was an intentional choice in how to setup the controls, they want to award percisely controlling the character.
Example: Try to turn the character around and do a spin jump (jump and push forward same time), what actually happens is you do a backward jump (jump and push bacward same time), what you need to do is turn, then spin jump.
The controls take a while to get used to but this is a fun game with a unique style and charm to it. It might not be the end all of the genre but its worth the price.

Project Root is sort of an open-area arcade shooter that feels like it came from the 90's.  I was enticed by what I saw, bought it on sale, and merrily jumped in.  20-ish hours later (which was in Offline Mode and thus not displayed here), I was done waiting for it to become worth my time OR money.  It's got a good arcade-y feel to it, the objectives are (most of the time) clearly marked, and the game DOES work as intended.  HOWEVER....it is heavily marred, and I shall focus on those details.
The English is sloppy.  Even one as pedantic as I can forgive the occasional mistake, but this is pre-high-school level, and it grates on me.  Some of this is presented in pre- or post-mission cutscenes that alternate between two ugly character stills and an uninteresting story poorly presented through text.  The rest of this mess is given by all the text frequently sprawled across the bottom during the action.  This is distracting at best, and often meant I had to back away from all combat to catch what was going on before the text rapidly vanished.
And the controls....I don't know about keyboard/mouse, but I played this on a controller, and it was not fun.  There is never a need to stop shooting.  You should be shooting during the majority of the time.  You need to be holding down a button to shoot.  These missions are upwards of 20 minutes each.  That makes 20 minutes or more of holding down a button more-or-less constantly, which gets uncomfortable, and the ensuing cramps disuaded me from that third mission in a sitting.
But what about aside from that, what about the gameplay?  Well, there are upgrades!  Upgrades that don't necessarily explain what they do.  "Elite kit: Rockets" doesn't tell me much.  And these felt minor, easily forgettable, and like the points on "Whose Line Is It Anyway?"... didn't really matter.  Honestly, the game should've just left out the upgrades altogether.
The view feels too zoomed in.  If you want to avoid getting shot from off-screen or rushing past an enemy nearly as soon as it appears, you need to keep your eyes OFF of the scenery and on your mini-map.  The shooting and the dodging just don't feel GOOD this way.
Now, some of you may like the idea of infinitely respawning enemies.  Keep the pressure on as you go for the objectives, right?  Well even that just feels clumsily done in Project Root.  I found one of the spawn points.  A ship appearing in air right in front of me, and another instantly appearing right in front of me as its predecessor died in fire.  I should not have been able to see that.  That aside, the constant enemy spawns are just an aggravating nuisance during the boss fights, which go on too long anyway.
This game's graphics and settings are also subpar.  It felt a little sluggish on my quite-decent machine, despite not looking the part of a modern game.  Reducing the graphics settings yielded a result, and smooth play...but the distant background went from fog to black abyss.  A black abyss that sometimes swallowed or spit back out varioius terrain features of this background layer, based on which direction I was facing.  There's a difference between giving a game a more basic graphical style, and just poorly-executing your visuals.
In short, if you want a budget version of a modern-day imagination of an older-style shoot-em-up that has a very open area, you could probably do worse than Project Root.  There's a gulf, however, in between that and a recommendation from me.  That gulf is hidden in a glitchy black abyss.

There are a lot of things about this game that could make it great but, unfortunately, there are a few things that thwart that possibility and the game is ultimately just bad.  There are very few options available for any kind of tweaking - those that are there don't seem to have a lot of effect anyway.  The levels are way too long, with many "primary" objectives strung together one after another - by the time I reach the end of a level, my hands and arms are strained so bad that I can't continue.  I think each level could be split into two, or even three, separate parts - as it is, it makes the game more difficult than it needs to be, even on easy.
One of the biggest flaws with the game is the fact that no achievements you earn will show up on Steam.  Reading through the discussions will show you that dozens, if not hundreds, of people have reported this issue but the game has long since been aboandoned by the devs in order to pursue their recently Greenlit game "DOGOS", which seriously looks like nothing more than an update of Project Root.
While Project Root has all of the potential of a truly excellect twin-stick shooter, it feels like it's only 95% finished.  Sadly, that lack of polish and bug fixes makes this game not worth the $10 sticker price.  I paid $2.49 and I'm actually still disappointed.  If the devs come back and fix the issues with this game, I'll gladly change my review but, as it stands, I will not recommend it.  NOT RECOMMENDED.

Let's get the cons out of the way.
I paid more for dinner than they budgeted to make the menus.  Very frustrating to use and navigate.  Story is lackluster; spelling and grammar are atrocious.  Controls are a little tough in practice since both triggers require near-constant use and the right bumper gets used for special abilities.  You have to contort your hands on the controller to make it work.  Camera doesn't let you see shots behind you.  Radar is very confusing.
Think those are petty, minor cons?  They are.
Project Root is a fine game.  The difficulty on Normal is still scathing.  The radial gameplay is a cool feature used to great effect.  It runs smoothly and cleanly.  Shmup fans will find something to like about it.
