It's worth every minute of your time if you're into social studies, philosophy, and like hearing people telling stories.
Definitely not for everyone, not even for walking simulator aficionados...yet this 'game' welcomes everyone who wants to (try to) understand it.

You might be asking yourself? Marble Blast Ultra, where art thou? Maybe not in those exact words, but if you are... GET OUTTA HERE SHAKESPEARE! Anyways, Marble Void is a game inspired by Marble Blast Ultra (yep, that Xbox Live Arcade title on the Xbox 360) and another title called Marble Madness (that I never played). The game adds more to the formula of the Marble genre of game, but takes away from some things too (which isn't a bad thing).
I've managed to beat the Easy Difficulty levels after doing some exploration with the game. It took me about 30 minutes, but that's only if you're going about figuring out the game itself. There's a ton of potential for speed running like the past Marble titles. There's also these things called "orbs" that grant you unlocks if you "bank" a certain amount. Banking orbs just happens after collecting and clearing a level, and each level has a certain amount of orbs to collect. The unlocks you are granted after banking are new modes, and I believe even new marbles (I have yet to see that yet though).
The reason I purchased Marble Void was to finally get my Marble Blast Ultra fix, and let me say it delivered 'marbleously' (get it?). At the beginning it had me thinking, "well, it's not Marble Blast Ultra", but eventually I had mixed thoughts of, "it might as well be" and "it's not trying to be". The game teaches you how to play the game and what the game has to offer right at the beginning of the levels. During these points of being taught the game's level design and physics you'll compare the games you've played before, and think "This isn't Marble Blast Ultra or Marble Madness - this is Marble Void!"
The game has a few things that obviously need to be addressed such as:
This is Marble Void, a game where you'll be saying things like, "what about Marble Blast Ultra?" in a 'who cares' manner? Marble Void does a lot better with the Marble genre, but although it has it's weaknesses on pacing, it's still a game where you can't deny having fun with.
You guys should get this game, or the expansion it's on sale this weekend.

I bought this on sale, thinking there was probably no way I'd lose my money. Wow...I was completely surprised by how this game sucked me in and became one of my favorites.
I like city builders, but usually I get to a certain point and discover that my strategy thus far isn't aplicable in the later stages of the game, or I hit disasters of some sort that I just can't deal with and I get beaten on by the game mechanics. The other thing that usually turns me off is getting to the point where you're just waiting for the things you've put into motion to bear fruit...and you just watch time go by, waiting for the chance to get involved in the game again. This game manages to solve both issues in a very nice fashion. I did not enocounter any problems (at the standard play level) that I could not recover from with a little effort, and the micromanaging on this game is presented in such a way that you're constantly optimizing your resources, but it's not a burden.
It really impresses me that the game is not complete at the time of this review. It's 100% playable and a lot of fun. Challenging, but not overkill for the casual gamer. If you have any love for city builders, I highly recommend giving this game a try. Go through the tutorials, and pay special attention to the part where assigning your workers is discussed....this will make or break the game for you. Remember to plan ahead. Things take time to happen, but you will get enough warning to make effective changes to your resource strategy if you're watching carefully.
TL;DR : Great city builder game with easy to understand mechanics that solve many of this issues that can make city builders boring or discouraging.

A bug-hunters wet dream. Horribly broken menus (not that you can actually access the options in-game, because apparently this is 1995) and the inability to even fix it yourself because the player configs are in encrypted binaries. Menus are both slow to respond, and hard-coded to use xbox360 controller icons, regardless of control preference (oh yeah and the controls menu causes the game to grind to a halt). Which is probably just there to foreshadow the fact that the mouse controls in-game are abysmal and pretty much unusable. The ship will continue to rotate long after you've actually stopped making any input with the mouse, regardless of sensitivity settings - high sensitivity only results in massive over-compensation from any input, and low sensitivity results in the feeling that you're stirring tar. The standard troubleshooting (vsync, pre-rendered frames, etc) will offer you no remedies here, this is all game mechanism.
This could have the best gameplay in the world, but it's completely irrelevant thanks to an atrocious input interface with the user. Of course in reality, the gameplay is nearly as poor; it's marred by the usual suspects - invisible walls (with enemies that can shoot at you through them, but you can't shoot back - oh and they can do this with some standard geometry too), backtracking and just painfully bland & repetitive gameplay.

...David Cage is weird...
Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy is an adventure game from the prestigious David Cage of Heavy Rain and Beyond Two Souls fame.
Despite its original release in 2005 and this remaster released  in 2015 the game still very dated. Not in a performance or visual way but in its overall feeling or vibe. You can use gamepad or mouse and keyboard, typically I don't bother to bring this subject up but other than the obvious differences. The game actually plays quite differently. As in you have direct analog control with a gamepad and should you choose to play with mouse and keyboard (as I did) You will be greeted with tank controls. Which can be a bit jarring when camera control is taken away from you and to the games credit it when it is taken away the camera seems to direct you in very helpful ways as to not get you lost but does indeed take some getting used to try and find your roots again with tank controls.
The game has this feeling of Resident Evil mixed with Eternal Darkness. Both because the general horror nature of the game and Eternal Darkness because there is a mechanic in which you must monitor your every action as it effects the mental fortitude of the player character.
You play as 1 of 3 characters. Lucas Kane, Carla Valenti, or Tyler Miles. You switch in between them after their specific sequence is over. In the beginning it feels a bit odd. As if you are being forced to take a side. As you probably know, its in the trailer, it happens in the first 5 minutes, this game is old; its not a spoiler but Lucas Kane murders a man in a bathroom. Carla and Tyler are the detectives assigned to the case. So right from the very get go you are given subtle clues as to which side you wish  take as well as have plenty of character moments. This is a David Cage game after all and every little decision means something down the line.
The main interaction with the game is walking around and finding clues or talking with people. Action sequences are either directional quicktime events, a sort fake simon says game or a test of endurance by pressing left and right a bunch. There is also a couple of sequences which I didn't find very enjoyable and tested my patience quite a bit. Without saying anything explicit, it involved moving very slowly, regulating your breath and searching for a clue relevant to the situation.
There is also some VERY strange sequences with licensed music. Specifically with the band “Theory of a Deadman”, a band I listened to in High School. It felt very strange, maybe a little forced but in all honesty is wasn't the first time the game started to feel a bit campy and stop taking itself so seriously.

If you played DD1, you will quickly see that this game is completely gutted. From the leveling to the gear to the social interaction.
Leveling:
-In DD1, leveling always was fun, at any time, you could pick which map you felt you were strong enough for, and you     were rewarded for completing more challenging maps.
-In DD2, it doesn't matter which map you choose, it is much faster to just play the quickest (hard difficulty) map possible, and keep repeating the process. The difficulty is trivial at best, and it just feels like a chore.
Loot:
-In DD1, loot is very diverse when it comes to the stats on the items that are dropped. There is a continuous search on any map for those rare pieces of gear with the perfect stats for your character. Many times, there are pieces with negative stats, because other stats on the gear are over leveled, and it is up the player to decide if the loss in some stats, is worth the gain in others. This makes you want to see how far you can push yourself in each wave to find the most overleveled piece of gear possible, even if it means sacrificing all of your character health and damage, for a full tower stat item.
-In DD2, all loot feels linear. You progress through the maps which have an indicator of what item level of loot will drop. You run the map and get gear that is slightly better than the previous map. You repeat the process, slowly getting better, but never standing out for pushing yourself. You never feel the need to push yourself.
Social Interaction/trading:
-In DD1, you get your own tavern, where you can place items on the floor of your shop, or in your personal shop. In your personal shop, you set prices on any items you wish to sell for mana(currency). Players tend to place the best items on the floor, in an attempt to barter with players that join their shop. It really makes you feel like you are selling something that has meaning, because items can have very unique stats. This makes the player WANT to go do more tougher and tougher maps to improve their shop. Having a personal tavern is one of the best aspects of the whole game, you can spend hours just setting your shop up the way you want it, and chat with customers who enter.
-In DD2, trading is non-existent. You get a personal tavern, but can't sell or trade.
Please Trendy, randomize stats on loot based on map difficulty instead of just increasing the gear by a percentage. Give us taverns that we can sell our items that we work for, and let us level up the way we want to, with more experience based on how tough the map and difficulty is.

Fahrenheit came out in 2005 and was the second game David Cage had produced under his development team Quantic Dream. David Cage has a unique style of gaming where your decisions advance the story, yet there is very little game play to be had. Cage likes to focus on story and presentation rather than how fun a game can be.
While Fahrenheit is a game that was considered good for it's time, when people come back to it they kind of realize how actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the game is. Granted it's a 10 year old game now so not everything looks as good as it used to, but the overall choices and stupidity you might expirence when you play this game leave you scratching your head. Now this in no way makes the game bad, in fact this remastering of the game is quite well done, but I feel as though when a character does something that doesn't make sense it's not really because Cage intended it but he just didn't understand how that should really work. Overall though this is a good story and was one of the first of it's kind, I reccommend it to people who enjoy story heavy games (The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, etc)
Potential Spoilers down below but nothing that isn't encountered within the first hour of the gameplay
Examples of Stupidity in this game
You have the option to move the body of the man you had just murdered out of sight, and this is basically to spare you a few minutes to get out of the restaurant. You drag him to the stall and it leaves a blood streak on the floor. You can then use a nearby mop to wipe up the blood yet your character completely ignores the blood smear he just created or his own blood in the stall he was just sitting in.
Shortly after you wake up at your apartment, a lone cop will visit your house, he asks if you're the man he's looking for and says your neighbors heard screaming coming from your place, you can say it wasn't you or say you cut yourself on some glass, the officer askes to come in AND EVEN IF YOU REJECT HIM he comes in anyway without a warrent. If you didn't have a chance to clean your house he finds a bloody shirt on the ground and proceeds to arrest you, mind you, you could have just told him you cut yourself on glass. But if you hide that shirt, but not your sheets in your bedroom, you can stop him and tell him not to go in, I've only heard one option but you can say your girlfriend is asleep naked in there, after which the cop loses all suspicion in you and then leaves. It's obvious David didn't really understand American law, and he also wrote a path that was to be expected for all players rather than an actual branching story where characters at least remember something they were told five minutes beforehand

I played this game off of Steam, yet I have done it all the way through before. This game is a really fun "Metroidvania-style" game. There are numerous upgrades to collect throughout the journey, but not all of them are necessary--Heck, you can even complete the game without the joke-upgrade that lets you turn around.
The gameplay is very fast-paced and not too forgiving about mistakes. You later gain the ability to use your extra lives, but until that point you're pretty much on your own. That's not really a bad thing. The bosses are challenging enough that having something to lose REALLY makes it feel worth the time spent when you actually beat them.
Another thing I love about this title is that it is so flexible about how you complete it. At least in Bunny's story, you can often do the bosses out of order, and they will change depending on what you do first. I actually managed to goof up a save-file doing this though. The first boss does NOT like to be defeated second. I couldn't beat her in pissy-mode.
Anyway, my rambling aside, I love this game and I'm glad it's on Steam. If you like exploring a huge maze-like map while searching for upgrades, battling hilarious yet difficult bosses, and following a goofy storyline that somehow drags you in despite its lack of seriousness, then you'll love this game.
Now if only I could figure out how I beat this thing in the first place. Going back to it, it's really hard T_T

(Don't worry, I love zombie games as much as the next nerd, they just get a tad tiresome after the 45th version). I'd say this game already has a lot going for it, despite it being early access.
The pros are as follows:
1) A weight system, forcing a realistic management of your supplies and how much you carry
2) A crafting system that includes human error, meaning sometimes your character might actually fail to craft items
3) The ability to recycle old tools, clothing, and what have you into materials for repairing your current gear
I'd say this game is a 9/10 in my book, I honestly cannot wait for a story line to go along with the already beautiful landscape that has been developed.

I was searching through the Greenlight section for games and this game stuck out to me, decided to buy it and give it a chance and I have no regret on it at all. The game is very good in my opinion and honestly, made me think I was playing a type of Metroid game, has quite a lot of similarities with Metroid, achievements/challenges for beating the game in a certain time with having all items collected, items/health to be found scattered in obvious and secret areas, bosses that are needed to beat to obtain items to open the next path, even a different suit that is purple and makes you stronger and take less damage, just like the Gravity Suit. When I had gone a few rooms to the right, I instanly thought of a similarity to Brinstar on Metroid Zero Mission, Dark King's Lair reminded me of the depths of Norfair from Zero Mission and there is even one dungeon further on in the game that will reminded you of Metroid games and Tourain (you'll know when you get there.) But enough about comparing this to Metroid, this game is hard at times as some of the bosses can be tricky the first time you fight them and you will need some quick reflixes on certain areas of the game. Overall it's not bad at all, didn't think it would be as enjoyable as it is. Controls weren't hard to get used to, lots of items to collect, soundtrack was done pretty good, nice boss battles that can be difficult or easy depending on how you go about the game and what items you have, another character to play as once you beat the game with her own story as well. Achievements in this game are quite the challenge on some of them, but that's what makes the game better, so if you're the type of person who likes challenges or going for harder achievements like me, then this will be perfect for you. I will say though, this game is going to bring back the older days with me, going back to speed runs which I haven't done in a long time. Amazing game, very enjoyable and very satisfied with my purchase.

Alright, so first of all, I gotta showcase my bias so you know where I'm coming from.
I am a huge fan of Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Sunshine. I'm hyped for explorative, but action-packed collectathons like Super Mario Odyssey, and I was indeed hyped for A Hat in Time.
So did it live up to the hype? Was it less so? The answer probably won't surprise you.
A Hat in Time caters exactly to the type of gamer that I am. I love cutesy stuff. I like a story that attempts to be genuine and heartfelt. And I sincerely enjoy a game that is packaged with different visuals and themes. Yes, this game has all of it, and it is an incredibly solid platformer to boot.
The main thing that we are told by the devs of this game when it comes to the moveset of Hat Kid, is that she was deliberately designed to be as versatile as possible, yet still within the realms of not being considered overpowered. Her versatility allows many players to make up for inaccuracies with their jumps, because of the combination of double jumps, dives, and divecancels, as well as the wallrunning move and walljumps.
You will be surprised just how far you'll be able to go with Hat Girl. Some jumps seem impossible, but you just might make them regardless. Some walls may seem just about too high, but you can do just the right maneuvre to climb them and make rapid progress.
The game's content is pretty much divided in 2 different styles of worlds. The traditional open-ended collectathon type, and the more narratively focused linear type. There are 3 of the former, 2 of the latter, and all feature super varied setups, characters, missions, and stories. Some may make you laugh, others may make you cover in fear.
I like to connect this type of game with the selfsame principle that Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door went for. It makes sure that every mission and world feels distinct and interesting. With the exception of the time rifts, you don't quite see much of the same here, and you can always count on being pleasantly surprised.
As for the collectibles? Most are used beyond the sole promise of story progression. You can collect gem pons to buy badges, you can buy badges to gain several abilities, and you can collect yarn to make different hats, which also grant you prominent abilities. There are also custom palettes for Hat Kid, as well as unlockable remixes for ingame music tracks, and different types of the hats that you already have.
All of this, and yet the Time Pieces are the only collectibles that count towards your completion percentage and bonuses.
It's kind of nifty I'd say.
So would I recommend it? By all means yes. As a guy who loves the genre and enjoyed the Gamecube era's take on it, I feel that I would say it's worth at least it's basic asking price. I myself spent about 11-12 hours getting all Time Pieces. People on average say that they took 13 hours just to beat the game. So you'll get your bang for the buck regardless of whether you are a veteran in the genre or not.
Are there shortcomings? Yes, but I would be spoiling the game if I listed them. Just know that my issues are entirely about some of the story, and you may disagree in that regard. Nevertheless, I loved this game, and I am looking forward to see what kind of modding we'll see in the future, because I will for sure come back to it when that workshop is open.

However, the Superhot Team have managed to create a narrative out of it (text based, apart from the expected though still awesome every time I hear it, "Super Hot" piece of dialogue) that feels like you're not just playing the same level over and over again. And whilst this certainly isn't the most challenging title you will stumble across, it kept me on my toes throughout - and had me cursing on more than one occasion as the number of times I had attempted a mission entered double figures.
The campaign itself is short, but I am appreciative of all the effort that has been put into it. Full marks to the developers for creating one of the most innovative shooters/titles this I've come across.

Technically, “The Beginner’s Guide” is a series of small games, created by a person named Coda and presented to us, players, by Davey Wreden, in chronological order with some immediate descriptions and overall narration. Davey talks a little bit about game development, but mostly about Coda himself. Very early (even in a trailer for the game) he says it’s cool, when you get to know someone through their work. Why someone makes games? Why this particular game? Were they sad or happy, while making it? Etc.
Story and game itself is linear. Don’t expect something like “
” here. And, actually, comparing two games is weird anyway. Don’t expect any plot twists (“I am your father!”) either — game’s story would evolve and shift focus, but in a very natural way.
And that’s, basically, it. Short simple games (it’s not wrong to call them “levels”, actually), with a little bit of gameplay (you mostly walk) and voice over narration. And the main attraction is that narration. It’s full of questions. Very interesting questions (funny, but one is about this, actually — about reviews and recommendations). And, I would argue, not a single definitive answer. Like, again, very early Davey outright says that he releasing Coda’s games without his consent. Is it moral? Is it even legal? Those questions are for you, player, to ponder.
Would you find in “The Beginner’s Guide” anything interesting for you, personally? Maybe. You don’t need to be a game developer to do so, maybe a little bit creative (and we all are, right?). But maybe not. Here’s the tricky part: I’m not recommending this game for you. Yes, you. ‘Cause I don’t know you. I’m just saying that it’s good and I liked it. Do whatever you want with that information.

The Beginner's Guide is... well,
The Beginner's Guide is different, the story it tells of a river that flows.
It's all, a part of the experiance.
Whether The Beginner's Guide is a work of fiction or a work of fact is something that is actually tearing me up inside, it is not often that I write reviews or actually make comment on a game's deeper meaning, but, the experiance is... Uncomfortable, and I feel that, The Beginner's Guide was designed to be just that.
After playing through it a few times, you begin to connect dots that you didnt even know existed.
So, should you Buy this game? Hell yea, buy it now and experiance it. The overall theme is something that, in this day and age, is more and more important.
==================================
Read Ahead if you wish to read my views on the subject matter.
==================================
.
.
.
.
.
.
.
If this is a work of fact, then... the subject has missed the point, but, that also seems to be the point, by continuing through the game you get the impression, through the tones used by Davey, his choice of words, and just the general feel of the final screens of the game, that as much as there is a need to continue to experiance the work of Coda, but, there is also deep deep regret within Davey.
In the second chapter, the whisper chapter, you are automatically skipped through a maze section, (in which you have the option to turn back and complete it if you wish) but this single act, shows that, Davey hasnt actually learnt anything from the ordeal. But that may just be a choice to depict his mental state at the begining. With Davey only coming in about halfway through Coda's game design career, it's understandable the excitement you get from experiancing these new and wonderous creations from a mind that isn quite on the straight and narrow.
Coda ensured that everything in his game's had a point, everything appeared done, from the gun that was useless and then skybox where you could see the end of the universe, things were done deliberatly. It's not my place to say that anything was done, or, if it was intended, or, if I could even have any minute semblance of an understanding of how  Coda worked. That's the point of the story. You dont know an artist through their work. Just like Davey when he told people that Coda was depressed, or in a bad state of mind, because of the theme of the little tidbits of game that he created.
Coda just enjoyed what he did, and the pressure that Davey put on him, the rush, explains why he slowed down his development, because, Davey couldnt, didnt, wouldnt, understand the demons he had inside of him, his need to be validated through someone elses work. Did Davey put out these works as his own? Did he really add the lamp-posts into the games? You cant know, not unless Davey tells us so, and yet, its only a game.
And you Cant know an artist through their works.

One of the best city builders I have ever played. Beautiful art assets with some of the most gorgeous weather effects I've come across and some fantastic building models. It's the sort of game you pause every few minutes to take screenshots of. The game is also nicely balanced with enough options to tweak the game from a tranquil city planner to a brutal survival game.
The game also seems to have been built with mods in mind, there's some great additions in the Steam workshop that really enhance the game experience so playing the game with a good selection of these is a must for me. Some notable mods include an Apiary with beekeeper profession, a butchers with butcher profession, a creamery that produces yogurt, cream and cheese, a Japanese building mod and the deer as domesticated animals mod. I can list off another 10-15 easily so go have a search through the workshop and you're bound to come across some good ones. Every mod I've tried has worked perfectly in the game with no crashes or performances issues.
In terms of technical performance of the vanilla version the game runs buttery smooth on my now mid-range system, at max settings I'm still getting a solid 60fps. As stated previously I've had no crashes and encountered no bugs (even with mods). The games looks, feels and sounds great, comes with a gentle, informative tutorial and a vibrant mod scene. I cannot praise this game highly enough, go get yourself a copy, even at full-price this game is absolutely worth it.

Overall great game, worth the $5 i paid on sale
Pros:
+aesthetics are amazing, they were the first thing i truly appreciated about the game.  rivers, woods, buildings are beautifully realistic
+plenty of features and buildings to keep you entertained for hours of play time
+the game isn't too easy, expansion takes a toll on the town (as it would in real life) that pays off in the long run.  The manegement during droughts and hard times were some of the most enjoyable and challenging parts of the game for me
+Overall worth the price and has plenty of playability, especially with additional mods that add buildings, maps, and new mechanics
Cons:
- you may get bored of this game pretty fast.  without mods, you'll find yourself constructing every type of building and resource only 3 or 4 hours into the game.  After that, it can seem like nothing more than dull expansion until you saturate the map and stagnate.  This won't happen after dozens of hours played on a single map however.
-there is no endgame, which may be discouraging for some.  i don't see this as a huge con, as i like the endless building aspect
-it takes a while to master efficient farming and gathering setups.  early on, you may struggle with food as your villagers are gathering inefficiently.
This game is great, certainly worth the money I paid.  Hopefully the devs include more in a future patch, as the game is still relatively new.

This game is amazing. You play as a reporter, who gets an email saying some dark things are happening in an insane asylum (why didn't the person who send the email just contact 4 stoners and a dog?), and you try to find out what happened. The gameplay is similar to Amnesia, where you can't fight back, leaving you to hide, or outrun your persuers. What I loved about this game is that it uses jumpscares correctly, because they happen to suprise you so your defenses would go down, rather than trying to scare you. The graphics are great, and it makes the game feel more 'alive'. The enemies are quite horrifying, and the ones that scared me the most were the twins and the doctor (I forgot his name), not because they jump out at you, but because what they do to you. I would recomend this game to avid horror fans, and I am personally astounded by the game, but I am a little dissapointed at the length of the game, lasting around 3 to 4 hours long if you don't try to find everything. Overall, I love this game, and I can't wait to get whistle blower.
(Update) I have gotten whistleblower on sale, and boy is it horrifying! I was not as scared playing outlast because I was playing with my cousin, and whistleblower gives you more reasons to be afraid. The main character in whistleblower is Waylon Park, who is a computer engineer for the mental asylum, who tries to tell Miles (the main character in Outlsat) about the happenings in the asylum. Before Waylon could send the message, he is taken and experimented on, but escapes and tries to find a way out. I have not beaten the game, but the enemies are really unpredictable, and Whistleblower is a great addon to Outlast. ONLY PLAY IT AFTER YOU HAVE BEATEN OUTLAST, AS WHISTLE BLOWER HAS A LOT OF SPOILERS! I will add more to the review after I beat whistleblower.

This is a wonderful game. I think that a lot of other survival games have attempted to pave a road, so to speak, and fallen a bit short. Whether they happen to be uninspired, or downright cliché. (Don't worry, I love zombie games as much as the next nerd, they just get a tad tiresome after the 45th version). I'd say this game already has a lot going for it, despite it being early access.
The pros are as follows:
1) A weight system, forcing a realistic management of your supplies and how much you carry
2) A crafting system that includes human error, meaning sometimes your character might actually fail to craft items
3) The ability to recycle old tools, clothing, and what have you into materials for repairing your current gear
I'd say this game is a 9/10 in my book, I honestly cannot wait for a story line to go along with the already beautiful landscape that has been developed.

The Long Dark is one of the only games I've ever written a review on Steam for. Why? Because this is a game that deserves to be played. The survival genre has seen a boom in the last year, but none so eloquently capture the real struggle of surviving in a harsh, unforgiving environment such as The Long Dark. This is a game that - unlike most - can and should be played without a walkthrough, taking in the breathtakingly stylized visuals, scavenging for food and supplies, and figuring out how to survive in the wilderness all on your lonesome. If you want to play a game where your main objective honestly and truly is to survive, this is the game to do it.
Having said that, you should know this game is in Easly Access and in the alpha stage. You should expect to find bugs, and you may be put off by the learning curve associated with the game. In the current build (v .183), there are several complaints with the AI (Hinterland doesn't seem to understand what balance is), as well as some real issues (e.g., AI behavior not being reset such that a wolf will be in a constant state of aggression at the bottom of the stairs even after resting for hours). Because of this, the game can be incredibly unforgiving in a way that may or may not seem fair. As well, story mode is not implemented yet, and the sandbox has "only" two maps. This isn't much of an issue, as the equipment you find acts on a weighted-chance loot table, where the gear is randomized with certain stuff more likely to show up in certain containers (e.g., you're more likely to find a flare in a metal box in an industrial area than in a cabinet in the kitchen). However, there is a noticable lack of wood-burning stoves in buildings despite this being the cold wilderness.
The mechanics are actually quite nice, such that you organically learn to do new things (as a player). There is a certain level of "skills," such that your chances of starting a fire are low to start, until you do it enough and it becomes easier. However, from the player perspective, it works very organically: you, like the real you, slowly learn the right ways to approach situations, when the right time to go out and forage is, how to find starters and fuel for fires, and so on. As well, all of these actions take in-game time and it becomes imperative to properly manage what you're doing for the day, planning resource gathering and management to maximize time spent alive.
The Long Dark makes me excited because it does what I've been looking for in other games. It makes me afraid to leave the safety of the cabin, despite knowing that I have to if I want to survive; it forces you to face its world, and doesn't coddle you. If this game is on your wishlist, you should just buy it now. It's worth the asking price, especially if it's on sale.

Alright, so first of all, I gotta showcase my bias so you know where I'm coming from.
I am a huge fan of Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Sunshine. I'm hyped for explorative, but action-packed collectathons like Super Mario Odyssey, and I was indeed hyped for A Hat in Time.
So did it live up to the hype? Was it less so? The answer probably won't surprise you.
A Hat in Time caters exactly to the type of gamer that I am. I love cutesy stuff. I like a story that attempts to be genuine and heartfelt. And I sincerely enjoy a game that is packaged with different visuals and themes. Yes, this game has all of it, and it is an incredibly solid platformer to boot.
The main thing that we are told by the devs of this game when it comes to the moveset of Hat Kid, is that she was deliberately designed to be as versatile as possible, yet still within the realms of not being considered overpowered. Her versatility allows many players to make up for inaccuracies with their jumps, because of the combination of double jumps, dives, and divecancels, as well as the wallrunning move and walljumps.
You will be surprised just how far you'll be able to go with Hat Girl. Some jumps seem impossible, but you just might make them regardless. Some walls may seem just about too high, but you can do just the right maneuvre to climb them and make rapid progress.
The game's content is pretty much divided in 2 different styles of worlds. The traditional open-ended collectathon type, and the more narratively focused linear type. There are 3 of the former, 2 of the latter, and all feature super varied setups, characters, missions, and stories. Some may make you laugh, others may make you cover in fear.
I like to connect this type of game with the selfsame principle that Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door went for. It makes sure that every mission and world feels distinct and interesting. With the exception of the time rifts, you don't quite see much of the same here, and you can always count on being pleasantly surprised.
As for the collectibles? Most are used beyond the sole promise of story progression. You can collect gem pons to buy badges, you can buy badges to gain several abilities, and you can collect yarn to make different hats, which also grant you prominent abilities. There are also custom palettes for Hat Kid, as well as unlockable remixes for ingame music tracks, and different types of the hats that you already have.
All of this, and yet the Time Pieces are the only collectibles that count towards your completion percentage and bonuses.
It's kind of nifty I'd say.
So would I recommend it? By all means yes. As a guy who loves the genre and enjoyed the Gamecube era's take on it, I feel that I would say it's worth at least it's basic asking price. I myself spent about 11-12 hours getting all Time Pieces. People on average say that they took 13 hours just to beat the game. So you'll get your bang for the buck regardless of whether you are a veteran in the genre or not.
Are there shortcomings? Yes, but I would be spoiling the game if I listed them. Just know that my issues are entirely about some of the story, and you may disagree in that regard. Nevertheless, I loved this game, and I am looking forward to see what kind of modding we'll see in the future, because I will for sure come back to it when that workshop is open.

This game is awesome IMO. I consider it to be one of the better games on Steam that (unfortunately for the devs) hasn't got the attention it deserves.
First off, let me say that another reviewer mentioned "I like indie game, I feel that smaller developers tend to focus on gameplay over showy superficial junk" and I wholeheartedly agree with this. I am so tired of seeing games where clearly the bulk of the focus went into the presentation.
Blasting Agent is an excellent metroidvania style game. Although I suppose you could just move through levels as quickly as possible the way to really maximize the value of this game IMO is to just take your time and explore each level. Blasting Agent makes it easy to immerse yourself in the game and rewards you for doing so.
Everything is very high quality. The ultra low res graphics have a very unique look to them which makes the game stand out in a good way from most of the games on Steam. The game probably most resembles something like Environmental Station Alpha. The gameplay is very good with some nice areas to explore and power ups to find. The enemies are varied and the bosses (I've only fought one so far) are interesting as well.
I haven't encountered any issues with the controls or with crashing as some have mentioned so perhaps this is something that was fixed at some point.
SUMMARY: The whole game is very well done. This game is easily worth $7 to $8 and is a complete steal at the ridiculously low $3 price it is currently selling for.  If you like this kind of game take the plunge and buy Blasting Agent. It is a great game.

This game / experience has impacted on me that much that I this is easily within my top 5 games of all time. Very high praise indeed you say, well yes, it is, but it's thoroughly deserved.
Davey has collected all the works of his friend Coda that he had made between 2008 and 2011. There are 17 games to walk through that Coda made, but then he suddenly stopped. This is Davey's story of trying to understand the genius of Coda, to find out what insecurities he has and why he eventually stopped making video games.
One warning, this is not a game as such, this is an experience where we are told everything and we are merely following the instructions of the narrator, the creator, Davey Wreden.
Potential spoilers of theme and content from here on out:
Davey Wreden does a fantastic job of exporing the themes that are in this game, and I was sucked in from the start. This isn't the Stanley Parable 2, no, this is so much more, if anything i'd say the works of his friend 'Coda' influenced the Stanley Parable in many ways, and the anxieties and depression that Davey felt after making that Stanley Parable, and what many game developer's struggle with are so apparent in not only Coda's work, but also in Davey's search for reason and understanding of Coda's work.
I think this game does a great job of highlighting and raising awareness of mental health issues within the gaming industry, and I think this game could be taking in so many different ways. Is this game about Coda? About Davey? About insecurities? Depression? Anxiety? Self-loathing? Is this game about obsessive behaviour or about Coda's perceived genius from Davey's point of view? Is this about all of those points? To know that, or to question that, you NEED to play this experience for yourself. This game is one of a kind and touched me in places I never knew games could touch me.
I give this experience a deserved 10 out of 10.

Finding permanent weapon and life upgrades encourages exploration, as does unlocking perks when you find all the gold and kill all the enemies in a level. The bosses are pretty cool, too.
Having said that, the game has crashed repeatedly on me; sometimes on startup, sometimes after finishing a level and sometimes right in the middle of the action. Also, Sometimes the controls just go absolutely nuts. My character will autonomously decide to start an uninteruptable air-dash, sucking him off the screen and to his death regardless of what I'm actually pressing on the controller. Oh, and the achievements don't work at all, either.
The crashes and unreliable controls reduce what would have been a reasonably fun game into an exercise in annoyance. If these issues are addressed in a patch it might become worth playing.

Rising Storm/Red Orchestra 2 is essentially what Battlefield wishes it was.  It's a more mature and more advanced PvP shooter that demonstrates the difference between console gaming (Battlefield/Call of Duty) and PC gaming (this game).
Many of the game modes are similar to what you'll find in Battlefield and Call of Duty, so what separates RS/RO2 is the gameplay.  It's like a realistic, hardcore version of Battlefield except with much better level design, better netcoding/hit detection, mod support, and no balance issues.
Some may say it bridges the gap between typical shooters like Battlefield/CoD, and mil-sims like ArmA.  Most of the gameplay, from the weapon functionality, complex vehicle functionality, and the high levels of intensity are closer to ArmA, while the scale and game modes are closer to Battlefield/Call of Duty.  Although not as strategic as Crysis/Crysis Wars or Natural Selection 2, anyone who likes PvP shooters should get this game.

Wow, this is a tough "game" to review.
It is one of the relatively new genre of "walking simulators", a term I don't much care for, but it seems to have caught on. There isn't a great deal of player interaction, although there is a lot more than in Dear Esther (which I hated). Most of the game is spent wandering through part completed Source engine levels supposedly made by an amateur level designer while what sounds like a directors commentary (not by the designer) describing and analysing the level and the motivations of the person who made it.
I bought the game based on the authors previous game The Stanley Parable, in particular the self contained demo, which is awesome. The full game of The Stanley Parable didn't tickle me nearly as much. The Beginners Guide has a sort of similar mini level design concept, but the mood is very sombre, and is almost completely lacking in humour.
It is a mixture of analysis of game design, art, philosophy and a reflection on the mental state of mind of the possibly fictitious level designer and of the human psyche as a whole. As such I can't say I could wholeheartedly recommend this game, the average gamer who buys this would probably hate it, but if you are into something short (about 2 hours of experience with little replay value) that will tickle the grey matter you may like it.

''Outlast contains intense violence, gore, graphic sexual content, and strong language. Please enjoy''
-Quoted from the game before you start playing Outlast.
As quoted here, this is exactly what Outlast is all about and is extremely well done, Especially the camera since you play as Miles Upshur, an investigative reporter whose ambition earn him an intimate tour of hell on earth. You start of as Miles driving towards the Mount Massive Asylum to uncover the secrets while you investigate the place that no other reporters would dare to do.
And since your only options are to proceed forward and uncovering the truth you either run, hide, or you die.
There will be a lot of unexpected things happening to you and the controls are very smooth, Especially while you use the camera, The battery only gets drained when you use the night vision that has a green view to it, and isn't very strong you can see a few meters ahead and should you run out of battery you will almost be completely blind adding a lot of tension to not consuming all of your batteries.
Navigating in the corridors of the Asylum, you're terrified of what awaits you and what as you uncover more of what has happened and is still happening, The secrets you find out that you never imagined was possible and as you're stuck in the Asylum trying to escape from the place. The language in this game surprises you kinda as it intesifies the experience in the game, It feels so real as if you were there.
In short, I really do recomend playing Outlast for those that enjoy playing horror games on evenings in the right atmosphere with a good headset so you hear well aswell.

The controls are weird, unintuitave, and unecessarily complicated. You hold "S" and release to jump. You have to tap the down arrow as you fall to make a clean landing. For advanced tricks you hold "S" but then press and hold another key like "A", release "S", then release "A" to jump and do a different trick. Then the really advanced tricks which still don't always register in the tutorial, you hold S, press D, release S, hold a right or left arrow key, release D, keep holding the arrow key during the jump but then release and tap the down arrow as you come in for the landing.
From what I've seen in the other negative reviews it doesn't get any more fun after that as it continually ramps up the complexity and timing of the tricks, so I'm going to go ahead and return it.

You play as Bunny, who got stuck in the Devils Labyrinth and is trying to find a cure for her cat-ear curse. As you navigate through the labyrinth, you have to fight enemies, get through obstacles and puzzles, fight bosses and find items to power up and unlock new places to go to.
The game is a pretty solid metroidvania game. It rarely has a "What do i do next?" moment. It has no indicators as to where to go next, but the items and minimap make most of these things clear. The music is great. I liked both the original and remixed soundtrack. The game is propperly translated, which allows non-japanese players to join in on the nonsensical humor this game provides.
Bunny Must Die also features an unlockable second character, with her own story and gameplay mechanics, doubling the fun of this game. The story of Bunny and this other character are sequels, and explains some mysteries in Bunny her storyline. It also has some room for skipping/sequence breaking, adding some replay value for hardcore gamers. Doing so will cause certain events to act different as well (like the 1st boss getting a different dialogue and becoming more difficult).
Unlike regular metroidvania games, Bunny Must Die also introduces some elements of bullet hell shooters. People who played the Gundemonium series will recognize some elements that have been copied from the other games. These extra elements make this game quite difficult on certain points. Although I wouldn't label it as insanely difficult, the game gets very tough at some later points in the game.

As evidenced in at least a handful of the other reviews I've written, the 3D Platformer is one of my all-time favorite genres. Combining tight, reflex-intensive gameplay with sprawling, diverse levels is a recipe for excellence in my book, although in recent years the genre has somewhat fallen into neglect. There have been a handful of games in the past year that attempted to breathe some life back into it, though, with different approaches. Yooka-Laylee vied to bring back the Collectathon genre. Clustertruck is a different sort of 3D platformer, based around fast, constantly-moving autoscroller levels. Super Mario Odyssey, out in just under three weeks, looks to be a love letter to Super Mario Sunshine and 64, my two favorite 3D platformers ever.
When I Kickstarted A Hat in Time, I expected to get a game that aped Sunshine and 64, had a handful of great ideas, played well, and was a fun game in a genre that was woefully underserved, especially on PC. Instead, Hat took its lengthy development time in order to polish, expand, and perfect its core concepts, and the result is a fantastic game that doesn't pay homage to its predecessors so much as graduates from them with flying colors.
You start the game in your novelty-shaped spaceship, on your way home from adventures unknown. You're passing by a small planet with a load of strange, unique regions, when you're hailed by a Mafia member who tells you that you need a permit, or can't fly by the planet for free, or some such nonsense. Hat Kid has no time for any of this nonsense, and attempts to break free, which results in the fuel for her spaceship, Time Pieces, being scattered all over the planet below. Now marooned, she heads to the planet's surface in order to get these hourglasses back by any means necessary.
This sets a tone that you'll see for the rest of the game: Hat Kid will help people with their issues, but her main goal is absolutely to get the heck back home. True Neutral.  This encounter with the Mafia also shows you the kinds of characters you'll be encountering: goofy, bumbling grumps with writing that I expected to grow old quickly, but which kept me chuckling until the end.
The first world is Mafia Town, a bustling seaside city where bald, broken English strongmen who all look the same rule with iron fists. You quickly team up with Mustache Girl, a character with just as much spunk as you, but who is decidedly more good-aligned. She helps you get your first couple Time Pieces in levels designed to teach you many of the mechanics of A Hat in Time: the double jump, the dive, the dive cancel, and hat powers.
Almost immediately, you'll see just how much effort has been put into making every single part of this game feel exceptional. 3D Platformers have long been bemoaned for their attempts at camera control, whether they opt for an automatic camera or user-controlled. I can safely say that there was not a single time in this entire game that I felt like I was fighting the camera. In almost every scenario, the camera is smart enough to adjust automatically, letting you focus on the platforming. When you feel you need to take control, you can make minute adjustments that don't autosnap back, letting you control the camera as you run, jump, and dive your way around tricky platforming sections.
Mafia Town is an incredible vertical slice of A Hat in Time for multiple other reasons besides showing you the ropes, though. Not only does the world offer a good amount of quirky characters, both in the mafiosos and the hapless townspeople, it also has a decent amount of collectibles to find, including Yarn which allows you to knit new Hats (which grant powers that can often open up sections of prior levels to find new items, including Yarn, and so on), Relics that allow you to play a slot machine where you'll unlock cosmetic items, and one of my favorite features: Time Rifts. These small glowing orbs are unlocked after certain Acts, and show up in the world screen as photos of locations in the world. You have to study the photo and then pick an Act, then hunt down the orb. Once you touch it, you're transported to one of two level types. The first is a love letter to Super Mario Sunshine's F.L.U.D.D.-less levels, great abstract blocks in space with incredibly tight platforming that's often a lot more challenging than in the core Acts. The second are strange, memory-hunting collection levels where you must find relics and pieces of a journal in order to progress, which will let you view a short picture book at the end with the memories you collected. The former are some of my favorite levels in the game, but the latter are fun in their own way, especially as a cooldown from some of the difficult levels of the core Acts.
There's one other core Hat in Time concept that Mafia Town introduces, and that's the stunningly fun boss fights. There's a miniboss that is played on a purely horizontal plane, where you must jump over barrels and dodge them, and that core dodging mechanic carries through to every other boss fight in the game. Boss fights in A Hat in Time feel akin to Donkey Kong Country boss battles in 3D, which is not something I would have anticipated working (or being fun) but they are some of the highlight encounters in the game. Each boss has multiple phases and attack patterns, and often has in-match cutscenes and dialogue (which is skipped if you retry the boss - one more excellent Quality of Life feature). These are not your 3-hit Mario bosses or 5-hit DKC bosses, though -- often, each boss takes 20-30 hits to defeat, meaning each boss battle is a test of stamina, reflexes, and patience. I'm not usually a boss guy in platformers, because I find them to often be trite or unnecessary, but Hat's bosses shine with the same polish as everything else in the game.
The boss encounters also have some of the best music in the game, with bombastic tracks that call to mind everything from Mario to Undertale. These are far from the only standout songs, though: the entire soundtrack is a delight, with each track suited perfectly for its area. Sound design in general in this game is fantastic, whether it's the Link-style groans and oofs when you bash into something or the thousands of voice-acted, well-written lines.
I don't want to talk too much about the other three worlds in A Hat in Time, to avoid spoiling some of the best levels in what is unfortunately a pretty short game (I finished in just under six hours, with over half of the total Time Pieces, although from looking around I was on the short side), but rest assured: each world introduces new concepts, enemy types, and even entirely different gameplay mechanics. There's a murder mystery, a parade, and a sneak-and-hide horror level (which is genuinely scary!) as well as levels that are nothing but good old-fashioned platformer fun.
A Hat in Time is one of the best games I've played all year, and one of the best 3D Platformers ever. With two worlds coming as free DLC, as well as co-op in an upcoming patch, mod support, and more, it looks like this instant classic is going to stick around for some time. I hope that anyone who likes the genre, great writing, fantastic music, and genuinely perfect controls picks this up, because they will not be disappointed.

I have always been a fan of atmosphere-driven games, where you get thrown into the thick of it and have to figure out what's going on for yourself, letting the environment tell a large portion of the story. To me, Half-Life and Dark Souls were such titles, and Outlast is yet another. There is something decidedly off-kilter about the way this game portrays itself, delving into the depths of the human psyche and showing the horrors people are capable of.
As a gamer, I rarely get queasy or frightened, but the first few jump scares of the game reliably gave me a rush of cold sweat. You will feel lost, helpless and in the thick of it as you explore this old '50s mental ward, recently repurposed as a research facility into things that are best left alone, and playing host to all manner of creeps.
As much as I would recommend this game though, Outlast has a few major flaws in its execution that detract from the immersion, one of which being repetitiveness in its set pieces. Multiple times throughout the game, there are sequences where you need to either activate or collect several of something, and during this task you will invariably find yourself being hounded by an enemy you can only run and hide from. By the time you get to the third such sequence, you'll pretty much go in knowing what's about to happen. Some of the enemies behave eratically, and can decide to spot you out of nowhere, occasionally leading to a slew of frustrating deaths, and if you do get stuck somewhere for a long time, repeatedly getting killed by the same enemy will quickly become more annoying than scary, even for the most fearful of gamers I wager.
Exploring this incredibly visually and thematically dark place is definitely a reluctant pleasure, but I do not recommend playing this game through in one sitting. Not because it is so scary, but because it may wear on your patience otherwise. After four hours of play, I even found myself getting bored, and a scary game should never be boring.

Outlast is a unique horror experience that most games don't offer. I played through the entire game before writing this review. I am a huge fan of the horror genre, and it is very hard to find a game that scares me. While this was an amazing game, it was not very scary. This may be different for other people, but there were probably about 10 jump scares, and there wasn't really any psychological horror in it. The game was atmospherically horrific however, because 75% of the game takes place in the dark. The enemies in it were decently scary, and what I enjoyed was that you can not fight back. I loved the graphics on this game, they had their own king of feel to them. The gameplay was okay, but it got very repetetive because you were constantly having to find two things while being hunted by an enemy. One of the cool things about the gameplay was the use of the camera, which has limited batteries and has a nightvision mode. Throughout the game you can find bonus documents and read about different psychopaths and such, which was a very cool collectible experience. The story in it was okay, it wasn't too story driven, but there was a story. The game is not at all like a Silent Hill, or any other game that just uses psychological horror. Difficulty wise, the game wasn't hard, however there were parts that I died in over and over. The game should take at least 6 hours to beat without a walkthrough, so it was decently long. Overall, Outlast is a great game to play and I highly reccomend it.

This game isn't Tony Hawk, nor does it try to be. OlliOlli 2, like OlliOlli is a skill based game that takes place on a skateboard.
There are similarities, such as doing tricks to try to get high scores, but you have no control over which direction you're going. You're always going to the right.
That isn't necessarily a bad thing though. What OlliOlli 2 does, it does well. It is very challenging and you will find yourself getting frustrated as you fail over and over. I have noticed a lot of the reviews have an issue with the game, saying the controls aren't responsive and I want to address that as a fan.. Just because you can't get the timing down, doesn't mean the controls are bad. People think the timing is off, but the only thing that is off is their ability to correctly time their moves. I haven't had a single issue with timing.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game, especially over the first one for a couple of reasons. Number 1, there are more tricks and you can do manuals in this. Second of all, the newer game is going to get more dev attention and this game is only 2 dollars more than the first. It makes no sense to get the first one.
If you want a number score, I'd give this an 8 out of 10.

It has alot of potential to be a great game, the kind to play a few matches in everyday or tinker around and create some ships. But because it's a game in development it does have some issues still.
You can start by doing the short tutorial and build your own spacecraft to fight other players.
Building your own ship starts very simple (with the Rookie class) and it gives you more options to expand upon as you level up in the game. At rookie level 10, you can access the other types of ships in the game and build all of those too, like a heavy weapons battleship or a fast moving frigate.
Building ships is my favorite part of the game.
You really have to think of a ship that fits to your playstyle and build it accordingly.
After a few matches you might think of a way to make your ship better, or level up so you can add more stuff to it (like additional weapons or armor plating). It's fun to get creative with it (although that probably won't always make a great ship to fight with).
As of now, the only gamemode is pretty simple; a PvP deathmatch arena with a few different maps. The outcome of the battle will reward you with experience in the class you are using and scrap to purchase upgrades.
It could greatly benefit from some additional development time.
The game still has some minor technical difficulties, for example lag and balancing issues where weapons range and distance in the game seems to be the most important factor to win at the moment (read: you will get sniped alot).
Also levelling up classes and earning scrap goes ever so slowly which makes it frustrating as you cannot try out new things. Some more map variation and new gamemodes would be welcome.
Hopefully nothing that can't be fixed in the near future!
All in all the game is pretty straightforward and fun to play and that's why I recommend it.

The game is pretty fun, and the customization and building of ships is easy and fun too.
Pro: Ships are very customizable, and can be made to tailor many different play styles
Cons: Ranking up in a ship class makes you significantly better than a person in a similar class, but only slightly lower. This works in RPG type settings, but in an arena type game it gives too much power to people based solely on amount of time spent playing.
Researching new modules etc to use is very difficult, and you must play through many games just to unlock the weapons that are more powerful, while not having access to comparable firepower to defend with.
You'll spend your first several hours dying, or hiding in battles as you're completely outclassed regardless of skill level. Once you unlock new ship classes you'll be in a similar, but less disadvantaged state until you can earn enough to research the requisite modules to allow your class ship to actually function as a battleship etc.
Conclusion: It's fun to play, but needs more game modes, which will hopefully come in time. Balance needs MAJOR work. As of writing as mentioned above you don't stand a chance against anything for your first several dozen matches regardless of your individual skill or ship design.

“We could keep you here forever” is one of the many prompts that the system displays during your bullet-ridden romp through the digital world in Superhot. Developed by the SuperHot Team, this is a first person game with a peculiar twist: time only moves when you do. This allows for some intense sequences where you kill multiple enemies while bullets and limbs whiz past you, and it feels very satisfying to clear an entire level after rampaging through the room and killing half a dozen enemies. I now know what Ryan Reynolds felt like in that masterpiece of a superhero movie, Green Lantern.
The first thing you notice after you boot up the game is the graphics and presentation: the menu is presented as a computer terminal, and the narrative is often delivered in the form of one of those old IRC chat rooms. The enemies - red, polygonal humanoids - explode into small crystals when killed, and the lack of a HUD adds to the game's immersion by making it look like you're in an action movie's trailer. Sound design remains minimalist, and you will only hear a few different effects throughout the game, such as the hollow 'click' as the gun you are holding is empty and the obnoxiously loud 'SUPERHOT SUPERHOT SUPERHOT' at the end of each level.
The game's crown jewel is, evidently, the gameplay. The levels themselves are not overtly challenging, the enemies normally coming from all around you, converging on you like the hired thugs on a D list action movie, and while they all die with one bullet so do you. This means you need to be constantly on the move in order to avoid a hail of bullets and pre-empt the enemy movements in order to shoot them successfully. The final few levels do allow you to ''superswitch'' and control an enemy's body, but this does little to change the game's flow.
The story itself is quite straightforward, just like a binding road. It seems quite clear at the start but turns into quite a mess - that said, the story is never at the forefront of the game, and instead takes a back seat to the gameplay. It is important to keep in mind that each level does contain ''secrets'' or items hidden in obscure areas of the levels that offer an insight into the story for those brave adventurers who stray off the beaten path. However, these secret items are not necessary to complete the story mode and consequently, the story mode is able to be completed in just under 2 hours.
Once you complete the game's story mode, the challenge and endless mode are unlocked, from which most of the additional replay value comes from. The challenges offer a variety of different elements such as only using katanas, and there are also speed runs in which you must race the clock to complete a level, although this added replay value is only present for as long as the tight gameplay entices you.
Overall, the game is definitely innovative and utilizes an interesting and refreshing mechanic. It is a blast to romp through the game's 2 hour story mode but this may be the game's weakest point - given the price, some might feel the price tag to be a bit on the salty side of things. While there are challenges to complete afterwards, they can get quite repetitive after a short amount of time and things could've easily been enhanced by the presence of a level editor. A fun, albeit short, game.

Wow!  I haven't finished the story yet, but Outlast is something special.  I'm a man that hates jump scares as a general rule since for the last 10 years it's the only trick in Hollywood's bag.  Sure, jump scares abound in this game, but they aren't a crutch.  The camera mechanic, the sound design, voice acting, and environments nail the atmosphere.
I also love how the game doesn't pull any punches.  Sure, we've been stalked by monsters, mutants and maniacs, but rarely by deranged, unnervingly well spoken naked men.  Seeing full male nudity adds a certain extra creepiness not only to being chased by said naturalists, but when you see test subjects obviously missing their front bits, you know it's not from a standard video game "Ken doll" approach.
Really, the only drawback (and I realize this is the crux of what makes Outlast so delightfully uncomfortable) is the total and complete lack of combat.  I don't want to be pulling elite silent takedowns and whatnot, but I do wish there was more to evasion than merely running.  If you get cornered or grabbed it'd be cool if you could fight your way loose.  Just getting whomped on the head with a pipe without any kind of defensive action takes me out of the game just the tiniest bit.  A very minor complaint.  I really hope Red Barrels keeps it up and delivers more visceral experiences in the future.  Great job.

I don' really know ever where to begin with this. I'm writting this review to serve as a warning, Zestiria is a masterpiec that has suffered a terrible accident, it recovered enough to limp back to life but is forever crippled for it. That's the best way to describe the travesty of this game.
*As a notice the following may contain spoilers*
Zestiria is a tales game, a member of one of the few JRPG linages to survive to the modern age. It was hyped as most of it's kind is of being the greatest new thing. Beautiful open and traversable areas, HD graphics [ though since I played it on a modest laptop most of that was turned down to avoid inducing a computer anyersum],  and flawless control - there were problems with the PS3 release, the system was just not powerful enough and the game was poorly optimized for it, but that's a a different can of worms. For the most part it delivers, accompanied by the as usual amazing Tales Soundtracks.
The Characters are a blast and have that classic interaction and quirky fun that one expects from Namco, and the expected interactions are all there.
BUT... that's pretty much all of the good parts.
While it is a vast, and beautifuly expansive world, it is rather empty. There are a grand total of 7 towns in the entire game   in addition to 4 destoryed villages (that are simply desolate areas related to simple side quests ) and the final dungeon which is a town in a similar state as the other four - destoryed houses little to explore and no soul living or dead inhabiting it.
Much of the game consists of vast open plains with few sights and the forest dungeons are all horrendously similar to the each other similar to repeats of the maze area before the bladlands in Xillia 1. The actual dungeons are even more depressing, save for the 4 shrines and the beginning and ending dungeons, each one is identical in features differing only in the color of the walls  - from blue, red, gray and purple metal/stone among other colors - and their basic layout. The remind me more of fallout out bunkers than any ancient ruin.
And here is where it gets frustrating, because Zestiria isn't just bad, it has a lot of good, which makes the bad worse. The first Dungeon, is an amazing stone ruin featuring a theme of South American temples and shrines, most closely resembling - at least in my view - Mayan, Incan and Aztec architecture. Since this was the first dungeon and I had seen nothing else, going off what I had heard of the game I had hoped the future areas of the game would continue this trend and take various styles of native ruins from around the world or perhaps just the Americas even. I was wrong, and it is quite possibly the best designed and most colorful of the dungeons.
Things unfortunately get worse from there. A JRPG has many unique elements but the essencial one is the story. And that's where Zestira drops the ball... HARD.
I'm not going into a ton of detail but basically the story is abysmal and barely makes sense. It's full of more plot holes that Swiss cheese. Further the story seems to just shift around a lot, I don't know how to describe it more than that, that it's unstable.
A big complaint is that the first Female MC gets replaced 1/3 or the way through the game by another girl who remains the Female MC for the rest of the came. It was poorly advertised and handled. It feels that either the second character was either shoehorned in or her role greatly expanded at the last hour without changing the story to compensate. Some have suggested that perhaps the game was meant to in the second half alternate back and forth between both female protagonists and their respective wind elemental partners, there do remain some parts of the story that might suggest that. The second female MC and her wind element partner are part of a group of assassins that feel like they were forced into the game. You could take at least the assassins if not her and the her partner out of the game and make a few small changes and nothing would be really different.
Further it's clear that the story was cut appart and put back togeather several times and at diffrent stages either to adapt for gameplay or differing ideas. It gives the feeling of several versions of a story from roughest draft to final copy un paper cliped and tossed around then reassembled without any regard that page 44 is from the final draft page 22 from the first and pagest 31-8 from various middle stages.
Because of all of this other segments of the story suffer. A history with most Tales villains is that they are well intentioned extreamists, they do what they do because they sincerely believe it is the key to utopia or a better life for all, even of many must be sacrificed along the way. This is charactistic of Mithos, Van, Ratatosk and Richter, Richard, Nachtigal and Gaius. The villain of Zestiria has none of that, he was basically cursed, by a corrupted god and an insane priest for being a pragmatic miliatary leader. Horrible things happened to him, so he turned evil or rather finally gave into evil and wants to destory the world as it is now his job to do so, if anyting the real villain of the whole story is never really given much back ground and it's just hand waved that he died after cursing the bad guy.
Further evidence of rushing with the game can be found in mentions of a third "northern" region that pops up in conversations towards middle of the second half of the game. This region is never visited but had ample map room, further more in a desert area in the end of the game there is a giant castle like gate covered with markings similar to Egyptian hieroglyphics. It is never mentiond by the characters or the game and appears as but a piece of scenery. It's attention to detail howerver shows that it must have clearly served a purpose and it is in the perfect position to be a gate to these northern regions that form a large blank spot on the world map.
Further, there seems to be no Tales twist, the ubiquitous event near the middle of the game that turns the player's and often the character's notion of the world completely on it's head. For Symphonia it's the existence of Te'thala, Graces Fodra, Dawn of a New world Emil is Ratatosk, Abyss the world is floating over an ocean of miasma and Luke is a clone. Xillia, the existance of Elympios. There is no such twist in Zestiria, yes there is the idea that you come from the so called "doomed town" but that has no importantance on the story's plot and is found out at the end of the game.
Another thing is all the tales games seem to have some sort of "moral" or center to them. Abyss is "you define who you are" Symphonia is "what is best may not always be right" Dawn is "Walk a mile in another's shoes" Graces is "Friendship conquers all" Xillia "compassion and understanding can build a better world" (it also had an underlying enviromental message). Zestiria ... I don't know what I got out of it..."Killing is okay if the person is evil." And okay I somewhat jest but there's really not much there... maybe "self-sacrifice or don't carry burdens alone" if you squint a look at it at a 42 degree angle in the right light.
So, in the end from a play and visual standpoint Zestiria is a rather good game. But the lack of elaboration given the visual capabilities the game had at it's disposal, and the train wreck of it's story make it a disaster that at least at it's current price I cannot recommend in good conscience.
-JHEE

I like this game, but I can't recommend it at full price. There just isn't enough there.
On the whole, Banished is an exceptionally slow game. This isn't necessarily a bad thing; it gives you far more control over your village, but the player grows past the speed pretty fast, and then you're stuck staring at the screen waiting for the glacier to move.  Population is the biggest thing, as it crawls up so slowly creating new, necessary jobs to keep your town alive is difficult. Seasons pass without much fuss or difference. I never had a problem with starvation or disease or... well, anything, and I was playing on medium. It felt like easy. I went 20+ years in game time without a single disaster, although I had it turned on. If you're going to have a disaster system, you should have a disaster system. The trading system takes about five years to start even after you build your dock, and then they only trickle in once every two to three years if you're lucky, and they only ever bring one or two items. Better hope it's what you want. Ordering my sheep took well over ten after the traders started coming, although I was very excited when I finally got them. Excited over buying sheep- the citybuilder life.
Citizens seem to constantly swap jobs around with no rhyme or reason. They almost basically refuse to move outside the town's radius to harvest resources, and as of such you find yourself running out. You can't prioritise what business gets the resources first, so it ends up being grabbed by whoever wants it over the business that actually needs it (logs & the woodcutter). The hunter AI is absolutely moronic- I watched one stroll casually through a herd of deer, then wander off, still apparently working. This was not an isolated incident. The tiny size of the hunter's radius is another big no- I would've expected it to be a great deal larger because surprise, animals move around the map. I liked they didn't hunt them to extinction though. Coupled with the hunter's terribad abilities is the lack of leather, which creates hide coats, which is a main trading chip along with firewood and iron tools. They also keep your citizens warm, but whatever, they're worth a lot at the trading post. #priorities
The music is beautiful, the graphics are nice, and I love the trees when they're mid way through growing (pine trees, but tiny. it's adorable). It's a charming game, and a decently relaxing one too (I do say this as someone who has never had a disaster, though. I imagine that raises the stress level). The controls are lovely, although in a game with micromanagement there needs to be... an easier way to do a couple of things? For instance, I should be able to stockpile items I don't want the town to use, I would've also liked the ability to move things from a storage unit to another- think Pharaoh, and 'accept all/get maximum'. (to those of you who have never played Pharaoh, do so ASAP. it's my favourite city builder by a longshot, and holds up extremely well despite how old it is... but set speed at 90%, not 100%).
So, in short. I guess I like Banished, It's enjoyable, but it's mind-numbingly slow, even for a citybuilder, which aren't exactly known for their high action gameplay. I think it's worth $5, but it's not worth $20, so buy it on sale and give it a go if you like games that are slow paced.
