Fun city builder which focuses on micro managing resources and the jobs of individual citizens. Unfortunately, I always seem to get to a point where my population starts dying off in the boat loads due to conditions which seem completely out of my control. I'll have a handle on my firewood production and consumption, and all my people living in stone houses and wearing protective clothes. But all of a sudden, my firewood all disappears seemingly over night, it won't replenish no matter how much I try to force it to, and everyone freezes to death. Or something similar happens with food. More often than not, they starve to death despite almost everyone working in a job that produces food, they just can't produce it fast enough to support themselves. I get the necessity for this game to be harsh and difficult, but it seems like you should have more control over certain factors to keep your entire population from dying out unexpectedly.
I tend to start playing this game when I want something easy and relaxing to play while I'm listening to a podcast or after a rough day at work or something like that. This game can be great for that. But it does get frustrating at a certain point and I won't get the urge to play it again for weeks or months after. I enjoy this game and I do recommend it, but I would say that you shouldn't pay full price for it. Get it on a sale and it'll be worth your money.

Comparing to the Playstation 3 version , the graphics in the game have also received a slight upgrades and the characters looks a lot sharper , the game environment and background is "cleaner " . It is however , still primarily a Playstation 3 game so don't expect anything you will see from the triple AAA games in 2015. One of the major complains from the fans is the game is still locked in its good old-fashion 30 Frame rate . It shouldn't be too notice-able unless you are a graphic and performance police  , but even by the general standard in 2015 , a 60 fps solid port will make your fans much happier  , Namco Bandai.
Additionally , there is a fan-made mod that seems to enable 60 fps but I have had occassional game crashes with that , so I wouldn't recommend installing it ( at least at the time of writing this review )
And what makes this Tales game special ? This is apparently the Tales team first effort go Open-world with Tales game , the world map are pretty large to explore and traveling from town to towns may take a while , with the occasionally interesting discovery . Despite of having a larger world map  , most of the location are still somewhat boring and bland to look at .
The combat system itself is pretty fun  , your typical Tales - smash N smash . Easy to play , hard to master . And great thing is this time you get to quick-switch among all your active party members in the combat , nobody is left behind.
So why wouldn't I recommend the game ?
Because the Game Story is a complete mess. And that is actually an understatement .
Not only the writing is a disaster , the presentation is boring , the game setting uninspiring , game characters also lack depth , almost making less sense than your local music channel.  To be fair , the Tales team did attempt to grow out of the jRPG stereotypes and try new things . While the open world seamless combat transition works pretty well here , Bandai Namco had hired a proper writer , because many of the game aspects are not only getting old but becoming worse.
It's a jRPG ,  many may argue the recent jRPGs don't really has good story , but this one has probably one of the worst out there.
TL;DR : good port from the ps4 version ,  with pretty fun combat at first which eventually gets too complicated , grinding for high end equipment takes years , story doesn't make senses , plots a mess .

Meld is a puzzle game with a simple mechanic - you need to create coloured paths from one node to another. There are coloured hexes on the boards you can (or can't) move, you can mix the colours to better suit your needs, and you have various "powerups" that can alter the colours, or even the board itself.
Based on the above, the game's 200 levels seem to be excessive, but having gone until 50, I daresay it may be feasible. The levels all manage to be interesting some aspect, and while difficulty is quite up and down, I regularly ran into some rather challenging ones - at least if I was to make 3 stars with no extra powerup purchases.
So Meld is a pretty good game - probably not quite worth the 10 bucks asking price, but at 50% discount it's perfectly fine.

TL;DR This game is a work of sheer genius. If you're a puzzler you owe it to yourself to buy Meld and if you don't relish every minute of it I'll eat my hat!
At first glance it looks pretty tame. Make a line of hexagons to join the terminals. How hard can it be, right? Wrong! The first few levels are straightforward but you'll soon be scratching your head as the complexity ramps up. Various types of obstacles start appearing on the board and new powerups are introduced at intervals (16 of them in total!) Each new powerup is explained very clearly and the first couple of levels ease you into it gently so its usage is clear in your mind before you start exploring its potential.
With most puzzle games I usually reach a point where I can't finish a level so I finally give in and go to Youtube or Steam Guides for the solution. I'm invariably disappointed because now the level is spoiled and I'm convinced that I could have done it myself if I'd thought about it a bit longer but I'll never know because I can't un-know the solution.
Meld is a newish game and there are currently no guides to be found online which means no temptations, but the mechanics of the game have completely neutralised any urge to rage-quit and google the solution because you can set your own difficulty preference. Each level gives you a set number of moves and a small number of powerups, if you run out of moves you fail. You're awarded 1, 2 or 3 stars for completing the level, the fewer moves you make the more stars you get - time taken and number of restarts are shown but this doesn't affect your score. 1 or 2 star solutions are fairly easy for the first 100ish levels so total failure is unlikely but just in case you do get stuck you can use your supply of plasma, which you amass throughout the game, to purchase extra powerups if you want to cheat to improve your score or if you just want to get the level out of the way to unlock the next one.
If you want the hardcore challenge - 3-star solutions with no purchases - you'll often tell yourself "this level is simply not possible to 3-star!" but if you stare at the board long enough you'll eventually have that Eureka moment and congratulate yourself on your mental prowess. You always have 'lesser' solutions to fall back on, but some of these puzzles will leave you mentally exhausted. When the Fusion powerup first appeared on level 115 I felt my melted brain oozing out of my ears. Many levels have crystals placed around the board and if you want to go hardcore++ you can try the long route via all the crystals.
Every level is possible to 3-star (including all crystal routes) with no purchases. I can tell you this because I've done it!! If you play into the advanced levels you'll swear I'm lying but my conscience is clear. There's a special place in Hell for whoever devised level 192 though. As you gain experience you'll become more proficient and the previous levels that you couldn't 3-star earlier will seem easier when you go back to try them again.
There's an astronomy theme: shoot a comet through a wormhole, place a black hole etc. with nice sounds and animations - starbursts, energy-blur and a lot of zapping. Enough to make it pleasant to look at without interfering with the gameplay. The background music is unobtrusive and can be left on, although I prefer listening to my own music.
The Meld logo doubles as the key to the game. It's shown prominently on the level screen and you find yourself checking it constantly against the board to see which colours meld with which and how to apply the powerups. Brilliant.
There are only a handful of user-contributed levels so far but I plan to add to them. The tormented becomes the tormentor.
6 trading cards and 20 achievements - some interesting ones as well as the usual progress-related. 20th one isn't dropping though (see below).
... is OUTSTANDING. 200 puzzles (plus more user-contributed), and every one of them is carefully crafted with unique combinations of obstacles and powerups. At no point does it feel samey or repetitive, but at times you may wish it was just to give your poor battered brain a rest! There's a lot of replay value as you'll normally do 1 or 2 stars for many of the levels on the first playthrough, then go back to try for 3 stars. Unlike other puzzle games you will get full satisfaction from every level without the temptation to look up spoilers. You can see by my play time above that there are many hours of puzzling to be had.
What I think happened here is that the genius (really) devs completed construction of the magnificent 200th level and decided to celebrate by getting blind drunk, so they took their laptop with them to the pub and created the UI while they were there, in between tequila shots. Here are the results of their folly:
Puzzle games are my thing. I've played a lot of them and this one is a strong contender for my all time favourite. The mechanics are simple, you move hexagons around, but the puzzles are so cleverly contrived that you'll be grinning from ear to ear when you find that sweet 3-star solution. The gameplay is so good that I can forgive the mess of a UI. It's been on Steam for 3 months now and only 13 reviews, I feel sorry for all the people missing out on this hidden gem, it deserves to be a bestseller.

Did you ever like mixing colors together as a kid? Do you also enjoy puzzle games? Well, perhaps Meld is the game for you!
Meld is a deceptively simple puzzle game developed by Axis Games, who also apparently made a football game (Axis Football 2015)? Well, this is a weird departure for them I suppose, but oh well. Upon first glancing at the game, the graphics were kind of off-putting for me since they were so simple and bland, but after playing I can definitely say that the fun and challenging gameplay makes up for it.
See, Meld combines a few different puzzler genres in some interesting ways. Namely, it's a hex/tile puzzler mixed with those pipe puzzles in certain games. Oh, and there's color mixing thrown in the mix too. It may seem a little complicated but it's actually quite simple in theory: make a path from one end of the level to the other using only the same color as what the ends of the path/"pipe" (if you like to think of it like that) is. So, if the ends of the "conduit" (that's what the game calls it) are green, you need to make a green line of tiles to beat the level. You do this by dragging tiles of that color to form an unbroken path. Easy enough, right?
Well.....not exactly. See, tiles of base colors (red, yellow, or blue) can be "melded" together to make new colors (orange, purple, or green). The game starts off quite easy but as you progress the game introduces powerups and obstacles, which really amp up the difficulty as more and more are introduced. There's some basic ones like a lock on certain tiles which makes it so you can't move them, or meteors that can destroy both these locks and individual tiles if needed. Later on, some really wild stuff is added into the mix. I mean, just look at the store page description for what I mean - stuff like Black Holes, Supernovas, Superconducters, etc. It gets pretty crazy, but all the additions only serve to both add complexity and depth to the seemingly basic gameplay. Honestly I thought that this was a great way to make the game not get old fast.
One thing I will say is that the game can get quite hard very fast. I made it to about level 20 to 25 or so before I started to constantly get stuck, which would be a problem since the game has 200 levels (I believe). However, there's an in-game store where you can buy extra moves or various powerups using a currency the game gives you as you play, plasma, to help make levels easier. Though it can be pretty easy to run out of plasma if you're bad at puzzle games like me, I felt like this system helped compensate for the difficult nature of the puzzles. Plasma could be given out more frequently, but it's still a decent way to help people of all skill levels enjoy the game for at least a while.
The game also includes a level editor if you're into those. I didn't check it out since I'm not very good at making levels, but I did check out some of the user-made custom levels and those were pretty fun. If people keep making levels, there could be tons of replayability here, so it's definitely worth checking out if you somehow manage to beat all the main game's 200 levels.
In the graphics department, the game is clearly unimpressive. The only background in the game seems to be one of outer space and the only other noteworthy thing is the animations when using powerups, which may range from a small explosion to other weird jolts or whatnot. Sound-wise, it's a little better, with the music striking a decent balance between being pleasant and slightly repetitive while the sound effects are just about what you'd expect - some whooshes or explosions when necessary. Not too shabby I guess, but both areas could be improved on.
Meld is perhaps not necessarily the best puzzle game for those who aren't above average at games in the genre, but for both skilled players and novices alike, Meld is a great, fun, and challenging puzzler with great replayability, definitely no lack of content, and decent variety to its puzzles. For puzzle fans who are confident in their skills, this game will definitely test you, but even for those who aren't very good, the game provides ways to still beat levels. Check it out if it sounds interesting!

Unlike many color puzzles, Meld requires economical conversions, like converting currency in a trading simulator. I’ve never seen a trading sim with multiple currencies, but after playing Meld, I realize how fun the conversions can be, and certainly hope to find more games with this concept.
I do have several color-mixing games, and none use this concept of conversions to this extent. Of course, the others lose interest for me very quickly. But, the strategy involved in the conversions of multiple colors holds you all the way through these levels, and it lends itself to multiple replays to beat previous scores.
As a side note, the title reminds me of the meld collectable resource in XCOM: Enemy Within. Yeah, remember how the squaddies would say, “Meellllddd!” when spotting the canisters?! It sounded like they had become addicted to the body augmentation afforded by this new rare resource. Well, Meld is a lot like that, as you’ll find yourself drawn to replaying levels just to beat your last run through.
The tutorial is top-notch! Instead of spending 30 minutes explaining the mechanics, you get a simple one level instruction to perform an action that demonstrates the basic moves. Then, new power-ups are brought into the game one at a time, about every 25 levels or so. What is great is the way many are available on a map a level or two before introducing them, to encourage exploration.
When I first noticed new “things” on a level, I had no idea what they were, so I just avoided them hesitantly. But, then when they were available in the store to purchase with my plasma in-game currency, and the tutorial move popped up, I realized I could explore those ahead of time. And, that is definitely one of the best features of Meld, the variety of special power-ups that allow you to really get creative in finding solutions. You don’t feel like your hand is being held, but at the same time, if you think outside the box, you’ll find a solution fairly quickly that usually is much simpler than you would have thought possible at first glance. It rewards you for being lazy enough to complete the puzzle in the fewest number of moves.
The mechanics are incredibly smooth and enjoyable. Not only do the pieces move in the way that you would expect, but they move without thought, so that you are able to focus on the puzzle itself. That’s the way it should be with any game. You don’t want the mechanics to get in the way. Meld does this very well.
The graphics are simple because the game is a minimalistic puzzler. It looks good, and the music is enjoyable enough that I kept it on, unlike many puzzlers where you cut the music off after 30 minutes of solutions. But, the sound effects themselves really add to the experience, with a moving field of stars visual in the background. The power-ups are items like asteroids, planets, comets, etc. When you use a meteor, it has a sound effect with it. But, when you use a meteor shower, you see and hear 7 meteors strike the puzzle hexes, pretty awesome effect! It’s a very satisfying sound effect system, with quite a bit of imagination drawn into it.  Of course, this substitutes for the fact that there is no narrative, and essentially carries the game into a cohesive whole, with the theme of celestial objects.
*The symmetrical layout of maps can create or obscure symmetry.
*Color key is visible on-screen, and optional color-blind mode
*Hexagonal shapes are eye pleasing with many unique map designs
*High Replay Factor
*Level Creation feature via sign-in on game server
*The Dev responded fast and in detail to a bug with the achievies
*Suggest addition of speed run bonus levels every quarter to gain plasma
*Needs undo move button/ would be a nice feature
*Level Creation not on Steam Workshop share
This color melding puzzle game is a perfect ten! I highly recommend Meld for everyone.

Still retaining her long lapine ears as well, she is vexed by the fact that no one can tell if she is a rabbit or a cat. She even went as far as to seek the aid of a wise old bunny, but unfortunately he was brutally murdered by a rampaging bull and has left Bunny stranded in the cave of the 7 devils. If you think sounds mightily effed up, you are probably right, but no matter. It is time for Bunny to set forth and kick some devilish♥♥♥♥♥
Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 Devils is a classic example of the tried and true Metroidvania formula. It was created pretty much singlehandedly by Murasame of Platine Dispositif (aside from voicework), and like his other works the game can be punishingly hard at times. The original release was only in Japan, with 4:3 graphics and a midi-ish soundtrack. However this localization offers many enhancements over the original release, such as new widescreen graphics coded in by Murasame, a wild soundtrack arrangement by Woofle, and a fresh English translation.
When starting BMD the first thing you'll notice is the lush hand-drawn anime graphics. The next thing you'll notice is that you can't walk to the right. You must first walk to the left a few steps to collect "The Gears of The Past" to be able to turn around. This quirky bit of humor quite obviously pokes fun at the general mechanics of the Metroidvania genre, and trust me when I say that a whole lot more will be lampooned before you finish the game. The game even pokes fun at you (and then throws a viciously hard boss your way) for sequence breaking. Yes, the large-foreheaded first boss lady will fly off the handle if you skip her.
Now despite the amusing jokes and cliches blown out of proportion, the gameplay in Bunny Must Die is your standard Metroidvania exploration with plenty of Castlevania-style combat. You also gain the ability to bend time to your will, and that opens a whole new dimension in gameplay and puzzle solving. I should note though that no matter how good you are at this sort of game, you WILL die often. Just go into this adventure knowing that fact and you will have a good time. The way we learn is by making mistakes, right? And sometimes being repeatedly run over by a turret-tank while it fires laser beams up your♥♥♥♥♥♥is a learning experience too.
Rockin' Android has definitely gone all-out in the process of making Bunny Must Die a breakout title for the western world. They have go so far as to give the options to use the original graphical mode and soundtrack, despite the overhaul that is provided by default. This speaks volumes of their dedication to customer satisfaction, and to their preservation of the original product's values. Just as with the Gundemonium Collection, Rockin' Android has taken an already awesome property and further polished it to gleam like a diamond and stand out on it's own in the rough sea of indie games.
So to recap: Bunny Must Die! Chelsea and the 7 Devils offers frenetic platforming, Metroidvania-inspired exploration, kickass brutal bosses, a rocking re-arranged soundtrack, a superbly localized and hilarious story, a cute as heck main character, a super secret hidden character with a second playthrough, and tight controls that ensure that if you screw up, it's your own damn fault. What the heck are you waiting for? Bust out your favorite gamepad, buy the game, and kick some demonic patootie! Bunny's fate depends on YOU!

Having played the first game, Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45, the sequel is nothing short of stunning. While the AI hasn't improved all that much and the tank combat could use some more work, the remainder of the game stands as a testomony as to the horrendous conditions of the last great global war.
Snipers of legends were forged by this hellfire. From these elites, you'll be dead before you know what hit you. If you hear the gunshot, you are lucky enough to still be alive when you hit the floor. That can't be said for the falling corpse that used to be a man, who didn't stay far enough from the windows.
Machine gunners are the plague of the streets. Accurate and deadly, they can stand their ground for hours on end, picking off whoever is unlucky-or stupid-enough to wander into their vision. All they leave behind are chewed-up flesh that once constituted a human being.
Submachine gunners are the spearhead of an assault. If you miss your first shot, their eight returning bullets will certainly not miss you. Their bottomless magazines will make sure they outlast you in the hunt through the rooms and hallways of the ruined city.
Somewhere behind the enemy lines is their commander. A man of rank and influence, sent to this same hellhole as the rank and file soldier in this everlasting struggle. He may only be armed with a pistol, but it is his capacity with his rank that makes him such a grand target; this man can direct the flow of war against you, call down artillery and make the heavens fall on your head, and spy upon your each and every move from the skies. Only the most competent of men can fill this role, making him yet another deadly adversary.
Tanks, the mighty steel behemoths, are impervious to all but the largest of calibers. These rumbling machines of death, armed with their massive cannon and multitudes of machine guns, will bring a swift end to all those that oppose it on the streets. The only ones who can truly oppose a tank is another steel behemoth, or one of those lucky enough to be holding an anti-tank rifle.
Nine times out of ten, you are none of these.You are merely one of the many cannon fodder sent to their deaths on the front in an attempt to push the enemy out of this part of the street. You are a fresh recruit with nothing but a single grenade, two rolls of bandages, and a simple bolt-action rifle. A true relic  from the last war, yes, but it is your only true friend in this world that wants you dead.
tl;dr,
Red Orchestra does not merely tell you the horrors that we call Stalingrad, as the boring old history books always tell us in class. It is a ticket to the front row of this hell that had once descended upon our very own world.

The Cat and the Coup is a nice little addition in favor of the 'games can be art' debate.  It's quite short, but doesn't need to be long to get its point across.  It is part history lesson and part surrealistic visual story, and although the game play is sparse, it's still there.  This game wasn't 'fun' in the traditional sense, but rather it was more intriguing, as well as somewhat haunting with it's bizarre imagery coupled with the sad lingering soundtrack.
For those who didn't understand the metaphors in this game, I will explain below.
Scroll down or 'read more' for spoilers.

You play as the black cat, traditionally established as a symbol of misfortune, who manipulates the various items and situations in a series of rooms.  By doing so, you move Dr. Mossadegh through those different rooms as he struggles to adapt to the changes you are indirectly creating.  Note that at no time is it stated that the cat belongs to Dr. Mossadegh, but rather it is a cat that incessantly follows him around.
The rooms are a double-metaphor serving as both the various political/social occurrences at the time, and as stages of Dr. Mossadegh's life.  The cat is a metaphor for the CIA.  The cat's behavior is the covert tampering that CIA agents performed to maneuver Dr. Mossadegh into the situation where he would be removed from power.  The bulldog represents British interests who, behind closed doors, asked the Americans for undercover aid to depose Dr. Mossadegh from power.  The reasons for Britain doing this are spelled out at the end of the game in the vertical assent back through the imagery the cat initially fell downward through.  So, long story short, when you play this game, you play as the CIA covertly creating a social/political environment necessary to bring about a coup in Iran in the 1950's.
Why was the story told in reverse?  I assume that is just artistic license in story telling, but I could be wrong.

Red Orchestra 2 is one of the best, if not the best shooters I have played. The game is supposed to be realistic and it executes it really well. Not only that, it probably is one of the most atmospheric games I have ever played.
It can be hard to get into this game if you are completely new to this genre, but if you stick with the game for a while, you'll have a blast. But, it can take some time. It will be a one shot kill most of the time, however, sometimes you can survive it. The maps are pretty big, but despite that, you will always find action. If you know what you are doing, then the experience will be epic, however, if you don't know, you'll just get shot from left and right. It does take time to develope a game sense, knowing where your enemies can potentially be and so on, but it really is worth it.
Aside from a few clunky mechanics, which mostly occure on servers that you have a high ping on anyway, it plays really well. The game has a progression system in which you can unlock different types of things for guns, such as a bayonet, bigger clip and so on. Nothing too fancy, since it is WW2. It does take a lot of time to earn this experience, but if you enjoy the game just as much as I do, it won't really bother you. Besides, it doesn't put you in much of a disadvantage if you are level 1 anyway. The graphics are pretty decent, can't say that they are bad. The game did come out a while ago, but I think it does hold up.
Realism in shooters doesn't sound like much fun, but it is when you know what you are doing. If you are willing to take some time to get the grip of the game, you'll have a blast.

Lets talk about the game. This game will put on display for you the works of one person, narrarated over by a friend of his. The friend of course has a lot of bias about these games, and will push the notions he has about them on you. SPOILER: the narrarator will try to make it seem like the author of these works is a broken and lonely person, when really it's the narrorator himself who is seeing himself in the game (his own thoughts, views, etc). It's a sad dichotomy and the game does not end happily. In fact it's somewhat upsetting.
In short, to anyone considering buying this game, don't pay ten dollars for this, just go to the Library and check out a book on existential philosophy or chinese maxims or something. It will probably do a lot more for you than this emotional catharsis of a game.

Tales of Zestiria brings Bandai Namco's latest entry in its long line of fast-paced JRPGs to Western audiences, and notably for the first time to PC via Steam. It sports a cheery anime style and offers a meaty ability system for players to delve into, as JRPGs tend to do, capped off with the series' well-known (and trademarked) action-based combat.
The story follows a young man named Sorey, who has been raised away from humanity and early on in the story discovers he is their saviour - their "Shepherd". Along the way he meets entities representing the various natural elements and that he is able to fuse with ("armatize") in combat.
Combat is the defining feature of any Tales game, and Zestiria makes a few tweaks to the system such as battles no longer taking place in a separate arena.  If there's a rock to your left when you encounter an enemy on the map, it'll be there during battle.
The rest of the combat system remains fairly intact - for the uninitiated, that includes chaining combos, a mix of physical and magical abilities, and an elemental strengths and weakness rock-paper-scissors system.
The fusion ability that Sorey unlocks early in the game is incredibly fun and powerful, but there are also genuine tactical reasons to not fuse. It's not like a Final Fantasy-style limit break that you just want to fire off as soon as it's ready, though doing so
is rarely a truly terrible idea.
What really lets Zestiria down, though, is its equipment system. Each piece of equipment can come with up to four skills on it which represent a tile on a grid. Match the tiles either horizontally or vertically to enable bonus skills, and fuse matching pieces of gear together to create stronger gear with the skills you want... or in theory, that's how it works.
In practice, it actually restricts you - you make your way to the bottom of a dungeon, kill the boss and he drops an awesome weapon, but you can't use it because it doesn't have the right skills, breaking your horizontal or vertical lines, and equipping it is a net stat loss. It's a really unsatisfying feeling.
Zestiria sits in an odd spot within the market. For fans of the series, and JRPGs in general, it offers little in the way of surprise, and while enjoyable does come off a little trite. Gamers of this persuasion can probably pick up Zestiria with little fear of a poor experience, but shouldn't expect to be completely blown away.
Newcomers, however, are thrown head-first into the game's convoluted equipment and fusion systems. The game does offer the option to (further) simplify combat, but its true intention is to remove any necessity to correctly upgrade your equipment.
Outside this, enjoyment will come down to the individual's tolerance for Zestiria's anime influence in its appearance and in its story. If you're more of a cringer than a cheerer, then you may not want to follow this Shepherd.

A disappointment in the Tales franchise.
This one fell short in several key instances that keep me from honestly recommending it.
I won't say the plot had holes, instead I'll say that the world is inconsistent with how it follows its own rules.
I can't say more without revealing spoilers but it's enough to say that if you start poking around, you'll find more than enough events that make no sense and feel like they were pulled out of nowhere just for dramatic tension.
The combat feels like it's on autoplay half the time, with several multi-hit attacks going off of single button presses.
May seem cool at first but it makes it near impossible to block or dodge when you want to without first coming to a complete stop. You'll be wanting to block but will be stuck in a several second long attack animation.
The dungeons are awful. Most of them have absolutely nothing interesting besides the combat. And that gets old fast, especially when the camera gets stuck looking into a wall when fighting in tight spaces.
There's almost nothing in the way of puzzle solving, something that was a staple of dungeons in previous 'Tales of' games.
When you use a Holy Bottle to avoid combat, and find yourself running through dungeons with absolutely noting to do in them besides run to the end, that's when you know the designers utterly failed.
Not just because there's nothing interesting besides combat but also because the Holy Bottle doesn't fade away until you rest at an inn. And since you aren't getting into combat, that could be for a long while.
This game has too many flaws for me to recommend it.
Go play Tales of Symphonia instead. Graphics may be older but it's so much better in every aspect.
Don't bother with Zestiria unless it's on a really good sale.

I don't often write reviews for games, but I recently picked up OlliOlli2 again after not having played it for a while, and remembered just why I love this game so much.
TLDR, this is almost a perfect 'flow' game.
Some background: I love games where I can learn to work on an almost subsconscious level, turn my brain off, and just get into the flow. Stepmania and similar rhythm games are great for that, but I also love things like the Tony Hawk Pro Skater series for the same reason (I played an ungodly number of hours of THPS3 on the PS2)
OlliOlli2 scratches that exact same itch. It's 2D, so you may think it's overly simplistic, but I would personally say 'refined'. No, it doesn't have the 3D freedom and massive trick selection of the THPS or Skate games. This is a far more arcadey take on the same idea, but it absolutely lets you get into that perfect flow, and when you learn to combo all the way through a level it becomes seriously addictive. It's challenging enough that you won't master it easy, but laid back enough that you won't want to smash your joypad in frustration - at least once you get the hang of the basic controls. They're a little unusual, so it's tricky at first, but it doesn't take long to sink it.
The music is absolutely fantastic. The graphics suit the game's style, no complaints there.
The only negative really is that while there are good number of levels, most of the ones beyond about the mid-point of the game are so tight in terms of the timing required to get through them that there's pretty much only one correct way to do them, leaving no real space for freestyling or developing your own routes. The earlier levels, however, offer a lot of scope for doing them your own way, trying to beat your high score and best combo, etc.
Also, I've heard a couple of people complain about weird problems with analog controls. I've had that a bit too, phantom inputs and stuff. The solution for me was dead simple - I just use the D-pad. There's no real analog turning in this game, so it actually makes sense to use the D-pad for input. For what it's worth, I'm using a Playstation 2 controller via a USB adapater, with the analog mode disabled, and it works great.

So with Just Cause 3 on the horizon a review for JC2 seems late, but a good game shoud be honoured as such and Just Cause 2 certainly is a good game. If you are looking for an extremely open-world enviroment with many methods of travel, a vast array of weapons and destruction, and the choice between doing missions or casual wandering then this is for you.
Ok so the story is not entirely original, brilliant or generally packaged and delivered well, but for what it lacks in this area it makes up for in the gameplay mechanics and the open-world enviroment.
This map is huge, like huge-huge. I will stick my neck on the line and say it's probably bigger than GTAV's map, and it diversifies in each setting. You have your dessert dunes, wetlands, beaches, rainforrests, artic tundra and a murderous Japanese fog island. The weapons array is quite large, and can be upgraded, but the most instrumental part of the game lies in the grappling hook which serves as a weapon, travel method and a destructive tool for laying bases to waste.
I tend to play this vey causaly, and can choose to explore the islands and bases in any way I want. When you choose missions, although targets are painted and objectives are there, you can still tackle the mission with whatever is at your disposal.
Overall, Just Casue 2, It's a beautiful sandbox with some devastating toys in it. Dont play nice, Smash the castles.

First off, I want to warn you the game may not run on your system if you are on Windows 10. The only way I could get this game to run is with a 3rd party community patch. A game IMHO should never be released in any such form! You have been warned. Go to the discussion board and get the community patch first.
I have trouble reviewing this game because it divides me so much.
I'll start with the positives by saying the game has a fantastic story and set of characters. All characters (annoying or not) are voiced well and likeable. The story is complex and so are the characters and there is a lot to love when the two coming together. This game does a great job of telling a story, as I think an RPG should.
The game has lots of great cut scenes, or mini cut scenes called skits. They do a great job of giving characters thoughts, ideas, and expressions in a fun anime like way. It's kind of a unique system that I've never seen and it just adds a lot I think.
They also have an Anime based on the game in the works, would totally watch.
As great as the story and character are, which really hold the game together, the game has issues.
Even with the community patch, the game does have some graphical issues during combat. Certain effects cause massive graphical slowdown on a GTX 970, which shouldn't happen. Then again the game wouldn't even run for me without a community patch.
The camera in the game does not work exactly as you would expect. It turns super slow. You will adapt mostly, but it's just something that is so weird it's worth mentioning because you will battle it all game.
One thing that was kind of good / bad is you lose a major character like 1/3 of the way through the game. It's not that it really changes anything it's just a really bizarre thing like they started making the game and decided they didn't really want this character to be in the game and then hastily wrote them out. Although the game's director downplays this, it seems almost evident.
The combat system is overly complex, but here is an “easy mode” if you wish to take some of the complexity out of the game. It gets easier the more you play it but sill takes a bit of time before you can really confidently fight “epic” type monsters and survive. The few strong enemies will clean your clock though, and it drives down the fun value.
There are a few times where you will not have clear goals and need to basically wander around until you discover where you are suppose to go. Some better hints would be nice rather than wasting literally hours of my time trying to figure out where to go. Wasting players time should not be considered good. It is a tactic used by bad games to extend their play time. It really kills the pacing of the game.
TLDR;
Overall the game is above average in terms of story, and the characters are great. It's a shame however that the game suffers from poor pacing and other problems that really just make it a mediocre game. The game tries to do too much and stretches out too long for the content included.
I'd say play it with tempered expectations going in, it's an interesting game but it's not going to probably make your “greatest RPGs ever” list.

I survived the first days, making my way around Mystery Lake, scavenging everything from the tourist huts which seemed to be useful. I know that I could not survive, only eating those ugly fish I could catch from the ice holes, so I gathered my last supplies and began my way towards the deeper woods. Avoiding any contact with the aggressive beasts roaming the lowering and paths, I finally reached the Trappers homestead, just after the weather turned and a snow storm began chilling me to the bones. In this lonely hut I established my homebase. During the next days I started a slow but sustainable economy based on foraging firewood, scouting the surrounding for the best spots to set up rabbit traps and slowly crafting new and better equipment.
When I became used to the routine and also quite optimistic, regarding my overall chances of long term survival, the disaster struck. When on one evening I was patrolling the rabbit snares I discovered a wolf hunting down a deer. While the beast feasted on it’s pray I sneaked nearer from his side. I aimed and killed it with one shoot. Now both carcasses were mine for the price of only one round!
The only problem was, that sunset was approaching, and I was already heavily encumbered from the spoils of my traps. So I decided to take what I could carry to make my way back to my hut. I arrived soon after sundown. In the evening I fed the fire, which I would not allow to go out because of the precious matches need to ignite it. I also processed the pray I had acquired during that day before I went to bed.
On the next morning, I foraged some firewood and consumed some supplies for breakfast. Unfortunately, I confused the uncleansed water with already boiled save one. This resulted in a bad case of intestinal sickness. I treated it with the needed drug which I had luckily in supply. Still the sickness would need 10 hours for curing. Instead of returning to bed for the rest of the day, I still decided to make my way to the carcasses left behind the day before, so they would not further decay. I found my way back without any problems, it was not that far away and the weather was quite good at that time of the day. After I spent some time gutting my pray, I decided to take another route back to my hut, so I could check some of the rabbit snares I put in place two days ago. Already the sickness took its toll and my condition was worsening but I suspected that a little detour would not put me in any grave danger.
Soon I arrived at one of the snares and indeed it had cached some pray. At that point I made a dangerous mistake.
Instead of checking my surrounding before getting to work on the carcass, I just started the gutting as soon as I arrived, eager to return home as soon as possible. When I finished my worked I suddenly heard the fast approaching footsteps of wolf. I knew I had only mere seconds to live if I now made a mistake. I managed to turn around and also raised my rifle, but the shoot I fired in haste missed its fast approaching target.
Only an eye-blink later, the beast was at my throat. A frantic life or death struggle followed and I knew, that all the days I survived before were meaningless, if I would lose against this hellish creature. In the next moments my fate would be decided. With two mighty blows of my hatched, I drove the beast away! Howling it ran wounded into the woods. I had won this fight but now the real misery began.
The encounter left me seriously injured. After treating my wounds, I realised that my condition was down to less than a third. I was highly fatigued and also quite dehydrated because of my sickness. I knew that I needed to return to my hut as soon as possible, but I could only make a few steps before the weather changed and a raging snowstorm hit home. Suddenly the temperature dropped dramatically and the surrounding vanished behind a white wall of snow. I soon lost my orientation and I started to freeze to death. Because of the fatigue I could only move very slowly through the thick blizzard.
Down to 2/10th of my condition, I knew that I soon needed rest and a heat source to survive. I could have used my bed role to camp outdoor, but due to the violent storm, it was not possible to ignite a fire outside and without one, I would certainly freeze to death in my sleep. I decided that my only chance was to find the hut in the storm and I needed to move faster to do so. In haste I dropped nearly everything I had with me. My hunting rifle, the tools, all the priceless spoils of my hunt and worst of all, my hatchet. Now I was a little faster.
After further stumbling around aimlessly through the raging storm, I began to lose any hope. When my condition still dwindled I started to resign myself that this play through, which was my personal record, would find its inglorious ending here, freezing to death, lost in this storm, maybe only a few meters away from the safe heaven, but unable to find it.
Suddenly, out of nowhere, a fence became visible through the storm. I could not believe my eyes! It was the fence leading up to the entrance of my hut!
I was down to 6% condition when I reached the entrance. I took the rest of my fire wood depot, casting it into the oven, gorged down some food and drinks to treat my dehydration and hunger. Still my condition was dropping because of the dangerous fatigue. I know hoped that I had not overseen any other need which could kill me while I sleept and went to bed with only 4% condition left.
The next morning I awoke, a little surprised that I indeed survived the night. The weather was great on that morning and I was happy that I made it through this perfect storm. But the good mood was only short lived. I had spent most of my medical equipment. Also my food and water are now in short supply. To make the situation worse, all my tools are now lost in the woods together with my food supply for the next days. Also, with my rifle and hatchet lost, I am practically defenceless against the beasts in the woods. My survival over the next days is now still on the edge, so I gather the rest of my supplies, leaving my hut and the struggle against the forces of nature starts anew.

The basic mechanics of Meld are clean and easy to understand, with a solid twist on tile-based and pipe-based puzzle games. The game started out very simply as the game eased you into controlling the various mechanics of the game, however the difficulty curve rose sharply around the 25th level. If you're looking for a more challenging puzzle game I would certainly recomend this, but more casual puzzle game players might be turned away at the overall difficulty.
The biggest boon to the game is the built-in level editor. The replay value for this game is extremely high thanks to being able to access user-created levels from around the world. The editor is nice to use and does give players a lot of freedom when designing their own levels.
I would love to see a mobile release in the future, a platform where I believe a game like this would shine.

Imagine you could somehow deal with the camera angles (which are comparable to a square wheel in functionality) but the QTEs make you ragequit hard time after time.
The game just tells you to get ready and then slaps you in the face with a task that you fail at least three times before figuring out which buttons you're even supposed to use for this particular ♥♥♥♥♥how, then you fail some more going trial-and-error -style about HOW EXACTLY to move the analog stick up or something, and THEN some more failing because what's required of you is more or less inhuman, or just stupid. It's never intuitive, logical or the least bit pleasant.
Every single time that doomed "GET READY" appears on the screen you find yourself moaning in agony, screaming "WTF am I supposed to do?" at your controller and in the end watching your character ♥♥♥♥ing up again and again and again.
It gets to the point where you're not focusing at all on the story or what's actually happening on the screen, but instead on the controller and the pain you feel in your fingers and brain trying desperately to decipher the ridiculously bad controls. Every chance you give this game ends with you curled up in a ball in some corner, crying how you just wanted to play a nice story-driven game for a change.
Does this sound like an immersive or fun gaming (or "movie watching" as they call it) experience yet?

So,  I really wanted to like this game. Maybe I could've, if only playing it didn't feel like doing 4 kitchens worth of dishes with only a toothbrush and your own spit. For everyone else I recommend just watching a playthrough on YouTube, as the story is actually OK (if you're into the unintentionally funny B-movie type).
In the end I'm just bitter, oh so bitter and considering a refund, maybe getting something from TellTale in exchange. And some therapy. And maybe new eardrums for everyone else in the room who went deaf from my screaming (Sorry!).

It's really easy to use but powerful - simpler than Flash because you don't have to learn the syntax. All you need is common sense and an adventurous mindset.
Either you tinker together the default assets, with sounds, music, sprites, maps, items, animations, enemies and what have you... or you can customize everything to your heart's content. Like adding scripts from a forum or changing tilesets. Everyone can develop on their own level. And frankly, if you're a person who finds it fun to work with graphic tools or level editors or sandbox type of games, you'll have a blast.
Naturally, a finished and good product doesn't come quickly and there is a lot of problem solving, testing, tweaking and mindless tedium to be done. Also, you might get disillusioned when you realize that every rpg is basically the same. Or you come to appreciate more the outstanding work and elbow grease of some of these games.
It would be a good idea to start humble and experiment and make a couple of games, not just the one and only. Ease yourself in, maybe watch a video tutorial at some point.
Even if you're not that interested in developing yourself, owning this software allows you to play all the stuff in the workshop, simply by subscribing. When you do that, give something unpopular a chance and feedback for those you don't get any. There is a lot of trash there or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes. But don't just play the same stuff everyone is playing, because everyone is playing it. Encourage others and they encourage you. If they are worthy your encouragement that is. You can easily detect how much effort someone put into his game if you study their workshop page. If it has a generic, crappy title, a flat or nonexistent description and no pictures or videos then they are most likly not very proud of their work. It would be benefical for everyone if more people took their stuff more seriously.

I previously had this game reviewed as a thumb up and great but I feel I have to change it until some glaring issues within the game change. This is not to say the game does not have great features and that I hate the game or anything, but I currently do not play it and I will mention why.
1. There is not really any fair match making system, you can be in matches with players who have leveled up equipment and you have non leveled up equipment. I understand this is early access and under heavy development, but this is making game play pretty annoying for new players.
2, Leveling up, both EXP and JUNK wise, takes extremely long currently, I see how the devs added daily missions but that is only a bonus, and even if you recieved the reward of a daily mission in each mission you played, it still would not be enough junk and exp in my opinion. The Junk and EXP you get for playing is just wayyyyy to low for your time investment.
3 Frigates, they still have stun and invulnerability.
4 bad lag and optimization issues still make the game very unfun and un competetive when you are having these issues.
5 these issues have been here for a while and have not been adressed, when they are the issues that are chasing away the most players, myself included.
So this is my review, it will be subject to change as the game changes and more things come to light. All in all, dont let my review turn you away from the game, try it for yourself and see if you may like it.  It does have some pros, like its free, its not pay to win at all. No micro transactions for anything that gives anyone any sort of gear or power advantage. You can sort of build what you want to an extent also which is nice because not enough games let you do that.
They do occasionaly give away free premium, to speed up the grinding process, so I would advise playing on those days and using the free codes. Although even with premium I still consider the grind too long.

This isn't an FPS game.

A short review, for a short (15 minutes) game; essentially it's a 10-20 minute long history lesson (depending on how fast you read, and figure out the puzzles).  I liked the way the story was told, and the music (some of it from Nine Inch Nails, released under a Creative Commons license) complements the artsy visuals really well.  I was actually a little surprised, given the "documentary" nature, that it didn't have some kind of interactive bibliography at the end; that's not a complaint, just an observation.
As a puzzle platformer (which, from a mind-numbingly pedantic genre classification standpoint, this is), this game is a solid 1/10.  :)  Technically, there is platforming.  Technically, there are puzzles.  Neither of the above will present more than a minor speed bump to all but the most absolutely novice gamer.  You can also see "clues" for most of the "puzzles" in the Steam video trailer.
If you've ever wondered whether you might be interested in computer-based visual novels, this is a title to check out since it's free; not to mention, you'll learn a little history along the way!
Be aware that I'm stretching a bit on that recommendation; I really don't know anything else in the "visual novel documentary with a bit of gaming" sub-genre.  "The 39 Steps" is purely an interactive novel.

First off, I want to warn you the game may not run on your system if you are on Windows 10. The only way I could get this game to run is with a 3rd party community patch. A game IMHO should never be released in any such form! You have been warned. Go to the discussion board and get the community patch first.
I have trouble reviewing this game because it divides me so much.
I'll start with the positives by saying the game has a fantastic story and set of characters. All characters (annoying or not) are voiced well and likeable. The story is complex and so are the characters and there is a lot to love when the two coming together. This game does a great job of telling a story, as I think an RPG should.
The game has lots of great cut scenes, or mini cut scenes called skits. They do a great job of giving characters thoughts, ideas, and expressions in a fun anime like way. It's kind of a unique system that I've never seen and it just adds a lot I think.
They also have an Anime based on the game in the works, would totally watch.
As great as the story and character are, which really hold the game together, the game has issues.
Even with the community patch, the game does have some graphical issues during combat. Certain effects cause massive graphical slowdown on a GTX 970, which shouldn't happen. Then again the game wouldn't even run for me without a community patch.
The camera in the game does not work exactly as you would expect. It turns super slow. You will adapt mostly, but it's just something that is so weird it's worth mentioning because you will battle it all game.
One thing that was kind of good / bad is you lose a major character like 1/3 of the way through the game. It's not that it really changes anything it's just a really bizarre thing like they started making the game and decided they didn't really want this character to be in the game and then hastily wrote them out. Although the game's director downplays this, it seems almost evident.
The combat system is overly complex, but here is an “easy mode” if you wish to take some of the complexity out of the game. It gets easier the more you play it but sill takes a bit of time before you can really confidently fight “epic” type monsters and survive. The few strong enemies will clean your clock though, and it drives down the fun value.
There are a few times where you will not have clear goals and need to basically wander around until you discover where you are suppose to go. Some better hints would be nice rather than wasting literally hours of my time trying to figure out where to go. Wasting players time should not be considered good. It is a tactic used by bad games to extend their play time. It really kills the pacing of the game.
TLDR;
Overall the game is above average in terms of story, and the characters are great. It's a shame however that the game suffers from poor pacing and other problems that really just make it a mediocre game. The game tries to do too much and stretches out too long for the content included.
I'd say play it with tempered expectations going in, it's an interesting game but it's not going to probably make your “greatest RPGs ever” list.

Tales of Zestria jadi seri Tales pertama yang dirilis di PC dan kedua yang saya mainkan setelah Tales of the Abyss. Saya sendiri cukup menaruh ekspektasi besar pada seri ini.
Cerita (7/10)
Bercerita tentang Sorey, manusia yang dibesarkan oleh kaum seraphim. ToZ berpusat pada petualangan Sorey & para seraphim mengalahkan hellion yang disebabkan oleh malevolence dan sumber malevolence, Lord of Calamity.
Cerita ToZ sangat berpusat pada Sorey sebagai karakter utama, namun karakter Sorey sendiri terasa kurang di-explore. Hanya karakter Edna & Zaveid yang terasa begitu unik, selebihnya terlalu generic. Hubungan antar karakter pun minim konflik & emosi, pusat cerita ini hanya 1, bagaimana mengalahkan LoC.
Alur plot yang terasa datar, tidak ada yang dapat membuat kita merasa excited kecuali saat menjelang akhir cerita.
Namun di antara itu semua?
Satu yang menarik adalah skit dialog yang muncul di saat2 tertentu yang dapat menutup plot hole pada cerita utama. Banyak scene yang bisa di-unlock setelah mengalahkan optional boss tertentu yang mampu menjelaskan sisi lain karakter & cerita pendukung. Beberapa cukup lucu dan menghibur, mengingat cerita utama ToZ cukup 'dark'.
Grafis (6/10)
ToZ ini berasal dari port PS3 yang merupakan engine lama. Tidak ada yang luar biasa di sisi grafis.
Berita 30 fps lock cukup membuat banyak orang tidak mau menghabiskan uang untuk beli game ini, apalagi kaum yang merasa game di pc 30 fps = bad port. Untungnya tak lama kemudian muncul ToZ fix yang membuat game ini dapat berjalan smooth pada 60 fps. Saya sendiri hampir selalu memainkan ToZ pada 30 fps & merasa ini bukan masalah.
Satu2nya masalah ada pada kamera & point of view saat battle yang menyebalkan bahkan terkadang susah diatur.
Gameplay (8/10)
Banyak sekali yang bisa kita explore di sisi gameplay.
Dari segi battle, berbeda dengan seri2 sebelumnya, dengan adanya konsep manusia & seraphim, kita bisa melakukan armatize yang merupakan penggabungan (fusion) manusia & seraphim. Stat kedua karakter akan dijumlahkan (HP, BG, Atk dll). Party terdiri atas 2 manusia & 2 seraphim, namun jika Sorey sendirian, maka hanya 1 seraphim yang bisa bertarung bersamanya.
Adanya skill yang dipasangkan pada equipment (senjata, armor, aksesoris dll). Dengan menyusun skill tersebut menjadi G-Union, E-Union & Stack akan memberikan bonus skill yang dapat mengubah karakter dengan stat pas2an menjadi begitu overpowered, sehingga kita bisa menyusun strategi melawan boss tertentu dengan kombinasi skill yang tepat.

I have a hard time recommending this product. That's why I'm going to select "Not Recommend" as an option. I wish Steam had a "Maybe" option. The biggest problem I actually have is with the resolution this engine is locked at. It is locked at 800x600 I believe. I also believe the assets are locked at 32x32. It's a good introduction engine for those looking to get into game development, and it's a cool tool to mess around with if your bored and just want to make some place neat that you can just screw around in. I don't know what you like to do in your free time, man. I don't judge. Now, I have to say, if you're a seasoned game developer and using this software, you need to step up your game. If you plan on using this engine, and exclusively this engine, to develop games, I can't say that's the best decision. Often in the gaming community, people see an RPG Maker title and assume it's just another throw-away, mediocre RPG with a sub-par story and premade assets. Sometimes, they aren't wrong, but there are some good, and somewhat successful, games for this engine. Take "To the Moon" for example. The engine is certainly flexable, but you can really only flex so far with the assets that you are given to work with. Sure you can install plugins, and make your own things (which I recommend you do), but this engine can really only go so far. It really does have limits, and very significant ones. Sure this engine is flexible and it gets the job done for an amatuer developer, but you need to ask yourself "How professional can I look while using this engine?"
In all honesty, if you're planning to sell games from this engine, you, most likely, won't make your money back. So if the money doesn't matter, and you make games on this engine because you enjoy it, good for you. Don't worry about the money. The engine is definitely fun to use, and it's reasonably simple. I'll give it that. Honestly, if you ever want to be taken seriously as a developer, step up your game. If you are looking for an alternative, go to Unreal Engine or Source Engine. Those are both reliable and solid engines. I'd easily recommend those two over this one any day. Buy this with caution.

RPG Maker VX Ace promises something that just about every gamer has dreamed about at least once -- the ability to make your own game, where you are the creative dictator. You write the story, you design the gameplay, you pick the music, you do everything. No corporate suits telling you what you can and can't put in, no deadlines to meet, and no profit margin to worry about. Sounds awesome, doesn't it? For sure. But is it really?
Yes! Absolutely. If you love RPG's you will love trying to make one. The fun I've had with this software has paid for its somewhat high price tag many times over. I can't stress that enough. But can you really make your dream RPG with it?
No! Well, probably not. There are just too many limitations to the system.
First and foremost -- lack of resources. Too often there simply isn't any content available that matches your vision. Let's say your RPG is set in the modern day, and you want it to start with an exciting car chase. Alright, you're already feeling it. You rub your hands together, set up a new blank map, and -- wait. Where is the graphic for the car? Hmmm. *Click, click, click, click* Huh, there isn't one. Weird. Ok, we'll figure that out later. Let's at least get the street set up and -- oh. There's no road tileset.
The base resources the game comes with are EXTREMELY limited. Forget about a modern day setting, it's impossible. Your game is going to be a fantasy game with forests, dungeons, castles, and medieval towns. Period. Still feel like the creative dictator?
"Ok," you might be thinking. "I can work with that. I'll just make a fantasy RPG. With my writing skills and artistic vision I can still make it good." Sorry, but It doesn't matter. Time and time again, whatever you want to create isn't going to be one of the options you can choose. Want to make a cool looking knight? Better hope you like one of the two you get. Want to make a jester for the castle? There isn't one. Nine tenths of your ideas have to be scrapped before they even get anywhere.
In the software's defense, this would be a problem regardless of how many resources they packed with it. All of the resources in the world wouldn't even begin to cover all of the possibilities you can imagine for your game. But nevertheless, the amount included is much lighter than it could have been, and severely limits what you can do. There are DLC packs available to add content, but they are VERY overpriced and limited in their scope. "Oh, awesome!" you say when you discover the Modern Day Tileset DLC. But then you see that it's $15 and just gives you some roads, a couple of buildings, and some cars. You still don't have nearly enough to set your entire game in the present.
As with resources, there are also some game functions that just aren't available. The default battle system is pretty basic and, frankly, bad. Want to change it? Hope you know how to program. And if you do, why do you need RPG Maker? This isn't limited to just the battle system. You'll find that there is a whole list of things you can't do with the event system. Almost anything can be done through scripting in the game's RUBY language, but if you're using RPG Maker it's probably because you don't know how to do things like that in the first place.
So. Do I recommend RPG Maker VX Ace? Yes, wholeheartedly. Just keep your vision realistic. What you are going to do with this software is assemble parts and pieces of your dream game, tiny pathetic fragments of great ideas. You will never finish it and it will never be released, and it will probably kind of suck. And you will have a ton of fun making it.

This was not a decision I made lightly. It's a bit of a shame that Steam reviews only have a thumbs up or thumbs down, not any sort of in-between score.
I expect that fans of the game will downvote the hell out of this review for not recommending it.
Truth is I'm a huge fan of this game. Despite a couple technical hiccups (which may not be actual bugs, given the nature of the game), the game is ridiculously fun and stylish as hell. Though SUPERHOT has really only one gameplay gimmick, it never grew stale. Killing a room full of red guys in impossible situations never got boring, and the game's narrative actually kept me very engaged.
Since time only moves when you do, the game feels very far away from any other first person shooter made before it. It's impossible to run-and-gun, you need to carefully plan your steps to dodge deadly projectiles, while also aiming carefully and lining up those perfect shots; with so little ammo, you can't afford to be careless. It's the freshest breath of air an FPS fan has been able to inhale for the last long while.
So why am I not recommending this incredible game?
The price.
I've defended games like Jazzpunk and McPixel, even Undertale, when faced with the criticism of a game being too short. I truly believe it's about the experience. But SUPERHOT has pushed my limit.
$35 Canadian dollars for a game you can potentially beat in a few hours?
It's not quite worth it.

To start, I'd like to say that while I'm no Tales expert, I've played Tales of Vesperia, the Abyss, Xillia, Xillia 2 and now Zestiria, so hopefully that'll give an idea of where I'm coming from with this review.
As a whole, Tales of Zestiria is quite possibly the most enjoyable Tales game I've played to date.
There's a bunch of reasons for this, but I'll start with what's (probably) the most important: the gameplay.
As the thing you're gonna be doing for the next 40+ hours as you run through this game, the combat needs to be solid if a Tales game is gonna work and, thankfully, I feel like Zestiria pulls it off.
As always, the game sticks to the traditional hacky, slashy Tales format but adds its own unique twists, in this case the SC system. Every attack you do is gonna cost you some SC and if you don't have enough, then you've just gotta wait or block/dodge in order for it to charge back up.
At first, I found this to be a really tedious and dumb system. There were plenty of occassions where I was just stuck standing there staring at an enemy rather than introducing Mr. Sword to his face in a timely manner but, eventually, it grew on me. It adds an extra layer (as thin as it may be) to the combat, forcing you to ration out your SC. During some of the more difficult late game fights (especially the super boss at the end), blowing all your SC too early can really cost you. So, the SC system is a mixed bag. I personally enjoyed it, but I can see some of the more gung-ho players getting really sick of standing around.
Next up in the gameplay department, the combo system. While similar to usually Tales formula of pressing up, down, left or right along with your attack to change what you do, Zestiria tried taking it one step further. Now, each directional attack is linked to an Arte (provided you've unlocked it) that can immediately be chained into any other Arte or regular attack that you happen to have on, capping out at 4(5?) attacks.
At first, it's nothing new. You don't have access to many Artes so you're just hacking and slashing as normal but it's the late game where this system really shines. Once you've got all your Artes unlocked for your regular combos and your special moves, the amount of variation you can pull off in one string is staggering. Granted, given the fact that enemies being weak to certain elements is far more important than before means you're probably just gonna line up a certain element combo (i.e: smack the thing that's weak to wind with a wind combo), it's still impressive to see just how many different ways you can pour 40+ hours of your life into beating monsters.
However, Zestiria does fall short in the variation department when looking at another one of its mechanics: your party. Tales games (at least the ones I've played) have always boasted a unique set of party members that really allowed you to fight the way that you wanted to. In Zestiria, however, do to certain aspects of the story, you either use two party members where one of them is fixed or four members where two of them are fixed. This means you're gonna be seeing an awful lot of the main guy, Sorey and the main gal. That was a pretty big letdown for me since I found the fighting styles of some of the other characters to be a lot more interesting than Captain "I have a sword and a bit of magic" Sorey.
On the other hand, there's weapon variartion up to a giant's eyebrows, which is usually nice. Unfortunately, it's implemented worse than a rejected kidney. The way that weapon skills work in this game is something that, even after my 50 hours of gameplay, I still don't really get. Something about a grid and lining up the skills on it to get more bonuses? Cool idea, patchy at best implementation. If there are multiple tutorials around something and I still don't really get it, then something was probably done wrong.
Speaking of done wrong, did you know that Tales of Zestiria has a pseudo-open world that's fully rendered now? Did you also know that it's completely and utterly pointless? They make this big, pretty world but it lacks any real substance. You run from area to area through giant open planes that just have nothing in them. Sure, there are a few chests littered around each map and there's some things to inspect for brownie points, but the whole thing just feels empty and lifeless. It really contrasts with the towns which do a great job of replicating the hustle and bustle of city life when it's appropriate. I feel like the game really should've been more focused in this regard, as they make it linear by stopping you from going to certain areas anyway. The big open map just isn't needed.
Speaking of a poorly done transition, how are the characters, an oh so important part of Tales games? I'm fairly sure I'm in the minority here, but I actually liked them a lot. Sorey (earring guy in the trailer) follows a fairly standard character archetype; country bumpkin has a coming of age story as he realises the world isn't as nice as he thought, but they put a few twists and turns in there that really made me invested in him. I won't say what 'cause spoilerooneys, but I was very satisfied with his character at the end of the game. I won't go into much detail on the other characters as you should experience them for yourself, but it's a fairly well rounded cast with mostly good characterisation and voice acting that totally isn't overshadowed at all by the best girl that is Enda.
Speaking of being overshadowed (eyy, I got it that time), the music in this game is really just meh. I don't have it in me to call it bad because there were a couple of occassions where the music really stood out, but it just didn't have much of an impact. This was made painfully clear when I slapped on the Zaphias costume for Sorey. If you don't know, that costume changes Sorey's look and the in-game music to things from Tales of Vesperia. As soon as that guitar riff kicked in during a battle, I realised that the music here just wasn't on par with the standard I usually expect from Tales games.
As this is a Steam review, let's talk about the PC port. The planets must've aligned because it's a first time PC port from a Japanese company and it's actually pretty good. My PC's nothing amazing but I had no trouble running this on max settings. It is locked at 30FPS which I'm sure will trigger some master race members, but there's a mod out there already that fixes that problem. is a gud port.

I'm just going to get out of the way that I love this game. Now some details: OlliOlli2 is a minimalist skateboarding game which is kind of like a mix between Canabalt and Tony Hawk. In it, you have to complete a track from left to right avoiding a number of obstacles while mixing in some sick tricks. The tricks are built into a simple mechanic using the joystick and requires good timing to stick a landing and keep momentum. Timing is also key in maintaining grinds which are dotted throughout levels. Finally, you can also put in manuals which will maintain your tricks into a (potentially) level long combo. And when this happens you feel like a god, rocking through levels feeling and looking cool (completing optional side quests to get better stars). And for the 100 attempts before it clicks for the level...you still feel awesome because the game has great stylized graphics, music that perfectly suits the "Just One More Level" gameplay style and the total lack of a gap between runs had me playing more and more and more. I never got round to finishing the final area but that came down to a period of time away from my computer but that's something I'm going to try and rectify soon.
All in all a very satisfying and challenging game!

I can say without a doubt that 'A Hat in Time' is an excellent game. While calling back to games of the Nintendo 64 and GameCube eras, 'A Hat in Time' isn't afraid to mix things up and get out of the conventional 3D platformer's comfort zone.
Though the story as a narrative isn't much to write home about, it is more than made up for by the game's quirky, lovable, and especially humorously-written cast of characters.
The presentation is fantastic, with sickeningly adorable character design, expressive and alluring worlds, both silly and awesome visual flairs, and a top-notch soundtrack to boot. The voice actors/actresses chosen varied on quality of their performances, but the cast as a whole fits the game near-perfectly.
Perhaps the greatest quality of 'A Hat in Time' is its gameplay. The game's lead, Hat Kid, controls similarly of Mario back in Sunshine, though she has many a trick up her sleeve. Jumps, dives, and short wall dashes, in conjunction with an assortment of various, wacky hats, make Hat Kid one of the most versatile platforming characters that I've ever seen, yet much of the game's controls feel very natural and easy to pick up. Each of the worlds Hat Kid explores are filled with goodies to collect and obstacles to face. In terms of difficulty, the game makes a steady incline in progression, with perhaps a few exceptions.
All this said, there are a few noticeable issues, one being that completion may be impossible, at least in regards as to the game's "Rift Tokens", used to unlock cosmetic bonuses and soundtrack remixes, as after searching high and low through every world (with the game's dedicated item hunting skill equipped), I found myself short of two final goodies. Secondly, the game has its share of noticeable bugs here and there, mostly a handful of segments simply lacking the spit and polish of others. Of course, it's only been a matter of days since the game has released, so these issues are subject to a possible patch.
At its core, 'A Hat in Time', is practically a masterpiece, despite some issues/nitpicks every once in a while. I binged this game over three days, playing from 11 in the evening to 3 in the morning, and I don't regret it. I can easily see myself replaying this gem over and over again, much like 'Banjo-Kazooie'. 'A Hat in Time' not only honors the 3D-platformers of the past, but breathes new life into the genre, making the genre's revival seem much more hopeful than previously. Do yourself a favor and play 'A Hat in Time'.
tl;dr: This game is an excellent successor to 'Super Mario Sunshine', 'Banjo-Kazooie', and the like. If you're a fan of the genre or of great games made with passion, play this now.

Indie used to mean something, man.  It used to be about special little games crafted with love and care by a cottage industry of largely unknown but certainly not untalented developers.  Nowadays, when someone uses the term "indie" to describe a game, what they're really saying is that it isn't worth your time.  And Freebie is an example of the new indie at its absolute direst.  Barely any graphics.  Barely any sound.  Barely any gameplay.  Barely any effort.  Avoid.

I really, really like this game. It scratches an itch for me that hasn't been scratched since the early Tony Hawk games. Once you get used to the controls (which actually remind me more of the old Trasher game than Tony Hawk), you can really get into a flow with this game. Having said that, I think there are some problems with input recognition. There seems to be a minimum amount of time you have to spend grinding on a rail before you trick out with anything other than an ollie, regardless of how fast you're handling the controls. Maybe there's a reason for that, but it really just makes the game feel like it's not responding well. I've also noticed that if you want to trick out of a landing very quickly, you have to land in a manual as opposed to landing normally (landing normally gets you stuck in a crouched position for an extra second or so where you can't do anything). I think that the input handling could be done in a way that feels more responsive. Restarting 10 times in a row at the start of a level to land a trick you've done hundreds of times before gets pretty old. But anyway, bottom line: I really enjoy this game and definitely got my money's worth.
