This game is very simple, it's a square which has a green angle and a red angle. The objective is to throw a fire ball (looks like a fire ball) into a spining bar in the middle of the screen to make the ball touch the green angle.. Sounds simple, eh?
Well, it's not.. since you have 3 tries before the game over, and after each 10 points (10,20,30,40...) the speed of the spining bar increases. Once you reach 30 points the bar moves so quickly that is really hard to predict where the ball touches the bar.
The controls are very simple you can use your mouse or press the up and left key to throw a ball from the top left corner or the right and down key to shoot the ball from the bottom right corner. Clicking the boxes with the mouse was much easier for me.
In the main menu you can choose 3 different 8-bit music, which are nice, but in the long term it makes you more frustrated with the game. There is also the option 'No Music', though you still have the sounds of the game.
My veredict: 7/10. Easy 100% (completed it in 1 hour or so), has trading cards, and overall is a nice little game.

Hello,
At the beginning I would like to say that the game itself isn't bad, but there's no "Neutral" button to press and my personal game preference pointer is slightly towards "Wouldn't recommend", that's why my review is negative.
The game itself isn't that bad, just so you know.
As a new player to the "Action-Tower Defense" games you'll probably like it. The opposite goes for players that spend XXX hours playing the first Dungeon Defenders.
Anyway let's write about few things that I would like you guys to know...
1. This time they've made a game as F2P(free to play) with cosmetic microtransactions(mostly) as Cash Shop. Don't be fooled by this. Character slots are limited to 4 - you need to pay to get more slots. And you will need more, when new characters will be introduced to the game. The second problem is you Inventory, starting bags are limited, they fill with items really quick - more bags of course are available with cash. It wouldn't really be that big problem if the items like chests or pet stuff would stack, but sadly it doesn't...
2. Unlike DD1 you characters here have more skills to use, which is kinda nice - 3 skills + heal, but you have less towers to build, only 4.
3. Game looks a bit better than DD1, a bit more cartoony I would say.
4. If the game host got crappy connection or his internet will start doing some nasty stuff(high ping, dropping packets, etc) you and other players will be laggy as hell, be ready for that.
5. Pet hatching time, 48h to hatch an egg - hatching can fail(no pet, sorry)
6. Number of trash items dropped isn't bad, like it was in DD1, it was earlier in alpha but they've reduced trash drops.
7. No character customization - just outfits unlocked via chests.
I think that would be all I can think about at the moment.
To sum it up, DD1 sucked me in for many, many hours of fun, and I really enjoyed it and love the game, while DD2 just doesn't feel this way, it lacks something that keeps you interested in the game.
In a bit funny way I will type this:
You sit at the table and you see two things on this table - 1. Sandwitch with cheese(represents DD2) and 2. Pizza(represents DD1). Which one would you pick? - This is how I see this two games.
DD1 - 9/10 (-1 for the number of trash drops)
DD2 - 4.5/10

This was not a decision I made lightly. It's a bit of a shame that Steam reviews only have a thumbs up or thumbs down, not any sort of in-between score.
I expect that fans of the game will downvote the hell out of this review for not recommending it.
Truth is I'm a huge fan of this game. Despite a couple technical hiccups (which may not be actual bugs, given the nature of the game), the game is ridiculously fun and stylish as hell. Though SUPERHOT has really only one gameplay gimmick, it never grew stale. Killing a room full of red guys in impossible situations never got boring, and the game's narrative actually kept me very engaged.
Since time only moves when you do, the game feels very far away from any other first person shooter made before it. It's impossible to run-and-gun, you need to carefully plan your steps to dodge deadly projectiles, while also aiming carefully and lining up those perfect shots; with so little ammo, you can't afford to be careless. It's the freshest breath of air an FPS fan has been able to inhale for the last long while.
So why am I not recommending this incredible game?
The price.
I've defended games like Jazzpunk and McPixel, even Undertale, when faced with the criticism of a game being too short. I truly believe it's about the experience. But SUPERHOT has pushed my limit.
$35 Canadian dollars for a game you can potentially beat in a few hours?
It's not quite worth it.
SUPERHOT is amazing. But $35 is a very steep price for a quick game. I suppose there is replay value in the Endless Mode, trying to do sections more efficiently, and trying to uncover the game's secrets. But really, as excellent and fun as it may be, there is no variation in gameplay.
Tons of AAA titles boast campaigns that barely register 6 hours and they cost twice as much, I know this. But, having paid a much smaller price for games I felt carried more weight, I still don't think SUPERHOT has a justifiable price.
If it came down in a sale or something I'd push this game onto every person within reach and earshot of me.
SUPERHOT is an incredibly creative and well-crafted game.
It just costs too much right now.

All dead hype aside; this is a very decent horror game. Scott Cawthon, the creator of the FNAF series (which you probably already know by now if you've been keeping up with the fandom since this got released) has made a very simple concept something that kept me up at night for weeks.
((This is paying no attention to the fandom whatsoever and my opinion of this game is based off the game itself - I've been out of the fandom for quite a while now as it's become too toxic and full of negativity; although I still really enjoy the games ^-^))
You play in the role of Mike Schmidt, a security guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. The objective of the game is to make it through five nights in an office checking the cameras around the building (using your trusty touch-screen tablet slamming you in the face whenever you use it) and protecting yourself from killer animatronics by checking the lights of the doors to your sides and closing them when an animatronic is peeking in.
The simplicity of the game sounds so easy yet when you actually load it up it can bring out your worst fears - I've played it enough to get used to the noises and jumpscares but when I first played it I couldn't stand checking the lights in the doorway because of the chance there would be someone looking back at you.
Scott has a great skill with this game in taking what would be seen as harmless and turning it into your worst nightmare, and I really congratulate his skills on coming up with something so unique in both the horror genre and the entire gaming community. A very well done to you, Scott Cawthon :3
I recommend this game and series to those who enjoy horror, and not to those who just want it because they're in love with a particular robot or want to "yiff" Foxy (he wants to be left alone - didn't you read his "SORRY, OUT OF ORDER" sign?? XD)
Thanks for reading this review and I hope it's helpful to you! ouo/

This is an excellent engine to make your own games in.  It's simple enough for the beginner and versatile enough for the professional.  While the main engine is geared toward making a standard JRPG, its script system literally gives you tools you need to completely transform the engine so you can make any type of game you want.  I've seen isometric adventure games, side-scrolling platformers, and even first and third person shooters made on VX Ace.  I'm currently building a tactics RPG that uses both 2D and 3D isometric elements.
Pros:
An essentially limitless scripting system
Easy to use and understand interface
A complete database with everything you need to make a full game without alteration (although even beginners will probably want to do some alteration)
A clearly organized and easy to use event command window (a definite improvement from previous makers).
Cons:
Does not support pointer variables (No, you're variables cannot point.  With the release of XP, which also had full script support, pointer variables were deemed unnecessary)
Loses a good amount of the functionality that RPG Maker 2003 had
The run time package may not be to your taste (I know it isn't to mine, though I do like some of the songs...and I some of the graphics assets are okay.)
In spite any complaints, VX Ace worth every dime you'll pay for it.

If you want to build a simple RPG, RPG Maker VX Ace is a great tool for you. Some professionals have made incredible games with it, but almost all of their games would have been better if they had used some other software to build their games. RPG Maker VX Ace (and all the others) greatly limit what you can do. And that's the point. The software provides a perfect guide for making a 2D RPG rather quickly. Assets are provided so you can use their artwork, sound effects, music, animations, backgrounds, title screens and so forth.
It's fairly simple to get into the programming aspects of RPG Maker, but you don't have to. You can just boot it up and go.
I've used the software for funsies to build a little game world. I've used it to teach my children about game design and programming. And I also use it to build Treasure Hunts for the
community where I build a complex world with lots of hidden parts to it and then hide codes to games in it.
You can redistribute your game and it does not need Steam to run.
VX Ace is more difficult to use than 2000, 2003 and XP. So if you're just getting started, I would recommend picking up RPG Maker XP. It's not too expensive (especially on sale or in a fairly regular bundles).

In order to get further into the brief history lesson, you have to interact with the environment in such a way that leads the human to fall out of the room you're in and into the next room. The music in the game, paired with the art and photos, gives it a great atmosphere. I am definitely having my history buff friend play this, just because it was an interesting game. I got to have fun while learning something new. Now if only all history classes were taught like this, I think more kids might pay attention.

Music: 10/10

This was my first full playthrough of a "Tales" game. I've played some Tales of Symphonia but never the whole game. I know a lot of fans of the "Tales" find Zestiria to be the low point of the series, but I found it quite enjoyable.
The story is about a world that has been plunged into chaos and darkness due to a lack of Shepherd. Not to be confused with Commander Shepherd from Mass Effect, although that would have made the game more interesting. Shepherds are people who can interact with beings known as Seraphs and purify evil beings known as Hellions. Basically they're the peacekeeper between humans and mythical things. You take control of Sorey, the new Shepherd, as he travel the land gaining Seraphs to help him to end the era of chaos. The story is fairly entertaining, although it can be a little slow to start off, but it start to pick up around the middle point.
The game play involve moving across a 3D open world. As you move across the map you will see enemies roaming about  and if you run into one you get put into battle scene. Basically in a battle, a small boundary is placed around the player and 4 of his party members until the enemies are defeated. The combat is a hack and slash, but with the gimmick of being able to merge with party members to use stronger attacks. Their are elements in this game, so as you can guess there is a rock-paper-scissor system in place for what type of attacks enemies are weak against. Combat feel good although just watch what level you and your party are. If you're too low then you'll find some enemies beating the tar out of you, but if you're too high then you'll find you're beating the tar out of the final boss.
The music felt right although don't try to ask me to remember any particular tracks, it just kinda blended into the background for me. The character english voices wasn't too bad (I've heard some horrible dubs before). The game really a good game, and I've no problem recommending this game anybody who is looking for a JRPG to play.

Edit: so I went back and decided to play a large map. At this scale the game started to show some shortcomings in the management of people and resources. Having arrived at 500 citizens I started to have problems when I set up a second town hub. In a sense I set up a second town away from the starting one with its own market, production buildings, etc. Then I noticed the game does not assign people and resources to a closest logic. So I had citizens from one hub working in farms on the other side and plenty of resources on one side and people starving on the other.
You also do not have the option to decide for each resource if it should be stocked or not in a particular warehouse or to completely disable consumption of that resource if you want. These are little features that help manage the flow of resources and exist in other such games.
All in all it is a fun little game but it is not designed for big city building for lack of optimization. The point and challenge it seems is to see if you can survive the first years and challenge comes from starting in hard maps.

I've seen that the reviews for this game are very mixed, and I just want to really explain why people might and might not like Tales of Zestiria.
First thing, right off the bat, my view of this might be skewed a little bit because my computer is... less than top of the line. Forgive me if I miss something hugely different when playing on a decent system.
The major issue that I had with this game, and what I feel most people had problems with but were unable to articulate, was that it failed to be engaging. I would rather sit and watch all of the skits than actually play the game. The visuals are beautiful, the characters are charming, the story is interesting; however, Zestiria failed to engage me. To put it simply,
than play it myself. And even then I would expect them to do a lot of skipping around to get to the important parts that people actually want to see.
I'm going to compare this to what I believe is one of the greatest JRPG's in recent years, Xenoblade Chronicles. Xenoblade is very similar to Zestiria is a lot of ways, but Xenoblade just does it better. The world is immersive and much more interesting than Zestiria, the visuals are fantastic for a game on the Wii and even better on the 3DS, and the characters are so fun that the people in your party are more often decided by how fun they are to have around than their combat potential. And Xenoblade engages the player, much better than Zestiria ever does.
In Zestiria, the combat felt really lackluster to me. Not to say that it wasn't flashy, but
If I felt particularly lazy, I could just set my characters to auto combat and let them take over. And even if I wasn't lazy I didn't have the ability to participate in the story. Sure, you play as Sorey learning about your Shepherd powers and fighting Malevolence but I felt more like an observer than a player.
Back to Xenoblade, the combat requires the players full attention. Rather than just spamming the attack button (which is an entirely viable strategy in Zestiria), one must pay close attention to which character has the enemy's aggro and what arts your partners are using and what status the enemy has. And the story requires more than just walking places and watching cutscenes. Plus,
When the story progresses no matter what decision you make, and there aren't any side missions to take your mind off of the endless cutscenes, the game just becomes a slog of walking to the next set of cutscenes and scripted battles.
Now, Zestiria is not a bad game. It's a good anime. Seriously, if Tales of Zestiria were an anime I would watch the entire thing like three times. But when the game says walk here, which takes twice as long as it should on my slow computer, just to watch another cutscene it really bothers a player who expected to do something during this game.
To conclude, Zestiria has a lot of potential as a game. It has wonderful characters, a really good looking world, and a story that I wish I had time to experience. But this game fails to recognize the players role in advancing the story, aside from walking to the next objective on the map. So I wouldn't recommend it to anybody who wants to play something. But if some studio decided to make Tales of Zestiria as an anime, I'm very interested.

At some point I was wondering if I was playing this game or very story driven Sims. I was at least relieved that the sex scene didn't have quick time events.
The first half of the game is the best part: the setting for the mystery is very well put and there are actually some really good point and click elements going on. I was loving Lucas' psychic abilities to gather intel to make better conversation choices or actions, and even the work of the investigators was a pleasure to follow when they tried to reason the weird crime circumstances. But then the storytelling decides to focus on completely unrelated happenings that really drag the flow, like playing guitar, basketball, or boxing sparring. All these actions are just repetitive quicktime events, there's no reason to spend several minutes of minigames on those parts, a simple cutscene would have done the trick.
There are also issues with controls and the camera, but those are relatively minor because of the genre. The main issue is the inconsistent storytelling, I really, really wanted more from the story itself, and got very frustrated when I was forced to do some unrelated actions, and the ending gets rushed because of that. And please, if you decide to create a branching storyline, make it split in some other ways rather than succeeding/failing in lenghty QTE events. Any other system would do, depending on your karma, character relationships, discussion choises or anything.
This game is one of the pioneers of visual storytelling, and I respect it for that, but by today's standards it has outdated really bad.  I feel like the developers had the full focus on the story and directing, but didn't have a clue how to make it work as a game, and they tried to include all kinds of elements that were either slapped on the story (pointless QTE during a normal cutscene) or ended up being almost completely unrelated to anything. The final impressions are really mixed for me, the story hooked me in so much that I couldn't stop playing 'til the end, but I honestly can't say it was a pleasure. I recommend Heavy Rain instead.

Ok so I'm going to write a new review based on early access now that the game has gone offline in preparation for launch. I would give the early access game 6.5/7.0 out of 10.
I have played over 5 hours with friends and got a good level of enjoyment. The player base was a bit small but with the relaunch and new game modes it should grow. The game defiantly needed more game modes as 6 v 6 team death match is all that was playable. The game did need a bit of balancing and some new maps but early access has been a pleasing experience. The only thing overpowered in need of tweaking was the support ships being able to shield and give buffs will little cooldown other than that the rest of the game worked nicely.
Essentially Galactic Junk League is a PvP ship battle game. You aim your weapons with your mouse and shoot pieces off the enemies ship until you destroy their core. You can take out the engines or weapons and leave enemies dead and just floating around. You have abilities like speed boost, shields, slows and power ups assigned to keyboard keys. Flight wise you accelerate, slow down and can pitch up and down. The game is basically build a ship go into a match and blow up other players ships to earn currency and experience. The devs are adding base assault/defence and capture the flag upon release.
The way you build a ship is according to your class as you have abilities and a certain amount of cpu and ap to put things like armour, engines and other types of blocks onto the ship. As you level each class you can unlock and research more stuff and your ship gets stronger. However level does not mean you win, there is a certain amount of skill involved and learning how and where to place armour and weapons is important. At the start of a match you can view other peoples ships to try and determine where they are weakest... for example someone may have no armour blocks on the bottom of their ship so if you have a fast ship for a example you could fly under them.
I played many matches where people had ships just made of weapons and they couldn't do a thing..... its about finding a balance and learning your class.
A lot of people moaned that in early access that certain classes were overpowered or that the person with the highest level ship wins, this is NOT true. Having played with two other friends in a group of 3 we had a support ship, a tanky ship (me) and a long range sniper ship. We found this combo to be very effective and won 70% of games because other players would keep going for my tank or were unable to get close to my friends sniper ship as they were using a slow class.
The way you build your ship and where you place your core, abilities blocks and engine blocks make a huge difference.
All in all this is a nice free 2 play game... there is a minor element of pay to win in the fact you can pay to level a bit quicker but I never found anyone with a paid account to dominate early access and most of the paid content is cosmetic anyway and paid players would get matched with other paid ones.

Yeah, it's scary....at first.
You say "Oh god stay away!" the first few times, then after a while you start saying "Dammit Chica go away....! Stop HOGGIN MY POWER!".
I personally loved the idea of this game, preserving power by keeping yourself open for attack. And jumpscares are one of my weaknesses in video games, but it started to effect me less and less as I played.
Your job is to guard the resturant at 12 at night till 6am in the morning, while fending off 4 animatronic animals that want to kill you by stuffing you into a suit. They come to your door, say hi, you say ♥♥♥♥ off, and close the door. You see them on the security cameras messing with you and taunting you. The four are Bonnie, Chica, Freddy, and Foxy. Bonnie and Chica roam the halls taunting you and making faces at you through the security cameras while Freddy silently makes his way toward you after a few nights. Foxy waits at "Pirate Cove" and if you don't watch him from time to time he will run straight to your security room and kill you.
Your only defence is your doors and lights, which apperently run on AA batteries, so you can't keep the doors shut at all times, you have to keep the doors open and keep yourself exposed to survive the nights.
When I played, I would check Foxy and Freddy, then turn off the camera, checking my lights, then repeat. I only died once due to my power running out and Freddy singing his song for 2 seconds.
This is where frustration more than fear kicks in.
I never got suddenly killed by Foxy or the other two characters because I kept checking my lights every good 7 seconds, then checking my cameras to keep the other 2 at bay. That makes you run out of power fast, but what other strategy do you have? What if you don't check Freddy or Foxy at all? What if you don't check your lights? You die. Just by not checking anything, not even the cameras or lights, after 15 seconds, I'm down 10% power.
The game failed to scare me after watching youtube video's of people getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that they lost because they actually played the game right and because of how random things are, they died.
After the 2nd day, I wasn't scared at all, I was more happy that I made it to the next night without getting killed from some accidental miss click of the lights or I checked the cameras for too long.
I only recommend this game to people who have a short time spand to waste, I beat the game in an hour and only died once.

The Beginner’s Guide… to what you may ask? That’s all up to interpretation, as are many aspects of this game. You are narrated by Davey, the maker of The Stanley Parable. This game isn’t to play like Parable though. This is a slice of Davey’s life where he talks about his friend Coda. This game is almost a memoir in that respect.
I’ll just get gameplay stuff out of the way real quick: It plays like a source game without guns and you simply walk around just like in Stanley Parable. I feel that this is only a game because Davey knows this best as a medium to get this story out.
And he is right for that, because the main “plot” of the game is to talk about Coda and his games. But it’s what the games mean and how the player and Davey interpret them. He gives the player a model of what he is talking about, which is a really rare thing in storytelling. From after this paragraph there may be game spoilers that reveal what actually happens in real life. Anyone reading this review to decide whether to get this game can stop here. If you want a story that can make you feel something more than any work of fiction can, absolutely get this “game.” It’s really thought provoking and special not only to those who play it, but to Davey himself.
If you want my explanation for the events of the game, continue reading. Otherwise the review and summary of the game is over.

Superhot is a really innovative new shooter that does a lot to immerse you in the world it creates around itself. It is extremely fun to play around with, and can certainly be a game you can play with friends to see who can do the coolest things, but $25 is a bit too much for what is being bought.
For one, Superhot's main story is only about 2 hours long. Even with a dozen retries on some levels, I still completed it in under 2 hours. That is quite ridiculous, as the replayable content doesn't go very far after that either. The only modes available following the main story are Endless Mode and some Challenge modes. You can probably squeeze a few extra hours out of those if you're in love with the game, but other than that... you won't be playing this for long, and as such, you definitely won't want to cough up $25 for a 3-4 hour experience in a video game.
Is Superhot worth playing? Yes. Like I said, it is exhilarating to play. It's an experience I've never had before, and would love to have again in a different aesthetic. Maybe a more realistic one. If you can buy Superhot on sale, go for it. But at it's current asking price, I just can't recommend the title.

Edit: so I went back and decided to play a large map. At this scale the game started to show some shortcomings in the management of people and resources. Having arrived at 500 citizens I started to have problems when I set up a second town hub. In a sense I set up a second town away from the starting one with its own market, production buildings, etc. Then I noticed the game does not assign people and resources to a closest logic. So I had citizens from one hub working in farms on the other side and plenty of resources on one side and people starving on the other.
You also do not have the option to decide for each resource if it should be stocked or not in a particular warehouse or to completely disable consumption of that resource if you want. These are little features that help manage the flow of resources and exist in other such games.
All in all it is a fun little game but it is not designed for big city building for lack of optimization. The point and challenge it seems is to see if you can survive the first years and challenge comes from starting in hard maps.

After finishing the game I've decided to put in additional thoughts and provide the perspective of someone who hasn't played any other recent Tales games. I didn't expect a lot about the game and by all means I enjoyed it, some points in this review people might disagree since some of them expects a lot and so on. Nevertheless, here are my thoughts:
+Deep battle system, it does not encourage you to just mash buttons on your way to victory, which is true if you're playing in higher difficulties.
+Skits are very entertaining and always a thing I look forward to.
+Lots of character development among the main characters of the game and everyone is likeable in terms of personality. Some secondary characters also provided a huge part in the story.
+Difficulty system rewards you with better drops and allows you to learn the battle system much faster.
+There's still post game content once you've finished the game and lots of stuff gets unlocked once you start NG+
+The music of the game was spectacular, mostly the music inside the trials.
~ I'd stay neutral story-wise as it is a subjective matter on how you take the game, it feels lacking at some point on some characters but other than that it all made sense to me.
- Equipment system is too complex and grindy. If you want to maximize the potential of the system, you need to grind a lot and I find it hard to maximize everything in your first playthrough it would be better if you try to maximize it on subsequent playthroughs.
- Unless you're really good, some, if not most, battles forces you to use armatization since some monsters/bosses can kill your characters pretty easy. This happens most of the time on higher difficulties (Intense, Chaos) since the level of the enemies grow a lot and damage potential is increased.
- Armatization can be abused to the point a battle can be very cheap. i.e. spamming a seraphic arte over and over until the enemies die.
- Camera during battles becomes awkward when fighting in small corners as the camera gets zoomed in a lot to the point you can't see anything. A slight fix would be to use the "Free Walk" button to be able to see your character.
- The AI of your allies doesn't really help you much in battle, yes, they die a lot for no reason. I find this very frustrating on some boss fights, even on some random encounters, since they tend to target your allies a lot or cast huge spells which your allies just tank. They also tend to split from armatization then die immediately afterwards even if you try to armatize them. In order to alleviate this, you have to micromanage everyone during fights to minimize the deaths and hope that they don't mess up everytime you switch into another character.
Great overall game, which you can play at your own pace (which I did), I finished my first playthrough by finishing all the sidequests and doing what I can to improve my equipment.

Now, some people have given this game, a bad review. I respect that, it's your own opinion, you're entitled to it. But I disagree. DD2 is a very good tower defense game with friends. I can't stress that enough, WITH FRIENDS. In the single player campaign, (Spoiler Alert) The later enemies are very hard to do alone. And I mean really hard. When you get to the ogres, your defenses will be crushed, along with you. So, you try online. Warning: You made a bad choice. People online are good at the game, I don't dispute it, but not as a team. Everyone has their own playstyle with the game which makes the experience so good with friends. With friends, you have ways to communicate like Skype. With only online, you don't have that verbal connection. Online, you have a chat bar, but it's small and in the human brain, you don't have any reason to listen to them. And if you do, you are most likely doing it wrong because as stated before, everyone is unique. When your Skyping with friends you have lighting fast connection to talk, and you also have an emotional one, compelling you to listen to them, when online, your just with strangers. Now that that's out of the way, lets move on to the gameplay. The gameplay is great for when you have some spare time. The graphics are amazing, sometimes I even found myself looking around during the build phase because the scenery was just so stunning. Also, the community has great people in it, and there's always help around the corner if you need it from other players. The developers even post very frequently, so you can always see what's going on with the game. All in all, Dungeon Defenders 2 is worth the download. It's early access, but it seems like a full game because of the progression the developers made. So, I give Dungeon Defenders 2, the deal of the thumbs-up. If the Developers read this, I hope you can fix some of the issues stated. Thank you for reading all of this.

UPDATE:  I got it working. I turned down anisotropic filtering down to 8x instead of 16 and turned front-buffer effects off. I suspect the front-buffer effects were the culprit though.
I tested it again and the front-buffer effects were the problem. I'll change my thumbs down if I go through the complete game without anymore annoying issues.
FINAL THOUGHTS: Leave the anisotropic filtering at 8x. Later in the game, I experienced problems when I wanted to undo my actions/choices. How do you do this? Simple, pause the game and go  to "Stop" then when on the Main Menu, "Continue" . Eventully turning the filtering back down fixed a problem where my PC would freeze when I did this (and I'm a perfectionist on one of my playthroughs  so doing this is a must). So once I did that, I had no problems whatsoever with the game. Oh, and my PC is pretty good if I say so myself... so save yourself some neckstrain and implement these settings... it might just save you time where you could be playing the game instead of fixing it.

I think most of us have a few ideas for games rattling around inside our heads. If you're just looking for a way to tell short stories to share with your friends, everything you need is right here- for more involved stories or for the more ambitious gameplay mechanics, you'll still need to put a lot of work into it. It's easy to use as-is and is tremendously modifiable- I've seen people making platformers and vertical-scrolling shooters in this engine.
Some of the interface quirks can be awkward- movement paths have to be input one step at a time, and dialogue has to be input one window at a time, but there are mods to change the behaviours of those too.
All in all, a very cool stepping stone for anyone with a game in their minds, but it doesn't do ALL the work for you.

In SUPERHOT, you control time! It's more of puzzle game than a FPS though because you need to have patience to plan your movements. If you rush in, you will likely die. When you stop moving, time nearly haults as well. You can use this time manipulation to dodge bullets, narrowly avoiding death as you destroy all of the enemies in each level. Throw weapons or various objects to block bullets and disarm your enemies, hot switch to change places with one of your enemies, leaving them to die instead of you.
Overall, the story was well done, and the gameplay was very enjoyable. This game has a lot to offer, and you can pull off some really crazy plays. If you enjoy challenge modes, timed modes, and/or endless modes, this game is certainly worth the full price. However, if you intend to play ONLY the main story, I suggest waiting for a sale.

Wanna make a fourth generation-style RPG? A horror game? An adventure game? Anything at all? Then this is what you're looking for. Every new version of RPG Maker had its shortcomings; XP was too choppy and the scripting was too complicated, VX was dumbed down a lot, etc. This is where they really outdid themselves. It brought back features everybody's been clamouring for, like actual battle backgrounds, the scripting is more eloberate but easier to use at the same time and there are some cool new features which had to be inserted manually back then, like your party members following you on the overworld, stacking buffs, custom damage formulae and so on.
The interface is still largely the same as in the previous iterations, so I can't give it full score for originality. Also, the translation is still kinda iffy. Remember that default skill called "Breath Weapon / Breath Armour"? Yeah, that's a mistranslation of "Bless Weapon / Armour", which makes a lot more sense if you consider that it increases stats... but all of these are minor nitpicks when compared to the lengths they went to fix everything and deliver a complete package.
I'd recommend this for anyone who wants to get into game development, because even if you don't actually finish a project it's still massive fun and you'll definitely learn a thing or two.

そういう次の戦闘に役立てる為に死んでいく事こそがこのゲームの醍醐味であり、このゲームでは立ち回りが非常に洗練されると、私は思う。
このゲームは悪い事ばかりではない。
このゲームのプレイヤーの肉体は貧弱だと言っていたが、それは自分だけではない。
相手も同じ立場なのだ。遠距離から不意打ちすれば相手は倒れる。
慣れたら前線に出て眼前の敵を殺したり殺されたり出来るようになれば、君は一人前の兵士であり、皆から信頼されるような心強い味方であり、敵にとっては悪魔のような存在になれるだろう。
購入を検討するのならライジングストームの方をオススメする。
【レッドオーケストラ2】
武器が万遍なく強く、お互いの力量が強い方が勝利に直結するし、タンク戦など独自の仕様がある。どちらも連射出来る武器が使えるし、高性能な狙撃銃が魅力的である。だがこれといって尖った武器がある訳ではなく、どちらを選んでも同じ様な強さを得る事が出来る。どの陣営を選んでも勝敗を明確に分けるものではない。
【ライジングストーム】
これはレッドオーケストラ2とは毛色が違う。まず日本と米軍に分かれて戦うのだが、史実を忠実に再現してしまったせいで、日本の攻める公式マップが(2014/7/31現在)3つしかない。
そしてレッドオーケストラ2とは違い武器の性能差が激しい。
まず米軍は歩兵レベルで半自動小銃が携行可能であるし、殆どが短機関銃や軽機関銃を携行可能だし、武器はかなり恵まれた状態でスタート出来る。なんといっても米軍にしか装備出来ない火炎放射器、この強力過ぎる武器は私も常々頭を悩ませる存在だ。これに関しては是非その悪魔の炎をその身体にうけて感じてほしい。
さて、比べて日本の武器ではあるが、殆どがボルトアクションライフルしか装備出来ず、連射性能がある武器といえば数が少なく、それでいて選べる数が少なすぎる。お世辞にも性能が良いとは言えない、米軍がeasyモードならば日本はhardモードでプレイみたいな感じと思ってもらっても構わない。米軍は適当にやってるだけで勝利出来るが、日本側は防衛戦が多すぎるせいで、知略の限りを尽くして防衛しなければならない。

The controls are solid, the hats are fun, there's quite a lot of collectables and badge-power-ups you can buy.  I havn't 100%'ed the game yet, no, but I have reached the final world (which currently only shows a boss fight, and required I have certain hats to access), in about 8 hours while I was doing a lot of side content.  There's also only one hat I don't currently own, that I'm lovingly calling "ZA WARUDO!" until I can get it. ;P
If you like 3D platforming games like Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie, you will enjoy this game.  I'm honestly surprised at how much fun I'm having with it.  The soundtracks are great, the bosses can be quite tough at times, but the game is playable, possible, and above all FUN.
+Music
+Bosses
+Tight Mechanics
+Perfect Controller Support
+If you prefer harder games, there is a way
+Fun Platforming
+I can unironically say "This is a better Super Mario 64 Sequel than Super Mario Sunshine" even though it's an unrelated indie game (fan game I'd say, there's too many connections to SM64...  mansion is a space ship, coins are gems, stars are hourglasses, paintings are telescopes, etc etc...)
+/- Platformer
+/- Lack of combat outside of bosses
+/- Bosses can be far more challenging than their leading up levels
+/- LOADS of collectables that *do* effect gameplay
-Rather short (~8 hours)
-Only 5 worlds (6 if you count 'The Moon' bonus levels)
-"Effects" aren't as optimized as the other options (but my processor is outdates, just be sure to check your sysreqs)
-Shopkeeper is inconsistant
-(?) No map badges for finding yarn, coins, or any collectables other than "Artifacts"
-has a "weapon" tab in the menu, but only has one weapon that cannot be changed or accessed
-sometimes wall running activates when you don't want it to
-due to the games color scheme and soft shadows, landing on wires can be a pain with no clear indicator of where you're falling, I'm good at games and I usually over/under shoot them
-my BIGGEST complaint: The Camera can be VERY finicky at times
Foot note: I'd rate this the old "K-A 7+", some bosses are too hard, some levels quite terrifying (Luigi's Mansion meets Amnesia Dark Descent), and there's one level (on a movie set) with quite a bit of 'blood' on display, for kids 6 and under.  But in a world where game ratings are rarely accurate, I felt I should put my two cents in on this one.  If it were a movie, it would be "Toy Story 3" brand of "PG".

The Cat and the Coup is a visually arresting, surreal history lesson chronically the life and death of Dr. Mohammed Mossadegh. Half edutainment, half bizarre art project, it's an entirely unique and wonderfully creative 15 minute fall down an abstract rabbit hole, reinforced with the snippets of real world events that somehow only make it all the more unusual. Personally I found it a brilliant experimental experience, though for as odd as it is I can just as easily imagine a dozen entirely different opinions about it, which perhaps says something to how weird a game it is. Thankfully I don't have to decide for you whether to give The Cat and the Coup a look, as it's entirely free and will take just a small portion of your day to complete. At the very least it's almost certainly the oddest use of a Nine Inch Nails song I've ever found, which in itself I find strangely compelling.

First and foremost, I would like to say I am brand new to the Tales Of series in terms of playing the games, as Tales of Zestiria is the first game I actually have the proper platform for (PC). I guess that makes this a more or less unbiased review in terms of series nostalgia, which may make it more or less appealing depending on who is reading it.
I'll get straight to the point here -- this is my first ever review on Steam, and I am writing it exclusively to say that this game is amazing. Downright incredible. From the very start, it pulls you in with charming designs, likeable characters and interactions, and a battle system that feels unique, flexible, and interesting. And as you go along, this feeling never diminishes, even once. Steam doesn't seem to have clocked all of my hours since I played a good number of them offline, but I have been playing for a fairly good amount of time, and I am still marveling at the novelty of the characters, the exciting variety in the gameplay, and the beauty of the world built around everything this game has to offer.
If you enjoy action RPGs, I would say don't hesitate for even a second in picking up ToZ. If you enjoy story-driven games, DEFINITELY do not wait. ToZ is largely driven by a charming and engaging story which doesn't feel tedious or exhausting, largerly due to the characters it focuses on. If you like games purely for aesthetic reasons, you have a real charmer here, too, with exciting and gripping character and location designs.
In short: play Tales of Zestiria. It's wonderful, and you won't regret it.

I awake from a tragic plane crash to realize I am stranded in a snowy forest. I am already starting to freeze from the brutal temperatures of this world. Due to my knowledge from most survival games, I decided to try knocking down a tree. I came to realization this is not any survival game, but an extravagant and realistic adventure. Suddenly, I notice that I will die of hypothermia if I don't take action. I begin to run off into the unknown to hear a dreadful snarl to my right. A wolf leaps upon me leaving me to fight it with my hands. My blood began to trail behind me in the snow after managing to scare it off. My hearing begins to fade as my senses drift off. After 1 hour of being in a snowy forest, I die.
Time to try again.
I awake in the same situation, in a new area, mainly surrounded by large hills. The sight before me was fantastic. There were many downed trees and stumps in a clearing. There was a deer, a mountain, and upon that mountain, a manmade structure. At last! I have found shelter! Within the viewing tower, was a rifle, medical supplies, a fireplace, bed, and more. I helped myself by making a fire with some supplies I found and resting. I felt invincible. That was until I heard noises outside. Frozen in panic, I ducked down, took out my rifle, and snuck outside. I shortly concluded that the sounds were just the wind causing the building I was in to creak. As soon as I felt safe, in the distance, I heard the howl of wolves. I realized I ate my food, used up my firewood, and had nowhere to run. The structure I was living in surely wouldn't support my life, judging by the fact there was a man's corpse at the bottom of the stairway. I had to leave.
After wandering around, the cold and my poor injured ankle from taking a fall off a short cliff, there seemed to be no hope. As soon as I was about to give up, a hidden hatch came into my view. My excitement began to climb higher than ever, as I climbed down the ladder.
As I type this to you now, I am in the underground room underneath the hatch. My food and water supply is efficient. The amount of adventure and fun that I have picked up from this game has led me to write a review telling you how much I love it. I am positive I will continue playing along with the development and following the full release.
Keep in mind, this game is in the alpha stage, as an early access game, and has a great performance. If you may think there is not enough in this game, I can see your reasoning, but there is still an excellent future for The Long
Dark. I still think there are an incredible amount of objectives and strategies that may be used for entertainment.
Also, keep in mind that when I wrote this review, I was in the middle of my first time playing it, and only, at the time, had about 20 minutes in it.  Plus, a story mode is planning to be added.
This is NOT a stereotypical survival game. Great graphics, (for an alpha game). No zombies. No punching down trees. There are realistic features and it expresses the challenging aspects of survival. You don't just have the danger of starving or dehydrating, but you may be attacked by wild animals, you may die of hypothermia, or be crushed by something collapsing. Who knows.
Trust me. This is a masterpiece, and if you love survival games, or any games, The Long Dark is for you.

Never have a spent so much time with a computer game/program of any kind. The time spent alone makes this the best value for my money ever spent. But it gets better....much better.
I first bought this to make a game for my daughter when I was unable to find a fun computer game with reading as a main component. Naturally I made her the main character. I have always enjoyed writing, and now I had a whole new platform to craft a story.
In time I became attached to my game, even with the default assets. As an educator, I thought this could be a good story-based game for other kids as well.
Thus began my attempt to gauge interest. It fared well on Greenlight Concepts...but receieved a lot of criticism on the actual Greenlight, mostly due to using default assets. They liked the concept (a family-friendly RPG), but hated seeing the RTP.
Now here is where the versitility of RPG Maker really shined. I was able to import custom made characters and sprites, cutscene art, and original music (bonus: if you compose, you get to use your own music!)...even voice-acting. With the new assets in, my votes increased dramatically, and my game was Greenlit.
It was by no means easy. The amount of time and effort is monumental to create a game that others will pay for and enjoy. There are those who will tell you that your first game will never make it commercial, and they are usually right. I had a lot of support from the very helpful RPG maker community. I had some money to invest in the assets. I listened to my crtics, even the ones who blasted me. I had kind people (familiar with rpg maker) alpha test,; their suggestions enabled necessary improvements over many different versions.
Having my RPG Maker game Sydney's World up on Steam is an accomplishment I am proud of. But irregardless, the personal satisfaction I had when I played through my final version was priceless.

このゲームは往年のFPSとは一線を画するゲームである。
新兵となった君はチュートリアルもせずにマルチプレイヤーモードで適当な鯖に入って遊ぶ事になるだろう。
そして今まで培ったFPS技術が音を立てて崩れさった時、君はこのゲームに惚れるか、アンインストールして次の戦場に移っても良い。私は敗北主義者と罵って後ろから撃たないから
取り敢えずこのゲームはプレイヤーが貧弱であり、一発受けただけで大抵死ぬ。所謂リアリズムなゲームだ。立ってるだけで死ぬのだが、君が賢き者ならば今度リスポーンした時には「立っていると危ないからしゃがみながら行動しよう」と考える。
そういう次の戦闘に役立てる為に死んでいく事こそがこのゲームの醍醐味であり、このゲームでは立ち回りが非常に洗練されると、私は思う。
このゲームは悪い事ばかりではない。
このゲームのプレイヤーの肉体は貧弱だと言っていたが、それは自分だけではない。
相手も同じ立場なのだ。遠距離から不意打ちすれば相手は倒れる。
慣れたら前線に出て眼前の敵を殺したり殺されたり出来るようになれば、君は一人前の兵士であり、皆から信頼されるような心強い味方であり、敵にとっては悪魔のような存在になれるだろう。
購入を検討するのならライジングストームの方をオススメする。
【レッドオーケストラ2】
武器が万遍なく強く、お互いの力量が強い方が勝利に直結するし、タンク戦など独自の仕様がある。どちらも連射出来る武器が使えるし、高性能な狙撃銃が魅力的である。だがこれといって尖った武器がある訳ではなく、どちらを選んでも同じ様な強さを得る事が出来る。どの陣営を選んでも勝敗を明確に分けるものではない。
【ライジングストーム】
これはレッドオーケストラ2とは毛色が違う。まず日本と米軍に分かれて戦うのだが、史実を忠実に再現してしまったせいで、日本の攻める公式マップが(2014/7/31現在)3つしかない。
そしてレッドオーケストラ2とは違い武器の性能差が激しい。
まず米軍は歩兵レベルで半自動小銃が携行可能であるし、殆どが短機関銃や軽機関銃を携行可能だし、武器はかなり恵まれた状態でスタート出来る。なんといっても米軍にしか装備出来ない火炎放射器、この強力過ぎる武器は私も常々頭を悩ませる存在だ。これに関しては是非その悪魔の炎をその身体にうけて感じてほしい。
さて、比べて日本の武器ではあるが、殆どがボルトアクションライフルしか装備出来ず、連射性能がある武器といえば数が少なく、それでいて選べる数が少なすぎる。お世辞にも性能が良いとは言えない、米軍がeasyモードならば日本はhardモードでプレイみたいな感じと思ってもらっても構わない。米軍は適当にやってるだけで勝利出来るが、日本側は防衛戦が多すぎるせいで、知略の限りを尽くして防衛しなければならない。
しかし日本側も決して弱いだけではない。日本の兵士だけが使える「バンザイチャージ」これは使いようによっては戦線を一発で覆す性能を秘めている。
これは簡単に言えば「気合で能力を底上げする」であり、リスポン位置から遠い事で有名なガ島や速攻で戦地に戻らなければならない硫黄島のFなどですぐに舞い戻るにはこれを有効に活用しなければならない。
長くなりすぎたようだが、もしも君が普通のFPSに飽きていたのなら、新鮮さを求めるようにこの戦場に舞い降りて見ないだろうか？

This is a game you are meant to spend as much time as possible with, souly on one map, to achieve anything.  You need to have several spare tombs for your pharoh as well as he can die suddenyl without warning (I had one pharoh die two years after his father died and didn't have a tomb ready because of it).  You need to establish the school, then healthcare, funeral and temple buildings quickly (I do it in this order as the school is basically the first thing you need to get more graduates to power all other buildings that require them).  You need a large low class population established by the time you reach a point where no more villagers are on the map to milk people from.  I tend to build all 4 types of buildings farms, labourers, soliders and servents for this reason even if I don't need them.
If you don't have more then half your population as low class, you may find slowly over time your Low class population disappears, and as their population works the entire city... You can easily end up with an econimic crisis on your hand as there won't be enough Low guys to fuel the class descent systme from low to high society.  So you have to make sure tyour middle class populance never goes above more then half the size of the lower.  Likewise, at no point should your high class guys take over more then 1/4 or 1/5 of the population of middle.
Also despite the games advice that you must locate buildings close to the source of raw materials they use, you can really put them anywhere on the map.  Only a few will greatly be impacted by this when they can get to a template or healthcare building in time.  Some buildings like shops can use the exchange, saving the need to worry where in the city they are placed.  For others like perfume makers who gather their sources, honestly, they get their resources from 4 possible sources so they may spent days walking all over the map making careful placement almost impossible.
Other then this... Building as many small tombs as possible keeps the nobles happy as they need tombs as well as pharoh an there are no consquences if a royal family member dies (not pharoh) so you can forget about supply them with tombs (unless they are pharoh).  Brick layers and brick makers can more or less be placed anywhere on the map. They are essential tot he city, but by the time you have two dozen of them, most projects are then catered for forever. If you have more then ample farms, pulling back some of the nobles food for the sake of the poor is not a worry and honestly?  The nobles numbers support the city via farms, loosing them means the city collaspses (it happened to me once).  It best they are allowed to keep as much food as possible even if the citixens of the city suffer becase of it.

The only question I had when I put this on my wishlist was "Is this game actually going to be as charming, colorful and fun as it looks?"
Now that I have played it - turns it that the answer is a resounding "Yes, and more". It's also funny, clever, full of endearing characters, relentless positivity and blink-and-you-miss-it gags. I spent most of my fifteen hours smiling from ear to ear. It's basically 12+ hours of concentrated happy. I collected all the time pieces and most of the collectibles and I'm just kind of sad it's over, and glad I got to experience it.
It's NOT a hardcore platformer - it's specifically designed to limit frustration; if you fall off a high-up platform to the floor of a tower or other multi-story platforming sessions, it will respawn you from a checkpoint instead of forcing you to redo the entire climb from the bottom. If you die a couple of times in boss battles, the game will help you by granting health for simply hitting the boss successfully, so you can make it even if you don't learn the pattern perfectly. If you're looking for a challenging experience, look to achievements, self-imposed challenges, or try speedrunning.
Probably going to be my favorite title of 2017 when it's all said and done.

I preordered A Hat in Time a little over 2 years ago when I first heard about it. The hype I had for this game was unimaginable, and now that it's here, I can review it.
Story:
The story is as basic as they come. Girl uses things to fuel spaceship, things get removed, find things. A simple plot, but engaging and fun.
Characters:
Every character is amazing and full of charm. Hat Kid herself has many different animations, and each npc has different interactions with her. Just the Mafia members alone make the characters 10/10, but combine that with the Snatcher, the Crows, and Moustache Girl, and you have a magical cast.
Voices:
Speaking of voices, this game has a full cast. And it's splendind. There are some stand out names in the roster including YouTubers such as Jontron and Yungtown. Yungtown in particular does and AMAZING job, and it's nice to see Jon in this game even after the whole "controversy". Every character really comes to life with the voice acting, but there is the ability to hear things in the retro mumbling effect we all know and love.
Graphics:
This game is vibrant and colorful, just as is advertised. It is, as the developers put it, "Cute-as-heck"
Music:
Just buy the soundtrack. I promise you won't be disappointed. Every track does a wonderful job setting moods and adding emotions to areas.
Final Verdict:
Please, please buy this game. This game is an example of Kickstarter games done right. I love this game with everything I have. I give it a recommendation and a 10/10 to go and play it for yourself.

I have mixed feelings about this game, but ultimately it is worthy of a playthrough, or at least a partial playthrough. The concept is brilliant, and I applaud the idea of bringing attention to causes, plights, opinions, politics and philosophy through the gaming medium. This game is also actually a game on a technical level, as it has challenges to solve through manipulating a character, although it really just barely qualifies as a game. The animation and art is really wonderfully done, and is stylized in a way that has aristic value and restraint not usually seen in gaming. The downside is that it is boring, as a story, and that the gameplay is essentially a frustrating element designed to keep the story from being told in a rapid series of clicks. So in the end it is worth looking at the concept, as it is entirely brilliant; the content, however, is hit-and-miss, with the art as the major notable hit and most everything else a near- or far- miss. Mixed bag. [ 6 / 10 ]

単純なランゲームだが、多彩なトリックをコンボで繋いでいく面白さがある。ステージを完走するだけなら簡単だが、高得点を狙うには技とコースを覚え、トライ＆エラーを繰り返す必要がある。BGMは軽快で心地よく、背景も色合いが美しい。キャラクタの動きも凝っていて操作感は良好である。キーボードのASDW及び上下左右のみで操作が可能で、またリトライもワンボタン（R）でやりやすい。コース数は5×5で25本だが、障害物の配置が異なるプロと合わせて実質50本。また各コースに5つのチャレンジがあるので一つのコースを何度も楽し（苦し）める。まだ自分は出来ていないが高難易度のRADモードなるものもあるらしい。実績全解除は至難の業だと思う。他にスコアを競うスポット、一回きりのデイリーグラインド、ローカルなマルチモードなどもある。
少し残念なのはメニューの遷移方法が微妙に優しくないこと、ステージエディット・シェア機能が無いこと、日本語の誤植があることである。特に最後はチャレンジ達成不可能となるもの（5-5アマのチャレンジ「すべてのグラインド、マニュアル、ローンチなどをパーフェクトに」は「Spinを30回以上決めてフィニッシュ」が正しい）があったので注意が必要。

I am absolutely in love with this game. The art, the atmosphere, and especially the audio are all amazing. They nailed all the little things that make for an immersive experience; one of my favorite examples being the sound of a cold howling wind outside of the shelter of a cabin. Getting caught out on a lake in a blizzard is actually terrifying, especially when you end up back at the same fish shack you swear you just searched.
The Long Dark is already a winner for me, and I can't wait for the story mode. A couple things I think would be cool to add to the game would be:
1) A compass as a obtainable item: would make navigating the maps a little easier, especially in bad weather.
2) Being able to craft a place-able bear trap out of scrap metal, same idea as the snare but would be able to take down a wolf or deer. Useful for protecting a home base and general food gathering. Could also maybe inflict damage to your character if you accidentally stepped over one...
Would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a challenging but fun survival experience set in a beautiful world that kinda feels like you're inside a Lawren Harris painting.

and, finally, Hinterland gave me just what I was asking for!
My first three attempts at the game had me lasting for a little over an hour, in-game time, each. My fourth attempt I lasted nearly an
day.
I sit at my computer desk in the warmth of my own home and I'm struck by the realization that I practically feel the biting winds of that blizzard coming through. I can nearly feel the snow crunching under my feet. I feel the panic set in when I realize that I've lost my sense of direction and, with the storm picking up, I can barely see 5 feet in front of my face. I head back to my cabin, or at least in the direction that I
my cabin is in and my breathing gets heavier. I consider running but I need to conserve as many calories as I can. I just keep soldiering forward, trying to get back to my cabin, when I hear it. I hear a wolf howl in the distance. Maybe he's 100 yards away. Maybe 50. It's hard to tell. My heart races while I try to give the wolf as wide a berth as possible.
Now I'm freezing. My condition is dropping rapidly. My breathing gets heavier. I'm thirsty and I'm hungry but the wolf is out there and I'm afraid that if I stop to take a drink he'll be on top of me. I'm not sure I'll survive a wolf attack in my current state, so I keep moving forward, trying to tell myself that the wolf is far enough away.
That's when I see the frozen corpse just ahead. I know this place. I'd been here just a few days earlier and had already scavenged that body for whatever worthwhile things it had on it. I'm heading in the
. My cabin. My shelter. My food stores and supplies... they seem
now.
I've got to make it. I've got to get back to my home base. I head in the right direction, now, and just push forward with everything that I've got. I take a much needed break along the way to eat what little food I have on me and drink some water. I haven't heard the wolf in a while, perhaps he got distracted by a rabbit. My condition is rapidly decreasing but I just may have enough left in me to make it home and get a fire going.
I climb that last hill and I see my cabin shortly ahead. The storm has died down quite a bit and it looks like things may be calming down. I see a deer up ahead and it makes me happy to finally be able to get the rest and nourishment that I need to survive for another day. It reminds me that as brutal and unforgiving as nature can sometimes be... it's also quite beautiful.
Just a few more yards and I'll be home free, at least for the next few hours. I smile, but the smile quickly fades as I hear the snow crunch behind me. And then that growl. I'm done for. I'm not gonna make it.

I've loved every minute of The Long Dark I've played so far. First off, the game is a work of art: visually, it's beautiful, and the landscape is interesting sylistically. The world feels big and dangerous, even while playing on the easiest difficulty. So far, I've survived 50 days and haven't really come close to death (again, on easy), but it's never felt boring, and I've never felt like the world has lost its edge.
The way your character interacts with the landscape is satisfying, and even though you may spend time exploring and getting lost, it feels like the game has a clear sense of direction.
Even in early access, The Long Dark is totally functional for me. I'm so used to early access games being a wreck of bugs and dead ends that I didn't even feel like I was playing an early access game. The game is decidedly simple (with a clear goal: survive), but the elements and mechanics that are already in the game feel complete and well thought-out. I am optimistic about what this means for the remainder of the development, and am eager to see what happens next.

It feels like most of my Steam reviews are just a paraphrasing of "it's a great game, but it's not for me", followed by the template "the game's XYZ aspect is great, but here's a paragraph of a single mechanic that mostly ruined it for me". And that's what OlliOlli2 is to me, sadly.
This game has excellent great presentation and polish out the wazoo, and the mechanics to back it up. But man, I am not a fan of the controls, which involve flicking the stick in various motions and then letting go. It just never felt right to me, and I could never get into the "flow" I was looking for. That, and a lot of the objectives in the game involve going for score, which invariably means you have to be really dextrous and masterful in nailing lots of tricks and grinds in quick succession. There's nothing inherently wrong with that, but I don't feel like investing the time in getting good if I find that the core mechanic of using the thumbstick clumsy and un-fun.
And for what it's worth, I've played my fair share of board-based games such as Tony Hawk's Pro Skater and Skate 3, and tolerated the trick/style aspect of those games because they felt good enough for me not to care too much. I can't say the same for OlliOlli2, as good of a game as it is.

I have to confess, one of my weaknesses is games that are under a quid on Steam. I just can’t help myself. Anything over that magical threshold and I might question whether it is worth my money, but below that? I’m game. So of course I wasn’t strong willed enough to resist Freebie’s value based allure. Not even the fact a game called “Freebie” cost me 47 pence could turn me away.
Freebie’s premise is simple. You bounce balls off of a rotating panel in the centre of the screen and gain points if the ball hits a green wall while avoiding the red walls. The paddle slowly ramps up in speed, increasing the difficulty. A solitary high score counter keeps track of your personal best on the main menu.
When not on sale, Freebie costs £0.79 pence on Steam and to be quite honest it certainly looks like it. As you are greeted by the dreadfully plain main menu, the deafening silence is jarring until you choose which of the three tracks to play. A nondescript play button sits near the top of the screen and blends far too easily into the rest of the text. I’ve seen more exciting main menus on ZX Spectrum games.
Things don’t get more exciting as you get into game, unfortunately. The concept itself is sound on paper, but is more timing dependent than skill based. There is no timer on firing the ball so any urgency in the game is removed when you realise you have the luxury of being able to calculate the perfect line of attack. As your score increases there is no real sense of progression. There is little to no fanfare about reaching any milestones, save for steam achievements for 10, 20, 30 , 40 and 50 points reached. The backgrounds stay the same, the music does not change, the only thing that changes is the speed of the paddle. At no point do you feel that it is ever ramping up or "getting real". The whole experience feels very muted.
With the above said, however. I got 20 minutes enjoyment out of it, which is about ten times longer than any Kit Kat for the same price has lasted me. A fun enough little game with an interesting premise that feels like it cost 79 pence and not a penny more. It is worth a try, but have something on standby to fill the longing for something more this games leaves you with.

Hey folks MrChimp here, I recently sat down and played SUPERHOT on my stream which usually runs for about 2 hours a night 3 nights a week. Thinking this game looks great I will get my two hours in and call it good. That didn’t happen. Once I was in the game had me reeled in and I could not put it down. Played through the entire story mode in one sitting and started to pick at endless mode and challenges after that.
SUPERHOT just throws your right into the action with its intuitive controls and addicting game play. You start out just killing red dudes because they want to kill you and then your roped into this swirling story that leaves you wonder “What the hell is going on?” and you keep wanting more, you become a slave to the system until it “Frees” you.
This game has a ton of replay ability built in with 100ish challenge to complete and many levels of endless madness after the campaign. The mechanic that this game is made on is truly one of a kind! Time only moves when you move so you find yourself jumping into a level and getting into it then dying, trying a couple more times. After a bit you get the pattern down and start working on a path to victory but the great thing is every playthrough is different based on how you move through the map.
The graphic style is great, and it's one that could run on practically any system. The game play is seamless and enjoyable. I cannot leave out the awesome soundtrack as well.
In closing I would give this game 10/10 and would recommend it to anyone that wants a challenging game that they can pick up and play without too much set up or grinding. All you have to do is enter the system and start killing red dudes.

Having not really played any collectathon platformers prior to this, and therefore having not much of an opinion on the genre, I have to say that A Hat in Time is easily one of the best games I have ever played.
The game is great to control, the protagonist Hat Kid moves fluidly and at no point did I ever feel like I was fighting the controls to do what I wanted. The level design itself is amazing - the environments that you explore are unique and varied, and are open to explore and search for collectibles and secrets. The collectibles themselves never feel like a chore to find, as they help unlock both upgrades for Hat Kid to improve her arsenal, and cosmetic changes to allow for you to customise Hat Kid.
Charm oozes from this game, between the world and characters that inhabit it. Hat Kid is simply a very adorable protagonist, shown mostly through her animations in the game and the few small lines of dialogue that she speaks. Most of the characters are memorable and have genuinely funny dialogue, which is backed up by good voice acting. The places you visit are all unique, vibrant and full of things to look at and explore, which backs up its already great level design. The soundtrack is fantastic, Pascal Michael Stiefel, Grant Kirkhope, and the rest of the composers outdid themselves, with every track being great to listen to, which really helps you get immersed into the experience that this game provides.
Overall, you should definitely give this game a look, and possibly even try it. It's one of the most fun, charming and polished games that exists right now. It's left a massively good impression on me, and I plan to keep on playing it in the future, especially once the modding support comes out (which will be very soon), as well as finally go and try out the games that inspired this wonderful game.

I feel like Outlast is one of those games nearly everybody and their mum has heard about, as when it was released it was absolutely everywhere. People were playing it left, right and center. And for a very good reason! This game is bloody good!
It's set in a first person perspective, where you go around, nervously turning your camera on and off to see any glimpse of salvation using the night vision esque effect on your camera, which from time to time you'll have to reload with a fresh batch of batteries. And I swear, whenever a dark area came up, I seemed to be on my last two and couldn't find a single damn battery anywhere to help keep my nerves in check. Now that right there, is not a good feeling to have when you're navigating a house of horrors!
The game does a very good job of creating a nice, dark, scary atmoshpere. Certainly so when a big, insane guy comes chasing after you with the intent of doing horrifying things to your corpse!
When I think of popular horror games, the first two in my head, without question is Amnesia, and of course, Outlast. I personally enjoyed Outlast a whole lot more than I did Amnesia. Hell, I even beat, Outlast and I expected it to be one of those games that I would never finish, and boy am I glad I pushed through and continued to play. The more I played the more I seemed to enjoy, and a little part of me was dreading when I finally beat the game, and another part of me was thinking, thank the lord I won't be terrorised anymore. But when I think back to my time with Outlast, I can't deny how much I really did enjoy the game.
Honestly, Outlast is a game you need to experience if you're even remotely a fan of horror games. It just does it all so well, and most certainly deserves your attention.

In my opinion, this game is a masterpiece. Why? Simple: First of all, the controls are easy to learn, and the animations are smooth and realistic. The graphics are extremely good, the lighting creates a terrific effect, and the AMAZING sound design makes you feel nervous ALL THE TIME. There's nowhere you can feel safe, even if you're hiding. Running away from the enemies is absolutely desperating, and when you finally think you got away safely, they find you. That's what makes this game special: it's not the typical modern horror game that uses jumpscares to frighten you. Outlast does have some jumpscares, but what makes it completely terrifying is the fact that you can't protect yourself, just run. And sometimes, even running is useless. No matter where you go, they can find you.
The story is not the best part of the game imo, but it's really cool anyway, specially if you buy the DLC. The main thing that makes you wanna keep playing is the intrigue: You're trapped in a terrorific Asylum, knowing almost nothing about what happened there.
The main problem of the game to me is the lack of freedom to explore the Asylum. Yes, you can enter different rooms and find some secrets, but if I could explore the whole place on my own instead of being guided by the game, it would be much better. Of course this is just a personal opinion. The good thing about the game being so lineal is how it takes you through the asylum. There are no invisible walls or closed doors, but the enemies will chase you to the places you need to go, and the blood on the floor will help you find the way out of some places.
In my opinion, this game deserves an 8.5/10. Taking in mind that not a lot of modern horror games deserve that score, every horror game lover should definitely buy this title.

Death by Game Show is a mixture of Tower Defense and strategy.
The purpose of the game is to defend the character in a limited time, using the map to to create bot minions, build buildings and use consumables. At the end of the time, a space ship will arrive to rescue you of the scene and to take off, then you will return at the stage of the show and the challenge will end.
There is a reward system based on coins that drop during the game. With the funds you earn in each stage, you must purchase upgrades to your buildings, your army of robots and even personal means of defense and offense. Although, unfortunately, the game is not completely descriptive as to the function of every purchase you made, so you has to determine the efficiency of the objects and buildings by trial and error.

Skateboarding and videogames go together like peanut butter and jelly.  Just like the Tony Hawk and Skate games left their mark on the industry so too did OlliOlli.  Although the sequel may not be revolutionary it does are great job of capitalizing on what made the first game great while simultaneously improving itself in almost every aspect.  New stages, tricks, and challenges will make this second installment a worthwhile play for those who have already finished the first game.  If you're new to the series don't worry, excellent tutorials will catch you up to speed real fast.
OlliOlli is a fast-paced, side-scrolling, skateboarding extravaganza.  Those who played Skate will feel right as home as this games main tool for tricks is the analog stick.  By flicking the analog stick you can jump up in the air and perform various flip tricks.  You'll also need to hold down the analog stick right before hitting a rail to grind.  To land any other tricks you'll need to tap the A (or X) button right before landing.  As you proceed father into the game you'll need to be able to quickly transition back and forth between rails and the surface in mere seconds.  Its a thrilling experience that requires you to find the right rhythm to flow smoothly through each stage.
The atmosphere in OlliOlli 2 is incredible and the art is gorgeous.  The game has a very slick, colorful, presentation..  Although it clearly resembles the original, this time around the art is much cleaner and a lot less pixalated.  Each location offers a unique theme from the jungle, to the old west, the carnival, and beyond.  The highlight however is the soundtrack.  A wonderful selection of pulsing electronic music is bound to put you in a trance as you play.  The best part about the music in this game is that it keeps playing continuously, even as you reset a stage or open up various menus.
The most notable change to this sequel is the new tricks, specifically manuals.  Just like manuals revolutionized the second Tony Hawk game so too do they this game.  The ability to manual coincidentally lets you combo your tricks trough the entirety of each level.  This is especially import for the Spot mode which only let you perform one combo per stage.  Manuals are pretty easy to do so if you really want to achieve a high-school you'll need to combine them with two of the other new tricks, grind-switches and reverts.  Grind-switches let you mix things up on long grinds while reverts let you switch your stance as you land a trick.
This is clearly an enjoyable title in many ways.  The gameplay is very smooth and rewarding while the soundtrack is exciting and motivating.  That all being said this really isn't that drastically different from the first game.  If you played the original OlliOlli you can pretty much expect more of what that game offered.  The new stages and tricks, along with a magnificent new soundtrack, add quite a bit of value and incentive for picking up this game.  Whether you played the first one or not it, definitely check this one out.  OlliOlli offers a thrilling experience for gamers and skaters alike.

I’m always pleased to review games that defy conventional genre classifications since I’m fully aware that if Steam is in dire need of one thing, that is certainly originality itself. With Steam Greenlight being mostly the cesspit in which all the cheap knock-off indie titles seem to gather, is getting harder and harder to find A & AA games that can stand out. Fortunately, Death by Game Show is just what the doctor ordered. A humorous hybrid from a debutante developer.
A 2D Side Scroller which doesn’t involve any jumping or platforms. A tower defense, perhaps? “Defense” is a keyword in this game’s case but same goes for “survival” and “escape” while the sideways perspective isn’t traditionally associated with many TD games. You’d mention to me, 2009’ Plants vs. Zombies but that one seems severely limited when compared to Death by Game Show (DGS) in both variety and scope. If one thing most players can agree upon, is that DGS is entertaining even after it begins to show its limits. Sure, it gets repetitive fairly quick but as with most indie titles, its charming personality almost forces players to push on. Storywise, we have form of satire that addresses the societal problem of humanity’s increasing dependence on artificial intelligence. A robot dictatorship which suppresses human freethinking through violence disguised as a game show. Imagine Hunger Games/Battle Royale with robots pitted against humans. It would have been quite a grim subject if the robot overlords wouldn’t be as equally dimwitted as they are cartoonishly evil.
Against this Big Brother which shoots himself in the foot, protagonist U.H. Wutt stands a fair chance of winning. Our chubby hero has been accused of “Smarts” and thus sentenced to death through participation in an increasingly lethal set of challenges that will test his patience and strategic thinking. He must defend himself from wave after wave of mechanized foes, with the help of building placement and even robots of his own. A reward system is in place, through the drop of coins and automatic funding. Even a wheel of fortune that provided unexpected help from time to time. With the funds you earn in each stage, you must purchase upgrades to your buildings, robotic army and even personal means of defense and offense. The goal of each individual level in DGS, is to survive the onslaught until the “rescue” shuttle arrives to carry you onto the next stage. Since some of those have sublevels of their own, you can expect a decently lengthy gameplay. Some griding is present in the form of restarting a level in order to attempt a higher score and thus more funds since the best upgrades are obviously not gonna be affordable.
Graphics are standard 2D sprites drawn in comic-book style and the sounds could have benefitted from more diversity other than the handful of effects present. Alas, I reckon Death by Game Show is decently priced for all it’s satirical value and quirky hybrid of genres along with Trading Cards and Achievements. As always, you could wait for a Sale or bundle but the game itself is worthy of any Steam gamer’s collection regardless of when you purchase it.
