Journey through the continent of Glenwood, purging evil in the land! You play as Sorey, a bright-eyed, ruin-loving youth, his adoptive brother, Mikleo, and others who dare to purify evil with them.
This is a fairly basic story. They set out to cleanse evil, and they do so. What more could you want?
...Well, actually plenty. But it's a servicable story, and there is nothing wrong with it. I just wished it had some more to it.
In a humorous statement:
We've got a ruin maniac, an invisible ruin maniac with control over water, Princess Not-Mary-Sue, a plucky assassin, a rocking sarcastic loli, Pun-Mistress Turbo (She's on Fire), Professor Wind, and that funny guy that's simultaneously awesome.
But yeah. These characters, while summed up rather crudely, are quite memorable for their interactions, as are most
games. I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with these characters, and I'll probably remember them more than others in other games/VNs I've done so far. I just wished that they would have fleshed them out some more.
We've got the paragon of good, and the epitome of evil; the Shepard and the Wolves that threaten it. Well its actually not wolves but that's the idea.
LORE DUMP INBOUND!!!
There are three beings that exist on the continent of Glenwood:
Humans (SURPRISE!! :D)
Seraphim
Hellions
Humans are what you expect. You know, because we are human.
Seraphim are beings who are similar to humans, possessing great powers and significantly longer lifespans but only perceivable by a select few who are capable.
Hellions are either Humans or Seraphim that have become corrupted by evil; malevolence. They can be purified of their evil by a certain group of humans and seraphim.
These humans who can purify are referred to as Shepards. The Shepards use the power of the Seraphim to purify malevolence. There are two categories of Seraphim in reference to the Shepard: the Prime Lord and the Sub-Lord. The Prime Lord is the one who enables the Shepard to purify, and Sub-Lords are those who have bound themselves to subservience to the Prime Lord, allow the Shepard to wield their power and giving those Seraphim the ability to purify as well. Other humans can gain the power to purify in addition to the Shepards. They are known as Squires - they only make pacts to become bound the Shepard.
It is the duty of the Shepards to quell Hellions by quelling the source: the Lord of Calamity - your wolf to your Shepard.
I think it's fairly solid lore. Wish they would expand it some more, but this is plenty enough for decent lore.
Holy crap this is an actual overworld! Everything is scaled up to match the player models on screen. It can feel lifeless at times with the lack to fauna skittering around, but that's where the Hellions come into play - they appear on the world as the fauna, and can be engage in combat.
Last two times I saw an expansive satisfactory overworld was in Skyrim and Middle-Earth: SoM

Never reviewed a game before, but I think The Long Dark deserves a few good reviews. I just finished my first attempt at this game. I survived for 7 days, 4 hours, and 26 minutes.
So, my first impressions with the game left me feeling quite good. I chose to play as the female character, and started in Mystery Lake. My first few days were difficult, especially since I was just learning the basics.
During those two or three ingame days, I took some time to appreciate the atmosphere Hinterland Studio has created with this game. Everything looks like a painting, from the sunset to the pebbles and ice on the ground. The music is rarely played, but is beautiful. Finally, the character I played as seemed very believable. Very good voice acting, and a badass at times.

I also learned 3 important fundamentals of the game: Food is scarce, Wolves are plentiful, and the Cold is everywhere. And lucky for the player, two of those things are almost always guaranteed to kill you!  For example, I went into the old Hydro Dam. Everything was going good (I had a plybar and was able to open locked containers) until I turned around. There was a wolf there, and he nearly killed me with one attack. I thought he was dead, and went back to opening other containers. I turned back for the door, and if I hadn't had my storm lantern out, I'm sure I would have died. He saw the light and ran away. He died on the stairs.
I've done enough rambling, so here's my final opinion on The Long Dark.
I am in love with this game as it is, but I recognize there are some flaws. Certain game mechanics will need to be refined before this game gets out of early access. As it is, this is currently a fun, challenging game. Much the game is spent lighting fires and melting snow, but somehow it's fun (?). I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy survival games. With enough support, it could be one of the top games of next year.

I discovered this game way back in 2005 on a demo from an old ps2 magazine. I remember thinking the somewhat short demo was one of the best things I had ever played on a ps2, however at this time I was not really old enough for the adult themes and never owned the full game.
10 years later I found this game on sale for Christmas and decided to play this "cool" game again. If I was to try and compare this game to anything it would have to be "Deadly Premonition" for it's obscure game play and bizarre ideas.
So the demo version of the game is the very first segment of the game and honestly it is possibly one of the best starts to any video game I have ever played. The game is set in New York during winter time and you start the game in a toilet in a diner. You have to watch you character being possessed and carving symbols into his wrists before murdering someone else in the toilet. Your character comes to and sees what he has done and the cut scene finishes you are then thrown into his shoes and have to try and clean up the scene and leave the diner before your are discovered. This was super cool to me then and now because it really creates a tense atmosphere and this game has a way of being very real. After escaping you are then introduced to the other two protagonists NYPD homicide detectives. You have to look for the clues left by your former self you have to find the mistakes that you made during the initial sequence. This could be anything from leaving the murder weapon to leaving traces of blood and this is what makes the start of this game so good its all about the actions YOU make. Having the two sides to the story also made for an interesting story line because half the time you want to get away half the time you want to find the fugitive.
However after this initial sequence the game begins to deteriorate, One of the biggest design choices in this game was to try and make it like a movie. Which is fine but for the rest of the game your either in a point and click adventure or a horrendously long quick time event sequence. It gets old and stale extremely quickly, but honestly I could look past all that if the game retained a solid story. But the subtle detective/ fugitive story has turned into a complete mess by the end of teh game dealing with themes of apocalypse and doomsday. It's really dumb.  I finished this game in one six hour sitting and my brief memory of the demo was somewhat ruined.
In retrospective this was an ambitious game for the time it was created where developers were less afraid to take risks and i can see why it got the appeal that it did. It is somewhat of a cult game branching out to a niche audience. But honestly if the game had retained the quality of it's initial sequences this could have been up there with the best games of that era of gaming. But in 2015 I cannot recommend this game because honestly after the first few hours the game just isn't very good.

The controls are solid, the hats are fun, there's quite a lot of collectables and badge-power-ups you can buy. There's also only one hat I don't currently own, that I'm lovingly calling "ZA WARUDO!" until I can get it. ;P
If you like 3D platforming games like Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie, you will enjoy this game.  I'm honestly surprised at how much fun I'm having with it.  The soundtracks are great, the bosses can be quite tough at times, but the game is playable, possible, and above all FUN.
+Music

+Perfect Controller Support
+If you prefer harder games, there is a way

+/- Platformer
+/- Lack of combat outside of bosses
+/- Bosses can be far more challenging than their leading up levels
+/- LOADS of collectables that *do* effect gameplay
-Rather short (~8 hours)
-Only 5 worlds (6 if you count 'The Moon' bonus levels)
-"Effects" aren't as optimized as the other options (but my processor is outdates, just be sure to check your sysreqs)
-Shopkeeper is inconsistant
-(?) No map badges for finding yarn, coins, or any collectables other than "Artifacts"
-has a "weapon" tab in the menu, but only has one weapon that cannot be changed or accessed

-my BIGGEST complaint: The Camera can be VERY finicky at times
Foot note: I'd rate this the old "K-A 7+", some bosses are too hard, some levels quite terrifying (Luigi's Mansion meets Amnesia Dark Descent), and there's one level (on a movie set) with quite a bit of 'blood' on display, for kids 6 and under. TLDR: Robocraft in Space
So at this point, I cannot recommend or disapprove of this game. I feel very neutral towards it, for reasons being that it is a cute little gem that plays on being robocraft in space. But what it lacks is depth, balance, and goals.  While there is ship classes you can level and build around, there is almost no point, since Sniper ships are the god weapon of this game and win every game. The Good: Excellent visuals, atmosphere, and ambiance, clever puzzles and unique scripted events
The Bad: Abrupt ending, not enough scripted events, extremely short, difficulty is all over the place, some obscure puzzles
Leave it to an indie game to be clever, atmospheric, and do things that AAA titles wouldn't dare do. Limbo starts out with just a simple message: Find your sister.  No voice acting, no characters, nothing just a black and white 2D platformer and a nameless little boy. This can be risky because why would you care about this with none of those elements? You won't need to because the game makes you care for the boy via your actions. He can be dismembered and killed in every way possible via deadly and horrific obstacles and traps like getting caught in a saw blade, getting hung, or impaled by a giant spider leg. You cringe at every death because this is a little boy and not some nameless soldier or thug.
Limbo offers tons of atmosphere thanks to the great ambiance and visuals cues that make you just wonder through the whole game. The puzzles start with simple ones that deal with gravity, pushing stuff around, and pulling switches and levers. Later on you have to manipulate gravity and these puzzles get pretty complicated, but the game also gets darker and more dangerous as you go on. Limbo approaches typical platforming elements like bosses, enemies, and puzzles differently. Enemies are few and far between, but there is such a unique way to eliminate them that you wish there was more of it.
This short 3 hour game feels like a sample because you really want more. With the sudden and seemingly unsatisfying ending is made purposefully to just make up your own ending in your head. Yeah, this isn't for the narrow-minded, but keep in mind that the game is juicy and give you tid bits along the dark journey to make you feel satisfied at the end. Limbo delivers a lot more creativity and atmosphere than a lot of top budget titles because it uses subtly over explosion and big scares. My only issues is that some of the puzzles are pretty obscure and the game can be very difficult in spots which will frustrate you to no end.
I also didn't like such an abrupt ending that didn't solve anything for you. However, this is a case by case basis on if you like this sort of thing or not. The game has a lot of variety, but I wish there was some more of the unique scripted events that made Limbo feel really fun and intense.
~Score: 8.5/10

It's a nice game, if you can ignore that. The gameplay feels really good. Music is pretty decent. Animations can go from pretty good to reaaaaally stiff and ugly, but it's nothing that I feel harms the game that much. The zones themselves are really pretty and fun to explore.
You get a sprint hat, and that's pretty much the only useful hat. Very similar to Mario 64/Sunshine/Galaxy. I figured it'd be more like Banjo Kazooie, but MUCH much closer to 3D Mario games. Bosses are very uhh... inoffensive is probably the best way to put it. They're not bad by any means, but probably nothing I'd feel the urge to replay again. They tried to make it pretty fast paced, and look exciting though, so I give em credit. They're all right.
Voice acting can vary. it feels really strange at times. I guess I got used to it as time went on. EVERYONE is voice acted, for EVERYTHING except until later when.... they're not?? Overall though, the gameplay feels good. You have a ton of movement options, and it feels good to abuse them. Also, very easy game, but still felt rewarding.
It's a decent game, and I hope we can see more indie devs follow this game's way of doing 3D platformers. Pretty high quality, and pretty fun. It's not going to blow your socks off and be GOTY, but it's a good stepping stone for bringing back 3D platformers for sure.
I think if you're interested in an INDIE 3D Mario-like game, you should give it a shot. 30 dollars might be on the expensive side for a 15 hour game, so maybe wait for a sale.

I have found that I both like this game and dislike it, for many reasons. I'll start with the good of this game, because I feel it did keep with the feel of the previous Dungeon Defenders:
-New looks for almost everything! I especially like how the heros are designed, they're noticable but not overwhelmingly so. The outfits are a nice touch, and you can even mix-match them to make it more your own.
-New monsters, bosses, and levels! The scenery is wonderful; the colors are vibrant but aren't blinding, and they textures for everything are amazing. Not only that, you can actually interact with the world you're playing in, which can be really helpful in some of the more chaotic maps.
-New weapons, armor, and accessories! Every piece of armor has a function, and the new items they added in really help to boost your character all around.
-New traps, towers, and ablilities! The game introduces new ways to completely to destroy the enemy, while also bringing back some classiscs. They redid the UI to make it not so screen consuming, and even added a mini map!
-The tavern looks AWESOME! I feel like they picked up the old one and dropped it in a mini-mall. There's so much more going on, and so much more room to run around and practice in.
-New pets, and bringing back the classic ones! (I havn't played enough to get a pet yet, but I've seen other players pets and I adore them!)
-More quests and missions than I could have hoped for! Theres's always something to do, so you can never really get bored.
And now for the bad side, which almost outweighs my positive notes:
-You can't customize your characters like you used to. You get all these really neat outfits, but that's about it; no way to alter your color scheme at all, which I really miss. Not only that, but you can't customize your crystals anymore. You also can't set up your character stats for how you want to play the character;
-Why do we have gold? Why do we have 'ablility mana'? What was wrong with the all around mana-does-everything system? All the gold you get from grinding for who knows how long can only really be used in tavern shops, and it's for equipment that is either not as good or worse than what you have, or something that isn't your level. And on top of that, you can't just save up my in-game gold to buy the outfits, instead of spending real money. Look at the lockboxes - you have the option to open it with either a key (which I still don't know how to get by this point), or a bunch of this... I guess crystals? Who's idea was this??
-Speaking of real money and bad ideas, why does this feel more like TF2 than a Dungeon Defenders game? Basically, you have to spend money to either make real advances in the game, or make yourself look good - again, the lockboxes are a good example of that. At least in the first DD if you got an outfit it came with a unique map, and actually made the outfit a reward for beating it instead of just some trinket that you can go out and buy. But I guess I should have expected this from a free Early Access game.
-What happened to the chat system? You can only see what other players are saying, the chat log option is gone, and you can't really tell who is saying what unless you look quick enough. After that, you don't even remember what you just said, because it doesn't show up on the next-to-nonexistant chat window. I'm sure that people complained about the chat log in the past in some way, but I would really like to have that back. Communication with your party is key to success.
-No more upgrading stuff - what you see is what you get, unless you get the right gear and so on. Either that, or you can just spend forever grinding and replaying levels until you find equipment you like. (I've only played about 4 hours all together by this point, so I'm not sure if you can upgrade things or not.)
-The levels are too overwhelming too fast. The game now makes you - almost forces you - to play with other people in the beginning, or else face innevitable failure. Either that or you just need to make all the classes right away, and practice with all of them at once, and spend forever replaying the same levels until you get used to everything. In any case, the way the monsters are set up makes you feel like a failure the moment the round starts.
-What is with the cutscenes? You can be running around trying to find new gear or something, and suddenly you're pulled to the main crystal, having no other option but to sit there and wait for it to finish. Then after that, you have to watch the stupid chest clip, where it turns from stone to wood or whatever. In all the time that's happeing, you could have been suited up for the next level, selling old stuff, maybe even trading (if that's still a thing we can do), and you could have done that several time - if not for these annoying and mundane cutscenes.
-The newsletter. Dear Lord, the newsletter. Every time you go back to the tavern for any reason, there is a massive window in your face telling you about something that you either are still working on, or just don't care about, due to the frequency of its apperenece. Technically, it's a monthtly exclusive 'quest', so it should just stay in the quest log, and allow you to look at it whenever you feel like it. Or, you know, USE THE MAILBOX! WE GOT A MAILBOX FOR STUFF JUST LIKE THIS, STICK THE LETTER IN THE MAILBOX AND GET IT OUT OF MY FACE!
I want to like this game, there are plenty of reasons for me to like it, but the way things are being done makes it not fun and almost a chore to do. I'm not writing this review because I hate how things are done, I'm doing this so I can give the feedback the developers need to hear to make this game better in the future. As of right now, I'm giving it 5/10, until things change for the better. Play if you want, but you've been warned.

Never reviewed a game before, but I think The Long Dark deserves a few good reviews. I just finished my first attempt at this game. I survived for 7 days, 4 hours, and 26 minutes.
So, my first impressions with the game left me feeling quite good. I chose to play as the female character, and started in Mystery Lake. My first few days were difficult, especially since I was just learning the basics.
During those two or three ingame days, I took some time to appreciate the atmosphere Hinterland Studio has created with this game. Everything looks like a painting, from the sunset to the pebbles and ice on the ground. The music is rarely played, but is beautiful. Finally, the character I played as seemed very believable. Very good voice acting, and a badass at times.

I also learned 3 important fundamentals of the game: Food is scarce, Wolves are plentiful, and the Cold is everywhere. And lucky for the player, two of those things are almost always guaranteed to kill you!  For example, I went into the old Hydro Dam. Everything was going good (I had a plybar and was able to open locked containers) until I turned around. There was a wolf there, and he nearly killed me with one attack. I thought he was dead, and went back to opening other containers. I turned back for the door, and if I hadn't had my storm lantern out, I'm sure I would have died. He saw the light and ran away. If you're a Tales fan you should be getting just about what you expect. For anyone else, if you're looking for effective story moments with likeable characters, satisfying battle mechanics and a vast world full of content to explore without minding some cheese and repetition, then you'll enjoy this game. The story in the Tales franchise never comes down to black and white, and while Zestiria doesn't really shine in the plot or the character department as well as some other Tales games, it does have some genuinely touchy moments as well as humorous ones through its course in common Tales fashion. The artstyle is also clean and vibrant, and the animated cutscenes by Ufotable are pleasing to watch.
The battle mechanics are a positive trademark of the Tales franchise, focusing on fast, action based real time combat that revolves around evading attacks and locking the opponents into combos by exploiting their weaknesses. It's easy to get into and hard to master, starting out extremely simple and then giving you more and more to work with, although you can also simply transform into a different form and murder everything without that much thought. Battle mechanics have been done better in a couple other Tales games, but Zestiria is still good at creating a system where skill plays a considerable enough role and beating bosses doesn't always have to come down to more grinding. There are also 5 different difficulty settings to work with starting out with 3, with harder difficulties yielding better drops.
As for the equipment system, you have 5 equipment slots with every equipment having 4 skill slots, and there are a total of 50 skills in this game that you can stack or combine in specific ways to create bonus effects. You get the skills you want by fusing copies of the same gear together, but getting those copies of gear with the specific skills you want before the fusion process is based too heavily on RNG and ends up being way more trouble than it's worth, so for the most part you'll just end up ignoring this whole mechanic, and fortunately it isn't needed in any way to make progress even on harder difficulties. Still, it's an unsatisfying aspect that will hopefully be executed better in the future, as it is a neat idea.
The world is split into several open overworld sections, towns, dungeons and fight arenas, with unique discovery points, collectibles and optional boss monsters to find in each separate area. The fight arenas are an exception however, as they seem to be designed mostly for equipment grinding. While there's a vast number of optional dungeons, they can be quite repetitive as they're all very similar with each other. Most of the main story related dungeons are fine though unless you're specificaly looking for clever design or complex puzzles, as there won't be much of that here.
New Game+ system is something that the franchise likes to give attention to, letting you earn points called Grade on your playthrough that you can use to buy bonuses and special traits for your next playthrough. Zestiria game has a new approach to this, letting you acquire guardian spirits called Lords of the Land for each town which you can then level up through battle performance and by offering them items, and the Grade you get after your playthrough is based on their levels. This process also unlocks other advantages, making it an interesting system, although one confusing aspect about it is  that the points used for leveling up the spirits are also called Grade despite having nothing to do with the actual Grade you get for NG+ bonus purchases.
While Zestiria falls a bit short of where some other Tales games have set the bar, it's ultimately a good game if viewed as a standalone and as such I can recommend it to any RPG fan.

Short review: It's incredible but there's some serious issues that can be game-breaking in some cases.
Longer review:
Okay so it's a remaster of a game back from 2005. In 2005 this game was amazing. Is it now? Well..yes. It is.
The visuals are a little dated but they're still really good for what they are.
The gameplay is a mix of free-movement and QTE's but they're done in a way that don't become immediately boring. You can even crank up the difficulty of the QTE's or even tone them down [if you're wanting to play it simply for story]
The story? Damn it's crazy. It's a supernatural murder-mystery with emphasis on the characters. Not just character development but managing a characters feelings, stress and things like that.
The puzzles are great but what makes it unique is how you handle them. The best way to explain this is a particular part of the story where you're supposed to composite a sketch of the murderer. If you do it right then it will depress your murderer and make it harder to play as him. If you do the sketch wrong then it'll depress the investigators and make it harder for them. It's a real risk-reward system that I adore.
That all sounds positive, right? Well..there's issues.
A lot of people are reporting getting a black screen and issues even setting the game up. In my case I literally have to spam enter when I boot it up and then I've got to go through a set of menu's in French [I don't speak French so it's not fun].
I've even got a couple of friends that have said flat out that this won't run because of the issues. The Dev's know of the issue and I've come across forums where they've admitted they don't even know what's causing the issue.
All in all, I think this is great. I loved it 10 years ago and I love it today.
Also make sure you use a controller.
Also David Cage is in this game and he can't pronounce English and it's kinda hilarious :')

I originally played Indigo Prophecy on the XBox and can happily say that this port does a decent job of bringing the bananas plot to a PC audience. All the stupidity, poor writing, bad voice-acting, and left-turns into full-on Crazyville are there for the player to observe and gape at in all their David Cage glory. Unfortunately, the gameplay (or lack thereof) also makes the transition, which undermines the experience by being just as garbage as it was when the game was first released. David Cage's obsession with QTE-based action sequences and the 3D equivalent of pixel-hunting will forever baffle and confuse, but as with the original release: it all works to the game's credit, because we play David Cage games for the same sort of entertainment found in watching The Room.
I would love to give this game a recommendation, but I can't. The port is glitchy: it took me two hours to figure out how get it to stop crashing to desktop every time I tried to start a game, and it crashes anyway every time I have to reload. These problems are all solved by running the game in windowed mode, but playing a game that's pretending to be a movie in window mode is like watching TV shows in the little PIP box while the menu takes up the rest of the screen. If you buy this game, figure out if it will work immediately and refund if it doesn't. It isn't worth the time to make it work when you could be playing something else. Unless, like me, you're a massive fan of David Cage's lunacy.

Do not expect drastic changes when you see "Remastered" label. Yes they have done quite a lot of works but remember this is a game from 2005 and originally released on PS2. Of course you can switch between HD and SD version by pressing F9.
I got a copy of Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy (GOG version, uncut and SD only) a long time ago and I'm so happy that it has been remastered, as well as released on Steam recently. The gameplay is story-oriented. Which means, if you're into fast-paced, high speed action or even sparking RPGs, then this is not what you're looking for.
The best word to describe this game is "interactive movie". Everything you do may affect the storyline, which then leads to different endings. Even if you chose a "wrong" route, the game still refers to a conclusion (and yes you can restart from last checkpoint after all).
Pros:
+ Awesome story line, with different endings based on choices made by the player. No, it's not simple to describe the whole story within some paragraphs here.
+ Great voice actors.
+ Well-done remastered version with controller support, Mac+PC ports.
+ Uncut version (yeah, there're sex scenes in game).
+ Cheap (got this when it was 75% off on Nuuvem, about ~$1.89).
Cons:
+ Annoying quick-time events. They're based on PS2 control scheme. Beware: ASWD is your left controller analog and mouse is your right controller analog, use them wisely when you're playing guitar.
+ Dated graphics.
+ Random crashes during gameplay.
Overall rating: 8.5/10.

Not much to the overly vague story in this game but that hardly matters. SUPERHOT has some of the most unique gameplay I've ever experienced in a shooter. Here's a quick rundown.
- Goal is to kill everyone
- Time moves at normal rate when you move, dramatically slows down when you're standing still
- Gun-to-gun gampeplay, similar to Hotline Miami but in 3D space
- Bullets travel at a dodgeable speed for both you and your enemies, makes leading difficult and rewarding
- Ability to swap bodies, which allows you to evade foreseeable death or just use a body swap to kill an enemy
- Multitude of guns/melee weapons (pistol, AR, shotgun, katana, household objects, etc)
Price tag is a tad steep for the amount of content you get.
I still definitely recommend it though.

Line-defense
Hard
8/10
The narrative element of the game is presented through the intro of the game, through the announcer's banter, in-game signs and the descriptions of droids, buildings and level descriptions.
You play as U.H.Wutt. It is your task to help Mr. Wutt through the Game Show and earn your freedom from the droid tyranny.
8/10
In every level you are presented with different goals, which varies from destroy all enemy buildings and droids, survive for X amount of minutes and collect X amount of money.
In order for you to destroy enemy buildings and droids and help you survive, you will have to build buildings and droids of your own and send them to defend the line. Enemy droids and buildings drops coins, which you can collect with your hook in order to collect money.
There are 10 different types of buildings and 10 different types of droids that can be unlocked as you progress. You have 4 basic type of droids unlocked from the start, but no buildings. As you complete levels you will unlock access to the 6 other droid types and the 10 building types, though it should be said that the unlockable droids and buildings act as one-time consumables purchased with the in-game money earned through levels. There are also consumables that can be bought for the player's character that gives bonuses such as faster move-speed, healing and allowing your hook to do damage to enemy droids.
All levels are replayable and even failure to complete a level will earn you money if you collect any coins on the failed map. There is a difficulty bar at the start of level where the player can adjust the difficulty of the map, making it easier will reduce rewards while making it harder will improve the rewards. This basically adds infinite replayability as the game challenges you to challenge yourself. Every level will offer you a challenge even if you make the level easier. Every level require a different strategy and the game is hard, but the frustration the player will likely feel will stem from a feeling of not being able to figure out the strategy rather than the game being unfair.
The game also features a level designer for you to design maps that other players can try to beat.
8/10
Death by Game Show has a cartoon-style that will be hit-or-miss for most. It should be said that the game has steam workshop and all sprites in the game can be modded. The game is well-optimized and will run smoothly on most computers.
8/10
The soundtrack is lovely and very fitting for the game, but as with the visual style it is very much hit-or-miss. The sound effects are top-quality and fits very well within the genre.
8/10
If you are looking for a challenging line-defense game with infinite replayability that has no hand-holding this is the game for you. I wholeheartedly support this game and I most certainly would say it is a well-worth purchase for any fans of strategy and line-defense games.

I received this game at Momocon for free in a contest/panel that the creators were running, which was cool in of itself, but I'll stick to the game.
I wasn't really sure what I was expecting, coming into it, but the game itself was very unique, right from the get-go.  You had your standard platforming elements where you move left and right, and space to jump and that was all well and good, and then it changes things a bit by allowing you to reverse the polarity, allowing you to stand on the ceiling.  Of course this opens up a whole new world of challenges, but they don't stop there.
Then not only can you shift that polarity up or down, but with certain locations in-game, you can rotate your map (and the polarity) 90 degrees to the left or right, depending on the button pressed.  So now you've got four ceilings and four floors, in some levels virtually all at the same time but there's still more added on.
They allow you to add color to your cube with certain areas and when your cube matches the color of a wall, you're now allowed to traverse through it.  So now you've got all these things, all going at once and it's a puzzle platformer that really requires you to think on how you want to proceed.
The only negative problem I have with the game is that there are enemies...and not necessarily that they're there, but they feel a little tacked on.  You do get varying methods of attack, which is interesting itself, but it feels to me that the main draw is the puzzling itself, and the enemies don't really add or take away from that.  I would like to see them be more incorporated into the puzzles themselves, rather than as an obstacle given that once you get a few of the better attacking methods, you can one-shot most of them and there's no real challenge or point to them being there in the first place.
However, all in all the puzzling is a high level of fun and thought-provoking in Pixel and I would reccomend that people give it a chance if they're looking for a puzzle game that requires you to think in multiple dimensions and laterally all at the same time.

show is inspired by the great movie
but goes beyond. A blend of strategy and twitch-based genres, baptized as “Twitch-Strategy” by the developers, and as such it might not be that normal tower defense and strategy game that one would expect. Forget about defeating waves of enemies on a single map with fixed building spots and upgrades, instead, embrace your limited freedom and walk freely on the map, trying to survive by strategically spawning droids and placing structures within a limited time.
The game has a cartoonish 2D style with a unique feel to it. The focus lies on a futuristic look while keeping it as a tribute to those old game shows, maybe a bit too detailed which make it look messy, with too much going on, like the billboards filling the background of the battlefield with witty anecdotes; sadly there is not enough time to read them all, but the effect is still there.
The audio is very simplistic and yet very fitting, but sadly there isn't much variation in it, therefore it looses some attractiveness and might get irritating in a longer game run, considering that the soundtrack is pretty much the same as it fits the the theme perfectly.
As it a more casual game there is not very much voice acting going on. The lines are brought in an attempt to sound stupid and funny, but in the end the humorous might not get appreciated by all players and a bunch of references might go by unnoticed with the younger players.
The story plays in the future where robots dominate the human race. The player plays the role of U.H. Wutt. A typical fat nerdy human who is too smart according the droids and is sentenced to death because of it. The 'truth' about it all, is slowly reveal with the messages on the boards, the cries heard in the battle and many other elements in the background. The story also packs some parodies, references and puns from cult classics, but most of them can easily be missed by younger players, while olders might find it overdone. At the end, the story seems to disappear along the gameplay rather fast.
The first level sort of acts like a tutorial but still leaves an aftertaste of confusion. A lacking of "how to" or a the function of replay the tutorial makes the game confusing at times and might force the player to replay certain levels before realizing what needs to be done.
As the game will progress, the gameplay will only be getting harder, and your buddy (a chained mobile factory or G.I.M.P., standing for Gameshow Intimidation Machine of Pwnage) also has an energy bar, which needs to recharge if you spawned too many droids in a short time. You also must place buildings around the map, which will help with defeating the enemy droids, but some will help by generating other friendly droids.
The has a simple premise which consist in each level Wutt getting transported to a planet, then he needs to accomplish some goals before getting on a rescue ship. The ultimate goal is always to survive until the timer runs out. Even though the field is small and is side scrolling, the space above is filled with flying enemies and sinking coins that Wutt will use to grab with his equipped hook.
Killing enemies, grabbing coins and getting upgrades while text balloons with funny lines shows up; dying re-adjusting and repeating is all what will be left of the strategy as the levels get harder and faster. The game has particular power-ups available through spinning the wheel, but they are so far and in-between, you’ll never have enough. It would be great if the money could be used to buy more units. But that is unfortunately not possible.
The challenges or levels have a high replay value. In fact the more it gets replayed, the fun factor rises together with the understanding and goal of that level. None the less, for certain gamers it could get repetitive, while others might quit or get bored with the string of dying and restarting due to the difficulty spikes in some levels.
Adding to the replayability value, the levels do not only have a difficulty setting, which is easily changed by a slider, but the also provides a in-game level editor, as well as different languages packs, custom sprites and levels in the Steam Workshop.

Clearing Pro mode will unlock RAD mode, which is skating flawlessly or eat dirt for not nailing everything perfectly. Safe to say it's not for the faint of heart or those who never experence having sore thumbs for gaming hard.
For those that look to boast their scoring abilites after handling what the game has to offer, look no further to Spot challenges and the Daily Grind that has online leaderboards. You can also play locally with up to 4 buds in a split-screen Combo rush mode, which is a nice plus to what the game already has.

I first encountered this game three years ago in a little booth with two of the main devs working on this game. I've watched it grow and develop a story and tested levels yearly to date. I haven't played much on Steam itself (yet) but I would say I have at the bare minimum twenty hours of gameplay with this game in various iterations. It's honestly one of the best experiences I've ever had with an indie game for years; I'd dare to say I haven't enjoy the unique nature and gameplay of an indie since Cave Story, though it's a rather brazzen comparison since I only mean in appeal and not in the style of the games at all.
You play as a single, intelligent pixel and manuever through puzzling platforms to align the pixels in the background to form a picture. You also shoot virus-infested pixels, and not in a silly way most platformers do, with weapons such as (At the time of writing) a single-shot gun, flamethrower (Yes, it lights pixels on fire which can light other pixels on fire), a laser, shotgun and a rocket launcher (Which you can rocket jump with). In addition to weapon type, there is also weapon color. Naturally, the virus-infested enemy pixels have a color, but in order to harm them, the opposite color weapon must be used against them. For example, a yellow pixel will be unharmed by red, but hurt by blue. If an enemy is shot by a color that is neither the same nor opposite of their color, their hue will shift and you will need a new color to defeat them than what was needed originally. This can, however, be used strategically, as multiple enemy pixels of varying colors but close proximity could be shifted to the same hue, then all three could be blasted into oblivion with a single rocket launcher shot of the opposite color. In this regard, combat is both a puzzle and skill-based ordeal.
What sets Pixel apart from most games is the scoring system. Everything consumes or gives resources with the exception of basic movement. Your resources, from the start of ever level, begin at zero and decrease into the negatives. This is where speedrunning skills come into play. By quickly gathering resources in the form of color-changing squares or killing virus-infected pixels by shooting (Which requires points based on which weapon is in use), points are gained. By rapidly collecting resources and destroying rogue pixels, your negative score grows into the positives and shows how much time was spent, bullets were shot, enemies were killed, resources were collected and deaths you accumulated from start to the goal. But thanks to intuitive level design, there isn't one single "best" way of beating a level. So you can keep going back and trying to overtake a friend's score and eventually beat it by thousands of points all because you took a better route or did so more efficiently than the competition. The scores will never truly have a best only because skill, route selection and RNG elements influence your run to the millisecond.
What strikes me most about this game is that it not only covers many genres (Such as platformer, puzzler, shooter and mostly speed runner) but it does each one justice. It's by no means a regular shooter, but it utilizes its own setting and movement to make a challenging, fast-paced system that shines in a light all its own. Rather than mimic the big boys in the gaming industry, they take tried and true ideas and make them work in a balanced and non-gamebreaking way.
Overall, I think this has the potential to be an incredibly popular game if it gains a solid fan base and skilled player base. The puzzles require a lot of thought but also a lot of skill and most levels can be finished in multiple ways with differing scores. This combined with a workshop for level creation will prove a great many levels requiring unique skill sets that will test the limits of both skill and patience as the pros go at the same level for hours on end in search of a "perfect" run. Which could very well be debunked the following day.
It may not utilize the best graphics engine on the market or have the most detailed characters or levels, but the devs have really put together something incredible. To me, at the very least, this is a hidden jewel on the Steam market.

The atmosphere in this game is incredible; possibly the best I've experienced, I'd say. The art style is charming, but it's the sounds that make it for me. Waking up in the morning only to hear the wind screaming outside, I immediately check my food and water reserves to see how long I can last in whatever shelter I've found, because I'll be damned if I'm going out in that storm. It creates a sense of peril and foreboding: "Could this storm mean my demise?" And in this game, yes, it very well could. Sure, you might have enough supplies to make it through a day of being stuck inside, but that's a day's worth of supplies spent doing absolutely nothing. In other words, a day's worth of supplies spent
getting supplies for tomorrow. Can you afford that luxury? Perhaps, but it's going to make the next few days more stressful, and you're going to be more pressed to find supplies.
The game, as it stands, earns my recommendation even given its flaws (which, to be fair, are very possibly the result of it simply being a young game). It does something new and fresh. The threat isn't from zombies, other players, or really even wildlife, if you're careful (other reviews make it out like wolves will ruin you every chance they get; unless you're not paying attention or are being a little too brave, attacks are rare, and even then they're plenty survivable). The threat is simply the environment and your inability to provide for yourself. For the simple act of trying something new, and doing it well at that, I think Hinterland deserves praise and support.
That said, and though I think it is one of the more promising games I've seen in a long time, it isn't perfect; not in my opinion, at least. There are some things that are just silly. I go to bed with my thirst 100% quenched and wake up 12 hours later dehydrated, to the point that it's affecting my "condition" (think: health). It's a little obnoxious. Clothing durability is also a little screwy, to me. Be prepared to have to repair your clothing once a week or so. While I think this is much too fast for clothing to be deteriorating, I can understand if that was the intention. If this wasn't the case, you'd have to play for months (game time) before the threat of not having proper clothing loomed on the horizon. Most of this stuff, though, is just annoying, not game breaking - and it's also stuff that may be hammered out before release.
Bottom line: I spent $10 on this while it was on sale, and now having played it, I would happily spend twice that (its normal price of $20). It's a fun game, it's new and fresh, and I am more than happy to support people that are brave enough to try something out of the box, especially when it's a good time.

Short and artsy, with a good sound track, The cat and the Coup tells the story of Dr. Mohammed Mossadegh, the first democratically elected Prime Minister of Iran. This is the first game from the Tales series that I've played so I'm not sure how it compares to the other Tale games. However, it certainly got me interested in trying out the other games. Tales of Zestiria is a good place to start for anyone trying out their first Tales game.
The characters have a unique personality and what makes them even more interesting are the skits in this game. The combat can be confusing at first, but once you get the hang of it that's where the fun starts. Enemies get more challenging as you proceed and encourages you to prepare before going into battle. The music in this game is amazing. Some people may say the story is not as great and I wouldn't disagree with that. It could have been better, but I wouldn't say it was bad. The animations and voices were well done and fits with the rest of the game.
The camera can be in a weird position when fighting near walls or narrow hallways of a dungeon which will prevent you from seeing anything. It also moves pretty fast outside of combat unless you lower the camera speed settings, but the problem with fighting near a wall remains. Some skits and sidequests can easily be missed if you continue on with the main quest or pass by these "points of interest" without noticing. They don't tell you much about how things work in the game except for some parts such as monoliths that give combat hints and other things you could miss like skits that explain how fusing equipment works.
Interesting combat system with armitization, decent story, great music and animations. The camera could be improved, but works fine as long as you are not fighting near walls. Overall I'd say Tales of Zestiria is a great game and I would recommend this game to people who are interested in anime and RPGs.

Initial Review - 31/12/2014
I've never purchased an early access game before but was intrigued by the concept of The Long Dark and the overwhelmingly positive reviews it has received so far. Suffice to say I was not disappointed.
The Long Dark is an Incredibly tense, beautiful and engaging wilderness survival game. Although the wildlife and combat are quite limited in the current version, the survival mechanics are very deep as you find yourelf in a constant struggle to stay alive as you scavenge for food/water and try to keep your character warm, healthy and rested,
The difficulty options are neat - allowing you to opt for a more ambient experience, a brutal survival experience or something in between - and it's nice to see you can choose your gender and environment before starting.
There's alot of fun to be had with this game in it's current state (sandbox mode) and I can only imagine it will get better as new mechanics, modes and environments are added.
Recommended for fans of games like Don't Starve but I also encourage players who enjoy exploring vast yet delicate environments to give this a try.
-----
Review Update 1 - 11/6/2015:
Following my review from December 2014, this game has went from strength to strength as the devs have added a host of new environments, wildlife and mechanics. Each update has been of a consistently high standard and I have no doubt they will continue to improve/refine the game as they push towards full release.
Each of the sandboxes has a very distinct feel - forcing you to adapt your survival style as you progress - and the transisition areas between each sandbox are unique and challenging. The bears are a welcome addition as are the new crafting mechanics: such as curing of animal skins (which makes crafting of animal-based clothing a little trickier) and the bow and arrow (which provide a nice alternative to the rifle).
The general balancing has improved alot since I started playing this - providing a good mix of thoughtful exploration and harrowing survival - and the backpack interface has evolved nicely.
The Long Dark is undoubtedly one of the finest products on Steam and surely one of the best examples of Early Access done right.
Highly recommended!
-----
Review Update 2 - 13/2/2016
Following my June 2015 update, the Hinterland team have added even more environments: including the oddly-sinister Desolation Point - where the ominous Processing Station contrasts starkly with the cosy Lighthouse - and highly-challenging Timberwolf Mountain - which requires nerves-of-steel to navigate its lakes, forests, slopes and caves.
New gameplay additions - such as the flare gun, rope climbing mechanics, ability to pick up stray wood and ability to break down items in the game world (one of my favourite additions since purchase) - serve to deepen the already-refined gameplay; nothing feels quite so humbling as finding a cosy cabin in the middle of a fierce storm then being forced to break and burn any remaining signs of humanity in order to stay warm.
Hinterland have overhauled the UI side of the game too with a much improved backpack interface, detailed logbook and stats screen and the ability to create multiple saves at once. You can also choose to start from any region now: a welcome edition for new players who will likely benefit as they attempt to hone their own survival style. You can now play the game with a controller as well as keyboard-and-mouse: the former feels good but the latter remains my weapon-of-choice.
Since my last review I've clocked in almost 100 hours of playtime and reached the peak of Timberwolf Mountain: a great achievement indeed. I look forward to the impending Story mode but even without that feature, this game is already more than worth your time and money.

Though the facts might be intruiging and not widely known among Americans, and the visuals be beautiful and strange, The Cat and the Coup is a diorama; a visual and marginally interactive history lesson. Not a game. That aside, and other issues (below) notwithstanding, it's also only a fistful of minutes long so it never adds up to being enough to be satisfying.
Despite the particular history it covers and its intrigue to me personally, between the popular allegorical preachiness of some of its imagery and the breakdown of play to the point of throwing up rote data less than halfway through, i couldn't help but feel the crassness of propaganda running through "Coup"'s fabric. It may be that that's due more to its being billed as a game than anything else, and that somewhere in the back of my mind i felt a little tricked when "Coup" quit being interactive. I'm a huge fan of Joe Sacco's purely journalistic comics, and interested in similarly untraditional ways of telling people's personal histories, but I guess part of why I felt tricked might have something to do with the fact that this wasn't a person's story. It was mere names and dates, and seeming laziness on the part of the illustrators and programmers. Like they made a third of a game and got tired of it, deciding to just get the process over with and publish. If you can get past this, and the history is unknown to you or interesting enough to spend fifteen minutes on, have at it. You'll enjoy it. And to be fair, this is my first encounter with subject material like this being disseminated in this way and for that the publishers deserve credit.
I'll recommend it with a "Meh".

Do not expect drastic changes when you see "Remastered" label. Yes they have done quite a lot of works but remember this is a game from 2005 and originally released on PS2. Of course you can switch between HD and SD version by pressing F9.
I got a copy of Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy (GOG version, uncut and SD only) a long time ago and I'm so happy that it has been remastered, as well as released on Steam recently. The gameplay is story-oriented. Which means, if you're into fast-paced, high speed action or even sparking RPGs, then this is not what you're looking for.
The best word to describe this game is "interactive movie". Everything you do may affect the storyline, which then leads to different endings. Even if you chose a "wrong" route, the game still refers to a conclusion (and yes you can restart from last checkpoint after all).
Pros:
+ Awesome story line, with different endings based on choices made by the player. No, it's not simple to describe the whole story within some paragraphs here.
+ Great voice actors.
+ Well-done remastered version with controller support, Mac+PC ports.
+ Uncut version (yeah, there're sex scenes in game).
+ Cheap (got this when it was 75% off on Nuuvem, about ~$1.89).
Cons:
+ Annoying quick-time events. They're based on PS2 control scheme. Beware: ASWD is your left controller analog and mouse is your right controller analog, use them wisely when you're playing guitar.
+ Dated graphics.
+ Random crashes during gameplay.
Overall rating: 8.5/10.

Having not really played any collectathon platformers prior to this, and therefore having not much of an opinion on the genre, I have to say that A Hat in Time is easily one of the best games I have ever played.
The game is great to control, the protagonist Hat Kid moves fluidly and at no point did I ever feel like I was fighting the controls to do what I wanted. The level design itself is amazing - the environments that you explore are unique and varied, and are open to explore and search for collectibles and secrets. The collectibles themselves never feel like a chore to find, as they help unlock both upgrades for Hat Kid to improve her arsenal, and cosmetic changes to allow for you to customise Hat Kid.
Charm oozes from this game, between the world and characters that inhabit it. Hat Kid is simply a very adorable protagonist, shown mostly through her animations in the game and the few small lines of dialogue that she speaks. Most of the characters are memorable and have genuinely funny dialogue, which is backed up by good voice acting. The places you visit are all unique, vibrant and full of things to look at and explore, which backs up its already great level design. The soundtrack is fantastic, Pascal Michael Stiefel, Grant Kirkhope, and the rest of the composers outdid themselves, with every track being great to listen to, which really helps you get immersed into the experience that this game provides.
Overall, you should definitely give this game a look, and possibly even try it. It's one of the most fun, charming and polished games that exists right now. It's left a massively good impression on me, and I plan to keep on playing it in the future, especially once the modding support comes out (which will be very soon), as well as finally go and try out the games that inspired this wonderful game.

A weird, brilliant, beautiful game that's still my favorite, after ten years and hundreds (thousands?) of other games. In the first scene you're standing over a body that you can't remember killing, and it doesn't slow down from there. There's a "stress" game mechanic where you have to drink coffee, have sex, and do other morale-boosting things to keep from going totally insane. Which, under the circumstances, is a challenge. (Doing things like leaving bloody clothing where people can see it? Stressful, and there may not be enough coffee in the world to make up for it.)
I'm having trouble explaining why this game is so amazing... the epic plot is one not everyone appreciates (it could've used a sequel or two to expand on what's eventually revealed about the underlying world and causes) but that's not really the point. You're fighting to survive, make sense of the world, and keep your mind intact from one scene to the next. It's immersive to the point that if your character gets hit, you wince.
By the way, you play as three distinct characters (mostly) so you'll be thrown into the shoes of people who sometimes have different agendas, one after the other. Have fun trying to simultaneously cover up and investigate a crime - it'll make your head spin, but in a good way.

To sum it up, Quantic in 2005 tried something new and extremely innovative. Albeit in 2015 we had many examples of such, in 2005 there was no instance of it. Their advanture game was supposed to be interactive movie. The way you use your mouse / controller or even QTEs was supposed to reflec that. And no, in 2005 QTEs were not oversused all over the board and were acceptable by community.
Playing as three characters, of which one is trying to evade other two and other two are hunting him is extremely interesting. When on a scene you forget something, make a mess, you give incentive and easier job to detectives in question. Mix of mystery and detective work is where this game excelles even 10 years after its release.
BUT. This does not hold up to the hype. I don´t know what happened to writers team, but at half of the game, they started pushing story and extremely interesting dialogues into the background and bringing up the kung-fu, matrix cutsenes. Which looked in 05 really cool, however story suffers because of this. This can be overlooked if not for the last several chapters where plot twists are so ridicolious, the explanation behind everything is insulting and the main character suddenly becaomes zombie with all walking dead zombie characteristics murders it. It seems writers started with great idea, expanded upon it and than started to get stuck and when trying to invent the end they just went with this because "♥♥♥♥ it, we have deadline to make".
Still, even though the end if horrible, the rest of the game is so great that I am here, 10 years later, replaying the game for 5th time and purchasing the remastered version for 9 euro. There are very few games which can say the same about themselves.

As of writing this review i have played 1.5 hours (90 minutes). I Will be writing about the gameplay and the graphics, i will also write about all the good and bad things i came across while playing the game.
In this game you are a smart human, the world has been taken over by robots called bots. You look your part, a classic fat kid with wierd glasses that looks smart, this game does alot of that, using stereo types and issues in society like STD's. It uses all these things and makes jokes of them, which it manages to do with success. You have been captured by  the bots because you are too smart, you are put on a game show by bots for bots and your goal is to survive and escape the game show (as far as I could tell).  You are put through a bunch of challenges by the bots, you land on a planet you either defend from the bots or attack them, and there is always a timer to make sure some preasure is applied. By killing robots and their buildings you get money, in some levels you need a certain amount within the time limit and in some levels its just for the high score. However, you dont have any guns, or melee weapons, how do you kill bots? By fighting fire with fire, you use bots of your own to fight their bots, by spawning them from your mobile flying factory that is chained to you, you can accually defend yourself from the robots or attack their buildings.
Some robots fly, some walk, some drive, but they can all fight. For example some robots are used to blow up buildings on the fron lines and some are used to blow up buildings on the background. In some levels you get to place these buildings yourself. When you need to defend from the robots for example.
In many levels there is a difficulty slider where you can set how difficult you want the level to be. I have only played on 100% difficulty (probably the way the game is supposed to be played) but if a level is to hard you can half difficulty.
One thing i dont like about this game is that with the money you win you can buy extra bots to fight for you, special ones that are better but here is the deal, you get only one of them and one costs around 10 million I believe. In my oppinion this should be a matter of unlocking these bots and then you can spawn them in a challenge when you are able to spend your entire energy bar for example. Also with the money you win you can buy buildings, you can place one. I think it would be better if the amount you bought would be replenished at the start of every challenge.
The game lacks clarity of how to do things. A couple of times I ran into a situation where I finnaly realized after playing the level a couple of times what to do. The tutorial is a one time thing, meaning that once you click through it you cant get it back and you are on your own (as far as i know).
The graphics of this game are cartoon-ish but with more detail which is nice. it fits the game well i think. After all the whole game is based around a future where the robots have taken over and are producing entertainment for dumb humans by putting smart humans through deadly challenges on TV. The sound is just as cartoony, same for the music, it fits this game well, it goes along with the art style which is think is one of the most important things for sound and music.
Its a fun little game, with humor. I like the game because its goofy and you can quickly hop in and play the game for a few minutes. The gameplay itself is fun although it sometimes does not make it clear what, how, when or why. The single use bots and buildings are a minor downside since you could probably pass every level without them but i would like to see that change as i described before.
After taking all of this into consideration i give this game a 7/10. Its not a big game with tons of story to be had, the gameplay is simple yet fun. It could definatly improve on some pretty important aspects but i like it.
7/10. Fun Gameplay, good Graphics, nice sound and music, but gameplay could be improved uppon in diffrent areas.

Death by Game Show takes a new twist to what tower defence games are al about. Instead of being stuck onto a single map and having to defeat enemies wave after wave, Death by Game Show removes that element and replaces it with being able to walk around the battle feild spawning droids to help you survive.
This game takes a new way of playing tower defence games, and makes this game a very unique one at that. The way that you play the game is you are on this planet, there will be enemy droids spawning that will try to kill you. You have your buddy, which I can't really indentify what it is, that spawns friendly droids that will kill the other droids. The first few levels are fairly simple, you spawn in a bunch of droids to survive until the ship gets back so you can exit the level. But after the first few easy tutorial levels have finished then the game starts to get a lot more strategic. You cannot simply spawn in a bunch of friendly droids to kill all the others, as there is a energy bar that limits you to how many you can spawn at once. This game is fairly fun and easy to pick up and play. With a nice variety of different droids and buildings that you can place down to hekp hold off the opposing droids, there really is a lot of content in this game to play around with for the strategic side of the game. The game does seem to take a steep difficulty curve when you hit a specific level, dying over and over until you can either win or just exit the game completely. The soundtrack on the otherhand is truly brilliant and well suited to this type of game. I feel like there needs to be a bit more content in the game generally, as the game does seem to get repetitve after a little while of paying the game.
The graphics of this game are alright enough to stand upon looking at. But after a while of playing the game, it does get a little bit boring to look out. I think that most of the levels don't have much variaion in the background, and just seem to be copied from the previous level and added some buildings that spawn new enemies around the map. Although some of the buildings do look nice, there still just seems to be a lack of variation in what is in the backgrounds of each level.

Overall a very good survival game capable of producing some very tense moments, whether it's cresting a hill and coming face-to-face with a hungry wolf or fighting through a snowstorm hoping to find a deer carcass so you don't starve to death.
Pros:
- Great atmosphere: the map isn't extraordinarily large, but even after 15 hours I still get turned around in snowstorms and get lost.
- Very effective UI: looks good, is fairly intuitive, and does everything it needs to do.
- High quality voice acting.
- Unique and interesting graphics: the environment art especially is very good, frozen corpses could look a little better.
Cons:
- No jump button: for the most part, you can get where you need to go but there have been times where I've been stuck behind a waist-high obstacle.
- Loot spawns could be a little better: most times I find a nice assortment of loot, but from time-to-time I die simply because the loot I need just isn't available (for example: I ran out of water because there literally were no matches / firestarters / magnifying glasses anywhere, I searched for multiple real-life hours and was unable to melt snow or cook tea - just bad luck but could be implemented better).
I would definitely recommend, and am looking forward to future updates.

I so want to like this game and for that matter the series, because it has a lot of potential. But wouldn't recommend it to friends for the flaws - not just of the game but the series - particularly if single-player mode is of primary interest. Not that I have friends I recommend games to, but otherwise why would I leave a review here? However, please note that this is a review of the SINGLE-player campaign.
What I like about the idea of TW:Napoleon is the clear campaign, even if only the Europe scenario really counts. The problem lies in the execution, which simply isn't good enough in terms of AI at the normal level. I should add that I am not interested in multiplayer at all, in part because I'm bad enough at micromanaging on the battle map in part thanks to the utterly terrible interface for placing and moving units. But at least in single-player mode it has a pause button on the battle map, and I'm not afraid to use it.
On normal/normal I resolved to only use autoresolve, whether attacking or defending, figuring that as the leader of the armies of all France I'm more interest in grand strategy (I didn't twice, more on that later). Not that I didn't use Napoleon as my primary general, of course. Admittedly I did reload for misclicks and very occasionally to go back in time to correct a stupid mistake - stupid because of course I should have checked every single info panel every single turn.
Although it is very much a "one more turn" game, at a certain point as France you become sufficiently dominant to be able to afford 6 full stacks, keeping two of them in northern France for defence, one behind Napoleon, and the other two nearby, after you backstab the Austrians who are forced into a peace treaty after taking Vienna. So far, so historical. The thing is, the campaign is supposed to take from 1805 until 1812, but on normal/normal I had already taken a fair chunk out of Russia by the end of 1806 doing absolutely nothing special other than disbanding my navies on the first turn and autoresolving all battles with two full stacks, as well as leaving a full stack and some support in Vienna. That winter I rolled up the Ottoman Empire and then came back with Napoleon by sea to take Gibraltar.
But this is Total War! It's all about the battle map! I hear fanboys cry out. Again, the pathetic AI makes a mockery of that. Once Gibraltar was taken, it was WAR! Nelson's mighty fleet smashed a fleet of mine and dropped off Wellington in Corsica of all places. For some reason, I dropped off a three-star general and his smallish stack of militia there in the hope of achieving something, as well as launching a cross-channel operation on London that was fortunate enough to cross safely - my range of sight had grown showing it was not full thanks to my research of all but the very top tier technologies.
So anyway, I autoresolved that battle, slightly miffed that taking the rest of Britain wouldn't magically make their navy disappear, and went on to the next turn. I'd been building ships in the summer of 1807 to take back the armies of northern Russia that had taken the Northern Baltic over to Scotland, but the wonderful boarding "feature" failed so often I needed to go back to the autosave.
What the heck, why not fight the battle. So in town are four units of cannon fodder, that I spend about three minutes while paused trying to spread out in straight lines across the town. Wellington's Dragoons approach to just beyond musket range, the artillery starts shooting at the the townies, who in turn must be sh**ting themselves. The *** general appears at the far corner of the map, with four units of militia. Wellington realigns his forces in the direction of the approaching "danger", despite it being nowhere in range even for the three units of artillery he has. The remainder are Elite Foot Guards, and although it isn't a full stack, there are perhaps eight of them. The Dragoons attack my militia as they mass to form lines of attack rather than columns vulnerable to cannon fire, and in fact the cannons ROUT my general. And yet, the townsfolk in their four units are left to shoot at two of the three six-pounders - horse-drawn ones at that - with impunity before also aiming at Wellington and running him off to recover in Dublin to be vanquished in November 1807.
I could write far more scathing words on the user interface in terms of being able to do what you want to do, like attach a spy to Napoleon's entourage that won't stay in every town he conquers, or not being able to prioritise certain types of construction, or for that matter that only building the top tier of buildings in the capital will allow all research. Yes, 'groups' can be made in the battle interface, but essentially if you are playing to win on the battle map - or even survive with minimal losses - you have to micromanage unit by unit to an even worse degree.
In summary, although it is ludicrous that a battle between a balanced AI stack of elite units with their top general can be beaten by a similar sized stack of the lowest tier of general who leaves the battlefield first and militia supported by an additional four town defenders sallying forth, it's the AI of the campaign that leaves me even more disappointed. Yes, I know there is a hard and also a very hard mode, and for fans of the series who also like exploiting the stupidity of the AI when fighting human players I'm sure there is some enjoyment.

. "Killstagram" (Now called "SUPERHOT Video" for PC reasons I imagine) is also a really sweet and unique feature.  You can seamlessly upload replays in game to
to be shared on social media.  All in all this is a fantastic game, I am a big fan of endless games and I will be putting many of hours into this.  Easily one of my favorite FPS games.

Right, alot of downvotes because I am not bashing the game with an ignorant and/or snarky three sentence review.  Let me clarify, I could care less whether or not you like the game. However, it is common knowledge that the game is a score attack/mechanic driven game. So, when you buy and then write a "wtf 2 hours for 25 dollars!1!1" negative review you are making yourself look like a fool, and  perpetuating a fallacy.  I agree SUPERHOT isn't for everyone. As I stated before, complaining the story wasn't long enough
is utterly absurd.
SUPERHOT was funded for the SOLE purpose of having tons of endless and challenge modes. If people bashing the game bothered to research before purchasing they would have known this. If you even did a quarter of the challenges available you would get your moneys worth. Criticizing a game for what it isn't trying to be is the very definition of entitlement. I legitimately haven't seen a vaild criticism of the game yet besides "hurr durr it's 2 hours".  Look at the description, it doesn't even mention a campaign. This game is probably one of the best to come from crowdfunding, it delivered EXACTLY what the backers wanted.
At the end of the day whether or not it is worth the price is dependent on what you think of the time slowing mechanic. If you saw the mechanic and went "meh" you will be bored probably within three hours. If you were fascinated by a revolutionary step in an otherwise stagnant FPS genre seeing thousands of opportunities, you will be occupied for HOURS.
I have never been one to take Steam reviews as the gospel.  Especially now after seeing all the negative 2 sentence snarky reviews getting thrust to the top of the SUPERHOT page.  I am very glad that the critical reception has been very positive.  However, in the user Steam reviews I have seen a vocal minority insulting the dev's artistic vision, questioning their character, even going as far as to call them "disingenuous".  Frankly, it is really childish to me to hate a game just because it wasn't what you expected.  I wish the team the best of luck and I hope they make enough cash to embark on another endeavor, they deserve it.

When I saw the price, my first thought was that it was too high, but after beating the campaign and going through some endless levels and challenges, I realized that I could be wrong... I mean there's enough content here to justify the price, but ONLY if you truly enjoy the gameplay, and if you're also into speedrunning, or getting every last achievement. Those are the 3 biggest factors you need to consider when making your decision, which is why if you're on the fence, I highly advise you to try the prototype on their website(
). The only gameplay difference between the prototype and the game now, is the ability to throw anything you can pick-up. Hitting an armed enemy with a throw, disarms them, allowing you to grab their weapon mid-air.
One thing you may notice after playing the prototype, is that it can actually get pretty difficult. In fact some of the levels in the campaign and a majority, if not all the challenges, will test your ability to cope with 'Super Meat Boy' levels of frustration. Now if that sounds fun to you, great, but also consider all the achievements you can collect, and how you can show off to all your friends how fast you can finish every challenge and level. Neat!
So basically, if you like dodging bullets in slow-motion and are somewhat of a masochist, you'll get A LOT out of this game, but if you're still on the fence, there's nothing wrong with waiting. I mean you can always play Evolve... ok realistically, there's Unturned's BR-like arenas (which is free), or 'Paint the Town Red' if you want to go on a killing spree.
Now I'm not going to give it a score, but I will say that I enjoyed the challenge and it's overall aestheic. It did get tedius at times, but the stylish kills, along with the end-of-level video replay kept me going. I can also see myself playing the challenges and endless levels to kill time... literally (...ok what do I even mean? ...Kappa)

This game really encapsulates that nostalgic feeling Yooka-Laylee was trying so hard to hit on, while also being an entirely new IP. The controls are really tight when using a controller, but the game really isn't at it's best when played with mouse and keyboard. The only thing I found took a little getting used to was wall running and triangle jumping. Hat Kid does it automatically when jumping into a wall, not when you press the jump button again.
The hats seem really varied, and they are, but outside their main uses they don't really do much else. The ice hat turns you to ice so you can catapult yourself, and nothing else. Only two or three of them really help at all when it comes to combat, and even then it's very situational.
Hat Kid is absolutely the cutest protagonist in any platformer I've seen, and that design really carries over to the rest of the world and its characters. It's a very visually pleasing game to look at, and the whole game oozes with creativity and charm. The tone is all over the place, however, though that sometimes works to the game's benefit. One mission is a hilarious romp through a city, the next is teeth-grittingly difficult, and the one after that is a mini horror game (yes, really).
All in all an enjoyable, fun game with it's own style and humour that really lets the game shine. A few minor kinks here and there don't ruin the overall experience that really, really makes me want to boot up Banjo-Tooie again.
