Now, its final conclusion isn't something that mindblowing, it's just barely thought-provoking. I've read that you can only truly understand the game and love it if you've been through a depression at some point in your life. I gotta say, that might be true, because I (fortunately) haven't been through such kind of phase, ever, and the game didn't connect with me on an emotional level. Or rather, it did, but only to disappoint me.
You see, the final message is somewhat interesting - when judging other people through their work, don't cast the shadow of your own values, fears, ideas or expectations on their persona. Don't assume someone is lonely because they drew an empty room. Don't assume Seth from Superbad is gay because he couldn't help drawing c*** all over in middle school.
And that's it.
The game is just tedious and a bit pretentious, really. Not much else to read into it.

Everything, from the level design, character design, sound design, etc is completely polished to a delightful degree. The controls are pure butter, I have honestly never played another platformer that felt this good to control, and it feels extremely rewarding when you start to get really good with them.
The game is adorable from head to toe. The characters are charming, the levels are intriguing and incredibly varied. There are quite a few glitches that have to be smoothed over but with a reasonable amount of community input I can see that not being a problem at all in the near future.
And the music. My god, the music. Stiefel didn't just emulate the styles of Kirkhope and Kondo, he created a masterpiece of constantly evolving tunes that occasionally make you set the controller down and just listen.
As many have said, the game is very short, taking less than 15 hours to fully 100%, but every single collectable feels like a fantastic journey in and of itself, the game trying its hardest to never feel stale and succeeding forthright. In the end, it feels like the perfect length to a sweet little quest.
I really can't say enough good things about this game, it's just so incredibly satisfying. It makes obvious what it takes its inspiration from but does not hang from their coat-tails. I think GfB have a very promising future in this business!

A Hat in Time is a solid, charming, and fun little gem of a game.
I backed this game when its Kickstarter launched, and the moment they had the Alpha up I knew it would be good - it definitely needed time in the kettle then, and now, three years after the Kickstarter, it's finally out. Definitely worth the three year wait.
The game plays solidly - it's a 3D collect-a-thon platformer in the same vein as Banjo Kazooie (which I've never played) and games like the old Spyro trilogy (which I've played a ton of.) It certainly plays smoothly, even on a mouse and keyboard. There were a few spots where I struggled to get timing right, mainly with stuff involving the Dweller's Mask, but overall nothing would really frustrate you for bad handling.
Graphically, the game is a beauty. The characters are absolutely charming, and the environments are lush and beautiful. The game even gets a lil creepy at certain parts, and works it out really well! The levels are varied and carry a unique feel to each one.
The music and sound design is fantastic - the voice acting is great, although I'm pretty sure they ripped out a certain NPCs voices due to dumb backlash - which is a huge shame, in my opinion. Each level has really great music, with a few getting remixes as well due to the Kickstarter stretch goals. You can also opt to go for garbled dialogue by getting a badge, if you want it to feel more like Kazooie.
Everything about this game is great - really, the only thing that's bad is that it's pretty darned short, so hopefully Gears for Breakfast will find a way to give more content some time!
Absolutely recommend this game if you love platformers or if you loved old platformer games like Spyro and such, it carries a lot of the charm that those older games had in a nice, modern package!
Really good to see this be such a success!

My go-to local multiplayer game.
It's a game you can play with anybody who has ever held a controller, right away, without really having to explain in great detail what you are supposed to do and how.
"You shoot your arrow with X and you jump with A. You have a limited number of arrows. There are treasure chests with bonus items poping up from time to time."
When they get the hang of it by the second game: "By the way, you can dash with the shoulder buttons. While you are dashing you can grab arrow flying at you out of the air."
Everything else can be grasped by playing, and once you have those few rules down, you can start building your strategy, trying new stuff, and see what works.
There is of course a level of mastery you can get to in the game that will make you more or less unbeatable by someone just starting to play.  But that's par for the course for great party games that are not based on luck alone, and the default settings try to help out the players lagging behind in points by giving them a extra hit point a the start of the round.
There is also a great, and really challenging coop mode.
No online play, and playing alone against the CPU can be fun, but the game is first and foremost build to be a great local multyplayer experience.

Imagine a DVD player which is powered by you playing Guitar Hero on Expert mode with a mouse. Combine it with a terrific thriller to get Fahrenheit: a horrendous video game hiding a great cinematic experience.
When it came out in 2005, Fahrenheit offered something new by focusing exclusively on the narrative and nothing else. It was a true interactive movie with cinematic techniques like split scenes displaying the same events from multiple points of view (like in the TV show ‘24’).
The plot is entirely character-driven and focuses on three main leads: Lukas, a murderer on the run; and Carla and Tyler, the two detectives on his trail. Their stories are split into more than thirty chapters on two separate threads that eventually meet in one big finale.
A finale about superpowers, Mayan prophecies, an artificial intelligence, and somehow preventing the freezing of the planet with a martial arts showdown against an immortal priest. If you thought the end of Matrix: Revolutions jumped the rails, it has nothing on this game.
Sadly the derailment of the plot is vastly overshadowed by gameplay issues. The controls are horrid, no matter what control scheme you choose: for example, basic actions like picking up something require at least four-five mouse or stick gestures with bad movement detection. The few puzzles make absolutely no sense, and all key scenes are progressed by playing a double quick-time event that obstructs the entire screen. By the way, on
mode, this minigame leaves roughly a quarter of a second window for each action before failing.
I have no doubts that Fahrenheit was one of the best things ever in its time, but it aged horribly. If you missed it originally, you are far better off just watching a longplay than trying to suffer through its controls.

Red Orchestra 2 manages to straddle that fine line between semi-realism and gameplay. This is one of those rare and excellent Second World War shooters to play. It is highly thrilling, tense and satisfying. Weapons and bullet drop are represented impressively and the sense of accomplishment from survival and completing objectives make it worthwhile.
An authentic level of vulnerability, tension and stress makes the game harrowing. It is rare to find a game that almost captures the brutality and intensity, but I find that Red Orchestra 2 comes quite close.
Athough not perfect, with several awkward flaws (weapons unlock and casual modes) and rough implementation (campaign mode), for someone like myself not inclined to shooters I cannot seem to figure out how Red Orchestra suceeds. Teamwork matters between the commander and squads while caution and bravado occasionally nets results. I am not sure I will find another game in the future as compelling as this, in an age of shooters too afraid to offer tactical depth at the expense of accessibility

This game reminds of a mashup of games like Life is Strange, Shadow of Memory's, Broken Sword and Silent Hill with a few others I'm sure that other people might pickup on. Overall the game is fun, visually interesting and has a reasonably strong atmosphere and soundtrack. However, there are quite a few flaws. The controls and camera are frustrating, even more so on stealth and timed sequences. The action sequences distract the player from what's taking place on the screen and are too easy once the player has got to grips with it and it's difficult to define what constitutes a passed or failed attempt at hitting the required buttons in time. Another major flaw is the story, which starts out as quite an intriguing mistery but ends up a completely confusing mess with elements that seem to be thrown in the mix for the sake of it. The characters don't have much depth and It also feels like developments in character relationships take huge leaps in short spaces of time and theres some parts that just absolutely make no sense towards the end and other parts that appear completely unecessary. I'd probably say this game is worth playing because it's fun, atmospheric and innovative but it could have been so much better.

Death by Game Show is a 2D strategy- type of a indie tower defense game. Game is based in 26th century where apparently everyone else is stupid and our hero is way too smart and is therefor sentenced to rehabilitation. Rehabilitation turns out to be a TV-show where audience awaits your death and the main idea of the game is to avoid dying.
Right from the beginning I found the graphics really appealing for an indie game, lacking only the differences between two of a kind of robots or buildings. Every explosion and critical hit is presented in a comic book- way which adds a nice little touch with matched sound effects. The one and only background tune that is constantly playing, however, quickly becomes annoying and you start wishing for any Justin Bieber song instead. Extra points for the Big Arnie's
phrase, always could be more of these!
The death match happens on a circular planet- map between two electric fences where you will have to use strategic skills and planning in a strategic view in order to destroy enemy robots and buildings, as there is never enough time nor energy. You spawn the robots by pressing keys 1 - 0 on your keyboard and build the buildings as well as use the boosters with your mouse, which sometimes didn't respond correctly to my actions.
Game is fun for the first 40 minutes where you finish the tutorial and do some of the easy levels of the game. I found it hard to follow the instructions since there were a lot of text content on the screen, but after 5 minutes of playing you get used to the excess signs between every inch of the screen.
After 40 minutes of playing, game becomes grinding hell where you need to run previous levels multiple times to buy yourself a good amount of boosters and buildings to finally pass the next round. Level 14 alone took me 40 minutes to pass, even with 0% difficulty slider - which I think is way too long for an indie game that has 50 levels, with even harder achievements.
After a few level optimizations should become greater than Fallout
!
PLUSSES AND MINUSES:
difficulty of levels
background tune becomes annoying after a while
becomes grinding in terms of replaying
many levels
achievements and trading cards on Steam
random comments such as "Get to da choppa!"
hours of fun

Banished is the closest a city builder can get to a survival game.  You start off with a small number of families banished from another town sometime in the Dark Ages.  With these few families, you have build a new self sustaining town that can supply it's own food, firewood, and clothes.  It's not that easy and it took my at least 20 hours (and countless restarts) to get a town up to 100-200 people. I have a special place in my heart for city builders, and this game puts enough of a new spin in the genre that sucked me right in.  You have to balance expansion with your food/clothes supply and things can go really bad really fast. It is not unusual to have one bad winter where half of your population just dies off.  Like FTL and Spelunky, you learn from your failures and there's this desire to immediately restart with new ideas. Here is a list of ways my town has utterly collapsed.
1. I forgot to build a tailor. We had a terrible winter and people started freezing to death.  By the time I realized my mistake, I was down to 2 people (out of about 50).  Those two dudes froze to death while building the tailor building.
2. Ran out of food. A band of nomads wanted to settle in my town, so I let them.  Unfortunately, I didn't have enough of a food supply to satisfy all the extra mouths.  Everyone was dead within a year.
After all of this, the music is really good.  This is the most relaxing game I've played all year.
5/5 Recommended.  This game puts a nice take on city builders.

Overall a very good survival game capable of producing some very tense moments, whether it's cresting a hill and coming face-to-face with a hungry wolf or fighting through a snowstorm hoping to find a deer carcass so you don't starve to death.
Pros:
- Great atmosphere: the map isn't extraordinarily large, but even after 15 hours I still get turned around in snowstorms and get lost.
- Very effective UI: looks good, is fairly intuitive, and does everything it needs to do.
- High quality voice acting.
- Unique and interesting graphics: the environment art especially is very good, frozen corpses could look a little better.
Cons:
- No jump button: for the most part, you can get where you need to go but there have been times where I've been stuck behind a waist-high obstacle.
- Loot spawns could be a little better: most times I find a nice assortment of loot, but from time-to-time I die simply because the loot I need just isn't available (for example: I ran out of water because there literally were no matches / firestarters / magnifying glasses anywhere, I searched for multiple real-life hours and was unable to melt snow or cook tea - just bad luck but could be implemented better).
I would definitely recommend, and am looking forward to future updates.

When I saw the price, my first thought was that it was too high, but after beating the campaign and going through some endless levels and challenges, I realized that I could be wrong... I mean there's enough content here to justify the price, but ONLY if you truly enjoy the gameplay, and if you're also into speedrunning, or getting every last achievement. Those are the 3 biggest factors you need to consider when making your decision, which is why if you're on the fence, I highly advise you to try the prototype on their website(
). The only gameplay difference between the prototype and the game now, is the ability to throw anything you can pick-up. Hitting an armed enemy with a throw, disarms them, allowing you to grab their weapon mid-air.
One thing you may notice after playing the prototype, is that it can actually get pretty difficult. In fact some of the levels in the campaign and a majority, if not all the challenges, will test your ability to cope with 'Super Meat Boy' levels of frustration. Now if that sounds fun to you, great, but also consider all the achievements you can collect, and how you can show off to all your friends how fast you can finish every challenge and level. Neat!
So basically, if you like dodging bullets in slow-motion and are somewhat of a masochist, you'll get A LOT out of this game, but if you're still on the fence, there's nothing wrong with waiting. I mean you can always play Evolve... ok realistically, there's Unturned's BR-like arenas (which is free), or 'Paint the Town Red' if you want to go on a killing spree.
Now I'm not going to give it a score, but I will say that I enjoyed the challenge and it's overall aestheic. It did get tedius at times, but the stylish kills, along with the end-of-level video replay kept me going. I can also see myself playing the challenges and endless levels to kill time... literally (...ok what do I even mean? ...Kappa)

Banished is a city-builder game which is mostly about survival. While it may seem that there is not that much content (types of buildings etc.) you won't notice since the game plays relatively slowly and it takes a time to build a solid town. You will find yourself struggling mainly in the early years as the firs few winters tend to be the hardest, yet you musn't let your guard down even in later years as the careful planning is crucial and key to be succesful in this game. Me for example I was able to build a city of some 600 people and I was doing great, but since I had bad infrastracture and didn't place the buildings in efficient manner, the whole system collapsed on itself... population dropped by roughly 400 individuals due to starvation and my town became a ghost towm... The game is challenging and quite addictive despite being relatively simplistic, I'd say there is a steep learning curve, as beginners will probably struggle for first two or three games but once you pick up basics (and there isn't really much to pick up) it is relatively easy. Despite the game being fun you will find it a little bare and with low content once you master it, but until you do, it should be fun. Definetely grab it if it's on sale!    7/10

First and foremost: if you were hoping for another Tales of Vesperia you should look elsewhere. Even without unfair comparison, Zestiria is not a great game. Thankfully the port runs smoothly and looks great (a promising sign for the future) but almost every facet of the game is disappointing.
Going for the low hanging fruit, the plot and characters are hideous anime cliches through and through. The protagonist is wide-eyed and bushy-tailed but naive and idealistic, one of the female protagonist is kind of the same but calm and royalty while the other one is kind of wild and energetic. All the seraphs are just different shades of anime: mother figure, cynical one, older realistic brother figure, dark mysterious dude. Really tiring and boring garbage.
Combat is frankly a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Without barfing a dissertation onto you, there are three different types of attacks that break each other in a rock-scissor-paper fashion which is often obnoxious to put to any use. Combat often felt like a cluster♥♥♥♥ of getting the right combo off at the right time and praying the enemy didn't start channelling an attack that opposed yours. Bosses require that you armatise with their elemental weakness in mind otherwise you will straight up get stomped every time.
Equipment sucks as well. No learning neat abilities or artes, they just have various stat boosts and other assorted passives. You can only fuse the same pieces of equipment to produce higher leveled versions of that (e.g. vest + vest = vest +2!) and the boosts, of which there can only be a max of four, interact to make new stat boosts. This interaction further depends on whether the equipment is mastered or not either. Mastering equipment does nothing outside of fusion. It's pretty tedious and extremely bad.
So yeah, there is little to really like about Tales of Zestiria. I very stupidly tried to push myself through this game and at 35 hours I realised I still couldn't see the end in sight and was completely sick of every single aspect.
TL;DR? This isn't Tales of Vesperia.

This game really encapsulates that nostalgic feeling Yooka-Laylee was trying so hard to hit on, while also being an entirely new IP. The controls are really tight when using a controller, but the game really isn't at it's best when played with mouse and keyboard. The only thing I found took a little getting used to was wall running and triangle jumping. Hat Kid does it automatically when jumping into a wall, not when you press the jump button again.
The hats seem really varied, and they are, but outside their main uses they don't really do much else. The ice hat turns you to ice so you can catapult yourself, and nothing else. Only two or three of them really help at all when it comes to combat, and even then it's very situational.
Hat Kid is absolutely the cutest protagonist in any platformer I've seen, and that design really carries over to the rest of the world and its characters. It's a very visually pleasing game to look at, and the whole game oozes with creativity and charm. The tone is all over the place, however, though that sometimes works to the game's benefit. One mission is a hilarious romp through a city, the next is teeth-grittingly difficult, and the one after that is a mini horror game (yes, really).
All in all an enjoyable, fun game with it's own style and humour that really lets the game shine. A few minor kinks here and there don't ruin the overall experience that really, really makes me want to boot up Banjo-Tooie again.

Short but sweet.
This is one of the most satisfying and fulfilling games I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. Everything, from the level design, character design, sound design, etc is completely polished to a delightful degree. The controls are pure butter, I have honestly never played another platformer that felt this good to control, and it feels extremely rewarding when you start to get really good with them.
The game is adorable from head to toe. The characters are charming, the levels are intriguing and incredibly varied. There are quite a few glitches that have to be smoothed over but with a reasonable amount of community input I can see that not being a problem at all in the near future.
And the music. My god, the music. Stiefel didn't just emulate the styles of Kirkhope and Kondo, he created a masterpiece of constantly evolving tunes that occasionally make you set the controller down and just listen.
As many have said, the game is very short, taking less than 15 hours to fully 100%, but every single collectable feels like a fantastic journey in and of itself, the game trying its hardest to never feel stale and succeeding forthright. In the end, it feels like the perfect length to a sweet little quest.
I really can't say enough good things about this game, it's just so incredibly satisfying. It makes obvious what it takes its inspiration from but does not hang from their coat-tails. I think GfB have a very promising future in this business!

I'll be quick (which, for me, is a rarity). This is a perfectly fine game - competently designed, handles smoothly, controls like a twin-stick shooter should. It just feels slightly unambitious, or like Wizbyte got it as far as "solidly functioning" and chose not to go any further. Balance problems pop up early, with a bit of a "hurry up and wait" flow to the game. The fact that the main enemies have strict pursuit AI means that the game does not demand the chaotic hand independence of, say, Robotron 2084. There are a few instances of lacking in polish, too - I run the game in a downscaled resolution, and the bomb count and score multiplier are on top of each other, so I have no idea what my value for either is.
If you cannot get enough twin-stick shooters, or if you've never played one, you probably won't regret buying this, but it's hard to recommend when, even in my limited experience, I've played a few others that better capture the essence of this style of game.

Wow! Five Nights At Freddy's is fun. It may be repetitive, but it is also addicting. The complete story of the game is that you find an ad in the paper. If you like repetitive games and jumpscares as well as excitement and dread every second you play, I highly recommend "Five Nights at Freddy's".

After having some time to think about it, I'm kinda bummed on this "game". It wasn't a bad experience, it just wasn't fun. I feel like I just watched someone go through therapy, and while it was engaging I don't feel like I should have paid money for it. This was Wredens anxiety about The Stanley Parable's popularity made into game form...at least thats what I made of it. It was so personal I almost felt intrusive, but then I reminded myself that Wreden was the one that put his psyche on display for the world to see for 10 bucks, and looking at it that way kind of made me mad. I'm a bit put off by the fact that this guy thought his dilemma was so special that I would pay money to experience it. Had I known thats all this "game" was I wouldn't have bothered. He could have at least had the decency to make a game around his very self-centered theme, instead of just making a (kind of boring) walking tour.
I think the thing that bugged me the most early on (and pretty much put this "game" in the "psuedo-intellectual hipster BS" category) is the way Wreden keeps referring to his (or Coda's, whatev) creations as "games", and rambling on about what makes them so special. Art may be subjective, but games are not. There are a few rules as to what makes a game, and The Beginner's Guide had none of them. There was no way to fail or succeed, you just went along for the ride...in fact it kind of reminded me of a dark ride. It honestly would have been no different as a non-interactive movie.
Also, and this is just me personally, but the heavy-handed "moral of the story" was not very revelatory to me. I could even identify with it, having been on both ends of the dilemma, but it wasn't something worth making a whole "game" about.
Its an interesting experience but I wouldn't call it a game...or pay money for it.

A Hat in Time is a solid, charming, and fun little gem of a game.
I backed this game when its Kickstarter launched, and the moment they had the Alpha up I knew it would be good - it definitely needed time in the kettle then, and now, three years after the Kickstarter, it's finally out. Definitely worth the three year wait.
The game plays solidly - it's a 3D collect-a-thon platformer in the same vein as Banjo Kazooie (which I've never played) and games like the old Spyro trilogy (which I've played a ton of.) It certainly plays smoothly, even on a mouse and keyboard. There were a few spots where I struggled to get timing right, mainly with stuff involving the Dweller's Mask, but overall nothing would really frustrate you for bad handling.
Graphically, the game is a beauty. The characters are absolutely charming, and the environments are lush and beautiful. The game even gets a lil creepy at certain parts, and works it out really well! The levels are varied and carry a unique feel to each one.
The music and sound design is fantastic - the voice acting is great, although I'm pretty sure they ripped out a certain NPCs voices due to dumb backlash - which is a huge shame, in my opinion. Each level has really great music, with a few getting remixes as well due to the Kickstarter stretch goals. You can also opt to go for garbled dialogue by getting a badge, if you want it to feel more like Kazooie.
Everything about this game is great - really, the only thing that's bad is that it's pretty darned short, so hopefully Gears for Breakfast will find a way to give more content some time!
Absolutely recommend this game if you love platformers or if you loved old platformer games like Spyro and such, it carries a lot of the charm that those older games had in a nice, modern package!
Really good to see this be such a success!

TL:DR for ex-robocraft players: You are playing Mars Crater and everyone is playing Rail Walkers.
TL:DR (for everyone else) - Small maps, little cover and auto-spotting
favor the point and click nature of long range armor cubes.
The game itself has massive potential, though it's currently plagued by a couple of problems that complement each other resulting in a huge issue..
By reading other reviews you are probably aware of the "long range" builds issue with about 44.2% of the community focusing on two longest range weapons. You can find the data on the Dev diary #21 on the official site.
I mean Jesus, how do you end up with almost half the community using only two weapons out of 7 total?
We'll I'll tell ya, now buckle up, this is gonna be a long one.
(As usually happens with my rants when I have a love/hate relationship with something)
The major factors that are causing this issue:
1. Automatic spotting regardless of distance
2. Relatively small maps with huge open areas and very little to no cover
3. Simpler ship design when building a long range build. (fewer things to worry about)
4. The "buffer"
#1 - Automatic spotting regardless of distance
Looking at this alone doesn't seem like a huge deal, and in
areas of
maps its not a big problem. But it gets worse, or better in the case of 44.2% of players. xD
#2 - Relatively small maps with huge open areas and very little to no cover
Now when we look at the number 1 and 2 together, you don't need a PhD in map design to figure out which classes will benefit the most out of that. Add more stuff to maps, don't leave such massive open areas that allow the long ranged ships spot and engage threats the moment they get in range.
Some potential weapon solutions can be seen in Robocraft ( I know I keep comparing these two, but alot of the problems are pretty much interchangeable). The range advantage was was reduced by adding the laser indicator that lets the targeted player know that they are being targeted, so he can start dodging or engage back. Other things that reduced the effectiveness of the long range (railguns atleast) were the slow turn rate and somewhat long recharge time between shots, leaving them vulnerable to fast moving close range vehicles and forcing them to pick their shots and not just spam left click at the first name that turns white.
#3 - Simpler ship design when building a long range build.
It's like point building characters in RPGs, you will have dumpstats, aka aspects that will get neglected to the lowest possible state that doesn't overall compromise the build in a significant way.
You don't need insane speed, or incredibly fast turning rates, mostly because you can outrange or match anything that can threaten you the moment it's in your line of sight. Not to mention, you'll probably be aware of the threat long before they get to threaten you due to how the spotting works right now.
So the result is people simply making so called "Borg cubes" that cover a large portion of the map, particularly from the top.
4. The distance "buffer".
You will notice that gauss based builds end up dying far less often than average (in the graphs I initially mentioned). Atleast in the case of cannons, they have that buffer distance which allows them to engage the short/medium ranged enemy long before they are within range to respond. That usually results in you loosing a component, getting your core exposed or even getting outright destroyed before reaching cover.
Now some will argue that they "need to git gud" and dodge, which you can try, but as mentioned in 1. and 2. the maps are universally open if not to all sides then atleast from above. to amplify the problem further, you will be constantly marked as long as you are in the line of sight of any other enemy, which is pretty much all of the time, resulting in the long range ship being ready for you once you pop out of cover whether to engange him or run away.
Essentially the effective range importance goes up as the map size and complexity go down. You cover a much bigger portion of the map and you end up threatening other ships from further away, while they have no effective way of fighting back.
Imagine encountering a group of such long ranged ships (with ~44.2% of people playing like that, that is statistically unavoidable) that can virtually make the entire map their killzone, while being able to cover each other at the same time. Countering something like that, well it leaves you with with few options out of which the most popular one is "Leave match".
The change the devs did on these weapons is welcome (largely futile), but it's only treating the symptom, not the cause.
Nerfing the cannons is merely a bandaid measure. As long as the maps are designed with large open areas where you'd get spotted the moment you pop out the domminant weapon will be whichever weapon has the longest range and the lowest skill requirement to use. Nerf the cannons and ubers bellow 3000, cruise missles will become popular, nerf the missles, heavy lasers will become popular. Balacing weapons this way can only go so far as it turns into a race to the bottom.
Other issue I have to mention are the range/damage abilities. This is an issue I often see with games that have any sort of customization.
If you intend to give players utility, stick to utility. The moment you give them ways to shorten the TTK (TTK - Time To Kill) those abilities will become the go-to abilities.
Anyone who has played CoD4 MW1 knows this, with everyone picking Stopping Power perk +40% DMG, essentially shortening the TTK by 1 hit on average. And in a game where most automatic weapons kill in 3 to 4 hits, lowering that by 1 is a huge deal.
Warframe also fell into this trap of the "game of numbers" years ago, with all weapon and warframe builds being laser focused on dishing out the highest possible DPS and some CC (though CC is another story).
So these are all the problems, but what of solutions. Well those might be obvious at the first glance, but will take a lot of work and time.
Larger maps, add some complexity, like those holes in that rock platform that cant fit oversized ships (forgot the name of the map).
No auto-spotting, use radars and jammers if you have to have an automatic way of spotting. Rewarding scouting and supporting in general would be a good idea as well.
The reason I wrote the "Great Wall of China" of text is that I really like this game and I'd hate to see it go down the same road of mistakes I've seen so many games follow. You guys have a good thing going here, don't let it go down in history like another robocraft.
Also from the data devs gave in that table show other implications besides the sheer popularity.
Average K/D ratios
Gauss Cannon: 1.47
Gattling Gauss: 1.34 (despite having the highest average kills)
Heavy Laser and Uber Cannon: 1.75 (the difference is 0.01)
Cruise missle: 0.97 (Probabbly due to the fiddly nature of the rocket AI)
And then the interesting part
Phaser: 0.84
Rocket Launchers: 0.71
So it must be a coincidence that the weapons that have the lowest K/D on average are also the weapons with the shortest range.

Red Orchestra 2 manages to straddle that fine line between semi-realism and gameplay. This is one of those rare and excellent Second World War shooters to play. It is highly thrilling, tense and satisfying. Weapons and bullet drop are represented impressively and the sense of accomplishment from survival and completing objectives make it worthwhile.
An authentic level of vulnerability, tension and stress makes the game harrowing. It is rare to find a game that almost captures the brutality and intensity, but I find that Red Orchestra 2 comes quite close.
Athough not perfect, with several awkward flaws (weapons unlock and casual modes) and rough implementation (campaign mode), for someone like myself not inclined to shooters I cannot seem to figure out how Red Orchestra suceeds. Teamwork matters between the commander and squads while caution and bravado occasionally nets results. I am not sure I will find another game in the future as compelling as this, in an age of shooters too afraid to offer tactical depth at the expense of accessibility

I honestly don't recommend it. The game is quite good and solid. It's a "super meat boy" style of game, with short "hard" stages but without the refining meat boy has. And that makes a great difference.
Super meat boy everything happens the same way, the same time, which gives you a learning curve for every stage where you learn the position of things and the timing to do them. Here in demon hearts you don't have the "timing" nor the "monsters" learning curve. The monsters position don't reset after death, or they reset at random positions, which nullifies 100% of the learning curve through "timing". Also some stages has moving plataforms that also doesn't reset or resets at random position.
Because of those two points, you most likely will be meeting the monsters with different timing and different positions which will result a slighty different comportament which will nullify the "monster" learning curve.
Not having this learning curve makes this game a completely different type of game and i didn't like it at all.
Most of the game is pretty easy and straight forward, but there was 2 stages (last boss and the last "cursed one" before the last boss) that were just way too hard. Since there's no "timing" and the monsters and the plataform would aways change position/comportament they were just annoying. Feel like you know pretty well how to finish them, but the slighty changes would break you off over and over again. That didn't gave me any satisfaction after i finished them, not having the "static stages" made me feel like i just had lucky that time and i were so annoyed that i just felt relieved rather than satisfied.
Still, the game, like i said before, IS solid and well made. It's also cheap, despise being quite short, so the price follows the time to beat it and for that i won't "not recommend".

Death by Game Show:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Life in the 26th century is a bit strange to say the least! Take the example of U.H.Wutt who was tried in court for being too smart! Yes, you read it right. To make even worse, he was sentence to rehabilitation . . . In the 26th century, rehab means you are going to overcome serious challenges to stay alive, as you are being sent to this strange game show called. . .  Death by Game Show! Sounds like a walk in the park to me. Oh, I do not want to be rude but I think the game host is about to present our new contestant and I have the feeling it might be our dear U.H. Wutt!
Death by Game show is a strategy/action/tower defence game where you play the smart and groovy U.H.Wutt, who was sentenced to . . .  Death by Game Show! When the opening scene ends, you will be dropped by a rocket on a groovy stage show, where droids will take pictures of you (a bit like Japanese tourists, the flashlight never stops)! Here you will be able to see your next challenge, as well as the reward allocated for successfully completing the challenge. It might be reaching a specific number of points within a time frame to gain a structure or a new droid.
You will spawn on a field which will have an electronic fence on each end of the screen. These fences are not too far apart and all the action will take place within them. You will have to defend U.H.WUTT and his G.I.M.P.
The G.I.M.P is a giant floating locker strapped to you. It is also where your droids will spawn but it has a limited amount of energy. If the energy bar is at its lowest, you will still be able to order droids but they will be deployed rather slowly.  You will have up to 10 units to use, 6 special moves and 11 structures to choose from. You will be able to gain additional structures, units and special moves through the wheel of fortune (well, this is what I call it). To be able to spin the wheel you have to collect a specific number of coins. How do you get coins? It is rather simple; just destroy the enemy units and buildings, run over the coins or use your grapping tool to get them. As soon as you get the right number of coins, you will be able to use the wheel but it does not mean you‘ll get an extra unit, special move or structure - you could get nothing at all! Just the luck of the draw, I guess.  Just keep picking up coins! Plan and get the right gear to succeed in your next challenge.
This is a game that has a fair bit going on at once, and to be truly honest with you, could deter people. But I think it is a charm that makes this game stand out from the others! You will have plenty of failure, but as we say, a failure is one step closer to success.
I really like the artwork in this game, it just fits so well. Great humour too, I like really like the voice saying “GET TO THE CHOPPER!” The controls are fine but it will take you some time to get used to all the units, special moves and buildings.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great artwork
-	Challenging and fun to play
-	Good humour
-	Plenty re-playability
-	Trading cards & Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Challenging levels can become frustrating at times
Death by Game Show is a challenging game with great artwork, humour and plenty of episodes/levels to play. Great fun!

OlliOlli2: Welcome to Olliwood is a hard as hell sidescroll arcade skate game, which is probably the best "skate" game you can get on Steam.
I'm a huge fan of the first one aswell, but in my opinion the developers managed to make a great game even better.
Here's why:
+
The first one had a great soundtrack, too and OlliOlli2 doesn't disappoint in the slightest with it's choice of music. It's a mixture of electronica, glitch & and hiphop (artists like CidRim or Kyle Cook) and does just fit so well to game. One of the reasons I like that game so much!
+
What makes OlliOlli2 such a great successor is the fact that they added plenty of new mechanics which make the game for one part more difficult but also way more entertaining. Now it is possible to get even bigger combos due to the new manuals and reverts. Also they added a bunch of new tricks (Double Treflip, Darkslide and others) and you're now allowed to change your trick while grinding (f.e. from Nosegrind to Crailslide). This makes the gameplay just so much more fun, as you have way more options to finish a level. The tricks are done similar to the game Skate by using the leftstick to perform different moves.
+
Another positive aspect is the overall more polished presentation and more responsive controls. While still retaining the retro look they also managed to make game look better overall. Also in the first part it sometimes felt like some controls weren't executed by the game (resulting in starting all over). Roll7 did a good job in fixing some minor issues.
Plus, the new levels look pretty great and have (especially in the later pro levels) a really nice level design. I sometimes had problems distinguishing some objects and obstacles in the first one, now everything is quite good to see.
+
The game isn't that expensive and for a really nice price you get a lot of content. You basically have 5 levels per world and 5 challenges per level. It takes a while to beat everything (took me around 8 hours for the amateur challenges), also you have lots of achievements and a nice feature called daily grind where you can play a level and compare you points on a worldwide leaderboard.
Oh, and there is an extra "spot" per level you have to skate in one combo, which also will be visible on a leaderboard.
~
I generelly like everything they added but I feel like they easily could add even more, f.e. Grabs, real Lateflips (can only be done with a trick combo f.e. Hardflip-LateShuvIt) and Flatlandtricks while manualing. I guess they keep that for another sequel.
~
I generelly don't see it as really flaw (I actually like it, you have quite a high skill ceiling) but it should be mentioned that it is a really difficult game and for some people maybe a lil bit too difficult.
-
I'm having a hard time finding anything bad, but there are some minor flaws I should mention. For example the game occasionally freezes for 2-3 seconds, which is absolutely deadly for such a fast paced game. This doesn't happen often, but it is still annoying. Also it would be awesome to see the different runs for highscores, which they sadly didn't add. (Maybe also a future thing).

Pros:
-Very good combat system
-Seamless transitions between battling and traveling
-Very good music
-Most in-depth character customization of any Tales game so far
-Well written dialogue (although delivery is all over the place in quality)
Cons:
-Much weaker story and characters when compared to older Tales games like Vesperia or Symphonia
-Animations and voice acting can be a bit goofy at times
-A bit of a slow burner. The game doesn't really start coming together until about 3 hours in
-Very easy combat unless you're playing on hard difficulty
Zestiria is kind of a "two steps forward, one step back" game. Compared to Xillia, the combat system and actual gameplay has been vastly improved. One of the biggest problems I had with Xillia was that it was simply too easy and the combat was unengaging. Zestiria fixed those problems and made the combat fun again (although you still need to be playing it on hard for it to be properly balanced). The step back is in the story. Its not bad by any means, but Zestiria probably has the most generic plot in the entire Tales series. The actual writing and dialogue between characters is fine (although the voice acting is all over the place), but the overarching story is a huge step back.
I don't think Zestiria brings the Tales franchise back to the glory days of Symphonia and Vesperia, but its definitely a step in the right direction.

So I may try to start again with this game later in the future, but the options of video games that I have have to change.  Simply, I don't see the point in playing this game with what games I have available.  With that said, there is more to it than that as to why I have stopped.  Really, the only good thing going for this game is that it is pretty in my opinion.  I enjoyed the tone of the game put forth by the graphic engine.  Other than that, I didn't really enjoy it, here's why:
1.)  Battling system is a mix between command oriented battle and hack in slash.  Let me tell you, they don't mix.  The control scheme is really peculiar.  For example, in order to run around, you have to hold down LT.  That was weird.  They made changing targets RB + direction.  For me, a better approach would be to make the battling hack n slash, which I don't understand why game designers don't do this.  In which case, you could make RB a dash.  The beginning of the game at least, the attack scheme is mindless.  Just bash B and press A every once in a while to get stun, and you win every fight.  Boss fights just require some dodging and using healing herbs that you pick up and you don't even have to pay for.  The cool part about the system is the right joystick in real time sends commands to your NPCs.  That's cool.  I hadn't gotten to the DPAD yet, I was wondering if they could just use that to switch targeting, but something tells me there is a purpose to it.  I am giving them the benefit of the doubt.
2.)  Battling system information.  The beginning of the game is filled with these stones where you get AP (useable) for reading them.  It's about this overly complex battling and equipment system.  Honestly, there is a part about equipment with how different logos align in the top right, that really over complicates things.  How these align, determine the bonuses that these equipment bring.  Or, you can just look at the resultant bonuses and just negate the whole color rune system.
3.)  SO MANY CUT SCENES.  Maybe there isn't as much as the game progresses, but I am barely fighting anything in my game and have to listen to a boring anime.  There isn't even action.  The game is really really slow, and I have barely leveled up.  This may change at the game progresses, but it takes a good while for the game to progress.
4.)  Storyline is completely predictable.  I already know what is going to happen in the entire game.  I won't "ruin" it for you, but you can piece it together in the very first part of the game.  That to me, makes the game very uninteresting.
Wonky controls and battle system, overly complicated equipment system, barely playing and a lot of cut scenes, followed by a story line that I already know the outcome, just makes me want to play another game.  I will only beat this game if I literally have nothing else to play.  Quite frankly, that won't happen for a long time.  I would advise people to try other RPG's.

Banished is a city-builder game which is mostly about survival. The game is challenging and quite addictive despite being relatively simplistic, I'd say there is a steep learning curve, as beginners will probably struggle for first two or three games but once you pick up basics (and there isn't really much to pick up) it is relatively easy. This was perhaps one of the best impulse buys I’ve made on Steam. Everything about it is quite excellent. The single player gameplay is a fun and exciting mix of turn-based grand strategy campaigns and real time tactical battles (which are entirely optional btw), neither of which require too steep a learning curve from past titles or comparable games. The graphics are top-notch for it’s time and I was pleasantly surprised that my HP notebook would keep pace. However, you will need to modify you’re preferences script to access higher levels, if you need help I’d be happy to provide instructions. The campaigns are excellent and can be completed on the lowest difficulties at around an hour (perfect if you’re short on time). The exposition given between campaigns by Marshal Louis-Alexandre Berthier does a great job in painting a rather charismatic and sympathetic picture of his emperor and friend. Finally, the sound and music provide an immersive, and sometimes cinematic, feel to an already great game. I can’t attest to the multiplayer because that’s not really my thing, but from my understanding there’s little difference from single player. The only complaint I do have are the relatively long loading times, which otherwise give little trouble.
Overall I’d have to say that for my first Total War game, Napoléon has been and impressive and memorable experience. I truly recommend it to anyone interested in Total War, grand strategy, or even the time period.
Final verdict: 10/10

Gameplay is fun, but battles become very quickly repetitive. There are a lot of fun mechanics that kept surprising me to the end. Side quests are meh but they do feel like they are part of the main quest rather than just for the sake of grinding. Once you finish the game, the game opens up with new content to explore either through new game+ or simply reloading a previous *cleared* save. The worst place was the trial of water, you have to avoid being seen by a blue eye by using one of your abilities. If you do get seen, you are transported all the way to the start of the trial which frustrated me to no end. My advice is to look for the eye on the ground, because you must be seen by that one in order to move on. There is neither dialog, nor any form of hint to tell you that, and it is only by running on it in frustration I figured that one out.
The story is generic and typical Japanese i.e. kids save the world, hesitant hero that can at times be annoying, he gets his♥♥♥♥♥kicked but through some dialog arise to kick♥♥♥♥♥
Music is without a constant genre, so it changes, while this is interesting, it pulled me out of the game a lot. Also, I don't remember a single song so thematically, it is underwhelming.
Most of the audio memory bank went to dialog and there is a lot of it. I found the acting of Mikleo to be the best one. Sorey had great moments too, but it fell flat on certain scenes. The female cast, I fear, had to imitate the Japanese performance too much, which caused them to become caricatures and fail. Denzel was pretty bad too.
Some of the best acting came from side characters.
Japanese audiences like when characters say the name of their abilities as they are cast. Unfortunately, it becomes very annoying too quickly and it got to the point I had to mod away the battle voices.
There is also a name mistake in the game. During one of the combat victory scenes, Sorey says Mikleo as Mikleeah
Sound design had some interesting moments but I felt it was really lacking outside of the anime cutscenes. Weapons sound the same, characters have no foley (cloth and armor movement sounds) when they move around, though Alisha  got some armor sounds during cutscenes, which was a nice touch, and spells are without any power behind them.
Graphics are fine, but I had to download a tool to make it run in 60FPS which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. At times, the eyes look very dead and you have no idea who they are looking at. While I really like the 2D skit scenes, I rather do without it if I can customize my characters as this is not reflected in the 2D art (Obvious why it isn't.) I am not a big fan of equipment you can put on that doesn't change the look of the character save the weapon. The customizing you can do, feels at times too silly and not very impressive though I did like the topknot. There seems to be a bug that causes characters to pop in and out very quickly, which annoyed the hell out of me.
While I can recommend the game, I would shy away from it if you are looking for a deep storyline, great voice acting and mind blowing graphics.
If you don't care about any of those too much, you'll have around 50-70 hours of gameplay.

As opposed to other game development tools I've experimented with, RPG Maker is one of the easier ones to understand and use, namely thanks to its hassle-free, WYSIWYG interface. The most basic features provide enough choices to make your RPG game stand out (with custom graphics, items, weapons etc.). For advanced users, there's also what's called RGSS3 - a scripting system with which you can modify your RPG game further, even as far as to turn it into an RTS or a 2D platformer! Different members of the RPG Maker community have made many awesome custom scripts and other resources for developers to check out and use.
In short, if you want to make your own RPG, get RPG Maker. Trust me, you won't regret it.

Let me just start by saying this: The game is not bad.
I won't spoil anything, but the last act of the game IS bad. Up until that point, the story was incredible. I felt attached to all the characters, was genuinely interested in seeing where the story would go, loved the music, and only closed the game out once in my time playing. Beat it in two sittings. Both were in the same day. Until I reached the ending, my only real complaint was the controls. They are pretty lackluster and it chock full of weird little gimmicky button sequences. Early QTE's if you will.
The last..oh..two hours however, in a roughly eight hour game, are bad. The plot gets completely thrown out the window and it feels like a new writer came in with no idea of what happened in the game prior to their arrival. It makes the ending feel really disappointing, undeserved, and off-putting.
I do like the game, honestly. But in the end, I really can't recommend it. You will love it up until that last act. If you really want a game that plays similar and has an infinitely more satisfying story, then I suggest Heavy Rain instead.

So, here we have a copy of Robocraft. One would think that the developpers learnt something from it, but actually it has exactly the same flaws as Robocraft. Yay?
Good stuff: Now fully 3d fast paced combat, controls are quite intuitive and the battle flows good.
Also building a robot... Sorry, I mean, an "space junk ship" is quite satisfying... the first three times. Then its always the same stuff: battle, get some coins (or pay for them if you wish), unlock new skills and modules and repeat.
But now let's be honest: How comes that you kept EXACTLY the same mechanics than in Robocraft?
Do you want to build an all-purpose ship? NOP! You can only select one kind of weapon.
Do you want to fully protect your ship? NOP! You are limited on the ammount of pieces you can add. Cheap mechanic as f(word). They could balace it so if you have a very heavy ship you will be slow, or loose power, or require more engines to actually keep flying... But Nop! Let's just limit the number of pieces you have!
The battles are short. WAY too short.
And, exactly as it happened in Robocraft, the players that have been playing longer are simply overpowered, so they will always lead the battle. Skill, you ask? Nop, simply better weapons and pieces.
Sill you may enjoy this game for... let's say 2 hours? Maybe a game you want to have installed to play something while the good games get updated.
Still free to play. I don't think much people would spend money on this.
Only good thing I can actually say: This is still an early access. Maybe the developpers will lsiten to the reviews and actually make this an appealing game. As it is right now I expect a very short life for Galactic Junk League.

Immediatly as you get the credits you get a new upgrade to research. The price?
12.000 credits.
Do you want to have anything good in a reasonable time? Pay. Becuase if you don't have this stuff you simply can't compete in game.

When I first heard about Death By Game Show, it was touted as a game inspired by the great film Idiocracy.  I would call it a guilty pleasure film, but it deserves more than that.  Then I read up on the game, discovering that the developers were also declaring this game was blending the strategy and twitch-based genres in what they coined as ‘Twitch-Strategy.’  Intrigued, I requested a copy and gave it a whirl.  I’m not a huge fan of strategy games, but like speed chess, the merger of speed with critical decision making was something that greatly interested me.
The game starts in the 26th century, where your character U.H. Watt stands trial for being too smart for a human.  You’re sentenced to rehabilitation, otherwise known as Death By Game Show.  This is the full extent of the story.  Obviously, when they said ‘inspired by’ the designers thought it meant referencing lines from the cult classic.  All of the writing is borrowed dialogue from a full gamut of films, including The Dark Knight, Office Space and even Predator’s ‘get to the choppa’ line.  If you still enjoy hammed up ‘Awnald’ impersonations, then you’re going to love this game’s wacky sense of humor- sadly I found it kind of grating and childish.  The story is basically non-existent, so I’m going to move past it and looks towards the gameplay.
You’re transported to a planet at the beginning of every round, where you run around the planet’s surface with goals to accomplish before you can take back off on a rescue ship.  Despite it being a side-scrolling experience, the developers have utilized flying enemies to use the space above, buildings behind the front row that can only be taken out with particular robots, and coins that sink underground that you can pluck out with a claw right out of Bionic Commando.  You can also adjust the difficulty before a stage, with the lower the risk, the less coins your enemies will drop.
You’re strapped to The G.I.M.P. (Gameshow Intimidation Machine of Pwnage), an automatic and personified locker, which has a limited amount of energy as it shoots out your selected fighters.  If you push him past his limits (indicated at the lower left by a power meter), he’ll fall over exhausted until his meter fills back up.  You can still send out robots while he’s down, but it’ll be at a slower pace, and you’ll have to drag it if you decide to move.  As you take out enemies and blow up buildings, you’ll collect coins and upgraddes (the extra D is for a double dose of pimpin’).  Once you’ve taken out the buildings or raise enough money, you return to the studio audience, and your money continues to rack up (as long as you don’t die).
I have to say- when I first started with the tutorial levels, I understood the innovative spark behind the design.  Being on a two-dimensional plane, you’re robots have a nice blend of offensive and defensive purposes, while you focus on grabbing coins that fall beneath the skirmishes.  You have a mobile wall that pushes back enemies and standard troopers you can send out to swarm the opposition.  There’s a fast-paced missile that blows up upon collision with an enemy building or robot, and flying robots that take out background infrastructures.  Your opponents come out of lockers as well, and you can see a timer counting down until their release.  It’s quite innovative.

Sadly, these ideas aren’t as developed as they need to be, and the strategy and choices evaporate as you get further along in the game.  This is clearly the opposite of how it’s supposed to be.  I should be getting more confident, and discovering new ways to utilize my abilities.  My paths should be growing instead of narrowing down to one.  Because everything starts moving at a breakneck speed with very limited resources, you’ll discover a level’s needed order of attack, and what you’ll need to defend against the pushback.  You don’t spend time strategizing; you’ll just die, figure out what went wrong, adjust and try again.  Eventually, you’ll ignore the coins that fall into the ground (they’re not worth the risk), and you’ll be focused on remembering the patterns.  It’s more like learning an overly complicated dance fad, knowing that when you do finally nail it, it’ll be meaningless, and you’ll have to move onto the next one.
The game does try to change things up; perhaps a stage will be based on points, or destroying every building on the planet.  However, considering most of the time you’ll need to kill everything to get the points you need, the goal of every stage is the same- leave nothing standing.  The game has particular power-ups you can only get through spinning the wheel, but they’re so far and in-between, you’ll never have a nice reserve.  What would’ve been nice is if I could’ve used my money to buy additional units, but sadly the game doesn’t offer that- making money useless outside of high scores.
Visually, the game is very imaginative with character designs, but the frame is cluttered without any mercy.  The GUI just has too much going on for me to pay proper attention to any one area.  When you release robots, they speak with a giant text box saying some 90’s Back To The Future reference that fills the screen.  Huge black and white billboards have even more witty anecdotes, as planets rotate around the background as you move.  All this sensory overload doesn’t matter too much either, as most of the time your eyes will be planted on The G.I.M.P.’s power meter as you release enemies as quickly as you can.  The only time your eyes will be needed is when you look up to defend against hovering opponents or missiles.  Then, occasionally you’ll get to spin a giant wheel that gives you a random perk- that ends up filling the screen while enemies continue to push towards you.
Mike Judge should be blushing because this new take on the strategy genre has been infused with his magical extract of vulgarity and satire. Regarding style, the game has a distinct feel. The speedy gameplay has an innovative approach. Sadly, the execution is entirely off, and everything from the mechanics to the audio comes across as muddled and half-baked. There’s simply too many missing opportunities to be recommended. Soon, “twitch strategy” becomes as impressive as combining empathy and action into a “walking shooter.” I would only recommend this game to hardcore fans, who are willing to wade through poorly implemented ideas to experience this fast-paced strategy game.
I recommend this game to only hardcore fans, or those interested in the idea of breakneck strategy.

When it comes down to it, Death By Game Show will be for strategy players that has a high tolerance for frustration, and want something a bit different in the genre. The core strategy and the different combinations of buildings/robots leads to a lot of dynamic challenge that players will enjoy, it's just a bit rough to get accustomed to it while you fail over and over again. The dynamic difficulty setting and the real risk that comes with pushing forward with reckless abandon or not thinking about your next move will keep your mind thinking. So the core gameplay works well...it's just got a set of functionality around it that could use some improvement to make it easier to play. It's nice to see though that steam workshop support will be there, and I feel that it will make a huge difference for the life the game. The humor of the game is hit and miss, and that's really what I feel about the game in the end. It's going to be very hit and miss with the different audiences out there, and while it hit with me, be weary if you like more general strategy experiences, because this game will probably frustrate you.

This game is awesome. Not because it's graphics are stellar (which they aren't, and that's not the way the developers want the graphics to be), not because it has a great campaign (which it also doesn't as of yet), and not because of the limit on things the player can do (it really is very limited at this stage of development, you light fires, scavenge for food and resources, and if you're lucky enough to find a rifle, might survive a few days).
No, this game is great because of the atmosphere and work that the developers have put into it. When you start into the world, it gives you no instructions, and you have to feel your way about controls to figure it out, and a fair amount of guess and check is to be expected when figuring out how to get different supplies. Soon you realize that you absolutely need to find some sort of tool to gather things, without it, you will certainly die. On your adventures you can find rabbits, deer, and wolves (once again it's in alpha so more wild life is to come I'm sure), you may even see a wolf chase down a deer/rabbit and begin eating it once it has killed it. The wild life in this game is superb, even though they only have three types, the programming for them is awesome, the wolves can actually be seen howling if your timing is correct, and it forces you to wonder where they are just in case you are about to be their next meal. The deer can also be heard making noises akin to those made by elk.
While there isn't much to the game as of yet, the work that the developers have put into it has incredible charm. The comments made by your character, the lonely sound of footsteps on ice/snow/wood accompanied only by the sound of a raging wind around you, incredible views of the sky at dawn/dusk, eery howls and calls made by the only other living things, and the overall sense of solitude in this ice-age-esque world, create one of the best atmospheres possible for this post-apocalyptic survival game, and assuming the developers continue to put quality work into it, it should turn into a great full game in time.

This is less a conventional video game and more like an interactive documentary with some clever physics puzzles thrown in. On that level, it's supremely compelling: a visually striking, info-rich, contextualized narrative about the political career of Dr. Mohammad Mossadegh, the first democratically elected Prime Minister of Iran, and how it intertwines with the country's role in the global oil industry. I realize that this isn't usually the remit of most titles on Steam, but if you're even remotely fascinated by the subject matter, I would highly recommend checking it out.
The rich graphics are combination of traditional Persian art with Terry Gilliam-esque cutout animation -- think Monty Python's Flying Circus, and it meshes effectively with the political content.
The moody, atmospheric soundtrack is adapted from two Nine Inch Nails songs, released under a Creative Commons license, and it's a surprisingly appropriate fit with the rest of the game.
The physics-oriented puzzles are rather simplistic, but I can't begrudge the designers for that -- they're really just an artificial mechanism for regulating the pace of the story, rather than anything intended for true gaming pleasure.
Best of all, it's completely FREE. Really, The Cat and the Coup deserves all the attention, support, and praise that it can get.

Let's get this out of the way to start - a good game with major set-backs. I'll come back and revamp the review in the future, but for now, I need to take a break.
I've played this game for hours upon hours in it's pre-Steam beta. Most of that time was just spent blowing up PVE ships in test mode to try out a cool new ship I had just built. That's really the fun part of the game and still is. The multiplayer rounds in Galactic Junk League leave something to be desired, however.
Other game have a much better "feel" to them. Perhaps it's atmosphere? Possibly "community"? World of tanks, for instance, is also free to play but the rounds seem more lively. People chat, map gets "pinged" and tactics play a large role. Crossout, also has more of a lively feel to it, mostly because it has a very specific post-apocalyptic atmosphere.
Galactic Junk League just has a "meh" atmosphere about it; a generic sort of sci-fi spceship feel, with very little communication taking place in rounds and almost no tactical approach to battles. Furthermore, the other games mentioned have a specific goal the teams work towards, other than blowing other people up, so you feel a reason to keep playing round after round. Star Trek Online does much better in most areas than this game, but you can at least design ships in this game, which makes it a bit different.

So as long as you don't expect to sell your work with little effort, have at it.
The event system (basically you embed scripts in a single tile and make it have actions) takes little bit to get used to - especially if you're used to actor/component based tools, but the help/manual is sufficent. After that you are well on your way to making your own JRPG. For it to be any good and to avoid the collective sighs of the masses "another rpg maker game" - you'd probably need to invest a lot more time than you think.
The level editor is great since it has autotiling - no need to tediously place matching edge tiles - and also has easy copy paste chunks from the tileset or existing level. In comparison tools (AFAIK) like gamemaker/construct/fusion/even unity are missing such a simple feature (auto tile) that makes level creation a breeze and has you end up finding a way to get Tiled into your workflow.
A consideration is with RPG Maker MV out, you may consider that instead as it supports more platforms. Ultimately you may want to go for a trial first (I know it's out there with some limitations) and seeing if you agree with the software before throwing any money down (barring huge sales or humble bundles).

This is a short synopsis of my early impressions.
Pros:
-Great tutorial.
-Learning curve very small.
-Overall game mechanics are simple.
-Game progresses nicely, not an unpleasant grind for a new (and free) player.
-Lots of complexity and variation in ships and strategy.
-Very cool low poly/hand painted graphical style reminiscent of borderlands.
-Fair matchmaking
-Runs on low spec machines (I have a 3gb card and can run this game on ultra at highest res)
-Have already had very memorable gaming moments
Cons:
-Feels like it should work great with a controller, but you can't really be competitive without a keyboard and mouse.
-Only one mode in multiplayer at the moment (Team Death Match)
-Hard to put down
Minor nitpicks:
-Environments are beautiful and varied, providing tactical interest, but they are often so crowded that I feel less like I'm in space and more like I'm underwater.
-Vertical combat is a bit dicey. Since the "3d" aspect of the combat comes by raising or lowering your ship's position on a 2d plane, aiming can tend to be weird and awful if an enemy is directly above or below you.
I posted a short guide for new players on r/galacticjunkleague.

I want to recommend this game.
Superhot is an FPS with an interesting and unique premise and that's that time moves when you move. The claim here, however, is false. When one here decides they wish to stop in the face bullets, these bullets continue to move. Men with guns will continue to aim, and brutes oozing to bruise will still turning around after you've decided to jump over them, but very very slowly. So it is then needed to predict not only where everything will end up once time flows normally, but also weither these minor changes will affect your next action.
This is inline with the biggest part of the game, which is mental eyeballing of distances of bullets relative to your exterior. An exterior that you don't know the limits of, however. There's no way to judge your own hitbox, other than the idea that if it's not under you or towards the center of your view then you're probably safe, but this is not always the case. This might not seem important, I mean most FPS don't have or need full body awareness, but this game is about Spacial Awareness and I am not aware of my own space. SUPERHOT really does like to tout itself as the most innovate shooter to come out in a very long time, and I have to agree with them. Never have I played through an entire (albeit short) campaign with a goofy smile on my face the whole time before today. The mechanic of "Time only moves when you do" is pretty easy to grasp, but this doesn't inherently make you a god. Pretty soon you're juggling between keeping track of weapons, bullets, enemy placement and so on as you barrel into a room with 4 people shooting at you all at the same time. Bullets can be shot, sliced, or blocked mid-flight, which leads to some butt-clenchingly tense moments where your last bullet gets shot out of the air and have to change your plan accordingly.
A lot of people have been using the complaint of "Game is only two hours, not worth the money," and I don't necessarily agree with that. The campaign is good, but short, sure. Upon completing your first run of the campaign, challenge and endless modes become unlocked. Endless mode throws you in an arena and throws enemies at you, and challenge mode puts different modifiers and restrictions on the campaign. And these modifiers change up the way the game is played, drastically in some cases: KATANAONLY restricts your weapons to, well, a katana. No longer can you spray down that hallway with an assault rifle, and you must approach the level in an entirely different way.
So yeah, the campaign is two hours, but saying that's all there is to the game is like playing through one ending of The Stanley Parable and saying "Wow, that's it?" Frankly, this game is like the lovechild of Hotline Miami and The Matrix, and if you're looking for a game that makes you feel like a total badass, this is your fix. SUPERHOT is, forgive me, super hot, and if you're willing to play the campaign again in different ways, is well worth your money.

It's very, very different from the original. The Huntress is still a DPS monster, but I'm pretty bummed that there isn't a Summoner as of yet.
Anyways!
The Good:
-The loot system seems less all over the place, likely because it is. Instead of a random heap of stat boosts/debuffs, you get tower-centric and hero-centric stats on items. They're also much simpler.
-Seperate mana for self-heal / abilities and towers.
-In an Orcs Must Die 2!-esque fashion, during the build phase, little white indicators show you where the enemies go along their path. This has the negative side effect of blatantly pointing out any and all choke points.
-The costume design is /all/ ridiculous. See: The fact that the Monk's shirt is just a sleeve. Not two. One.
-The microtransactions are for things like costumes and inventory space only, not stat boosts.
-Loot is sorted by color in terms of how good it is.
-Auto-loot!
-The devs are just really nice people.
The Bad:
-As of now, only four classes.
-Not much like the original. You get a hotbar instead of the neat circle-y interface there was in the original (at least with a controller.)
-Does not have Xbox controller support, as of now.
-The Huntress holds her bow sideways. I get it, fantasy, but you hold it vertically so the string can be pulled behind your ear. (Her bows are too small for that, though.)
-The campaign feels like a really big tutorial.
-Speaking of the tutorial, the tutorial text+art is shown on the right side of your screen, but it covers part of the map.
Overall, worth a try if you liked DD1.

I don't know if I liked this game. I know that I wouldn't tell anyone else to play it, but I might encourage them to watch a playthrough or read about it. I found many points in the game relatable but I also felt like there wasn't a lot of room to think on any of it. It's certainly a thing that favors telling over showing. It is probably just personal preference, but I found being guided through every emotional turning point a bit annoying. I know things about the pieces of the story but I didn't come to many of those conclusions on my own. Even now, as I think about what opinions I have about it, I can't tell how much of that is tainted by the long diary that I just listened to. When there was a moment of silence, music came in and performed whatever emotional rigging it could manage. I can't stand any form of art doing that let alone a game. It feels disrespectful to its appreciator in that it almost doesn't trust that person to feel what they should feel as a result of what they've just learned or heard.
I'm not the kind of person that needs to have a hand in every action to consider something enjoyable as a game, or whatever one might want to call The Beginner's Guide-- so, while I found myself tremendously bored at times, I was okay with the nature of the game. However, I think there is definitely something to be said about the fact that, even though the nuances of this relationship between creator and player was, at times, the central conceit of the story...I felt like that didn't matter as much as the creator's relationship with the creator as evidence by the near abusiveness of the exercise in general. Maybe that was the point. I don't know. I'm an appreciator of all forms of art and a game designer myself, but I really wasn't feeling this one. Again, could be personal preference. But I don't know if I liked it.

I really want to like this game (I mean, it's Robocraft in space!), but I just can't see myself getting into the game at present time. The problem is that the game feels incredibly slow - the Destroyers, Battleships, and Cruisers all feel ridiculously unresponsive (Frigates too but to a lesser extent), and I'm getting the sense that attack range is EVERYTHING. Further excaberating the point is that you start with guns that have 2000m range at best, and you are getting put up with destroyers with 4500m+range beyond level 7. It is possible to put up with that once you get Gauss Cannons so you can build your own destroyers, but it makes Cruisers and Battleships feel worthless, especially when the ships move so slow it's dirt easy to hit a target (with the exception of Frigates)
The grind is also terrible. If you are not already good at the game, you can expect to earn 500 Scrap at a time (and the cost of getting new parts starts launching to 12000+ even before you unlock the other classes). At least you only have to buy them once and you can have as many as you want though... Even with the Pilot Liscence (the GJL name for Premium), you can only expect to get something new every 12 games (and each game usually lasts 10 minutes due to the terrible responsiveness of ships.
Perhaps if ALL ship classes were 3x more responsive (speed AND handling), the game would be much more interesting.
