VX Ace is a great program for beginners and hobbyists. There's a lot you can do with this program, you just gotta get creative. If you're on the fence about RPG Maker, I say go for it. It's usually on sale or in bundles so keep your eye out!
From just the surface you can easily make your own RPG using default assets. But, if you want to take it a bit further the community has provided tons of scripts and resources for you to add to your game.
Within the program there is a help file that a lot of people tend to ignore, but please read it! It has so much information and explains a lot of the features of the program and how to use it. If you have specific questions the official forums are extremely active and a great place to go for resources, tutorials, and information.
VX Ace vs. MV (the newest RPG Maker):
MV is fantastic, but if you're new to RPG Maker I highly suggest trying Ace first. Mainly because you'll be paying less. It's also extremely likely get to a point where you'll want to try something not available without scripting and since VXA has been out for years there's a huge database full of ready made scripts you can use to plug and play. If you're considering VXA it would be a huge benefit to learn the basics of Ruby or at least to understand how to read it.
With that being said... MV is also great and the plugin database is already pretty large for how long it's been out. It offers a handful of new features and to me, personally, it feels a lot more flexible.
VXA scripts are written in Ruby while MV plugins are written in Javascript. If you have more knowledge about one over the other I would keep that in mind.
My final note is that I actually love both programs. I'm currently working on a small project with MV and I'm able to do a lot of what I couldn't in VXA. However, I have been considering making my next project in VXA as there are a lot of readily available resources.
TLDR: New to RPG Maker? Get VXA. It's definitely affordable at it's sale prices and great for beginners.

I'll start by saying that this might just be the best local-multiplayer brawler on PC. Super easy to get into, fun to get better at, and perhaps most importantly, infinitely replayable.
It's also ridiculously polished. The art, music and sound design are all top-notch. The game manages to have this unique atmosphere that makes the matches that much more compelling.
Even unlocking things in this game is a blast, with stuff getting unlocked just from playing multiplayer matches like in smash bros. That's not the reason why unlocking the stages is fun though - it's the unique animations that play. For example, a piece of the moon in the background of one stage falls off, which then crashes down to earth on the map screen and BECOMES another stage! A very hype moment indeed! After that, the piece of the moon will be missing in the background of the original stage. It's attention to detail like this that make TowerFall that little bit better than other indie local multiplayer games. All these little quirks, and yet the gameplay doesn't suffer at all. You can tell a lot of love went into this game.
If you like having friends round for a night of gaming on the couch, then buying this is a no-brainer. I've not got the Dark World expansion yet, but I'll definitely be getting it as soon as it goes on sale!

Pros:
+ Great, responsive controls
+Lots of content
+Looks great
+Few glitches (other than some clipping with death animations that are mentioned below)
+Very difficult, yet rewarding enough to keep you going
+Very addictive
+ Has free-play mode for all levels
Cons:
- $17 might be a little bit much to ask for a 2d side-scrolling game, but value isn't really a concern if you end up liking the game and pumping hours upon hours into it (like I am likely to do)
- Death animations are hilarious the first few times but are ultimately on the glitchy side with some clipping, and obvious disregard of physics, although intentional, I would've prefered somehting a little less over-the-top
- Menu controls on the controller are more than a little finicky
- No 21:9 support (although, it doesn't crop like some games, it just adds black bars on the side, but it would've been really useful in a side-scroller like this to have that kind of support, enven if my high scores didn't count)
Bottom Line:
As someone who was a huge fanboy for the Skate series on Playstation, and a huge advocate for sports games, seeing another skateboarding game on PC is refreshing, even if it's quite a lot different looking than Skate. But removing that third dimension, they still managed to keep the element of difficulty in this game while keeping it very simple.
This is a simply addictive skateboard game that is a must-buy for anyone who liked Super Hexagon, Skate, or the Tony Hawk games, and I would still recomend it to anyone else who is looking for a simple game that's easy to learn and run, but addictive and difficult enough to keep you angrily fascinated enough to keep playing.

My favorite shooter...which is saying something, as I play almost exclusively shooters.
This game is about tactics. If you're looking for a run-n-gun, then don't bother. If you like the pace of games like Insurgency, then pick this up: the intensity and tact of Insurgency + the scale of Battlefield. There are few things more terrifying than being surrounded by bad guys--in RO2, if you are outnumbered, you're probably going to lose.
This is almost exclusively a MP game. Yeah, there's a single player campaign, but the bots are dumb enough to ruin the otherwise eh-"story" and fantastic-gameplay. There are campains online in which you play on a server and fight on one side--Axis or Allies--as your team competes to dominate the war or drains the energy from the foes.
This is a hardcore game: the losers get weakened, the winners get stronger. There's not much of a HUD. You'll have to learn the colors of each team because there is no red reticle when you're aiming at a baddie. If you hesitate, you're dead. If you shoot a teammate, he's dead and will likely punish you (take your lumps, bud). You will rely on your teammates for ammunition, cover fire, suppressing fire, artillery, etc. If you're a solo player (ignore everyone else), don't buy.
From a technical standpoint, this game leaves a lot to be desired. The game is very CPU-heavy and is poorly optimized. The graphics are only "meh", although the sound elements are fantastic, as are the effects (getting shot at in this game makes your vision so blurry that the best thing you can do is go prone).
At the end of it all, if you can run it and like tactical, hardcore FPS action, then pick this up. You WON'T be disappointed.

Although it's entirely based on one sole idea: Archers in a small space, there is enough polish and gameplay to hold your intrest for a long, long time. It is a true example of a simple theme, perfected. The pixel graphics and gameplay are polished to a "T", and feel entirely modern.
The beauty in Towerfall is you never really "beat" it. You can beat the campaign, and the expansion's levels, but the campaign was never designed as the main attraction. Towerfall is meant to be played against your friends, side by side, on the couch. The campagn provides a challenge to complete with your friends, a sort of distraction from beating each other up, and a place to earn more stages and characters, but the real joy is  in the arena.
The awards at the end of each match are hilarious, and pages of gameplay modifiers add to the depth. You can customize just about anything. There are hours and hours of intense, fast-pased, competition to be enjoyed here. A must-buy for anyone with people to play locally with.
There is no "skill cealing" here. With most games, once you reach a certain skill, you can play with just about anyone and there's no garanteeing who is going to win. The outcome of  a match in a game with  a skill celing is no longer based on the player's skill but other lucky or unlucky elements. In Towerfall, you will learn more and more new moves and techniques, and can really push the envelope on what you think should be possible in the game. There are guides on dash-cancelling, power-booping, and binking. Should you want to get competative, this game offers a similar scene to that of Super Smash Brothers. There isn't much more you could ask for in a couch multiplayer game.

There's a lot of single-screen platformers out there -- both single-player and multi-player based. And finding a marvel in the pile of shovelware is always nice, even though it's an extremely rare happening. As you might've guessed already, this one is one of the good ones.
So, basic gameplay is simple: you choose a hero, you enter a level, you shoot baddies with your bow. You have a lot to unlock, though -- new levels (each with new enemies), new difficulties, new challenges, new heroes even. Depth of the game is one it's main perks, honestly.
Another great side of Towerfall is the gameplay, of course -- fast paced action all around (speeding up even further on higher difficulties), it's as fun as it gets, especially if you're playing with a friend.
All in all, I would rate this game 8.5 out of 10 and would definitely recommend it to people who enjoys great pixel art, fast-paced platformers and casual archery. Also, consider the DLC if you'll like the game, as it adds on even more content.

The beginning of this game has the most amazing moody atmosphere you'll ever enjoy.  And in the beginning, it's a mix between melancholy and spooky. (Also, this kid's jump?  PATHETIC.)
For the plot, you have to go out-game (he's looking for his sister), and the ending...yeah.  It's meh.  (Full confession: I accidentally spoiled the ending for myself, looking up reviews).
If you're an artist, play it for the aesthetics, but I there are stronger platformers out there with atmosphere just as rich.  If you liked this, or if the concept of a beautiful, lonely platformer piques your curiosity, try anything by Nifflas, like Within a Deep Forest or NightSky.

Scenario : Good, but could have been better. Still captivating, decent and enjoyable.
Sound :

- Original voices : perfect (as usual) !
Graphics : Colorful, diversity of environments, good character design. But it remains a Tales of game, don't expect 2015 blockbusters standarts !
Charisma of Characters : One of the best point of the game !
Battles : Quite technical (it's not press A and win at least at higher difficulties, boss = multiple death), any new equipment is to balance whether or not to equip for a complex bonus system is behind. Some will find this bothering, others will like the complexity.
Conclusion : You will enjoy the game, it's not one of the few legendary JRPG but a decent top tiers one. And it's the first Tales of series game on PC !

I really, really hope I'll have to change this review. I think The Long Dark will merit a thumbs up, but I do have to say that, for the asking price, the game is not there yet due to a few crucial flaws.
One of the most critical issues does not effect everyone, however. If you have a high-end PC, skip this paragraph. If you have anything other than a high-end PC, prepare yourself for some lag. This game is horribly optimized. The game runs smooth indoors --about 45-60fps-- but although I'm just a bit below the recommended requirements, the game chugs around 20fps tops whenever I step outside. Luckily the game doesn't rely at all on twitch gameplay and is naturally very so this isn't game-breaking, but it's still feels awful and makes an already slow game painfully sluggish. The game is in early access, and I believe that the developers know that their game needs serious optimizing, so I think this will improve. I hope it will, at least, as it's low framerate is a huge turn-off for playing.
Most of the problems in this game stems from the fact that the games just not done yet. In fact, it's no where near done.
The maps are too small for this kind of game. After a few games, the player more or less knows exactly where they are all the time, and it makes the gameplay far more repetitive and trite. The developers have tried to remedy this by adding a second map, which does help, but only for a while. I'm not sure if there is an easy solution to this problem, but it's a problem nontheless.
The combat is atrocious. It's just confused buttonmashing.
The environments are empty and static, which is good and bad. It does give off a very lonely feel, which is good, but it also makes it largely uneventful. When I see a moving object sloshing through the environment, I just think "deer or wolf." There are rabbits and birds, but they seem to be little more than table dressing.
Although at first it seems like there's a lot to manage and consider The Long Dark, but I quickly realized that it's really quite simple. Finding food, melting snow, boiling water, scavenging for wood, and not going outside during high winds is all you need to know. Finding tools just adds efficiency, but rarely changes your daily activities. This makes an awkward pattern in the game. If you know what to do, winning is just luck. If you find an axe, a gun, a knife and a box of tools you can harvest with enough efficiency to be self-sufficient, andyou'll survive until you eventually mess up and get eaten by a wolf or freeze to death on a short trip (which is very easy to do). If you don't find those tools, you'll live for a bit before running out of finite foodfrom abandoned backpacks, bodies, and lodges (water and wood is renewable and very easy to produce). So, no matter how your run goes, it will always boil down to harvesting wood and food, then melting and boiling snow. The only item that opens up any extra dynamic is the rifle, which allows you to stand up to wolves and hunt deer. However, the gun seems to be extremely rare (although ammo is plentiful). To summerize, the game's mechanics are extremely bare bones. There is little to offer besides managing three with a few one or two step processes.
However, the game is incredibly atmospheric, beautiful, rough, and immersive. It can be a really, really good survival game. It's just that the game is no where near done. If someone would ask me if they should buy this game now, I would say no. You should wait. The game is not even close to being worth twenty dollars in its current state, I wouldn't even recommend it for five dollars. You don't need to buy this game yet, you'll probably be disappointed. Wait a few months for it to go on a few sale with half a dozen more updates under its belt, hopefully it'll be worth it by then.

The people who say this game is hard are correct. It is hard. There is no 30-minute, hand-holding tutorial, at the end of which you're given your essentials and pointed in the right direction. You spawn in a random location, could be day or night, clear skies or a blizzard, and you're expected to find your own way to safety. But it's not difficult just for the sake of being difficult - it gets easier as you learn, and you learn by playing. You'll die. A lot. But given time, you'll also figure out where the certain landmarks are, where to look for supplies, how to fight off wolves, and so on.
You also have to keep in mind that this game is still in Alpha. Sandbox mode might not be for everyone, if you don't like the idea of not having set "goals", but be patient, it's coming. Hinterland are some of the best devs I've ever seen, who actively listen to the community and take on board suggestions, releasing updates and bug fixes regularly. I haven't even been playing the game for very long, but in that short time I've seen it grow and develop so much, and it's easily one of my favourite games ever.
As many people have said, if you're looking for a survival game that moves away from the typical tropes, this is the game for you. Difficulty settings have recently been introduced, so you can now take the time to explore without the threat of wolves, with more updates planned in the new year. I'd also recommend the Coastal Highway map for those who are new to the game - it's a little easier to navigate, I find, but poses its own challenges. The graphics are perfect, the scenery and lighting is stunning, and it runs impeccably on my three year old laptop. Whether it's on sale or not, buy it now. You will not regret it. Watch it grow, and it might just restore any lost faith in the gaming industry.

A game where you start with a bunch of happy, healthy citizens, and ends two winters in where you have three sad, dying elders. No doubt this game is brutal, but the 'realism' can only serve to commend the game and raise it above its peers.
Initially it appears hard, but unlike some other indie games there are countless guides online which will help you find your way to success; though if they prove unsuccessful there are enough mods on steam workshop to help alleviate the pressure by giving you more resources per tree/rock, or just giving you the option to 'cheat' resources.
One mod i would wholeheartedly recommend if the alternate start mod, or of similar name, the ability to start with a doctor's family in a pre built town, or a whole hoard of settlers (plus more) really revitalises the game from the vanilla Easy, medium and hard line up you start with. Though i would recommend playing at least three vanilla games initially just to get the feel for the game.
The music and art style is beautiful and one can easily spend hours looking after their little village, town or minor city, depending on how long the game has been progressing. If you want to lose a few hours, then you can easily spend a while just trying to jump the first hurdle, to survive the first winter, with subsequent winters being less and less difficult, unless there is to great a population boom.
Overall:
Pros:
+Art style is lovely
+soundtrack sounds epic or mellow (depends on track)
+mods can increase the life of the game
+Just a really fun game
Cons:
-there isn't a banished 2
-initial hurdle can be hard, not necessarily a con, depends on what your opinions are

The Scourge of War series has superb attention to detail as always. Unfortunately, SoW:Waterloo suffers from the limitations of the series raised to the power of two.
Worst of all, the unit AI near buildings is atrocious. Unlikes in the Civil War series, fighting near forts and in cities was a major aspect of Waterloo. I cannot make my units enter buildings and not get stuck in walls and other obstactles. The AI has no problems and will wipe the floor with you as your units repeatedly bonk their heads into the wall.
The unit AI is still dubious. Giving units normal movement order cancels immediately if there are enemies even remotely close by, meaning you have to either order forced attacks or take command of every single unit you want to move. The AI simply refuses to move units to effective fire range, preferring to keep them 100s of yards away. There's no proper AI unit facing either, meaning that half your units will be facing the wrong way unless you constantly babysit them. This will likely get them mowed down from the flanks. I cannot imagine leading an entire army with such half-baked unit AI.
The scenario time limits are way too strict and every scenario will end in a defeat, making it pointless to play them.
Half the UI commands were invisible so I could never figure out how to unsplit my units or even how to order a charge! The manual gives is nothing but text, making it impossible to figure out where these actions are supposed to be performed.
Avoid this at all costs unless you're a veteran of the series.

This American Life:  The Video Game.
Some say that it's the ultimate defence for the 'Games as Art' argument, as the narration and design attempts to fortify and demonstrate an example of this philosophy, but this player believes it's more than that.
It's a documention of a man's passion and 'life's work' up to now.  It's a declaration by developers who feel that their work should be a means of expression and not mere entertainment for others.  It's a rebuttal to the many who believe that gameplay trumps other aspects of a game.
Walking Simulator?  Well no.  Dear Esther is more of a walking simulator.  In this game the narrator is talking to you instead of just talking.  And this is nothing like The Stanley Parable where the narrator openly mocks you and challenges you.  It is far less interactive than The Stanley Parable, but probably just as immersive.
People who played The Stanley Parable may or may not like this game as it is less interactive.  However, people who love ramblings and insight on the radio as well as The Stanley Parable will probably enjoy this game, like I did.
If you want to consider what it means to develop a 'game', and whether a game minus gameplay can still be a purposeful and meaningful experience, install this and contemplate for a time.
...  I do miss Kevan Brighting's voice though.
EDIT:  The Ending demonstrates a reason why creators (be it writers, artists, game developers) who are friends can just so easily get into a fight over personal space, distrubition rights (for each other's work) and so forth.  It's...  A call for help...  Players must reach the ending if they wish to truly make sense of what this 'game' is.
...  And whether you agree if it should have been released at all.

A masterfully done documentary-game.
This game presents history of an individual in such a way I found so strangely compelling and so unique I would even say I would pay for it, considering it is free. It follows the story of Prime Minister of Iran, Mohammed Mossadegh, and his subsequent downfall through a CIA- and MI6-engineered coup during the 1950s despite being the first democratically elected leader..
It's rare to find a game that teaches you and wonderfully presents itself in both gameplay and how each segment of Mossadegh's life is shown through old Persian-rug weaves. There is a mix between the mystical and the imaginable, the real and the ethereal and I believe that Peter Brinson and Kurosh ValaNejad who made the game did a superb job on the way each conflicts with each other.
An exemplary for those who wish to claim that 'game as an art'.
Or perhaps it is just me being a niche-game collector/player... hahaha..

At the time of writing, this game is currently in Early Access on Steam for 20 dollars, and is probably the best 20 dollars I have ever spent on a game. The scenery is spectacular, the gameplay is smooth, and the feeling of the winter landscape is absolutely terrifying. The Story Mode is currently being worked on, and I shall be waiting with baited breath until it is released.

I first reviewed this game upon one of its first major sales - 50% off during the winter sale.  I live up north on the Canadian border, so playing this game while it was at times a lower temperature outside than it was in the game came to be incredibly immersive.  I had written 10/10 would frostbite again.  Since that time, the game has undergone several updates, patches, and content upgrades.  Most notably of the additions is Pleasant Valley. I didn't think the game could become more trying on its median difficulty, but I was proven wrong.  This game is still early access, but has come a long way since its initial offering.  New crafting, plantlife, and items lend to increased survival options.  There are still missing mechanics that bug me - no jumping, incredibly slow crouch speed (stealth is not necessary so far, so perhaps it will become so) and purely defensive hand-to-hand combat mar some of the more beautiful facets of the overall product.  Some rock and snow formations only 6 inches high can prevent you from moving further.  I'd like to see a jump or vault action to overcome some of these minor, unrealistic obstacles.  The close combat system is kind of weird, and daunting.  It's more of a pray-you-never-have-to-use-it deal, as odds are stacked completely against you if you find yourself underneath a vicious wolf.  If you win, the wolf likely scurries off, merely wounded but by no means incapacitated.  You're left bleeding and very susceptible to exposure, as if you weren't already.  It might be easier, and more engaging, if it were real-time combat.  Despite that, the wolf population was skimmed a bit in one of the patches so its not as much of a threat.  I still love this game.  I can't wait to see what they'll do with the story mode.  Definitely recommend.

VX Ace is a great program for beginners and hobbyists. There's a lot you can do with this program, you just gotta get creative. If you're on the fence about RPG Maker, I say go for it. It's usually on sale or in bundles so keep your eye out!
From just the surface you can easily make your own RPG using default assets. But, if you want to take it a bit further the community has provided tons of scripts and resources for you to add to your game.
Within the program there is a help file that a lot of people tend to ignore, but please read it! It has so much information and explains a lot of the features of the program and how to use it. If you have specific questions the official forums are extremely active and a great place to go for resources, tutorials, and information.
VX Ace vs. MV (the newest RPG Maker):
MV is fantastic, but if you're new to RPG Maker I highly suggest trying Ace first. Mainly because you'll be paying less. It's also extremely likely get to a point where you'll want to try something not available without scripting and since VXA has been out for years there's a huge database full of ready made scripts you can use to plug and play. If you're considering VXA it would be a huge benefit to learn the basics of Ruby or at least to understand how to read it.
With that being said... MV is also great and the plugin database is already pretty large for how long it's been out. It offers a handful of new features and to me, personally, it feels a lot more flexible.
VXA scripts are written in Ruby while MV plugins are written in Javascript. If you have more knowledge about one over the other I would keep that in mind.
My final note is that I actually love both programs. I'm currently working on a small project with MV and I'm able to do a lot of what I couldn't in VXA. However, I have been considering making my next project in VXA as there are a lot of readily available resources.
TLDR: New to RPG Maker? Get VXA. It's definitely affordable at it's sale prices and great for beginners.

OlliOlli2 is an awesome arcade game,
with simple basis but complex advanced techniques,
so you can have a lot of fun  with any skill level,
by trying to finish a level, or doing a level-long combo
to reach the world record.
Concretely, the game is a 2D skating game, I think you noticed it,
but what the screenshots and the trailer don't show you,
is that this game has a particular gameplay.
You can enter tricks with the left stick, and do spins or special tricks
with the triggers of your pad (pad game,  almost unplayable on keyboard).
but you need, when landing your tricks,
to press the A (or cross)  button before hitting the floor to validate your trick.
(and also not slam your head on the asphalt)
and this is a really particular gameplay mechanic,
so you will need a little bit time to get used with it.
bit by bit, you will try more advanced tricks,
and pretty insane techniques to do a level-long combo,
but you shall first humbly try to finish the levels
without falling in deadly spikes or getting burned in lava!

GRAPHICS: cool, a little bit generic and not really varied,
but you won't really focus on it.

leading to moments where your actions are synced with the music,
just by chance. also, no dubsteb. so really cool.

pretty much time, from 10 hours if you want to go straight,

the game has a local splt-screen multiplayer, which is really great,

(but really fun with a minuimum of practice!)

buy it.

SUPERHOT is a game that starts out with a videodrome-like plot built around simple gameplay, a lot like the Jacob's Ladder experience that was Pony Island.
But whereas Pony Island was more about the strange twists things took, Superhot's shorter simpler plot arc doesn't do much more than act as bumpers for the gameplay, and is ultimately an unsatisfying narrative.
But what great gameplay!  The real 'meat' of the game actually starts AFTER you finish the main story and start working through the challenges and endless mode.  In fact, the main reason for anyone to buy this game in my view is that it will help train your quick-thinking skills - this game is a wonderful 'workout' for your nervous system when you get into it!
When you do get far into the challenges, you will find yourself going into 'the zone' an awful lot, and pulling off amazing combos at near-realtime.  It's extraordinarily satisfying and great fun when you do.  This game and its challenge modes warrant multiple playthroughs in my view, to keep training your skill and improving what combos you can pull off.
PROS
-Fantastic core gameplay built around a simple well-done premise
-Trains your quick-thinking strategic skills and reflexes
-You can see yourself physically getting better as you tend to play more in 'real time' as you get better
-Some interesting little side-gimmicks
-A uniquely surreal and bleak sense of humor
-Pretty to look at for such simple graphics, and very nice sound design
-Challenges and endless mode are the real 'meat' of the game, and fantastic satisfying fun
CONS
-Gameplay could have been developed and expanded upon much more than it was (more enemy types, more weapon variety, more gameplay twists than just bodyswapping, more level scenarios pushing what you can do)
-Some minor annoyance with some melee attacks not quite connecting in spite of swinging close
-Weak and altogether too short story
Overall: 8/10 - With the asterisk that I feel this is a 'must-buy' for anyone who fancies themselves and esports player. This is a game you can play on your downtime to train your reflexes or warm up your quick-thinking skills.  Additionally I would bump this to 9/10 if post-launch sees free updates with additional content.

An evocative intrusion into the mind of an unwilling stranger, and a desperate friend.
I started playing The Beginners Guide with my heart in my throat, I was so excited. I saw it was from the creator of the Stanley Parable and instantly added it to my steam library. It soon became apparent that this was not a game. This was a message, a one sided conversation to you as the “gamer”.
Much like Davey Wrenden I saw something in the creations of “Coda” (I don’t use parenthesis to distance myself from the genuineness nature of the name, but out of respect to the creator of the “games” I’ll continue to assume that “Coda” is not a name that they want spread around publically) that resonated with me. It’s entirely presumptuous for me to assume I know the mind of Coda, but the sense of anomie, disconnect from society that I’ve suffered for years was very clear to me in these “games”. They aren’t games though; it’s unfair to label them as such. They are miniature art installations, expressing, through a limited interactive way, the innermost thoughts and feelings of a person who feels different. Proponents of the notion that video games can be an art form (of which I am such a person) will surely hold this up as an example of everything that proves them right.
As the “games” progress, we get further and further into the feelings of “Coda”. The natures of the levels change, and increasingly topics of imprisonment, loneliness, and psychological fatigue feature prominently. For those who have suffered from mental illness, or even development disorders like Autism, will recognise themselves at their darkest times.
I, like Wrenden, felt the need to reach out to “Coda”, to comfort, protect, and help. This is a fundamental mistake. Someone already reached out to “Coda” and ruined their work for them, that being Wrenden. It’s hard to understand unless you’ve played the “game”, the final level is a direct, painful, honest admission of the damage that Wrenden has caused “Coda”. Wrenden himself realises this, knows this, and yet has still chosen to continue the same mistake that cost both “Coda” and him so dearly. Showing the world “Coda”’s work was never the intention, the meaning behind why “Coda” made these. These were self-expressive tools with which to understand themself, something they clearly feel they have lost.
I hope, I wish, I pray that somewhere, the person that is “Coda” is ok. Maybe not by societies standards of what “ok” should be, the standards that Wrenden tried to enforce. But on their own terms, their own way of getting by.
For all my criticism of what Wrenden has done, I am not in the slightest un-empathetic to why he’s done this. This is a statement of grief, one last begging at the doorstep in the rain, one last late night text message, desperate for a failed relationship to continue. The overwhelming need to validate ourselves by loving and caring for another, proving to ourselves that we’re ok, by making other people “better”. I feel that, I’ve been there. I empathise, but I do not condone it.
I felt like an intruder, near the end. During the epilogue, I felt like I had walked into the house of a recently deceased person. Empty, devoid, unwelcome. I was keenly aware that I was never  meant to see this. This was never meant for me to enjoy, so I did not, I aimed to be as respectful as possible in the home of someone who had ran away.

You need to have some patience to get into this game. Let me get the negatives out of the way first. The graphics are poor to very bad. You often hear wargamers say that graphics aren't important for strategy titles but they seem to conveniently forget what the origins of tabletop wargaming are all about - a painstaking focus on colour, detail and having visually attractive models to use on the battlefield! The sprites in this game are poorly rendered. They move around quite jerkily, and soldiers walk through walls. It is also hard to move units properly because you have to wheel the line around and sometimes it doesn't move as it should. A battalion will often line up on a diagonal when it should be in line with the enemy. Movement is quite slow as well.
Some of the scenarios are quite frankly stupid. I chose one scenario where I had to repel a mass French cavalry charge. I moved my infantry forward and put them in squares. The French had zero infantry and the cavalry didn't even charge my squares it just milled around them for 30 mins. I went off to make a cup of tea and came back to see that I had won the battle. I couldn't even see a way to speed up the battle. For gameplay purposes there should have been a little infantry support just to make it interesting even if we were supposed to be following a historical event. Artillery should have been pummelling my squares.
In light of everything I mention above, I am finding that fighting on the defensive is much better. You can get your troops set up and with minimal movement the game becomes more enjoyable. You don't have to watch soldiers plod along to the top of your screen or watch artillery keep slipping away even when metres in front of the enemy. The scale of the battles can be awesome. You can be commanding a division and under severe pressure only to see reinforcements come out of nowhere to help you out. This is when the game really shines and gets you engaged. Over the years Total War games have almost become skirmishes with the size of armies dropping quite dramatically (I remember in Medieval I when you sometimes had a third rebel army to fight plus allies). This game returns us to the proper battlefields of yesteryear when huge numbers of men fought each other over a whole day as there is a choice to command the full army at Waterloo, instead of just brigades and divisions, and this takes 7 hours to complete!
I will have to play this game more but at the moment I can only give it a 7/10. If the designers could spruce up the animation and sort out the movement mechanics then you could have a really good game to play.

Oh, and SMGs will melt literally anything in range. I've made skirmishers with 4-8 SMGs on them and I've just turn through anything entering range before their phasers or missiles could even hit me.
Disappointing. It's an obvious spiritual successor from the days of non♥♥♥♥♥♥Robocraft, but done a lot worse than the old version of said game. There's no real variation on ships from what I can tell (Not that I can, being relatively new and all that.) All ships have thrusters, all ships have gyroscopes. In Robocraft, you could see from the same second you opened your "Research" tab exactly what your end-game would be, not unlocking♥♥♥♥♥♥as you level up and having no bloody idea when you'll get something that you actually want. They had tracks, wheels thrusters, planes, helicopters blades, hover discs, walker legs which allowed for railgun scorpions. It was viable to make a main-battle tank in Robocraft due to the fact that you could continously stack layers of armor upon Itself of different levels of protection to protect against what you felt was the biggest threat. Plasma? Have weaker armor in front and thicker in back. Railguns? Thicker up front with a squishy interior usually worked, as long as you spaced out the squishy with strong blocks.
SMGs giving you trouble? Making a varying layer of strong / weak / strong / weak would often ♥♥♥♥ up their day until you managed to kill them.
If you wanted to make a flying carpetbomber, you could. If you wanted to make a wheeled, weak but extremely fast skirmisher, you could. That game used to leave all the choices up to the player of what they wanted to do, not go "Well, you either do X or Y or you don't do anything at all."
I've no doubts that the developers of GJL will eventually fix all of these problems, and I sincerely hope they do, but until they do, I would not waste the time It takes to download and uninstall this game. I'dd rather do something more productive and fun, like smashing my skull on a brick wall.

Apologies, as this is my first review and this is long...
Bottom Line up Front: I wish there was a "mixed feelings" rating. As much as I want to love this game (and I do get enjoyment out of it, especially fighting Division-level skirmishes) I do not believe it meets expectations based on how it's advertised (Large scale Army vs Army Battles). Most of these let downs are from a poor AI, especially on the friendly side.
First off I'm a big Napoleonic buff. Besides doing ungodly amounts of reading, I've played the John Tiller Battleground series games Waterlooo and Napoleon in Russia back when they were new and I've played Waterloo and Austerlitz based off the good ole Sid Meier Gettysburg engine. When I came across SoW: Waterloo I was extremely excited. I will say I do not mind the graphics engine since the amount troops portrayed more then make up for it. I'd summarize my experience so far as thus:
PROS:
+Excellent and historical troop representation. All the various units are in their unique uniforms. Especially impressive are the British battalions have their unique regimental facings (1st "Royal Scots" with Blue, the 28th in Yellow, etc.) and the few British regiments that still wore the older Stovepipe shako at Waterloo are portrayed as well. French units are shown in their grand uniforms,which makes finding certain units (Curassiers, Imperial Guard Units, etc) easier when you have large formations.
+Scale. The default 1 sprite to 6 men really sets the mood of the late Napoleonic Wars. Nothing beats having thousands of men marching across a open field during an assualt (...if you can get them to actually advance...)
+Sounds. The sharp rhythm of musket fire interrupted by the boom of a cannon, especially when zoomed to ground level, really adds to the atmosphere. Many battles I simply parked the camera POV beside a line of my artillery and listen the the sound of fire while watching enemy formations take casualties. Really makes you feel like you're there.
+Courier system. If you can figure it out it really adds to the feeling of being a commander. In the larger sandbox battles, it's exciting sending off messages to your far-flung subordinates, ordering them to consolidate at a terrain feature, only to have your first arriving units make contact with enemy troops. Lots of exciting moments wondering if that last division will make it in time to save the day.
CONS:
-The "Friendly" AI is compeletely incompentent. I understand the game's creators believe they've made a system that simulates having subordinates, with all their personality traits. Some of your junior leaders are supposed to be more aggressive, others more cautious. This is supposed to determine how they will react to the enemy whether that means conducting a counterattack or simply establishing a defense and requesting reinforcements. However I find that friendly AIs either don't react at all or will execute completely moronic orders you didn't give them. I've ordered units not even in enemy contact to advance straight ahead, only to have them not move, move in the wrong direction, actually fallback some, and in many cases simply turn away and exposing their rear to enemy. I've ordered a brigade to form a simple line in defense, only to have the units criss-crossing each other in a jumbled mess.  I understand the point is to have the frustrations of being a commander with real humans, but it's so awful as to be completely unplayable several times. Most of my battles become exercises in micromanaging and simply "Taking Command" (the button to turn off the AI) of each individual unit. The friendly AI couldn't find it's way north, even if it was smack dab at the south pole.
-The Enemy AI, however, seems to know your subordinates are idiots and reacts in ways that seem to take advantage of your inability to command your subordinates. I've had several battles where the AI simply sacrifices it's cavalry, sending them to parade in front of my troops but never attacking. No matter the orders given, my units refuse to do anything else but form square and suffer hundreds of casualties from artillery within a matter of minutes (see notes on artillery below). Should you actually get your men to stay in line and advance, the small decimated squadron (less then 80 men) of enemy cavalry then simply brushes your battalions of 600 men aside, despite the battalions firing a full volley.
-The enemy AI is especially crafty with a his artillery in that you can never seem to overrun his own guns unless you can get a lucky cavalry charge in. Even as your infatry sprites cover the guns, suddenly the enemy battery appears limbered up a hundred paces to the rear and races to safety. Amazingly the crews are able to unlimber and fire more canister before you can close the distance before retreating again. I've  surrounded enemy batteries on all four sides only to have them simply ride away. Musket fire appears to have little to no effect on the artillery for some reason.
-The artillery is also way overpowered. For some reason the creators and most of the mod makers for this game are obsessed with the supposed killing power of artillery, possibly due to the game engines roots in the American Civil War (when artillery began to approach the deadliness that became it's hallmark in WWI) . I've had many battles were up to 70% of casualties are from only a handful of gun batteries. A little research into this shows that in the extreme cases, like at Waterloo, artillery inflicted 20-25% of the casualties at most. see Dr. Rory Muirs "Tactics and Experience of Battle in the Age of Napoleon" for a great explanation of casualty statistics and causes.
-Sandbox Campaign engine. Everything about the Campaign map is clunky. Armies are only able to move on the primary roads, so no overland marches are possible. Time on the campaign map freezes once two armies meet, and will not move forward until you resolve the battle. What this means is it's absoltely useless to split your forces to attempt a diversion. In my case when playing as the British in defense of Brussels, I had split off and sent forward several cavalry brigades to locate the approaching French. Finding them, I kept my cavalry in place to screen, while moving my main forces towards the location. When the French and my screening cavalry made contact, time on the campaign map froze, with my main army only 30 seconds away from joining the fight. However, I was forced to fight a 4 hour long battle against the whole French army with only the single cavalry brigade. Despite being only a moments march from the fight, you apparently can't receive any reinforcements during a campaign battle. Furthermore, should you not win the battle, you apparently have no effect on which way you retreat. I've tried fighting defense in depth, inflicting heavy casualties and withdrawling before the enemy can mass against me. However I'm then frustrated when the game has my army retreat *BEHIND* the enemy army I just fought, completely exposing the objective I was trying to defend. It means you have to win every battle you fight, which means it's not really a strategic campaign.
-Poor community reception of new players having difficulty figuring the game out. I have never posted the developers support or discussion forum becuase I've watched other people get shot down for even minor criticism (mostly from long time fans from the game's American Civil War days). People with what I would consider valid complaints are told they haven't bothered to learn how the game works.
In closing, I REALLY wanted to endorse this game. While I understand they want to give you all the frustrations of being a commander, that seems to be the focus of the game as it is right now. It simply becomes a clicking simulator as you have to take over the lowest level of units, while you're left wondering the AI commander you've just ordered still won't move 30 minutes later.

You play as an unnamed, and apparently mute, boy searching through dark woods and city landscapes for something. According to the game description, you're looking for his sister. Oddly enough, there is no mention of this in the game though it's implied. There isn't much of a story in this game. You simply wake up in a forest, with no idea who you are or what's going on. In the background, you see trees and as you go along you start seeing buildings, plants and factories. It is almost as if your in a side world to the "real world" but the game never really explains this. The game has a distinct ending, but its a bit abrupt and isn't that satisfying to me. There isn't much to spoil about the ending of the game, but I won't spoil it so you'll have to play it to find out what happens.
This story's character is no saint, to say the least. While one could make the claim that it was kill or be killed, he does some things that make me wonder. There are certain parts where the kid will kill the other kids via traps. There is also one point of the game where you have to pull a leg out of a spider that's been trying to kill you in order to progress further. Usually, you feel justified to an enemy, but ugh, doing that really made me queasy.
So what about the puzzles themselves? Well, they weren't too bad. They tended to range from jumping around, moving objects to the right place, using the physics engine and jumping at the right time, otherwise you were dead. It also includes some gravity puzzles as well as a part where an insect limits your movement. The overall difficulty curve is gentle and gradual for most of the time. None of the puzzles got to the point that required a ridiculous amount of precision in order to progress though. However, I did find some of the puzzles can be frustratingly opaque. I ran into a couple that required some help from guides. One other thing I should point out is that while the game auto-saves as you progress, there are a few puzzles that if you screw up, it sets you back a little bit more than I would like, which can lead to some frustration as you redo the steps over and over again until you get it right.
PC settings are fairly limited though you don't need many for 2D Games. You can change are controls and brightness levels. No V-Sync, AA, AF, resolution options or anything else. It's limited but to the game's credit, seems to scale well from my experience. I never had any lag or crashing or other issues crop up during gameplay. The game is very light on graphic settings, though your not going to really need to change them as long as you have a decent computer. It is controller compatible if you prefer controllers. The keybindings aren't changeable, but I found the default ones are smartly placed.
The game's OST is very atmospheric. At first the music stays in the background, but as you progress along and get into the city-section, the music starts getting in your face, almost overwhelming you as you try and solve the puzzles all the way to the end of the game. The sounds itself sound very realistic, though sometimes muted. There is a flying insect in the game that slightly creeped me out thanks to the sound design.
In the end, I had more fun that I thought I would with this game. The unique visuals sets this game apart and makes it memorable, helped in no small part by how brutally dark this game is. It only clocks in at about three to fours hours for a run through it. But I was satisfied with the length of the game given how cheap it is and how well designed it is. There's a reason that a lot of games are based on the Limbo formula and why so many people played this title. It's worth giving a look for the moody atmosphere, the dark music and tight platforming.

The isolation of being able to obtain notes or see in the dark only through your video camera makes you feel completely vulnerable, much like Amnesia or Penumbra. A lack of being able to defend yourself heightens the anxiety for sure. I would say that this game fits more on the side of psychological horror, however, as much of what the player sees or experiences is meant to elicit a visceral or uneasy reaction rather than complete and utter scares; not that those have been neglected, either.
All in all, a good game, significantly long enough, the DLC is worth the money, definitely a favorite of mine, with a fun and different story. Buy it! Enjoy it! Pee your pants!

Refunct is an entertaining first person platformer and parkour game.  It has a minimalistic and clean visual style that, while being colourful enough, maintains a sober feel to it. The game scenery consists on a series of platforms that arise above the surface of an endless calm sea as the game progresses. Other elements include spring platforms, elevators and sort of vacuum tubes. Looking up there's a beautiful sky which transitions from one dusk to the next, making the ambience light vary accordingly.  The music is beautiful and contributes to the game's mood and pace.
Player's aim is to traverse from one checkpoint to the next using parkour style movements, uncovering rising platforms and picking a series of cubes until the game's done. It is a short game but there's much replayability if you accept the speedrun challenge and another one that requires you to reach the end while touching the floor the least times possible.
Really worth playing, and cheap!

Albeit I have only played for a short while, I have gotten a clear picture how this game works, and even though it is very similar to the first game, this one takes the simple idea and then tosses it in a river.
The RPG, loot collecting, and tower defense, is fun as ever. However, when you first start off playing the game, you are met with utter confusion. The first maps start off as hard as most maps were half way through the game in the first game. By the way I reached the third or fourth map; It had four places where monsters kept pouring out, and the items I were to defend were placed in a haphazard manner. The maps are in general just poorly designed in comparison to the first game.
So, right from the start; This game is impossible to play alone to get a hang of it. So you are forced to play with people online, which I figured is the way it's supposed to be played, of course. Well, it would have made a bit more sense to let a person who is new to the game actually start off in a brand new game, and not throw the poor player into a group that is already half-way through the map, leaving you unable to build any towers. So you stand alone in the onslaught, doing no damage, simply waiting to get your free loot.
Also, throwing all the leveling info, stats, customization, and everything of the sort ALL AT THE SAME TIME, is extremely daunting and off-putting. Slowly introducing mechanics to new players would be extremely helpful, since most info you get is either too detailed or not detailed at all.
It's not a terrible game by all means. But it would at most get 4 out of 10, where the original DD would easily get 8 out of 10. If it was as simple to learn as its predecessor, the game would have been better in general. But the useless stats thrown around, no proper info or pointers given, poor optimization, and the maps being completely rubbish in comparison to the first game, does make it feel extremely lackluster.

After playing for 5 hours I'm not sure why people say the game is so terribly unbalanced, unless they are old reviews. It's simple game mechanics like every other game, you find a style you like then you exploit the environment and your abilities to best support that style.
I personally play a ship with high DPS, short weapon range, light armor, and low mobility. Do I get killed every time I try to approach a ship geared for long range combat? No, because I'm not a dumbass who flies straight at them in the open. I watch the team and as soon as I see the opportunity, I rush in and melt through 3 ships before they know what's going on.
I've seen ships with missiles, gausse weapons, and lasers all be the top ship in matches(and ships with extremely heavy armor and no armor). If you're not doing well either find out how you can use what is available to you better or start from scratch and try something else.
A little about the game, the matchmaking seems very balanced to me. What you do in the match easily decides who wins. In my experience 80-90% of my games are close enough that it could go to either team. If you've never played this type of game before, then you should try it to learn how pleasing it is to build a ship completely yourself and then perform well in it. It's extremely easy to learn and is fun the minute you get into a match - even in a rookie ship.
For being EA and Free to Play I'd give this game at least a 9/10 at the time of this review. (And I'm not the type to just throw big numbers around because I like one thing)
PS: It's fun as hell to make Eve Online ships. My friend made a Coercer that actually looked extremely similar and performed well in matches.

So, I bought this a few months ago, and decided to try my hand at making a game out of one of the stories I've written in my spare time. Long story short, although I personally still have a lot to learn(particularly in the scripting area), this is a fairly easy to use software, and is especially useful for making your stories come to life before your eyes!
The setup is fairly simple, and you can easily figure out what certain terms mean by hovering your mouse cursor over the term, making it very user-friendly. The basic tilesets and characters that come with the software are nice, and the character generator, while limited, is still pretty well put-together, and the fact that you can add more parts to it yourself makes it pretty versatile. The music that comes with the software is decent, though you'll probably find better tracks in one of the DLC packs. I would mention the scripting, but I know very little about it, if anything at all, so I feel like saying anything about that would be a bit unfair.
Really the only cons I've found were the limited default parts, but as I mentioned above, that can be easily remedied by the user.
If you're a writer or artist, want to learn game design, or just want to make some cool stuff for you and your pals, VX Ace is definitely worth it!

As many others have said, this is not Total War Napoleon despite an initial superficial similarity.
The Negative:-
By today's standards  the graphics are mediocre and the UI is clunky and the fps and sprite animations are maybe not what one would expect, also can be a little unstable on occasion and there are features not yet implemented described in the manual but not in the game .
(Norbsoft have a good record of supporting their titles though, and this one will remain in development for a good few years yet I suspect, they are a little specialist publisher that are really in it for the long haul. )
However all that can be forgiven  (by me anyhow) , because of what this is.
The Positive:-
This program like its Gettysburg predecessor  is the closest that a small  indie team can get to a SIMULATION of this battle (+ the DLC battles if you like it enough to try them)  and  realistic Napoleonic era tactical warfare with obviously quite limited resources.
The attention to detail and the work that has gone into the OOB's, the orders systems, the terrain, the AI and the engine that runs it is unprecedented.
On the more realistic levels you can command from the seat of your horse from a particular individuals position. You send written orders by courier to your subordinate commanders, couriers can get killed so orders don't arrive, subordinates have their own personalities and don't necessarily interpret what you wanted them to do as you expected...its controlled chaos and  and a huge incite into warfare of this period.
This is not a light title, you can jump in and play by going through the tutorials , but you will not really know what you are doing unless you read the lengthy manual and make a study of the game.
Mita's How to control AI and other tutorials in the discussion section is pretty much mandatory.
This really is a niche title and if you love the period and are prepared  to put the time into learning a complex and relatively hardcore system, it has a lot to give and will repay your time + a lot more I suspect.

Its a title I keep coming back to, the fun increases the more I understand the system as I can keep increasing the realism levels (the scenarios are very challenging even on the easiest levels so you have to learn the game pretty well before having any chance with the more realistic features such as HITS (head in the the saddle).
Almost certainly a 'grognard' wargame title, but if you are a 'grognard', its a feast.
Though the 20/20/20/20 mode is near impossible the game is both fun to play and will scare you half to death

The game has been stable for me so far. The graphics aren't bling, but do the job more than adequately. And the AI varies from 'clever girl' as it pulls a surprise from the hat to making you want to take it behind the woodshed as your subordinate divisional commander totally misinterprets what you wanted him to do. Just about right really.
My biggest gripe with the game is the rather sluggish performance at times. One of those times where a powerful single core could perhaps be of more benefit than a multi-core CPU.
Otherwise, I've been enjoying the game so far. It's one for taking your time with and over. Adjust to the pace of early 19th century warfare.

I've started to name this and Rising Storm personally under the title of "War" as simply, at times I can't describe it as anything but. Barring the horrid singleplayer campaign and Action mode (a more casual mode and the least popular mode in the community) RO2's Multiplayer is balls out amazing. It's terrifying, tense, frequently brutal, realistic, at times hopeless and all around fun.
John Gibson, Tripwire president tried hard to keep the game realistic while also being easy to get into for people not used to such realism and it pays off, helping newbies to not struggle with controls so don't be amazingly afraid of RO2.
The game also has a great first person cover system, weapon mounting system, and even a nice damage system that makes every kill feel earned.
The maps for Heroes of Stalingrad and Rising storm give off experiences so different they're almost different games. Heroes of Stalingrad displays the struggle between the Soviet and German forces between 1941 to 1945, both equally matched albeit fighting on different sides with different weapons across large open, bleak colored battlefields on the snow covered bunkers of russia or the brick, dirt and concrete buildings and battlefields of germany, fights usually either at long range or extreme close range inside buildings.
Rising Storm however shows the Pacific Theatre of World War II, with the Japanese with their superior positioning and more brutally effective tactics (you can plant grenades in the ground like boobey traps and suicide rush for a bayonet stab) against the Americans with their generally superior weapons (You'll get to know the terror of the flamethrower well from the other end) albeit nowhere near the will to do the things the Japanese do, fighting across the tropical battlefields of japenese islands.
And the best part? If you own RO2 you can play Rising Storm's maps albeit stuck to a bolt action rifleman.

I have very, very low expectations for the writing in Tales games to begin with but this is a new low. The generic characters are complete imbeciles, even those who aren't supposed to be naive. They constantly draw conclusions that made me go "Wait, what?!" and their decisions rarely make sense. Villain runs off (as they like to do between large stretches of hanging back and doing ♥♥♥♥-all), threatening to now end the life of a friend of yours? Meh, was probably just kidding, let's continue with our elemental collectathon quest straight out of the early Final Fantasy games. There is no sense of urgency or wonder that drives most of the plot and the characters' journey, no feeling of being involved in larger events, it's just "follow the yellow star on the minimap to the next dungeon because video game" The moralistic theme is even more botched and hamfisted than the environmentalist one in Xillia. Lailah jumps in with her non-interference shtick whenever it makes the least amount of sense for her to do. And the customary Tales story twist is a predictable dud.
Bottom line, Tales of Phantasia had more original and engaging writing 20 damn years ago.

I really loved this game for many reasons
Here's why
First of all - Atmosphere
Really great overall
The pixel graphics are neither too complex nor too simple wich is ''cozy'' for the eyes

The best i've ever seen in a while honestly
At the start, all the controls are simple and easy to use (Press to aim, release to shoot - press to dash, press again to cancel - etc...) wich makes it easy to learn for new players.
BUT THEN, when you really get into it and practice, some crazy tech becomes available (Jump-cancel dash, crouch dash jump-cancel, dash-cancel shorthop etc...) wich can get really competitive.
So perfect for casuals but with a complicated side for the hardcore ''tech-ers''.
Finally - FUN
Play with friends, laugh, have fun, don't take life seriously etc.
You're gonna have a great time.

So being a massive fan of most of the Tales" series I have to say this is a disapointment.
I'll start with my biggest issue, the story:
-What story?
Literally the entire story is thus: Friendship is magic, and know your enemy so you can understand his past, but not do anything differently as a result.
At first it seems as if the story is going to go into some psychological stuff about being a hero and not flaunting your power but any and all pretenses of a story deeper than a kiddie pool are dropped completely by the time you get to the second town. It get's worse too; Key story points for obtaining certain party members are dropped and never mentioned again in any fashion after an hour. And to top it all of there are NO sidequests of any kind. Each and every one of the "optional" quests you can do turn out to be not so optional within minutes and are forced upon you to progress. The story itself, for what it is, is also rediculously short. Synopsys (Ya ya spoiler warning)
-you save woman
-you follow same woman to save her again
-become hero by necessity (also the cliche that you are the only one who can do it BS)
-lose to boss man
-complete 4 "trials" that are not trials at all
-forced running around to complete the "side quests" to learn the past of the boss man
-beat boss man.
---> As previously stated it looks like it would dive into some good psychological depth early on but it's all dropped in 5 minutes.
Now for combat:
-Limited to 3 attacks at a time NO EXCEPTIONS. Enemies are not limited thusly.
-Also limited by "fatigue" (called something else). Not sure if enemies have this or not.
-all magic only costs fatigue and nothing else
-Magic is convoluted, especially healing
-all magic is uselesly long to cast unless the caster goes mellee, completely making magic pointless as your casters get mauled because their AI is so derp no matter the settings. Casters also don't have the health, defenses, or physical attack to do any good as non-casters. (starting to see the problem?)
-Enemies gain magical-Jesus-BS-armor randomly, even mid juggle, and become immune to all stagger and take massively reduced damage. This usually results in a party wipe as the AI stands there and dies one after another as you try in vain to pull the enemy off of them.
-Some enemy attacks are stupidly broken: For example one enemy throws his spear at you, bu instead of being a line attack it is battlefield wide AOE that instagibs the entire party. This enemy is just regular world type too, not even a sub-sub-boss.
-all in all combat is difficult because of poor design, not legitimate dificulty.
There are possitives though:
-the world is pretty nice looking and so are all the entities. Though graphics don't at all make a game in my opinion it is nice to look at.
-character names are very original and most character in your party actually have a personality.
I cannot recomend this game to anyone.

It's a precision platformer where you go really fast. It has a Street Fighter-like combo system, but you rack up points instead of damage, and you're trying really hard to not hurt the little guy instead of beating someone up. It has the constant silly deaths of I Wanna Be The Guy, but with better art and less crashing.
50 levels spread across 5 worlds and 2 tiers of difficulty, each level has 5 badges for meeting certain challenges on the level. One is always to get a certain score, one for getting a certain size combo, and three that make increasingly absurd demands on your dexterity and concentration. As I've gone from struggling to complete world 1 to being able to speed-run through half the game, I have kept running into challenges that make me say "what? That's possible? How?" -- and I am still hitting them!

I love this game. I've played a lot of tales games and this game plays a bit differently. The combat and battle encounters feel nice and a bit more simplified than other tales combat systems, which isn't to say it's bad. The combat encounters have no load times, attacks are done in a flow chart for comboing and there are different elements. Your stats and passive abilities come from your equiptment which you can combine to make better equiptment etc. Your artes are unlocked from your titles and leveling up. Dungeons can get boring. The story is what kept me playing, I really enjoyed it. On the surface it seems like a happy and fun game but then the story's tone dramatically changes dark unexpectedly/randomly, which I didn't mind too much. The tone varies a lot at times. It didn't exactly feel too forced and they were able to tie in the dramatic dark tone changes in the story. The unexpected reveals are what kept me thinking about the game long after I beat it, especially the entire ending/aftercredits. Even the little things in the game's story like the subtle characters interactions with one another kept me thinking about it. I figured the english voice actors would be mediocre  and sound annoying so I switched to japanese. The game was overall a lot of fun and the characters were great. I feel like a few things might have been/were lost in translation but I'm okay with that because I enjoyed the game and got what I wanted out of it. 8/10

This is truly a great game, and with over 300 hours played, and me trying for 100% completion, it beats Skyrim for playability. The world is immense and beautiful. The missions are as easy or as challenging as you want them to be, based on your perceived threat. The story is a little silly, but nonetheless it does sort of hold together based on the silly nature of the game; despite the fact you're committing wanton acts of terrorism and genocide across the whole of Panau.
Even though this is a great game, it just doesn't do anything exceptionally. Yes, it has some beautiful subtle touches, but it just doesn't come together like a classic game should. The driving mechanic is an absolute nightmare, and you can be racing down the highway at breakneck speed when your car decides to spin out and flip over killing you instantly for no apparent reason. The AI is pretty generic. Running for cover, but then deciding to rush your position. Okay, it can be pretty intense with a host of mobs, but once you deal with the heavy machine gunner/sniper, the rest go down pretty easy. One thing I don't understand is if your threat level gets to maximum, the best Panau seems to send out against you is a chopper, even though they have tanks and fighter jets sitting in the bases. Perhaps the biggest complaint though is the QT events to override the control systems. On some missions the key inputs just wouldn't register, and in some cases time is critical.
I do hope they sort all these little niggles out in JC3, because this is still a great game and on the brink of being a pure classic.

Picked this game up after hearing the Scourge of War had a Napoleonic option after Scourge of War: Gettysburg and always like to take a chance on an evolving engine.
I like both levels of the Napoleonics - both battles and the politics.
This hits the spot that I like for battles allowing you to dig into the OOB (Order of Battle) structures and various tactics and formations (column, line square, double-speed, etc.)
Graphics: I usually play this on my laptop and even with lower specs it plays quite well.
The ground is solidly displayed and the units are colourfully done.
Good graphics and has plenty of graphical options - things like draw distance, trees transparency, and objects control.
Sound is good and classical and keeps up with the battle.
Controls and Gameplay: Camera Control has a lot of options with options to spped up camera movement(at first I found the default too slow)  And with the OOB button, you can find units in your command structure.
A lot of the direct unit control has been done through a Context Toolbar menu(moddable).  After you select the unit, you right-click the ground where you want to that unit to go and a menu comes up giving the formation options(that you can chain together.)  And off they go.
There are lots of scenarios that are not easily winnable(replayable) and for both sides as well(France/Allies).  There is a sandbox that I found impressive with many options, different levels of complexity, and starting terrains.  On top of that there is a sandbox campaign that allows you to string together scenarios.
And at the higher levels of difficulty, you have limited views and have to send couriers to get your commands done(HITS HQ In The Saddle). I ain't good enough for that.
There are some OOB mods and many in the community use the Grog Mod that expands the Context Toolbar(often shown in the YouTube videos)
Learning Curve: You need to go through the tutorials and to keep the fairly thorough manual nearby.
You can select any of the seven difficulty levels(Untrained, Militia, Normal, Seasoned, Veteran, Historical, and Grognard) and can tweak AI effectiveness.  You can select brigade, corps, and division levels for your scenarios.
There are more than a few tutorials on Youtube for different subjects.
For any questions, there are both the Matrix and NorbSoft Developer forums
Matrix -
NorbSoft -
Check out both for answers, mods, and After Action Reports
Overall:  For Napoleonics, it is worth it to get into the nitty gritty of the tactical.
The AI offers a challenge.  The game is stronger than most tactical games for content - many scenarios are available with both sandbox and sandbox campaigns.

This game is excellent.  In a way you probably wouldn't expect.
I am taking command of General Girards 7th Infantry Division, under Marshal Reille's II Corps, with two infantry brigades and Capitan Barbeux's artillery battalion. A Courier from Reille arrives and tells me to mobilize to a small town on the far western end of the map, far away from the rest of the army.
We arrive at the objective ahead of the Prussians, and I organize General Piats brigade in the treeline, whilst Brigadier General Villier stays on the hill to act as a reserve. We await the enemy from the south but they unexpectedly approach from the west. Without cavalry to scout the area, I did not know where the enemy would come from. Luckily, the AI is fairly capable on its own and general Piat mobilizes his brigade to turn and face the enemy.  My artillery begins to fire and a brigade of Prussian Landwhere approach me. In the distance, I can see a large force of cavalry and infantry with artillery support mobilizing. I estimate that the enemy is in Corps strength, so I dispatch a courier to the Marshal, requesting support and prepare to hold my defensive position. If I can delay the enemy here, a full Corps of enemy troops will be away from the main battlefield. I do not know where the rest of my Corps is, or how far away the rest of the army is but they are out of my sight so this is a dangerous situation for me. However the terrain gives me an advantage, and if the rest of my Corps arrives in time, the tide could turn easily enough. The enemy advance slowly, and we manage to maintain the upper hand for the first part of the battle, we both send out skirmishers splitting them from our regiments and a slow grueling infantry duel begins. After about 30 minutes of fighting though, my men are exhausted. General Piats brigade has barely held, and then General Villiers begins an ill fated attack against the Prussian right flank. His men are mowed down and massacred, until only a single regiment remains. His troops pull back to Piats position and my artillery also repositions itself. Finally, a messenger from Marshal Reille arrives, I am to hold my position at all costs, support is on its way. Angry at General Villiers for beginning his attack without me telling him too (The AI officers under you will do things like this, my favourite part of the game actually), I take direct command of his few remaining troops and continue to skirmish with the enemy, buying time as their cavalry closes in, routing half of Piats remaining men and I am now utterly screwed.
Then most of the Prussian force breaks away, turning to face a new threat in the distance. The rest of the II Corps is marching towards me, from the rear of the enemy force. I withdraw my men back to the crest of the hill, using the distraction to rally them and rest. As the battle begins in earnest again I march my troops into the now rear of the enemy, wiping out the small landwhere brigade under general Von Frunk (Maybe wrong name, I don't remember) and eventually breaking into the enemies center. Another long battle ensues, and one hour later it is over.
My men had held our position, and reinforcements had arrived. We had beaten back the enemy in the west, and I recieved new orders from the Marshal. We would march south and hit the allied Army in the east. Despite the poor condition of my men, barely a thousand left out of four thousand strong, I followed the rest of the Kollum acting as a rear guard. We arrived at the central battlefield, a river standing between us and the flank of the enemy, Then I saved my game and took a break. This game is amazing, but ♥♥♥♥ is it exhausting. This was not a proper campaign mission either, simply a "Sandbox" battle.
Hopefully this small thing will give you guys an idea on the scale of the game, the ingenuity of its AI, and sheer grand tactical options (I say grand because most of the time you are operating at the grand tactics level). (Will finish this part in a min, gotta go)

It reminds me of robocraft. Robocraft you can build ships, tanks, or robots. The building system is essentially the same. Robocraft also has 50x the amount of pieces of content. Robocraft also plays a bit smoother, but its hardly noticeable. You feel like you are flying a freighter in this. That being said, Robocraft has several flaws that make Galactic Junk League Better.  GJL chooses to go for a inked in aethetic similiar to Borderlands and others, which to me at least is more interesting than the visuals in Robocraft. Parts are very limited, but all building parts you can get from game currency earned by playing. Parts in Robocraft are behind microtransactions and 100s of dollars of DLC. Also the best weapons are bought, which makes Robocraft pay to win. There are balancing issues in GJL, but the devs even acknowledged the issues with snipers and are working on it. There are microtransactions, but they are for aethetic skins, and exp/currency boosters for playing games. Which in my opionion is totally fine. Put money in and support the devs and you will progess quicker. That being said, they don't hide any peices needed to build or win behind paying. The tutorial was also more user friendly then Robocraft and the narrator character added some charm. The game has character. Lets hope the Devs keep up thier integrity, and other parties don't intervene. A lot of f2p games built up communities just for the devs to change the system to pay 2 win, or another party takes over and kills the game balancing. I expected to play it for a bit and delete it like robocraft when I downloaded it. Now, I think I'm going to stick around and maybe throw some money the devs way to show my support with some exp/bot boosts.
