Do you like games that focus mainly on the story such as The Walking Dead (or every game by Telltales)? If so, you should like that game. Fahrenheit Indigo Prophecy is a point-and-click adventure in which you control Lucas Kane, a guy who wakes up in the toilet of a restaurant with a knife in his hand .. and a body on the ground just next to him ! Also, you control two other characters, the two cops that are in charge of the investigation for this murder.
First of all, the gameplay. It plays like a regular point-and click adventure game but an important part of the game is the cutscenes . The problem is that in some of these cutscenes, you have to do QTEs (Quick Time Events) in the form of 'Simon Says' with 2 pad of 4 arrows. Sometimes, it's just useless since there is no action at all and it's distracting. Some other times, it might be too hard and unforgiving for some people (I had no problem with that but read a lot of bad comments about that). The game is quite easy. You won't be stuck anywhere since the characters always tell what to do.
My favorite part of the game was the story. Really interesting story. It starts out as a thriller. Why did Lucas did that? Why did he mutilated himself in the toilet before commiting the murder? Why doesn't he remember? There's a lot of questions that are answered later in the game and I won,t spoil anything. It's better that way. I had no idea what this game was about and was pleasantly surprised at the end. There is also different endings depending of the different choices that you make during the game !
Another really good thing about this game is the voice acting. It sounds like a movie and it's definitely a good point. In French (don't know about the English voices), the voice-over is perfect and really intriguing. The music is really great too. It's mysterious and it adds up to the atmosphere of the game (and you can buy some good songs with bonus points in the 'bonus' section !)
Last thing that I really liked was the camera angles throughout the game. Sometimes, you'll see 3-4 views at the same time to show more informations of where the people are or where to go next. Really fun and useful !
In conclusion, if you don't mind about the QTEs, get this game. The story is amazing, the writing is engaging and you'll definitely want to know what happened. Also, it's long enough to be well worth the price of the game (Took me 6 hours to complete it)

Red Orchestra and Rising Storm are truly amazing WW2 tactical shooters. Very realistic and challenging gameplay with no room for silly mistakes. Rising Storm will take the player to the Pacific Ocean theatre of WW2.
US Army and Imperial Army are extremely well done. Using US superior firepower to take stategic locations in places like Iwo Jima or Saipan is a great experience.
In my opinion the thing that makes this game so great is definitely the Japanesse Imperial Army. They do not posses such good equipment as US forces, but they rely on their unmatched feriocity and fanatical determination to fight to the last man. Booby traps, ambushes and other treacherous tactics are in common use. Watching an entire squad rushing into enemy position with swords/bayonets/grenades and fanatical screams is something that could not be forgot - Banzai Charge is an unique gameplay mechanic of the Imperial Army.

First off, I'd like to say this is a tentative recommendation. Buy it only if you are a major jrpg / tales fan or it is on sale.
I'll add that I'm a huge fan, starting like most fans with Symphonia. Anyhow, I'll split this into the good and the bad so you can make your own summary.
- Obviously, the graphics are a pretty big step up being the first Tales game to land on a new platform and PC as well. They've clearly done their best to make sure the character models are both pretty and expressive. Personally, I really hope they continue make the model more animated, it really is a nice touch. The environments, especially the greenery tends to look very nice.
- Honestly, a lot of the music in the game is fairly non-descript. It serves it's purpose as BGM. However, there are a few key pieces by Go Shiina that completely blow everything else out of the water. Don't know who that is? Doesn't matter - you'll recognize this music the second you hear it. It is used sparingly in some of the most key moments of the game. It is so well done, that it might be the best music I've ever heard in a Jrpg.
- Tales has been building to this for a while. While Xillia came close, it couldn't quite shake the feeling of fields just being corridors between dungeons and towns. Zestiria has the most realized overworld so far. They are truly huge - maybe too big.  Some fields feel ludicrously huge, such that it take quite a while just to cross back from one direction from the other, with not much in between,
- This is the big 'but'. The battle system is obviously derivative of Graces. This isn't a bad thing - Graces is widely regarded as the best combat in the series - but honestly the combat system would've worked fine if it was just that. But one thing ruins it, that is armatization. With armitization, battles are reduced to just button bashing for victory. This is a shame, because the base combat system does have some interesting complexities. I often found myself ignoring it just so I could enjoy a battle more. Unfortunately, this often has the effect of dragging out already long boss fights even longer. Bosses often feel like they have a ludicrously high amount of HP.
- This is likely one to irk RPG fans the most. If you're familiar with the tales system, you normally receive 7 party members in total and can construct any party you want out of them. For this game, you're forced to have two certain characters in your party for the entire game (sans moments where they are removed from your party for story reasons). The other two will likely be determined by the enemies elemental resistances.
- Zestiria made the bold decision to have battles take place dynamically in your current environment. While a cool idea in practice, this means that the battles are entire optimized for the area. This will result in the camera getting stuck on almost anything. Walls, enemies, even trees. While some attempt has been made to fix it, there's only so much that can be done for it. This will be a perpetual annoyance.
-This is more of a personal thing than anything, but the anime custscenes are sort of a strange holdover from older tales games. In the current state of technology, they simply don't seem necessary any longer. They used to be used to show events that couldn't be performed using the in game engine, but should be perfectly possible now. Honestly, they just seem rather jarring to the flow of the story where they pop in.
- I don't have much to say except: jesus christ stop making so many of the dungeons be the same cave with a slightly different layout. It's overused to a ridiculous amount in this game.
You might've noticed there's something I haven't mentioned - The story and the characters. That's because they are very decidedly average. The narrative feels very cheesy in a way I can only compare to Graces. The characters oftentimes only feel like caricatures. Compared to the strong character and story in past Tales games, this is a big let down.
I'd like to make one final point before I end this, that is, the localization. This time, it felt very definitively different.  There were noticably a few 'internet voice actors' included, which may be a positive or negative for you, but I felt was very stiff and lacking, especially as one of them plays a main character. Finally, please stop with the memes. It's terrible. Memes and immersion don't belong in the same sentence.

It's also very fun to go for unique shots or trick shots with different kinds of arrows (Bomb/Super Bomb, Drill, Reflecting, Etc.). I'm looking forward to playing it again in the PvP modes and replaying co-op with harder difficulties.

With its stark black/white artwork, layers of film grain, and analog hiss the effect is a bit like the video game equivalent of a Guy Maddin movie (Don't know him? Take 5 minutes and see:
.
Of course it is a bit strange that a game would take the silent era of film as its "retro" model rather than, say, the 8 bit era of video gaming (there's something odd about using digital technology to so lovingly recreate the analog imperfections of another medium), but it's just so gosh darn pretty you don't have much time to think about how it doesn't make much aesthetic sense.

- SPOILER FREE REVIEW! -
What a wonderful example of a 3D Platformer done right. A Hat in Time is a game that obviously draws inspiration from certain N64/GCN titles, but it does so subtly and even improves on their formulas in both fun and interesting ways. I don't intend to provide an in-depth review, but I hope to convince a few 90's gamers to try it out! Without further ado...
Worlds/Graphics:
A Hat in Time will throw you into a delightful selection of worlds, each with their own unique style of both graphics and gameplay. I can honestly say that each of the worlds almost feels like its own game -- everything from the stage selection screen to the NPCs and flavor text contribute to the thematic style of each area. Graphically, the game is wonderfully cartoonish, and I think best described as a blend of Wind Waker's bright colors alongside Super Mario Galaxy's alien environments. I experienced the game Maxed out at 2560x1440 and can honestly say it's one of the most beautiful games I've played. It also looks gorgeous at higher framerates if your monitor supports it.
Music/Soundtrack:
Many indie games fall flat when it comes to their soundtrack, given that their development team usually isn't large and doesn't contain a dedicated composer. With "A Hat in Time," this could not be further from the truth. The game's soundtrack immediately grabs you with its unique space-y sound and happy-go-lucky attitude, and the experience only gets better from there. Each world has its own "theme," but the music undergoes subtle changes as events take place and you progress throughout each mission. Everything from the area themes to the boss music is a home-run. Simply a phenomenal job. If you're a fan of VGM soundtracks, you'll be coming back for it later, I promise.
Gameplay/Mechanics:
With any platformer (especially 3D platformers) it's important that the controls function well. Given that "A Hat in Time" does require precision platforming in some of its areas, it is clear that the developers spent a lot of time tuning the physics and controls to ensure tight, responsive movement. Hat Kid generally goes where I expect her to go, and keeping her aligned to platforms/tightropes/etc. usually works as expected. Not everything works perfectly, however-- wall kicking is more difficult than it should be and it often causes the camera to jitter if done incorrectly. This is something that could easily be addressed with a patch, so I expect this won't remain an issue forever.
Conclusion:
Although this might seem a bit cliché, the biggest problem with "A Hat in Time" is that it's too short. Not for the price, mind you -- $30 is completely reasonable for a game of this complexity and length. It's too short because it leaves you wanting more. You want to take Hat Kid on more adventures. You want to hear more of the entralling soundtrack. You want to stand in awe of the next enormous environment, precisely crafted to its own style. In theory, two additional worlds will be arriving at some point as free DLC. If so, that's fantastic news -- I just hope the Developers take their time and put just as much effort into the DLC worlds as the originals. Don't rush them; just make them fun.
In a way, that's the whole theme of "A Hat in Time." It wasn't rushed, but rather carefully crafted over many years of hard work. The result of that work, however, is an experience brimming with such a pure, genuine fun that I haven't felt since playing Super Mario Galaxy nearly 10 years ago.

This game has a lot to offer, and... I want to like it. I really do. But I can't.
It offers a simple "village builder," where you can lay out your town as you please - no need to worry about setting up inefficient trade routes between islands (here's looking at you, Anno) or spamming area-of-effect buildings (SimCity) throughout the map. You build what's needed (a quarry to cut stone out of the ground after you've scavenged everything from the surface, for example), scale appropriately (farms to produce food as more families populate your town, for example), and you should be good-to-go.
Alas, it is not so. The AI - your townspeople - will ruin the experience of building a settlement for you.
Simply put, the moves your AI townfolk will make are terribly inefficient bordering on the outright nonsensical. Once your town seems to reach a certain threshold (greatly exacerbated in the "mountains" style maps, where small pockets of population separated by terrain features dot the terrain), your workers will simply scramble in random patterns while resources go uncollected, buildings lay incomplete, and food goes to waste.
Don't count on workers to live near their place of employment - instead, count on workers to live in a random pattern, where they'll necessarily need to run all the way across town to get to work, only to find themselves exhausted at the end of the journey, turning around to get something to eat or warm up at the house - while the aforementioned projects lay idle. Your townspeople will, despite having plenty of food or resources stored for use, starve themselves for lack of time to collect and use those resources as they run clear across the expanse of whatever settlement they live in...
Unless you're extremely tedious in building housing immediately prior to putting a new production site down - something that's not feasible unless you're spending a ton of time deliberately planning every move versus "going with the flow" of managing input/output as resources are built up or dwindle under the strain of new citizens - you'll simply watch your town(speople) self-destruct under the weight of the AI's ignorance. Not for lack of resources, mind you. Just that they're too stupid to locate closer to home, even if you intend for the queue to line up that way.
Ultimately, this wrecks the game and, unfortunately, I cannot recommend.

I absolutely love city builders. This may speak to some problems with micro-managing, but whatever, that's not important right now. What IS important is that, if you do not already have Banished, you buy it right now. I am one of those people who's least favorite part of most city builders/RTS games is the military aspect. Bansished has none. Even without the threat of invasion, there is plenty to worry about; primarily ensuring that your entire village doesn't starve or freeze during their first few winters. Throughout the game keeping your population growth and possible trade goods in mind is also incredibly important.
There are several ways to make the game more or less difficult. Aside from difficulty modes, you can also decide if you want mild or harsh weather, the size of your map, and the elevation of your terrain (mountains are important for mining, but make farming difficult). Admittedly, playing on easy is incredibly boring for me, but if you're new to city builders it would be a great place to start.
It's a slower-pace game than something like Tropico or Age of Empires, but with so much going on it will keep you entertained for much longer than you had planned to be playing it at all.

Red Orchestra 2 is simply one of the finest if not the greatest WW2 game that has hit the market to date, and there are numerous features that make this game sine in almost every aspect to back this statement up.
First of all the graphics.When maxed out on the ultra graphics i dare say this game looks as realistic as a game can look and can compete even with the graphics of games such as Battlefield.In addition all the maps are geniously desinged so as both team work and tactical thinking are needed in order for a team to progress while at the same time maintening a balance between the 2 sides.
This also brings me to the next key aspect of the game that makes it so appealing to me ,which is TEAMWORK and i simply can not strech this enough.Forget about all your call of duties and battlefields and such where all you need for the victory is one effective player.In this game if teamwork is not utilized defeat is inevitable.Even the slightest hindering in a teams teamwork such as for example a gunner that doesnt know where to place his mg to provide supressing fire can mean the deference between a point captured and a point lost.And to back this importance of teamwork a finite amount of classes are being introduced ,each one utilizing different guns and equipment for different purposes.In addition each gun comes with up to 3 REALISTIC attachments that can be obtained through the extensive use of the gun.These attachments can vary and are all historically accurate in contrast to the ones in game such as call of duty (for example there's no apperture sight for the mp40,an attachment clearly completly fictional).
Moreover the games realistic feel is further increased by certain aspects that the HUD and the gun mechanics have.For the first time in the history of gaming there is no bullet counter and instead the player can have a rough guess of how many bullets he has left by quicly releasing and weighting his mag or by extracting his bolt half way to have a look at the clip if he is using a rifle.Most guns are also usually 1 shot kill if a player lands a headshot,a heartshot,a nutshot or an upertorso shot.If the player doesnt land one of these shots the player he hit will become wounded and will have to bandge immediatly if he wishes not to bleed out.Therefore the chances that you will hit and enemy and he will either kill you or run away are very few ,as they should in my opinion.The game also uses a realistic ballistic system accounting for gravity and such,and it is for that reason that the ability is given to the player to ajust his sights for the proper range.Actions availiable to the player such as changing barrels of an overheated mg,aiming through the iron sights of a snipe rifle and changing through the rate of certain machineguns also add to the realism.
Tank combat is furthermore a feature that sines in this game.Never before has the intirior of a tank looked so realistic in a game and never before have the correct seats within a tank been utilized correctly.In order for the tank to be used to its full potential, the gunner, the driver,the tank commander and the mg gunner will have to work together.
Last but not least a feature that i just love and think every game should have is that when the server is not full of players ,bots take the empty slots.In this way even if only 2 players are palying on a server the game wont feel empty and dead.I must however in account of fairness admit that the AI for the bots is nothing to be really proud of as they will often stay in the spawn running back and forth,stuck in various places or wont advance as the match progresses.I have met this bugs however only a handfull of times and i also have to say that they are not so game breaking as they sound,plus when the server has 56 bots 2 or 3 stuck or glitched isnt really a big deal.I have faith that Tripwire Interactive will adress this issue in a future patch however and so i do not count it as minus for this review.
To conclude Red Orchestra Heroes of Stalingrad is game that can be charectarized as realistic,graphicly immersive and thought provoking as it requires the player to strategically work with his teammates to achieve victory.It has only 1 minor issue that can be easily adressed in a later patch and is made by a company that is known to maintain its games freshness through patches,updates ,contests etc.It is a game with a staggering amount of inovative features and is sure not to disapoint you ,as long as you are not a casul 13 year old cod-loving tryhard.If I were to rate it I would definetly give it a 11/10.I hope this review has helped you and that i will see you online playing this marvel of a game.

Outlast-Hell Is An Experiment You Can't Survive.
So, Well, Hey there. This is gonna be my first article. I am not serious about going into Videogame Journalism but still, I decided I'd do something 'productive' with my time. I'll begin with a game I fell in love with, but sadly, can't marry it, Outlast.
Outlast, the description is terrifying in it's own sense. The game is about a guy called 'Miles Upshur' who is a freelance journalist. He receives an anonymous tip from a guy who says that he worked in the Mount Massive Asylum. Miles feels this is gonna be a nice thing to take down the Murkoff Corporation and goes. Indeed, Miles had a bad childhood since he didn't watch much horror movies or he would've known what was gonna happen, but anyways, Miles did that so that we may enjoy.
BACK TO THE TOPIC.
Outlast is developed by Red Barrels, a company composed of ex-AAA developers. The devs used to work under big names like Ubisoft and EA. Well, Red Barrels used Unreal Engine to power their game.
The game has stunning visuals for an Indie. The description itself says, 'AAA Quality'.
To provide us with immersion, the game has amazing soundtrack, sound effects, and of course, No HUD.  Yep, no HUD. Of course, this is not a typical FPS.
I'm a soundtrack-♥♥♥♥♥. I'll play any game with good soundtrack. And seriously, this game has a DOPE Soundtrack.
Starting with Gameplay
The game is a FPS. Of course, you knew that. The gameplay is like Mirror's Edge with horror. It focuses on your camcorder and quick wits rather than those twitch reflexes.
The controls are not too extensive like Bohemia Interactive's Arma. There is a key for journal, another for Nightvision. Just these two. The remaining are simple WASD, Shift and Space.
Let's get to the mechanics.
As I said, the game features no HUD. You don't fight, you run. Yep, Run and hide. But majority of the gameplay, you'll be hiding. Why? You'll simply be toooooo scared to go on. Like me.
The game has good physics, although, Environment doesn't play a major role, except from climbing. To be honest, if you've played Mirror's Edge, and then play this, you'll notice striking resemblance in freerunning and parkour mechanics. Although, Outlast doesn't have wallrunning and stuff, of course, Miles is just a journalist.
You happen to have a camcorder with you during the game which let's you record events, on which Miles writes his notes. I prefer having the camera out all the time because you never know which event is important. Your camcorder also has a Nightvision inbuilt, which you'll be using all the time. Realistically, your camcorder requires AA batteries to function. You'll have to think before turning on your NV or else you'll be running blindfolded from the variants until colliding with a wall and getting beaten to death.

Story Time!
Yeah, the game has a good storyline. It feels real. Although, it's not open ended. The game is linear and thus the choices don't affect the story. You don't get any choices to be exact. The only choices you get are whether you should run or hide. Yup. Just those two.
Aaand remember, for the first time, Hide.
Is it difficult?
Well, not really. Everything is difficult at first. There are a few difficulty levels. I recommend you Nightmare, sounds tough, but I recommend it for high immersion and fun. Insane is not recommended because you don't get saves.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Comparions are of the devil, but sometimes they are necessary. This game is known as being "from the same guy that did the Stanley Parable", so comparisons with that very game are in order.
And I'd like to say that this game is nothing like the Stanley Parable. The former's about defying the narrator and breaking sequence, this one's a long, narrated corridor of interactions. Sure, it has a plot (which I feel has more than a few holes in it); but it's a simple, linear experience - much like reading this review, your only options are to continue or go do something else.
The plot, which is then the major selling point of the game (since interactivity really is not one), didn't feel that strong to me either. Without going into spoilers, I feel like the points it wanted to make could've been made in much less time and that the game was just artificially stretched to meet the 90 minute mark - and, throughout the whole experience, I'm simply a random spectator caught between Coda and the narrator, who really does not matter at all for the process. Like the message the game is trying to send is not meant for me.
So, much as I wanted it to get better, to make a sudden reveal and turn into a second Stanley Parable that amazed me and filled me with wonderment at every step, I'm afraid I must say it really is nothing of the sort. If you like short, linear games that talk about personal issues, then you may enjoy it - but then again, there are also other games that deal with those subjects in a much more engaging way than simply as a spectator.
Not A bad game.

Approx. 65 hours in:
I've never really been much for making reviews, but I guess I could say I would gladly recommend this, would even pay 10-20 euro for the game at it's current stage or better.
I do like that they decided to make the game F2P, with microtransactions for costumes, that would never affect gameplay (many people are upset, and I don't see why since it only changes your appearance, but fair enough).
Many seems to complain about having to buy extra inventory space, and why? I've reached level 50 on all 4 characters, sure I've grinded a little bit, but with the monthly mission, and daily missions, all different characters, lots of different maps, I'd say I haven't grown bored yet from always having variety of a certain kind. Sure, the characters are each amazing for one specific build and suck at the rest, but does it matter? It does come into play with tactics when you reach the end, because the dropped gear is most likely useless if you want defense gear for a tower builder, and you're playing on your hero character, since the "passives" will be made for that particular character you play as. That adds challenge, in my opinion, to using your characters and towers correctly.
Also, fun to play with friends, I haven't put money into it, and probably won't put any money into costumes since they, easily unlocked by real money, can still be unlocked with the in-game special currency, that (as far as I know) only comes from Dailies and Monthly missions. I really think people should consider playing the game a little, before complaining about it being all "Microtransactions? This will be a pay-to-win game for sure!"
So, all in all, I recommend this game, whether you're a solo player or have friends to play with, though it's always better when you have friends to play with :).
P.S. If any developer see's this, I'm curious, when we step out of Alpha, will people keep their characters and items, or will it be reset and we receive stuff based on our playing? Something else maybe?
P.S.S. I noticed only 2 bugs in the game so far.
1: Sometimes (SPOILER) Harbinger may stay around even after you finish a "phase" with him, where you can't touch him, he can touch you easily aswell as the ship.

Honestly, I bought this game because I remembered playing the first 15 minutes of it on a demo disc for ps2 years ago, and what the game turns out to be is much different than what I expected of it.
It starts off that Lucas kills a man while possessed or in a trance, and after he flees the scene, you control two detectives, Carla and Tyler, in charge of the case. Lucas tries to figure out what happened to him, and Carla and Tyler notice there is something strange with this case. Soon after, the plot takes a twisted dive off the deep end into a river of burning sh*t, like someone decided to drop acid part way through writing this game. I'm pointing my finger at you, David Cage.
So, after that huge spoiler alert, I stopped trying to figure out what was going on, and ultimately stopped playing the game before I could finish it.
Since the story decided to f*ck my brain, I forced myself to concentrate on the actual gameplay mechanics to try and get through the rest of this game. Which may have been a bad idea, as I may have had better luck tolerating this game if I took my skull-f*cking like a man and tried to figure out the story. First, you control the most mundane tasks for the characters.
*swipe left to open top drawer*
"It's empty."
*swipe left to close the top drawer*
*swipe down to open the bottom drawer*
"The thing I need is in here."
*swipe up to take the thing*
*swipe down to close the bottom drawer*
I'm pretty sure the only reason why the game didn't make you swipe left to move your left foot, and right for your right foot, just to walk forward; was because you had to do that for a few climbing sequences, and it was unbearable for those short periods of time; also QWOP wasn't made until a few years after this game came out. Second, if you aren't walking around looking at things, or talking to someone, the game plays a cutscene with a quick time events overlay. Which, turns every badass fight scene in Indigo Prophecy into a game of "Simon Says." The overlay is literally simon says, I wish I was making this up. Finally, there's the conversation mechanic. There is literally no way to predict how the other character will react to a topic you bring up (unlike how it is in Mass Effect or Deus Ex: Human Revolution). But, all their reaction can do is raise or lower your "mood." I can't figure out what the mood bar does; characters don't act different and even at zero ("wrecked" mood) the character won't go off and kill themselves, there's plenty of ways you can do that on your own, on accident
So, I didn't mind conversations that much, since there was no way to mess them up.
- Story that took M. Night Shyamalan off guard
- Controlling every mundane task
- Having to play Simon Says over every cutscene
+ Conversation control wasn't bad
+ Character mood doesn't change a thing

I absolutely love city builders. This may speak to some problems with micro-managing, but whatever, that's not important right now. What IS important is that, if you do not already have Banished, you buy it right now. I am one of those people who's least favorite part of most city builders/RTS games is the military aspect. Bansished has none. Even without the threat of invasion, there is plenty to worry about; primarily ensuring that your entire village doesn't starve or freeze during their first few winters. Throughout the game keeping your population growth and possible trade goods in mind is also incredibly important.
There are several ways to make the game more or less difficult. Aside from difficulty modes, you can also decide if you want mild or harsh weather, the size of your map, and the elevation of your terrain (mountains are important for mining, but make farming difficult). Admittedly, playing on easy is incredibly boring for me, but if you're new to city builders it would be a great place to start.
It's a slower-pace game than something like Tropico or Age of Empires, but with so much going on it will keep you entertained for much longer than you had planned to be playing it at all.

Honestly, this is one of those games where you get halfway through the tutorial and you're already saying "man, I love this game". At this point in time I haven't progressed very far into it,heck, I'm only on the second stage, but everything about this game is just fun, the controls are fluid, the humor is spot on, the level design is easy to memorize and a fun to blast through, and this is one of 3 games I have bought the sountrack to, and I only had to listen to a handful of songs before I made that decision. It's very well optimized for pcs as well, I have a gtx970 and an i74790k, and while playing this game at some of the highest settings possible, I have yet to see it drop one fram below 60, and my dualshock 4 controller works from the start without having to instal 3rd party software (take that dark souls). This is one of those rare cases where I honestly reccomend buying it whilst at full price because the developers deserve every penny of it for the amount of love and hardwork put into this game. I'd say my only issues with the game are that the dash doesn't go in which way you're pointing your analog stick, but rather where your character is currently facing, which has led to  a few deaths, and the game seems to have a philosphy of "Come back when you have the proper power up so you can get this collectible" ie: banjo-tooie (I'm just not a big fan of this kind of design, I much prefer being able to get everything in one go if I can), but these hardly detract from everything else this game has to offer. If you have an itch for a 3d collecthon platformer, especially if you feel like yooka-laylee blueballed you, then you have no reason not to pick this game up, it's everything I wanted from it and more.

What is it?
Leadwerks Game Launcher is a platform to play games made by people, such as myself, using the Leadwerks Game Engine (which is also available on Steam). No external software is required - it's all handled by the launcher and Steam. Find a game you like the looks of, click 'Launch' and it'll download the files and start up once it's ready.
What games are there?
Lots! The best thing about Leadwerks Game Launcher is that it enables you to play anyones' creations that they've made with Leadwerks Game Engine. Keep in mind, however, that these games include titles made by complete beginners to those made by people with considerable more experience. Some of the games are demos, some are prototypes, and some are proof of concept. In any case, there is a description within each game by the author so you know what to expect... mostly!
Of what quality are the games?
They differ. As above, they're made by people of all different abilities and experiences. Some are quite rough around the edges - and that's part of the charm. These are not AAA games (yet!) but you never know what might happen.
What does it cost?
Absolutely nothing. And that's a really nice thing. No harm in trying it out!
Can I talk/suggest things to the devs?
Yep, sure can. You can leave comments for the games on the Steam Workshop pages!

I really wanted to give a positive review on this game, I REALLY did. Fallout 3 is such a good game, but instead of saying the good stuff, I'm gonna get the bad stuff out of the way.
1) The graphics. First and foremost, the graphics to this game are downright ugly. I mean, this is 2008, so maybe I could give them some slack if 4 years ago, Half-Life 2 was released, and it still looks good today, in my opinion.
2) The broken gameplay. Now this is the main reason I gave it a negative review, because of how broken the gameplay is compared to Fallout 4. I have 2 reasons as to why it's broken.
2a) The aiming. The aiming in this game is horrible. Now, I use a controller to play Bethesda games (I play Fallout 4 on PS4), and I thought that it was just because the PC version wasn't designed to have a controller, so I tried using my mouse, and somehow, that was even worse. I literally can't headshot an enemy without having to constantly use the VATS all of the time. And yes, I have tried adjusting my sensitivity and yes, I do use a crosshair.
2b) The lack of dificulty variety. Now Fallout 3 has 2 dificulties. Hard, and balls to the wall hard. I have tried playing the game on every dificulty, and nothing really changes. I keep dying over and over and over again from raiders, ghouls, super mutants and even goddamn radroaches! I mean, if normal mode meant average dificulty, then this'd be a fun game. But no, it has to be the same as hard. Well, after saying all that negative stuff, I feel like saying some positives.
1) The characters. Fallout has (for the most part) had very memorable characters. I still remember Gob, that ghoul that works in the bar. Anyone else remember him?
2) The world. Now, this is a Bethesda game, so the open world aspect is the biggest draw to it. Whilst everyone looks more plastic than a Lego figure, it still feels alive.
3) Perks and desicions. OK, one thing that Bethesda messed up with Fallout 4 was the dumbed down perks and choices you could make. Let's talk about the perks first. The perks in 3 are really in-depth. The game encourages you to level up if you don't have level __ in ____. Also, whilst your character isn't voiced, his/her voice is meant to be your voice. Because of this, Bethesda made whatever you choose to say is what your player avatar really says. Unlike Fallout 4, where it barely describes what you're saying, and there's the dreaded "sarcastic" option. (If you ask me, it'd be better if it was saying nothing instead.) Also, this game makes you feel like your choices affect the world around you. Kinda like Telltale (aside from GOT).
In conclusion, Fallout 3 is not bad. But, it would be a better game if it was remade/remastered into the new engine. If you have read this far, cheers and have a good rest of your day.

The resolution IS small, however that is intentional. This game's tilesets are the standard size for almost any JRPG, making it so much simpler when seeking out resources online. I've grown to like it. It's simple, and I don't feel overwhelmed when creating for it.

You see, there is just you and the animatronic dolls. Thats the horror of the game. You have nothing to do but to sit there and wait for the evil presence kills you. You're trapped.
As with Amnesia this game is supposed to be played in a pitch black room with your headphones on. Unlike Amnesia this game has tonnes of jumpscares but no cheap ones. Since the entire game builds up for them so well. Infact there arent much else. But a well places jumpscare with a lot of build up can make or break a game. The atmophere is key to horror games and this game NAILS it.
There have been 3 great horror games during the last 5 years. Amnesia, Outlast and Five Nights at Freddy's. All of wich are horror to their cores. All of wich put you up against horrible creatures and all of which you are helpless against. The feeling of not being able to fight back is so horrifying that it's not even funny but in this you have nothing else but to sit and wait.
You dont have an objective to escape or take revenge, something to keep you from dreading the monsters chasing you. In this your objective is to survive. Not to run but just to last til morning. You cant run, you cant hide and you cant fight back. All you can do is wait for the clock to tick. Add the creepy setting, sounds and general feel to it and you sit there and just hope for the in game clock to have mercy on you so can make it to 6:AM.
Oh and did i mention the amazing reason you place yourself in this position. 120 bucks. For an entire weeks work. Life kinda sucks sometimes, you know that?
I sure hope I could make games.

Four hours into the game, the story was intriguing and well-told, but the gameplay was so horrendously bad I had to stop playing.
The exploration parts are simple and plagued by terrible control of locomotion, quirky interaction controls, and terrible camera cutting, all of which are even worse for the action sequences.
The quick-time events are excessive, repetitive, lacking of any sort of substance due to the absolute lack of player choice or any skill in general beyond a low reaction time. This is worsened by the repeated use of very long sequences of quick-time events without any intermediate checkpoints or the like (the flying-objects sequence in Lucas' apartment comes to mind) which ultimately lead to frustration over repeated failures which the player can do nothing to avoid except mindlessly retrying and hoping to randomly be a little faster or a little more accurate on the next try.
Lastly, the puzzles are trivial and feel like those of a point-and-click, rewarding brute experimentation more than reflection on mechanics and comparison against previous puzzles, perhaps due to a high dependency on puzzle-specific rather than systemic mechanics.
On top of that, many puzzles (e.g. the bookshop/library) and quick-time events (e.g. boxing, basketball practice) are mostly unrelated to the main plot and feel unsubstantial and redundant.
All in all, this game would have been a lot more enjoyable as a movie. At the very least it should have been stripped of all the shallow quick-time events and received some adjustments to controls and camera behavior. In any case, I personally ended up reluctantly discarding it when my frustration with the gameplay began to outweigh the quality of the story.

Superhot is an indie first person shooter running on the Unity engine. It has such a novel premise I'm surprised it hasn't been done before.
In this game, time slows down to a near standstill when you stop moving. And progresses forwards when you move and when you fire. The development team implemented this very well. Bullets fly through the air and are very easy to spot among the white level textures. The game has this very Hotline Miami feel to it. You can throw your guns at enemies to stun them, you can throw objects to block bullets, and you can even shoot bullets in midair as they fly towards you. For a game that should feel slow and calculated, it feels very fast paced and rhythmic.
Stylistically the game is very interesting. The UI resembles a DOS based operating system. Enemies resemble low poly characters from old video games. At the same time the environments look very crisp and everything stands out very well. If you're a fan of films like Tron you'll definitely like this game.
However, all that being said the game is not perfect, and it's very hard for me to recommend. For the 25$ asking price there's very little content and you can mostly beat it in a handful of hours. The level design also maintains the same white sterile aesthetic and doesn't have that much variety to it. While the core gameplay is pretty solid it appeals to a certain kind of player. It appeals to the kind of player that wants to play a level over and over to try and achieve a perfect run.
If you're that kind of player I do recommend this game a lot. But to everyone else I'd say wait a little for the dev to either create a level editor or lower the price.

I GUESS PEOPLE CAN ONLY COMPREHEND SPOILER WARNINGS IF THEY'RE IN ALL CAPS, SO SPOILERS AHEAD PEOPLE. ALSO, AND FOR GOOD MEASURE, IN CASE YOU SKIP THIS LINE, TOO-
*SPOILERS AHEAD*
The Beginner's Guide will inevitably polarize the slice of gaming public that plays it (as evidenced by the reviews trickling in). And that is as it should be. It's a game about the death of the author/programmer, and it is deeply ironic, confusing, and sad. It also questions the cultural desire to canonize some things as "art" and discard others, as if there's some apotheosis of meaning to be found in a so-called grand narrative.
The hour and a half narrative experiment features a narcissistic auto-narrator named Davey Wreden who tries futilely to grasp the meaning behind a collection of unfinished micro-games that his friend, Coda, presumably made, stored away, and forgot about. The player explores these little interactive abstract expressionistic games and observes as each programmed space gets increasingly desperate, dreary, and claustrophobic. Most of the time Davey annoyingly lectures about the meaning of each game, which actually violates player agency in a way few games manage (and I think that that might be what makes so many people uncomfortable. It certainly made me uncomfortable). Whereas most games contain programmed boundaries for the player--and the meaning of the experiences in these games unfold based on the choices the player makes or is impelled to make--in this case the narrator acts as an extra constraining force that imposes meaning on works that otherwise feel deeply ambiguous.
I feel the need to defend this game for precisely these ambiguities, as well as for Davey's constant need to fold those imposed meanings back in upon himself (something that I think we all do when looking at an art piece). Many of the criticisms leveled against this game range from thoughtful (e.g. unlike Stanley Parable, which forces players to reflect upon their choices by showing how games constrain mobility, this game spoonfeeds meaning to players and holds their hands during the experience) to irrelevant (e.g. why pay this much for a bunch of unfinished games?). I'm interested some of these responses because so many of them showed that the game caused a stir, and the most compelling of those responses were ones that almost couldn't decide what to think. Stanley Parable was a complicated game because no other game before it had intentionally done the work of exposing the boundaries of the game world. No other game had discussed so completely how games are such powerfully rhetorical devices (a discussion we need to have more frequently, especially given the legacy of brazen violence in video games that comes, in part, out of a history of military involvement with the games industry).
But The Beginner's Guide is something different. Instead of forcing players merely to reflect upon themselves as they engage with the game world, it also asks that the player recognize how one's interpretation of an artwork is colored by personal experience, and that as a consequence it is always already misguided to attribute an absolute intention behind an authored piece. So what do we make of Davey, the actual author? Leaving aside for the moment that the auto-narrator is nothing more than a mirror (or picture, or simulation) of Davey, the author of the game is always inaccessible and non-existent. Once the product is out there, it is up to the player to decide what it means. In other words, everybody's interpretation of a thing is simultaneously subjective (lonely) and socially constructed. That makes meaning both dynamic and intersubjective. Because Davey is an added constraint on the player (metaphorically figured in-game as imprisonment), the player is left to wonder what the hell they just experienced. Was it someone else's loneliness? Was it a desperate game designer crying for help? Was it a massive cliche about how tortuous the creative process is? Or was the game just forcing us to ask these questions in ways we never have before?
The player sometimes occupies multiple subject positions in order to feel loneliness and uncertainty. For example, the player is at one point a student in a lecture hall. With the exception of a professor at the podium confidently spouting off pseudo-intellectual nonsense, the entire lecture hall is empty. The camera shifts to different seats two or three times before settling on the professor, who perceives behind the lone student in the auditorium (his pink cube head reading "listen" on all sides) a massive black hole sucking in everything around it. Meanwhile, the player gets to choose what the professor says. Yellow highlighted phrases are what the professor would actually say to his students. The grey options, always vulnerable or crass or self-defeating, are the honest ones. Maybe I found this scene so touching because I teach college, too, but it confused the hell out of me because at this point in the game I was so critical of Wreden for being an absolutely pompous jerk, and yet I found myself needing to fold this moment back in upon myself. More than anything, that's the sort of confusing push and pull that makes me endorse this experiment.
I recognize that my review might come off as a little ironic, since it seems like I'm attributing absolute meaning to this game. But I'm not. I am just offering a way of thinking about it, and a lot of people might find this way misguided and stupid. That's fine. In the end, it doesn't matter if people do or don't like this game, because what it did is it elicited a confused response that didn't before exist. The cool thing about meta-narratives in games right now is that they suggest game designers are starting to leave behind the tired narratives of hyper-masculine men lugging around heavy weaponry through destroyed cityscapes. Instead, gamers now have to think about how lonely the experience of playing a game is. They have to reflect on the types of questions games are able to raise in ways other media cannot. The possibilities are utterly exciting, and I for one look forward to what developers come up with next.

- SPOILER FREE REVIEW! -
What a wonderful example of a 3D Platformer done right. A Hat in Time is a game that obviously draws inspiration from certain N64/GCN titles, but it does so subtly and even improves on their formulas in both fun and interesting ways. I don't intend to provide an in-depth review, but I hope to convince a few 90's gamers to try it out! Without further ado...
Worlds/Graphics:
A Hat in Time will throw you into a delightful selection of worlds, each with their own unique style of both graphics and gameplay. I can honestly say that each of the worlds almost feels like its own game -- everything from the stage selection screen to the NPCs and flavor text contribute to the thematic style of each area. Graphically, the game is wonderfully cartoonish, and I think best described as a blend of Wind Waker's bright colors alongside Super Mario Galaxy's alien environments. I experienced the game Maxed out at 2560x1440 and can honestly say it's one of the most beautiful games I've played. It also looks gorgeous at higher framerates if your monitor supports it.
Music/Soundtrack:
Many indie games fall flat when it comes to their soundtrack, given that their development team usually isn't large and doesn't contain a dedicated composer. With "A Hat in Time," this could not be further from the truth. The game's soundtrack immediately grabs you with its unique space-y sound and happy-go-lucky attitude, and the experience only gets better from there. Each world has its own "theme," but the music undergoes subtle changes as events take place and you progress throughout each mission. Everything from the area themes to the boss music is a home-run. Simply a phenomenal job. If you're a fan of VGM soundtracks, you'll be coming back for it later, I promise.
Gameplay/Mechanics:
With any platformer (especially 3D platformers) it's important that the controls function well. Given that "A Hat in Time" does require precision platforming in some of its areas, it is clear that the developers spent a lot of time tuning the physics and controls to ensure tight, responsive movement. Hat Kid generally goes where I expect her to go, and keeping her aligned to platforms/tightropes/etc. usually works as expected. Not everything works perfectly, however-- wall kicking is more difficult than it should be and it often causes the camera to jitter if done incorrectly. This is something that could easily be addressed with a patch, so I expect this won't remain an issue forever.
Conclusion:
Although this might seem a bit cliché, the biggest problem with "A Hat in Time" is that it's too short. Not for the price, mind you -- $30 is completely reasonable for a game of this complexity and length. It's too short because it leaves you wanting more. You want to take Hat Kid on more adventures. You want to hear more of the entralling soundtrack. You want to stand in awe of the next enormous environment, precisely crafted to its own style. In theory, two additional worlds will be arriving at some point as free DLC. If so, that's fantastic news -- I just hope the Developers take their time and put just as much effort into the DLC worlds as the originals. Don't rush them; just make them fun.
In a way, that's the whole theme of "A Hat in Time." It wasn't rushed, but rather carefully crafted over many years of hard work. The result of that work, however, is an experience brimming with such a pure, genuine fun that I haven't felt since playing Super Mario Galaxy nearly 10 years ago.

First off I’m going to say this game is amazing, if you want to know if it’s worth it, absolutely yes! If a cute, fun, solid 3D platformer is what you’re looking for this is the game for you! Now on with the review!
I'll start with the pros and cons. Cons first, so let’s get these bad boys out of the way.
Cons
- The length
- Visual glitches
- The lack of voice acting near endgame
The worst thing about this game would be its length... Well if you do the bare minimum; which is getting 25 time pieces and not going out of your way to grab collectables. In which the game is about 10-15 hours. If you however, collect everything, the game is much longer and more enjoyable in my opinion. This also negates the length problem; however even after finishing everything I could, I was still left craving more.
This game is definitely beautiful, but one thing that happened a decent bit were visual glitches, mainly shadows on some  characters being off and clipping on models, a lot of clipping. An example is a cut scene after the first boss. Where hat girl closes her eyes and shakes her head, her eyes clip through. Though that only happens in that cut scene.  Distracting but that's about it.
Another thing that is merely distracting is the lack of voice acting near the end of the game. Some characters were voiced while some were not. Note that these same characters were fully voiced earlier in game. That’s the reason why this is distracting, IS because it is fully voice acted other than those handful of lines.
Pros
- The visuals
- The camera
-The voice acting
-How hat kid controls
-The Characters
To start right off the bat you’ll notice this game looks good, but not really detailed, most textures are relatively simple. However what makes this game’s visuals mostly simple but down right gorgeous, are the visual effects. From sand and snow sparkling, to partials and butterflies in the air. The wind blowing, dust and fog hanging just above the ground, and ambers floating in the air around fire and lava. And probably more that I’m missing. That alone makes this game so beautiful to look at; really it’s just a treat for your eyes.
They defiantly took a lot care with the camera; it feels like an extension of yourself. It never got in my way, nor did I have to fight it. To the point that hardly noticed it. The only two problems I had with it. Were that sometimes I couldn’t make a sharp turn fast enough; likely do to my settings. And that you can clip the camera through a lot of thing ever so slightly.
I’ve got to say the voice acting is wonderful, some of the best I’ve heard! Not much to say, the character’s voices are distinct, and fit perfectly with each character. Lastly the lines were read with so much character and emotion.
Hat kid controls beautifully, every move can flow into each other. You’re given so much control over how you move. Not to mention how fast you can move, do to being able to have each move go from one to the next. I don’t think I’ve ever played a platformer that allows for such movement. To go from one side of an area to the next with lighting fast speed and simple but accurate controls; well one just has to feel for themselves, to truly appreciate it.
Last but not least the characters, oh the characters. Every character has an distinct and quirky personality. They also play off one another beautifully. From two characters fighting for a trophy, by all means possible, do to believing the other will cheat to win. To one that your obligated to do, let’s say “chores” for. And not to spoil anything ends up in a disagreement that goes back and forth in a humorous way. I’ll leave the rest for you to see for yourself.
And that’s A Hat in Time. A must play if you ask me, so what are you waiting for, pick it up and play it already!

While I'm normally loathe to play, let alone recommend an Early Access title, The Long Dark is not only well into a playable state. Not only is it playable, but it is exactly what a wilderness survival game should be: cold, unforgiving and lonely. Your survival will depend on your ability to make snap desicions, your ability to spend your resources well and your ability to navigate. The Long Dark is not without its flaws however: it is not exceptionally well optimized, I experienced fps drops on a  machine that ran the new Wolfenstein at 50-60 fps, navigation can be a chore as the shadow system is not working properly though there is dynamic lighting, hunting is a little less realistic than it should be and it is a little jarring, on medium difficulty wolves survive .303 headshots. All things told, the game is an 8.5/10 in its current state, and it looks like it's only uphill from there. A definite buy.

Don't let the hours fool you. I've already logged a bunch of hours while my internet was down...
Regardless this game is a great strategy game. But be warned watch a video, this isnt a visually advanced game, its all sprites and what not. It is also not fast paced. But it is in-depth and in my opinion exciting, and despite the slower pace, the... intense moments of watching your line trying to hold, or ordering a division commander to fulfill orders or being that division commanding officer. You can chose from a variety of command levels on the Order of Battle. You can play the battle of waterloo or make your own. As I now play larger and larger battles I have found more... frustrating things. Such as a simple notice like... when a major player is killed on the battle. Playing a massive battle on the campaign (my much smaller dutch army w/ fewer infantry, fewer cannons and no calvary trying to hold off a larger french army that including cavalry) where a win was critial as if the french were to break through the town, that army could have caused havoc until I could have mustered a large enough army in the area to counter them (if that was even going to be possible). The pressure was intense, the battle a fantastic reperesentation of what this game has to offer and a billion things going on. Trying to hold a thin line, meanwhile the cavalry rushing in scaring my men into squares where they became easy pickings for my infantry, on the flanks a back and forth of me trying to flank the french and ease pressure on my center before not once but TWICE did the french counter attack with near fresh divisions. The battle itself was absolutely enjoyable. Would I love for some portions of the battle to not become so... laggy. Of course who doesn't want a fluid game? Why when there are i7s and i5s out is the engine rocking some 1.5 crap? Is it too much to ask that the same awesome smooth marching and fighting in smaller battles be capable on the larger scale? Regardless thats absolutely minor and doesn't take away from the fun what so ever, just being picky.
Back to my original point in all this mayham, the bloody Prince of Orange, the commander of the entire dutch army died. No courier to my next in command saying your in charge now. On top of that I find the end stats loaded with info that I dont get a chance to look over cause the game keeps promting end of battle but while your trying to read the stats and find out just who is left in command of your regiments, divisions and corps, the battle is raging on for some reason behind the screen... And maybe I havent found it yet on that screen cause it keeps bumping me out when the end battle newpaper pops up, but the stats you can find midbattle of wounded, missing, and killed for each battalion is great, but why isn't on the end stats. Finding out which of your commanders was killed can be tedious. Or before that just having a courier saying that this commander is dead and so-and-so is taking over. I'd like to look over his stats and see what kind of person he is, seeing as it could someone important or crutial. I think finding out a reliable or favorite division commander was killed would help immersion of being connected or invested in your forces. Finding out after words is like... Oh well that blows. And keeping in touch with historical aspects... I think the chain of command would notice that the PRINCE OF ORANGE was killed and orders were coming from someone else... Haha it's really too bad, now I've got to fight the rest of the campaign without such a leader (who was replaced by a MAJOR/sure hope that was just heat of the moment in battle and someone else is appointed commander, have yet to see).
And the screens for spliting and merging portions of your forces can be a pain, and I dont understand why it isn't possible to merge different units to form difference corps or divisions. I've been having fun playing the game, yes, but that doesn't mean there aren't rough edges.
Pros:
The building is very fun and intuitive. Very similar to Besiege and From the Depths and others like it, but not as much depth or complication as those two.
Combat, when you get a good match up, is satisfying. Grouping up in a squadron and punishing lone wolf enemies feels great.
Flying the ship may feel sluggish or slow, but that is usually the player's fault; add gyroscopes and thrusters or cut weight. This is where much of where the balancing went right; it's difficult to build a truly 'over powered' ship, as you will lack in one area or another, be it fire power, maneuverabilty, utility or armor.
Cons:
The balancing feels very poor in terms of weapon design, especially with how open the maps are and how player spotting is handled. You will know where virtually everyone on the map is at any given moment. Flanking is hardly an option as the game tells you where almost everyone is at all times, except for a few seconds when they fly close to a wall. Which would be fine, except...
Longer range weapons will trounce shorter range weapons 9/10 times. This is where a lot of your frustration at lower levels will be. Gauss cannons and cruise missiles will shred you long before you even get within range of the enemy with them if you dared to use the weapons with sub 3000 meter range (which is all you have for the first few hours), and the devs think the solution to this is to tell us to go flank (see above).
And while not obvious at first glance, one glaring issue is voice communication. The game lends itself to teamwork but how can you really do that when you would have to stop and type to your team. This could be difficult due to how diverse the playerbase is but it would be a great help.
Also, by nature of being free, the game is loaded with micro transactions, but they are just cosmetic. Anything that actually effects gameplay can be won over time but it still makes it feel a little pay to win.
Over all, I'm giving the game a positive review because I feel it has a ton of potential and the issues can be relatively easy to fix. The concept is solid and the building is great, the issues lie mainly in some minor balancing tweaks.

Review:
RPG Maker is simple to get started and to use, however it is at times a bit too simplistic.
While you can easily create an Final Fantasy clone it's much harder to create the game accordance to your own imagination.
It's very much like Bethesda's approach towards their games, let the modding community flesh out the irks and qirks that nags them.
In this case it's extending RPG Maker, so while you may have seen titles such as Lisa and think you could easily re-create it, it won't happen unless you heavily extend it with libraries/your own coded scripts.
For example it treats everything as an event, as such you have extensive freedom in deciding what npcs, objects and effects are suppose to do, but it makes debugging and backtracking a nightmare, especially when dealing with non-native language games.
It's script editor and event editor is very clunky and outdated.
The script editor does not parse the code to check for errors, instead you have to run the game for the Ruby intepreter to print it out, thus coupled with the fact that you can not make the textbox (i.e. where you write the script) bigger, can't search for keyword cross files makes it very time consuming when debugging.
The event editor has a very Scratch like feeling to it, in that you put chunk of programming logic to create game logic, however as said before the editor suffers from poor design choices such as:
You are limited by about 5-6 tile set per map, where all the A sub tiles has to be of a certain type:
A1 -> Terrain
A2 -> Roof
A3 -> Walls
...
...
Also the lack of debugging and game testing mode, while yes it does exist, it is very, very, very basic.
The only thing you can change via debugging is the switches and variables but there is no way to spawn certain enemies, no teleportation, god mode without scripts or even to test the current map, instead you have to see it load the game, start the game as normal (again you can't skip the intro or do anything different than from a normal playthrough without scripts) play through the game as normal to get to the location you want to test and then you have to make sure you save it there to make sure you don't have to do it all over again.
In the end I do not know what to give it, it's annoying when it doesn't work as intended but rewarding when you start to understand game design and game logic.

Heavy Rain... I mean, Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered, is an update of the PS2 era game of the same name. Focusing more on being a movie than a game, it provides a unique experience built from the ground up with mechanics that AAA developers nowadays seem willing to inject into what should be purely action games. However, this title partially succeeds at using these elements to tell an enthralling tale.
Visuals: Sharper resolutions and cleaner textures combine with PS2 era animations and the camera catching things which shouldn't necessarily be in the frame. I noticed the latter issue during the end cutscene, with chunks of the sky and visual effects cutting off with a flat line because my monitor is too wide. Otherwise, for the most part, it looks okay. Also, the sex scenes look hilarious.
Audio: The soundtrack isn't very large, so a lot of the same music will be played over and over. Where this game is strong is in its voice acting. Every character is believable and delivers their lines with enough emotion to keep the player engrossed.
Story: With the exception of that turn for the (Steam censored what I said here, lol) in the last hour or so of the game, it's a very well organized plot with multiple paths. It's filled with people that the game gave me a reason to care about, and I rarely get attached a game's story. Also impeccable is the level of detail, such as how certain actions (or lack thereof) will affect the character, emotionally or physically. For example, forgetting to do one thing might force the player to hastily cover up evidence of that mistake, sometimes even in the presence of other characters.
Gameplay: If you are not dealing with Resident Evil controls or quicktime event overload, you cannot possibly be playing Indigo Prophecy. The tank controls, I can get used to, even in the pseudo-stealth sections. The constant quick-time events, not so much. Almost every task that does not have to do with walking, from having a drink, to having a superpowered fight with that old dude from Saw, is a quicktime event. It's boring, it's monotonous, and it oversimplifies some tasks while making others too complex. However, considering that it is clearly intended to be more of a movie, I can be a little forgiving in that regard.
More perplexing is how dialogue is handled. Short, one word descriptions representing my possible conversation directions do not adequately convey enough information to allow me to make an educated decision. Sometimes I'm not sure of the tone the character will take, sometimes I'm not even sure as to whose perspective I am controlling the dialogue from.
Other times, the system just seems impractical. For example, when talking with somebody who is standing perfectly still and will not leave until I do, why is the conversation still timed? Why can I only talk about 2 items off of my list of 4 items when the person I'm talking to has nothing better to do?
Overall, it feels like a Dragon's Lair arcade game with less cliché and an occasional ability to take a breather.

- SPOILER FREE REVIEW! -
What a wonderful example of a 3D Platformer done right. A Hat in Time is a game that obviously draws inspiration from certain N64/GCN titles, but it does so subtly and even improves on their formulas in both fun and interesting ways. I don't intend to provide an in-depth review, but I hope to convince a few 90's gamers to try it out! Without further ado...
Worlds/Graphics:
A Hat in Time will throw you into a delightful selection of worlds, each with their own unique style of both graphics and gameplay. I can honestly say that each of the worlds almost feels like its own game -- everything from the stage selection screen to the NPCs and flavor text contribute to the thematic style of each area. Graphically, the game is wonderfully cartoonish, and I think best described as a blend of Wind Waker's bright colors alongside Super Mario Galaxy's alien environments. I experienced the game Maxed out at 2560x1440 and can honestly say it's one of the most beautiful games I've played. It also looks gorgeous at higher framerates if your monitor supports it.
Music/Soundtrack:
Many indie games fall flat when it comes to their soundtrack, given that their development team usually isn't large and doesn't contain a dedicated composer. With "A Hat in Time," this could not be further from the truth. The game's soundtrack immediately grabs you with its unique space-y sound and happy-go-lucky attitude, and the experience only gets better from there. Each world has its own "theme," but the music undergoes subtle changes as events take place and you progress throughout each mission. Everything from the area themes to the boss music is a home-run. Simply a phenomenal job. If you're a fan of VGM soundtracks, you'll be coming back for it later, I promise.
Gameplay/Mechanics:
With any platformer (especially 3D platformers) it's important that the controls function well. Given that "A Hat in Time" does require precision platforming in some of its areas, it is clear that the developers spent a lot of time tuning the physics and controls to ensure tight, responsive movement. Hat Kid generally goes where I expect her to go, and keeping her aligned to platforms/tightropes/etc. usually works as expected. Not everything works perfectly, however-- wall kicking is more difficult than it should be and it often causes the camera to jitter if done incorrectly. This is something that could easily be addressed with a patch, so I expect this won't remain an issue forever.
Conclusion:
Although this might seem a bit cliché, the biggest problem with "A Hat in Time" is that it's too short. Not for the price, mind you -- $30 is completely reasonable for a game of this complexity and length. It's too short because it leaves you wanting more. You want to take Hat Kid on more adventures. You want to hear more of the entralling soundtrack. You want to stand in awe of the next enormous environment, precisely crafted to its own style. In theory, two additional worlds will be arriving at some point as free DLC. If so, that's fantastic news -- I just hope the Developers take their time and put just as much effort into the DLC worlds as the originals. Don't rush them; just make them fun.
In a way, that's the whole theme of "A Hat in Time." It wasn't rushed, but rather carefully crafted over many years of hard work. The result of that work, however, is an experience brimming with such a pure, genuine fun that I haven't felt since playing Super Mario Galaxy nearly 10 years ago.

First off I’m going to say this game is amazing, if you want to know if it’s worth it, absolutely yes! If a cute, fun, solid 3D platformer is what you’re looking for this is the game for you! Now on with the review!
I'll start with the pros and cons. Cons first, so let’s get these bad boys out of the way.
Cons
- The length
- Visual glitches
- The lack of voice acting near endgame
The worst thing about this game would be its length... Well if you do the bare minimum; which is getting 25 time pieces and not going out of your way to grab collectables. In which the game is about 10-15 hours. If you however, collect everything, the game is much longer and more enjoyable in my opinion. This also negates the length problem; however even after finishing everything I could, I was still left craving more.
This game is definitely beautiful, but one thing that happened a decent bit were visual glitches, mainly shadows on some  characters being off and clipping on models, a lot of clipping. An example is a cut scene after the first boss. Where hat girl closes her eyes and shakes her head, her eyes clip through. Though that only happens in that cut scene.  Distracting but that's about it.
Another thing that is merely distracting is the lack of voice acting near the end of the game. Some characters were voiced while some were not. Note that these same characters were fully voiced earlier in game. That’s the reason why this is distracting, IS because it is fully voice acted other than those handful of lines.
Pros
- The visuals
- The camera
-The voice acting
-How hat kid controls
-The Characters
To start right off the bat you’ll notice this game looks good, but not really detailed, most textures are relatively simple. However what makes this game’s visuals mostly simple but down right gorgeous, are the visual effects. From sand and snow sparkling, to partials and butterflies in the air. The wind blowing, dust and fog hanging just above the ground, and ambers floating in the air around fire and lava. And probably more that I’m missing. That alone makes this game so beautiful to look at; really it’s just a treat for your eyes.
They defiantly took a lot care with the camera; it feels like an extension of yourself. It never got in my way, nor did I have to fight it. To the point that hardly noticed it. The only two problems I had with it. Were that sometimes I couldn’t make a sharp turn fast enough; likely do to my settings. And that you can clip the camera through a lot of thing ever so slightly.
I’ve got to say the voice acting is wonderful, some of the best I’ve heard! Not much to say, the character’s voices are distinct, and fit perfectly with each character. Lastly the lines were read with so much character and emotion.
Hat kid controls beautifully, every move can flow into each other. You’re given so much control over how you move. Not to mention how fast you can move, do to being able to have each move go from one to the next. I don’t think I’ve ever played a platformer that allows for such movement. To go from one side of an area to the next with lighting fast speed and simple but accurate controls; well one just has to feel for themselves, to truly appreciate it.
Last but not least the characters, oh the characters. Every character has an distinct and quirky personality. They also play off one another beautifully. From two characters fighting for a trophy, by all means possible, do to believing the other will cheat to win. To one that your obligated to do, let’s say “chores” for. And not to spoil anything ends up in a disagreement that goes back and forth in a humorous way. I’ll leave the rest for you to see for yourself.
And that’s A Hat in Time. A must play if you ask me, so what are you waiting for, pick it up and play it already!

***NOTE: If you are interested in trying this game out, go to the developer's website and check out their demo for Scourge of War Gettysburg since they are similar enough.***
This is the game for the person that loves this particular period in warfare and is looking for the most authentic experience simulating those battles as possible. Sure, the game is not as pretty as Napoleon: Total War and is even mildly less appealing graphically than Histwar, but it makes up for this in spades by presenting as accurate a combat simulation that can be made of the Napoleonic Wars given today's technological constraints.
There is a lot more going on under the hood than what you can gather from the screenshots - you have the opportunity to play the full battle of Waterloo in real time, simulating the nearly 200,000 soldiers that participated, generally in 1:4 scale. The Sandbox Campaign also lets you simulate the campaign in Belgium during the Hundred Days, so you might be able to radically change history that way as well.
I am a huge fan of the era and so this game was a must have. Even though I am not as partial to Waterloo as other battles of the period (I would prefer Austerlitz, Wagram, Leipzig, or Jena-Auerstedt) the modding community has already provided a substantial amount of content and has created some of the OOBs for those battles already.
If you think this game would be a good match for you, go to the developer's website and check out their demo for Scourge of War Gettysburg since they are similar enough. Overall, I would say the game is worth it for any fan of the Napoleonic Wars.
