So let me first say that even with the negativity in this review, it's still easly recomended, it's a must have game for anybody wanting a REAL wargame, this is what a wargame should be.
I've played this for sevral dozen hours before it was out on steam.
Now lets get the negative part of the review out of the way.
I have only one major complaint but I feel this is part of a symptom with the developers.
My complaint is the horrible FPS, we are talking max 25 fps on small is battlers. and if you like me want a huge battle, expect 5-12 fps. Now this is a problem, it's party becasue the engine is old and glued, taped and rubberbanded togeater from older incarnations, The game only uses 1.5 cores yet the game is 90%! based on CPU power, with RAM far behind and GPU almost playing no effect.
Aperantly the reason for 1.5 core use is with more cores the multiplayer becomes unstable... So it was dield back 1.5,
So if you got a 3.5 x 8 CPU you will get worse FPS then a 3.8 x4  CPU.
Now this is bad, but worse is the devlopers complantancy with it, When this topic is brought up, you will be swarmed with "this isn't a first person shooter, you don't need 60 fps, or 30 fps" or similar excuses. They honestly think 12 fps is good enough. Now the same thing is happening on the steam forum, any complaint that 12fps isn't good enough and you'll be swarmed by people attacking you for pointing out this very obvious fact.
I personaly get slighly nauseous and can get bad headaches if playing on 7-12 fps, yet this complaint is ignored, like my experiences with the game isn't valid. I think all this stems from some of the developers and alot of the fanboys(I count my self as a fanboy of this game and all the games made by Norbsoft, also before it was nordsoft)  Are totaly separate from the rest of the gaming comunity. I honestly think they think 12 fps is fine. And do not realise that about 99% of the rest of the gaming world do not agree.
Ok Now to the good stuff, and there is alot of good stuff.
As mentioned I have played the pevious Scourge of war games, and the Two "Take command" games. Take command first bull run when it first came out was AMAZING!
The game from the name obvously deals with Waterloo, You get 20 "campaign missions"  10 for each side. With each battle getting bigger. The first battles are brigade sized game, where you control a few thousand soldiers. The last two battles are The full waterloo battle, one as Napoleon one as the Anglo-Allies/Prussians. This is an epic game, At 1:4 scale you will controll some 18 000 sprites representing about 70 000 men, And the enemy got about the same sized  army.
As the battle goes on, another 5000-10000 sprites will enter the battle.
I personaly feel the game looks great, sure it's not a total war looking game, but seeing tens of thousands of troops marcning is a beautifull sight.
As an Army general you will give orders to your corps and divisions, or even brigades,
But as a brigade general you are just a small clog in the big ben, You will have to do your best with your 1500-3000 men while the battle rages around you.
The ai while not perfect, is better then almost all other strategy games. each commander is based on the real one.
So Ai Picton will generaly perfrom better then AI Prince of orange. ect.
I do have one other complaint, the arty, and this has been a thing since first bull run. Arty is useless with anything less then canister. You can have 80 cannon fireing at 30 000 enemies and after an hour they will have killed 10 guys. It does remove the fact that arty did in general much more damage then muskets and sabers.(with some exceptions)
I can not comment on MP as I do not play it online, but aperantly it's fantastic.
You also have the ny Mini Campaign, map of belgium where you move, detach retach units, with sevral options for victory, from taking spesific town, to hunting down and destroying most of the enemy forces. Quite fun, and can lead to enormous battles. I personaly had one battle that totaled over 300 000 troops(so over 70 000 sprites)
There are other minor compaint that some people feel are more imporant then I do. like unrealistic movement of units, or "spagetification" as it's called, It might be I'm simply used it that rather odd sight based on it's been in the engine since First bull run some 10 years ago.
The game is far above any other Napoleonic game.
I also recomend the Scourge of war gettysburg if you are more a ACW gamer, Not sure if it will come on Steam, but matrix games have it in it's store.
Edit;  I've now run a  clean install of windows on  my  pc,  this is one of the claims by  the devs that this will help with the FPS problem. It does not,  not a single FPS is gained by a clean install.

The first I heard of this game was when it was featured in Two Best Friends Play's second annual ♥♥♥♥♥torm of Scariness. It looked amazing there, but I didn't follow up at the time to find out more about it. Some of my friends watched multiple LPs of it, and I kept meaning to, but didn't get around to it until much later on. Then I finally took the word of the internet and added it to my Steam wishlist, near the bottom. THEN I watched Markiplier's LP of it, and fell totally in love with the game's story. I knew it would take me a long time to get through, because I'm a huge baby, and it DID take me a long time, but it was worth it.
The story is top notch (the only flaw I've ever spotted is that most people would walk into the situation in the game, see blood and power outages, and immediately go back out the way they came and never look back). 10/10
The visuals are
, and not for the squeamish or faint of heart. The night vision mechanic is used perfectly, but the combination of that and the motion blur may cause headaches or motion sickness. If you're okay with guts and blood all over the walls and floor, and with proximity to people who have been physically messed up,
with brief, not technically shown personal harm to you, the player-character, then you'll be fine. This game pulls no punches with the total loss of control in this building full of insane, violent people. 10/10
The sound is fantastic, and beautifully used throughout the game. Sometimes it's too quiet (or you're too panicked) to hear anything but your own breathing and footsteps and heartbeat. Sometimes there's ambient noise from outside, or upstairs, or just down the hall, and it's difficult to tell if whatever it is is a threat to you or not. The music is perfect too, with no music if things are calm and you're not in any danger, subtle musical cues when certain enemies are nearby and you should be alert, all the way up to the chase music, which is theatrical and epic and really awesome. 11/10 because WOW sound is important in this game and they really nailed it.
This game is scary as heck and everyone should play it, even if it takes you five times longer than some other people. Five stars, A+++, 100/10, all the thumbs up that can be gathered from the dead bodies in Mount Massive Asylum.

Usually if you choose the wrong way when being chased (It's completely impossible to know before hand which way is a dead end) you will just die. Fahrenheit garnered critical acclaim when it first came out 10 years ago: its QTE events and story were something seldom seen before and more than made up for its shortcomings.
Nowadays its innovation is lost of course, and the game hasn't aged well but it is and always will be a classic.
-a good cast of characters,all fairly interesting
-a compelling story, the beginning is especially very strong and makes you want to know what's happenening
-the various game scenes feature a nice amount of variety
-great soundtrack
-good voice acting
-nice cinematic cameras in certain scenes
-story starts to become a bit too surreal towards the end, several different elements also seem to have been introduced just to try and make the mistery more complex
-the over reliance on QTEs is more distracting or annoying than anything else, some QTEs are also too drawn out for their own good or require inputs way too quickly
-having a limited number of retries for each QTes is annoying and feels out of place in a game like this one
-despite the HD treatment the game clearly shows its age with bland textures, fairly simple models and low res effects
-somewhat sluggish controls paired with a camera view that can sometimes get in the way
-wooden animations

- a few glaring elements left in the release really made me wonder, examples are a stretched texture on one of the main char's face (in a couple of levels only, luckily), the game client quickly dropping back to windows to refresh itself when loading a level and no dpad support

This game has suffered from a rough development, and for a long time my review said not-recommended. It felt like the developers were just throwing random ideas together and hoping they would create a fun game, and for years, their efforts failed miserably. They completely rebuilt major parts of DD2 over and over again, often leaving it even worse than it was before.
But somewhere along the line, something changed. I honestly don't know if they finally got their act together and laid out a real development plan, or maybe they just finally got lucky and stumbled upon a formula that works. Whatever the cause, I can now say that Dungeon Defenders 2 provides an entertaining experience that is worth the purchase price. It's still got some rough edges, but devlopment is active and moving in the right direction.
For those not familiar with DD2, it's a tower-defense game, where you build a variety of towers each with unique abilities and strategically place them to fend of a stream of monsters who are trying to destroy your magic crystals. What helps DD2 stand out from most other tower-defense games is the fact that you also play a hero who can run around fighting the monsters, helping the towers deal with bosses or groups of more threatening enemies. And in RPG fashion you will level up and equip new weapons and armor, progressing through the campaign and extensive endgame.
If you enjoy strategic thinking, fast-paced action, and RPG progression, and you would like to see all three blended together, then I recommend giving Dungeon Defenders 2 your money.

This is a game for those who want a unique city builder. Banished revolves around a group of people that, as the game describes, have been banished from their homeland for some unknown reason and must resettle elsewhere to survive. There are no enemies except nature itself. There are two major resources needed at all times: food and firewood. Having plenty of crops and firewood to get your people through the long winters is regularly an uphill battle. You also have a finite number of citizens to do the work and they can grow old, die, have children, etc. The children grow up and become workers for the town but they too can die. This game is not forgiving. Even with disasters turned off, things are difficult. Before you can blink, you can be out of food and/or firewood and be left scratching your head wondering how and why you ran out so quickly. All you can do then is sit back and watch helplessly as your people starve, freeze, and eventually die, hoping that spring will come so new crops can be planted and firewood isn't as high in demand...that's provided the graveyards don't fill up too quickly.

My town of Tomorrowland, a city-state that thrived from the humble beginnings of just a few friendly families banished from Great Britain to a colony meant to fail. However, those colonists thrived. After the complete disconnection from the king, they thrived and thrived. Self-sufficient! 3 farms, 2 orchards, a hunting cabin, forester lodge, gatherer's hut, and herbalists. We had medicine, food, clothing, and tools. By year 20, we had a HUGE population with mines, quarries, trading posts, and Adventurers searching for the "Curse of the Golden Llama." It was a COLONIAL CHARTER, and it couldn't've gone better. But the unthinkable happened.
We unwillingly traded with Britain. A trade boat came that seemed like Boni, our indepentent farming goods partner whom we have a great contract with. We traded a great deal of seeds and crops, boxed filled with crops. Inside one of the boxes *gasp* was a British spy.
Surveying our city-state, he noticed our distillery, great trade post, farms, pastures, palm tree lodgers, and great City Hall. He loaded our hall with firewood and burned the building down. HE burned almost everything. Left, was a group of 5 families with a stockpile of wood, stone, and very small pile of iron. Inside the lone storage barn were some tools, a couple of hide coats, and some leftover potatoes from last Spring's harvest. It was like the beginning.
Honestly, this game absolutely FANTASTIC. The vanilla game is pretty good, offers a great deal of fun and learning of city building and controlling villagers. Then the workshop comes in, and the mods flow in like a river during a storm. Colonial Charter (CC) Curse of the Golden Llama adds a♥♥♥♥♥♥LOAD I mean♥♥♥♥♥♥LOAD of content, and extra little mods like Intensified Fishing Dock and More Wood/Stone/Iron per Tree/Rock/Ore make the game like no other.
10/10 would watch my city-state burn again

I'd like to start by saying that I loved The Stanley Parable and hate that it's so hard to review The Beginner's Guide without looking at it through that lens. On the surface, they're fairly similar. In both, you just walk around and listen to a narrator.
In The Beginner's Guide the interactivity begins and ends with walking forward (mostly) through the story. There is also a single puzzle. I kept trying to go off the beaten path to find all the interesting stuff that surely must be hidden in the game only to find that there are barely any places you can even choose to do something unintended. Only twice in my playthrough did the narrator respond to anything I did.
Furthermore, unlike The Stanley Parable that had a perfect marriage of form and content, the story in this one could have been told in any other medium to the same or greater effect.
I hate to rag on The Beginner's Guide so hard because it's an interesting story told competently. I can't help but think that it would have been more well received if it had been released under a pseudonym. At least then, I wouldn't have to be annoyed by how it completely ignores the lesson of his last game.

There are wolves too, but they're rare enough that you can simply avoid them if you don't have a rifle and ammunition. The forces at work in this game create an excellent atmosphere of survival like no other, and I would definitely recommend this game to others.

Now that connection issues seem to have been largely sorted, this is actually a fun game.
The ability to design your spaceship from scratch results in a lot of interesting possibilities and wacky entertainment.
One thing I do have to question is the matchmaking system. I understand wanting to limit queue times and therefore would expect some variance in ship strength but at the moment it's just completely ridiculous. Just had a game where the entire enemy team was destroyed by a single ship on our team which had maxed out hitpoints and damage as well as a ton of abilities. The guy had 14 kills by the end of the game and it left very little to do for either the remainder of our team or the enemy team, most of whom were piloting rookie ships. Would much prefer waiting a tad longer if it meant rookie ships were matched up against other rookie ships for one. A somewhat more extended tutorial and more elaborate single player campaign would also be highly beneficial as what is present right now is extremely basic.
An option to reset your account would also be extremely desireable. Research costs (which give you access to new building blocks and items for your ship) are prohibitive to the point where if you research the wrong thing early on, you're going to be stuck with a subpar ship for dozens of games afterwards which is just needlessly frustrating.
Overall the game definitely has potential but at the moment the main enjoyment for me comes from the ship design rather than the actual matches. Still worth a try though.

I've used many game maker programs but never completed a game with them, with RPG Maker I took a risk even at a sale price and gave it a shot.  Suffice it to say I made my very first video game and now working on the sequel!

Cons:
- Decent amount of content but if you want more, you'll need to either purchase the content or find it.

Overall:

This game has suffered from a rough development, and for a long time my review said not-recommended. It felt like the developers were just throwing random ideas together and hoping they would create a fun game, and for years, their efforts failed miserably. They completely rebuilt major parts of DD2 over and over again, often leaving it even worse than it was before.
But somewhere along the line, something changed. I honestly don't know if they finally got their act together and laid out a real development plan, or maybe they just finally got lucky and stumbled upon a formula that works. Whatever the cause, I can now say that Dungeon Defenders 2 provides an entertaining experience that is worth the purchase price. It's still got some rough edges, but devlopment is active and moving in the right direction.
For those not familiar with DD2, it's a tower-defense game, where you build a variety of towers each with unique abilities and strategically place them to fend of a stream of monsters who are trying to destroy your magic crystals. What helps DD2 stand out from most other tower-defense games is the fact that you also play a hero who can run around fighting the monsters, helping the towers deal with bosses or groups of more threatening enemies. And in RPG fashion you will level up and equip new weapons and armor, progressing through the campaign and extensive endgame.
If you enjoy strategic thinking, fast-paced action, and RPG progression, and you would like to see all three blended together, then I recommend giving Dungeon Defenders 2 your money.

If you want to experience large scale (64 players), asymmetric (i.e. each side has different weapons), multiplayer warfare set in Europe or Japan, then this game is for you. The action is intense, realistic, and punishing. Running down the field whilst spraying the air with bullets does little but get you killed. To succeed, Rising Storm demands patience, caution, and strategy. It only takes one bullet to die (most of the time), and even minor wounds, if left untreated, can cause you to bleed out. The graphics are great and the audio authentic.
Rising Storm is not problem free. Leveling feels slow and gives few rewards in the form of unlockables or upgrades. The realism is awesome, but getting sniped over and over again shortly after spawning can become frustrating, especially if you’re unlucky enough to endure 23 second re-spawns. Team work is vital for success, but rarely do other players utilize microphones. Lastly, Japanese mortar bombardments and artillery strikes can make for breathtaking moments of epic havoc and death, but constantly getting picked off by random mortars can get infuriating. All in all, the game is fantastic. This mini-review may appear very critical, but that’s only because I prefer writing about shortcomings rather than accomplishments. For twenty bucks (or less) you really can’t go wrong giving this game a shot!
Red Orchestra 2: Rising Storm: 8.5 / 10.0

This is a difficult game to like.
If you are into super cheesy Japanese RPGs, and are generally familiar with the Tales genre, it's worth picking up. But even as a fan of the series, it's been difficult for me to sit down and play the game for more than an hour.
Story-wise, the game is...ok.  Tales series are not necessarily known for their wonderous stories, but I've always found them a bit less stereotypical than most typical RPGs.  This title however just feels a bit more forced - you see the gears grinding too hard, and the games nearly 3-hour long tutorial doesn't help.  The plot is also confusing - some characters can't be "seen" by most of the characters, but then you still fight with them...it's just confusing, and I feel that it takes too much hand-waving and exposition to setup.  The characters don't help the game along. Unlike some other titles in the series, the characters are very stock, almost perfect, and cling around one or two traits which just get tiring to play listen to. The lines are basically exposition, the jokes are flat, and cring-moments are high even for a series that takes it as a given.
Combat wise, as a fan familiar with the series, I just wanted to get in and learn the system while fighting in actual combat. But the game holds your hand for so long, it just gets boring.  Yet, it's difficult to just zone out during these moments; the game's combat system is very complex, so complex that I feel newcomers will be put off, and old fans will have to sit through the monotonous basic zones in order to pick out the more complex systems that come during these otherwise trying segments.  Still, if you are into micro-mangment, it can be fun. But to perfectly min-max your combat battles takes a level of computer-controlled player management and menu-screen fiddling that makes you question why you're not just playing a turn-based game in the first place.  Playing with friends locally, however, really enriches the experience if you have some buddies who will actually put up with the dialogue and down-time.
Honestly, just wait until Tales of Symphonia is released on Steam.  Its a far, far better game despite being so much older.  It's a much better example of the series being done right. The storyline is as cheesy, but its characters feel human, and and the heart of its gameplay and story beat lies a complex moral question that just feels much stronger than "angels saving the world."

My review started off with a recommendation but because of the constant cheating of enemies in battle, I can't recommend it anymore. It gets worse and worse as the story progresses so my impression changed a lot over time.
The story:
Is nothing that will set your world on fire, BUT (Spoiler - kind of - incoming and I only played ~40 hours, so there's the chance I'm wrong) it has a different story than most of the other Tales games (like Symphonia, Abyss, Graces, Zillia, Hearts etc.): there are NOT two worlds competing in some way or the other with another and you are not on a journey to somehow get those worlds to coexist.
I know... that's really a change up!
The characters:
I never really liked the lead in Tales games, they are mostly boring and pretty uninteresting, sometimes even unlikeable (I'm looking at you Luke) - Lloyd being the exception - but I don't mind Sorey to be honest. So that's something! The rest of the cast is interesting and the interaction is again really funny.
Graphic and sound stuff:
Graphics are fine, but you can see, that this game was developed for the PS3, the music is in parts really damn good and never bad.
Gameplay:
The gameplay/battles feel definetely a bit dumbed down from previous entries. It incorporates the weakness/power hit system from Zillia 2 and tries to bring a bit more depth into the game by introducing the armatizing feature (combining with a seraph character of the different elements), but it removes the freedom of binding martial artes to any button and the attacks have a specific spot in the combo. Like certain attacks are always the third in a combo and so on.
I certainly miss the option to bind my 16 (or 20? has been a while) different attacks to every button I choose to and execute them whenever I want to, like in Zillia.
Only hidden artes are bindable and very limited (5 can be bound at any given time), so overall not a lot of freedom there.
Of course there's no cooking and no wonder chef... you have to buy food when you sleep in an inn.
The bad stuff:
- Little variety in your party setup: it's always 2 humans and two seraphs, but as far as I've gotten now, you only have two humans at any given time, so you can only experiment with different seraphs in your setup (4 so far)
- The camera... god damn this camera... especially in narrow hallways or near walls...
- Countless tutorials but some stuff is still confusing. Like leveling your weapons, I've still don't really get it, mainly because I can't memorize the 50 different boni and there "place" in the matrix... To really make a good item you need a tutorial or a reference sheet I guess
- The game cheats... a lot. A lot of the time enemies are able to become invulnerable and stay invulnerable for easily half a minute or even more. Indigo Prophecy first released in North America in 2005 to mixed reviews. It couldn't compete graphically with many of the AAA titles of that time, and the gameplay was something the industry hadn't seen before. At best, it was a neat experiment that (critically) fell short of greatness. The story felt like a sped-up version of Lost. Engaging, exciting and mysterious at the start, with a ridiculous theological (or in this case science fiction-y) ramp-up approaching the end. Because of the game's strict adherence to its "dynamic story" feature, oftentimes your play-through would result in not enough information or justification for the ridiculous plot points. The only way to get the full picture was to play the game perfectly. While that wasn't particularly difficult, it did require subsequent runs through the game, which is a clumsy way of providing a satisfying conclusion. The new HD remaster, by definition, addresses none of those issues apart from the graphical fidelity. As with my REmaster Review, it is unfair to rate the game based upon story or gameplay elements ten years after the fact, so this review will cover how well the developer remastered and ported their game to PC, Mac and Linux. Graphical Upscaling: Where other remastered games add things like newly rendered cutscenes, character models, environmental or weather effects, light bloom, dynamic lighting or increased particle count, Indigo Prophecy Remastered does nothing of the sort. Visually, the new version is almost unrecognizable as a different game. The only noticeable differences are that it runs at a solid 60-ish frames per second (which is a huge leap from the PS2/Xbox era) and the "film of standard definition" has been wiped from the screen; it's no longer blurry or fuzzy. Object outlines are clear and concise, the snow particles don't make traversing the street segments a chore, and it is now easier than ever to spot clues or interactive elements. While that certainly makes the game more playable, it doesn't match up to other more intensive remasters. Read the full review at

Cranky Cat is simple (if you know Puzzle Bobble/Bust-a-Move) - it's PB with the board rotating, rather than you aiming new bubbles. The big problem is that especially later on, a lot of the boards will feel identical, and if you're going for 3-stars, the RNG nature of each stage is going to become a pain because sometimes you get a good run, and sometimes it just won't give you that one bubble of the right color to clear a path to the last two.
There's a Puzzle mode but it's hardly worth mentioning, because it comes down to "find the opening spot, rotate board appropriately to make all the bouncing pieces clear things". In fact, a huge part of why I find Cranky Cat kind of unfun stems from either a) gimmick boards where you can't blow up the biggest mass, or else the entire board will shift off-kilter and go out of bounds until you blow up two layers of bubbles, or b) reused boards over and over. I've seen one show up at least three times.
It's not a classic game by any means, is all I'm saying. The formula has some kinks.

If you’re interested in A Hat In Time at all, pick it up. I wouldn’t call it cute-as-heck, but instead lively-as-heck. There’s a lot to say, so let’s get to it!
As far as the size of the game, I would say it was shorter than expected. It took me 10 hours to beat (while looking around for stuff), 12 hours to get the achievements after that, and 14 hours to get all of the pins on the Collectibles Map. HOWEVER, this isn’t actually really a bad thing! Every 1/40th of the game is very sizable and unique in its own way, and it also means the game doesn’t overstay its welcome with padding.
The main selling point of this game is Hat Kid’s movement. With a double jump, a far dive, a jump after that, and a wall climb, her horizontal movement is insane. There are a lot of moments in the game where you see a platform far away that you MIGHT be able to make, jump and dive to it to see if you can make it (since failing a jump isn’t much of a penalty thankfully), and ACTUALLY DO. It makes you feel like a gosh darn GENIUS, especially when you skip other platforms. The fact that there are very few enemies in the game is telling that the focus went into the platforming level design, and it compliments your movement options extremely well so that every moment of the game is “Can I get to that ledge?” Hat Kid’s vertical movement being very limiting is a smart way to “balance” this out. She can only run up the wall for a second and her wall kick only goes outwards, so you need to be crafty to get UP to places. Finally, Hat Kid’s dive is really fast if you get the timing right , which makes navigating any more open areas more fun and satisfying than, say, spamming a long jump.
As for the bulk of the game, the missions, the thing that stood out to me the most was how most of them felt like they told a part of a story and were distinct in their own right. Your objectives never really felt random or misguided, and this makes it feel like much more than a game about Hat Kid’s ability to platform. The dialogue’s a part of this. The thing is that there’s a lot of dialogue, and even with the Hold A to Skip mechanic in parts, feels like it could be obnoxious for repeat playthroughs, but it’s important for worldbuilding. As for the worlds, they’re pretty bulky and fun to run around in sometimes (except for Chapter 2, which is more “individual missions), but thankfully getting to each mission isn’t a struggle. For example, my favorite Chapter is Chapter 3 because the world’s big and relatively flat, so it’s easy to see a new point of interest, check it out, then repeat a la open world games. There are three Time Rifts per world, and they show up anywhere in the area with only a picture of its location to go on. With how big the worlds are, I figured this would be tedious and awful…but the worlds are designed with enough distinct areas that I actually ended up enjoying the little scavenger hunts. The Time Rift levels are pretty short and a series of floating platforms that are “pure platforming,” and they’re really fun. And a little tidbit that goes a LONG way is the game telling you if you don’t have an item to complete a mission instead of leaving you to flounder and find out for yourself.
Now, with the base parts of the game out of the way, we can talk about my favorite part of it: just how alive and real each world feels. Like I mentioned before, every platform is there for a reason because it’s a part of an environment. Buildings, leaves, piles of crates, etc. all feel like a part of the environment first and a platforming challenge second. And, of course, the game uses colors that are appealing to look at and aren’t samey in both light and dark areas. The game gives you a camera for a reason! The most obvious part of the game feeling lively are all of the characters, and not just all of the ones represented in the logo of the game itself. Everyone either is doing something or has something helpful or witty to say, even if they use the same model as another character in the area. A lot of characters have motivations, some silly and some understandable (like in some boss battles, for example). I’ve heard people knock the voice acting, but I think the full voice acting is excellent and helps the “alive” feel exceedingly well, as even the minor “set piece” characters talk and are a joy to listen to instead of having to read a bunch (since this game has a lot of writing for what it is). In fact, only the forest minions, the foxes, and the Chapter 4 people had voices that I didn’t like. And of course the music ties the environment feel up perfectly. Each song is fitting, and even the more subdued and ambient songs are interesting to listen to. The subtle dynamic music per area also helps make each sub-area on a stage feel more unique. Not to mention, the unique title cards for every mission are nice.
This game has collectibles, but it’s not labeled as a collectathon for a reason. To me, the collectibles were really fun platforming challenges to get them, fitting the game’s excellent platforming and giving you more to do in certain areas. You can see most of them since they are surrounded by light (with others being findable with a map badge), so it really does become a matter of “How do I get over/up there?” A little cheat is that the camera badge is helpful for looking around areas, whether they intended that or not. You could get yarn for making new hats, coins to get different clothes colors/hat skins/stage remixes (customization options I love in any game), and relics to unlock Time Rifts. I never needed to stop progress to get yarn for a hat I needed or to unlock a Time Rift, so putting those behind collectibles isn’t a nuisance thankfully. There are badges that you can buy with little orbs strewn around the stage called Pons, but none of them are really NECESSARY and are just nice boosts to have. Another extra are the achievements. Their simplicity makes them fun to go back and do post-game.
The game’s not without flaws, though. They’re all minor, but let’s list my bigger gripes. The Golden Safe mission didn’t make it obvious you could touch it for trails. I never struggled with Pons unlocking some levels, but it seems arbitrary and pauses the fun. If you mess up in a subarea, there’s no Restart Area option and you have to start the WHOLE MISSION over. Getting everything is kinda a nuisance when the game says you have 100% when you get just the Time Pieces, the Relic Badge only shows an arbitrary amount of things, and some things like yarn are inside blow-upable things. The X counter thing felt kinda weird and finicky sometimes. I also feel like the grappling hook is too important to be a badge, even with three badge slots. Smaller complaints include the camera freaking out sometimes and Hat Kid clipping into things, but bugs are bugs. I feel like gold tape around objects didn’t quite scream “You blow this up!” The Ice Hat is criminally underutilized and should’ve been available for Mafia Town where the ice platforms are beautifully placed (but it’s great for bosses). The stealth section lights are shorter than the actual hitbox.
But despite all this, none of it REALLY got in the way of my enjoyment of the game. Just minor nuisances with some collectibles I can’t be bothered to get for a true 100% completion. Each Time Piece is packed to the brim with fun platforming, environments/characters/music with personality, and little collectibles to go for along the way. I’d say it’s one of the richest games an indie group has put out and makes a name for itself among bigger developers with its charm. I’d say that the full $30 is a great price…but if the low play time makes the price seem not worth it somehow, then definitely pick it up in a sale. It’s an enjoyable experience front to back.

Absolutely one of my favorite games ever. Probably the only game I've ever 100%'d. I was a slacker backer for the Kickstarter, so I bought my copy like... 2 or 3 years ago? And honestly, it was like a gift from my past self to my present self.
This game made me feel like a kid again. The absolute joy of taking control of Hat Kid for the first time, discovering what kind of jumps and leaps you can do onto platforms. The controls are just so tight and responsive, and everything just works together so well. The worlds are all so incredibly unique, and no mission is like any other. The characters you interact with are well voice-acted and full of character. The bosses you fight are unique and memorable. The music is STELLAR! There is not a single song in the game that I don't love!
One issue is that the game does not keep track of your progress on certain collectables such as the pages in Time Rifts (unless you're currently in said Time Rift), yarn, or tokens. It's very difficult to tell if you've completely cleaned out a world of its things to do when there's no stats on the menus to tell you. This is pretty minor, as it doesn't really detract of the general experience. It'd just be icing on the cake if they fixed it.
This game is getting workshop soon! Which will involve custom hats as well as custom made levels with modding tools! Meaning that when you're done with the game, you won't truly be done. Even after I 100%'d this game I still want to play more. Hopefully we can get some level ports of Super Mario 64 so we can play through them as Hat Kid!
Overall, the entire game is fantastic. It's unforgettable to me. It made me genuinely feel like I was playing Mario Sunshine for the first time again. It's truly unique, and a great result of a long time development cycle.

If you want to experience large scale (64 players), asymmetric (i.e. each side has different weapons), multiplayer warfare set in Europe or Japan, then this game is for you. The action is intense, realistic, and punishing. Running down the field whilst spraying the air with bullets does little but get you killed. To succeed, Rising Storm demands patience, caution, and strategy. It only takes one bullet to die (most of the time), and even minor wounds, if left untreated, can cause you to bleed out. The graphics are great and the audio authentic.
Rising Storm is not problem free. Leveling feels slow and gives few rewards in the form of unlockables or upgrades. The realism is awesome, but getting sniped over and over again shortly after spawning can become frustrating, especially if you’re unlucky enough to endure 23 second re-spawns. Team work is vital for success, but rarely do other players utilize microphones. Lastly, Japanese mortar bombardments and artillery strikes can make for breathtaking moments of epic havoc and death, but constantly getting picked off by random mortars can get infuriating. All in all, the game is fantastic. This mini-review may appear very critical, but that’s only because I prefer writing about shortcomings rather than accomplishments. For twenty bucks (or less) you really can’t go wrong giving this game a shot!

I can't stop playing this game, I mean, I really should play all the other games gathering virtual dust in my steam library, but this game keeps pulling me back. It reminds me of Day of Defeat's extremely dangerous combat paired with Battlefield's emphasis on teamwork. 64 players try to take objectives through the map much like Battlefied's Rush mode during the pacific theater in WW2.
The realism in this game is unparalleled, what other game lets you dial in your sights on a gun? It can get frustrating as at first it feels as if your poor little soldier is constantly getting riddled with gunfire or blown to bits by artillery after every spawn. However, amidst all this chaos and death if you stick with it you'll eventually get a feel for the game's flow. Positioning, marksmanship, and even knowing when to flee from danger will all start to become second nature. For every death resulting from a mile's off sniper or random nade will be a rage fueled killing spree as you pick off targets one after another in between each bolt chamber, barely seeing the enemies through bloodrage like you're Jude Law in Enemy at the Gates. You'll use bolt action rifles the most by far (unless you play mainly allies), which may seem disappointing (realistic however) but you'll learn to thrive with this long range death machine. The moments of frantically shooting charging baddies alongside your teamates in a trench and awkwardly trying to shoot someone who's almost on top of you are really great and something that I've missed in recent games.
Other weapons have specific roles, MGs providing bases of fire and SMGS for close range room clearing. There is a cover system, which even allows you to blind fire, but it is truly blind as you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥in the first person view while in cover. It adds together to form an impressive action game on its own, even without the coordinated team mechanics.
In order to truly excel at this game it's important that you are part of a competent team. Like Battlefield, there are squads within each team who all report to a commander. The commander is capable of calling in artillery or UAV... I mean recon planes. All this teamwork, when it all comes together creates one of the most intense scenarios in a FPS. Huddling in a bunker from enemy artillery and watching screaming japanese charge through clouds of smoke is an unforgettable sight. Obviously you get some guys who go off and rambo into battle, and it is a good strategy for "ninja-ing" into flanking positions, but you'll find most victories arise when people are following a competent commander's wishes.
The Japanese vs. Americans asymmetry is really well done as well and surprisingly balanced. Whereas the Americans have vastly superior firepower (literally, they have a flamethrower that barbeques entire bunkers full of people) the Japanese have to rely on shock and ambush tactics. The American's M1 Garand is a brutally effective weapon, chambered in 30.06 and is semiautomatic, so it is essentially one of the aforementioned death machines that can fire as fast as you can click. They also have automatic riflemen who use the BAR (pretty much a fully automatic Garand that destroys everyone). The Japanese have two bolt action rifles and a kinda meh SMG. On paper, this seems unfair, but the Japanese have the ability to set booby traps and do banzai charges which increase their stamina and health while sprinting. This feeds the need for more teamwork as the banzai ability stacks the more people who do it at once. I enjoy charging holding a katana with teamates yelling and dying all around you in a glorious suicide rush. Yes, you'll probably die, but in order to win some measure of bravery is needed to succeed in Rising Storm.
Buying rising storm also comes with Red Orchestra 2 multiplayer, which is set in the Russian theater. I'm not a huge fan of the tanks or the urban slaughterhouses that most matches seem to devolve into. It is still cool that some servers alternate between the two theaters though.

Edit:
Due to certain induviduals expressing their displeasure with my review, and probably many others as can be seen from one out of every 4 people finding it not helpful in any way, i have decided to expand upon this comment on the game, and give my true opinion.
This was my first tales game. I have long been a fan of RPGs, mostly in the form of final fantasies, but i have never found the oppurtunity to play from the tales series, mostly due to the lack of them on PC.
While this may be common knowledge to some, it will not be to all. To start off, i will talk about the battle system. To be honest, i found it very confusing at first. It's all real time fighting, and everything is based off of combinations of clicks and certain keyboard keys. you use your left click for basic attacks, and your right click for attacks such as special techniques or spells. later, after learning more abilites, you will be able to set certain skills to different combinations of buttons. for instance; right+mouse button = a move, left+mouse button = a different move. when you get the hang of what keys to press for what move, you will have a LOT more fun. It's simply learning the games mechanics. While this takes time, when you learn how, you will have an amazing experience exploiting weaknesses and finding cool technique combos.
Combat summary - difficult at first, but very fun when you learn how to use your techniques well. Doesn't take a lot of time, but be prepared to learn new things. 8.5/10
Now, we come to the equipment and skills it comes with. Each piece of equipment you find in either a chest or an enemy drop will have some ability on it. Examples being; +4% attack, +10% attack against this certain type of enemy, +10 hp gained when blocking, etc. While these may be useful, it does not make or break fights. The certain item you get is far more important, leaving the little perks it comes with to be fairly insignificant. You can also fuse two of the same items together, allowing the new item to be everr so slightly stronger, and with perhaps new abilites. I went through the entire game without fusing a single piece of equipment or trying to find the best setup of abilites. The ONLY time i needed to make custom gear with lots of fusing was for the most difficult, optional, and final boss. Also, it's confusing as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Here's an example of what you can get if you spend 10 hours farming for specific equipment.
Equipment/fusing summary - interesting, but too confusing to pay attention to. Can easily go through the game without having to worry about it. Unless you're a min-maxer, don't worry about fusion unless you really want to. 6/10
Finally, the story and characters. I've heard many complaints about the characters, and how it's difficult to be attached to them. I, on the other hand, absolutely love them. This may be because i have little experience in the tales games, but i found the main protagonist to be a perfect fit. Naive, courageous, a little innocent, and an incredibly strong willed induvidual. While i don't like some as much as others, there is a lot of variety among the group. you'll get a lot of good laughs with certain interactions and side conversations, while also feeling quite emotional at points. I'm keeping this vague because i would like to keep this review as spoiler free as possible. Which is why, with the story explanation, i will keep it short. I very much enjoyed the story. While the pacing seemed a little weird at times, and some things were a bit rushed, hard to follow, and sometimes never even explained, it was largely unnoticeable due to the large amount of positives you'll find throughout your journey. If you read all of the dialogue (no skipping please), you'll find the storyline very interesting with some very unique concepts.
Storyline/characters summary - against popular opinion, i found the characters to be very funny and easy to get attached to. While the story is a little rushed at times, it's overall a very cool experience. Don't skip the dialogues. 8.5/10
Would i recommend this game to a friend? Of course. Would i recommend this game to everyone who is even a little interested? Of course. As long as you're willing to put a bit of time and effort into learning the mechanics, and have previously had an RPG or JRPG that you have played and enjoyed, this is a must have.

After just finishing the game, which took me 240+ hours, I thought I'll write a review.
The story is fairly generic. I mean, you're a hero, born for one single purpose - to fight evil.
There aren't that many plot twists and main character(s) are mostly teenagers.
Still, I loved all of the main cast. The great part is that they all have strong personalities, and funny stuff happens when they clash. Expect to hear lots of funny convos. Serious ones, too.
There's sidequests too, which are pretty important. They aren't fetch quests. They are mostly "go beat that big bad monster" quests. They're important, because of their rewards. Seriously, you don't want to miss them!
It doesn't take long to level up characters and learn new skills. I am not entirely sure, but I think you will have all skills by the time you reach level 50, or around that level.
It might not seem like there's a lot of skills in the game, but I think it's a good amount.
Thing is, that if there were more of them, then the game might need a whole different system.
There's also titles, which give various bonuses to your character(s), which you unlock in various ways.
Loot is hard to get, while you don't have drop rate boosts. Once you get those - it becomes a lot easier getting stuff, which you want.
There are also exp boosts, which you can get after finishing the game for the 1st time. It can go as high as 6 times the exp.
Max level is 200 and getting there isn't hard, I would say, because I was still gaining levels at endgame. I finished the game at around level 136.
The last difficuly and the hardest one, is called "chaos". Unfortunately, it just increases monster level, damage, hp ... All that stuff. The monsters won't act any smarter, or whatever. They will just be more annoying. Fortunately, you can get the best loot in this difficulty, so it's worth fighting with this setting, if you can handle it.
The difficulty of the game depends on how well geared you are. I had a lot of things on +99, so I managed to beat the final boss on chaos difficulty.
+ Nice art, anime-style movies
+ Interesting story, just not one-of-a-kind
+ Interesting characters, all with their bright personallities
+ Good skill and leveling system
+ Each weapon features unique design
+ Nice selection of difficulty settings
+ Lots of boss monsters, all with different behaviors
+ Interesting and new "Lords of the Land" system
+ New game plus option with lots of cool features
- If you want to get great gear with +99 fusion and 3x skills, then prepare to grind. A LOT.
- Linear story-telling might not appeal to some
- While you progress thru the story, some areas get locked out and you can't backtrack, for some time
- The ally AI might be hard to get used to, and setting it up might take some time
- The battle camera will annoy you, when you will fight in tight spaces
It's worth buying, if:
- you're looking for a new experience. I would say, that, not many games offer such an experience amongst current steam games
- you like anime

My opinion on it is easy to express : it's simply awsome ! :D
Whenever we are aving LANs with friends or are just a small group gathered there is often a time when we want to have fun with a local multiplayer game and Towerfall is the go-to game in this case.
It's really simple to learn but offers a lot of surprising and intense enconters thanks to the variety of arrows, the little interaction with terrain, the warping of the map in a snake-like fation, the dodges...
And all of this awsome gameplay is coming with beatifull pixel art graphics and a variety of little fun touches that you enjoy discovering throughout the game : the characters and map unlocks, the hats that can be removed by an arrow coming too close, the original awards at the end of each match...
Add to this a coop and a challenge mode that are both solid (even if for me the core of the game is the versus) and the possibility to tweak the rules of the match to add interesting twists (controlable ghosts, exploding bodies, slow time...) and you've good an awsome game with a clean and elegant design that is always fun to play for one more match :D
Plus, the extension is good too but I'll talk about it in a specific review if I do one (spoiler alert : new cool maps/arrow/character design and bosses 4-player coop => it's really good ^^)

First I have to point out that one of the main reasons I bought this game was the preorder bonus of "Tales of Symphonia" since I was a huge fan of that game during the Gamecube era. With that out of the way, I can honestly say I was blown away by this game.
I really had miminal expectations before playing this game - but I gotta hand it to Bandai Namco, this game is a great way to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the "Tales of" series.
This game starts out kinda slow - actually not kinda, but really slow, but after playing for a couple of hours while you gather all the party members, this game picks up huge steam and goes with that awesome pace up until the end.
The story starts like it's gonna be one of those happy go stories of let's save the world! but the deeper you delve into the game the darker it becomes while still maintaining a lot of fun moments. The story holds well with good backround lore of the characters.
Speaking of characters, the cast of this game is really great, the interaction between all the main characters is awesome, especially Edna - what a great and funny character.
But not limited to Edna, all the characters are fleshed out and great.
The game is filled with fun dialogue in the form of "skits", a mainstay of "Tales of" games. The game makes great use of cinematics, both in-game engine and also thhe well animated cutscenes.
The game is full of moments that make you genuinely smile, while other will make you genuinely tear up. This was only possible because of the well written characters.
In my opinion, having played 4 games in the series, this game has the best OST of any of them. What a beautifully made soundtrack.
Battles have nice BGM that will pump you up, Boss battles have their own too - but one AWESOME song plays in one of the final battles that really cemented this series as the best soundtrack.
Dungeons have good BGM, but what truly shines is the BGM of the Trial Dungeons which are masterfully done.
As in any Tales game, the combat is what truly shines. Developed by Namco Bandai, the Advanced Battle System (ABS) is an action based combat that let's you freely move in the battlefield while using combos to fight.
The abilities in this game are categorised as Martial Artes, Hidden Artes and Seraphic Artes - these abilies make the basis of the Battle System.
Also, this game has a fusion system where 2 characters can fuse in battle to gain hightened battle abilities. In addition, all characters have a finisher move that does massive damage called "Mystic Artes".
there are 5 elements in this game - Fire, water, wind, earth, and physical. All enemies have specific weaknesses and resistances to these elements - in order to win boss battles and harder enemies, you need to exploit these weaknesses.
In addition to the massive content, I'm 58 hours in and still have plenty of optional bosses and dungeons to complete and even a New Game+ with many optional difficulty or quality of life choices for people who are into that.
All these elements make this game a great addition to the fabled "Tales of" line-up.

Cranky Cat offers a new twist on the marble-shooting, bust-a-move genre, and it does it well.
Instead of firing spheres upward, they float in from the sides and slowly gravitate toward the center of the playing area. The player can (and has to) rotate the "board" to match the marbles. Three or more of the same color will remove them from the board, which then causes now loosened marbles to bounce off and gravitating back, which allows for quite spectacular and fireworks-like combinations.
There are numerous special marbles, such as the traditional bombs, and power-ups, like those that remove all marbles of a specific color. The game includes hundreds of levels in the story mode, and it also features a variety of endless/random modes, with the "lightning" mode perhaps being the most enjoyable one.
There are also Steam achievements and local highscores. The only feature I've been missing are Steam leaderboards, but this aside, this is a fairly enjoyable, fast-paced (at least deeper in the story mode and in Lightning) and smoothly running casual game (which can be quite hardcore). The developers have been very responsive to feature requests.
Worth checking out, especially at the very inexpensive super-budget price.

Okay well this is an interesting little game going on here. Before you read my pro and cons i'll give generally review now which is the game is mixed for me but just slightly on the good side and that is because the game (on steam that is) is still in it's infant stages and could have the potential for good development (provide the dev's do some serious work on it big time) plus my current experiences of playing this game at the moment (which is about a weeks game play).
Well lets start with the pro's for it....
1) Ship combat construction game: Well Every word speaks for itself and it speaks good, ship building your own designs, yep that's right up my alley. Testing what you've built against other players another big tick there. Flying around different places, pretty cool.
2) Ship classes system: Having several different classes of ships in this game provides the players with different advantages and disadvantages on the playing field for their specific style of gaming.
3) Early Access: I know this is an odd one to put up but I feel its relevant in this context. Because of it being out on steam for like only a week theres a chance that we might some significent work done on it. This I feel helps the current player base to remain interested in sticking the game out in hopes of getting something more out of it which will help build the games community I feel
4) Decorative customise options: Now this is going to be one of those good and bad points for this review, so lets go good for now. The ability to customise the appearence of the vessel is a nice touch to this game as it allows you to expand upon that already unique design of ship which you have made with your blocks to something with your own personal touchs whether it be a ship with sharp pointy blades on them (ouch that hurt) or a menacing pirate bridge (well that's ..... different) you can create the ship of your dreams. :D
5) Researches: Here's the second on of those good and bad pointers, the tech tree idea is good in the fact that it allows you to advance those powerful weapons and strong armours into something that makes you ship truly menacing.
Cons.....
Well here we go, the bit of the review I always hate doing but lets get to it....
1) Glitches: Yep Lord clang has defo hit this game hard (sorry space engineers reference there to things usually going horribly wrong when your doing stuff), you'll run into things like the game not wanting to load up battles or your targetting reticles disappearing or my personal favourite you spending precious space whiskey to try and get that all so sweet and delicious reward benefit only for the game to go and give it to some other player (9/10 times being on the opposing team).
2) Deceptive build up beginning: If your like me and you haven't been on this game before outside of the steam workshop zone but decided to join it anyways because it looked good, well kids you better hold onto your pants cause your about to hit a major smack in the head. you'll get a rookie ship to begin with which you'll hammer to lvl 10 thinking "brillient, what an excellent game so far", then you'll unlock the other ships and think "Marvelous, now i can get a battleship and lvl it up well easy and make it powerful and rule the game" (sorry my world dominating devils trying to sneek out again) well yeah getting that battelship leveld up to lvl 10 is easy but once there oh boy don't you know about it. Your stuck on a life sucking grinding treadmill cause at this point practicular every single player out there as done the same thing as you but  with upgraded versions of the weapons and stuf thatf you have on your ship so your pretty much stuck at this point cause you can't beat them.
3) Decorations: While the ability to purchase ship customizations is a good idea for this game, the fact that some of the really cool looking ones are and your guessed right folks premium pay currency only really sucks. I personally would have had two options either pay the premium or grind for junk to buy it. Not everyone out there has like £100 a week to pull out of their parents to afford this stuff you know.
4) The Research Tech Tree: My god, which ever idiot came up with the cost system for this really has not gone through what we're going through right now. I mean seriously the costs are ridiculous for the more advanced stuff in the this tech tree especially considering that about 90% of the new players are now stuck behind stupidly advanced players.An  Example of this Gauss cannon lvl 6 upgrade which cost the player about 23,000 units of the space junk resource. i yourf team loses the match, you only get like 400 units of junk at best. That means the new guy has to lose at least 60 or 70 times before they can afford the upgrade, then it goes up to a new stupid amount so they have to do it all over again and then some.
5) More content: While player vs player combat is good, in this game it loses its appeal real quick. Most of the high level players are now shouting out for some sort of campaign system to be added to this game to help give it some much need variety.

A hat in time is a gorgeous 3rd person platformer drawing inspiration from games like Super Mario 64 and Banjo Kazooie. Ever since the release of Yooka-Laylee earlier this year Iv been on the hunt for more of these great games from the golden days of rare 64, it seems many developers and or publishers no longer want to make these games as they feel there isn’t a big audience for them...thank god they are wrong. And thank Gears for Breakfast for making this. Thankfully I only found out about this game a month ago so the wait hasn’t been too bad unlike some who have been waiting 4 years :/
We open with our main protagonist Hat girl setting off in search of the stolen time pieces that were lifted from her space ship. The ship serves as the hub of the game and will allow you to enter any given world, you can also revisit at a later time with new powers to access previously locked areas. Something we see most games of this genre do and do well.
The “hat” part of the game are your powers, you craft hats through yarn (collectible currency) and they function as both fashion and functional abilities.  You have the usual double jumps, air dash which help navigate the open worlds as well as offensive and other various but useful tools. Alongside that are  many passive abilities in the form of badges which are pinned onto your hat.
It’s easy to lose yourself in long gaming sessions here, the bright fun worlds are brimming with characters and content that offer a decent challenge whilst not being hairpulling or a breeze. Some of the humour I thought was quite good, its not quite adult mature but its also not childish..that decent middleground we can all enjoy. The sound and audio had all the charm and polish you would expect from a title like this, with added options to unlock remixes of each worlds theme/music.
A Hat In Time is a great game regardless of wether or not you grew up playing these games, everyone can get something. I look forward to future DLC and the modding community, special thanks to the people who helped me hunt down those last few achievements for 100%.

Alapha Stage REVIEW -
I really enjoy this game. Survival games are one of my favorite game genres so I had to get this one.
I grew up in the woods and spent most of my childhood out in the woods day and night, so I know the feeling of a cold wind blowing through the trees, wind howling, walking through deep snow through the trees.
The moment I loaded into this game and started it felt real. I felt stranded and an urgency.  The sound effects, the wind, the frost, trees, lighting, shadows, crunching of snow, cracking of ice are all great. For an Alpaha it's great, I can't wait to see it finished. I played for about 2 hours and tried out the two different maps they currently offer in Alpha.
I was honestly more scared playing this game than a lot of the "horror" games I've played. You never know when an animal might attack you, it gets darks, your vitals drop, you can see a cabin just over the hill but you have to travel across a frozen lake and past a pack of wolves to get to it, and then it might not even have anything that will help.
You can feel the tension, urgency, and risk. Do you leave your shelter for water? Where do you go? Do you travel by day or night?
Even in the early Alpha, I LOVE THIS GAME!

One of the few hyped-up horror games of 2013 that deserved its hype in full.
The nuanced movement, while seeming a bit like Mirror's Edge, at the same time feels smooth, almost second-nature after being given a lobby area to get it down (though it won't take long to adjust to Outlast's controls).
The cam-corder mechanic creates the situation wherein not only is the flashlight trope avoided in a creative way, but the story and focus of the gameplay is built upon interestingly without feeling like either is made simply for the sake of the other.
Normally, whilst Asylums can be  bit of a trope of their own in horror games, and this game is really no exception, the handling of the environment working in tandem with the story blows previous torch-bearers of the Asylum trope (Nightmare House 2, Dementium) away.
The game doesn't feel like its objectives are intrusive like many modern FPS games out today, you practically don't have to look at the objectives; your movement and exploration compliments the objectives anyway, as the objectives and tasks are simply to continue progressing, and they don't feel fetch-quest-like to the point of seeming like your path is only blocked occasionally so the game has an excuse to make you grab something.  Many times your obstacle can be bypassed using an object you can find before you even noticed your path is blocked, so said blockages never feel contrived.  The no-combat basis is a standard of the 2012-present survival horror game revolution but the camera system here lends credibility to the no-fighting-back inclusion here.  The "Hiding" mechanic is perfectly handled as well; the ability of enemies to see where you are - even if you're hiding - creates a kind of tension and fear that stacking crates behind a door in Amnesia just can't hold a candle to.  The atmosphere is very SCP-Containment-Breach-like.  Silence is your only friend in the shadowy corridors of Mt. Massive, with camera static taking up foreground mostly, and string-instruments stabbing you at key scare moments to enhance the effect.  While the violin-stabs at jump-scares can be seen as a horror trope, the atmosphere playing upon monotony allows for the player's vivid imagination to take over, imagining what lurks behind the next corner, hoping for something to break the silence, even though the only thing that can break the silence is something you don't want.
All in all, if you're willing to look past the tropes of the Asylums & Nazi Doktors, Outlast's atmosphere, story, and gameplay will haunt you (in a good way).

Man, this was a journey. I just finished this game after buying it about 3 weeks ago, and I have to say my 50 Euro were well spend. (Warning: this will be long. But it will also be insightful, so if you don't mind reading long reviews, this is for you.)
First off, as a fan of the series myself (my first Tales-game was Tales of Symphonia), I am aware that this game got quite a lot of flack from the following of this series, for various reasons that I won't get into in order not to spoil anything. It's the reason I was so skeptical about buying this game myself. But then I was in a very bad place 3 weeks ago, and I needed distraction, so I thought "might as well." And I don't regret that decision.
This game has its issues, sure. The graphics aren't outstanding, there are quite a few plotholes, the item fusion system and skill sheet are too complicated, the camera spazzes out during battle quite a lot (honestly, if you get attacked in a small corridor you better choose the flight option cause chances are you won't see a thing) and for those of you who care about it, it's locked to 30FPS (I personally don't actually care, I guess my eyes aren't trained enough to even see the difference between 30FPS and 60FPS. However I know some people care, hence...).
Other than that though, I think of this game as just as stellar as the other entries of this series I have played. There are issues, yes, but which game doesn't have them. Ultimately I enjoyed it, and that's what counts. I wasn't like "Thank God it's over" when it ended, but I was actually sad.
Other than the issues mentioned before, it has everything that makes the Tales-series special and enjoyable: interesting characters that you get attached to and actually feel for, super entertaining skits, an engaging world and story, a moral that teaches you a LOT if you let it, and a fun battle system - if you ignore the camera issues.
Yes, the fusion system is quite complex too - if you like spending lots of time in menus and perfecting your gear etc., great, but if you don't, that's also not much of a problem: I beat the game without any big issues, and I never really paid too much attention to those systems. In fact, I still don't fully understand how they work. lol
Actually, this game also has aspects that I think have been handled WAY better than in all previous Tales-Games I have played. For one, the music. It's AMAZING. It really is. This music sounds like it belongs in a Hollywood movie, not a Japanese role-playing game. Especially the intro song and also Go Shiina's tracks are marvelous. It's SO good, I put the soundtrack on my phone.
Also, they know how to UTILIZE their music. Which leads me to the next point that stood out positively to me: The atmosphere. They knew when to play which song, there were no abrupt song changes when the characters started changing behavior (this is something that bugged me in Symphonia), every scene has a track that fits it to a tee. And when the atmosphere requires there to be no music whatsoever there IS no music whatsoever. This game knows how to make you feel the significance of a moment.
Another really outstanding point is the voice-acting. I have only played the game in English so far, however, I am 100% positive the Japanese voice-acting is great, cause it always is. What's special though is that the English voice-acting - save maybe for Mikleo's - is just AS great as your typical Japanese voice cast in my opinion. The voices fit the characters and the voice actors are doing an amazing job at delivering moods, emotions, personality and really bringing these characters alive. Now, the voice-acting for English releases of the Tales-series has always been decent, but this one is stellar, in my humble opinion. Not once did I feel the need to switch to the Japanese audio track, something that I did wish I could do in previous Tales-games I have played (but sadly those didn't have the option to do it).
The anime cutscenes are also amazing, but that part goes without saying. It's ufotable after all.
There's also much attention to detail. Not in the world map (sadly), but in other aspects of the game. There's actually something I realized when finishing the game that I don't think I've seen anyone mention yet: (SPOILERS)
I find that details like this make the game very enjoyable.
All in all, it's a great game. It has its issues, but it's very enjoyable throughout its 50+ hour-ride, and it never bored me or wanted to make me quit. It's not perfect, but none of the entries to the Tales-series were. They ware all great in their own ways, with their own issues. In the end, if you allow yourself to be immersed in the story and listen to its teachings, this, just like every other Tales-game that I have played, is an amazing game and an experience that might actually change how you think about some things.
I absolutely recommend this game. It's one of the very few I have actually had the nerve to finish recently.
P.S.: I have not yet played the Alisha's Story DLC, as I had no chance to purchase it yet and I am waiting on Bandai Namco to make it available for purchase again after fixing some bugs and (apparently) testing if it really fixed the issue for people who already own he DLC. So my review doesn't reflect that part of the game. Once I have completed Alisha's Story, I will update this review accordingly.

I'd like to share a few thoughts about this Remastered version.
Now I understand the people saying that this game shouldn't be called Remastered, since the graphics haven't been really touched, so it is somewhat a letdown if you look it that way.
However, I still think that this version is a success in other ways.
1. The textures haven't been replaced, but the game still has a native HD resolution and to be honest it looked pretty good even on my 55" television. Okay, I can't and won't compare it to any new title, but it was certanly a nice improvement over the original version.
2. X-Box controller support. Now this might seem like a minor thing, but honestly when I first tried out my controller with this game I instantly noticed how great it was. It was far more superior than the keyboard and mouse combo  I usually prefer in PC games. I felt that this game was ment to be played with a controller, for example the moves you have to make to open a door or make a decision can be done with the controller sticks. Playing with a controller simply boosts the experience.
3. Un-cut version, nothing to say here really, about time we got this. :)
4. Price tag. I bought this game for 8.99€ and that was it's full price. If you consider that this is an improved version, and the original game has been taken off Steam a long time ago, not to mention that this is a quality game, you'll see that it is not a high price to pay. Still think it is a bit much? Wait for a sale and get it for half the price or even less! You can't go wrong.
Overall it was a great fun for me to start the game again after all these years just laying in my bed with my X-Box controller in my hands looking at my 55" flatscreen. I'd recommend you to do the same. :)

Farenheit is a game that has been compared to the Matrix in it's wacky story achetype.  The real congruance in the stories lie almost in the pace at what they are told. About half way threw, Fahrenheit suffers from invalidating it's own premise (as a video game, not a story.)
For the first several hours of play, we are lead to believe this game is a form of law and order police drama where you are playing two sides of the same story.  Seemed rather original; as it was a throwback to the adventure games I used to love growing up.
However; somewhere halfway threw this game loses it's direction and almost forget's it's a game.  Gone suddenly is the feeling that exploring the environments matter.  Suddenly it becomes apparent that choices and adventuring become unimpactful on the story.
The biggest tragedy comes about in the endings of the game.  Like Mass Effect 3, no matter how the player chooses to live the daily lives of the main charectors, we are left to realize that none of the adventure aspects in this adventure game matter.  The endings are only up to choises made in the very last sequence of the game, as if the creators forgot we were emotionally attached to the journey getting there.  This left me with a hollow feeling, as if in real life scenarios lacking closure.
This game could of benefited from endings with more ties to the unique perspective of each players journey.  Instead, we as players are given an illusion that there us freedom to partake and a world to expierence and mold.  But sadly in the end we realize this isn't the truth. It's unfortunate the developers chose to embrace a story driven second half and leaving the player to wonder where their impact in the game truly game from.
It's really sad to see a (Great first half) game ruined it's own creditability by being daring in story (which is nice) but ruining away from what made it truly intriquing.  Despite, the voice acting was wonderful, the remaster graphics we're great, and the pace of the gameplay varied at points and the game never felt boring.
Despite the erradict decline in gameplay half way in, The story has many twists and turns and flat out "WTF" moments that are engaging.  The game maintains interest throughout because of it's good story pace.  The ultimate conclussions seems to fall somewhere between the matrix and a dragon ball z storyline.
It's just sad the gameplay couldn't keep up that the storyline's quality shines in.
It is still a steal for 10 dollars.  Worth playing and enjoying despite it's flaws.  It's just a shame I felt so detached from what began as a very promising game to start.

A survival game without the zombies for once!
Although still in early access (at the time of this review), this game still provides hours of fun.  It's realistic and unforgiving - just what you would expect of a survival game that plops you into the middle of a Canadian winter.  You must find food, shelter, clean water, and warmth all while steering clear of hungry wolves that make your life much harder - or much shorter.
Beware that this is a one-life game!  Once you die, you start over.  There is no going back to the last save before you were mauled by that wolf, or foolishly walked out into a blizzard without pants on.  Let this make you more wary, stealthy, and smart about every action that you take.
It's a lonely adventure, as you're the only living person around, but it's worth the trip.  The stylized graphics are really quite beautiful - reminiscent of a painting.
Master piece, it shows that with a low budget you can do great things.

Male Shep + Fem Shep go innawoods.
There's an interesting tug of war with your main resources:
* Food / Calories
* Water
* Sleep
* Fire
* Shelter
* Combat/Safety
* Shelter
* Warmth
And the unspoken constraint of Time.
(There's also a 1-dimensional knapsack problem but you'll only run into it on easy mode)
You're managing time by taking risks in each of those dimensions and balancing it with time.  For instance, foraging outdoors gets you cedar (great for fire) but you run the risk of being caught in a snowstorm, compromising safety (wolves), warmth (immediate and long-term damage to clothing), and calories.  You could get reclaimed wood indoors (half as good and half as reliable) but at a far lesser risk.
This is an excellent way to learn bushcraft, by failing in a very safe environment, with the voices of Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale helping you along.  Even though it's in Early Access, it's a great game as is.  Just know that the wolf AI is broken and you should treat them like the droids from Alien: Isolation, basically.  Just pretend they're polar bears.
