Remember the chucky movies?
A creepy killer doll is on the loose and out for murder. It spawned a franchise spanning 6 movies (so far...)and if these movies did one thing well, it was to create the world's creepiest little plastic killer  ever! That is until now...
Five Nights at Freddy's places you in the role of a security guard working the "dead" night shift at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.
A family friendly pizza place popular for kids parties and famous for its animatronic  robots, Freddy Fazbear and his pals. These happy, clappy, little fur covered robots entertain the kids during the day but seem to have a tendency to wonder the dark and empty rooms and corridors at night.
That's where you come in, the job of night security guard has suspiciously become vacant and you're the lucky applicant.
Starting the game, you will find yourself sitting in a cramped little security office surrounded by CCTV monitors, a phone,  a door on either side of you and couple of light switches.
It's a pretty oppressive setting to start with, but before too long the phone will ring and you'll start to get an idea of the situation you've gotten yourself into.
The game-play itself couldn't be simpler. You flick between grey, fuzzy security feeds, watching out for anything unusual. You view the empty tables, the dark corridors, the animatronics room.
You'll get your first glimpse of the "puppets" themselves.
You remember how I said earlier that the Chucky doll from the Childs Play moves was creepy?
Well the unnerving smiles leering through the metal and fur present on these animatronics captures that sense of menace perfectly, but there was only one chucky, here you'll find yourself stalked by a few of the creepy buggers!
The only other controls you have beside flicking through the CCTV screens, are the door controls (you can lock yourself in your office) and the door lights (CCTV doesn't quite cover the dark access to your office, A blind spot which can prove fatal.)
Wait, did you just say fatal?
Oh yes, Freddy and his friends have a habit of wondering around at night, and should they manage to find their way into your little office... well.. . It's game over man!
So why don't you just turn on your lights, lock the doors and wait till morning?
It's a question of power management. You only have a limited amount of electricity you can utilise throughout the night.
Keeping the lights on drains power, keeping the doors locked drains power and trust me, you don't want to be out of power when you see  that creepy bear leering into the security camera just outside your office!
Don't go in expecting a triple A release here or you will be disappointed, what you essential get for your money are a series of static screens you can flick between and some creepy audio, but this bare bones description doesn't do the experience justice.
With such a simple premise and game mechanics it's a surprise that this game works, but it does.

9 out of 10:
Some of the original Silent Hill games, the first F.E.A.R. game were among the few horror games to truly scare the $%@! out of me and make me really uncomfortable.  Now that I've finally played Outlast (which I luckily got during the summer sale) and beaten it today, I can add it to the list of games to actually scare me and not use only cheap jump startles like some other "horror" games (because being startled is different than being SCARED).
There are definitely jump scares in this game, but the real terror comes in the tension in the atmosphere and the build up.  After the jump scare, the terror is made worse when you find out what is chasing you or see it up close.  One of the most terrifying moments I had in this game was in the beginning when I was being chased by the first prisoner and I decided to look over my shoulder.  Turns out this was a terrible idea as he was RIGHT BEHIND ME and I screamed bloody murder.
Silent Hill is the only other horror game that actually made me scream out loud before this.  Normally I just curse a lot when I play horror games or make a loud gasp, but even in times where I tried my hardest to bite my lips together and stifle my sound, the game somehow still got me to scream.  The way the atmosphere and the ambient noise #%%s with your mind is absolutely insane.  But I love it and no matter how scared I was, this game was definitely worth it.
The only negative I can think of is It will be frustrating and you will die many times.  You may even become a little numb to certain scenarios once you have to repeat them after death, but the levels and areas have enough differences between them to keep you on your toes the entire time.  Claustrophobic?  The game has it.  Agoraphobic?  It has that too.  Something that might be considered negative by others would be the battery duration, but unless you're playing on Hard or higher, most of the time you can find plenty of batteries if you're not too chicken to explore.
Regardless, this game is worth it and you must play it the only way that I believe it should be experienced:  In complete darkness, with a pair of headphones (surround sound or amplified gaming headphones recommended) and a controller.  Make sure you crank the volume up and you're in for a wild ride.

The technical aspects of this game are all excellent: the graphics, the animations, the camera direction, and the sound. The first half hour when you're entering the asylum is tense and creepy stuff.
Then the gameplay hits and ruins everything.
Basically what ruins the game is the annoying stealth mechanics and nightvision. Far too many sections are pitch black, forcing you to use your camera's nightvision to see where you're going. This isn't so bad when there aren't any enemies and you're free to explore (in fact, the game is at its best when there aren't any enemies and at its worst when you're running and hiding from them), but it's annoying and frustrating when you're constantly using it to check for enemies and to run from them. The nightivision cuts your field of view depth perception which is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you're trying to sprint through twisting corridors while being chased. Imagine trying to sprint through a maze while looking through a video camera; it's just as difficult in the game as real life.
It really can't be stressed enough how the camera ruins the entire game. You have limited batteries with ridiculously short lifespans, and several sections are pitch black forcing you to use nightvision. So you're forced to "pulse" the camera constantly turning it off and on real quick. There is a beep and static sound every time this happens. What should be tense moments of immersion are shattered by the constant BEEP bzzzz BEEP bzzzzz BEEP bzzzz as you alternate between pitch black and Paris Hilton sex tape nightvision mode.
The enemies are equally frustrating. They are all very scripted and so is the solution to bypassing them because the stealth is arbitrary and makes no sense. Get ready to constantly reload from the last checkpoint (no save anywhere) as you die a lot during "practice runs" to memorize the layout of levels, the location of spare batteries, and the scripted triggers of enemies. There is no way you'll succeed at many levels the first try because you have to devote several deaths to simply mapping this stuff out.
There could have been a really effective indy horror game here. The technical aspects are all great and if they weren't so in love with that damn stupid nightvision camera and 30 second lifespan batteries then they could have salvaged this. Limit the mandatory nightvision to a few exploration segments or at least not during chase sequences. Ditch the limited battery life. Take a note from the Thief games and impliment a stealth system with enough feedback to make sense of it. I could see the hide & seek & run mechanics working if they didn't combine them with scripted triggers and nightvision.

REAL REVIEW:
SUPERHOT is a fun game, even a well made game, but it's not worth the current asking price unless you really like completionism. As of writing it took only one and a half hours to complete the entire "story" campaign and a few challenges, and I feel like there's not a whole lot left for me personally. If you like finding every secret, doing every challenge, and playing endless modes there's probably $25 worth of content in this for you, but not the rest of us.
The gameplay is fun, and the "time moves when you do" mechanic works fairly well, except for a huge flaw.
Looking uses time.
This doesn't SOUND like a big deal, but when the game starts spawning enemies around you unless you're checking or simply memorize levels you will die a LOT from people you never saw, simply because while turning to look for them, you will have used up enough time for them to kill you. I feel like this is a HUGE flaw because of how the game flows, you die far too often from enemies you will have never seen because looking eats up a surprisingly large amount of time.
Your character's hitbox is also oddly large, I noticed quite a few deaths occuring when a bullet grazes by my player but then again it could have easily been someone who spawned behind me. The game is also locked at 60 FPS with barely any graphical options, something that irked me considering the price.
Honestly it's not a bad game by any means, quite the contrary, but the asking price is too high for anyone who isn't interested in trying to 100% the game. If I had to give it a numbered review, I'd give it a 7/10.

Tales of Zestiria is the fifteenth game of the long running JRPG franchise "Tales of". 15 games man, and all these games manage to feel different from each one, but keeping the action battles that makes a "Tales of" great.
The main story is good and engaging, the characters are charming and they mature as you play the game, also, the sub-events are interesting enough to do the side missions tied to them, specially the ones where Rose is the main protagonist.
Combat is nice and fast, the new mechanic in this game is called "Armatization", which is a fusion that you can perform with one of the four Seraphs in the game (Fire, Water, Earth and Wind) when you are in this shape, your moveset stats and artes changes completely. Combat is not as deep as other entries (Like Vesperia or Xillia but is fun enough to do 100+ hits easily)
Battles takes place in something they call Fusionic Chain Linear Motion Battle System. What does that means? Well, battles are not played in a separate screen or a special stage as usual, battles this time take place in the same space as exploration, so the enviroment and topography can affect the combat this time.
Soundtrack as always is amazing, specially the song called Rising Up!
That said, there are some little annoyances that can spoil the fun at times:
- The camera angles break often
- Some bosses have Artificial Difficulty (I'm looking at you, Eizen, Angel and Turtlez)
- >30 fps lock in a pc game (can be bypassed by a mod though)
- Playing with a keyboard can be a nightmare
- Petrify can't be healed
- The Item fusion feature is unnecessarily complex (Although not hard)
With over 50 hours I can easily recommend this game to anyone who likes JRPG or the "Tales of" franchise.
ALSO ROSE IS THE BEST GIRL, EDNA IS A CLOSE SECOND, LAILAH IS A FUNNY WAIFU AND ALISHA IS PRETTY BUT KINDA STUPID.
p.s: The Im@s dlc is great and so is the Tales of Characters costume set

There are few games on Steam developed in full by just one person, and even less that manage to be something more than small indie titles easily passed by. Banished is one of those titles and benefits from its ground-up design which results in unique survival elements in a fresh take on city building.
Bigger titles have more variety in terms of buildings, structures, technology and scale, but this game can stand on its own and is still very much worth checking out because of the tangible, residing-in-memory nature of citizens and other assets which gives them lifetimes, seasonality and the ability to affect each other, creating for a subtle but immersive ecosystem that you wont see in other titles of this genre.
All the delight of this game comes from it's memory storage of everything as objects. This gives life to everything from chickens and citizens to trees and mushrooms, and adds consequence to their lives or seasons coming to an end, which ultimately ends up in a more cozy, but deeper and genuinely reactive world and life cycle that doesn't exist in other city builders. It's also what produces the survival elements of the game.
A bad season, for example, will mean not enough food being generated which can't be collected and stored, which might result in your citizens having not enough to get some of your children or old-timers through the winter, which affects the birthrates in future generations, and a whole street or village might die off too soon, which in turn affects the amount of workers and everything else, and the cycles and trends all weave and mix and affect each other. It's a rich and very interesting thing to witness and feel the affects of, and forces you to keep track of multiple different things to understand what's happening in the different parts of your town.
* The great User Interface and tracking deserve special mention. Finding out population changes, food and resource statistics, work information and more is all very helpful and also very easy to understand.
* Feelings of struggle and survival, and a network of subtle dependencies are rewarding when solved and help keep you engaged.
* Gorgeous assets and engine make your town really relaxing to just sit back and watch at times.
Similar to Dust: An Elysian Tail, Banished was developed in full by a single person, and really benefits from it, but it also hurts a game like this by limiting it's updates and scope, and taking feedback from the players. Little things like the achievements, for example, have been broken for most of the time this game has been available on Steam.
The other big problem with Banished is the lack of end-game content and wider approach. There's great mod support in here which adds a plethora of new foods, animals, buildings and more, and helps extend Banished's life, but as with the core game, there's nothing new once you've explored everything and no means of alternative play other than hardcore survival. All city building sims suffer from this problem to a degree, but they help alleviate it by offering things like monuments and a larger variety of building types and interactions so that there's always a slightly different take but in Banished, once you understand how everything works and how the networks interact with each other the game becomes fairly straight forward and building becomes more labour and less love.
* An awful lack of end-game or content for enthusiasts, though this is somewhat mitigated by good mod support.
* It's very limited in scope and even small things like map generation options or more tech upgrades would go a long way.
As a city builder, Banished doesn't have a set playtime, but you'll likely get at least 20 hours out of it before you're likely to feel the need to move on. It's available for £14.99/18.99€/$19.99 on Steam and that feels very fair for the playtime involved. It's also available (and sometimes slightly cheaper) on GOG and Humble Widgets, so shop around.
* The developer created an informative and interesting Devlog which is worth a read from start to finish here
if you're remotely interested in game design and development
* Banished has a great, and very useful sub-reddit which is full of information

As someone whose image has been a google search result for some years, I am intimately familiar with the idea that once you have created/shared something on the internet, it no longer belongs to you. It belongs to everyone.
I think the same can be said for a videogame. Once a creator has made something, it belongs to everyone.
So the message I took away from this game seemed a bit pretentious. If you make something and share it, other people will be affected by it. Will take it and change it's shape. Will share it again.
That's the way the world works.
That's not condoning plagarism, of course. Owner's rights should be given to an individual that created something, but they can't reserve the right to have their work not be interpreted by anyone they choose to share it with.
That's stupid.
So this game? It's a fun piece of fiction. An interactive matinee. But as a game developer myself I have trouble relating with the core message, or at least what my interpretation of it was.
So if the game's goal was to make me think: Mission accomplished. It was worth the entrance fee for that. But I hesitate to recommend it to others. But I suppose I will, because I'm glad I had the chance to think about what the game meant, and others deserve that experience.
If there's some hidden meaning that I'm missing out on, then I wish the game would have tried harder to clue me in on it.
Very short, but it's free to download and play, and you might learn something. A work of art.

This game probably will become much hated. Forget Gone Home: whenever anyone wants to complain about "pretentious pseudo-artsy indie non-games killing the industry", they'll remember this one now. Well, it surely has very little to do with conventional gaming as we know it (but, ironically, much more to do with what games were before there was a munlti-million industry). It is a barely interactive short story, a confession about ruined friendship, wasted effort, artistic struggle, creativity turning harmful -- all told through short surreal non-games. It is by no means "fun", but you might find a lot to relate to. If you play games professionally, as a designer, or a critic, or an art scholar, it can also give you some insights into the way interactive storytelling works (though, unlike Stanley Parable, it's not this game's main focus). All in all, it gives you plenty of food for thought, which is still rare (and frowned upon) for this medium.

This game leaves me so conflicted.  The Beginner's Guide has a really great message to deliver about the relationships authors/artists have with audiences and other artists, and about the consequences of those who pride themselves in validation by association. Where the Stanley Parable felt like a true discovery as you uncovered more about its narrator as you explored, this game instead chooses to lecture you about its narrator as you walk down a hallway.  The 'twist' at the end feels very hollow and empty, and it left me heartbroken, for an entirely different reason than it should have.

Hat in Time is one of those rare gems that comes out of nowhere, and is a great example of what crowdfunded games can be when the developers really care about the product. This game spent a grueling 5 years in development, and the undying passion throughout those 5 years from the Gears For Breakfast team really shows. Every chapter a with it's own unique personality, and no two acts feel the same despite the fact that you're usually playing on the same map.
This game is a love letter to 3D platforming from the N64/Gamecube era, right down to having Gamecube controller support (seriously, the number of different controllers I can run on this game without configuration is nutty). In many ways I could imagine being a kid and playing this on an oldschool Nintendo system. The controls are really tight and everything feels great. You start off with a whole bunch of movement options and abilities right off the bat. Wall jumps, double jumps, slides, so I don't see repeat playthroughs being frustrating.
Speaking of gameplay mechanics and options, I'd like to give special attention to how much tech there is in this game's movement. The fact that the devs left in an achievement for sequence breaking should tell you everything you need to know. Whenever I wanted to move fast and freely but needed a certain hat for something, I found myself chaining slides to keep my speed up and the levels, although having linier objectives, are designed in such a way where you're rewarded for finding unique ways around them and exploring. You have one primary objective per act but there are loads of small side objectives you can do, such as finding collectables, secrets, or just fun little easter eggs.
Personality wise, this game oozes with it. The dialogue is always spot on and the voice acting is insanely good. I found myself sitting and listening to all the voice acting, even if it meant slowing down the gameplay to enjoy it. The atmosphere in the levels is always perfect, with the music dynamically changing through a lot of the different environments (oh, by the way the soundtrack to this game is phenominal) to just the game generally creating the atmosphere through the gameplay.
A few downsides I will mention, just because I find myself wanting to look at this game critically so it can be improved upon in later patches. First off, I'm two timepieces away from finishing the game. The current build of the game only has 40 timepieces. By the time I finish the game (which unless something supernatural happens will be tomorrow), I will have only gotten four days worth of gameplay out of it. That's not to say that there isn't more I can do. I have the option of grinding out for the rest of the cosmetic items and remixes, and possibly trying the game again with One Hit Hero mode enabled, but for now, that's it. The devs did say they're planning on adding two bonus chapters later down the line in a free update which should hopefully bring our timepiece total to a cool 60 or so, but for now, this is what we have.
There are quite a few bugs left over in this game. Most of them are minor bugs such as small visual glitches, caused as a result of sequence breaking, or just minor things that got overlooked, but there were a couple of times I got stunlocked, or took several consecutive hits from an enemy all within the same few frames, and one time where I straight up got softlocked. Having said that, since the devs have already promised continued development for this game for a little longer, I expect many of these issues will be patched.
All in all though, I will make a couple of bold claims about this game:
1) It's easily in my top 10 favourite games of all time
2) This game is hands down one of the best single player gaming experiences available on Steam, if not one of the best games on Steam period.

Allow me to be straight, is this the game to resurrect the 3D platformer genre? No. God no. Far from it, it takes much more than a decent game to do that. With hype abound for Mario Odyssey (Myself included on that hype train), we're all excited for any high quality platforming game. So, ill be very straightforward in this review.
A Hat in Time is a wonderfully made 3D platformer, it nails each aspect of a 3D platformer and does it in spades with seemingly minimal effort! This game is simply a joy to play, it recaptured a part of my heart that was lost long ago. Here are the scores.
Gameplay 11/10
Simply a joy to play. The most important part of literally any game is the Gameplay, and the most important aspect of a 3D platformer is the movement. This game nails gameplay with flying colours!! The movement is fluid and becomes second nature! Each time I play this damn game i cant stop running around in circles or finding new areas to explore and find, this game has a few secrets too! It encourages explorative nature, but it also discourages it in a sense (Ill move into that a bit later). You have a group of worlds to explore, this game is HIGHLY derivitive of Mario Sunshine and BanjoKazooie, so much so to its detriment! This game has a severe loss of identity, as it tries too hard in the opening worlds to be like Super Mario Sunshine 2! It tries waaay to hard to be Mario Sunshine, and it really hurts because this game can stand on its own two adorable legs. When you unlock more worlds, you see the identity in this game, this quirky and really ♥♥♥♥ing funny game is a marvel at times!
Music 8/10
Not the worst soundtrack ever, but definitely not the best. Some tracks drone on in the background, while others dont match the mood of the overall world at all. The music is servicable and, in some cases, beautiful, but its nothing stellar. Dont buy THIS games soundtrack unless you really want some upbeat drone to listen to, and NO thats not a bad thing! The music is upbeat and is always pleasant, but it just drones all the time and rarely changes. When it does change, its jarring and not fluid at all in some cases, and fluid and welcome in others! Its hit or miss for me, but when it comes to the quality of the music? Thats where it gets its points from. Each track is good on its own in an isolated environment, but if you listen to it while youre playing the game, it can deliver mixed feelings.
Aesthetic 10/10
Positively marvellous, the careful symbiosis between Graphical style and Gameplay style is struck immediately in this game! No point in the game is odd, even the one actually creepy level i played made wonderful use of the graphical style, making it a very creepy game even with its absolutely adorable art style! Hat Girl is one of the cutest characters made in gaming to date, I say that in full body and mind, me and my friend marathon'd this game over the course of 8 hours (My internet was down during the first 3) and we simply couldnt stop saying "This game is adorable" and where it isnt adorable its just plain pleasant! The mobsters are so damn cute I cant hate them! The ghosts had me saying "awww" al the time! You cant go wrong with this games cartoony and colourful artstyle!
Sound 9/10
For the most part, the nail is hit on the head with voice acting and sound clips, but there is one instance where it feels a bit weird. The primary antagonist in the game, Mustache Girl, her voice is a bit weird to hear coming out of the character. Accents are also something that is a bit weird, but I can easily look passed that. The voice acting is absolutely top notch, one level is set in a spooky forest, and the primary enemy in it is a sinister large ghost who's voice actor has the PERFECT EVIL LAUGH!! And his voice is actually intimidating, so to hear him say all these adorable things and throwing out small cute quips here and there, it successfully makes an endearing character! This game nails that aspect again with flying colours, minus a few characters here and there. Two in particular are a bit annoying, Mustache Girl herself and the Owl in the second world. Other than that, marvellous.
Performance 9/10
I have an Intel Core i-5 2500k processor and an NVIDIA Quadro 1000m graphics processor, its not a bad PC and it gets me by with Indie titles. I had a lot of chug on higher settings but when i bumped all settings aside from character detail down to the lowest itll go, I was perfectly fine throughout the game. Now, depending on your PC, I would say stave off till the console releases, but if you truly cant wait and are sure you can deal with some frame drops here and there, youre fine. This games primary gimmick is the acquisition of hats, which give special abilities. Now this is cool in concept but I personally have issues with that, as finding Yarn can be difficult at times and♥♥♥♥♥♥easy at others. It makes you reconsider grabbing on piece of yarn over another because that piece is on a tree branch that takes 5 minutes to get to, or you can go get the one frozen in ice with an explosive literally right next to it. Its annoying how hard it is to get 1 single piece of yarn while you can get 5 perfectly fine with NO effort whatsoever in other worlds.
Another small issue is Boss Fights. Some are imaginative and interesting while others are so damn boring. My least favorite thus far was the fight with the primary Ghost Boss. Its visually impressive, yes, but its also incredibly tedious. I dont like how long these boss fights are either, you have 2-3 phases, and well thats good but also thats bad. You'd think 3 hits to get into the next phase, but one boss was like 5 hits while another felt like ♥♥♥♥ing 20! its infuriating to say the least. All in All buy this game if youre confident in your PC, if not, I would say wait until you're certain or await its arrival on PS4 and XBONE. You cant go wrong, best 30 dollars Ive spent nearly all year!

Game should be played in complete darkness and with proper headphones, or at least a good surround system.
The game masters mostly everything. It is very cleverly built. The usage of light and complete dark is used to an extreme advantage here, and done so very well. There are lots of surprising elements. Your character doesn't have any weapons and can do only two things: run or hide, often a combination of both. But still, when escaping an area successfully you get this great feeling of mastering something: you survived.
The scares in this game are endless. What I loved the most was that some of them were pretty silly, the game obviously mocking and laughing at you for scaring you. That said, the game is mostly very serious and deals with the theme of insane asylum in a proper "not safe for life" way, but it doesn't take itself too seriously through certain funny moments.
Monster and scare-wise Outlast is like a hyperactive Amnesia. What I loved about it is that certain enemies are the same characters that keep following you through the whole game, trying to catch you. This adds alot to the immersion, which otherwise is top notch.
My only tiny minus side was that a few areas were too dark, even with light turned on in-game. Feels like I missed some detail there, but this happened only in around 5% of the game.

This is a game that you HAVE to play with other people.  Its single player mode is tacked on and hollow (much like many modern games). I cannot recommend it if you're looking for a good single player experience. However, its incredible multiplayer more than justifies the game's reasonable asking price if you have a few controllers. While the Dark World expansion fleshes out the campaign, it is still best enjoyed when you have a few friends to share in the rage. One MAJOR caveat: the game has no online multiplayer. While the reasoning is understandable, (the game has mechanics timed down to individual frames and would be a subpar experience if there's any amount of latency involved) I believe having a poor online mode would still be superior to not having one at all.
Barring those few criticisms, Towerfall Ascension is a gem of a local multiplayer brawler. You play as one of several archers (that vary only cosmetically) and have a limited number of arrows (3 by default). Once you shoot an arrow, it is left on the world and you must pick it up by walking over it. Your movement and aiming is combined into a single control, which takes some getting used to if you're new to the genre. You are only able to move and aim in 8 principle directions. The arrows you shoot home slightly if there's an enemy in range, and there are multiple arrow types that range from exploding to bouncing to piercing. Each attack is an instant kill, regardless of whether it was through shooting your opponent with an arrow, hitting them with an arrow's secondary effect, or stomping their heads in. There is also dodging, which is both your defense and mobility ability. And finally, there is screen wrap, where the top/bottom and left/right of the screen are connected.
It was designed from the ground up to be played locally, and accommodates both casual and competitive play. The default game mode on headhunter is perfect for people who have never played the game, with just enough rubber-banding to keep everyone in the game without being egregious (nothing like Mario Kart's first to worst from a single blue shell). Each round is paced well, and no one ever stays hopeless or dead for too long. You can go down the list of maps to gradually introduce your friends to new items, and never really overwhelm them (unless you want to).
If you're playing casually with experienced players, custom game modes vastly increase the replayability of an already replayable game. Small tweaks like spawning with special arrows or returning as ghosts result in significant changes in how you play. And finally, making an asymmetric custom mode (2v1/3v1 team death match) where one player gets huge bonuses (such as regenerating shields and arrows) while the opposing team gets an advantage in numbers is almost like playing an entirely new game. Even the more chaotic game modes (like infinite drill arrows or infinite laser arrows) are good for a round or two before you abandon them and pretend they never existed.
And finally, the game is very well balanced competitively. Dodge cancelling and superjumping are difficult mechanics to master, and yield a surprisingly high skill ceiling. While there are a few oddities for a competitive game (bolt arrows finding your opponent's home from 3 zipcodes away, kicking their dog, then brutally murdering them right in the face comes to mind) it's nothing that custom rules can't fix. Because everyone has the same attacks and abilities, the only thing that sets players apart is their positioning, skill, and reflexes.
Towerfall Ascension is an amazing game that I highly recommend if and only if you play local multiplayer games. Do not buy this game if you're looking for a single player game or a good story (mediocre and nonexistent respectively). However, Towerfall Ascension is one of the best local multiplayer games out there. If you own a few controllers and have people over occasionally, this game is almost mandatory.

Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy could be best described as an interactive movie directed by David Cage and published by Quantic Dream during 2005. The player takes controls of Lucas, a man who finds himself a murderer for reasons beyond his control, and Carla and Tyler, two detectives from the New York police department investigating on the same murderers where Lucas is involved.
If you are familiar with the other works from Cage (namely, Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls on the Playstation 3), then you already know what you're in for. If not, Fahrenheit plays out as a typical adventure game: you must interact with items and talk to people in order to advance, the only difference being the whole "cinematic" feel of the whole thing (your movements are limited and you use quick time events to perform several actions). The formula is broken only on rare occasions (there are two stealth sequences, for instance) and the tasks you will be asked to complete vary a lot. At various points in the game you can take choices that will alter the main story, for better or worse: the adventure features different endings, with the very final sequences being a big factor in which one you'll get.
Another important gameplay mechanic from Fahrenheit is the sanity meter of the three characters: each one will get more or less depressed as the events of the story unfolds, with dire consequences if a character will get too hopeless. Performing certain actions or picking precise choices can increase or decrease a protagonist's sanity, althought this vary from character to character and honestly sometimes there is no any way to know in advance.
There are in-game bonus cards that can be found scattered across the various sequences, sometimes in view, sometimes hidden in drawers and such. They award bonus points that can be later used at the end of the game to purchase concept art, movies and other goodies.
One of the main problems I experienced in Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy are not about how omnipresent the QTEs are, but how tricky they can actually be. While playing expect to be suddendly tasked to clear various QTEs in rapid succession, with a lot of buttons to press at the right time. It's worth mentioning that failing most QTEs will result in a game over and the necessity to reload the game from the last checkpoint, but sometimes failing a QTE is necessary to achieve certain results, down to the very multiple endings: the game doesn't explain this at all. You should also know that using a keyboard could carry some technical difficulties too (button presses not being recorded and such).
Another problem from Fahrenheit worth mentioning is that the unexpected gameplay changes and some special sequences could be a serious issue for first time players and are mostly about trial and error (I'm referring to the far too many timed missions with Lucas, where you have to peform certain action in order to dodge a game over in the short time given, or two stealth sequences I mentioned above).
To end this review, you may have heard that Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy's story gets a bit ... twisted towards the end. I'd agree with that statement: while what we could call the first act of the game drags far longer than necessary, the second and the third act introduces so many outlandish and complicated elements that never have enough time to be properly fleshed out. While this was due to a severe executive medding, we can only judge what we have in our hands.
The remastered version doesn't add any new content whatsoever and provides mainly a graphical overhaul for HD displays.
In short, Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy is an interesting experimental game with an average story and a very tense gameplay, but it's very easy to find it entertaining at least

There are few games on Steam developed in full by just one person, and even less that manage to be something more than small indie titles easily passed by. Banished is one of those titles and benefits from its ground-up design which results in unique survival elements in a fresh take on city building.
Bigger titles have more variety in terms of buildings, structures, technology and scale, but this game can stand on its own and is still very much worth checking out because of the tangible, residing-in-memory nature of citizens and other assets which gives them lifetimes, seasonality and the ability to affect each other, creating for a subtle but immersive ecosystem that you wont see in other titles of this genre.
All the delight of this game comes from it's memory storage of everything as objects. This gives life to everything from chickens and citizens to trees and mushrooms, and adds consequence to their lives or seasons coming to an end, which ultimately ends up in a more cozy, but deeper and genuinely reactive world and life cycle that doesn't exist in other city builders. It's also what produces the survival elements of the game.
A bad season, for example, will mean not enough food being generated which can't be collected and stored, which might result in your citizens having not enough to get some of your children or old-timers through the winter, which affects the birthrates in future generations, and a whole street or village might die off too soon, which in turn affects the amount of workers and everything else, and the cycles and trends all weave and mix and affect each other. It's a rich and very interesting thing to witness and feel the affects of, and forces you to keep track of multiple different things to understand what's happening in the different parts of your town.
* The great User Interface and tracking deserve special mention. Finding out population changes, food and resource statistics, work information and more is all very helpful and also very easy to understand.
* Feelings of struggle and survival, and a network of subtle dependencies are rewarding when solved and help keep you engaged.
* Gorgeous assets and engine make your town really relaxing to just sit back and watch at times.
Similar to Dust: An Elysian Tail, Banished was developed in full by a single person, and really benefits from it, but it also hurts a game like this by limiting it's updates and scope, and taking feedback from the players. Little things like the achievements, for example, have been broken for most of the time this game has been available on Steam.
The other big problem with Banished is the lack of end-game content and wider approach. There's great mod support in here which adds a plethora of new foods, animals, buildings and more, and helps extend Banished's life, but as with the core game, there's nothing new once you've explored everything and no means of alternative play other than hardcore survival. All city building sims suffer from this problem to a degree, but they help alleviate it by offering things like monuments and a larger variety of building types and interactions so that there's always a slightly different take but in Banished, once you understand how everything works and how the networks interact with each other the game becomes fairly straight forward and building becomes more labour and less love.
* An awful lack of end-game or content for enthusiasts, though this is somewhat mitigated by good mod support.
* It's very limited in scope and even small things like map generation options or more tech upgrades would go a long way.
As a city builder, Banished doesn't have a set playtime, but you'll likely get at least 20 hours out of it before you're likely to feel the need to move on. It's available for £14.99/18.99€/$19.99 on Steam and that feels very fair for the playtime involved. It's also available (and sometimes slightly cheaper) on GOG and Humble Widgets, so shop around.
* The developer created an informative and interesting Devlog which is worth a read from start to finish here
if you're remotely interested in game design and development
* Banished has a great, and very useful sub-reddit which is full of information

Air Conflicts: Secret Wars is an arcade flight simulation set in a world war I + II scenario. During the 7 campaigns the player has to fly and fight through 49 missions. Before taking off, the player can choose between different aircrafts, each with different strengths and weaknesses.

After some missions the player can upgrade one of his skills in order to maneuver the airplanes easier, have more endurance or have your wingman boosted. Further, the player can choose between two control schemes. Arcade and simulation. The first one makes the game easier to control, while the second one gives more options to control the aircraft.

Okay, so ordinarily I'm a sucker for games like this. I'm not interested in debating whether or not different projects can be called games, especially ones that are as narratively driven as this one. Ultimately, art and entertainment are what they are and I'm fine with judging them on their own terms. I should also say that I really enjoyed the Stanley Parable for what it was, especially the first time around.
That being said, there's something pretty pretentious and self-indulgent going on here. The Beginner's Guide presents itself as a tour of a series of short, abstract games produced by an introverted friend of the narrator, and the player is left to puzzle over their meaning. The narrator himself leaves very little to interpretation or imagination, steering the conversation and reflection as he sees fit, and it's clear early on that his obsession over interpreting his friend's work is in many ways his own problem. I don't think I'm spoiling much by saying that this is part of the conclusion of the game's meditations, which leaves me asking why the narrator ever put these games together and spoke up in the first place.
There are all these themes of self-awareness, validation, success, etc being thrown around. I understand that as much as some of us try to deny it these concerns are big parts of our lives, but without larger implications it just comes off really self-absorbed when it is all there is to the subject. If you're too theatrical about the discussion it just gives the impression that you're enjoying being a tortured, self-conscious artist. Maybe part of it was the writing and voice acting but I just couldn't buy the idea that any of it was sincere (Ironically something the game delves into at some point).
I'm getting off point, I'm still very confused by this game so it's hard for me to offer a focussed explanation of how I feel about it.
Multiple times I kept thinking that it would've been so much better with sparser or absent narration. The text scattered throughout the levels does more than enough without Davey's ponderous moaning about sincere expression.
I should've started this review by saying that the game left me feeling incredibly sympathetic toward "Coda", the producer of the games you're led through, the artist whose mind and motivations you spend an hour and a half reflecting on. The narrator recognizes himself as an abusive intruder into this guy's life, even recognizes that his attempt to reconnect by releasing these games which are not his to release is a transgression that makes everything worse. There's  no rule obligating me to be sympathetic to the narrator, and I'm sure Davey expected this turning point to be a revelation, but it wasn't. It just left me relieved that the narrator finally learned a lesson that should've been obvious from the start and shut the hell up. That's another problem, it's not a lesson you learn, even vicariously. It's a lesson he learns, you're just helplessly brought along for the neurotic ride, pinned to a chair and forced to listen to him heavy handidly talk about self discovery.
For all that I've said there's something fascinating about a story that concludes that it never should have existed in the first place.

It's much easier to say "Pick up and play Five Nights at Freddy's" to understand what the game is, than to describe it, but that's kind of obnoxious to say that and leave it there. It's actually because the game is rather simple, as opposed to complex.
Five Nights at Freddy's is a game that costs less than a footlong Subway sandwich, and lasts only a small amount longer, so perhaps simplicity and shortness are to be expected.
It's essentially a point and click, first person horror game. You're a night shift security guard confined to an office the whole game, and you have to (like the title implies) survive five in-game nights at Freddy's, a failing pizzeria in the vein of Chuck E.Cheese's, in order to win.
Each night, the four animatronics in the restaurant will try to slip into your office and kill you. The only way to defend yourself is with two sets of doors and lights, and a monitor of the camera feeds, in order to locate where everyone is. The problem is, though, that using the doors, lights (that show up anyone outside your door) and monitor will increase the rate that the nightly-allocated amount of power is drained.
It's a game where vigilance and observation will get you far, as well as managing your power. If you run out of power, then you're completely vulnerable to attack, so the game trades off how quickly you can look and react with how accurately you can look at the environment.
At least in my own opinion, the game does the horror element exceedingly well. I cannot speak for how another person would react to it, but the horror element is exemplary. The creepy ambient sounds, such as footsteps, breathing, demonic laughter and childish laughter, coupled some audio cues and nothing in the way of music except for Freddy's tune (a music box version of The Bullfighters' March from Carmen) make the game feel very tense to play.
There's some visual elements of horror. The animatronics can appear to shift positions, or even stare at the camera when you check and double check on them in the monitor. Background elements can subtly change between viewings. You can flick the lights on to see the animatronics gleefully smiling at you when you light them up. The animatronics may be cartoony and colourful, but there is a certain 'soulless' quality to their eyes, mouths and faces in particular- it's a game that is clearly playing off the fear anyone had of animal animatronics as a kid. FNaF is a very dark game, so it pays to give lots of attention to being obsevant- it is not very well lit at all, intentionally. We're talking about a game whose wiki has brightened versions of screenshots in order to help you better see it. If we're being cynical, it could be argued the game is dark to mask the graphical fidelity.
There is psychological horror in the tense, creepy atmosphere, but the game is also full of jumpscares. These mainly happen when you get caught by the animatronics, so the game might not appeal if you don't like jumpscares- if you don't like the characters literally being 'in your face'.
FNaF is over in about an hour, tops, but it packs in a lot of creepiness, horror and jumpscaring. The mechanics give a less-is-more vibe, and it's very competent at what it does.
I believe it's a game that's worth playing, but not for the faint of heart, or for those with poor eyesight.
In summary, it's a short but sweet horror game that delivers well on the horror and scares, that's intuitive to pick up and play, with some easy-to-learn-hard-to-master mechanics. It's not a game for everyone, but if you're prepared to risk being scared a few times, it's worth it.

Kickstarted the game a long time ago. I heard about it because one of the devs was involved in the TF2 modding scene for a while. It's been a while since I've played a 3D collectathon let alone enjoyed one, so when I checked my email to see it came out I was pleasantly surprised. I've enjoyed my time in it. It's got great music, I enjoyed the art style, the movement is responsive and feels good, and while the early voice acting isn't the best, the later voice acting can be great.
It does however have a few small issues that could be frustrating in the moment, but totaled maybe 5 instances throughout the game. Wall jumping is finnicky, and you kind of lose air control after wall jumping, meaning some jumps or maneuvers you think you should make, you don't. There's usually alternate paths to those things, though, and this is usually caused by me being stubborn and not looking around. In the settings, if you change the camera distance to far or very far, it will jitter and wig out if in any sections with pieces above you. I found the far setting to be the most comfortable distance, but whenever there was a platform above the character's head, it jittered around making it hard to see.
The bosses were pretty fun, and the music in all of them was great. Some bosses seemed to last way longer than I thought they would, and in some cases healing existed pretty much only at the beginning of the fight. This meant you had to do a 5 minute long boss fight while taking 3 or fewer hits for the duration. I found out after the fact that there's an item that makes the fights all way easier (and you don't have to do the fights before getting said item), but still.
The zones are varied and pretty fun to traverse, and there's a lot of neat little easter eggs or sort of left field jokes that made the experience overall more enjoyable. Over the course of a weekend, I beat the game (~12hrs total playtime) collecting all of the hour glasses (equivalent of stars in any of the 3D Mario games), with a few extra collectables I did not really go out of my way to collect.
Overall enjoyed the game, and if a 3D collectathon game where you change hats to use different powers and hookshot across the zones sounds like it's up your alley, I'd say give it a go.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a horror game in which you play the role of the security guard, Mike, and try to survive until your next shift against 4 (or 5?) bloodthirsty animatronics.
The gameplay is amazing, especially if you're a fan of the horror genre. There are 4 (or 5) animatronics in total: Bonnie the bunny, Chica
(not a duck), Foxy, Freddy Fazbear, and Golden Freddy (who is kind of an easter egg) and they're ALL out to kill you. You have a limited amount of power every night since the manager is a cheap♥♥♥♥♥ so you've gotta conserve your power (closing the doors that keep the animatronics out, using the lights in the hallway that illuminate your blind spots on the cameras, and using the cameras all take power). It's hard to predict what the animatronics' next moves are gonna be sometimes, which makes the game that much more terrifying.
One thing I didn't like was how the animatronics all have set paths. Bonnie and Foxy always come down the west hallway while Chica and Freddy come down the east. It's still scary when they poke their ugly heads out from around their hidey holes, but I hope it's more random in FNAF 2. The game does get really hard on the later nights though (and also
repetitive), and that takes away from the replayability value to me.
The sound in this game is probably what immersed me the most, so I've got no complaints here (other than the fact that they all seem to do a slightly different variation of the same scream when they pop up at you). From Night 4 onwards, Freddy is on the move and you'll know it. If you hear Freddy's signature laugh, close the door to the east hallway and CHECK THE CAMERAS. If you hear footsteps, force your hand to stop shaking for 2 seconds and close the doors to the west hallway. Foxy likes to chill in Pirate's Cove most of the time, but when you get on his nerves he hauls♥♥♥♥♥down the hallway. There's a lot more freaky sounds that the animatronics can make in the game that ALL add up to make beautiful ambience of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. If you hear Freddy's song... bye-bye.
The gameplay, sounds and music all together create an amazing atmosphere for a horror game that, depite its flaws, is sure to scare anybody at least once (unless you're extremely lucky and happen to glide through the game without dying once, but that's nearly impossible). If you're interested in this game at all, it's definitely worth the 5 bucks to at least try it out. If you're a horror fan, then I don't know why you wouldn't already have this and be eagerly awaiting the sequel by now. Have fun playing it, and sweet dreams!

Story: 8/10 Great, but cliché. Of course since it's an old game.
Gameplay: 2/10 The game mechanics are possibly the most annoying things you'll ever see. From evading a thousand props for no reason by pressing the same keys on screen (this feels like an extreme version of Dance Dance Revolution) to constantly running through the same hallway 10 times. Completely unnecessary, tiring, and repetitive.
Even when talking to other characters, and you've asked 1 or 2 questions to the person in front of you, for some reason you are later not allowed to make the other possible questions, which were offered just a few seconds ago. The game basically prohibits you from talking after a few tries.
There's also another game mechanic that is still here, which is spamming the LEFT and RIGHT buttons. It's horrible. And even if you get a program to spam it for you, the game adapts so horribly to your button-pushing that it misses your actions and says "oh, I didn't see you pressing the correct button (either L or R) so I'll just supposse you didn't press♥♥♥♥♥♥and make you fail".
Sound: 4/10 The audio is almost completely mono (1 channel) and it doesn't feel anywhere near from a "remastered" version.
Graphics: 5/10 They could've put so much more work into it, but apparently just making better face and clothing textures is enough for the game. This feels like Half-Life (1) made in the 20th century. Wait..
The game has a great story. But you'll be spending a lot of time progressing because of obvious but horribly designed puzzles and trying to get a goal by pressing a total of 150+ keys in just 2 minutes, because of its horrible, non-polished game mechanics that will literally make you mad and tired. The story is the best thing of this, but since the story is the ONLY good thing about this game, you might just want to watch a walkthrough on YouTube, instead of having to deal with the button-pushing, Dance Dance Revolution-like design of this game.
TL;DR If you have the old version of this game, stay with the old version. If you don't, then, for your own good (and for the health of your hands and wrists) watch a walkthrough.

I have been a Tales fan since pre-Symphonia times and was very excited when I heard that the newest entry in the Tales series, Zestiria, was going to go back to its classic medieval style. During the first few hours of the game I was absolutely captivated. The world of Zestiria had the classic Tales flair with many Arthurian style elements, but that enthrallment slowly faded away due to the lack of character development and the story plot.
Graphically the game is very beautiful despite being outdated PS3 graphics, and the world and character design are all magnificently executed. I really liked the characters in the beginning but as the game progressed I felt that the personalities they had become static. The story went from being interesting, to painfully predictable. The only thing that really kept me going was the battle system, which had some new wonderful implements, and my love of the Tales series.
My absolute biggest complaint was that I felt that the game was extremely linear due to the lack of side quests compared to that found in other Tales games. The side quests present in the game always felt like they were oddly timed between the few important story quests, and always revolved around optional dungeons. I did enjoy how optional dungeons were peppered into the newly improved world map system, but any quests that involved them were merely “go and fight X here.”
Despite these complaints I would still recommend this game to any Tales fan. It won’t be your favorite Tales game ever, but it’s a solid entry in the series.

Like a diamond in the rough, this masterpiece of a game has so much potential to become something greater, which I really hope it for to take and grasp that. Dominique Grieshofer has created a perfect, short and relaxing parkour/platformer game that brings you both fun and peace to your mind, along with many more positive features.
Pros:
- Remarkable Graphics
From the sea to the sky, Refunct has some astonishing design and graphics. The shadowing and water reflection are very well done, along with the stunning background that you play in. The lighting is great and the fact that it coordinates with the sun's movement, it leads to something even more amazing. Refunct has a night/day cycle, which lets you experience the beauty of the game during the light of day and the darkness of the night. The colors are very bright and lively, making sure that it helps make you feel relaxed and at home, truly remarkable.
- Melodious/Peaceful Soundtrack
The music in this game is exactly what it says, relaxing and emotional. It brings peace and calmness over you while you play the game to its fullest. With music like this, there is really no reason to be angry or rage during the game, since you will be enveloped by the tranquility of the music. The soundtrack is truly marvelous and the fact that the music also cycles with the day/night cycle shows that much effort has been put in the soundtrack.
- Simple, Charming Plot
The gameplay is like any other game platformer, but it comes with a twist. You parkour to restore the world around you and return it to its former glory. It gives the player a bit of purpose on why he/she should continue to restore the world around them. Even though it doesn't give you any idea of a plot or idea, this was my assumption, since you have to press buttons that would continue to bring the broken world up from the depths of the sea. It makes sense, since each time you step on a new block or piece of land, you restore it with its color and give it the gift of life. I kind of lean towards plots like this, that are straight-forward and easy to understand.
- Pure Gameplay
The gameplay is relatively forward like any other platformer game. You can walljump off of tall blocks, you can slide through pipes and low places, you can take lifts to higher places, or jump higher and farther from springs. Seems simple, but the real purpose of the gameplay is to not make you feel angry, frustrated or any other related emotions. The game was built to make you feel relaxed while you play the game, so the gameplay was designed to not overwhelm you with overly complictated actions. Despite that, the game is obviously not hard to play, meaning that many people with different platforming experience could play. However, the game is also not too easy to beat, due to the achievements and overall design, which gives it a bit more flavor and memorable to those who play a lot of platformer games.
Now to the cons; but I have to point out first that these are all in my opinion, meaning that some might not agree with me, but I'm sure that these opinions are ones that most would agree on.
Cons:
- Short Game
I know that the developer intended for this game to be short, but I enjoyed it so much that I want it to expand more. I really dont care on how it could be extended, maybe adding more parts to the one level, or maybe making an entire new level. With its already incredible graphic and soundtrack, its just so sad that you can finish this game so quick and not see the fullness of the game.
- MOAR Content
Now this was something I needed to point out, like I said in the beginning, 'A diamond in the rough'. What it means is when something (or someone) has hidden exceptional characteristics and/or future potential, but currently lacks the final touches that would make them (or it) truly stand out from the crowd. This game is exactly that to me because the developer could add so much more to this game to make it even greater. Now, I'm not saying that it doesn't stand out (Just look at all the positive reviews), but I kind of want more content within the game. Maybe the developer could add some sort of teleporting system, or maybe a bridge mechanic ( These are ideas I'm just throwing from the top of my head). To people who have already played, you might get where I'm coming from, but to the new player or those who are interested in this game. Just play it first and enjoy what its was made for, then you'll get what Im trying to say. Other than that, the game itself is already a masterpiece.
My Verdict of The Game
9/10

There are a few surprises you'll encounter in the game, one for me was that there is a pretty good amount of difficulty in some areas, necessitating repeating areas. Also there is a pretty terrifying Act in world 3, but I may be more sensitive since I don't play many horror games.

So far, the game looks promising and it has the potential to become a great open-world survival game.

TL;DR - Title in pre-alpha, developed by one teenage dude that already abandoned this game only to pick it up again after few months. He might do this again (I don't think he plan to but I guess that he also didn't plan to abandon it in 2016) so if you really want this game just wait for some 1$ bundle or -95% discount. With history of rocky development and in its current state the game is not worth its current price (9,99€).
Also, look at the reviews. Most people got their keys from bundles - this is why overall score for the title is MIXED. It would be Mostly Negative but you have to buy the game directly from steam to be included in 'User reviews' overall score.
FULL COMMENT
The game is in something that I would call pre-alpha stage. For example: environments are empty, some textures are missing, AI is really, really bad (soldiers barely move, they won't try to hide behid the cover during fight; in fact they will stand motionless in front of their enemies and exchange fire, really exciting), animations are broken, just like optimization and many other things.
I don't want to bash this game but in it's current state it should not be on steam. 'It is Early Access' you can say. Well yes, it is, but it's been there from at least over a year. You see, this game started as 'Lost World'. It was supposed to be multiplayer title but at some point thing went south. The developer went on some kind of war with community and eventually decided to abandon his game. Few months passed and he decided that he actually wants to finish it - he picked it up and restarted development, removing many features (like already mentioned mutliplayer) in the process.
I respect that he decided to try again BUT, as far as I know, the game is still being made by ONE teenage dude. We have no guarantee that he won't cease development again, leaving all potential buyers with unfished title. He addmited that he is busy (school and stuff) which means less time to work on the game. Unfortunatelly when he has time to work on it he seems to focus on adding stuff like ships on the sky (not interactable) instead of, I don't know, some kind of tutorial (might be useful when main menu is replaced with empty and boring hub where we can see our character in TPP) or at least AI that actually do something.
I wish him best but I don't belive that Lost World (aka LONE WOLF: Horizon) will ever be what he wants it to be. If he will ever finish it in first place.

I've had this game sitting in my library for I have no idea how long.  I don't know when I bought it.  I don't know where it came from.  Nothing.
"Let's give it a try!" I said to myself.
I started up the game.  There was a character on the screen.  I sat back and waited for a title screen or something.  A few shots rang out.  Someone exploded on my screen.
"Hit a few buttons maybe?" I said.
I did.  I moved around.
"Oh, there isn't a title screen," I told myself.
I then went about figuring out what did what.  I died a few times.  At some point I noticed a purple gun.  Legenadry apparently.  Honestly, I couldn't tell the difference.
I tried to hire new people.  I couldn't figure out how.  I looked around.  Right behind me was a mass of maybe 15 bad guys, just standing around.  I shot a few.  Their friends seemed ok with this.  I walked over to them, wanting to see if they'd attack me if I got too close.  Nothing.
I stood in the middle of the bad guy horde for a few minutes while I looked over the stats screen.  There was a "quit" button.  I clicked it.  Nothing.
Around this time I noticed more gunfire.  Some guys that looked like the Silver Surfer were standing around getting shot at by the bad guys.  I tried to get in the middle and "give me life" for the Surfers, but alas the bullets were not meant for me.  I killed a few more of the bad guy mass (now known as the "Tango Tumor" in my mind) and looked at their guns.  Nothing legendary.
I noticed another Tango Tumor nearby and went to hang out with them too.  I showed off that awesome green skirt I was wearing for some reason.  They seemed impressed but largely ignored me.
Off to the side there was a beacon of light going from the ground into the sky.  Surely that will do something!  Nothing, besides make my screen go white if I got in the middle of it.  Maybe that was the healing spire?  I couldn't find out because no one would shoot at me any longer.
I checked out the updates and saw that this game had been out for a year now exactly.  2/12/16.  The info here on Steam says they're going to aim for a Q1 2017 release.  All I can say is good luck to the dev.  This game sounds great on paper, but it needs a lot of work.

Firstly getting into start screen. The start screen is very basic, but it's very well done. It's easy to find the graphic settings, the controls, the co-op, and single player buttons, not to mention the audio itself.
Getting into the actual gameplay, It's amazing. Although the farmer is very annoying, but for what you pay for the game it is really good. The guns are really good, and powerful at low rounds, and as you progress it gets harder to kill the boars. Getting into the days, I think 101 days is a little bit long to play, but if you have the time it's fun, and the characters themselves are great to play as.
The bosses get harder every 10 days which is really challenging and fun. I love the aspect that they can heal so that they don't die so easily, and you have to actually do a lot of hard work to kill them, but the best part of the bosses is the names for the fat pig that's in the middle.
Getting on to the grinder. The grinder is amazing, but it is used for powerups which is also a great addition to the game, and make sit much better to play for something else other than just killing boars that are on steroids, but apart from that stuff that's all there is to the grinder.
Getting on the farmer himself. He is funny, but also annoying. His jokes aren't that great, and could be worked on a little bit, but apart from that the farmer is a great guy. Especially when you shoot him, and he starts getting mad, and eventually throws stuff at you.
Getting on the boars. There is a mix of boar's from small to large, and from skeletons, to bosses, and from boar's to pigs. The game on a whole is amazing, and I love it.
Getting on to the price. The price of the game should be more, because of how fun the game is especially when you play with friends, and have a laugh with them. So I recommend the price should be set atleast at £2.50, and not 0.75. I'm not complaining about it being so cheap, but I think it should be more.
On a whole I would recommend anyone to get this game that enjoys shooter genres, and loves to play co-op with friends.
I would rate this game a 10/10, and that you should buy it if you have a spare £0.79

Overview:
So this game is pretty much the good ol times in Robocraft, but with ships instead of robots.
Gameplay:
Rather simple but slightly cumbersome. More or less like Robocraft.
Graphics:
Well it's a F2P game so it can't be too intense. Still it's rather clean, UI may take some time to get used to.
Balance:
Well here's where things get tricky. There are classes which your ships are based around. Frigate, Cruiser, Battleship, Destoryer and Rookie ship. Some ships go really, really well with certian weapon and equipment combos, like the destoryer's artillery mode and heavy gauss. Heavy gauss has a range of 3500 and artillery mode gives you more range at the cost of speed. Right now that's the BIG OP. But aside from that everything will fall into place.
Free to Play: you have the bog standard goods, however it's mainly all cosmeticts, There are ships you can get but the ones that are used for Space Credits just have skins on them. You get a consumable that you can use once per match to incease the XP and money earned in a match, up to three peope can activate them per match to a bonus of 225%. These consumables can be brought or gotten via promotional codes.
Finals Thoughts: The game is nice, runs well. Well worth a try if you pine form the good old days of Robocraft.
I'll also link two promo codes. Don't know how long these will run for.
KOMPOT- 3 days of prem time and a free rookie ship.
SPACERAMBO- 3 days again but this time you get 10 of the premium consumable i mentioned.

Well, is it a good game? Yes.
Is it fun? Mostly yes.
Is it realistic? Kind of. The damage models seem realistic, bullets penetrate the skin, break bones and cause bleeding. If you're into that, great. Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm also have great gore if you're into that, I know I am.
Speaking of gore, the voice acting for when people die? I never thought sound could play such a huge role in selling the experience, I found myself getting more immersed from battle chatter and gunfire than from the plastic textures of the Unreal Engine.
There's also tanks in this game by the way, and I'm not sure if any other games do it like the Red Orchestra series which is a huge shame because I LOVE IT SO MUCH. The damage models aren't exactly true to life, but who cares, you have fully modeled tank interiors, realistic enough damage models, the tanks seem balanced, honestly, I have few complaints about them other than when you get stuck on a surface you shouldn't be on, backing up does more harm than good.
I guess that's all I really have to say for this review then, go buy Red Orchestra 2.

Like a diamond in the rough, this masterpiece of a game has so much potential to become something greater, which I really hope it for to take and grasp that. Dominique Grieshofer has created a perfect, short and relaxing parkour/platformer game that brings you both fun and peace to your mind, along with many more positive features.
Pros:
- Remarkable Graphics
From the sea to the sky, Refunct has some astonishing design and graphics. The shadowing and water reflection are very well done, along with the stunning background that you play in. The lighting is great and the fact that it coordinates with the sun's movement, it leads to something even more amazing. Refunct has a night/day cycle, which lets you experience the beauty of the game during the light of day and the darkness of the night. The colors are very bright and lively, making sure that it helps make you feel relaxed and at home, truly remarkable.
- Melodious/Peaceful Soundtrack
The music in this game is exactly what it says, relaxing and emotional. It brings peace and calmness over you while you play the game to its fullest. With music like this, there is really no reason to be angry or rage during the game, since you will be enveloped by the tranquility of the music. The soundtrack is truly marvelous and the fact that the music also cycles with the day/night cycle shows that much effort has been put in the soundtrack.
- Simple, Charming Plot
The gameplay is like any other game platformer, but it comes with a twist. You parkour to restore the world around you and return it to its former glory. It gives the player a bit of purpose on why he/she should continue to restore the world around them. Even though it doesn't give you any idea of a plot or idea, this was my assumption, since you have to press buttons that would continue to bring the broken world up from the depths of the sea. It makes sense, since each time you step on a new block or piece of land, you restore it with its color and give it the gift of life. I kind of lean towards plots like this, that are straight-forward and easy to understand.
- Pure Gameplay
The gameplay is relatively forward like any other platformer game. You can walljump off of tall blocks, you can slide through pipes and low places, you can take lifts to higher places, or jump higher and farther from springs. Seems simple, but the real purpose of the gameplay is to not make you feel angry, frustrated or any other related emotions. The game was built to make you feel relaxed while you play the game, so the gameplay was designed to not overwhelm you with overly complictated actions. Despite that, the game is obviously not hard to play, meaning that many people with different platforming experience could play. However, the game is also not too easy to beat, due to the achievements and overall design, which gives it a bit more flavor and memorable to those who play a lot of platformer games.
Now to the cons; but I have to point out first that these are all in my opinion, meaning that some might not agree with me, but I'm sure that these opinions are ones that most would agree on.
Cons:
- Short Game
I know that the developer intended for this game to be short, but I enjoyed it so much that I want it to expand more. I really dont care on how it could be extended, maybe adding more parts to the one level, or maybe making an entire new level. With its already incredible graphic and soundtrack, its just so sad that you can finish this game so quick and not see the fullness of the game.
- MOAR Content
Now this was something I needed to point out, like I said in the beginning, 'A diamond in the rough'. What it means is when something (or someone) has hidden exceptional characteristics and/or future potential, but currently lacks the final touches that would make them (or it) truly stand out from the crowd. This game is exactly that to me because the developer could add so much more to this game to make it even greater. Now, I'm not saying that it doesn't stand out (Just look at all the positive reviews), but I kind of want more content within the game. Maybe the developer could add some sort of teleporting system, or maybe a bridge mechanic ( These are ideas I'm just throwing from the top of my head). To people who have already played, you might get where I'm coming from, but to the new player or those who are interested in this game. Just play it first and enjoy what its was made for, then you'll get what Im trying to say. Other than that, the game itself is already a masterpiece.
My Verdict of The Game
9/10

I have been a Tales fan since pre-Symphonia times and was very excited when I heard that the newest entry in the Tales series, Zestiria, was going to go back to its classic medieval style. During the first few hours of the game I was absolutely captivated. The world of Zestiria had the classic Tales flair with many Arthurian style elements, but that enthrallment slowly faded away due to the lack of character development and the story plot.
Graphically the game is very beautiful despite being outdated PS3 graphics, and the world and character design are all magnificently executed. I really liked the characters in the beginning but as the game progressed I felt that the personalities they had become static. The story went from being interesting, to painfully predictable. The only thing that really kept me going was the battle system, which had some new wonderful implements, and my love of the Tales series.
My absolute biggest complaint was that I felt that the game was extremely linear due to the lack of side quests compared to that found in other Tales games. The side quests present in the game always felt like they were oddly timed between the few important story quests, and always revolved around optional dungeons. I did enjoy how optional dungeons were peppered into the newly improved world map system, but any quests that involved them were merely “go and fight X here.”
Despite these complaints I would still recommend this game to any Tales fan. It won’t be your favorite Tales game ever, but it’s a solid entry in the series.
