So, Tales of Zestiria. First of all, I'll inform you that I'm a bit of a “Tales of” fan, but with them being scattered across various consoles, I've played only 3 of them before Zestiria: Symphonia, Abyss and Vesperia. Given the background, I'll make some comparisons, but I'll try to stick to the game to itself.
I'll start right away with my overall impression, then if you'll like you can read the details behind my opinion. Tales of Zestiria it's an okay game: it's fun, it has interesting characters, the music is awesome, the battle system is quick paced. However, it's a bit of roller-coaster, with highs and lows, hits and misses; some aspects of the game are too simple, while other are too complicate. I'll stick on a 7,5/10 as a numeric value. If you're a “Tales of” fan, prepare for many changes; if you never played a “Tales of” game, this is a really nice JRPG, that needs some work on some things. In both cases, it will be a good experience!
So, why 7,5? Let's find out
Zestiria is a JRPG, so it's the usual mix of exploration, puzzles and battles, which are in real time: you command directly one of the characters in the party, while the others are guided by the CPU, that follows a series of guidelines customizable by the player. It's basically an action game, quick paced, fast, fun and enjoyable. However, you can still coordinate the attacks of the whole party, giving specific commands if you want to take on the battles with a more strategic approach.
Now, the system has really changed from the previous “Tales of” games: you don't have a mana bar, but rather an action bar, that depletes when you attack or when you dodge, but it refills automatically if you defend or simply stand still. You don't have 'basic attacks' as in the other “Tales of” games, but rather different techniques (Artes) that you can use. Point is, the close combat Artes common to all the characters (the Martial Artes) are 'linear': you can do four attack in a combo before being forced to reset it, but the possibilities are very limited. At the first attack, you'll have to pick one of two specific Martial Artes, at the second one one of four specific Martial Artes and so on; at the second attack you can't pick a Martial Arte that triggers only at the fourth move. And it's a bit of a pain, since every enemy has weakness related to specific attacks. There are ways to break their resistance of course, you are playing with four characters after all so one of them will be able to strike hard the enemy when you can't. But aside from that, the combos you'll be able to create are impersonal and limited: back in Vesperia, it was GORGEUS to see the characters fighting... I made a 300+ hit combo in there! That was SO fun! Zestiria, however, becomes too repetitive too quickly. Of course, you have other types of melee attacks (the Occult Artes) and the classic long range magic attacks (the Seraphic Artes), so there are still possibilities, but still... This battle system feels like a bit of step backwards in order to make new things. They also added lots of battle rules and specific actions that are simply too many: it's nice to improve a fighting system by making it deeper, but I think they got too far. They also added a range of 50 skills bound to your equipments: from them, it comes most of the fighting power your characters will be able to acquire; you'll also be able to fuse equipments to either power up existing skills or making new ones. But even here, it's a bit too much: as I said, 50 skills. You really need a guide to understand how to get the desired result.
In short, they took many risks, some paid off, some didn't. It's still enjoyable, but it feels like they added too much to renovate the system.
The characters are enjoyable; we've seen better in the “Tales of” history, but we've seen worse. Overall, I liked them, some more than the others (Edna, Dezel, Zaveid), but I didn't actually dislike any of them. They're good, they work well. The plot is a bit traditional (chosen hero needs to defeat the big evil guy), but the characters interactions and developments make the story interesting and enjoyable. The game world feels a bit small, compared to other “Tales of”, and it needs more sidequests... But, credit where it's due, they gave you a hint system to tell you where you need to go to trigger the sidequest... In the past, you needed to be at the right place at the right time and they rarely gave you a hint about it.
The music is AWESOME, I really loved it, it pumps you up during the fights and it makes you feel the emotions of the characters.

I see a few negative reviews here, and I feel the need to talk about why you might not like this game.  If you're more interested in going against the narrator...it's not the game for you.  If you need to believe the box you're placed in to begin with, this is not the game for you either.  This is a walking sim and a highly personal story, given a frame mechanic about being about some unknown game developer named Coda.  To me, the conceit is pointedly thin.  The narrator edits games constantly, and if you know games, you know that you don't...really edit other people's games.  This game is about the narrator, and his understanding of himself and his needs.  Coda, and his games, ultimately, don't matter.  And, yes, people who make games do make games like this...pointless little exercises in understanding, so the games Coda makes aren't the realm of a game someone who makes games to make them happy would make, but that doesn't matter.  This game is definitely a game about feelings, that takes you to a very unexpected place.  It's a very...emotional ride, and at least for me, I didn't see where it was taking me.  I knew from moment one that the narrator was to be questioned.  Is Coda a real person?  What's the narrator's real relationship with Coda?  There's a lot of room for interpretation, but one thing can be certain.  There is something wholey and unmistakingly wrong through the who game, and it's the questions that raises, not the gameplay or the conceit itself that are needed.  You don't have to play The Stanley Parable to play this, and honestly, I wonder if having played that game may take away a bit of the impact of this game as you're already at questions with the narrator and its hallways to begin with.  But, this is a, wholy, beautiful game.  Play it alone, when you have an hour to kill, and a little time to reflect.

Hat in Time is one of those rare gems that comes out of nowhere, and is a great example of what crowdfunded games can be when the developers really care about the product. This game spent a grueling 5 years in development, and the undying passion throughout those 5 years from the Gears For Breakfast team really shows. Every chapter a with it's own unique personality, and no two acts feel the same despite the fact that you're usually playing on the same map.
This game is a love letter to 3D platforming from the N64/Gamecube era, right down to having Gamecube controller support (seriously, the number of different controllers I can run on this game without configuration is nutty). In many ways I could imagine being a kid and playing this on an oldschool Nintendo system. The controls are really tight and everything feels great. You start off with a whole bunch of movement options and abilities right off the bat. Wall jumps, double jumps, slides, so I don't see repeat playthroughs being frustrating.
Speaking of gameplay mechanics and options, I'd like to give special attention to how much tech there is in this game's movement. The fact that the devs left in an achievement for sequence breaking should tell you everything you need to know. Whenever I wanted to move fast and freely but needed a certain hat for something, I found myself chaining slides to keep my speed up and the levels, although having linier objectives, are designed in such a way where you're rewarded for finding unique ways around them and exploring. You have one primary objective per act but there are loads of small side objectives you can do, such as finding collectables, secrets, or just fun little easter eggs.
Personality wise, this game oozes with it. The dialogue is always spot on and the voice acting is insanely good. I found myself sitting and listening to all the voice acting, even if it meant slowing down the gameplay to enjoy it. The atmosphere in the levels is always perfect, with the music dynamically changing through a lot of the different environments (oh, by the way the soundtrack to this game is phenominal) to just the game generally creating the atmosphere through the gameplay.
A few downsides I will mention, just because I find myself wanting to look at this game critically so it can be improved upon in later patches. First off, I'm two timepieces away from finishing the game. The current build of the game only has 40 timepieces. By the time I finish the game (which unless something supernatural happens will be tomorrow), I will have only gotten four days worth of gameplay out of it. That's not to say that there isn't more I can do. I have the option of grinding out for the rest of the cosmetic items and remixes, and possibly trying the game again with One Hit Hero mode enabled, but for now, that's it. The devs did say they're planning on adding two bonus chapters later down the line in a free update which should hopefully bring our timepiece total to a cool 60 or so, but for now, this is what we have.
There are quite a few bugs left over in this game. Most of them are minor bugs such as small visual glitches, caused as a result of sequence breaking, or just minor things that got overlooked, but there were a couple of times I got stunlocked, or took several consecutive hits from an enemy all within the same few frames, and one time where I straight up got softlocked. Having said that, since the devs have already promised continued development for this game for a little longer, I expect many of these issues will be patched.
All in all though, I will make a couple of bold claims about this game:
1) It's easily in my top 10 favourite games of all time
2) This game is hands down one of the best single player gaming experiences available on Steam, if not one of the best games on Steam period.

Allow me to be straight, is this the game to resurrect the 3D platformer genre? No. God no. Far from it, it takes much more than a decent game to do that. With hype abound for Mario Odyssey (Myself included on that hype train), we're all excited for any high quality platforming game. So, ill be very straightforward in this review.
A Hat in Time is a wonderfully made 3D platformer, it nails each aspect of a 3D platformer and does it in spades with seemingly minimal effort! This game is simply a joy to play, it recaptured a part of my heart that was lost long ago. Here are the scores.
Gameplay 11/10
Simply a joy to play. The most important part of literally any game is the Gameplay, and the most important aspect of a 3D platformer is the movement. This game nails gameplay with flying colours!! The movement is fluid and becomes second nature! Each time I play this damn game i cant stop running around in circles or finding new areas to explore and find, this game has a few secrets too! It encourages explorative nature, but it also discourages it in a sense (Ill move into that a bit later). You have a group of worlds to explore, this game is HIGHLY derivitive of Mario Sunshine and BanjoKazooie, so much so to its detriment! This game has a severe loss of identity, as it tries too hard in the opening worlds to be like Super Mario Sunshine 2! It tries waaay to hard to be Mario Sunshine, and it really hurts because this game can stand on its own two adorable legs. When you unlock more worlds, you see the identity in this game, this quirky and really ♥♥♥♥ing funny game is a marvel at times!
Music 8/10
Not the worst soundtrack ever, but definitely not the best. Some tracks drone on in the background, while others dont match the mood of the overall world at all. The music is servicable and, in some cases, beautiful, but its nothing stellar. Dont buy THIS games soundtrack unless you really want some upbeat drone to listen to, and NO thats not a bad thing! The music is upbeat and is always pleasant, but it just drones all the time and rarely changes. When it does change, its jarring and not fluid at all in some cases, and fluid and welcome in others! Its hit or miss for me, but when it comes to the quality of the music? Thats where it gets its points from. Each track is good on its own in an isolated environment, but if you listen to it while youre playing the game, it can deliver mixed feelings.
Aesthetic 10/10
Positively marvellous, the careful symbiosis between Graphical style and Gameplay style is struck immediately in this game! No point in the game is odd, even the one actually creepy level i played made wonderful use of the graphical style, making it a very creepy game even with its absolutely adorable art style! Hat Girl is one of the cutest characters made in gaming to date, I say that in full body and mind, me and my friend marathon'd this game over the course of 8 hours (My internet was down during the first 3) and we simply couldnt stop saying "This game is adorable" and where it isnt adorable its just plain pleasant! The mobsters are so damn cute I cant hate them! The ghosts had me saying "awww" al the time! You cant go wrong with this games cartoony and colourful artstyle!
Sound 9/10
For the most part, the nail is hit on the head with voice acting and sound clips, but there is one instance where it feels a bit weird. The primary antagonist in the game, Mustache Girl, her voice is a bit weird to hear coming out of the character. Accents are also something that is a bit weird, but I can easily look passed that. The voice acting is absolutely top notch, one level is set in a spooky forest, and the primary enemy in it is a sinister large ghost who's voice actor has the PERFECT EVIL LAUGH!! And his voice is actually intimidating, so to hear him say all these adorable things and throwing out small cute quips here and there, it successfully makes an endearing character! This game nails that aspect again with flying colours, minus a few characters here and there. Two in particular are a bit annoying, Mustache Girl herself and the Owl in the second world. Other than that, marvellous.
Performance 9/10
I have an Intel Core i-5 2500k processor and an NVIDIA Quadro 1000m graphics processor, its not a bad PC and it gets me by with Indie titles. I had a lot of chug on higher settings but when i bumped all settings aside from character detail down to the lowest itll go, I was perfectly fine throughout the game. Now, depending on your PC, I would say stave off till the console releases, but if you truly cant wait and are sure you can deal with some frame drops here and there, youre fine. It runs very well in most cases, and only struggles during highly taxing scenes. This is MY pc too, I had my Girlfriend test it on hers (She's got a magnificent PC with an i-7 6700k and NVIDIA GTX 1080i on hers), and she had absolutely NO issues throughout the game, only dropping to 30 on some parts and it was only for a second or two.
Verdict 9/10 - 10/10
This game is an absolute marvel, get it on PC and its about a 9/10 but get it on Console and im positive itll be a 10/10. And with updates coming along that add modding support and coop, you will NOT regret your 30 dollar purchase of this game. I didnt go over everything, mainly because I wanted to stave off a few details, but there are a few Ill mention before we wrap things up.
This games primary gimmick is the acquisition of hats, which give special abilities. Hats are limited to each stage you find them in, as in you wont find like the Time-Stop hat in world 2 or anything like that, but you do find yarn to create hats in each and every single world. Now this is cool in concept but I personally have issues with that, as finding Yarn can be difficult at times and♥♥♥♥♥♥easy at others. It makes you reconsider grabbing on piece of yarn over another because that piece is on a tree branch that takes 5 minutes to get to, or you can go get the one frozen in ice with an explosive literally right next to it. Its annoying how hard it is to get 1 single piece of yarn while you can get 5 perfectly fine with NO effort whatsoever in other worlds.
Another small issue is Boss Fights. Some are imaginative and interesting while others are so damn boring. My least favorite thus far was the fight with the primary Ghost Boss. Its visually impressive, yes, but its also incredibly tedious. I dont like how long these boss fights are either, you have 2-3 phases, and well thats good but also thats bad. You'd think 3 hits to get into the next phase, but one boss was like 5 hits while another felt like ♥♥♥♥ing 20! its infuriating to say the least. But, the boss figths arent BORING in any sense of the word, they are all fun and impressive visually, absolutely wonderful on most occasions.
All in All buy this game if youre confident in your PC, if not, I would say wait until you're certain or await its arrival on PS4 and XBONE. You cant go wrong, best 30 dollars Ive spent nearly all year!

RPG Maker VX Ace is the superior means by which to make role-playing games. Traditional RPG design is difficult and confusing, while RPG Maker’s simple and elegant design makes role-playing games easy to create. While traditional design uses clunky, unintuitive programming languages that complicate the process and makes only the most elitist programmers capable of making anything substantial, RPG Maker uses Ruby, which puts user needs first. RPG Maker allows even an unexperienced developer to effectively create a memorable, powerful experience. RPG Maker is better than classic coding in many, many ways.With traditional RPG development techniques, the majority of the difficult work is pure coding, and even the slightest issue can result in hours of searching through confusing code to find a solution, which can lead to further issues if the wrong part of the code is altered. Likewise, even if the correct piece is changed, the repair of one error can lead to further problems should there be multiple times when the code is utilized. However, RPG Maker VX Ace uses a special system where you can generate individual objects, character interactions, player characters, and levels without viewing any code whatsoever. No knowledge of coding is required, as entire games can be built through only scripting and imagination.Of course, programming is still possible, and made easy as well. Clunky, unintuitive programming languages made by and for elitists have been common for quite a long time, yet RPG Maker’s Ruby programming is built to be easy to use, and shares heavy similarities with the English language. Capable of computing addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and even exponents and percents in single lines, Ruby is a simple, powerful way to improve upon a program, such as an RPG video game.
Many developers have proven the powerful potential in RPG Maker, such as Kan Gao from Freebird Games and his games To The Moon and A Bird Story and Mortis Ghost and his game OFF. Each instance is an instance of someone becoming popular and making money thanks to the simple yet powerful elegance of RPG Maker allowing them to create a quality game. They were small names at first, with no major games to boost them ahead, until their RPG Maker games became famous, and they became famous for creating them.
RPG Maker is the simple, elegant way to create quality RPGs with ease. No need to mess with complex, clunky, and unintuitive coding and programming languages. RPG Maker’s superiority is unmatched. While elitists are struggling with complicated code and difficult bug fixing, RPG Maker users can use scripting to utilize their creativity more than code memorization. Ruby programming allows ease in the process of creating occurrences that scripting alone cannot do. Truly, RPG Maker is the superior choice.

Firstly getting into start screen. The start screen is very basic, but it's very well done. It's easy to find the graphic settings, the controls, the co-op, and single player buttons, not to mention the audio itself.
Getting into the actual gameplay, It's amazing. Although the farmer is very annoying, but for what you pay for the game it is really good. The guns are really good, and powerful at low rounds, and as you progress it gets harder to kill the boars. Getting into the days, I think 101 days is a little bit long to play, but if you have the time it's fun, and the characters themselves are great to play as.
The bosses get harder every 10 days which is really challenging and fun. I love the aspect that they can heal so that they don't die so easily, and you have to actually do a lot of hard work to kill them, but the best part of the bosses is the names for the fat pig that's in the middle.
Getting on to the grinder. The grinder is amazing, but it is used for powerups which is also a great addition to the game, and make sit much better to play for something else other than just killing boars that are on steroids, but apart from that stuff that's all there is to the grinder.
Getting on the farmer himself. He is funny, but also annoying. His jokes aren't that great, and could be worked on a little bit, but apart from that the farmer is a great guy. Especially when you shoot him, and he starts getting mad, and eventually throws stuff at you.
Getting on the boars. There is a mix of boar's from small to large, and from skeletons, to bosses, and from boar's to pigs. The game on a whole is amazing, and I love it.
Getting on to the price. The price of the game should be more, because of how fun the game is especially when you play with friends, and have a laugh with them. So I recommend the price should be set atleast at £2.50, and not 0.75. I'm not complaining about it being so cheap, but I think it should be more.
On a whole I would recommend anyone to get this game that enjoys shooter genres, and loves to play co-op with friends.
I would rate this game a 10/10, and that you should buy it if you have a spare £0.79

A Hat in Time is the platonic ideal of joy and fun translated into a series of ones and zeroes.
I backed this project on Kick Starter four years ago. Even with all the disappointments that Kick Starter has delivered, whenever I checked back in on A Hat in Time, I was confident it would turn out great. And yeah, it did.
I think the one thing that makes or breaks any platformer is controls, camera, and movement. If any of those are bad, then the game immediately falls apart, no matter how good the level design, art, or music is. And A Hat in Time controls like a dream. There wasn't ever a single time that I got frustrated while moving Hat Kid around the levels. Every jump, dive, and attack felt incredibly smooth and natural.
And yeah, what you've heard is true. This game has charm coming out of its ears, eyes, nose,♥♥♥♥♥ and toes. Every level has some new delight to share. Subcon Forest is absolutely one of my favorite gaming worlds of all time.
After a 100% run, I only wish there was more. Whether that comes in the form of a sequel, DLC, or fan-made levels, I'm itching to get more!

I personally enjoyed this game a fair bit.
This game was also very fun playing with friends and theory crafting strategies for beating maps we were having trouble on. Figuring out the most effective/efficient tower placements made it quite fun the first time around.
After the initial 50 hours I started to grow quite boring and tedious to do anything and everything.
The journey of getting your first max level character (level 50 at this point in time) is probably the most fun I've had in this game. Getting to max level and grinding out for the best gear you can and then replacing it instantly after climbing to the next Nightmare difficulty becomes less and less rewarding and feels like more of a chore.
With everything I've said, this game is fairly fun for the first 30-50 hours.
In that time you can:
-Learn about the classes
-You can reach max level on a character or two (or 3 if you're really diligent)
-Learn about every map
All the maps are given to you and you can play them all before you ever reach max level.
There is no real reward to reaching max level besides being able to start the Nightmare difficulties which are just a pain the butt and offer nothing new besides identitcal weapons with better overall stats.

The RPG Maker VA engine/software is to be used in various means, for diverse ends and is certainly a high-quality and appropriate software for every users interested in the subject.
I have used RPG Maker XP for 5 years and the release of VX Ace has undoubtably improved the XP engine in every single aspects. Not mentioning the fact that enterbrain had added new functions such as character creation into the software which is meaningfully innovative.
If you are an amateur at RPG creation or an RPG aficionado, this is definitely worth purchasing because if you are willing to invest time into it, it would be at least a fun experience of creation or would be a time-consuming, meaningful and slightly challenging hobby. In my case I have spent months making games with only the simplist element in this software and creating systems with my personal resources. And the software actually let me experience everything about making a game excluding game-engine designing which is too complicated anyway for an amateur like me. This software is intriguing also because the script based on ruby let you explore and develope functions yourself.
If you are truly into developing, have companions and sophisticated crew like artwork and scripting workmates, this is a rather simple but easy, efficient software if you intend to design a 2D/2.5D RPG game without the ability or intention to make the engine yourself. Again, the ruby-based scripting allows you to develope your own features and explore the engine freely within its manageable and quite strong capacity.
The only cons I can think of so far for it is that:
1.It can only design 2/2D-like RPG Games. However, since its name is RM, I doubt one who is planning to make other genres of games would have the interest of reading this.
2.Overpriced, with the same cost you can buy arma 3 and a lot of 3A quality games. However, it's usually 17$ when it's on sale so you can be patient and wait.
I also recommend RPG Maker XP if you would like a more open-source/classic engine. However, you have to fix with scripts/resources to make the graphics,battles and other elements comparable with the improved VA version.
Overall rating 9/10

Hard to review this one, as a fan of the original. Where to begin? Well...let's start off with what I don't like.
The game is quite a bit easier. The maps are visually more interesting to look at and have more full 3D depth to them, which makes them interesting to run around in at times. But each lane is identified for you immediately, and the maps are designed in such a way that you can't have an "aha!" moment as you discover a way to place a single tower to cover multiple choke-points. Either the developer placed the chokepoint for you and pointed you right to it, or the chokepoint doesn't exist. This can help to eliminate the feeling of "trial and error" gameplay that existed in the first game, but it also means you can never feel like you're outsmarting the developer when you find a good way to place your towers.
In some ways, this doesn't necessarily change the final feeling of the game, as in the first one, once you figured it out, you always placed towers in the best spots. I suppose this makes it easier to play the game in public groups or with friends that don't really play video games the same way you do, but it makes all of the maps feel a little samey after awhile, because you never get to experience that first moment of wonder as you treat the map like a puzzle to be solved.
The pricing of the cosmetic items is...quite high. I find myself learning to enjoy the default skins, since purchasing the outfits i'd like would quickly put this game at a higher price than an off the shelf, AAA title. I don't have a problem with the microtransactions themselves, I think it'd just be nicer if they were a little more "micro" so I could get a few skins and not feel like i'm getting robbed.
Now on to what's been improved!
The new hero-deck system will (eventually) prevent a single player from effectively filling every role. Playing with friends in the first game could be quite difficult at times, because you were capable of leveling up and gearing out the entire cast, and placing every tower type. Your friends could quickly outgrow you, and if you didn't play a ranger or barbarian, there was little reason for you to be in the game with such a person, since their towers would be better than what you could make. Being limited to a certain number of heroes encourages you to work together - once there are more hero types than there are deck slots, you'll need at least two players to do everything. It's forced co-op sure, but at least you can always be useful to your friends, since you can bring something that they cannot.
The way they introduce new unit types as mini-bosses feels good. Later maps and harder difficulties can repeatedly spawn mini-boss versions of these enemies too. Since there are a lot of things that can define an enemy (such as movement speed, walking or flying, special attacks, resistances), they keep your defenses in check and ensure that everyone has something to contribute. Defenses and your attentiveness get tested as each lane fights to divert your attention across the map. The new, proper bosses feel a lot more interesting than all of the bosses from the first game, too. They have mechanics that make them more than a "bullet sponge", and it was an excellent move making them a bit of an outside force that interacts with the map and the waves in interesting ways, instead of just being placed awkwardly and requiring that you blindly hit it with regular attacks and awkwardly placed towers.
The aesthetics of the game are sweet. Everything is much nicer to look at.
I think my biggest complaint is that I just wish the game was harder. Not in a "just make the numbers bigger" way, but that the maps were actually more interesting to play. It feels like the entire campaign is a tutorial to get you acclimated to the games mechanics. The maps never seem to get nearly as complex or interesting as they were in the first game....The revisited maps in 'the harbinger awakens' content update come closer and are definitely more fun than the maps that came before it, which gives me hope for the future. You really can't go wrong with "free" though, and I can see myself losing a few more evenings as I continue to play this with my fiancée. But ultimately, I don't think either of us will be sinking dozens or even hundreds of hours into it like we did the first time around.

I grew up playing this game, so take this review how you want.
Currently running it on a 32bit Potato and it runs smooth as butter just as, if not better than it did originally.
They have upped the resolutions to fit more modern 64bit machines, though i have witnessed a small issue when booting it up for some on such machines. A problem easily bypassed by setting compatibility to wXPsp2 much like most games from that era on modern machines.
The online community is still there all be it small they are just as fun and ferocious.
However, I don't play this to play online, i play it on LAN with my mates for 'retro' *shudder* lan party pissups and the experience reigns true to back in the day right down to the high pitched squeels people make when you run up to them with the Impact Hammer >:)
The maps and game modes are a true gem of this game.
The Maps are well balanced, exceptionally well designed and flow fantastically and a true testiment to the tallent behind it. The Game modes and Mutators keep it fresh even today. Getting bored? INSTAGIB FACING WORLDS BIIIISH
Not to mention the music, ooohhh the music. (DM-Gothic wins)
As far as LAN play goes, you will have to 'set up' a dedicated server on some ones PC that runs in the background.
It unsurprisingly, has little to no hit to CPU power, even in large populated games.
Which brings me to the UUUUUUUUGE catalog of amazing mods.
Due to the sheer amount of them i will name two of my favourites:
CHAOS UT: adds mele weapons like battle axes and really mixes up the game.
Matrix Mod: Adds wall running and Bullet time (i don't recommend the latter option)
The core gameplay is as fun as it was on release day with the added bonus of some mods that fix some niggling issues some might have.
I can't recommend this game any higher than I do. It is truly a piece of gaming history that still holds up.

This game reminds me a little bit of Alien Isolation, getting supressed is terrifying at first and slows the game down very much for you unless you figure out some way to flank, much like how the aliens and androids are creepy and terrifying at first. But after a long while, it gets annoying because you don't know where to go, you constantly die or get shot at, always pinned to a wall or something and you're just at maximum tilt. Assuming you've logged several hours into the game though, you can snipe MGs with ease which isn't much like Alien Isolation since you can't really kill the aliens or androids (Well you can kill androids, but that pretty much ruins your stealth.) Uhhh, anyway...

Well, is it a good game? Yes.
Is it fun? Mostly yes.
Is it realistic? Kind of. The damage models seem realistic, bullets penetrate the skin, break bones and cause bleeding. If you're into that, great. Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm also have great gore if you're into that, I know I am.
Speaking of gore, the voice acting for when people die? I never thought sound could play such a huge role in selling the experience, I found myself getting more immersed from battle chatter and gunfire than from the plastic textures of the Unreal Engine.
There's also tanks in this game by the way, and I'm not sure if any other games do it like the Red Orchestra series which is a huge shame because I LOVE IT SO MUCH. The damage models aren't exactly true to life, but who cares, you have fully modeled tank interiors, realistic enough damage models, the tanks seem balanced, honestly, I have few complaints about them other than when you get stuck on a surface you shouldn't be on, backing up does more harm than good.
I guess that's all I really have to say for this review then, go buy Red Orchestra 2.

"Fahrenheit: Quick Time Event Prophecy"
In Summary:
I am played this on SteamOS and it's a mixed feeling overall. You can't fault the game for being how it was designed years ago. I think Aspyr did a great job on polishing up the graphics for what they were (High Definition != High Detail!!!).  The sound seems to crackle a little in-game, noticeable in cutscenes or the main menu. The game has a great and weird story to it. The one thing that kills me, is the "DDR-Like" button quick time events. These use the Joystick, and if you know your Linux, Xbox 360 controllers can be hit or miss depending on the implementation. During the ...SPOILERS?......"Office Survival" QTE sequence, I was extremely frustrated do the the Xbox 360 controller's tendency to fling its resting "center" to the far right, which made some QTE actions register wrong. And when this sequence is as fast paced and forgiving as this one, it makes you angry. Play this one using a PS3 controller (USB or Bluetooth). You'll thank me later.
Pros:
Overall the game has a nice opening, and a very nice detective feel to it. The soundtrack is very good and the characters do get their fair bit of attention each in the character development department. The "mood" meter is a nice addition to the gameplay, and it forces you to carefully evaluation your actions and responses to conversations. The character models are ok, given the time this came out, and the games budget at that time of it's original release.
Cons:
The quick time event system is frustrating as can be. I soon lamented every "Get Ready" moment, especially when the game was unforgiving enough not to allow me collect enough "lives" to live through the tougher parts of the game (which I beat with one life..oi vey). Seriously, if you cannot tolerate QTE's whatsoever, this game will drive you mad. Furthermore, clunky movements, accelerated by the very odd "action" system (where in you push the joystick to do things), make it even worse. Many times, the center positioning of my gamepad lost it's way, forcing me to switch to a PS3 controller from an Xbox 360, due to the better axis precision. No other game I own on SteamOS / Linux / Windows does this.
The graphics were polished up decently enough for what the original game was, but there could have been more done. This is likely understandable given the team's budget. The story near the end takes a very odd turn, with some of the dialogue leaving you quite confused.
This remaster is most certainly for fans of the original, and it definitely teeters on the edge of Yes/No for a recommendation here. I'd say, if you can stomach the QTE's and wonky controls, give it  try.

A very simple horror game. You play as a security guard at, Freddy's. Sort of like a Chuck Cheese type place here in the states.  But, you're told that these animitronics move around at night. And guess what, they want to kill you!  For some reason they want to stuff you into a spare animitronic suit, thus killing you in the process.  Well your goal in this game is to survive till 6am.  So you need to keep an eye on the cameras and listen for them walking around the hallways.  But, there's a catch, you have a limited power supply. So veiwing the security cameras, turning on the lights on the hallways, and closing the metal doors at your office to stop them from killing you uses power. So you need to use your power wisely, if you want to live till 6am.
I played this over a friend's for hours, taking turns trying to survive. Also getting some jump scares in the process =P. made it to day 5 so far. Each day its gets harder and random so you need to really keep looking around. Each animatronic character Freddy, Chica, Bonnie, and Foxy have different patterns, so get to know them quick =).  Perfect for playing on a couch pc type setting too. With a wireless mouse and on a big screen TV and sound system. Oh jeez be prepared for a scare!
It's a single player game but, you can take turns trying to survive with friends. So play at night, turn off the lights, raise the volume a little bit and get ready for a scare.  You only need a mouse to control the game, by looking around, using the camera  and clicking some buttons in your office. Well worth the $4.99  If you see this on sale for lower its a steal bascially.

Fun fact: I played this game way back in the day when it originally came out on the PS2. Back then I knew it as “Indigo Prophecy”, and my teenage self was intrigued by its emphasis on cinematics and interactive storytelling, so I rented it for a weekend. I didn’t finish it during that rental period, and needless to say, I didn’t rent it a second time. The game’s story was just too weird. I think it was about the time that the main character began developing superpowers that I decided to let Blockbuster keep this one. So, ten years later and here I am playing this game again. Ten years older, ten years wiser… I’ve aged pretty well. Can the same be said for Fahrenheit?
The game gets off to a bad start when I’m greeted by French menus. This isn’t a big deal, but it’s a weird, lazy oversight, and it sets the tone for what’s to come. It’s especially weird considering this is supposed to be the “definitive” remastered edition of the game, but it just ends up feeling like a lazy port of a previous PC release. It does feature some updated textures for the new HD resolutions, but I honestly could barely tell any difference. Also, in another weird, lazy oversight, the game mode that features HD textures is actually the one with the old, low-res text and menus. I don’t know how the developers in charge of the port messed that one up. Anyway, after switching to English, I’m quickly reminded of director David Cage’s quest to create “interactive film” when, instead of “New Game” being an option on the main menu, there’s instead the option for “New Movie”. This, coupled with the game’s tutorial consisting of an in-game, low-poly version of Cage himself in a virtual movie set “directing” me, the player, through the game’s controls and promising a world where “anything can happen” creates an annoyingly pretentious vibe. Why must Cage remind me at every turn that this is an interactive movie? Can’t the product just speak for itself? Shouldn’t a game, or an interactive story, or whatever you choose to call it stand on its own as an experience instead of relying on the strengths of another medium?
I have to admit that I do like the game’s engine and core gameplay, though. Quantic Dream came up with a pretty good control scheme and game mechanics for a title focused on storytelling. Interacting with the environment and selecting dialogue choices is all done with the right stick or the mouse pointer, which is both intuitive and immersive. Holding left to slide open a closet door to the left, for instance, feels natural, and actions that require holding a direction longer, like turning on a light, do a good job of putting the player in the character’s shoes. It’s simple, but it works. With this engine you could conceivably tell any film-like story interactively, with quick-time events provided for action sequences or scenes in which characters must exert themselves physically. The characters are also all well-animated due to extensive motion capture, and are generally well-voice acted. David Gasman in particular gives a grounded, believable performance as main character Lucas, which is actually saying a lot given the ridiculous material.
That’s really where the problem lies. Despite the game functioning fairly well and providing a good system for telling an interactive story, the story itself is, ironically, the game’s downfall. It’s just poorly conceived. Cage is ok with dialogue and basic character emotions and relationships, but for some reason he isn’t content with just telling character driven stories. Fahrenheit is full of supernatural nonsense that only serves to alienate the player from any connection they might have felt to the characters. Full disclosure: I still haven’t finished the game, even after writing this review. I honestly can’t bring myself to; it’s such an unenjoyable experience. As a kid I stopped when Lucas developed superpowers; this time I couldn’t make it past the giant termites. I wish I were making that sentence up. Every now and then I will indeed feel as though I’m in the shoes of a character, making dramatic decisions with consequence in the film of their lives. I like the scene where Lucas’s estranged brother Markus gives him a call. It’s legitimately dramatic and interesting, and then it’s immediately ruined when Lucas tries to explain that he only committed a murder because of some magic mumbo jumbo. I instantly stopped caring. The vast majority of the time spent playing Fahrenheit feels like this; it feels like playing a stupid video game.  A poorly written one that takes itself too seriously and comes across as pretentious for it. I find this quote from Cage extremely ironic and extremely telling:
“During development, I discovered that this everyday facet of the characters was in fact the most interesting aspect of the game—much more than the supernatural side.”
Why couldn’t the game have just been full of moments like this, like the phone call between brothers who haven’t seen each other in years? Simple, relatable moments between real people with real problems.
Because of this I can’t really recommend Fahrenheit, even to fans of the adventure genre, except as maybe a historical curiosity. In the end, Fahrenheit is an admittedly ambitious, but extremely flawed and ultimately unenjoyable experience. It is interesting to see some of the strides it made, and its lineage can indeed be seen in modern adventure games like The Walking Dead, but in a genre that’s all about storytelling, and with a story as uneven and poorly-executed as this one, you may as well just watch a real movie instead of this cheap virtual knock-off. Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy Remastered is the pretentious poeticals of a college freshman.

is an important title. It is also a flawed title. It amazes and induces deep catharsis at its best, and removes you from the experience at its worst, but regardless, it is an important title. Leto Atreides II has written an excellent criticism of its failings, but I disagree with a few of those. I still contend that
is daring in ways that
wasn't.
At its heart, this is a very different game from
. Where the latter game is, in my mind, a heady critique of the illusion of player agency and artificial "freedom,"
seems more concerned with delving into the
of creation, rather than the creation itself, and in turn the true "ownership" of that creation once it leaves its author's hands.
The author, in this case, is the enigmatic "Coda," and is also the game's primary concern. Wreden plays a fictionalized version of himself, acting as your guide through Coda's many odd and striking interactive pieces. What initially offput me was the frequency with which Wreden interjected to present his own interpretations of the events on screen, even going as far as to change aspects of the game for the player's convenience - tearing down walls and bypassing labyrinths, speeding you through sections that weren't meant to be sped through and even, as you learn in an enormous revelation toward the end of the game,
. To a certain extent, it felt to me like Wreden was violating these personal spaces of Coda's without any means for him/her to object; there was something dirty about the whole thing. And it's those moments and revelations in which
truly becomes important, as a visceral, personal plea to consider the human behind the games. It's a piece which cannot be appreciated in a single playthrough; going back through with full knowledge of those revelations is essential to understanding Wreden as a character, and even as an artist himself.
Like any work,
is not without its flaws. There are certainly red herrings and curiousities strewn about several of the games which ultimately lead to nothing, and the game's linearity hampers the pace in several of the more open sections. There are also a few games that seem to be leading toward an idea, but ultimately fall short (then, perhaps that's the point?) There are a few more minor gripes, but they're largely overshadowed by the fantastic ideas at play.
Some will not connect with this game. Some will inevitably compare it to
and dismiss it for being so linear. Those are perfectly valid opinions. But if the discussion generated here is any indication, its release is certainly vital in some respect.
I still think frequently about what I experienced in this game. I find myself coming back to the themes and my own reactions to them again and again, and it feels as though something in me has been moved profoundly. That, to me, is the mark of great art.

This is a simple, silly little game that I picked up late friday night, just to play something while I watched some videos on my other monitor. I picked this game since its fast to download (300mb) , looked like a game that I could easily get into and the price is almost nothing.
The graphics are old-looking, but in my opinion kinda charming. If you just want a little bit of fun alone or with friends ( yes, it has co-op) then by all means pick this up. Just don't expect to much in terms of graphics or story. Blood and bacon does have 100+ levels though, so gameplay-wise it actually have a lot of content for the asking price.

As I do not do numbers, nor can I compare this game to others in the franchise (having not played many of them), I will provide a list of facts (from personal experience) and then some personal opinions.
Firstly, anything blanked out spoils the story and not the gameplay. As this is a JRPG, the story is the motivation for the gameplay. The story starts out simple and cliche, focusing on helping Angels fight off a Ever-Present-Evil and Monster Army, but it does develop into something more. However, the story tends to leave lingering sentiments that left me unfulfilled. Constant vagueness and intentional crypic nonsense from certain characters wore thin quickly, and the jokes character makes regarding such defuse anything potentially dramatic. Questions are posed, and then left either lingering or are simply taken as is despite whatever notion of doubt I felt or saw in characters.
Without spoiling directly, the game's story attempts to subvert cliche by being vague (for reasons that make sense in the game) and while I could understand why they acted in such a way, it was not entertaining.
There is a distinct emotional wall between characters, and the situation this creates in this universe may be lost on people without heavy RPG context.
I recommend this game for its combat, which is simple enough to get into and there are complexities to master. But such complexities aren't needed to complete the game. The game is made in such a way that battles can be made more difficult to satisfy needs for challenge. Equipment is not hard to gain, but does take time. You're never expected to invest more than you wish to in gaining said equipment.
The story has strong characters, though I have mixed feelings about the story. With a game like this, it comes down to personal opinion. That in itself is worth reccomending, if you are willing to think deeply about what is typically taken for granted or ignored in games regarding religion and long-lived beings like elves.

I can recomend this game, but it does have a few issues.  Most of the other reviews explain what is great about this game very well.
I feel these issues hurt the game-feel and break immersion.  Hopefully this could help people determine wheather this game is still worth it to them.  My biggest gripes with this game are down to the
The environments are terribly bland in most areas.  The ground and wall textures are very low resolution most of the time apart from the stone floors of ruins, which have designs and patterns on them.  The character models look great it's just a shame the rest of the world doesn't.  The lack of any foliage and loosely scattered trees was very unexpected coming from a ps4 game.  It would have made the world feel a lot more vibrant even with some more general foliage.
The animations of monsters outside and (sometimes) inside of battle a very abrupt.  Landing a preemtive strike was nearly impossible for me the first 20 hours of the game until I got used to the jerky animations.  If your playing ToZ vanilla at 30 fps, it can be pretty hard to predict enemy movements in battle.  This is an essencial part of the gameplay mechanics since dodging and blocking at the right moment gives you huge benifits in battle.  Plus playing at 30 fps can be really diffcult since you have even less time to react to the very fast enemy attacks.
I enjoyed interacting with the various party members and listening to their mediocre (but punny dialogue).  On the other hand the gameworld itself has very few ways you can interact with it.  Most of the interactable objects throughout the world will be question marks, (???) these are 4 abilities you gain later in the game that help you progress past whatever obstacle was in your way.  Besides talking to people this is your only way to interact with the world.  This system reminds me of a metroidvania style game but very, VERY, poorly done.   Press a direction on the d-pad, and you've solved the puzzle.
Sorry for the little rant, just though it would be important for people to understand some of the issues with this game, although I would recommend it for its combat.

The Beginner's Guide is a two hour walking introspection. It's not a walking simulator, it's a story. It's a very deep and very personal story about...a lot. A lot of what is human and can only be caused by human self-awareness.

Some people say this should be free, or a film, rahter than a 'game' or you should just watch it on youtube and if you can't buy it, do so.
It's funny, really. I don't think this ... story could've existed anything other than presented as a game. You can watch a film, but you can't walk
a film. You can't experience the virtual space of someone's imagination the very same way. And what's more this story is not about you. It's not about making you a hero, or feel important or good even.  But, it'll make you feel.

I almost pirated it. I almost did. I wanted this software for a particularly long time. I always did love RPGs; and I always loved game design, so when someone told me the same line of software used to make games like Yume Nikki, Five Nights at ♥♥♥♥boy's, OFF, Barbeque Quest among many other great RPGs was in circulation; I lost my♥♥♥♥♥♥with excitement.
The price label is high, but the reward is worth it. I worked in RPGMaker 2003 before this, let me tell you, moving to RPGMVXA was the greatest single decision I've made. It's far superior, and that's to be expected I guess.
I love VXA. It's simple at first with a learning curve that's reasonable, fast and easy to adapt to. With any RPGMaker program, in my opinion it's really fun to work in due to how simple or complex you can make things. It's perfectly adaptable to certain people's programming and learning styles. I haven't completed any major projects with it; but it's a load of fun, even when you're physically coding in Ruby.
Now on that whole "VXA vs. XP" debate; personally while VXA isn't perfect by any stretch of the imagination, personally I prefer using it over XP. I don't know what it is about it, there's just something I like more about it. Really though the XP vs. VXA debate is personal prefrence, I own both so it doesn't really matter in my case, but I don't use it enough to really tell you much about it; and they are very similar so I guess it's a matter of what style of games you're looking to make.
Is it better than 2003? Yes. Is it better than XP?... Well I'll leave that up to you. All I can say is, RPGMaker VX is well worth your money, your time and your ability. It's just as the labels tell you, simple enough for a child, powerful enough for a professional.
If you're absolutely sure you want to go into RPG game design, get RPGMakerVX, it's great, it really is.

I'm so glad I have this game a try. It manages to scratch my spaceship combat itch without being either P2W or overly gridny. It has differnt ship classes with interesting abilities, you can design your own ship using blocks, armor, random components and weapons, components that you need to chose and protect, abilities bound to some of those components. Battleships can even warp into the center of a few enemies with guns blazing, Battle Star Galactica style.
Like every early access game, it's got its flaws. Although balance isnt great, it can seem like a real game breaker to someone who just picked up the game. The rookie ship is almost useless when it has to fight a sniper that can insta gib you from 5km out, or a battleship with a shield and almost 10x your dps.
You have to be smart with your moves and know how to armor a vehicle effectively, or you will be easy pickings for the next guy.
I dont think MM is that big of a deal. The game is unfair, but the randomness of battle is kind of fun. Not everyone can be rambo all the time and there is some satisfaction in out smarting and killing a ship 3x your size.
The ship classes and some weapons could use a pass, though. The 5km sniper with almost hitscan accuracy is a little OP, give it a slower projectile and make it cost more to fire. Other than the sniper, the Battleship is the ususal end all. You can make the other classes work if you like the abilites, but the Battleships shield blocks +20% of income damage and does nothing to its own weapons damage. This means load up with batteries and generators, pop the shield and be an invincible gunship.
On the technical side, the sounds and graphics arent the best. There is no noise for getting hit, so you wont know if someone is pounding on your rear till  its too late. Graphics could use a pass, but it is good for the games current state. Controll and graphic settings are bare bones and there is no mouse sensitivity settings, but thats not a game breaker.
All in all, I am very happy with this game. If the devs give it a balance pass and dont make it pay to win, then they have a solid game right here.
Good luck, pilots. And remember, teamwork is OP.

Charming. Technically tower defense but not really. Hack-n-slash and pew pew game that takes almost no skill at all. Farm endlessly for no reason because there's literally nothing else to do.
No real strategy. Basically block off every path and prevent the mobs from getting through. Have good gear = win. Not having good gear actually makes it fun and challenging but the fun doesn't last all that long.
There's essentially one only one way to play each of the 4 characters. There is no depth to this game at all.
High level play, like level 30+, devolves to players swapping their high level characters in to place OP towers and afk every round. Bugged flying mobs are the only thing keeping people active because it slows down the farmfest. Beyond level 40 the game begins to feel nearly dead. Probably because people with half a brain don't keep playing hoping it gets more interesting like I did. There are barely any players to play with aside from the farmers. Once you find a farmer, you can afk and go do something better with your time. Literally anything.
You constantly replace gear because this game is all about ascending and descending in power. Take a few zeros off the numbers and check it out! It's as if you're still level 10! The difference is maybe your weapon looks cooler and your gear icons glow and have colorful borders.
The gear you are constantly replacing isn't shown on your character. The character goes from derp to Spartan warrior at the click of a button.
It's charming and could be cool but deep down, just like The Mighty Quest for Epic Loot, it's garbage and will be until time erases it.

A thrilling game with an engaging story that puts you at the wheel of unraveling its secrets. It's been a while since horror fans have been treated to anything of this caliber, and it's quite refreshing.
Much like in Amnesia: the Dark Descent, the game instills an immersive sense of helplessness by limiting the player's combat options to just two things: running and hiding. I don't want to give out spoilers, so I won't mention how, but they take this player-disempowerment model to a devious new level in one particular chapter. And don't worry--the brilliant level design makes sure to prey on all kinds of phobias--so if the nail-biting hide-and-seek moments don't get you, something else will.
A welcome break from the stiff, inflexible protagonists of other games, it's movement interface also provides the player with a great deal of useful mobility such as climbing, vaulting, sidling, and--most importantly--a decent sprint. Despite all of that, it still manages to remain believable by not having the character do anything unrealistic. (I don't know about other people, but I was getting tired of games where you had to play as someone who couldn't even figure out how to get over an obstacle at waist height!) Oh, and for what little spoken dialogue there is, I feel compelled to mention how well the voice acting was done; this game easily beats out the Dead Space series in it's ability to get me to really imagine the character's pain as he's being tormented.
Anyway, there's always more to say about it, so I'll try to keep it short. This game was really, really incredible, and I definitely plan to get my hands on the DLC some time soon.

One of the most humbling games I have ever played. If you played CoD when it was fun (CoD 1-4) and are considering buying this game, be prepared for a shock. This game takes the realism and immersion of sims like Arma, but keeps you in the action by taking out the parts in Arma where you trek for miles with no idea where the enemy or your squad is, and focuses more on the action. Remember how in CoD your character, even on veteran, could soak up bullets like a sponge, red jelly seemingly leaking out of his eyeballs, then duck behind cover and "squeeze" out the damage he had taken moments before? Forget that. Forget the crosshair in the middle of your screen. Forget when you would pick up a PPSH in CoD 2, fire off the entire magazine at the same target with nary a spot of recoil to be seen. Forget the ability of your character to sprint through an artillery barrage, dash across a field while being sprayed with MG-42 fire, and take out a tank singehandedly with nothing but your trusty TNT without even flinching. Try anything of the sort in this game, and, assuming you aren't instantly torn apart, your screen's color will drain away, your heart will be pounding, and you will find aiming immpossible. And I don't mean just in the game.
Each side, Axis and Allies, has its own strengths and weaknesses (although the Wermacht has few of the latter). Playing as the Soviet Union, unless you manage to snag one of the few special classes, such as sniper or commander, quickly turns into a meat-grinder experience, just as it would have been in real life. Playing as a rifleman, for example, will give you a Moison-Nagant 1895, two grenades and a life expectancy of about 30 seconds. You will charge across a field to a capture point which appears to be empty, and moments later a machine gun you never saw will open up from a window you forgot to check, or from behind a wall you passed without waiting for your team-mates to cover, and your brief, often pointless life will be over, as your squad members are often cut down around your darkening vision. Often a game spent as one of the more aggresive classes will turn in three steps: Spawn, die, repeat. Sometimes you will die without firing a shot.
This may sound dull, painful, or frustrating. In your first online match you may not get more than one kill. The learning curve in this game is quite steep, and this discourages many people. But eventually you will begin to learn the quirks, tricks, and rewards of each class. If you are patient, cautious, and lucky, just as the real veterans of the battle of Stalingrad had to be, and you will improve. Your name will move up the scoreboard, and you will begin to reap the rewards of the time you invest a hundred times over. This is when the game becomes the most fun. You will unlock bayonets, scopes, and new guns, and your player model will begin to show the wear and tear of surviving the battles, with medals, extra ammo and camo.
All in all, probably my favorite shooter of all time. The community is mature, and welcoming to new players. Stay away from the single player mode, and don't try the tank combat, and you will grow to love this beautiful, grim, and challenging video game.

This is one of the best survival horror games I've played in a very long time. It truly deserves the label "survival horror." You don't shoot a weapon a single time in this game - stealth and hiding is the name of the game. If you've played Amnesia you know a bit of what to expect in that regard. However, I honestly enjoyed this game much more than Amnesia. The story actually makes total sense in this game right from the beginning, something I can't say for other survival horror games (I'm looking at you, Amnesia... and Dead Space). The puzzles are also much more straightforward and less headache-inducing.
Everything in Outlast, from the gameplay mechanics, voice acting, visuals, etc. is just superbly well-done. One key highlight of the game is the incredibly immersive environmental sound design. It always dynamically changes to suit the current mood of the player's situation, and the quality of the sound is incredible. This is a good thing too, because unlike many games out there these days, Outlast does not give you a radar or minimap that shows you if an enemy is nearby or coming after you. You have to rely entirely on the sounds around you to assess your situation.
Another area in which Outlast excels is in how it tells its story. There are hardly any cutscenes in the game. Instead, most of the storytelling is done just as it accomplished in classic Resident Evil games, through notes and journals discovered in the environment. This is the best way to tell a story in this type of game, in my opinion, as it feels totally natural to search for clues in this type of mysterious, scary setting.
The only real drawbacks I can fault the game for are a few minor things. The first is the "closing door behind you" mechanic; often the game will tell you to press Left Click if you want to close the door in front of you, but when you do, nothing actually happens. This caused my death a few times throughout the game. It was only occasionally that I was actually able to close a door behind me to prevent a chasing inmate from catching me, all because the game refused to register my click. Another flaw of the game is the repetitiveness of the inmate character models. They generally start to look all the same after a while. This isn't a huge problem however since most of the time, you're supposed to be keeping your distance from them and not actually see them upclose.
I highly recommend Outlast to anyone who enjoyed classic Resident Evil games (1-3 + Code Veronica), and anyone who likes TRUE survival horror games in general. Picture this; you're walking into a supposed empty mental assylum that was used when Hitler was in power, not scary yet? Okay, you're walking and walking and then you see what looks like a man in a wheelchair..MOVING. But this place is supposed to be empty right? Except for that big fat guy who beheads you everytime he sees you. But the part that really affects you is you have no defense; no weapons, no hit button, nothing. Why? Because you're just a poor rookie journalist who was stuck with this assignment not knowing it might be the end of the line. The Total War series is a perfect blend of Real-Time Strategy and Time-Based Strategy.
The campaign map comprises of the entire european map (In this case as plenty of other Total War Titles have varying maps) that is turn-based. You manage your empire by constructing buildings, manage your economy, establish trade routes, research technologies, build armies, and, as the title suggests, Declare war on other nations for land. It is chock full of many ways you can go about managing the nation you pick from the selection screen. And yet, with all these things I have described about the campaign map. The games bread and butter is the battles. So how did they go about that?
The battles are a real-time map that give you a more detailed look on what your armies are doing when they are locked into conflict with their enemy. You place your troops, start the battle, and plan your way to victory on the battlefield. It is very simplistic in concept, yet complicated in execution. There is a huge learning curve that you have to bypass, but once you do, it can be either very relaxing, or mind challenging. Depends on the scale of the battle you engage in.
Before Napoleon Total War came out, multiplayer was a tacked on feature that was rather dissapointing. Sure it was fun to play battles with your friends and engage a player in a battle of wits, but a campaign coop mode was sorely lacking. Thankfully Napoleon Total War fixes this. It added a campaign coop feature where you and a friend can either dominate the world together, or be at each others throats in an almost never ending conflict. There are plenty of things wrong with the Coop campaign that irritate me. Dsych problems along with many exploits that can feel... cheaty. Overall it's a nice tacked on feature. Just wished they expanded on it further than they have.
In conclusion, Napoleon Total War is one of the most tactical Total Wars I have played, but it's far from the best. Its got its bugs here and there, but they are mostly patched.
My recommendation in playing this game, if you decide to buy it, is to install Darthmod with the game. It makes the AI smarter in the sense that they use tactics instead of bum rush you, and it overhauls the audios and visuals of the game with new musket sounds, smoke effects, blood (that you don't have to pay money for btw) and drums and fifes. It is a must have that is simple to install and easy to set up. I will post the link to the mod after my final score.
One other thing must be addressed. For newcomers in the Total War franchise who bought this game as their first Total War. Please take a look at this guide, that I will link after the mod, that will teach you all you need to know about battles and how to effectively fight them.
The final score for this game is an 8/10. One of the better Total Wars I have played. I recommend getting the game at the price it's at right now, as it's cheap and worth it, but for the dlc it is better to wait until it goes on sale. Some may argue that they are worth the price, but I feel it is a bit much to pay just to get extra units.

This game is truly amazing. Spend hours and hours of your life exploring a huge map, full of notable locations such as the Lost Island (an island based of the show Lost, there's a hatch, a smoke monster, and when you encounter the island by boat or plane, your ride crashes!), there's the Mile High Club (strip club a mile in the air), and the chaos filled Districts!
The first two missions are good for you to get to know the game. You can adjust the key and mouse settings to your liking, and it suits hardcore-casual gamers.
In free roam, after the first two missions, you can explore Panau. Cause chaos, massive explosions, and try to complete village's by causing chaos and finding resource items. If you wish to challenge yourself, try and complete military bases, military harbours, military airports, communication outposts, and more! Completeing areas earns you money, so you can buy things from the black market, including a series of weapons (including a rocket launcher, triggered explosives and a sniper, all for a reasonable price, as long as you work hard!) and vehicles (including jets with machine guns, boats with machine guns, and of course le' Tuk-Tuk Boom Boom).
You can at any time take a mission, which includes Military Strongholds, where you take over military bases while fighting off soldiers, trucks and helicopters. When taken over, you unlock Faction Missions where you are assained to kill traitors, steal cars, deliver people and trucks to your faction to increase the influence on the region, and help take back Panau!
You can also take Agency Missions, which are longer than Faction missions. Agency missions progress the story, and are quite fun.
With amazing graphics, an EXTREMELY reasonable price, a huge map, explosions and fantastic guns and vehicles, what more could you want?

Overall, not a bad game if you're a Tales' fan.  I've played a few in the past, and will just say that this one kept me entertained but didn't knock my socks off. As to some of the other reviews I’m reading on here, I personally really like the equipment customization/fusion aspect of the game.  It gives some breadth and actually easily allows you to manipulate your fighting style should you get bored (not that having 6 characters to choose from doesn’t allow that).
I also didn’t really ever have trouble with the camera as a lot of people are saying.  The combat system was very refreshing, and as someone who loves grinding it didn’t feel like I had to do much, if any, for the game given how much the equipment customization affects you and the regenerating stat herb items that can be found EVERYWHERE.  However, by the end of the game I found myself just fast –traveling and using enemy-repellant holy bottles when I was running around in the fields.
As for the insane amount of goofy, irrelevant cut scenes that come along with Tales’ games, at a certain point, puns become annoying.  There are other comedic devices you can use.
Which leads me to my biggest con of the game, the story/continuity…
Coming in, I'd expected (Knowing Tales’ games) the story to be convoluted and not make sense at various points.  I was not disappointed. Of the various times I asked myself “What’s going on here?”,  I will say that by the end of the game the story as a whole seems to make sense.  It’s indulging the writers to get there that’s tough.  The game is filled with so many holes and unresolved plot events that ruin continuity I can’t begin to go into them all. But the biggest, most massive, undeniably huge one is its basic premise (semi-spoiler)…
To not overcomplicate things with specifics, there’s 3 types of characters in the game: Humans, Seraphim, and Hellions.  Essentially, the story goes that Humans (minus our protagonist Sorey and company) are unenlightened, ungrateful, hate-producing low-lifes that normally can’t see Seraphim and Hellions.  Seraphim are enlightened, elementally powered spirit beings who live amongst humans.  Hellions are evil/corrupted humans and seraphim.   To try not go into a long diatribe with specifics on just how many times the game contradicts this most fundamental law it sets up for itself (It’s literally laughable), it is single-handedly the biggest issue I have with the game as it totally screws with continuity and any sane person trying to relate to the story would think that Sorey isn’t some sort of savior, but a bat$hit crazy person that talks to ghosts.  For instance, when he is conversing with secondary characters AND having conversations within their core group, wouldn’t it seem like he is talking to the air or that there are insanely long awkward pauses while our seraphim are discussing amongst themselves?
I’ll also say that character development is pretty flat throughout the game.  Barring the major event to set up the game’s ending, nothing really happens to change any of the characters’ outlook or core values.  And even that event doesn’t change much, as it’s more of a “I know what has to be done now” moment and Sorey continues to go on as a one-dimensional, pure of heart, do-gooder.
Looking back at the game, I’m thinking that the developers probably had a lot more content to put in. There’s a solid game in there but it’s just empty compared to other Tales’ entries.
