Tales of Zestiria is the latest Tales of game added to the Tales Franchise, which has been running for 20 years now. If you did not know, the Tales of series is extremely popular in Japan and is considered among the best of JRPGS along with Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest and Pokemon. It is an anime RPG series, so if you like Anime and RPG's keep reading. Or if you are generally interested in the title, you can continue reading as well.
I will divide this review into 3 parts: STORY, GAMEPLAY and OVERALL CONCLUSION.
STORY:
*Minor Spoilers ahead*
You follow the story of Sorey, a young ruin fanatic on an adventure with his best friend Mikleo. They stumble upon a young lady knight in booty shorts named Alisha and together they form a bond as they go on more adventures together.
Sorey shortly establishes himself as the Shepard early in the game, the only one who can purify "hellions" the monsters you encounter within the game.
As you travel together you meet more new friends; Seraphs, beings that are invisible to most humans, except Sorey and few individuals with the innate talent to sense/interact with them. Each of the ones that join your party are attuned to a different element: Fire, Wind, Earth and Water.
The main objective for Sorey's quest is to defeat the Lord of Calamity and bring an end to all malevolence brought forth unto the world.
Now with that aside and the overall gist of the plot explained loosely, I would like to say the Story is "nothing special". However I do say that, although it may not be an AMAZING story, it is still a decent and good one, generally easy to follow and not get lost in. The simplicity of your objectives and how they contribute to your adventure really set a nice steady pace for your journey and there are plenty of extras and sidequests to get lost in that do add more to your experience!
Never once have I felt that the story was moving too slow and it was not going anywhere.
Although the story does follow some cliches, they are cliches I enjoy and like and there are plenty of stuff done differently as well, so the journey doesn't feel empty. An example of a cliche used for the story is "A chosen hero bears the power to save the world". In my opinion, as overused as this plot device is used, it's still a great foundation for a story to start upon.
One of my favorite parts of playing through the story were the interactions between the main cast, as their personalities clash in times of joy and woe. Truly a wonderful cast is needed to bring out the story to life and I feel they nailed it for the most part. I will criticize on a certain design choice made on a character who later joins you, as SHE (there's your hint) can be annoying sometimes and in my opinion I would value a "certain" other character's presence over her, however this is unavoidable due to plot reasons.
Overall I would give the story a 7/10.
GAMEPLAY:
On the field, you control Sorey as you move from point A, to point B in a world that is connected by areas. There is no "overworld" so the only way to travel is run to your destination, or quick travel between save points. Quick travel is available early in the game, although it costs money and can't be used all the time due to plot points inhibiting your travel.
The game is divided into Towns, Dungeons, and Fields.
The map is easy to use and there are quest markers in case you get lost. Not everything is travel from here to there as there are sidequests to do as you play more, extra dungeons outside the story, and puzzles which can get to the point of "The Legend of Zelda" difficulty.  I enjoyed the puzzles and they are a nice distraction to keep the game from seeming like your running in a linear line.
The Battle System in Tales of Zestiria is one of the most FUN I've ever had in a Tales of game. If you are not familiar with how the series battle system works, the entire game is played in a real time action based combat system. You can freely move your character on the battlefield and attack when you want. No turns, no waiting, you fight like REAL men.
One of the biggest improvements to this system is that in past titles, you are put in a pre rendered environment to fight your enemies in, like older RPG classics, however this has changed. You are now placed immediately into battle upon encountering an enemy on the map, and fight exactly where you were prior to the encounter. You might be fighting on a staircase, there might be a rock you can hide behind, or a wall. It adds a great immersive feeling and depth to the encounter.
You control one of the party characters and attack via Martial Artes (No. Not really like Kung-fu movies), Seraphic Artes (spell based moves, with a cast timer) and Hidden Artes (Stronger versions of Martial Artes). The AI will then control 3 other characters.
A Martial Arte is your primary basic attack; fast combo strings that get more stronger and stronger as you chain into it. (Max of 4 chain attacks at the start). They are simply satisfying to watch and use, and you will most likely never get bored of watching your characters chain more and more combos together with your party, as you level up and grow stronger.
Seraphic Artes are for Seraphs only, and cast a spell with timers ranging from very short to long, depending on the level of spell you cast and when you cast it within your combo. For example casting a Seraphic Arte after 3 chains of a Martial Arte Combo will greatly reduce the cast time of a spell, making it almost instant if its a lower level spell. Each element of spell is interesting to use, and play with, and spells can also be combo'd into eachother within a 4 linked chain such as Martial Artes, making spells certainly entertaining to use as well.
Hidden Artes are just stronger versions of Martial Artes and can only be used with Human characters. They perform similar to Martial Artes except you don't have to be within a certain string of a combo to use them, unlike Martial Artes.
Now to put the icing on the cake the GREATEST addition I felt that was put into the gameplay was the....
FUSION SYSTEM!
Later on after obtaining the power of the Shepard, there is a skill called "Armatization", which allows you to fuse with Seraphs, obtain their element, and become an entirely different being.
For example when fused with Lailah, the Seraph of Fire, you wield a giant two handed sword with flames that purify evil-- literally!
Sorey and the Seraph he fused with stats are merged, making you a one man army. It is simply satisfying on how powerful you feel, when fused and the new Martial/Seraphic Artes you can use will simply blow you away on how spectacular they look when performed.
Now to put even more eye candy to your super form, each line the character now says is heard between two different entitites (Depending on who is fused) and I loved the nostalgic Dragonball Z feeling I got from hearing these.
Overall I would give the Gameplay a 10/10, fun/fun.
OVERALL CONCLUSION:
Now there is plenty of stuff I can go on and on about this game, but I would like to give the reader a chance to actually play the game themselves and learn what else the game has to offer.
There are tons of stuff I have not even gone over, which I assure most will enjoy such as "Skits" (Voice acted mini scenes between the party), and the very complex skill system used via equipment.
All in all Tales of Zestaria is a great game and has a tremendous amount of depth to overcome the flaws of it cliches, and the Battle System is straight up addicting. The characters are great for the most part, and the newest additions to the franchise are fantastic.
Give the game a try if you like Japanese RPG games, or are interested in it. I can guarantee it is worth your money.
I give the game an overall 8/10.

I really liked this game. It's my first Tales game, and it was very fun. I liked the combat, some of the story, the characters, the presentation, and I wasl satisfied with it. I also disliked the stat-system, a lot more of the story, the first-impressions of most characters, the vast, empty-except-for-monsters overworld, and a cople of nitpicks
The combat system is very, very fun. It's real-time in a small area, and there's a lot of good about it. Your "martial arts" will be your normal attacks, comboing into themselves and coming out quickly. "Hidden arts" sometimes combo into martial arts, sometimes finish combos, or just be stand-alone attacks depending on when and where you use them. They wont be interrupted by martial arts, but the same goes for enemy hidden arts. "Seraphic arts" are charged magical attacks, getting bigger and better and taking more time to charge as they advance. Mixing these up and killing all your enemies is fun, although good luck stringing together constant combos with the AI. Still, I took on the hardest boss in the entire game (Who, by the way, is a side-quest boss) while I was thirty levels under him. It took me a couple of tries, but the combat was so satisfying that I was ok with it.
The problem with the combat system is the stat system. Equipment changes in each area, becoming better as you go along. Unfortunately, it also doesn't. Each piece of equipment comes with up to four skills, the first of which is constant throughout across all other pieces with that name. Since all these akills are randomized, it tries to fuse linear and non-linear gear together, to terrible effect. There may be a set of skills for each tier of equipment, but I got so fed up with the system that by the end I wasn't really paying attention. It's an overly-complicated system that I ignored, and the game didn't punish me for it.
Another problem is with grinding. You don't actually have to grind much in this game, but you might want to just to make future bosses easier. I tried grinding a bit, but the enemies didn't seem advance with their levels when I raised the overall level of the area. It's not terrible, but I wish that there had been a more noticeable effect.
The music was pretty good, although not the greatest. It's good enough for long hours of playing, but not "soundtrack-of-my-life" levels of good. I also just liked the visuals in general, but the effect has worn off after... 75 hours? Where did my life go? Anyway, still one of the better looking games I've played in my life.
Now comes to the most important part of ny JRPG: the story. After 75 hours, I've decided that I kinda liked it. There's a lot of things that it does very well, some that I would normally face-palm at. There's a character focused entirely on puns, most characters are just fun and likeable. For reference, there's a group of "good assassins" in the story. Naturally I thought that that's kinda stupid and contrived. It's now one of my favorite points in the story. Unfortuantely, it's fairly average as stories go, and that's WHEN I did like it.
I may like the story and the characters, but if I had anything else to play at the time I probably would have stopped before the one-hour mark-- If the cutcenes were finally done at that point. For a long time the characters are just stupid and cliche and there si still a 10% chance that I like this story out of Stockholme's syndrome. For far too long, Sorey is "A wide-eyed, naive boy who's just learning about the real world, but keeping his chin up". Mikleo is "Sorey's best friend / Brother in all but blood, who always complains but always stands by his friend". The first time you meet most charaters, they are unbelievably cliche, and the main villain is essentially "The Darkness that lies in everyone's heart, mwahahahahaa". Eventually the characters become likeable, and the story picks up a sort-of theme about deciding taking your life's meaning and purpose into your own hands, but damn does it take it's sweet time getting there, and even then there are times when it's not that great. It's simplistic, somewhat cliche, and only saved by the combat.
Rants aside, I still liked this game. I pre-ordered it because it was bundled with a future key for Tales of Symphonia when it re-releases in 2016, and I've heard nothing but good about that game. I also got some extra costumes, which I like but could live without. Overall I'd reccomend this game, but over the Christmas sale when it is (hopefully) under $30. Until then, only Symphonia could justfy that price-tag in my mind.

The Long Dark has come a long way since I last reviewed it. It strives to offer a unique realistic survival experience, but falls just short. It requires some balancing and is still lacking some content, which I really hope gets added before being considered finished. In it's current state I would recommend it on sale, but not full price. I will not be discussing the "Pros" in this review, because there are enough that do that already. For the record, this is all subjective and based on my opinion of the game in its EARLY ACCESS STATE, but I think many will agree.
--- Lacking Content ---
There are not very many craftable items yet(?) and as you play, you can't help feel that some are missing. Like literally needing to forge arrow heads in a furnace instead of rigging some using scrap metal, flint or even just sharpening the arrow shaft to a tip.
You can find and read survival books that surely would teach how you to make and use a bow drill to start fires (while it is challanging, it's still possible) or pieces of flint.
I know in Canada your options would be limited in terms of out door shelters, but you should be able to build a small temporary lean-to out of pine branches to protect you some from the weather while you harvest an animal.
This is a minor complaint, but maybe another weapon or two? like some form of common pistol or compound bow, just to add some diversity instead of finding several identical rifles.
---The Balance---
Your chance to start a fire is too low for being indoors with an actual stove. Having matches, tinder and wood in those circumstances, should result in a chance of no less than 75%.
You eat too much. Your character is suppose to be an average person I presume, but eats as much as an Olympic athlete. Frequently eating an entire wolf, entire deer or several 2lb fish in a day? I think that's excessive. Should get more meat from animals or burn less calories to balance that out.
Tools break unrealistically fast yet and are repaired too slow.
---Other---
I understand not being able to chop down a large tree with a small hatchet, but I think you should still be able to break branches off with it?
Not sure anything can be done about this, because of how the games mechanics are implemented, but it's frustrating to waste a precious 2 hrs watching snow melt or water boil. You should be able to put it on the stove and do something else while you're waiting like fishing, crafting, fixing items, harvesting, etc.
- - - OUT DATED REVIEW - - -
EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Simplifying this review, because some people, apparently, didn't understand what I was saying.
This is not a bad game, but it has a few problems that prevent me from recommending it, at the moment. It will likely improve over time.
I'M AWARE THAT THE GAME IS NOT FINISHED.
With that said, lets get down to business. . .
You are not rewarded for critical thinking or your knowledge of the wilderness.
Survival in this game, seems to be a matter of luck an learning to survive the games mechanics.
Things break unrealisticly fast (e.g. Your clothes will break and fall off from walking).
Want to craft a weapon, like sharpening a stick to defend yourself from wolves, like Liam Neeson in "The Grey"? Can't do that. . .  yet? Have to fist fight them with your bare hands (You lose).
There is a gun, if you can find it and equally important, ammo. It's the only weapon in the game so far. I've plundered about 15 structures in my 2 hrs and didn't find it.
It seems like there will eventually be some sort of crafting system (via work bench), but its definitely not finished.
Plan on being hardcore and surviving the unforgiving canadian wilderness, by living off the land or out of a cave in a realistic way, without stealing supplies from people? No chance. You are FORCED to break into random structures and steal supplies.
It's fine if you want to do that, but be aware, there is no way around it. I can only assume, based on the way everything is currently balanced, that there are no plans to support that. If it bothers you, as it does me, you may want to wait on purchasing.
I'd like the option to survive off the land, because while thats impossible, I hardly consider it a survival game. You should not NEED to rely on buildings and the contents inside them.
It's rather new, so most of these problems will likely be fixed over time, but as of now, I just can't recommend it. I'm not trying to bash the game, but give useful criticism to the developers so they can improve the game and to you, so that you know what you're buying.

It's charming and could be cool but deep down, just like The Mighty Quest for Epic Loot, it's garbage and will be until time erases it.

It's such an intense game... It's so unlike other survival games, in the sense that there's nothing really trying to kill you (other than wolves), but even while you explore around, you're watching over your back, because the sound effects in this game are done so well, that it sounds real. Honestly, I was inside a cabin and heard the wind whistling, and had to take my headphones off because I thought it was coming from outside, but it was just the game.
A few tips? Don't stay in one place. That's an absolute waste of time, and you'll probably die. Every day, keep walking. Give yourself something to do. Got extra wood and fire starters? Cook some meat or canned goods or purify some water, find a work bench and fix some stuff. Don't let yourself have nothing to do. Much like real life, if you're going to survive, you need to keep occupied.
Oh, and also, don't ever carry too much, or become "encumbered". I thought there was a glitch or something at first because I could still sprint, other than my fatigue increasing quicker. Nope, no glitch. Your thirst and fatigue will shoot up, and if you don't take care of it, one minute you're walking across a frozen river, the next you're almost compltely blind and can only see a foot or two infront of you. Just, be careful.
Overall, honestly, I have no complaints about this game. For an early access title, it has amazing graphics, music, sound, base storyline (even though it's just sandbox mode right now, there's still some form of a storyline) and it all flows together and works. It feels real. I have high hopes for what shall come in the future.

One of the most humbling games I have ever played. If you played CoD when it was fun (CoD 1-4) and are considering buying this game, be prepared for a shock. This game takes the realism and immersion of sims like Arma, but keeps you in the action by taking out the parts in Arma where you trek for miles with no idea where the enemy or your squad is, and focuses more on the action. Remember how in CoD your character, even on veteran, could soak up bullets like a sponge, red jelly seemingly leaking out of his eyeballs, then duck behind cover and "squeeze" out the damage he had taken moments before? Forget that. Forget the crosshair in the middle of your screen. Forget when you would pick up a PPSH in CoD 2, fire off the entire magazine at the same target with nary a spot of recoil to be seen. Forget the ability of your character to sprint through an artillery barrage, dash across a field while being sprayed with MG-42 fire, and take out a tank singehandedly with nothing but your trusty TNT without even flinching. Try anything of the sort in this game, and, assuming you aren't instantly torn apart, your screen's color will drain away, your heart will be pounding, and you will find aiming immpossible. And I don't mean just in the game.
Each side, Axis and Allies, has its own strengths and weaknesses (although the Wermacht has few of the latter). Playing as the Soviet Union, unless you manage to snag one of the few special classes, such as sniper or commander, quickly turns into a meat-grinder experience, just as it would have been in real life. Playing as a rifleman, for example, will give you a Moison-Nagant 1895, two grenades and a life expectancy of about 30 seconds. You will charge across a field to a capture point which appears to be empty, and moments later a machine gun you never saw will open up from a window you forgot to check, or from behind a wall you passed without waiting for your team-mates to cover, and your brief, often pointless life will be over, as your squad members are often cut down around your darkening vision. Often a game spent as one of the more aggresive classes will turn in three steps: Spawn, die, repeat. Sometimes you will die without firing a shot.
This may sound dull, painful, or frustrating. In your first online match you may not get more than one kill. The learning curve in this game is quite steep, and this discourages many people. But eventually you will begin to learn the quirks, tricks, and rewards of each class. If you are patient, cautious, and lucky, just as the real veterans of the battle of Stalingrad had to be, and you will improve. Your name will move up the scoreboard, and you will begin to reap the rewards of the time you invest a hundred times over. This is when the game becomes the most fun. You will unlock bayonets, scopes, and new guns, and your player model will begin to show the wear and tear of surviving the battles, with medals, extra ammo and camo.
All in all, probably my favorite shooter of all time. The community is mature, and welcoming to new players. Stay away from the single player mode, and don't try the tank combat, and you will grow to love this beautiful, grim, and challenging video game.

TL;DR : 10/10 Game's good. Effort and care has been put in and it shows. Buy it.
I had backed this game a very long time ago from their website while it was in developpement. When it release, I couldn't wait to get back from work and fire it up. I was a bit nervous and truly hoped it was good. What I got was everything I hoped it would have been and more. The aesthetics of the game are wonderful. Vibrant colors, "cartoonish" logic object placement, lots of effects to make movement pleasing. In general : Polish and care can be found in every corners of the game. The controls are fun and the levels are refreshing for a platformer, throwing formulas out of the window and making their own. It is, of course, a kids game and has a very happy atmosphere. Until you get to Subcon Forest's "Queen Vanessa's Manor" level, that is. This level has been made by a sadist who wants to terrify children for a very long time. Young me would've been unable to finish that level again out of sheer terror (I was a scaredy-cat).
Moving on, there are four Chapters (levels), each with about 6-8 acts (sub-levels). You will often unlock multiple acts at the same time and can play them in any order. After certain acts, you will unlock "Time Rifts" which are hidden levels (think Mario Sunshine) that will give you extra Time Pieces (the main item you collect to progress). There are only 40 Time Pieces and it does make the game feel a bit short. However, there is a feel of "Quality over Quantity" to it so I personally did not mind. Time Rifts will also unlock flair items. Flair items allow you to customize your character and the music in-game to tailor it for your tastes. Taking all this in, I got through the game a bit quickly but I don't feel it's a bad thing. I feel I deeply enjoyed it and this gaming experience will stay with me for a very long time. If it was longer, I fear it would have diluted the "uniqueness" of certain levels, simply to add artificial game time.
All in all, I greatly recommend this game. It is a solid experience and an excellent exemple on how to revive a genre. This was everything I had hoped Yooka-Laylee would have been. I have always enjoyed platformers and I would like to give my contratulations/thanks to GearsForBreakfast for re-igniting my love for the genre. I do hope they will keep making games for a long time and can be sure to count on my support.

The best way I could describe this game to someone who's familiar with video games is to call it a spiritual successor to Super Mario Sunshine with Wind Waker's aesthetics and Banjo-Tooie's humour. But it's still so much more than just that. It borrows elements from so many 3D platformers that it feels like a celebration of the genre. Some level designs even had me reminiscing about Conker's Bad Fur Day and Psychonauts in terms of how they didn't feel like levels, but actual locations these characters would live and work in that are just very conveniently designed for your bouncy traversal.
You can notice as you move on from the first world that the development team was learning along the way, as many things such as animation and design become more fluid and professional, not to suggest the beginning of the game is unpolished or crude. It's all great, and only gets better the more you play.
My only nitpick, as a title that focuses on collecting, is that the game doesn't keep track of the total number of yarn balls and rift tokens you've collected like it does the time pieces. You effectively have to revisit every level of every world individually and search them to make sure, and even then I don't believe there's enough rift tokens available in the game to get every cosmetic unlockable.
I hate number scores, but for a 3D platformer this title is a 10/10 for sure.

This game is all about the experience of the small victories in survival. While some describe the game as an effeciency exercise--and I can't entirely disagree with that assessment--for me it is immersive enough that it doesn't feel like an artificial grind but the very real grind of surviving another hour, another day, in a harsh, unforgiving environment.
When I attempt to plan ahead by scavenging deer carcasses for their guts so that I can make fishing line, and I stock the ice fishing hut with wood fuel to keep me warm during a long day of catching salmon, and then carry an overburdened load of 30 pounds of fish across the ice and up a steep slope of snow to my lonely cabin, all before night falls, I am not entirely surprised of my own growing panic when an unexpected snow storm blows in, creating white-out conditions, and I realize I have likely over-shot my destination, and I am lost, with rapidly sinking temperatures, dangerously high levels of fatigue, and a high risk of spraining an ankle.
Cursing, I experience a sinking feeling in my stomach as I drop my heavy load of freshly caught fish and start running in the direction I hope my cabin is in. I blame myself for my own stupidity, for not staying in the fishing hut and waiting out the storm.
I tell myself that this is it, this is when I die. I knew it would come, but I honestly didn't think it would come like this.
But then, just as dark descends, and after not seeing a single thing while frantically running faster and faster, I stumble on a tree, and then a familiar cluster of rocks, and know that I am just a little ways from my cabin door. I thank God, but I try not to allow myself to feel completely relieved because I know something could still go wrong.
I am nearly frozen, can barely keep my vision from blurring--using the last bit of strength I have--when I reach the wooden gate. I stumble inside and slam the door to the howling wind. I creep over to the fireplace and use my last wooden match to light a fire. I begin to warm.
I can go upstairs and rest on the bed, but I choose to lay out my bedroll here, next to the fire. I crouch beside it, stare into the flames, and eat a can of pork and beans.
Today I know and feel, more than any other day of my life, that I am utterly alone.

A thrilling game with an engaging story that puts you at the wheel of unraveling its secrets. It's been a while since horror fans have been treated to anything of this caliber, and it's quite refreshing.
Much like in Amnesia: the Dark Descent, the game instills an immersive sense of helplessness by limiting the player's combat options to just two things: running and hiding. I don't want to give out spoilers, so I won't mention how, but they take this player-disempowerment model to a devious new level in one particular chapter. And don't worry--the brilliant level design makes sure to prey on all kinds of phobias--so if the nail-biting hide-and-seek moments don't get you, something else will.
A welcome break from the stiff, inflexible protagonists of other games, it's movement interface also provides the player with a great deal of useful mobility such as climbing, vaulting, sidling, and--most importantly--a decent sprint. Despite all of that, it still manages to remain believable by not having the character do anything unrealistic. (I don't know about other people, but I was getting tired of games where you had to play as someone who couldn't even figure out how to get over an obstacle at waist height!) Oh, and for what little spoken dialogue there is, I feel compelled to mention how well the voice acting was done; this game easily beats out the Dead Space series in it's ability to get me to really imagine the character's pain as he's being tormented.
Anyway, there's always more to say about it, so I'll try to keep it short. This game was really, really incredible, and I definitely plan to get my hands on the DLC some time soon.

This is one of the best survival horror games I've played in a very long time. It truly deserves the label "survival horror." You don't shoot a weapon a single time in this game - stealth and hiding is the name of the game. If you've played Amnesia you know a bit of what to expect in that regard. However, I honestly enjoyed this game much more than Amnesia. The story actually makes total sense in this game right from the beginning, something I can't say for other survival horror games (I'm looking at you, Amnesia... and Dead Space). The puzzles are also much more straightforward and less headache-inducing.
Everything in Outlast, from the gameplay mechanics, voice acting, visuals, etc. is just superbly well-done. One key highlight of the game is the incredibly immersive environmental sound design. It always dynamically changes to suit the current mood of the player's situation, and the quality of the sound is incredible. This is a good thing too, because unlike many games out there these days, Outlast does not give you a radar or minimap that shows you if an enemy is nearby or coming after you. You have to rely entirely on the sounds around you to assess your situation.
Another area in which Outlast excels is in how it tells its story. There are hardly any cutscenes in the game. Instead, most of the storytelling is done just as it accomplished in classic Resident Evil games, through notes and journals discovered in the environment. This is the best way to tell a story in this type of game, in my opinion, as it feels totally natural to search for clues in this type of mysterious, scary setting.
The only real drawbacks I can fault the game for are a few minor things. The first is the "closing door behind you" mechanic; often the game will tell you to press Left Click if you want to close the door in front of you, but when you do, nothing actually happens. This caused my death a few times throughout the game. It was only occasionally that I was actually able to close a door behind me to prevent a chasing inmate from catching me, all because the game refused to register my click. Another flaw of the game is the repetitiveness of the inmate character models. They generally start to look all the same after a while. This isn't a huge problem however since most of the time, you're supposed to be keeping your distance from them and not actually see them upclose.
I highly recommend Outlast to anyone who enjoyed classic Resident Evil games (1-3 + Code Veronica), and anyone who likes TRUE survival horror games in general. Refunct is a very smooth and beautiful 3D platformer where you progress by touching platforms, which colors them, and finding and pressing buttons located throughout those platforms. Each button raises more of the platforms out of the water to explore. The visuals for the game are very nice, especially the water and lighting changes brought about by the purely aethetic day/night cycle, and coupled with the great soundtrack lead to a very relaxing yet exciting environment. The platforming is extremely smooth with wall jumping and some jump pads and the jumps feel satisfying and fair.
Progression is measured by the percentage of platforms that you've colored, with 100% completion being reached when you've touched and colored every platform. The game is considered 'complete' once you've pressed all the buttons, but you can continue to play after to reach 100% completion or to just jump around the islands and swim in the water. There are small collectable cubes scattered around the islands and each is tied to an achievement for collecting it, but none are super hidden, and in reaching 100% completion you will almost certainly get them all if you haven't gotten them all already when completing the game.
A recent update has pushed the game more in the direction of speedrunning by providing sites to track records and achievements for reaching time goals. While I would normally be against such a change to a game I considered fun and relaxing, it fits well with the game mechanics and adds to the replayability of the game. Even with these changes, it isn't the longest game, but I have ~3.5 hours played right now, and given the price that's pretty good.
The only complaint I have about the game is the color selection when coloring the islands. Originally every island would be colored green, which led to a color sceme that I really liked. However, as of right now the color that the islands turn is randomly choosen upon starting a new game (it was changed in an update). While all the colors look nice, I would like it more if I was able to manually set it to green through an option. However, there have been a number of updates to the game, so it is quite possible that something like that may be introduced in the future.
In terms of achievements, a majority of them will be earned in your first run, especially if you focus on collecting all the small black cubes. The others require subsequent runs requiring you to replay the game to finish while meeting certain goals, specificly less than 33% completion (you need to hit the buttons while avoiding platforms when possible), having a run under 8 minutes, and having a run under 4 minutes. The 4 minutes run sounded quite hard to me initially but I was able to do it in just a couple tries after watching someone do a similar run and then learning a good route as I attempted to complete it. Completing the game used to be very easy before those last three were added in a recent update, and I would normally be really against adding achievements after a game had already had them for a while, but the developer did specifically offer to unlock the new achievements for anyone who had previously completed the game and was having trouble with the new ones, which was nice.
Overall the game is a really solid platforming experience in a very relaxing and neat environment, and is very satisfying and fun to play.

I originally played this game via PS+ for a number of hours on the PlayStation 4, but I had to get this when I saw such an enticing 50% discount. Of course, within two or three hours, I beat my progress on the PS4 version. This game is incredibly fun, and it's actually relatively versatile, too. Depending on how you like to play, you could:
•Play with others, where this becomes a fun, lethal, adrenaline-pumping contest, OR;
•Play on your own against the evil forces of something, where this becomes the single most stressful, rage-inducing, soul-destroying game ever.
The idea of playing with archers is really well thought-out, and it has several mechanics which are absolutely brilliant. The major one is dodging, where you can dash into arrows and collect them. You'll find out just how important that is in singleplayer, where you're often facing multiple enemy archers at once. Speaking of the archers, their AI is horrifyingly efficient, and they tend to kill you in CQC even when out of arrows.
The soundtrack for this game is absolutely beautiful, and right from the start of the main menu theme, you get the feeling that this is going to be a good game. And TowerFall: Ascension does not disappoint me. It's a beautiful game and it is definitely worth the money.

Judging The Beginner's Guide is a tall order; judging it objectively is pretty much impossible.
Please keep in mind I'm writing this from my own perspective, and that at the end of the day, whether or not you will get something out of this game depends a lot on who you are as a person.
That being said, I'd like to address an important point. This game is marketed as being by "the creator of The Stanley Parable". While this is true, this is also a hollow statement, because The Beginner's Guide has very little to do with The Stanley Parable.
The games do share a few similarities: they're both made in the Source Engine, both have a narrator guiding your through the game, and both offer a very limited gameplay (ie. walking around, looking at things and occasionally pressing other things).
The similarities stop here, though. While TSP was mostly humorous and absurd, TBG can be rather sad, depressing even.
TSP was about the story of Stanley, the character you played as, while TBG's story doesn't revolve at all around your character (or lack thereof). Your character isn't important. In fact, *you* are not at all important to the story.
TSP would encourage you to look around and disobey the game's narrator; TBG discourages you from doing so, and if you try regardless, you will be rewarded with very little, or even nothing. As such, TBG is much more linear and offers virtually no replay value, unlike TSP which could be played a good number of times.
Being different from TSP is not a problem; I wouldn't expect its author to rehash the same game over and over again. However, I find it a bit deceiving to mention TSP in TBG's marketing blurb. This can only make people think this game has similarities with TSP, even though there are more differences than similarities.
So, if you've considering getting this game because of TSP, do remember that they are wholly different. This doesn't mean you won't enjoy TBG, but if you go into it expecting anything like TSP, you risk being disappointed. It is better to go into it with a fresh head rather than with expectations.
With that out of the way, I'm going to try and address my issues with what the game is, rather than what it isn't.
The Beginner's Guide is, in essence, a story. The game itself is a series of smaller games that you will play one after another, but the game themselves aren't so important individually. While some offer some interesting gameplay mechanics, they are not there for you to really *play* them. What's important is the framing device, what all these games are wrapped around: the story of two friends, and the attempt of one of them to understand and help the other.
As such, the most important point The Beginner's Guide can be judged on is its story, since this is mostly what you'll be playing it for. And that story itself is good. Great, even. It's interesting, well delivered, surprising.
But the problem is, while the story itself is good, it didn't resonate with me. It didn't make me feel much of anything. It looked like it wanted to, but it failed. I got disappointed when it ended, because I felt like the game was close to succeed at that, but yet, fell short.
The reason why, I think, is that this story is meant to resonate with artistic people, mostly. Writers, or designers, or any other job or hobby that requires you to have ideas in order to produce something. The game touches a lot on this topic: what your ideas as a creator mean, what they say about you, and what happens when you run out of them. Unfortunately, I am not an artistic person. I have little imagination and would rather use concrete, already existing ideas, rather than make my own. As such, while I could understand what the game was trying to say, I couldn't relate to it.
And that's what this game requires you to do, in order to fully appreciate it: being able to relate to it, to understand and be influenced by it fully.
You may think this is a harsh judgment, then. I did, after all, find the story interesting, and it's not like I require all my games to have immersive, relatable stories. I've enjoyed games that made me feel no particular emotions.
But The Beginner's Guide, I think, lives and dies on your ability to get fully immersed in its story.
Still, is it the game's fault I couldn't do so?
At the end of the day, the reason I'm not recommending this game has more to do with me than the game itself. And maybe, just because of that, it was worthy of my attention. Maybe it will be worthy of yours, too.

This is a great game for JRPG fans. This is NOT good for casual gamers. If you're already familiar with the "Tales of" series, you know exactly what you're getting into. For those of you who only know Tales of Symphonia, this game is very similar, with a very improved combat system, and a bit shorter. If you liked other entries in the series, you'll probably enjoy this one as well. It's a little bit more complicated than the others, though. If you like JRPGs and aren't familiar with Tales games, this is a good place to start.
There's a New Game+ option with extra difficulty modes and other options that you can change from one playthrough to another, so if you're a completionist, you might want to replay up to 3 or even 5 times. There's also a DLC chapter focusing on a minor character.

Let's get this out of the way first: Tales of Zestiria is a JRPG, but it does not have turn-based combat and is not a grindy game. In fact, your characters' levels matter much less than what equipment they use and how you control them in the real-time battles, both of which are based on some systems that are difficult to understand at first and brushed a lot of people the wrong way (see below for an overview). The lack of a need to grind, the presence of a good Quick Travel system and the lack of needlessly big, empty regions (except for one) mean that the game flows very well, and except for a single bit near the end which doesn't even take 15 minutes total to clear, it never feels like battles and simple puzzles are being tossed at you just to increase play time, as it often does with so many other games of the genre.
The game's localization was very well-done. One particular character has a thing for puns and "dad jokes", which are very hard to localize because often they can't be translated and you have to come up with a new one along the same lines. The English versions of those might be one of my favorite parts of the game. The English voice acting is also very good for the most part. I don't know Japanese, so I can't compare, but the English language audio and text are on point.
The story is nothing exceptional, but good enough and well-told. The soundtrack is really good.The game world is immersive, there are interesting NPCs and sidequests, and I had fun just going out to explore places instead of actually following the story on several occasions. A big part of the game are the correlated Skills and Fusion systems, which I enjoyed playing around with, but which also frustrated many people. I'll get into those below.
There's an unofficial patch that allows the game to run at 60fps if you care about that sort of thing.
As I mentioned, character levels aren't as important in Tales of Zestiria as they are in the average JRPG. It's possible to take down an enemy twice your level or to be defeated by an enemy half your level, all depending on how you fight and on what equipment you have. Equipment stat boosts are much larger than your stat growth when you level up, but even more important than that are the Skills that your equipment comes with. Two otherwise identical weapons that happened to drop with different Skills on them can be significantly different from each other, depending on what other equipment you're wearing. In the beginning of the game, Skills aren't that important, but as the game progresses, they become more and more relevant. Certain bosses simply can't be beaten if you don't have the right Skills equipped.
When you encounter an enemy, a wide circular area will be closed around you to form the field of battle. You can move around freely,dodge, block, attack and defend in real time, and issue generic commands to the party members you're not controlling directly (spread out, focus on the same enemy, focus on attacking, focus on defense). By pausing the battle, you can enter a menu and order any non-controlled character to use a specific "arte" (the game's name for attacks, special moves and magic). You can also change which character you control mid-battle. There are five elements (Void/Non-Elemental, Fire, Earth, Water and Wind) to which enemies can be weak, neutral or resistant. In addition, each element is associated to a status ailment (e.g. Water to Poison) and a character stat (e.g. Void to Attack). Every single arte you use will have one or more elements, and every arte of a given element has the potential to cause the respective element's status ailment or give you a buff to the corresponding stat when used. Enemies also have Types (e.g. Flying, Armored, Beast) against which certain attacks are strong. An attack that's strong against an enemy type will deal bonus damage even if that enemy is strong against the attack's element. There are three numbers to keep an eye on during battle: your HP, your SC (Spirit Chain) and your BG (Blast Gauge). BG is used for certain especially powerful artes and for a unique mechanic called Armatization. SC is what you use for actually fighting. Your maximum SC is always 100 and everything you do in battle except running and blocking costs some SC. SC recovers over time during the battle, but if you attack too quickly or too often, you'll run out and have to wait. The lower your SC goes, the slower it recovers.
Each character has five different equipment slots, and each piece of equipment has four Skill slots. There are a total of 50 different Skills that can give you anything from stat boosts to increased HP recovery, protection against an element or status ailment, added damage against certain enemies, etc.  These Skills are organized into a 5x10 grid where each of the 5 lines corresponds to an element and each of the 10 collumns corresponds to a theme (e.g. the first collumn is stat boosts, the 9th collumn is increased damage of the respective types). Every Skill from currently equipped gear will be active on that character's Skill Chart.
Skills can be combined for added bonus effects, which can be even more dramatic than the basic Skills themselves (such as reflecting 30% of all damage of a particular element, having an extra Blast Gauge or gaining a 20% Max HP increase). The Bonus Skills depend on where skills are on the 5x10 Skills chart. There are three types of Bonus Skills: Stack (multiple copies of the same Skill), E-Union (two or more adjacent skills in the same horizontal line) and G-Union (all five Skills on the same collumn). Equipping two of the same skill, for instance, reduces the time you spend staggered by 6%. If you have multiple stacks of two, their effects add up - a stack of stacks, if you will. This means you can become completely immune to certain status ailments by equipping the right skills.
Every piece of equipment you get will have at least one skill and up to four. In weapon shops, it's possible to fuse two pieces of equipment and combine their skills, while also improving the equipment's stats with each fusion. Slots that have the same skill in both fused weapons, or any skill in one weapon and a blank slot in the other will keep that same skill in the resulting fused weapon. Slots that are empty in both weapons will continue empty. Slots that have different skills in each weapon will end up with a third skill that is different from both. Because of this mechanism, through fusion you can create equipments with the Skill set you want, to match your play style or enable a specific strategy against a particular foe.
If the above description of game mechanics didn't scare you, and you enjoy JRPGs, you'll probably enjoy Tales of Zestiria. If not, then you've probably stopped reading already anyway, but don't buy the game. That is all.

The Long Dark has come a long way since I last reviewed it. It strives to offer a unique realistic survival experience, but falls just short. It requires some balancing and is still lacking some content, which I really hope gets added before being considered finished. In it's current state I would recommend it on sale, but not full price. I will not be discussing the "Pros" in this review, because there are enough that do that already. For the record, this is all subjective and based on my opinion of the game in its EARLY ACCESS STATE, but I think many will agree.
--- Lacking Content ---
There are not very many craftable items yet(?) and as you play, you can't help feel that some are missing. Like literally needing to forge arrow heads in a furnace instead of rigging some using scrap metal, flint or even just sharpening the arrow shaft to a tip.
You can find and read survival books that surely would teach how you to make and use a bow drill to start fires (while it is challanging, it's still possible) or pieces of flint.
I know in Canada your options would be limited in terms of out door shelters, but you should be able to build a small temporary lean-to out of pine branches to protect you some from the weather while you harvest an animal.
This is a minor complaint, but maybe another weapon or two? like some form of common pistol or compound bow, just to add some diversity instead of finding several identical rifles.
---The Balance---
Your chance to start a fire is too low for being indoors with an actual stove. Having matches, tinder and wood in those circumstances, should result in a chance of no less than 75%.
You eat too much. Your character is suppose to be an average person I presume, but eats as much as an Olympic athlete. Frequently eating an entire wolf, entire deer or several 2lb fish in a day? I think that's excessive. Should get more meat from animals or burn less calories to balance that out.
Tools break unrealistically fast yet and are repaired too slow.
---Other---
I understand not being able to chop down a large tree with a small hatchet, but I think you should still be able to break branches off with it?
Not sure anything can be done about this, because of how the games mechanics are implemented, but it's frustrating to waste a precious 2 hrs watching snow melt or water boil. You should be able to put it on the stove and do something else while you're waiting like fishing, crafting, fixing items, harvesting, etc.
- - - OUT DATED REVIEW - - -
EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Simplifying this review, because some people, apparently, didn't understand what I was saying.
This is not a bad game, but it has a few problems that prevent me from recommending it, at the moment. It will likely improve over time.
I'M AWARE THAT THE GAME IS NOT FINISHED.
With that said, lets get down to business. . .
You are not rewarded for critical thinking or your knowledge of the wilderness.
Survival in this game, seems to be a matter of luck an learning to survive the games mechanics.
Things break unrealisticly fast (e.g. Your clothes will break and fall off from walking).
Want to craft a weapon, like sharpening a stick to defend yourself from wolves, like Liam Neeson in "The Grey"? Can't do that. . .  yet? Have to fist fight them with your bare hands (You lose).
There is a gun, if you can find it and equally important, ammo. It's the only weapon in the game so far. I've plundered about 15 structures in my 2 hrs and didn't find it.
It seems like there will eventually be some sort of crafting system (via work bench), but its definitely not finished.
Plan on being hardcore and surviving the unforgiving canadian wilderness, by living off the land or out of a cave in a realistic way, without stealing supplies from people? No chance. You are FORCED to break into random structures and steal supplies.
It's fine if you want to do that, but be aware, there is no way around it. I can only assume, based on the way everything is currently balanced, that there are no plans to support that. If it bothers you, as it does me, you may want to wait on purchasing.
I'd like the option to survive off the land, because while thats impossible, I hardly consider it a survival game. You should not NEED to rely on buildings and the contents inside them.
It's rather new, so most of these problems will likely be fixed over time, but as of now, I just can't recommend it. I'm not trying to bash the game, but give useful criticism to the developers so they can improve the game and to you, so that you know what you're buying.

It's such an intense game... It's so unlike other survival games, in the sense that there's nothing really trying to kill you (other than wolves), but even while you explore around, you're watching over your back, because the sound effects in this game are done so well, that it sounds real. Honestly, I was inside a cabin and heard the wind whistling, and had to take my headphones off because I thought it was coming from outside, but it was just the game.
A few tips? Don't stay in one place. That's an absolute waste of time, and you'll probably die. Every day, keep walking. Give yourself something to do. Got extra wood and fire starters? Cook some meat or canned goods or purify some water, find a work bench and fix some stuff. Don't let yourself have nothing to do. Much like real life, if you're going to survive, you need to keep occupied.
Oh, and also, don't ever carry too much, or become "encumbered". I thought there was a glitch or something at first because I could still sprint, other than my fatigue increasing quicker. Nope, no glitch. Your thirst and fatigue will shoot up, and if you don't take care of it, one minute you're walking across a frozen river, the next you're almost compltely blind and can only see a foot or two infront of you. Just, be careful.
Overall, honestly, I have no complaints about this game. For an early access title, it has amazing graphics, music, sound, base storyline (even though it's just sandbox mode right now, there's still some form of a storyline) and it all flows together and works. It feels real. I have high hopes for what shall come in the future.

This game is all about the experience of the small victories in survival. While some describe the game as an effeciency exercise--and I can't entirely disagree with that assessment--for me it is immersive enough that it doesn't feel like an artificial grind but the very real grind of surviving another hour, another day, in a harsh, unforgiving environment.
When I attempt to plan ahead by scavenging deer carcasses for their guts so that I can make fishing line, and I stock the ice fishing hut with wood fuel to keep me warm during a long day of catching salmon, and then carry an overburdened load of 30 pounds of fish across the ice and up a steep slope of snow to my lonely cabin, all before night falls, I am not entirely surprised of my own growing panic when an unexpected snow storm blows in, creating white-out conditions, and I realize I have likely over-shot my destination, and I am lost, with rapidly sinking temperatures, dangerously high levels of fatigue, and a high risk of spraining an ankle.
Cursing, I experience a sinking feeling in my stomach as I drop my heavy load of freshly caught fish and start running in the direction I hope my cabin is in. I blame myself for my own stupidity, for not staying in the fishing hut and waiting out the storm.
I tell myself that this is it, this is when I die. I knew it would come, but I honestly didn't think it would come like this.
But then, just as dark descends, and after not seeing a single thing while frantically running faster and faster, I stumble on a tree, and then a familiar cluster of rocks, and know that I am just a little ways from my cabin door. I thank God, but I try not to allow myself to feel completely relieved because I know something could still go wrong.
I am nearly frozen, can barely keep my vision from blurring--using the last bit of strength I have--when I reach the wooden gate. I stumble inside and slam the door to the howling wind. I creep over to the fireplace and use my last wooden match to light a fire. I begin to warm.
I can go upstairs and rest on the bed, but I choose to lay out my bedroll here, next to the fire. I crouch beside it, stare into the flames, and eat a can of pork and beans.
Today I know and feel, more than any other day of my life, that I am utterly alone.

tl;dr fun gameplay, alright but short story, repetitive challenge mode, subpar endless mode as far as endless modes go, gets stale quickly, devs need to add a level editor to come close to warranting the price
The advertisement and the positive reviews are generally accurate. You can expect some very fun, engaging, and unique gameplay. The story tries hard to be deep, and I found it interesting to some extent, but it's a bit too obvious and in your face. Also, there's a certain moment after the end that slightly soils the rest of the story, essentially saying "market our game for us" (incidentally, if you see all those positive reviewers repeating the same line, that's exactly what the game says to say. Maybe some of those people would have reviewed the game either way, but I feel like this inflates its positive reviews). Luckily or perhaps, unluckily, the story only lasts <2 hours. This says nothing of the amount of content. In terms of number of levels and weapon variety, I have no complaints. There are 25 campaign levels and 9 endless levels, most of which are well designed. As for weapons, there are fists/bat(and other bat-like weapons)/katana/pistol/shotgun/rifle, all of which are well balanced. In addition, there are a number of environment objects you can toss around. Even if that doesn't sound like a lot in text, I never wanted for more weapons because where most games will throw in a lot of weapons and most of them will be useless, all weapons in this game have some utility.
Most replayability will come from endless. Other reviews have said that the challenge mode will as well, but frankly, in challenge mode, you do the same 25 campaign levels with a little change (e.g. katanas only). It gets tiring quickly. I'm not sure why the challenges can't be applied to endless, especially since the game had a mechanism for doing so in beta. Given endless mode's importance, I have to question the lack of a leaderboard. Maybe I'm petty, but it's very nice rising on a leaderboard. I also have to question the presence of the hotswitch feature, where you basically posses someone else's body (also has a cooldown). It was probably easy to program, makes sense in the context of the story, and can be very useful in a tight spot, where you'd die without it. However, prior to getting access to the hotswitch feature, Superhot had a very nice flow and intensity. Afterwards, parts of the game were too easy, I outright forgot about the feature, or worried about when to use it. Superhot is better as a fluid experience. I can already guess someone might comment, "just don't use it," but my playstyle consists of using everything available to me. The levels were also probably made with the hotswitch in mind, so I'd be making it needlessly difficult. Furthermore, the time spent on hotswitch could have been spent on another part of the game (e.g. leaderboards, making melee opponents an actual threat).
The review thus far has actually been rather positive. The gameplay is good, the story is so-so but secondary to endless, and I have a few minor complaints. The reason it's negative is because much like other people, I don't believe the price tag is warranted, and it's not because of the short story as I've made clear, but because the endless mode isn't really that compelling (and that's partially why I made those points above, as possible contributing factors as to why). Perhaps part of this is the lack of a feeling of progression. Sure, the number gets bigger, but from what I've seen, endless just continues with the same thing forever. Given the name, that's reasonable, but the enemies' deficiencies become obvious, and the difficulty becomes too much about dealing with mobs of them. Melee enemies are rarely a threat, so the set of weapons I previously said was fine (and still is in the player's hand) is cut down to 3, just the guns (but they have infinite ammo for the enemies). The AI seems to be very basic, and often the game consists of just doing the same strategies in reponse to the same actions. This seems like it will inevitably become monotonus.
A level editor would break up the lack of content and tedium. The slowed gameplay very nicely supports strategy / puzzle type levels, where endless is more luck and figuring out what to do. To actually address my complaints, a massive amount of content would have to be added or changed, which isn't feasible, though I really wonder what this game's budget was to demand $25.
Edit: After playing some more, I'm further convinced the game isn't worth the price tag. Due to the slowed nature of the game, it's not a test of mechanical skills (which isn't bad in itself). It's about tactics and patience. Patience because while you CAN look around while in slow-motion, more often than not, there's nothing there, so it eventually becomes annoying and many deaths are the result of not bothering to look around. Furthermore, every enemy CAN be dodged, even the rifle and shotgun ones. The issue is: it's a lot of work, a lot of zigzagging, and a lot of jumping. So even more deaths are the result of bum rushing them in hopes that you won't have to bother with that. As far as tactics go, it's a very, very simple brand of tactics. You're only ever faced with a small amount of situations, and the response is always fits into a few specific responses. The levels seem increasingly poorly designed, given how easy it is to camp in a corner in most of them, which is easily the most effective strategy in the game because you just have to shoot down a single path and get an infinite supply of ammo from enemies. So, even the gameplay becomes tedious at some point, at least in terms of endless. I'd still be very interested in a level editor.

Pros:
+ It's a Tales of game.  If you are fan of the series, buy it now.
+ The music is incredible.
+ The main cast of characters is a lot of fun and they all have great chemistry.
+ There is a large amount of content (skipping side quests, it still took me over 50 hours to complete).
Cons:
- The story.  It's fairly simple, but at the same time there are a lot of odd bits here and there that don't make any sense.  I wonder if there were several changes in direction during development?
- The world.  The setting, the characters, the music, and the story (when it was coherent) all made me want to love the world.  But I don't.  The larger world map that the game features actually makes the world feel more empty and lifeless than past games.  The cities all felt the same, and I felt that in terms of locations--with the notable exception of four dungeons that occur mid to late game--fail to deliver on the promise that the opening of the game presents.
- The skill system in this game makes no sense.  I've played most of the Tales games available in the West and this is the first time I've found myself not understanding how a major portion of the battle system is supposed to work.  It can largely be ignored, but it's still frustrating that so much work and thought went into such a clumsy system for gear.
- The AI in this game is a new low for the franchise.  As usual, you can set tactics for the AI in the menu but more control over AI behavior would have been great for this game.  Your teammates flat out don't use the armatization feature correctly, and in the time it takes you to switch characters to make a change manually, the AI will have messed it up on your other two characters.  The AI also has a peculiar tendency to run straight into a boss as it uses a Mystic Art.  Depending on how lucky you get, the final boss and hard optional bosses can be a nightmare, because the suicidal AI will completely mess up a run.
Overall, I loved the game and would recommend it to pretty much any RPG fan.  There are some things the game did badly, but I only spent so much time on those things because the game itself is so great and could have soared to even higher heights.  I regret none of the time I poured into this game.

Bit rough around the edges but I find the game to be pretty enjoyable overall.
I'll start with what I don't like though:
- Fusion system is absolute donkey butt. It wasn't anything the Tales series needed, and back in Tales of Vesperia, it wasn't intrusive or forced on you unlike in this game. All-in-all, it's not an interesting system, and sometimes is really roundabout when you want specific skills, and fusion is NEEDED if you want to get stronger. That's just a no in my book.
- AI really needs work. Higher difficulties are fun and all, but nothing can sour you more than when the AI just refuses to guard when an enemy is telegraphing an attack, or doing an unblockable move (denoted by a "!!").
- Early on a lot of the wide open spaces are pretty bland, and the dungeon design is much the same throughout the game.
- English Dubbing. More of personal taste thing, but the Tales series dubbing has declined in quality since Symphonia 2/Xillia, and for me, voice acting makes or breaks the game, so I just stick to the Japanese setting.
The In-Betweens:
- Armatization. Extremely fun early on, but once you get late enough into the game, the combo variety is lackluster. The overeliance on it to actually feel like you're making a dent sometimes is problematic, but you don't actually NEED it to do significant damage, it essentially gives you the normal stats you would have in a Tales game by combining both characters, ensuring you don't get 2-3-shot, which will happen fairly often. You can force your AI characters into Armatization, but sometimes they'll undo it almost immediately, or undo it as soon as you switch characters, which is INCREDIBLY wasteful and could use a fix.
- Combo variety. Much different to previous games where instead of having basic attacks and being able to chain artes into each other, you have martial artes, which are essentially just preset combos, and seraphic artes. Every attack is essentially an arte, and the variety leaves a bit to be desired early on, and you have no basic attacks so you're limited to just 4 moves per combo. Feels really limiting and like an attempt at "Devil May Cry"-style gameplay. Stick to what you're good at, Tales devs! Later on though, it gets a bit more fun, and the moves are pretty cool.
- Banish Blasts. Are these a joke? I really can't tell. While they ARE indeed powerful attacks, they take long to wind up without the proper skills set, and they can be interrupted EXTREMELY easily, so I went without using them 90% of the time as they just usually wound up being a waste of BC. Could use some changes, unless I'm misunderstanding or not seeing something. Cool in idea, but not execution.
- Weakness system. Could be better explained. In order to stagger enemies and actually do significant damage, you need to hit an enemy with its weakness, or what it is susceptible to in order to get a "Power Hit" combo going. It's not a bad thing, but I don't consider it a good thing either.
The Good:
- I'm actually finding the story and characters to be fairly interesting. Malevolence is uttered A LOT, but the cast is a pretty likable bunch. I could've done without a lot of the Alisha-related things, but other than that, it was nice watching the main character, Sorey, grow as a sheperd.
- The character designs. Initially, I REALLY disliked the designs back when the game was first unveileved, but they're actually really nice and fairly pleasing to look at, and a HUGE step up from the cluster duck that is the transition of Xillia -> Xillia 2's character designs. Holy jeebus those were an eyesore.
- The soundtrack has been really great, and some songs like Zaveid's Theme or Rising Up really stick out as great tracks overall.
- Combat. Being a Tales game, and despite the lack of variety the player experiences early on, once you get later into the game and actually have more than just a "Mash the A Button" combo, it gets a lot more fun, and the variety becomes much more pleasing. The spells are pretty fun, and they make you feel pretty powerful as well.
- The skill system. I actually like the skill system in this game, but the fusion system makes it a pain to actually get skills you want sometimes. You can stack multiples of the same skill to stack the bonuses you get from them, and unlock more skills as a result, or you can fill up a whole row of skills to unlock stat bonuses that'll help you along. Though it does irk me a bit and makes me feel like min-maxing, and can feel overwhelming and like you need to choose too much in the beginning.
- Lords of the Land system. This time grade is earned through not only battles, but through the Lords of the Land system, and you can level those up for bonuses, and later unlock something in the game that allows you to boost enemy levels by a large margin, and that's one of the things I enjoyed a lot. There are plenty of more bonuses from the system, but that is one of the more outstanding ones.
Despite the bad things I've said about the game, I'm genuinely enjoying it, and if you don't mind a slow start to things, I'd recommend playing the game. It could've used some more thought and polish, but I think it's a solid entry in the franchise, and a solid game all around. Though hopefully they stop with all this DLC nonsense, 'cause that's just not cool mang.

Tales Of Zestiria is a game that is filled with action packed battles.  The visuals alone are sure to please the biggest JRPG hater out there.  Unfortunately, the game lacks in most other areas.  It has real time on map battles with stunning visuals and a huge array of attacks from all characters.  The fighting is a bit different from the previous games, but it is more than manageable.  You play as Sorey, a goody two shoes who never gets in trouble and NEVER DOES THE WHOLE FREAKING GAME.  And all the other characters....we will talk about this later
OK, now that I got that out of the way.  First let me say this.  I am a HUGE Tales series fan.  I would not call myself a fanboy. I do not get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if someone says something bad about the game.  It isn't everyone's bag.  However, it is important to note that I have loved all the other games tremendously, except for a certain one, which we will get into later. Lets start with some lists.
The GRAPHICS:  The graphics are down right amazing.  They are crisp, clear, and full of life.  It is a JRPG so it naturally looks like one.  It has a big open world and world map with monsters lurking around.  Nothing too different from before.  There is one hiccup.  The FPS.  I know what you are thinking, "oh god, another guy thinking the framerate is bad".  In fact, the framerate is OK.  I do just mean OK though.  It is perfect in the map and during cut-scenes and during in game cut-scenes.  In fighting, the framerate is near perfect too.  NEAR.  If you have a major battle, with a major bad guy or there are alot of artes (especially advanced ones) the framerate drops for about 1-2 seconds to about 5 fps, and it doesnt happen alot.  I noticed it only happening during the last 5 or 6 major intense battles near the end.  It is MORE than playable and excusable and should not be a reason to not buy this game, however, it should be mentioned.
The Story: The beginning of the game is amazing.  For about the first 2 hours or so I was very intrigued by the story and could not put it down.  Unfortunately, the fighting is very boring and mundane due to a lack of skills learned and being a very low level.  This was not the case in earlier installments.  You start off as a human about 16 years old named Sorey.  You live with a group of ghost like people called Seraphim.  They cannot be seen by humans unless they are pure at heart and taught.  You go on a journey to become the Shephard.  A guardian of the world that is gifted/cursed with the gift of defeating malevolence with his seraphim pals.  Malevolence is a dark force that turns humans and seraphim into bad guys.  It is basically the evil in their hearts.  So the entire game you play as a guy that never gets angry, never goes into battle all fierce, never gets mad, and never does anything bad EVER.  He is like a super religeous sheltered person that has never been outside.  It is very annoying.  ALL THE CHARACTERS ARE LIKE THIS!  Very very annoying.  No character development.  Good voice acting, but I still ended up hating every character.  That has never happened to me before n an RPG, and I play tons of RPGS.  I found myself skipping about 90% of the dialog because it was very boring and everyone was just sitting around crying in like every cut scene.  This is how the cut scene went: something bad happens, someone feels emotional for 5 minutes.  That person talks about it to 1 other person for 5 minutes, then your other party shows up and they talk about it for 5 minutes.  it is super annoying and dumb.  If I had to pick a deal breaker, it would be the story.  The end was cool, but the whole game was not worth the pay off.  There is one important thing to note, when you start a new game with zero save files, you don't get to see the classic opening.  I thought this was soooo stupid.  I hated it.  I thought the game was bugged.  I played it anyway and about 2 hours in something happens and it starts.  It is so fricken cool and gives me chills just typing about it.  Probably the coolest thing I have seen in a tales game to date.  Also there is a fast travel system.  It is very bad and the game hardly ever tells you where to go next.  You could literally spend HOURS trying to figure out where to go. and since the game won't let you fast travel, you will end up walking the world map FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE!!!!

The FIGHTING:  OK, so you have 6 characters in your party.  2 are human and the other are seraphim.  Te seraphim can bind with the humans giving special abilities.  It is pretty damn fun.  One thing I didn't like was how the seraphim are super OP and if you bind with Mikleo, you will kill everyone even on the hardest difficulty, rather easily.  It will just take forever.  There is no mana.  You get sc which depletes after a combo.  You then have to block to refill it.  It refills fast so not too bad, however if you use a special arte expect to block for a second or two.  Can be kind of frustrating.  I love the old orange gel system in all the other games. Skills are tied to weapons, which is dumb.  You will have pages and pages of tutorials over the fighting, but literally they can all be ignored.  It is very easy to get the hang of it. Almost all the stuff they say about special things tied to weapons don't matter nearly as much as attack power or magic power or whatever.  It is pointless and useless and serves no purpose.  Also, they fighting is like Graces F, which alot of people like.  I prefer the normal attack combo, then chaining specials together.  I do not like having special moves being apart of my basic attacks.  It makes for more button mashing.  Just a preference and not a reason to not buy it.  I personally didn't like the fighting at all, but all my friends did.
Basic RPG ELEMENTS:  It has then all, except, NO ultimate weapons, NO ultimate spells (unless you preorder), no mana.
Also, in all the other Tales games you get to find out a master chef for special recipes you can collect. This is not present in this game and it was rather disappointing.  Also there is no air ship or anyway to get around the map via vehicle.  There is a fast travel system, but I found it very annoying and vague.  Also, fast travel should not be in RPG's.  Other than that, it works great as a classic RPG.
The FINAL VERDICT:  If I had to choose a scale, I would give it a 5 out of 10.  So that means average.  Not bad.  I would definitely buy it, just not for 60 bucks.  The onyl reason I did was because Tales of Symphonia was free with preorder and that is like 30 bucks alone and one of my favorite games ever.  If I was iffy about this game, I would wait for a humble bundle, or a steam Christmas sale or something.  I think a good price to pay would be 30 bucks +- 5 dollars.  It was fun while it lasted and  exploring was ok.  And 30 bucks for a game that lasts 40-90 hours is a great deal, even if it isn't your cup of tea.  It is the second worst Tales game in the series, behind Legendia.  Legendia however should never be mentioned to anyone.  It was god awful.  It was made by the Project MelFes team and they were only allowed to make that one game cause it was one of the worst video games of all time.  Don;t even get me started on that garbage.  It almost made me stop buying tales games all together.  So legendia would be a 0 out of 10.  That goes to show you the huge gap Zestiria has over Legendia.  I would definetly buy Zestiria when the price is right, but next time you go to your game store and you see legendia, throw it on the ground and stomp on it then kick the guy behind the counter in the shins for selling it.  Say, "Matt sent me".
