RPG Maker VX Ace is a newer, improved version of a software which, as the title states, helps you make RPGs. It's not a game, but a software to make games. While with a lot of work you can make quite complex, not necessarily retro looking games, the base idea of RPG Maker is to make RPGs that are styled like those of the early 90’s: mostly 2D and 16-bit looking, such as the older Final Fantasy titles, or other such so called JRPG styled games.
I had used RPG Maker in the past -one of the first versions, in fact- and I’m glad to say the whole selection of menus and things you can do are much easier to find your way through now, and you can truly have a very short, very simple game out in a matter of days thanks to the wide variety of stock images they provide.
It might look quite confusing at first, but don’t be daunted by the amount of menus and options the program has to offer. Simply find a tutorial for beginners online and follow it, and you’ll be sure to be able to find your way around it. Or, if you’re the adventurous type, do what I did at first and learn by trial and error for the basics, it was also quite fun to learn this way!
So long as you're trying to make a game that follows the typical RPG rules, RPG Maker VX Ace makes scripting basic game features easy, as it will take care of most of the coding and you just have to fill in the options; it has some pre-made sample maps that you can use when you’re just starting out; as well as a character generator (for sprites and heads, you can change the eye color and shape, nose and mouth shape, skin color, clothes, and hair style and color between a few choices) that gives you a small amount of freedom on how your characters will look, while still working with the existing bases. This way you can busy yourself to learn the very basics of making a game thanks to not having to worry about the art and background.
The slightly more advanced basics (or should I say, intermediate scripting features) might take a little longer to learn (I still haven’t, I’m still only figuring out the basics of what this program can do), but if your goal is to make a small, simple game, you will surely find RPG Maker a great help. And, if you’re willing to delve into the world of scripting and use your own art, you can truly make of your game a masterpiece that might stand out from the rest, since with RPG Maker and some work you can customize everything: from the classes, through the damage formulas, to the menus and everything in between.
There's lots of user scripts to be found online that will help you with more complex stuff too, if you look for it! As well as free and paid packs of sprites, tiles, etc for download, some which are only allowed to be used with non-commercial games, while others have commercial licenses (be sure to check that when you download them!)
One thing that bothered me: Adding new tilesets to the default can be easy, but it’s not overly intuitive; some imported right and some not so, even though I added them as the tutorial told me to. Having better automation for this as well as for transferring tilesets you might make to someone else would be nice. Of course, since I’m new at this it could have been user error, but I feel like this step should be as easy as changing the images for the characters was, to make it more user friendly.
RPG Maker is good for beginners and advanced users alike, regardless of how big or small their project is. The only downside of it is that the official DLCs with music, new tilesets and characters can be quite expensive, but if you take into account that most of those are allowed for use in commercial games, it’s not too bad. They can, however, be quite an expense on an already expensive piece of software.
I’m not at all good with RPG Maker yet, and that is why this review for it is so short and not overly in-depth on all the possibilities you have, but as a beginner I can say: if you want to start out with a 2D RPG, RPG Maker is one of your best choices (though by far not the only one); if, however, you’re looking to make something a bit different from 16-bit styled games, you might find RPG Maker a bit more difficult to learn than you’d like to make a simpler game.

I first reviewed this game back in very early Beta, and even then I recommended this game. My opinion still has not changed. If you like survival games, but want a change from the standard zombie game that's flooded the market, pick this one up and give it a try.
Scores:
Gameplay   4/5
Visuals        4/5
Sound      4.5/5
Overall        4/5
Gameplay:
Depending on the difficulty you play on, random chance has a huge effect on your game. I've had games where I started in an ideal location with all the tools I need right at my fingertips, and I've had games where I walked around a rock and was mauled by a wolf less than 2 minutes after starting. The game isn't overly punishing for the most part, one of the few spots that I have a grump with is the food/water requirements of the character. On dificulties above easy, your character has to consume huge amounts of food every single day (multiple kilograms of meat for example) but relatively little water.
In The Long Dark, your character isn't MacGyver, s/he can't make jury-rigged stuff to do anything they need, you can improve your skills such as ice fishing or harvesting animals you hunt, but crafting takes a smaller role in The Long Dark than it does in many other games. I find this mostly refreshing. "Well of course you can't just machine a hunting rifle out in the wilderness from scrap metal and raw wood"
Visuals:
The Long Dark has some spectacular views in the game. It's not a photorealistic game by any measure, it's more stylized, like a watercolor painting. It's very pretty but it's not always perfect. Weather effects can all but whiteout the screen (which I suppose is rather realistic), and sometimes there's invisible wall effects that prevent you from moving somewhere that looks accessible. (The lack of a 'Jump' or 'Climb up' feature is strange, and frustrating)
Sound:
The Long Dark has amazing sound effects and music. The music is kept far in the background mostly and only brought up to noticeable levels at significant moments. Hearing the howls of a wolf pack tracking you at night is nervewracking, like it should.

tl;dr fun gameplay, alright but short story, repetitive challenge mode, subpar endless mode as far as endless modes go, gets stale quickly, devs need to add a level editor to come close to warranting the price
The advertisement and the positive reviews are generally accurate. You can expect some very fun, engaging, and unique gameplay. The story tries hard to be deep, and I found it interesting to some extent, but it's a bit too obvious and in your face. Also, there's a certain moment after the end that slightly soils the rest of the story, essentially saying "market our game for us" (incidentally, if you see all those positive reviewers repeating the same line, that's exactly what the game says to say. Maybe some of those people would have reviewed the game either way, but I feel like this inflates its positive reviews). Luckily or perhaps, unluckily, the story only lasts <2 hours. This says nothing of the amount of content. In terms of number of levels and weapon variety, I have no complaints. There are 25 campaign levels and 9 endless levels, most of which are well designed. As for weapons, there are fists/bat(and other bat-like weapons)/katana/pistol/shotgun/rifle, all of which are well balanced. In addition, there are a number of environment objects you can toss around. Even if that doesn't sound like a lot in text, I never wanted for more weapons because where most games will throw in a lot of weapons and most of them will be useless, all weapons in this game have some utility.
Most replayability will come from endless. Other reviews have said that the challenge mode will as well, but frankly, in challenge mode, you do the same 25 campaign levels with a little change (e.g. katanas only). It gets tiring quickly. I'm not sure why the challenges can't be applied to endless, especially since the game had a mechanism for doing so in beta. Given endless mode's importance, I have to question the lack of a leaderboard. Maybe I'm petty, but it's very nice rising on a leaderboard. I also have to question the presence of the hotswitch feature, where you basically posses someone else's body (also has a cooldown). It was probably easy to program, makes sense in the context of the story, and can be very useful in a tight spot, where you'd die without it. However, prior to getting access to the hotswitch feature, Superhot had a very nice flow and intensity. Afterwards, parts of the game were too easy, I outright forgot about the feature, or worried about when to use it. Superhot is better as a fluid experience. I can already guess someone might comment, "just don't use it," but my playstyle consists of using everything available to me. The levels were also probably made with the hotswitch in mind, so I'd be making it needlessly difficult. Furthermore, the time spent on hotswitch could have been spent on another part of the game (e.g. leaderboards, making melee opponents an actual threat).
The review thus far has actually been rather positive. The gameplay is good, the story is so-so but secondary to endless, and I have a few minor complaints. The reason it's negative is because much like other people, I don't believe the price tag is warranted, and it's not because of the short story as I've made clear, but because the endless mode isn't really that compelling (and that's partially why I made those points above, as possible contributing factors as to why). Perhaps part of this is the lack of a feeling of progression. Sure, the number gets bigger, but from what I've seen, endless just continues with the same thing forever. Given the name, that's reasonable, but the enemies' deficiencies become obvious, and the difficulty becomes too much about dealing with mobs of them. Melee enemies are rarely a threat, so the set of weapons I previously said was fine (and still is in the player's hand) is cut down to 3, just the guns (but they have infinite ammo for the enemies). The AI seems to be very basic, and often the game consists of just doing the same strategies in reponse to the same actions. This seems like it will inevitably become monotonus.
A level editor would break up the lack of content and tedium. The slowed gameplay very nicely supports strategy / puzzle type levels, where endless is more luck and figuring out what to do. To actually address my complaints, a massive amount of content would have to be added or changed, which isn't feasible, though I really wonder what this game's budget was to demand $25.
Edit: After playing some more, I'm further convinced the game isn't worth the price tag. Due to the slowed nature of the game, it's not a test of mechanical skills (which isn't bad in itself). It's about tactics and patience. Patience because while you CAN look around while in slow-motion, more often than not, there's nothing there, so it eventually becomes annoying and many deaths are the result of not bothering to look around. Furthermore, every enemy CAN be dodged, even the rifle and shotgun ones. The issue is: it's a lot of work, a lot of zigzagging, and a lot of jumping. So even more deaths are the result of bum rushing them in hopes that you won't have to bother with that. As far as tactics go, it's a very, very simple brand of tactics. You're only ever faced with a small amount of situations, and the response is always fits into a few specific responses. Well, where should I begin?
Dungeon defenders 2 is the sequel to what's probably one of my favourite games, to be honest, it's quite disappointing but I can't hold too much against it as it is only in alpha at the moment, if I haven't updated this and it's in like beta when you're reading this then you should probably just ignore it. This is what I will say for now, however:
The game is rather similar to the original DD but to me it just feels straight up bad in comparison. Let's talk about the main two components of both games, combat and strategy:
The combat of this game is quite different to the original, in the original you will be greeted by hordes of weak enemies who surround you and make combat a challenge as you smoothly slice or gun them down dodging lots of orcs (basically like big tank enemies who slowly swing big axes) and projectiles along the way, it sounds easy but as there are so many of them, it makes it an awesome but still balanced challenge.
However, in this second installment, it's changed for the worse, there are around 15 enemies on each part who all just feel a chore to kill, they have a lot more health but as it's not a proper fun horde, they are all easy to dodge and kill, it just takes AGES, it takes around 5 hits just to kill a goblin (a small enemy which is extremely weak, obviously there are a lot more in DD1). Did I mention melee? Using a melee weapon is just annoying as anything, every attack lunges you forward in the most awkward and uncontrollable way with a melee weapon. I've fell off cliffs trying to fight as a squire (the knight class in the game), so melee weapons and melee combat has just turned to total crap. Ranged weapons aren't any better though, really, all you do with one is move backward and shoot, which is no fun, I'd probably rather be a messed up knight, jerking uncontrollably. Basically, all the combat really is, is hitting and using your abilites when you can (just extra powerful attacks in this game really, and self healing). Squires can block but in this game it's useless as anything, I don't even see any difference in the damage they do me.
The strategy in this is probably even worse than the combat, let's start with DD1, all the maps could be built up in lots of different ways, some ways a lot better than others, all of the good looking builds worth trying, if you're smart (or you just have ridiculously high stats for the level) you can just build up and sit back to watch it perfectly working, or just grab a cup of tea. Now let's look at DD2, there are two obvious builds for every map, put turrets on the walls of the map and walls to block them off as they die, or just put turrets and walls on the obvious bits of the path. Both aren't really that different at all and no matter whether you chose the best out of the two possible decent builds or not, all the towers need constant supervision, repairing, fighting and all that. There are also environmental traps (such as valves you turn to release smoke and damage the enemies) which you NEED to use, forcing a lot of players in one game, it's hard to play with just one friend, you end up on a public game packed with 7 year old idiots. All the towers also have huge like spaceboxes so you can't place a tower within a meter's range of another, making placing them properly difficult, in DD1 they just couldn't overlap, unless they were monk or hunter traps. In short, there's no real strategy, you just need to run around like a headless chicken attending to your towers and activating environmental traps.
Let's move on to looting, this isn't that main a thing in both but it gets a verrrrrrrrrrrry annoying in DD2, you get a new, better weapon almost every wave and upgrading them does barely anything to the stats, all considered (In DD1 you need to upgrade your weapon to do good damage, which in my opinion is good). There is an option to automatically collect loot but it fills up the few bag spaces you have in DD2 very fast and you find yourself sorting good from rubbish after every level. There aren't many different models the items can spawn with either, so you will probably find someone with the same weapon as you in a public tavern. There's also only like 20 different pets in DD2 but tonnes in DD1 and in DD1 EVERYTHING spawns in different sizes and colours, nothing does in 2. This makes looting very bland. The items do spawn with different weights but this is broken so that heavier weapons do more damage per second, even with the same damage stats.
Now on to DLC, there's a lot of better, more optional and reasonably priced DLC in the first game, such as different characters with unique abilities but in DD2 it's inventory space for £20, More items and IN GAME FREAKING CURRENCY(!!!!!!!!!!!!??????????) for £30, how reasonably priced, fun and worth it this is (sarcasm BTW), oh and if anyone wants it's £17 for a costume pack on special offer!
Summary:
DD2= rubbish
DD1= awesome
If you like the look of this then just play DD1, you'll have a much better time.

This game is as entertaining as it is creepy and suspensful. You wander the 2D world environment in its ever spooky atmosphere with the D-pad, and use the Action Button on various items and objects to help you clear puzzles. Though don't let this single-button game get the better of you...

The only thing that can deter you from solving that pesky puzzle is how much patience you're willing to devote to this game.
While not -quite- on par with Portal 2 or some of those other action-y, high end puzzle solvers, LIMBO is definitely worth giving a try if you have ten bucks to spare, and an aching to dodge and escape flinging bear traps, shadowy figures with blow darts, an oversized arachnid and more, all hell bent on sending you to an early, prepubescent grave.

It's a very uniqe game, that's why it's gotten so much attention.
I for one, reccomend this if you like horror, and I will continue to go back to it when i'm feeling bored.

Here's another fad of the game industry which proves its cancerous state: hd remakes, remasters an the likes of them.

Actually, I do have to admit that remakes allow people like me - those who didn't bother to buy into something at the time - or fresh gamers to experience goodies from the past. It's just that I'm not okay with giving that much amount of money to a company which does not care at all how their final product turns out. The thought alone that some people acquired the rights to publish Indigo Prophecy in 1080p glory, did a poor job at updating the graphics and added mind-blowing controller support (which isn't needed, at all, but a nice extra) and are charging 9 € for it is quite disturbing. Those guys didn't do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥for that game and are cashing in dem Dollars and Monopoly Monies.
That's the problem with all those new old games. People don't give a ♥♥♥♥, in most cases. They just want to make money.
Buuuut besides that, Fahrenheit does not deliver the experience I expected it would deliver. Just look behind the qtes, that's the least offender. Personally, I can enjoy a video game if it delivers on some levels - eg story, artstyle, music, you name it. Problem is, the story of this game starts of really promising, only to show you one big middle finger after half of it. Seriously, don't even bother. I admit that I had fun for the first 2 hours, really, but everything after that is just one big disappointing mess of bad and unambitious writing. The godawful quick time events make matters worse.

Survive a challenging platforming segment, find yourself crashing against clumsy, chore-like puzzles. These two gamestyles do not flow together here. Also, anytime you change graphics settings on the game, it does not do so smoothly.  If these minor bugs could be resolved it would go a long way.  None of these bugs are game breaking, and once you get into the game itself, they are not present.
It is also nice that American audiences can now see the uncensored version of the game. I'm not sure how necessary it is, but still good to be able to experience the game the way the developer intended.
All in all, I hope Quantic Dream continues to support this game with a few patches to smooth everything out.  They've come this far, they might as well take it all the way.

This is a "remastered" and uncut version of Fahrenheit.
A strange interactive movie where you control almost all characters by walking around, branching dialog and quicktime events. The remastered graphics are nowhere to be seen but its acceptable for a good looking 2004 year game.  The soundtrack is really varied, but maybe a bit stereotypic.
The camera and controls are horrific. The clues for the quicktime events blend into the background so its hard to see what to do. Often there are no instant kill, but the miss system is not as elegant as for say Heavy Rain or A wolf amongst us.
Some of the voice acting is really horrible. The actors also overact all the time, swinging their heads back and forth when they talk. The audio is badly compressed, captured from a time when it was standard to have bad quality on voice because of how much space audio takes. (sad that the master tapes did not have full quality samples since it today would be no problem releasing with full quality voice samples)
So why recommend this game?
This is a classic games. Telltale games are clearly inspired from Quantic Dreams. I hope that many buys this game so we can get a PC conversion of Heavy Rain that was a great interative movie.
The story, using camera techniques, some of the adult themes are all a breath of fresh air even in todays gaming.
I do however hate Steam/publishers localized pricing system. I have always thought it was because of taxes (for example EU where some countries have 25% VAT). But no: Its just location based. The publishers have released the game cheaper elsewhere, they can afford to sell this on a sale.

As soon as I saw this game, I bought it on impulse, without a second thought. I went into this without watching any trailers, or reading any info. I would suggest it to anyone who has a folder full of unpublished games or notebook full of unfinished ideas, or just a mind full of untapped potential. This game is like a secret, warm space you can take some comfort in, because you are not alone.

The big problem I have is the level design, or I guess game mode type.
First to 20 kills and no objectives to play off of. So many games devolve into one side camping on a side of a rock, or in their own spawn, with no incentive to move forward. They get an improved position with the only cost being boredom. Not like any space on the map has any value with the lack of capture points, so it becomes a weird stalemate that is not very fun. So either both sides sit there bored, or a few people decide every so often to suicide to give the other team some kills.
Gameplay is fine, but the other issue hurting this game is the CPU progression limit. So you get to build a new ship in a new class yay! Oh wait you have horrible cpu limitations for building actual interesting looking ships, as well as not actually getting your abilities until rank 3 or 4. So chances are you like everyone else will just build a variation of box with a bunch of guns on it.
1 gun = 50 cpu
1 core block(4) + 1 armor on it(4) = 8 cpu.
So if you add and armor 6 squares, and you might as well have had another gun on your ship. Free blocks dont cost any that is true-and that is why everyone has small boxes with the most guns they can fit on them. I tried making a caracal from eve and the unneccesary, all cosmetic sidewings and nose section were 120ish CPU without armor. Been using this for the past week to try and make a game. I've had some experience with other versions of the program (2000, XP) but this is the first time I've actually tried to learn the program. So far, I'm satisfied.
RPG Maker VX Ace provides a pretty decent framework if you're trying to make an RPG (or a Yume Nikki clone or a horror game or whatever). The key word here is framework- the assets provided are beautifully made, but somewhat generic. If you really want to make a game your own, you'll have to generate your own assets or find them online. As long as you take time to learn how to use it, you can pretty much do anything, and what you can't do with the engine, you can usually accomplish with the use of scripts. Hinterland Studios is by far one of my favorite if not favorite game developers. Their dedication and love for this beautiful project shows in every design choice that they make. They rely on their fans, but know the direction they want to take. They want to push a product and keep people happy, but have no intention of rushing anything. Updates come when they're ready.
And when the updates do come, they're beautiful. I have to say I've never been disappointed by this game. I saw a glimpse of this game early in 2017 and thought it looked fun. I then sort of forgot about it, all up until it released 2 days ago. Now, having beaten it, I have to say that A Hat in Time will easily find its place in my top 5 games of 2017 list!
The game is a traditional collect-a-thon platformer, that draws heavily on classic 3D platformers. In my mind the heaviest influencers would be Super Mario 64, Banjo & Kazooie and lastly, but certainly not least: Psychonauts! This last inspiration becomes most obvious in a certain train-related level that I enjoyed immensely! It is also the influence of Psychonauts that sets this game apart from most other collect-a-thons of recent years.
The writing in A Hat in Time is not perfect, though, and I feel like it is struggling to decide on its audience. For the most part the game is funny and whimsical and could be considered an 'all ages' experience, but occasionally the game slips into using darker themes. At one point you are literally ordered to 'murder' a bunch of spirits. At other points another character openly suggests dismembering enemies, and towards the end of the game even character suicide becomes a thing, in a way. It seems that the writing tries to mostly go for a more mature audience, those adults like myself who's nostalgia for the 90's and early 00's this game feeds. Your mileage may wary, but in my case I found myself laughing out loud at many of the jokes in this game.
The gameplay is nothing too special. You run, jump, double jump, dive, then jump again. It's a bit surprising how much freedom of movement you have from the word go, and how much more the game expands as time goes on. New abilities are granted through, what else: hats! One hat lets you see into the spirit world, another turns you into a heavy ice statue, another yet lets you sprint fast or even ride around on a cute scooter!
That last one brings us to the most obvious thing about the game, though it is a point that bears repeating: this game is CUTE! The art style is impeccable and I was surprised to see the Unreal engine used in this way. The game is not without faults, though, and there are a few points in the game where you can see the engine not quite adapting to the style the developers wanted to deliver. However, for the most part, the game makes sure you don't get to see these shortcomings for more than a split second before moving you right along.
In the end, whether or not you will enjoy this game comes down to your nostalgia factor. If those old games I mentioned before, Mario 64, Banjo&Kazooie or Psychonauts tickle your fancy, then A Hat in Time may very well do you a world of good. If those games were not for you, or you never experienced them in their day, then the nostalgia-pandering of this game might end up irritating you in the long run and many of the jokes might not open up to you.
Still, I recommend the game and feel like this might end up being one of those rare games that even I 100% over time.

Okay, I haven't played Yooka-Laylee so I can't compare the two games. Regardless though...
A Hat in Time is one of my most favorite 3D platformer out right now (Not counting the classics.)
I think the art style is quite appealing and many of the worlds were beautiful to look at and explore. Chapter 1's Mafia town is admittedly a bit boring in comparison to other worlds and I found myself preferring anywhere else but there just because everywhere else was more interesting to me. The haunted Forests of Subcon Valley, movie sets of Dead Bird Studios, and the vast islands of Alpine Skyline was where I think the game shined and had me lost the most.
The collectables are fun to chase after and I found myself 100% completing the game. However 100% is a lie. It doesn't take into account the hidden Rift Tokens so that bites. There's also no good way of making sure you grabbed everything. No tracker for Yarns Balls so that also doesn't fall into the 100% complete and by the end I had every hat crafter but still 25 freaking yarns leftover. What's the point?
The music was really great listening to and getting a hold of the remixes through the Orb Machine was nice so you get some music variety in the levels. Customization was also great when you unlocked Hat Styles and Color Schemes. Howeve it's held back by the fact that all Styles, Remixes, and Color schemes are hidden behind a Slots style mini-game that uses Rift Tokens or you get a free one for beating a rift. There's a limited amount of Tokens and tries at the Slots and there's no current way I see of getting every customization item. Taking away against from completionists that want true 100%.
Story is lacking and it sounds like there's a build up between you an early ally, but then they never bring her up again until the ending. Clearly this was not the focus of the game. I enjoyed the little stories I got in each world with their respective main NPCs though. The final fight lacked the proper build up though in my opinion even though I loved the fight.
There's even an issue of the game's title. "A Hat in Time." Well aside from collecting the Time Pieces, there wasn't much of any focus on time in the game. Were we on a time limit for Hat Kid to get home? Is Hat Kid a time traveler? Never quite touched on. Time elements were just really few and far between. It's only there to justify your "rival's" motivation for wanting the Time Pieces.
Hat Kid herself is a fun and cute character. But that's where it ends sadly. She seems to have 0 concern about anyone else and simply wants her Time Pieces back. And that's fine, she's a neutral party. As the game currently is though, we don't know enough about Hat Kid to really care about her goal or understand her. Why is getting home important? We were shown and told nothing.
While it does sound like I've railed on this game, I can't help but still love it to bits. I sunk myself into finding everything and loved the other worlds out there and simply being lost in exploration. The controls aren't the tightest I've played with but that didn't matter to me. I had my fun running and jumping and never felt I messed something up or took damage because a control didn't funciton right. It was afun ride and I enjoyed most of the characters I was preented with.
Hands down though, the Crows are the best characters. Sorry, I meant my fellow Express Owls.
Overall 8/10 for me. Loved my time with it, but the areas that felt lacking hold the game back from earning a 10/10 in my book. I still reccomend the game a lot though. To me, it was worth backing it and I paid a higher price than $29.99 so at this price, it's quite worth it to me.

I'm going to break this down into a few sections, because i'm genuinely eager to convince people that this is a game worth buying. I was not supplied a code by developers, nor do I ever write reviews on Steam, but this game honestly compelled me to do just that.
First, lets talk about the plot. Without giving too much away, especially because there isn't really much to give away beyond whats left to interpretation, SUPERHOT is a game about a game. That doesn't sound too original at first, what with this new trend of metafiction we've been seeing in indie games like Undertale or Pony Island, but this game is just a little bit different. You find yourself playing a faceless protagonist. No, really, he has no face, nor does anybody else in SUPERHOT. Not much is revealed about the protagonist, or any of the "characters" for that matter, however what we do learn, aside from spoilers that i'll leave out, is that the character is a gamer in what is presumably the near future, because it seems that much of the gaming world is hooked on VR. SUPERHOT is just that, a VR game. However it is sent to you by an online acquaintance with the stipulation that it is a cracked and unfinished game that was stumbled upon.
I'm going to give SUPERHOT's gameplay a 10/10, because I really can't see anything that they could have changed or added to the gameplay that wouldn't feel unnecessary. SUPERHOT's gameplay really is right where it should be. There are two key gameplay mechanics in SUPERHOT, the first one being what the whole game really revolves around gameplay wise.
TIME PROGRESSES ONLY WHEN YOU MOVE.
This truly is a genious mechanic, and this is what makes SUPERHOT stand out. You often find that in any FPS you see only the highly skilled players pull off intricate plays that seem deliberate and smooth. In SUPERHOT, thanks to its slow-mo style, you can carefully plan where every bullet will land, when every poorly aimed martini glass will make contact with your foe's faces, and my personal favourite, staring at your screen with frustration as you come to the realization that the second you unfreeze time the volley of bullets in front of you will turn you into swiss cheese and you'll have to restart the level.
The second mechanic in SUPERHOT is "HOTSWITCHING", which lets you switch the body that you are occupying with that of any opponent you hold E on, with a cooldown of course. This is introduced a little while into the game, unlike the slow-mo mechanic, however it really helps when the levels start getting harder. It really adds a whole other dimension to the game being able to essentially warp behind your opponents, put yourself on the other end of a stray bullet coming straight towards you, or just position yourself a little bit better. This is another amazing mechanic, and although its been one visited in other games, I think this game got it right.
Lastly, being able to pull off some of the things you can, like grabbing guns out of midair, slicing bullets in half with katanas, or releasing a flurry of, well, basically any loose object you can find at your foes really makes you feel good when playing.
Overall, the gameplay in SUPERHOT feels extremely smooth, and there is nothing more satisfying than watching all of your meticulously planned actions come to life in the realtime recap that happens at the end of each level, all to the wonderful sound of the all too familiar SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT.
Ill cut this one short to say that this is either a 10/10, or an N/A. Simply because the effect the developer wanted to achieve was executed perfectly. That being, however, because it is a low poly game and graphics don't really come into play. Personally, I might be a bit biased because i'm a huge fan of low poly artwork, but I love the approach they took to SUPERHOT's visuals. Unless you have a seething hatred for low poly models, i'm sure you will too.
Much like graphics, to be honest there isn't much to say here. SUPERHOT utilizes three sounds frequently in its game. The ambient clicking of the protagonists keyboard, the whirring of electronics in the background, and of course, SUPER. HOT.
The first thing that comes to mind when I try to eloquently word an explanation of SUPERHOT's difficulty is that it is extremely reminiscent of Hotline Miami. For those of you who have played the Hotline Miami games, you're probably already pulling your own hair out at the thought. For those of you who haven't, it isn't unnecessarily hard, but you definitely do get that signiture feeling of frustration every time you get shot from behind, mess up a sequence, or get punched by an enemy you "killed". SUPERHOT is definitely challenging at times, but it's just the right kind of challenging, and after you get over a couple of waves of frustration it will absolutely leave you wanting more.
That being said, if you're Neo from the matrix you shouldn't experience much trouble completing SUPERHOT.
I'm going to end this review by talking a little bit about why I personally feel that SUPERHOT is worth its hefty $30 price tag, even though I had the good fortune of pre-ordering the game for a fraction of that. SUPERHOT may not be as long as a triple A release, and it may not have the replay value of a competitive online game, but it absolutely leaves you with a memorable experience, and if you like it like I did, you may just find that you'll put a lot of time into completing challenges, sifting through all the little side content and secrets, and playing endless mode. I have only dipped slightly into the content that lies beyond the main storyline, yet I am already very fond of the 15 minutes or so I spent watching the chat room characters talk to each other. Ironically enough, thats probably the most character development in SUPERHOT.
If you can afford it, I strongly suggest that you buy this game. It's fun, it's original, it has replay value to an extent, and it truly is the most innovative shooter i've played in years.

Fahrenheit is the second game by developed by French game maker Quantic Dream developed in 2005. Keeping this in mind, this is a review of the remaster as if the original did not exist. The first thing to be noted is the texture work. While impressive for 2005, the "HD" remaster is only a small refinement on the original.
Overall, the gameplay is far from inspired with most of the play revolving around controlling clucky characters and battling annoying and repetetive QTEs. There are times when Farenheit attempts to act as a game, but this is when it truely falls apart. The stealth section is poorly writen and overall frustrating without any real satisfaction in the end. The greatest failure of the stealth level is an entire lack of feedback given to a player, instead giving an arbitrary "Game Over" screen, not even indicating who spotted you.
The only redeeming element of this "interactive movie" is the story itself which holds a certain amount of interest. However the story does little to combat the gameplay.  Afterall, the story could have well fit into a 2 hour movie, yet was stretched into a  7-9 hour game. The amount of fluff is painful, with one section being nothing but lifting weights in a gym.
Perhaps this game has some value in a historical context, but unless you are doing so out of academic interest, it is best to avoid it.

I'm not sure what to say about the game.  I'm not even sure I got it.
There's a lot of narration, but that's not necessarily bad.  The environments are gorgeous and the music might have dethroned To the Moon for its ability to so perfectly create atmosphere.  The controls are simple, intuitive, and not noteworthy.  Most of the game is you experiencing--rather than driving or interacting with--a story.
The story is intentionally vague (seemingly intentionally), even when it all wraps up at the end, but there's enough there that a lot of people--especially anyone who's ever wrestled with depression, either chronic or temporary--can find something in it that will resonate on some extremely deep, often (for me) painful level.
It's short.  It feels about like Naissance, with more narration and less "just experience this world" (if you liked The Beginner's Guide, by the way, give Naissance a look.  The aesthetic and area layout have a similar feel).  It's...confusing, vague, and feels almost uncomfortably personal.  It's also one of those games where I can't say anything substantial about the story without utterly ruining it--so much of it seems to hinge on what it means to you, the player, and saying what it meant to me defeats the point of that first, untainted experience.
Above all, this is a game that should make you uncomfortable.  And that is joyous, and beautiful, and lovely.
If you like games that lean heavily on their story and atmosphere, and are extremely personal and individual and sometimes painfully blunt, this is one of the best games I can recall ever playing to do those things.  But otherwise, this game might noe be for you.

This game is a hoot with a full couch of friends. Its crazy how it got us all jumping and screaming for the entire time we were playing. I remember getting this in a indiebox and thinking "meh what a crappy game for this month". But being able to finally play it with a full group finally made it worthwhile.
The gameplay is fun and hectic. You get only a single life per round. Each round lasts anywhere from a handful of seconds to usually no longer then a minute. So players aren't left on the sidelines too long if they die in the very first second making a dumb move. Every arena is randomly generated and are usually very well balanced.  Every exit on the level links directly to the corrosponding opposite side. So that opens up a world of crazy encounters with groups that know how to use them creativly. The powerups add a whole level of craziness with the level moving vertically or horizontally. Which can disoritente some players and give others the chance to move in for a kill. Depending on who is winning and losing the game adds simple handicaps that gives others a chance to win even if they have lost a lot of rounds back to back. Some of the handicaps simply add a sheild allowing you to withstand a extra strike or helps bend your arrows to make it easier to strike a oppoent down. While leaders will have fewer arrows to start and most use pure skill to outwit their oppoents handicaps. It sounds like it make it unfair. But for me after all my years of multiplayer gaming. I can say this game is one of the very few that figured out how to make a fair and balanced handicap system.
Bottomline. If you have a local group of friends that get together to play games. BUY THIS. You will have a blast.

Does that make this a bad game? No. Doesn that mean that I will stop playing the game? No (I intend to buy a controller). Would I recommend the game? Yes, just not to anyone who wants to use keyboard controls.

Having now got a controller, I can now say that playing this game is a delight! By far one of the best games I've played! [Spoiler free review]
Gameplay:
The gameplay is best enjoyed with a controller (I used an xbox 360 controller) and relies mainly on Quick Time Events (QTE) of hitting the joysticks in different directions as events play out, with failure costing you "lives" or outright ending the game. Reaction time is important, but I played it on normal and found it somewhat challenging without being ridiculous. There are also events which require "stamina" like taping the L and R shoulder buttons to build up the strength gauge. Aside from QTE sequences there's third person "search" modes where you basically gather clues, talk to people, or interact with the environment, with the ability to move the camera angle through preset angles or move it independently using the joystick. Most dialog is on a timer, meaning you have to choose a conversation option before time runs out during an interview.
Concepts:
You play as each character in the story: the two detectives, as well as the perpetrator; It's interesting that you solve the crime you commit, haven't seen that in a game before. The characters are well developed, and are all unique enough to genuinely feel like a movie plays out (actually the New Game menu option is New Movie, the premise is kind of like you're playing out a movie.) Each character has an individual "stress gauge" in which you have to maintain their mental health, different events and actions will impact it one way or another, supposedly if the gauge gets low enough your character will commit suicide or something (I haven't tried letting it get that low, but there are moments when it gets close!)
Story (spoiler free):
The storyline I won't go into detail on for spoiler purposes. Let's just say it's well written, has some surprises, and isn't overly predicatable. The way it's "filmed" using multiple simultaneous camera angles at times, or unexpected cut-scenes is really effective. It feels like a movie, you'll have a different feeling play this then you would playing a typical adventure style game, it's incredibly unique and surprisingly gripping, haven't had that much connection with many adventure games other than "The Cat Lady" (also a very good, dark, serious-tone game.) It's not an easy story to predict either, takes a lot of twists and turns.
Audio:
There are dark, ambient tracks for music, as well as some real-world artist tracks (notably Theory of a Deadman did a lot of the music for this game.) The choices of music or ambience really fit the story. The audio is all spoken voice-recorded dialogs, and they're done quite well: some games have voice dialog that you can tell was recorded at different locations then slapped together, making it sound wonky. I would think all voice actors were present at the same studio for the conversations they recorded as the tones and inflections they used seem appropriate for the conversation.
Graphics:
Graphics are dated by todays standards, they're sharp enough on wide screen to appear "as good as they can" for using the original models and textures. I didn't find it hard to live with, the character models display facial expressions, speech matches the mouth movement. It doesn't look cheesy, it looks like it did: a high quality graphic game for it's time.
Remastered?:
There isn't a lot of "remastery" to this game, the textures have basically been made wide-screen compatible. Controller support was updated to support modern game controllers. It is also compatible with newer windows (I used windows 7) and didn't require any muck-around to make it play, something most PC gamers deal with. The audio is from the original game, the quality isn't as crisp as it could've been (in it's day a lot of compression had to be used to make it fit on media, therefore the spoken dialog is noticably compressed, kind of like listening to a lower bitrate MP3) It's not awful, but you'll notice it compared to modern games. The 3D models and textures maintain quality at the higher resolution option, but have not been redesigned by any means. Basically the remastery boils down to "works on modern hardware" in this case.
Summary:
I highly recommend grabbing this game. If you've never played it before, but enjoy crime dramas on TV, I think you'd really like what they offer. I'm a long-time gamer and this is one game I can't really relate to any other game, it's completely unique feeling (Dreamfall: the longest journey, is somewhat close.)
Games like these are a rare breed, and for $10, you really can't go wrong. I got about 10 hours or so of gameplay out of my first run-through, but that's just one option, I plan on playing it again to see how I can change the outcome by picking different decisions and such. The only reason I would consider against buying it is if you do not own a game controller for your PC, don't want mature uncensored sexual content, don't like QTEs, or do not like serious, gritty crime games. Otherwise, this is one game you don't want to miss out on!

A true classic of interactive movie remastered in High Definition!
I played Fahrenheit (Indigo Prophecy in US) when it was first released in 2005 and enjoyed it very much.
The Story is about Lucas Kane who finds himself in a bathroom with a dead man and a knife in his hand. Confused and with no memory how or why he had killed that man the story begins and will send you into a world full of mysteries and dark forces.
A very interesting feature of this game is to play different characters and each action of one character will result in different outcomes when you play the other character. Lucas can try to remove his traces from the crime scene and when playing the detective Carla Valenti you have to search for clues and evidence of the murder. This is something which makes this game so much enjoyable and replayable. It plays just like an adventure only with a thick cinematic touch, like a movie where you can interact and change the possible outcome.
This HD Remake enables you to play the game in high def resolution, the original version of the game only supports max resolution of 1024x768. Furthermore you will notice some sharper textures and there is also the possibility to change between the new and old textures while you are in the game with the key F9. Yes, the graphics aren't the same as in the latest games of Quantic Dream like Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls. But back in 2005, this was standard and with some playing time you'll get used to it.
After all if you are looking for an interactive movie with and interesting dark story and different outcomes then this is the game for you!

I'm not sure what to say about the game.  I'm not even sure I got it.
There's a lot of narration, but that's not necessarily bad.  The environments are gorgeous and the music might have dethroned To the Moon for its ability to so perfectly create atmosphere.  The controls are simple, intuitive, and not noteworthy.  Most of the game is you experiencing--rather than driving or interacting with--a story.
The story is intentionally vague (seemingly intentionally), even when it all wraps up at the end, but there's enough there that a lot of people--especially anyone who's ever wrestled with depression, either chronic or temporary--can find something in it that will resonate on some extremely deep, often (for me) painful level.
It's short.  It feels about like Naissance, with more narration and less "just experience this world" (if you liked The Beginner's Guide, by the way, give Naissance a look.  The aesthetic and area layout have a similar feel).  It's...confusing, vague, and feels almost uncomfortably personal.  It's also one of those games where I can't say anything substantial about the story without utterly ruining it--so much of it seems to hinge on what it means to you, the player, and saying what it meant to me defeats the point of that first, untainted experience.
Above all, this is a game that should make you uncomfortable.  And that is joyous, and beautiful, and lovely.
If you like games that lean heavily on their story and atmosphere, and are extremely personal and individual and sometimes painfully blunt, this is one of the best games I can recall ever playing to do those things.  But otherwise, this game might noe be for you.

Right first and foremost, if you're expecting an adventurous, first-person, action packed game of sorts; apologies this isn't what this game is about and you should stop reading from this point onwards.
Think of it as an interactive movie.
Literally just finished the game at the time of writing this review I'm almost speechless, so please understand if things said seem out of place.
Now attempting to make this spoiler-free as possible; the story explores the games created by an enigmatic game developer by the name of 'Coda,' the story not only explores Coda's games but Coda as a person, his thoughts and emotions.
The game truly is thought provoking. Both in real-life and in fiction there is a person, definitely not your average man but an enigma who pursues a field in art or similar, for example an expressionist (or in simple terms an artist). Such people instead of speaking their thoughts and feelings, they put it into their work, in such a expressionistic sense. Take for example the 'Scream' painting by Edward Munch, although not immediately obvious the painting portrays "nature's scream" as Edward has coined it, one day Edward walked down a bridge, and the sun began setting in a bright red color, at that moment he sensed nature's scream hense the blood red skies in the painting. This exact same situation occurs in The Beginner's Guide where Coda expresses his thoughts and emotions into his games, his games can be interpreted as art of sorts.
The narrator desperately tries his best to dig deep into the true meanings behind these mystic games, just as a normal person would to an expressionist's painting, but when he does pick them apart for what they really are it's just captivating. We're talking about the psychology that came when Coda created such games, and from my perspective Coda had a lot of thoughts contained. Coda didn't put much thought into his games when it came to an overall objective of a game, but instead he had messages. Everything in these games are designed the way they are for a specific reason.
I also feel like this game reaches out to those experiencing anxiety, depression or isolation rather. Some of the messages left behind to me are the epitome of such a person experiencing the above.
This game is certainly not for everyone, casuals may gain little or nothing from such an experience, but if you're a creative individual or pursue things like creative arts this is for you.

I tried it and it's ok but the balance is way off. Different weapons have different amounts of range and since you're always visible to the enemies (even through walls) it's impossible to sneak around and attack them from behind and even if you could many of the longer range weapons do enough burst damage to destroy you just as fast as the slightly higher damage close range weapons. If you place the hull blocks that you build on while facing different directions then it saves the direction it was facing and if you try to put down a row of diagonal pieces they will change the placement direction from block to block and you'll have to rotate each block a different amount of times to place it.

I don't even know what I just played.
Blood and Bacon is a wave survival game on a farm where you fight lots, and lots, and lots of pig-type species.
Obviously this is an indie game and not very full featured, but I paid about $.90 for it so whatever.
The graphics feel ancient, like N64 era, but it's not that big of a deal. The sound design isn't anything out of the ordinary but is satisfying, especially when you use the rocket launcher. Most of the guns have incomplete or basically non existent reload animations, and you can reload constantly even when your magazine is full.  The voice acting for the farmer is completely awful, maybe on purpose, but the voice acting for bosses and the sounds made by the pigs and grinder are spot on. There is some occasional humor to the game, most of it coming from the Farmer's lines, the bosses and hidden messages sprawled about the farm, but the game itself is pretty funny considering you are basically murdering a ton of hogs and pigs and undead pigs.
In many ways this game is like survival mode in L4D, just very barebones. Each pig you kill, you can push it's gibs or entire body into a grinder that magically turns them in to resources so you can buy grenades, revive pills, milk, ammo, nukes, and superstrength.
The only negative thing I have to say about the actual gameplay is that survival mode takes a long time. 100 days. If you are actually pushing everything in to the grinder, it takes quite a while to get through each day. Every 10 days my co op partner and I would be like "30 days and it's not over? Maybe 50 because we have like 2 guns left to unlock? Maybe 75? It's 100!?"  All in all though, sure, it's worth 90 cents for a few hours of fun until you get tired of it. I don't know what the original price of the game was but I'd still pay a few dollars more for it.

This is a decent program that suffers from Unity Syndrome (the market filled with low-effort products pumped out, dragging down the engine's reputation).
With a creative mind it is highly versatile and can accomplish most things that can be scripted through Ruby.
That's the rub, though. Ruby with RGSS is a high-level scripting language that's interpreted. A lot of more complicated features you might want to script could be hampered by jumping through too many hoops and lag the engine.
So don't necessarily believe that the sky's the limit, because it's not. There are limitations to RMVX Ace, understand that before you buy.
That said, if you want to make an RPG, especially but not limited to a turn-based 2D JRPG style one, this is a very useful framework.

I don't know what I was expecting. I wasn't super hyped for this game so I went in with what I'd say fairly low expectations. But now that I've fully completed the game, obviously barring challenges and endless mode, I can confidently say this game is the worst waste of time and money ever. About half way through my 2 hour absolute thrill ride (/s) I was already totally fed up of the text simulator that half the game basically is. If I took out all mandatory text scenes in this game it'd be little more than an hour long glorified flash game. Now, the game does offer neat little stuff like 'secrets' hidden in what I presume to be every level, but this has not interested me enough at all to keep me playing, or keep it in my library for that matter.
Gunplay is exactly how you'd expect. The whole 'time moves when you move thing' is pretty neat at times. I'm not going to lie, the game definitely has it's entertaining moments, for about 30 minutes, then it becomes frustrating. Hotswitching is fun for the what 5? 6? levels I was allowed to use it in, shame it was introduced too late. The level design is either sixty or total nought, with some levels making you purposefully die so you can play it again or some levels making you make mistakes because you just want it to be over.
The story is not particularly engaging, no spoilers, but it becomes GLARINGLY obvious what you're going to have to end up doing very early on in the game. The story is only advanced by compulsory text sections, which can range from short interactions to taking way, WAY too long. The large flashing text is an effective "cool" little feature for a while, then it starts to try way too hard to become intimidating and overbearing, which it fails at by being too frequent and 'obvious'? I guess?
Right, one more thing. I'm almost certain this is intentional, and somehow the secrets may be involved? Or maybe I missed things. BUT, the game has an OVERBEARING AWFUL LACK OF CHOICE. I seriously get the vibe the devs were going for, but man, is this game linear. It's painfully restrictive, if you're the curious type who tries to look for every way out of being told what to do, this game will be little more than a masochistic experience for you. Again, this may be all irrelevant with game elements which I have not explored.
Ultimately, not a good experience. Forgive my ignorance, but I honestly don't know what the devs were doing all those years. If you're a big fan of short games, and LOVE the mechanic of time moving when you do and are willing to play the game well into the challenges and endless mode, go right ahead, seriously, you will have a blast. But to the average player? I wouldn't. The game is good, but very slow paced, and the (unskippable!) text sections go on way too long.

Underrated. Unknown (for it's importance). Hostile Waters: Antaeus Rising brought the shooter, the vehicular combat, the RTS and the vehicle building/customizing games all together in a, not quite glorious, but rather a gritty, dark world where your team of professional uploaded-mind fighters chat commenting on their kills or just make small talk while each is playing his part in saving the world.
During a typical game you'll be commanding from a large navy ship that functions also as a manufacturing plant, and on occasion will ofter a salvo of its big guns for support, creating vehicles both airborne, ground and amphibious, equiping them with a weapon of your choice that radically changes their role, and with modules of your choice. You'll need to scavenge scrap for energy to produce units, ferry your land units to shore, and fight in 3rd person control of a vehicle. The AI is the personality of a handful of warriors from the past, uploaded in computer chips, which you assign to control a vehicle. It's not strategy with tons of units, you'll control maybe 10 at most, and won't be able to crew them all simultaneously. But the chit-chat on the radio when idle, the comments on the kills and cockyness will keep it more alive than most first person games ever were.
A great benefit is that you can build your vehicles for stealth, armor, efficiency, you are versatile, each one has its own strengths and weaknesses but you can go hit & run with attack helicopters, up close and personal with buggys, or you can take the snipers route and lure the enemy out where your turrets will take him down before they know it, and your support crew will be healing you and scavenging the enemy's parts to store energy for your next vehicles.
And it all ties in so well with the AI and the world, if you destroy their energy production plants they can build units only with their stores, destroy those and you'll find that they can hardly bring in any more reinforcements. Everything comes from a production plant, energy is countable, you can fight a war of resources on the enemy and it will work.
And then there's the story. Prepare for a surprise as the game pushes with a storyline and theme you rarely see in strategy games, and does quite well with it.
TL;DR:
This game is clearly the product of a team with skill, inspiration and an ambition to provide a game like none other. I would love to see them work on another game like this, and would gladly pay the full price, and I have no emotional ties to the game, I played it for the first time well more than a decade after it was released.

At one point I saved a game separate from my continuing save, just to have something to revert to when I want a new experience but don't want to go through the annoying beginning again.
My biggest problems with this game is a lack of content, and the logic behind the villagers. Honestly, the villagers in your settlement are really just not smart. It can take days (in-game time) to complete a building, while other buildings with the same amount of workers take less than half the time. The lack of content also makes the game get dull and boring after awhile.
I recommend this game for someone who wants to be forced to think; who can handle a game that goes from quiet to hectic in a split second, and without much notice either. You also need to be able to accept that occasionally, your settlement may basically self-destruct regardless of your skill level, and there's not much you can do about it.

Played this game for hours before purchasing on Steam, but from what I can recall after playing this game over the years; it's nothing short of a masterpiece. Sure, many people of the modern generation will denounce this game due to the aging graphics but there are plenty of redeeming factors about this game.
The first time you run this game, you're introduced to the kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack of Unreal Tournament. Many modern first person shooter games seem to make their soundtrack sound as if they are from some hollywood studio whilst this game's soundtrack doesn't many you feel like an actor but rather it makes you feel like you're going to unleash the ultimate killing spree. The soundtrack is probably by far the best video game soundtrack I have ever heard, it packs memorable beats and further encourages you to play this game.
The maps in this game are definitely unique to those of modern first person shooter games, the maps provide a consistent atmosphere to the environment the game is set in. The maps are also very well designed and take advantage of simplicity and maze-like patters to utilise the gameplay. It feels so awesome to be jumping in low gravity on a giant rock with two towers spinning around in space, or to be shooting bots off elongated platforms into a massive pile of biosludge. There is so many good maps (in my opinion Facing Worlds and Deck16 are by far the best maps this game has to provide) giving you plenty of different ways you could play this game, such as vast environments give you more room to dodge attacks etc. The maps on this game are fantastic.
The weapons offer you many different ways to kill someone, as most of them come with some pretty cool alt-fire modes (with the Rocket Launcher having the most combinations of these modes) which can solve many tough situations other players could place you in. The weapons include; The Impact Hammer / Chainsaw alteration (worst weapon in the game BY FAR), Enforcer Pistol (you can DUAL WIELD THESE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥S), Biorifle (Pretty useless, but best in confined areas), Minigun, Pulse Gun (You can shoot LIGHTNING with the alt fire mode), Razorjack (Shoot razors that bounce off walls and the alt fire mode can make them EXPLODE), ASMD Shock Rifle (Basically a plasma gun, has a really neat combo which allows you to make the alt-fire plasma ball explode creating a large explosion), Flak Cannon (Pray mercy for those on the recieving end of this weapon), Rocket Launcher (shoots sometimes guided rockets and also grenades, pretty good stuff), Sniper Rifle (alt fire just allows you to use the scope) and probably saved best to last... The Redeemer (a giant mother♥♥♥♥ing bazooka which shoots guided nuclear warheads, either ways anyone you fire this at is ♥♥♥♥ed). These weapons are fantastic and define most of the game's actions.
The gamemodes are really cool on this game, you could be spending hours playing on classic Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch, have great time humiliating the enemy team on Capture The Flag, run around the match capturing points in Domination, liberating bases from the enemy team's hands in Assault and finally see who will survive last in Last Man Standing. These game modes can be enhanced by mutators which can significantly change the gameplay of each gamemode.
The modding community, still active appaently and provides hundreds of new maps, mutators, character skins, weapons, voice packs for taunts, modding still makes this nearly 20 year old gem still feel fresh, not to mention they are all FREE so you don't have to pay for extra content when the community offers all of this extra content for free. The community itself is fantastic and helpful on the forums despite all the years that have went by.
Seriously there is so many awesome things I could talk about in this game which would've made this review even longer, but I give this game a solid 10/10 and would recommend this to anyone who wants to play an action packed FPS with friends or bots.

I recieved this product for free from a Steam support person to troubleshoot some issues I was having with the Steam controller on other games.  Man am I glad they gave it to me.  I never would've gotten it otherwise, but honestly I would even consider recommending this game at full price.  It doesn't look like it's remotely worth it's price at first look, or even necessarily at the first bit of playing.  But the boss design is AMAZING, the music is tight, and in general it's a real fun game.  The hardest levels/bosses on the hardest modes are extremely challenging, but well designed.  It sits on the cusp of what feels like artificial difficulty at times (as if certain attacks/events cannot be avoided), but then with practice you learn that even the hardest attacks or enemies are avoidable with enough skill.  The difficulty curve is also well designed in my opinion.
Funnily enough, I got almost nothing out of the versus multiplayer mode.  It's fine, I guess.  Very bland if you ask me, although if you're looking for something more fair and less chaotic it's good.  I think most groups of friends are looking more for smash bros and would have more fun playing that.
But the co-op and single player modes can't be beat.  10/10 coop, 10/10 single player, 8/10 trials mode, and 7/10 versus mode from me.  I have 100%'d the game and put about 100 hours in doing so.

MattMakesGames has always made crazy platformer games with high amount of death, which is NOT caused by:
- Falling down, because like the old platformer games, falling down a hole means you pop up upstairs instead.
- Falling on enemies. While colliding with the enemy causes you to die, booping on enemies (even players in a versus match) has been a method proven by magical plumbers everywhere as the best method of elimination.
- Running out of arrows. Have I told you this game is all about arrows? Shooting arrows, picking up stray arrows from walls, dodging AND grabbing arrows out of the air (the mystical tower archery training paid off). You will always find amusement in arrows flying everywhere and people trying to aim at little pixelated sprites with only 8 possible directions and a brilliant projectile physics...until you get shot in the face, of course.
However, glorious, hilarious deaths will certainly be caused by:
- DIfferent arrows that comes in form of a powerup from a loot chest. Be it explosions, bounces of walls, floor hazard generation, there's arrows to suit every kind of your archery needs.
- Flavourful enemies, some only spawn in certain levels. Be it the nearly-harmless slime, pestering ghosts, and dark hooded figures with pointy tools that can deflect your shots, it's better to end them before they end you.
- Getting shot in the face by a wily foe on versus mode
- Getting shot in the back by a sneaky foe on versus mode
- Getting shot in the back by an ally on co-op mode
- Shooting an arrow up, missing that goddamn bird and watch as the arrow plunge down right to your own character
- Lava. I mean, if Matt Thorson made a platformer game without floor hazards, people would flip.
- Getting shot in the face by your own bouncy arrow.
- Getting shot in the face by someone else's bouncy arrow.
- Trying to play single-string guitar with your bow...with Cursed Bow mod turned on.
- Getting divebombed from above (read: booped), Super Mario style.
- Failing dodge.
- Succeeding dodge and still get shot.
- Succeeding dodge, stole their bouncy arrow, tries to shoot them and ends up bouncing it at a wall and back to one's face.
- And many more.
It has huge replayability value when you play at couch coop with your friends. Done co-op on normal mode? Go hardcore. Done versus on normal mode? Turn on random mods and have a good laugh (or ruin your friendship). I wish they would expand on the story by adding narration and further the coop campaign, but I think that's what the Dark World expansion is for (I haven't checked). I have played coop with my brother and it has been such a blast that I wish the players can immerse further by adding background stories or certain triggers.
I highly recommend this for:
- Fans of MattMakesGames' old platformer games like Runman, Jumper and Untitled Story (that one with the birdthing).
- Those who are looking for a great couch coop game, playable sober or drunk.
- Fans of mechanically-challenging games. The platformer, jumping of walls, all the while trying to aim an arrow will be a great experience for you.
- Fans of great pixel arts and detailed, fleshed out game assets.

As this was my first 'Tales of' game, I was pleasantly surprised at what I got myself into. Being a JRPG fan, I was afraid the game would be too short or have other types of limitations. Quickly finding myself proven otherwise, I was really stoked at what the game had in store.
+ Overall a great PC port. Very much playable with keyboard and mouse, though I use my 360 controller out of preference.
+ A decent storyline that is not too overly complicated to follow. It's nothing spectacular or groundbreaking, though it was engaging enough to keep me playing.
+ The characters are also really good, maybe somewhat static at times but I enjoyed them. They were what made the story keep flowing as well as it did. The interactions between them are really nice as well.
+ A pleasant cell shaded artstyle that's quite easy on the eyes. Personally, I really loved it as the anime fan I am. Some places look really good, and I loved exploring caves and forests alike.
+ An astonishing soundtrack. Sometimes, I found myself walking around without doing much progress just to listen to the music. That's not to speak about the trial dungeons, which I find to be exceptional. The OP too. Just remember to patch in the version with vocals.
+ Solid gameplay, the combat is superb and rightly so as it's what made the game for me. However, the combat might not be for everyone. Look up some gameplay of it.
+ Good replayability due to the skill system, I'll probably play through the game again on some higher difficulty to try some different options, but I don't think that's necessary to get the full experience.
+ It's... Very long. Over a hundred hours and I've yet to beat the game, though I assume that's because I'm a tortoise when it comes to gaming. It wouldn't surprise me if you could beat it in 50h or so, probably less.
- Camera in combat can be a bit clunky sometimes, especially in tight corridors.
- The "open world" is somewhat lacking. You will find yourself running through empty large spaces quite often unless you want to spend money on fast travelling.
- Level design could've been better. They look good, but are quite linear and don’t give much room for exploration as the map is fully lit and shows you where to go.
- Minor occasional framedrops during combat.
- The skill system is really complex, especially the forging part of it and knowing which skill is better for each character etc. After so long of playing, I'm still not completely sure how to properly craft the type of equipment I want.
- Prepare to be bombarded with seemingly endless amounts of tutorials.
To sum it up, I can't say anything else but that I recommend this game. Everything just blends so well together and I found that the pros made me forget about the cons almost completely. I mean, who cares about crafting properly as long as you're having fun, right? I suppose one of the main things people will wonder about is the price, and yes, I can definitely say that it's worth it at full price. 49.99€ was a good deal as I got Symphonia as an added bonus, but even without that I personally think it's worth it. If you're still unsure, it might go on sale eventually.

Okay, I haven't played Yooka-Laylee so I can't compare the two games. Regardless though...
A Hat in Time is one of my most favorite 3D platformer out right now (Not counting the classics.)
I think the art style is quite appealing and many of the worlds were beautiful to look at and explore. Chapter 1's Mafia town is admittedly a bit boring in comparison to other worlds and I found myself preferring anywhere else but there just because everywhere else was more interesting to me. The haunted Forests of Subcon Valley, movie sets of Dead Bird Studios, and the vast islands of Alpine Skyline was where I think the game shined and had me lost the most.
The collectables are fun to chase after and I found myself 100% completing the game. However 100% is a lie. It doesn't take into account the hidden Rift Tokens so that bites. There's also no good way of making sure you grabbed everything. No tracker for Yarns Balls so that also doesn't fall into the 100% complete and by the end I had every hat crafter but still 25 freaking yarns leftover. What's the point?
The music was really great listening to and getting a hold of the remixes through the Orb Machine was nice so you get some music variety in the levels. Customization was also great when you unlocked Hat Styles and Color Schemes. Howeve it's held back by the fact that all Styles, Remixes, and Color schemes are hidden behind a Slots style mini-game that uses Rift Tokens or you get a free one for beating a rift. There's a limited amount of Tokens and tries at the Slots and there's no current way I see of getting every customization item. Taking away against from completionists that want true 100%.
Story is lacking and it sounds like there's a build up between you an early ally, but then they never bring her up again until the ending. Clearly this was not the focus of the game. I enjoyed the little stories I got in each world with their respective main NPCs though. The final fight lacked the proper build up though in my opinion even though I loved the fight.
There's even an issue of the game's title. "A Hat in Time." Well aside from collecting the Time Pieces, there wasn't much of any focus on time in the game. Were we on a time limit for Hat Kid to get home? Is Hat Kid a time traveler? Never quite touched on. Time elements were just really few and far between. It's only there to justify your "rival's" motivation for wanting the Time Pieces.
Hat Kid herself is a fun and cute character. But that's where it ends sadly. She seems to have 0 concern about anyone else and simply wants her Time Pieces back. And that's fine, she's a neutral party. As the game currently is though, we don't know enough about Hat Kid to really care about her goal or understand her. Why is getting home important? We were shown and told nothing.
While it does sound like I've railed on this game, I can't help but still love it to bits. I sunk myself into finding everything and loved the other worlds out there and simply being lost in exploration. The controls aren't the tightest I've played with but that didn't matter to me. I had my fun running and jumping and never felt I messed something up or took damage because a control didn't funciton right. It was afun ride and I enjoyed most of the characters I was preented with.
Hands down though, the Crows are the best characters. Sorry, I meant my fellow Express Owls.
Overall 8/10 for me. Loved my time with it, but the areas that felt lacking hold the game back from earning a 10/10 in my book. I still reccomend the game a lot though. To me, it was worth backing it and I paid a higher price than $29.99 so at this price, it's quite worth it to me.
