if you like JRPGs, this game takes the flaws of the genre and multiplies them by 2. There is ENDLESS dialogue for hours and it is not interesting. Most of it is just explaining what you just heard over and over. The characters are absolutely boring. The story is the laziest I've ever seen. There is "malevolence" in the world and you have to cleanse it. Malevolence is literally just evil. No one is held accountable for their own actions because if they do anything bad, it was just malevolence. There are humans and Seraphim, but Seraphim are just humans with some powers that humans can't see and apparently can never do anything wrong and it's always the human's fault.
For a game about saving the world and being heroes, the characters are all strangely judgemental and elitist. There was a horrible sidequest about following some stupid kids around (which is literally just walking around a small town and listening to 10 minutes of cutscene and barely any animation) and seeing if they're stealing from people because someone told them to. It turns out they were just stealing because they were!! So the game gives you an option. Send them to the knights and imprison them?? Or not?? I chose not to. So apparently that means going up to the kids and saying how evil they are. The kids are like "YEAH SO WHAT WE HAVE NO WAY OF FEEDING OURSELVES" and then the main characters just call the god damn knights any way and send them to a prison or whatever. These characters have no real empathy and don't seem to know how to react like even KIND OF normal human beings to situations.
Okay, so the story sucks, the characters suck, what about the gameplay? I could have let it off the hook, but no, the camera is the absolute worst I've ever seen. Especially if you are playing in multiplayer. I mean it when I say I've never seen a worse camera in a video game. It gets STUCK inside walls, as in you cannot move it out, and you are very often looking at a twitching mess staring at a monsters♥♥♥♥♥ Nintendo 64 games had set up better cameras for 3D
Not only with the camera, but the game rewards you for spamming. I know, I know, a lot of the other Tales games rewarded you for it as well, but this one takes it to a new level. All you do is armatize (basically fuse with a party member) and you will be put in a super form with MUCH much less moves. With almost every form, its best to just spam the spell casting abilities. They do absolutely huge damage and huge AOE and constantly stun the bosses and monsters. Sure, you could try just not doing that, right? But then you're at a huge disadvantage. The monsters tend to flinch way less, most of your moves are not very big aoes, and just are not very strong in general. Basically, every battle goes like this. See what weakness it has. Armatize to that weakness. Then just press your strongest spell over and over till the battle is done. Try to do it without armatizing, and its gonna take a lot longer or just not even be possible. It's just not balanced at all.
I haven't even gotten to the dungeon design. Oh the dungeon design is so, soooooo lazy. Most of it is just completely empty hallways with copy pasted rooms that have absolutely no detail in them. You'll go through caves that look exactly the same, except this cave is blue. You'll go through dungeons and find yourself getting lost because every room looks exactly the same and you have no landmarks to look to. There is absolutely no excuse for this. Previous tales of games, (vesperia, abyss, even symphonia) had better design and better puzzles. I'm not saying the previous games puzzles and dungeons were great, but the fact that this game somehow is WORSE than those is just sad. You're supposed to improve upon your games, not downgrade.
Oh, lets also not forget to mention the tons of worthless DLC. DLC costumes for a single player game. Beach costumes, that you used to just unlock in the old games for free, are now 7 dollars. A lot of it was just flat out day 1 DLC as well.
Overall, as a fan of the olderish Tales games like Symphonia, Abyss (well I didn't hate it at least) and Vesperia, this game is just a huge disappointment. I wasn't expecting much from it honestly, and it still somehow turned out worse than I thought. This game is just a soulless, lazy, and greedy cash grab. There was no heart put into this, no effort. They just wanted to make money and pump out a Tales game as fast as possible.
TL;DR. It's boring and bad. Even if you're a fan of tales games and JRPGS, find something better. Even the positive reviews for this game say it's the weakest game of the series so that must be saying something.

I don't know what I was expecting. I wasn't super hyped for this game so I went in with what I'd say fairly low expectations. But now that I've fully completed the game, obviously barring challenges and endless mode, I can confidently say this game is the worst waste of time and money ever. About half way through my 2 hour absolute thrill ride (/s) I was already totally fed up of the text simulator that half the game basically is. If I took out all mandatory text scenes in this game it'd be little more than an hour long glorified flash game. Now, the game does offer neat little stuff like 'secrets' hidden in what I presume to be every level, but this has not interested me enough at all to keep me playing, or keep it in my library for that matter.
Gunplay is exactly how you'd expect. The whole 'time moves when you move thing' is pretty neat at times. I'm not going to lie, the game definitely has it's entertaining moments, for about 30 minutes, then it becomes frustrating. Hotswitching is fun for the what 5? 6? levels I was allowed to use it in, shame it was introduced too late. The level design is either sixty or total nought, with some levels making you purposefully die so you can play it again or some levels making you make mistakes because you just want it to be over.
The story is not particularly engaging, no spoilers, but it becomes GLARINGLY obvious what you're going to have to end up doing very early on in the game. The story is only advanced by compulsory text sections, which can range from short interactions to taking way, WAY too long. The large flashing text is an effective "cool" little feature for a while, then it starts to try way too hard to become intimidating and overbearing, which it fails at by being too frequent and 'obvious'? I guess?
Right, one more thing. I'm almost certain this is intentional, and somehow the secrets may be involved? Or maybe I missed things. BUT, the game has an OVERBEARING AWFUL LACK OF CHOICE. I seriously get the vibe the devs were going for, but man, is this game linear. It's painfully restrictive, if you're the curious type who tries to look for every way out of being told what to do, this game will be little more than a masochistic experience for you. Again, this may be all irrelevant with game elements which I have not explored.
Ultimately, not a good experience. Forgive my ignorance, but I honestly don't know what the devs were doing all those years. If you're a big fan of short games, and LOVE the mechanic of time moving when you do and are willing to play the game well into the challenges and endless mode, go right ahead, seriously, you will have a blast. But to the average player? I wouldn't. The game is good, but very slow paced, and the (unskippable!) text sections go on way too long.

I've just recently finished the game, and as a fan of the Tales series, I'm sad to say I cannot reccomend Zestiria.
For reference, previous Tales games I've played are Phantasia, Symphonia, Symphonia 2: Gotta Catch'em All, Vesperia, and Abyss.
The dungeons are bland and samey, the side-quests are lackluster, there's very little in the way of end-game content and a notable absence of super bosses, and my major gripe with the whole experience? The combat system is awful from a Tales standpoint.
Coming from other Tales games, I recall the combat being fluid, and all about stringing together long combos. It was simplistic, but exciting. While playing Vesperia, I found myself performing long 100+ hit combos from somewhere near the midpoint in the game, and capping the whole thing off with a Mystic Art. The battle system was simple enough to pick up and learn that you could start exploring the kinds of Arte combos available to you quickly.
Zestiria's combat is anything but simple. Attacks have been split into three categories. Martial Artes (your basic attacks), Hidden Artes (Your Sonic Thrusts and your Demon Fangs), and Seraphic Artes (Spells.) These have been given a rock, paper, scissors style interaction. Martial Artes interrupt spells, Spells cast faster when struck by Hidden Artes, and Hidden Artes cannot be interrupted by Martial Artes. This isn't so bad, except for one glaring fact. This interaction is rarely relevant.
There are five elements in the game. Physical, Fire, Wind, Water, and Earth. The vast majority of enemies are resistant to most of these. If it's resistant, it takes very little damage and doesn't stagger regardless of what Arte you use. To make this worse, most of your attacks are now imbued with elements from the start, so you have to pick your combos based on what will deal damage, rather than what you think will be fun.
This cuts out some of the freedom to build your own fighting style that was present in past Tales games. But this is just the beginning of Tales of "No Fun Allowed."
You can only have 4 party members at a time. Two of them are permanently set. Sorey, and his human partner. Despite being perfectly capable of doing things normally, your other 4 party members require a 1/1 human/seraph ratio to participate in fights. So gone is the ability to choose 2 half of your party based on personal preference and combat style.
But wait, there's more! The four other party members each correspond with one of the four non-physical elements! I remind you, most enemies resist all but one or two elements, so you'll be forced to pick and choose which of those members to include in the party based of their element. Again, removing yet another element of choice from you.
So the game already goes out of its way to force your hand in choosing specific parties of characters throughout the game, but what else is wrong with the battle system? Surely it's still a classic example of Tales gameplay, right? Nope.
Enjoy your Over The Shoulder camera angle and full 3D combat arenas. In older Tales games, battles were mostly fought on a linear plane. You frequently had the option to move yourself around the battlefield, but the actual combat tended to take place in a straight line. Left to right. With the changes, I find a lot of my attacks just straight up missing. Sword cuts flying off into the ether and accomplishing nothing.
And I've saved the worst for last: The SC system.
In previous Tales games, mashing the attack button was a free action. It cost nothing. In Zestiria, that attack costs SC. SC replaces mana in this game, but where your mana pool could be increased in past games, your SC bar is permanently set at 100. And some of your Artes cost 25+ SC to use. You see where I'm going with this?
One SC intensive combo can drain your bar entirely. Hell, there are some combos you can't even perform because it will empty your bar before it's finished. So how do you refill your bar?
You WAIT.
SC refills very quickly, but the short 2 seconds where you're told "stop" by the game, over and over again, is infuriating. Past Tales games, you had to manage your mana if you wanted to perform a long combo using your Artes, but this was only an issue if the fight dragged on. SC becomes a constant problem every few seconds during fights with boss enemies.
You can refill SC alternatively by blocking or dodging attacks, but both of these abilities are slow to respond,
In addition, even if you're managing your SC well, enemies tend to obtain Super Armor after you've combo'd them once or twice, thus making them immune to a second combo even if they're in the middle of an Arte yours SHOULD in theory interrupt.
The game is, in essence, slapping you on the wrist for trying to play it in any way it doesn't deem acceptable. Compared to the freedom of previous Tales games, I personally found this awful. I never discovered a way to circumvent these problems in my 60 hours of total playtime, and  as a result, the game was a slog. Recommend this? No. Why? No major big reason, just little annoyances, that come from biases from other games. Yet if these things annoy me after playing other games, then well it's a good think to list them and comment on them, as if this isn't a good way to review a game, tell me what is.
1. The queue timer. Petty thing, but how hard is it to collect queue data for the last 5 minutes and average out the times? It'd at least tell me if I want to wait for a battle. This is petty as you can do other stuff while waiting for a battle, but at the times when you just want to get back in...
2. The minute long lobby screen followed by another loading screen. Why two loading screens? Why not have the second loading screen first, then once the map has been loaded give me the option to look at my teammates ships. This is part 1 of...
3. a poor ratio of wait time to actual combat. you've got somewhere between 1 minute and 30 seconds to 2 minutes and 30 seconds for a 6 minute match, not always that. You have a ratio of 1:3 in terms of boredom to fun. That is a kill joy. Robocraft, the gold standard for these types of game can be more than 1:20. And is very rarely less than 1:5. even it's shortest gamemode type, TDM, which is the only GJL gamemode right now, is 10 minutes long, unless you get a woefully poorly matched match, and the queue is less than 20 seconds. GJL just has too much waiting.
4. Complete abandonment of balance. There are guns out there that are definitively better than others, espcially of their own class. You can get matched against these when you still have T1. And when range is a very important factor in GJL, facing auto-locking missiles with a longer range than your lasers, which is the opposite way this is supposed to be, is not fun. RC had issues like this. It's been patched now so that the only thing that causes a weapon to be OP is player skill, not the actual stats. Heck in that situation, keep balancing figures out of it, the person with the missiles just needs to stay at range of everybody else. Then they dont have to worry about a thing.
Not to mention the class system. Mix the higher tier players, mix different types of ships against each other. Keep rookie ships out of there though, as the other ships are typically able to dispatch rookies with ease, simply because the class allows them to be better.
5. No autoheal. Or healing of any kind. This is going on my list of cardinal sins for games like this. In a normal PVP multiplayer game, having your character/ship remain functional until they die is good. It means you can always predict exactly whats going to happen. Having things stop working or be removed when they are damaged again fine, things need consequences. Being completely unable to fix that damage without dieing, is horrific however, espcially in a deathmatch style of game where not dying is the key to victory. It also removes the strategy of being able to run away, as whats the point? Take critical damage and you may as well sit there, as that way at least next time you fight you'll stand a decent chance.
6. 3 bays. If this has to be one place where RC can be said to be definitively better, no argument needed, no getting into personal preference, this is it. Robocraft offers 100 free bays. GJM? 3, and to get more you have to pay.
7. Maps. The maps don't stand out really. There's nothing to distinguish them from each other apart from a colour. They all have massive structures to use as cover and a floor and a ceiling and nothing to make each one stand out from each other. Not like a dam or a crashed ship.
8: Finally aesthetics. Not graphics, aesthetics. GJL is a mess aesthetically. Sure it all follows the same style, recylced scrap material. But it is not good to look at. There is a difference between "scrap" and "eyesore" and unfortunately GJL sits in the latter camp. Not to mention that it can be nigh impossible to tell the arnament of a ship before you get shot. RC, the guns are often big enough to tell what your going to be facing, and the bot itself will give some hints. Good look knowing if a ship in GJL has missles, lasers or ballistics before you close the range to it. If you want a good example of aesthetics when the games lore sets a scene of a decayed future, go look at StarSector. It's setting is one of things gone wrong and the promises of a bright future wrenched away. Some of it's ships are conversions of freighters to combat ships, some are hulks and derelicts rapidly repaired for service, despite belong to the same scrapyard as GJM ships. The difference? StarSector is nice to look at. The ships may look like junk, but they're easily distinquishable and fun to look. Now StarSector may be 2D and hand drawn, but making it so that something is easy to look at is not hard.
Though if I have to say one thing, it's nice that paying players in GJL directly benefit all the players, like RC used to. But... since RC has given that chance back.... so...
I have to say, if GJL came out 2 years ago, I would've enjoyed it no end. But now? It's overshadowed by games that outclasss it. Gameplay wise, RC steals it thunder with multiple game modes, multiple maps (that are distinct), more weapons, and having less annoying features. Ship flying wise, it's beaten by Elite Dangerous, where dogfighting is a fun thing to do. Aesthetics, it's beaten by RC, StarSector and pretty much anygame that isn't Dwarf Fortress. And lore wise, if you like Sci-Fi dystopia, Starsector.
But this is my opinion, and the game is F2P, so if you've read this far you're obviously interested. Try it and make your own opinion. I've just given mine.

2) The story is WAY too meta. It's a game about playing a game and it tries to make you feel like your being sucked in literally. Plus, the ending is a bit indulgent.
All in all, if you just wanted more levels, weapons, and a graphical upgrade, that's fine. This is a game.
However, if you were expecting something more for waiting 2.5 years, you might be dissapointed. To me, it felt a bit like the developers spent too much time polishing.

Anyone who played Sim City when it was actually challenging will appreciate this game.  There may not be UFOs or giant lizards that destroy your town, but it is somewhat similar.  In this game there is much more micromanagement.  You have to determine what crops will be grown, how many hunters / fishermen to have, how many houses, schools, storage locations (... etc) are needed to maintain a positive population growth.  You also need to pay attention to the ages of the population.  If there is a long streak where population growth did not happen (no kids born), or all of the people at the optimal range to have kids are wiped out, you'll be stuck watching your population slowly dwindle to 0 while everything slowly falls apart.
Very in-depth.

This WWII eastern front FPS will throw you right into the trenches! Awareness and allies are all you have standing between your brain and the bullets of your enemy. Capture and hold key positions in order to advance on enemy lines while keeping on the lookout for the ever present eyes of the enemy. This game rewards teamwork, stealth tactics, weapon supremacy, and skill in various and sometimes surprising ways. WIth my little experience in the game, I have found that the learning curve is higher than that of common FPS games, but easily surmountable within a few maps. Heroes of Stalingrad also features a solo campaign for those who want some story or the chance to learn the game at their own pace.
With all that said, I find it hard to locate much fault in this game. It may not be as flashy as some of the more popular war games, but Red Orchestra 2 promotes itself with soild gameplay and much honor to be bestowed to those who are willing to learn.

I found this game to be really, really fun and sometimes quite difficult, and sadly not too long of a game. It is really too bad that it wasn't longer because it is so unique as a sort of Battlezone-like real-time strategy/tactics mashup with third-person control. I wish I knew of any other games out there like this.
The navigation and controls take quite some time to get used to. I remember reading one arguably correct review that said that the control scheme (which I outline in detail below), while extremely responsive, is still so odd that you only REALLY become totally comfortable with it once you're more than halfway through the whole game. It's hard to even classify this game because it blends so many genres together:
- Your aircraft carrier is the only structure that you have (direct control of) per mission. Its onboard factory builds units instantly on demand, though it can only build a small max number of units, like a commando team that can keep being reconstructed as members die. The enemy, however, can slowly build a hypothetically infinite number of units.
- Your resources come from manually salvaging the wreckage of enemy units/structures and civilian buildings, while the enemy has oil derricks and other constant resource streams and C&C-style silos that you can take out.
- You can take personal, more effective command of any one unit (or let all of your operations go 100% automated, toggled by CTRL).
- There is no real-time eye-in-the-sky or top-down view at all, which may be disorienting or frustrating at first. Other than a super-pared-down, basic overhead map viewed while the game is paused, your eyes on the battlefield through the entire game come strictly from what your individual units see from their third-person perspectives, which you can cycle through one by one when desired.
One clear con that the game has for me is that once weaponry on both sides begins to get really advanced, it eventually degenerates into a range competition. Like the RTS Warzone 2100, eventually whoever can simply shoot from farther away wins. Or maybe that's just the way I played Antaeus Rising.
The gameplay mechanics almost remind me of Total Annihilation in how you can queue commands for individual units (attack this, repair that, salvage those parts). And like TA, Antaeus' story and in-game unit construction/reclamation also focuses on the nanobot rage around the turn of our last century. Such a fun game. Anyone who is fine with a learning curve that's on the steeper end should like this one.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand Rick and Morty. The humor is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of theoretical physics most of the jokes will go over a typical viewer's head. There's also Rick's nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation - his personal philosophy draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciatethe depths of these jokes, to realize that they're not just funny- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Rick and Morty truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn't appreciate, for instance, the humour in Rick's existencial catchphrase "Wubba Lubba Dub Dub," which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev's Russian epic Fathers and Sons I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Dan Harmon's genius unfolds itself on their television screens. What fools... how I pity them. joy And yes by the way, I DO have a Rick and Morty tattoo. And no, you cannot see it. It's for the ladies' eyes only- And even they have to demonstrate that they're within 5 IQ points of my own (preferably lower) beforehand.

I enjoyed this game far, far more than I expected I would  - I thought I would skip this entry as I thought the trailer betrayed lower production values than tales of Xillia, and I wasnt sold on the character designs. Regarding the latter, I still dislike Mikleo's clothes and Soreys stupid ear feathers, but after our 70 hours together I love them far too much to care. I loved them enough after 2.
However, The game does seem have Lower Production values than Xillia. The Field environments are far better spatially designs than the blobs of land seen in Xillia, but in parts are very, for want of a better word, polygony. The town and dungeon areas dont seem as well designed as Xillia but they arent quite so polygony. Possibly because most of the dungeons are ruins which could be made from repeatable rectilinear assets which would reduce the work needed.
The battle system is a bit of a departure from previous games. The battle system has been gradually become more are more 3 dimensional in each installment, and using the battle ability 'Free and Free' completly removes the 2d axis you traditionally fight on. I didnt. The ability to fuse with the different seraphim characters in your Party is good to really mix up the playstyle, whether it's for defensive reasons, in order the withstand a bosses blows, or just for when you get surrounded by enemies weak to water and want to maelstrom them into oblivion. The camera is not great. It is what it is.
One thing that has come under fire is the abilities on a grid system. It is quite complicated. There are 50 abilities which all occupy a grid. Line up 2 or more horizontally you will get different elemental bonuses, or of you get all 5 in a collumn vertically you get a stat boost. For example for the first collumn grants you 10% boost on all stats. However I was fearful of losing this bonus after I had gotten it and as as a result by characters were wearing 1st and 2nd tier equipment far too late in the game for them to be doing so. I later opted for equiping all the strongest equipments for their various strengths and making small consessions for certain abilities to make up for a characters weaknesses or provide abilities beneficial for certain bosses. For example I equipped Sorey with 3 peices of equipment with the Lindwer ability, providing 45% more damage against dragons (15 each), and the bonus for stacking 3 was adding an extra unit to my blast gauge (blast gauge being expended for fusing and special attacks).
The Strong point in this game in the characters. They are so likeable. I didnt think anyone would replace Jude Mathis of Tales of Xillia at the top of my list of most likeble Tales Protagonists but Sorey may have done just that. Theres lots of skits that expand on the characters, and even the enemy information is full little tidbits of Lailahs puns, Edna's snark and insults directed at Mikleo, and Sorey being so enamored with the little gun carts the goblins ride that he wished to be the first Goblin Shepherd (all the while being lightly chastised by Mikleo). Theres something quite refreshing about opening the enemy info mid boss and have rose making a Joke. Theres also a fair amount of fun in the item descriptions as well (Soreys not allowed to touch Mikleos hair, not since the incident) and its these little touches that really make Tales of Zestiria.
Theres also a good soundtrack, a few pieces being outstanding, an overall improvement on previous games in the series.
If the question comes down to whether its better than Tales of Xillia then the answer is no, but that comparing an excellent JRPG with a very good one. If you have a PS3 play Xillia first. If you dont this is still worth your time and money.

"The Long Dark" is definitely a breath of fresh air in a market where it seems every survival game is pretty much an off-shot of Minecraft - or just a clone of another one with different "enemies".
What I love, (and sometimes hate), about this game is how you start off with nothing more than the clothes on your back and a few meager items for first aid.   You won't have a gun or some super powered blade.  You will have just you and your wits to survive.   Due to this, you might just learn how spoiled other games have made most of us.  We expect to start off armed to the teeth, or be given weapons immediately.  This game won't do that.  You, and you alone, must find a way to survive on your own.
Now, that said - there are some mistakes, (in my opinion), that this game makes.  It's the same frustrating scheme other survival games use as well.  It's the speed at which your hunger, and other statistics run out.  This irks me with this game as it seems like they meant it to be a survival game that is more realistic.  In the real world, you won't become dehydrated or deathly hungry at the rate you will in this game.  Even the fatigue factor is set to increase a bit too quick.
The amount of wolves spawned in the game is a bit overused.  Meaning they are everywhere...
This, in a naturist sense, is not normal.
On that note - expect to be frustrated anytime you are attacked by a wolf.  Every attack will pin you to the ground, resulting in a click storm to try and survive the attack.  This gets old fast.  Even after you find a knife or a hatchet, the exact same "combat" routine will play out.
The only way this does not happen is if you are lucky enough to find a rifle and shoot the wolf before it ever gets to you.
I definitely hope this combat mechanic gets improved upon.
I'd like to note that there is no jump function.  This seems to be a step backwards for any game.
Anyway, on to the "pros" and "Cons"
Pros:
- Nice change from the other "survival" games out there
- Visually it is a great work
- It will keep you on your toes
- Good repair and realistic crafting system.
- Nice variation of items you can scavenge.
(I don't have too much to list here, it is a rather straightforward game).
Cons:
- Has the same problem mechanics as other "survival" games.  Stats decrease too fast.
- Item weights need to be tweaked a bit.  Some things are a bit too heavy.
- Walking and running speed don't feel right.
- There is no jump function... (Even if it serves no purpose, we all like to jump.)
- Fall height damage needs work.  I severely injured my character on what looked like 3 foot drop.
- Too many wolves...
- No real combat system against wolves.  It's just a click storm.
- Spawn locations are repetitive.
- No in game map.  (Not even one for places you have visited).
Would like to see:
- A map system showing where you are.  Even if it is a map you pick up in a station.
- A wider variety of spawn points.
- More buildings, (in ways that make sense).
- Trading posts or something of that nature where a weapon and ammo would/might be readily available?
- Different hunting weapons.  Bow, crossbow, pistol, scopes, etc.
- A little wider variety of items.
- Other animal types.
- Campfires deters wolves.
- Flares work a bit better when trying to scare off wolves.
- A real combat / defense system when taking on a wolf.  Even something as simple as swiping with the knife / hatchet.
I understand this game is still in development, and most of what I said may or may not be tended to.
We'll have to wait and see.  Though I would still recommend giving this game a shot!

I've played this game out of Steam for quite a while. It reminds me famous days of Robocraft, except all of us are flyers. As it is beta, many elements are not done properly or at all. I like it anyway.
Robocraft was destroyed by a greed of American Developers. Junk League is developed by a friendly independent team from Slovakia. It is pretty funny they made a mistake when translating the game into my mother language (Czech), which is almost same one (Slovakian developed from the Czech). It was saying that team with more -victories- will -win- the game. I didn't know they are Slovakians and I wrote it all English. They replied politely and friendly in Slovakian. I immediately realized it is a good team which will not ♥♥♥♥ the game like Robocraft. There is no either lack of communication or no respect towards community. All is good.
Game itself differs in many ways to Robocraft. First, it happens in an are without gravitation and we all are flyers. But there are still differences between classes. Some of them are slow and strong, others are quick and fragile.
Second, ships are divided in classes with multiple skills. These come in handy when you need to fight, tank, escape or do something else you wanna do. They all have different weight and armor of boxes resulting in additional speed or durability overall.
Third, you do have unlimited amount of bricks once you research them. This is extremely positive as you are not annoyed by buying more and more stuff as you progress each time, you are allowed to use additional CPU.
Fourth, most of the buy-able items are just cosmetics or boosters. They either have just visual effects or add income to the whole team (bigger to the owner). Buying a victory with real money is not possible.
Fifth, you are not supposed to destroy towers. The goal is to fight others and perhaps, there will be other mods. But mainly, a goal is to destroy as much enemy ships as possible. This is good thing, I have never heard of anyone liking destroying Robocraft towers.
Hopefully, I told you about some of the major differences and made you trust Slovakian developers. The review wouldn't be complete if I didn't write anything about incomplete features. The problem is I am not introduced to these much. I wish more abilities, weapons to come in as well as properly made collisions. Your ship cannot turn upside down, so the rotation may be added later.
I really recommend to get this game on to your wishlist or try it yourself immediately. From all the games I've played, this one is the best substritute for Robocraft and its potential is so big it may become a lot better one day. Really, developers learnt from mistakes of Robocraft and added their own ideas creating a stunningly new experience with Galactic Junk League. And I believe, this would become a new BOSS if all of the former RC players supported this. Give it a shoot.

So here it is, another Tales game. I love these games due to their active combat, good story, and not over-the-top art style. Many people want realistic games these days, but this series send it off to the side and give you +80 hours of gameplay with a good New Game+ system and replayability.
Now lets break this game down. Tales of Zestiria is....not the best tales game.
The story follows Sorey, a boy/young man (age 17 but should be more like 14/15 I think) as he leaves his home and becomes the savior of the world. He grew up as the only human in a village of Seraphim, Magical human-like beings that cannot be seen by people who do not truely beleive in them, The world outside of his home is filled with "malevolence" and he must become the Shepard to harness the power of the Seraphim and defeat the Lord of Calamity...and monsters...and dragons.
So I am going to start with the bad things about this game:
1. The world is very linear. I mean the map doesnt show it, but it is almost a straight line between towns and fields with dungeons to the side.
2. Learning skills is again not great, you level up titles and get skills but not the same way like Graces F. The title helps you select which skill you get, but it is a small pool.
3. Purchasing/customizing equipment is fairly staight forward but not great. Limited stocks, an annoying upgrade system, and how equipment bonuses combine is not explained well.
4. Cut content is clear. Some parts of the map, like a field towards the end of the game shows a fortress wall that it looks like you need to pass though and explore the world more, like another nation. Nope, this was cut from the game. It might have fixed some of the linearness but it was deemed unnecessary. You can find small bits here and there around the game.
5. Characters are not great. Example: Sorey, even though he is 17, seems to lack any libido or desire beyond friendship. Now, I am sure this is somewhat understandible but there is almost no, if any, relationships in the game. For a "story rich" game, I am sorry, but there should be some kind of relationship between ANYONE beyond friends.
6. The story. Well the story is okay at best. Unlike other Tales games, this is extremely straight forward. Xillia you couldn't hate your enemy and even respected all of them for their reasons, Symphonia was also complex, Graces was again another complex story where you end up respecting or atleast accepting your enemy. Here in Zestiria though, you are pushed to feel bad for your enemy but....I just can't do it.
Now the saving graces of the game:
1. The active combat of the game like other Tales games, weaknesses, resistances, and your need to guard/quickstep.
2. Replayability
3. Each equipment has it uniqueness with skills to it
4.The Armitization in the game, where you merge with a seraphim and change your combat style.
5. you can make weaker enemies more powerful by equiping "normin" which give you an augment party wide (like 4% def) and boosts enemy levels. up to 3 types of boosts and +30 levels to enemies. Makes weaker areas decent to farm in - if that is what you like.
All in all: It is not a bad game, it is a good game and fun. Gameplay is great though the plot could be better. Cut material from the game really makes is sad how much is lacking from what could have been. Battles are fun to play and can be avoided if you want (for the most part) as it is not random encounters. Not a game I will sit for hours on end playing, but I will play a couple here and there with breaks in between.

Like if I want to do some complex scripted event where I walk up to a chest, open it, find nothing inside, then walk away and want the chest to come alive, flapping itself open and close a couple times, then come charge at me and engage in a battle with a living treasure chest monster... This game is really something special.  There are games that look better graphically, sure.  There are games with bigger budgets, more insane AAA setpieces, and even longer games.  But there are few games out there with the kind of heart that A Hat in Time has.  It isn't just a Mario or Banjo clone (though the DNA of those games is certainly present). It is also its own game, and am I really glad it is.
I have seen many a comparison to Mario Sunshine, but that's just the beginning.  The different levels act as homages to different platform games in some ways, I suppose.  Mafia Town could be a Mario Sunshine stage, but the second level is more like a Psychonauts stage and so on.
I don't want to say too much else, but if you like games with heart and are willing to put up with a few technical problems to enjoy the kind of game that doesn't come along very often, A Hat In Time is something you just need to play.  It won't be a critical success and won't sell millions of copies, but it will be a cult classic and in a few years everyone will be telling you that you should play it, like Psychonauts before it.

Tales of Zestiria (RPG)
Story 5/10
Characters 7/10
Gameplay 8/10
World 5/10
Sound 8/10
Graphics 6/10
Verdict: Good with a few flaws
TLDR: Chances are if you're a Tales fan, you'll probably enjoy this game.
The Good:
All the standard hallmarks of a Tales game are here - the combat is as robust as ever, akin to a fighting game where you chain together combos. The game has one of the better soundtracks for an RPG. The skits(short scenes with the characters interacting with each other) are fun to watch.
The Meh:
The random loot system is in-depth but feels under-utilized. Graphics are servicable but strictly average. The setting has lots of potential but in the end, it sort of  hindered how the game was played.
The Ugly:
The story is painfully average. While there's nothing wrong with a classic Good vs Evil storyline, the plot feels barebones and the characters, while well written, feels under-developed. It's just not executed very well.
Conclusion:
Tales of Zestiria brings in some fresh ideas while sticking to a classic formula. Most of them work well to bring the series to the next stage.  It'll be interesting to see how the series contine to evolve in the next game.

The Beginners Guide is a perfect example of how computer games, when done right, are undeniably a legitimate platform for art, capable of evoking all sorts of feels. The game plays out over about 1.5 to 2 hours, depending on how much you choose to immerse yourself in the story. The game has no guns, no countdown clock, no flag to capture, and even when you encounter a puzzle you are handed the solutions.
On the surface the game is a compilation of someone else's unfinished works, smoothly connected and edited by the narrator/creator, but at about halfway through the game starts to feel more like an interactive diary, focusing on the relationship and mental health of two game designers.
Little more can be said for this game, it is simply something you must experience in a single, uninterrupted sitting. Because of its simplicity, it is also a game that anyone, regardless of gaming skills, can experience equally. 10/10

I have played about 15-20 hours of the game during the beta. If you want my review in Video form here is the review in video form.
I have also included a transcript below.
The basic premise of the game is that you Build a ship out of blocks. You jump into a match to see how it performs. Whether you end up wrecking or getting wrecked that game is fun. The match ends and you find yourself back at the start of that loop.
Except now you that you’re back you have a little bit more knowledge, more money, more experience and so you make changes just a few blocks at a time and then you loop this process of Build-Fight-Rethink again and you keep going through this incredibly rewarding, compelling and exciting gameplay loop until you’ve gained so much money and experience that by the end of a play session you’ve made this cube of death with guns sticking out of it and thats ok because you’re winning, except its not okay because its just a cube with guns strapped on it because the game punishes creativity.
In answer to the question “Should you play this game?” I say “Absolutely, why not? If you think it looks interesting you should play it, its free.” but another part of me would say “No, don’t play this game you’ll only be disappointed in it."
And the first thing I like is the aesthetic. And in all honestly its not even particularly well done but it just kind of works for the game. It has thematic consistency across the UI, the sound and the graphics. I don’t really know how to describe it but nothing feels out of place, it all feels like it belongs and that in my opinion means the aesthetic has been done correctly. It all just sort of fits together nicely in a neat little package.
I also love the core gameplay loop. I love building a ship, taking it to battle, getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked coming back changing my ship going back into battle kicking someone else’s♥♥♥♥♥♥getting myself some money f to buy new parts for my ship and then I rebuild it start getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked and then I go back to the start and just repeat that over and over for a couple of hours and its all just wonderful fun.
Taken without all of it’s flaws, theres a very fun experience to be found here. But oh my, the flaws, they come in droves and they hammer you into submission until that initial joy and excitement is refined into Free-To-Players Remorse, regret and frustration.
What frustrates me the most about the game is that there’s a amazing, fun little experience here. There’s a really rewarding and interesting distraction. But its just overshadowed, obscured and obfuscated by this crap that just sits on the game and ruins it all. And theres all this baggage on the game that just gets into every little nook and cranny ruining the game piece by piece. This baggage, comes from a few places. One of those is a Diabolical disgusting and devious place that you’ll all be very familiar with. And that place… is the free to play model. It just sits on every mechanic, it never lets you get away from it, it never gives you a break like an overzealous nihilist it just holds its hand under your nose saying “Wheres the money Lebowski?” And this is where the game dies in my opinion. The game forgets, that its free. The game forgets that free players are supposed to get a complete game and the paying players are supposed to get status, style and first dibs on new content in that complete game with a little bit of conveinience stirred in.
And thats just one flaw. Another glaring flaw with the game is related to the business model. You might have heard this called Seal clubbing or as I like to call it “The Fun wall” and make no mistake this wall is not fun. This wall is designed to keep fun out. It is designed so that people who have been playing longer have an insurmountable inherent advantage. Now don’t get me wrong. I’m not against advantages for players who’ve playing longer or use different playstyles, but when you’re loading up your first few games and theres ship in that game that will shoot you ONCE and kill you instantly then... then I have a problem. Either you need to fix your matchmaking, you need to fix your balance or you need to fix the fundamental progression model just anything SOMETHING has to give here in order for the game to reach it’s true potential and not be left broken and forgotten on the floor in hall of free to play failures.
I think the real take home here that doesn’t just apply to this game is that there are so many amazing experiences out there that are just being hamstrung in their ability to be successful by the very decisions that were designed to make those games successful. It breaks my heart, that time after time and time again the same mistakes keep being made over and over. These unsustainable, short term, whale centric market strategies have littered the annals of gaming with great games destroyed by their poor business models.  Some of my favourite games of all time are free to play games. But when you’re treated like just another bubble in a sheet of bubble paper that someone else gets to pop but you never get to be the popper unless you spend an absolutely outrageous amount of time or money on the game. Well, I lose interest and so do, I think, the majority of people.
I haven’t even begun to criticise the balance of the game. Which with a cursory glance after three to five hours of playing anyone could surmise either that through incompetence, deliberate action or some combination of the two it seems that every single element of the game’s balance feeds into making the previous problems EVEN more egregious, even more atrocious even more dare I say cancerous for the game. You have an inequality of strategies where a single playstyle completely dominates to the point of everything else not being even remotely viable. Now sure enough, its probably not fair to include game balance as a criticism for an early access title considering there are going to be patches new content and so on and so forth. However, I’m not criticising the game in 6 months after so many patches. I’m criticising the game now.
Right now once you hit highers levels of gameplay the game devolves into blobs of ships with sniper plasma cannons firing at each other this often means that the winner of the game is typically decided by which team had the least number of new players on their team who end up being crushed under the boot of these ultra long range plasma guns. This dynamic creates an incredibly unrewarding scenario, where the single ship type that gets extra range on it’s weapons completely dominates the metagame because the game just doesn’t give you the tools to deal with them or the tools they do give are inadequate to deal with them. I tried to make a high speed fighter with all sorts of weapons to counter this plasma balls strategy and I was met with some initial success but in the end as the number of people in plasma death cubes increased and  I found myself unable to beat them so I joined them and made my own plasma death cube.
Thats why I think the balance of the game leaves something to be desired and that just might just be the understatement of the year and its only January!
My final verdict? I love the game, I hate the game, I hope they fix it but I’m not optimistic yet I am optimistic about it. If it sounds like fun, play it. If all the baggage sounds like too much for you, avoid it. When you consider its just a silly little spaceship shooter where you build ships out of blocks you can forgive it’s lack of depth and look past its flaws and have a few hours of fun before uninstalling it. It needs more time in development, it needs balancing, it needs adjustments to it’s free to play model but at the core there is a fun game here.

I've been a fan of this game for many years, still got it on CD somewhere.
Narrated by Tom Baker of Dr. Who fame, and with Paul Darrow (Avon from the cult BBC series "Blakes' Seven") voicing one of the main characters, the voice acting is of exceptional quality, unsurprisingly. Let's face it, any game that starts with the Fourth Doctor talking to you is already on a winning streak.
In play, the game is a mixture of Strategy and Shooter, and a very well executed mixture too, the game allows you to smoothly swap between piloting vessels and issuing orders to your AI troops, and it's with those AI troops that the game really takes on a unque aspect, because they are characters, with strengths and weaknesses that you need to use.
Drop Ransom in a tank and you are not only not going to get a great performance, you are also most likely, going to get a sarcastic comment from Ransom himself ("I'm an Aviator Ay-Vee-Ay-Tor!"). Put Sinclair into anything that moves and he'll be off like an over-eager puppy with no sense of self-preservation, put him in a stationary laser-turret, however and he's deadly. You have to manage your troops.
The story itself is well constructed, based on an interesting premise and the diificulty curve is steep, but not unmanageable, though strategy is important, the game never gets to the stage where you can face the enemy on equal terms, producing energy, and destroying the enemies ability to do so will always be the primary concern in every mission.
There ARE a few wierd 'blips' in the game that can be a frustrating, certain stealth missions are more irritating than challenging, and the ending
, but all in all, if you can forgive the fact that the engine looks as old as it is, this is still a great, entertaining and challenging game, even after all these years.

I was so excited to try out this game, and when I finally got my hands on it I loaded the game, and tried to start a new game... And... It crashed. Fortunately, the community had found a fix to the problems that were keeping me from playing, so I patiently followed those instructions and was able to load up the game successfully.
Once I started, I was exceptionally underwhelmed by everything about the game. The intro was worse than Skyrim's start, with extremely awkward cutscenes treating the player like an idiot that needed their hand held through fairly simple mechanics. I hoped once I got through the opening scenes it would get better, but unfortunately it got worse. The conversations remained boring. The plot never got interesting.
I think an important part of RPGs is being brought into the world and feeling a weight to decision-making. But nothing about the world was interesting. The characters are mostly paper thin, with boring acting performances. The moral decisions in the game are laughable (should I blow up a town because some random people asked me to?), and the quests feel like busy work. The shooting mechanics were decent, but not that special. The asthetics of the world weren't particularly great, and the fact that enemies blow up into little pieces when they're shot by a pistol didn't help draw me into the world.
In short, I think it's an overhyped game with nothing interesting to offer players.

One of the most criminally underrated and unknown games out there.
You play as the last functional Adaptive Cruiser, the Antaeus - a vessel capable of building combat units from scratch with its on-board Creation Engine - fighting on behalf of the global utopian society that had abolished war. Your advesaries are the Cabal, the "old guard" of tyrants that had once ruled the world, and seek to do so again.
Pros:
- Great voice acting, the characters... have character. They'll chat to one another during the missions, complain if you put them in their least favourite type of vehicle, each have lines for calling out specific enemy units, reporting their vehicle's status, even whether or not they're able to engage an enemy they're being attacked by.
- A pretty interesting plot, narrated by Tom Baker no less. Nothing amazing, but the worldbuilding and the way the plot progression influences the gameplay is.. cool.
- Simple arcade-vehicle gameplay but with a relatively deep strategy/tactics layer on top.
You can spend the entire mission just ordering your units around from the map and watch them do their work (Though the "RTS" view is not Real-time), or build a unit without a soul-chip (ie an AI pilot) to use for yourself. You can also take direct control of any vehicle piloted by your NPCs, which is another thing they'll comment on.
You have a lot of freedom to set your own objectives and tackle them in whichever order you see fit. Some mission-critical objectives require you to act pretty fast, but generally speaking you can go at your own pace.
The enemies will have their own production facilities meaning you're almost always either attacking, or defending your resource operations. Sometimes they go hand-in-hand. You can destroy their energy production which will (after the reserve power runs out or is destroyed) prevent their facilities producing vehicles, or go straight for the buildings themselves. You'll have to watch out for the million flak cannons that are in each mission though.
- Diverse "cast" of vehicles, weapons and components; Shields, Armour, Cloaking, Long-range precision Lasers, Howitzers, Missile launchers, Helicopters, Hovercraft, Tanks. Each combination of weapon, vehicle and component(s) can be effective.
- Likewise, lots of enemy stuff to destroy. They have Tanks, Self-propelled Guns, Mammoth tanks, Attack and Scout helicopters each based on real-world designs. There are emplaced AAA sites, howitzers, autocannon turrets and bunkers. Each poses a differing level of threat to each of your units. They're.. "upgraded" later in the game, and ultimately replaced by things much more sinister.
- Simple in-game ordering system. Though the interface/controls for it are a bit archaic, after a few minutes using it it becomes muscle-memory. Order all your pilots to follow your vehicle and engage targets at will along the way, tell a specific unit to attack a specific target etc.
- Resource system: Instead of a mine or forest you gotta tell your little people to chop down, there's only really one way to gather resources in this game: Blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up. The enemy vehicles and facilities you destroy will be turned to debris, which you must harvest either with a helicopter sling-loading it to your carrier, or by a dedicated Recycler unit, the Scarab. Some of the situations you'll find yourself in will prevent you from keeping a resource collector at a source Later in the game, you will gain access to a vehicle that can carry out both this and a combat role at the same time.
Most missions will have areas full of pre-existing debris, or empty structures for you to harvest, but they will only net you so much energy before you have to move on to the next.
Cons:
- The game has poor replayability. There's no facility for loading a specific mission after you've completed the game (Unless you save for each one - however there are only 9(?) save slots and more than 9 missions), there's no skirmish or multiplayer modes. That hasn't stopped me coming back and playing through it again every couple years. For the asking price now, that shouldn't be much of an issue because other than that, the game stands as it is.
That said, there are cheats that let you skip through missions and access the entire tech-tree in any mission, but I'd advise against using them your first play-through.
- Slightly archaic control schemes - As I mentioned earlier, this mainly extends to the command interface - When you're not using the map, if you want to order a unit to do something, you press the appropriate number for that unit, and use W/A/S/D/Q/E to navigate the menu. The problem here is those are also the controls you use to move. This results in 1: the unit you're controlling stopping dead while you issue the order and 2: Possibly inadvertently issuing the wrong order because you were also using those buttons to move.
If you really need something done at that specific moment and the unit you're controlling is going to die if you rescind control for even a second, you're better off just going to the map screen and issuing orders from there since it pauses the game. Not a huge issue, but it's probably the most prevalent throughout the game. Otherwise, it's easy to get used to.
- No difficulty levels. The game is sufficiently challenging, but there are a couple of missions, one too easy to the point of tedium and one that's pretty damn hard. Fortunately the latter one is later in the game, so hopefully you'll be prepared for it.
Neutral:
- This game doesn't hold your hand. The first three missions serve as a tutorial essentially, letting you get to grips with the resource collection, combat and ordering mechanics. Beyond that, the only direction and help you'll receive is from the mission briefings by Church and Walker - And what they say is almost always relelvant.
- Mandatory stealth mission. Yeah, one of those. The mission fails if you're detected (Up til you've completed a particular objective), but as above, the guidance offered by your superiors will help you prevent it.
- Little music. There are a few tracks, but they're reserved mainly for the main menu, the briefing and cutscenes with none during gameplay, bar one (short) mission.
- Graphics are obviously dated, but still serviceable. Probably one of the better-looking games of its time.

Developer Quantic Dream, makers of Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls, made this gem too, if you played any of those before then you will know what to expect here. if you haven't then beware, this isn't the regular type of action game you know. it is more like an interactive movie where you have to make choices and do some QTE (kinda like Telltale games) to progress. I found this to be an immersive supernatural thriller, introducing Quantic Dream's unique brand of "interactive movie" gameplay that they do so well.
There's an overall cinematic feel to Fahrenheit that lends a unique atmosphere to the presentation. This is evident from the very beginning, which is probably one of the best opening scenes (not better than Silent Hill 2 though).
- regarding the story (no spoilers), it's a psychological thriller that, as it progresses, takes on more and more over-the-top supernatural elements. I think many would be turned off by the far-fetched twists and turns that the plot takes, but I really liked it and was hooked till the end.
- Gameplay is a mixture of moving around like the known adventure games, look around for stuff to interact with and doing many QTE (Quick Time Events) which kinda looks like the old toy (Simon) where you have to follow the lights sequences and push the buttons in the direction of the lights. also, it has the "choose your own adventure" style of dialogue (several conversation options at select points  (you're asked to pick one quickly to determine where it goes from there). sometimes if you fail you will die and have to restart the sequence.
- The graphics of course looks really dated (kinda similar to Max Payne graphics). while it isn't the remaster i was hoping for it is still better than the original and much better than the PS2 version. the price is fair i think. i even saw the option to play it at 4K but my screen is only 1080p so i went with that. but no matter what resolution you use the textures aren't gonna improve much, I highly recommend playing it with a controller (Xbox 360 or xbox1 controllers works perfectly).
- I really have huge respect for Quantic Dream, they took big risks in making this and their later games in a way that won't appeal to everyone and won't sell like other AAA games but are great and unique none the less.
- The port ran fine for me so far except one scene in the office where all characters vanished and i was just hearing voices then the game froze and crashed, other than that one instance eveything went fine and dandy.
- Small note to the developer, it would be better if i could highlight the resolution i want then click apply than having the screen flashing on me while scrolling through resolution options.

This is an addicting title.
When I started playing, it kept reminding me of RUST, somehow. But make no mistake, this game is much harder. I started it like five or six times, every time being suddenly killed by a wolf - once, I even ran over a frozen lake with only a few % of life left, only to die from freezing the moment a warming, safe hut creeped out of the snow storm and into my view. Needless to say, I was frustrated - but I started the sandbox again anyway.
The entire survival system is very well thought out. Calories (though correctly, they should be Kilocalories, but I don't want to be the nitpicker here) show a known, realistic measure of how much energy one has remaining, and the four values Fatigue, Cold, Hunger and Thirst give a simplified but sufficient overview of the character's status. Items are mostly spawned at random, though some keep staying the same (such as specific animal carcasses).
The artwork and sound is beautiful. Treading my way through a snowy valley, I heard my footsteps, the sound of wind in my ears and a wolf howling from afar, which all made for an eerie, but hauntingly beautiful atmosphere.
Would buy again.

So here is the thing, TOZ is a great game, no really a great game, but not one without flaws, however this game is also the pin point change of the franchise to the famous open world genre, its a test for the future and my vision tells me is a nice step to it, hopefully Berseria (coming one) will have perfected everything I am going to tell.
PROS:
-Open World : this is the next step for the franchise and its a nice step they took it with Zestiria, everything looks awesome and pretty well connected, travel around it as much as you want and the battle transition is so seamless you will feel you are playing a game without loading screens.
-Combat: the addon of SC as a combat mediator is amazing, it will avoid the player to resort to hack'n'slash in the battle, thinking of timing, defense, evasion and new tactics makes the battle liver and more intense.
-Characters: the same as every Tales of game I have played, entertaining, funny, you get to form a bond with them and understand their problems and vision of the world, I actually cared for these characters a lot. The amount of skits is also nothing close to small and they are pretty interesting to see, I often resorted to just listen to them instead of playing.
-Animation: even with the casual hate for 30fps the game has a great animation you wont even think you are playing at 30fps, the technology behind the game make everything very vivid and inmmersive for an anime looking JRPG.
-Soundtrack: the music behind the game is astonishing mainly the music from certain dungeons and the song RIsing Up inspired me so much that I have them with me all the time.
-Story: the history is pretty much inspired in the good vs the bad, its nothing new in the genre however the way of telling is what is different in a world when only a few ones can see the Seraphim race, the telling of the Sheperd becomes a more related one to the tales of Don Quixote de la Mancha, where the Sheperd is fighting a giant golem and everyone sees simply a rock, funny and yet makes you think what lies beyond the common eyes.
-Tons of quests and customization: from the equipment to fashion, from simple quests to quests that can customize the very influence you have in certain areas of the map that will affect not only the enemies you fight but the rewards you will get.
CONS:
-Combat: even if the combat is going in a good direction is not one without flaws, the 3rd person camera becomes almost a 1st person one when combating in narrow spaces or when the back of the player is against a big object. Also the camera being so close to the character makes it really difficult to observe your surroundings, a fix is using the Free Run abililty however since it disabled the SC recovery its a double edge sword.
-Story: even if the telling is amazing the main bone of it is very basic compared to other Tales of games, mainly compared to the next entry in the PC realm, Symphonia, its not bad but for the first entry as an open world is lack lustered, not many inspirational moments will be found in this game.
-Skill/Fuse interface: the whole game interface is really good however the other side of the coin is when you are going to fuse an equipment it becomes a pain to distinguish how it will affect your equipment skills (which are tremendously important in the game, if you dont keep them checked you are going down), I ended up leaving the fuse window to check which skills I was going to get and back again to check which fusion will benefit me the most, a pain certainly.
-Open Empty World: even if the world is wide open and big, the empty spaces between enemies is pretty big so sometimes it feels like a very empty world, dont be discouraged by this but be prepared by it.
-Sorey is your only character outside the map. You wont change it, its a minor thing but since in the other games you could change them I feel like a backstep when I discovered this.
MIXED
-Party Setup: the party is stucked at the two humans characters meaning you wont move them from the party, the only thing you can customize is the initial seraphims that will start the battle with you, fortunately this can be changed at any point even during battle with ease. This also is influenced by the story of the game, thats why its a mixed opinion. I didnt liked it at first but seeing how the story unfolded I understood it has to be done.
DLC
*SPOILER ALERT REGARDING ALISHA*
-Alishas Story DLC: many think this was bad since Alisha should be a permanent character in the main game, but as with the mixed opinion I had with the party setup Alishas Story is also mixed, I think it Alisha should have stayed in the main game however the story unfolded so well I didnt see a problem with her separating from the main cast. This DLC made me realize it was a brave move and I support it fully.
*END OF SPOILERS*
-Costumes: all the costumes are amazing and hilarious, they are unneeded and they do not affect your gameplay but after playing for many hours you wish you could change your characters a few things here and there, costumes are for that. There are some unlockables in the game but most of them will appear as future DLC, so get your card ready ;)
-Free Skits: get this DLC its full of funny skits that will make you laugh a lot! HOWEVER! Listen to this Skits only and ONLY when you have finished both the main game and Alishas Story DLC so you wont be spoiled of some elements of the story and characters.
TIME TO FINISH IT: Straight forward 30hrs, with side quests and extra dungeons: over 65hrs
GAME RATED: 75~80/100 = GREAT
RECOMMENDED: YES!
BEST IN THE SERIES? Nope, but its the first being an open world so its understandable that the transition will take its toll somewhere.

The Long Dark is, in my humble opinion, the best survival game available.  Even though it's in its early access stage it looks and plays as well or better than most titles not made by big name publishers, e.g. Activision or Ubisoft, I've played for six hours now and have yet to run into any game breaking glitches or bugs although you will run into invisible walls but you can easily get around most of these by side stepping or approaching from a different angle.
Some +'s and -'s:
+ The gun is iron sightable and the sight itself is crisp and easy to use/aim.
+ Survival is mostly common sense and believable.
- The survival 'traits?' themselves, namely food drain way too fast, you'll need to eat constantly and you won't last more than a few hours before starving.
+ The world perfectly captures the savage beauty of North-West America.
+ Effect's such as wind, fog, smoke, snow, light, and shadow are included and they are very well done.
- Limited Item crafting, well not limited but will leave you wanting more.
- You can't walk away from boiling water or leave food to cook whilst you tend to other things.
Some things I would love to see added to The Long Dark are:
* Bow's, Javelins, and Spears.
- Craftable and more pratical than a rifle when ammo is scarce.
* Snowshoes and Ski's.
* These should be included because you shouldn't be able to walk on snow without them, more like wade really. Also increase movement speed and lower carb consumption.
* More animals such as bears and lynx.
* A dog companion:)
- The game needs this it really does, if included the dog should be trained to stay, fetch(e.g. rabbit corpses), protect you from wolves and other preditor's, and maybe be a sled dog... disreegard that it should DEFINITELY be a sled dog "Mush Balto mush!"
* Maple Syrup, I mean come on it's Canda! also hockey memorblia for the same reason.
* More traps available than just rabbit snares, also ice fishing should be passive like trapping. In Alaska we use a cross shaped set with the line attached to the end too short to touch the sides when a fish is on line the side(flag) opposite the line raises and lets you know that you've caught something.
Thank you for reading my review and leave a comment if you'de like or if you wish to add to my The Long Dark wishlist and if you still can't decided whether or not to get the game all I can say to you is that there is a very good reason why out of thousands of reviews the feedback is "Overwhelmingly Positive" for a reason and well worth the charge.
P.S. Sorry for any Spelling or Grammar errors it's well past time my bed time but I just had to show my support for this game.

While this has a lot of potential, and is fun for starters, it gets way to repetetive quickly.
Every single takeover mission is the same, and the NPCs always say the same basic things. Start -> Open the gates -> Shoot -> take out minigun emplacement -> shoot -> takeout minigun emplacement -> protect the NPC while he hacks , using the minigun -> take out base comander, who is in a chopper -> listen to your buddies cheer your name
The other faction missions also don't have an awful lot of variety. Most boil down to:
Get in a car or hijack a car -> get to specific location
Get to a location -> Kill a target
Disarm bombs / hack computers (which basically requires you to do the same)
The design of the map also works against it's theme: causing chaos. It doesn't really provide you with enough oprotunities to do something incredebly cool, especially considering how cool the first couple of missions are
Most of the map is just empty landscape, where there isn't a whole lot to blow up, and you'll just end up losing heat if you go there. It really could have benefited from a smaller map with more creative secrets, like having to bring in a chopper and use it with your grapling hook to lift up some junk, allowing you to get down a hole and get your reward. Land vehicles are also completely useless offroad, due to most of the map being mountains and islands, meaning the best way to get around is a combo of your parachute and grapling hook (which admitedly is pretty cool, but will get tedious eventually). To add to that, vehicles just seem to handle horribly.
Combat also gets old, and is too easy, even on hardcore mode, and most of the time you can just shoot without having to use cover. It doesn't change much depending on which weapons you use, and they honestly don't feel that different. Upgrading weapons also upgrades them by the game's own rules, instead of letting you chose what you want to upgrade. I bring this up because the magazine size is completely useless, as reloading is so fast, you'll barely even notice it. Plus the difference in reload time is small to none-existent between weapons. It actually seems like a shotgun, which would take longer to reload has the shortest reload time. I didn't feel much need to upgrade weapons at all, and when I did, I noticed little to no difference.
All that said, there were some really awesome moments, when you get to do them. Like near the beggining of the game, where you can jump between enemy jeeps, place explosives, jump back to your car, and blow them to s**t, or even simply jumping on the roof of your car during a high speed chace, take out your persuers, and jump back in, continueing to drive.
The grapling hook is also really cool, and really feels like there's plenty of untapped potential with it. This should have been THE item to upgrade.
TL;DR : Too repetetive to be fun in the long run.

My biggest complaint, is that the main character is supposed to be BIG into dungeon diving and relics. Yet the only thing you will find in the dungeons of this game, are enemies, treasure chests, and corridors. Here is a small example of how barren the dungeons are. After playing 40 or so hours, walking into a dungeon and seeing a torch made me suspicious. I went over to the torch to see if it was something I needed to activate. If a single light source makes me think something is out of place in a dungeon, then you can imagine how barren it is. Literally rooms and corridors. Maybe a decoration bit here or there, but you will always check them because they all scream out of place. All of these dungeons are like this that ive been in except the very first.
The overworld is beautiful and the skyboxes are quite nice. Yet you will see the same enemies throughout the game just with different color schemes which is a con. -Some of the voice-work is kinda bad, though that is balanced out by some very stellar performances with some characters. And most of cast sounds fine.
-Camera is a bit wonky at points, but it's not bad. Just expect the standard 3D platformer yank.
-There's no easy way to see how many minor collectibles you're missing from each level. This one really sucks, if you are planning to go for absolute 100%. If you just want your file to display 100% clear, I guess it's not a problem since that only counts the Time Pieces, and not the Rift Tokens or Yarns.
-I don't think there is a way to change the control mapping? Which is really weird, given how good rest of the settings are.
But really, the positives far outweight the negatives. If you are into 3D platformers and objective based collect-a-thons, I totally recommend this.

It's time for my Review.
I finished the game just now and it's so much better than what I first thought would await me. Do you remember games like Sonic Adventure DX that tried to tie Story and 50 minigames into one? It failed at that and couldn't deliver. A Hat in Time however, completely does. From racing portions to horror sections, sky exploration to mail delivery, Hat Kid goes on an adventure to return all of the Timepieces after a tragic accident involving her and a planet's Mafia.
Throughout the Adventure, you will be spoiled with a wonderful, colorful word, funny and sweet portions of comedy, an engaging gameplay Experience filled with optional, yet rewarding pieces that will make your time playing this game just so much more exciting.
The soundtrack of A Hat in Time, partially composed by Grant Kirkhope, THE Grant, the same man who composed for Banjo & Kazooie and other popular Rare titles of the past, adds life to the visual style of the game. The spooky bits are filled with spooky music, the lively towns emit joyful tunes.
If your friends haven't recommended this game to you yet, I hope I can convince you to at least 'try' the game out. If you don't like the first hour, you can still refund the game.
After talking to the developers and artists for many hours, I really couldn't feel bad about spending 30 bucks on a game again. It's been a wonderful experience and the money goes to forthcoming people that put their heart into the game.
Sadly, some portions of the game were sometimes confusing (The spooky world more than once) and glitchy, which subtracts from the overall Rating I am giving this game:
9/10
The game's length is just acceptable for an indie developer team that worked on it for so many years. I went into this experience with no expectations, not being a backer but being intriged 3-4 years ago by the prototype build. I was BLOWN away. This game is everything I wanted it to be. Collectibles that are both intresting and worth collecting. A beutiful world of intresting locations. A control scheme that, even with a mouse and keyboard, controls wonderfully. That being said, there some things the prospective buyer should know. First off, the game, even with its bright, cheery exterior, does contain some scary imagery that may frighten children, though most adults and teens will probably be unaffected. Second, the game is about as difficult as the old platformers it tries to repliate, like Spyro or Mario 64. Just getting to the end credits is easy enough for a child, but colecting all the time pieces is actually preatty darn challenging. Third, the game has a comedic element to it. I thought it was truly funny, but the humor is kind of like that of Paper Mario, the Thousand Year Door, it is inofensive and family-friendly, yet still well crafted and funny. The one complaint I have is that the naritive elements are somewhat uneven. The second chapter, Battle of the Birds, was very naritive intensive, and had lots of great jokes. On the other hand, Mountain Peaks had almost no humor or story. I just personally wish the whole game was as over-the-top as Battle of the Birds, but that is probably just me.

Invite the Demons into your Computer with Five Night's At Freddy's, a unique, one-of-a-kind Horror Experience brought forth from the crazy/genius mind of developer Scott Cawthon. No movement, no fancy mechanics. Simple point-and-click horror at its best. These monsters take the form of your inner childhood fears and stalk the corridors of a derelict pizzeria, eager to, without heistation, force your weak human form into a walking Iron Maiden and kill you in the most horrific way imaginable. One second they're there, the next, gone. But, always watching you.
Simple mechanics. Open a door, close a door. Turn on a light, turn it off again. Open camera view, close camera view. Five Nights (give or take a few, if you play long enough) alone with 4 (5 *wink*) murderous animatronics. The question falls to you.
Are you ready, for when Freddy comes for you?
