Blegh. Not the best fallout by a long shot. Sure, I enjoyed it a bit, but that was before I hit teenage years and started to understand what makes a game fun. And I determined that this is quite a miserable excuse for a good game.
This open-ended, *riveting* first person RPG game with a complex moral system is essentially what happens when you have an hour to do a piece of writing. The concepts are thoughtful. Morality and karma are a good idea in most RPG games in my personal opinion. So Bethesda spent time and money thinking of all the features of the game.
By the time they thought of everything they could, they had 5 minutes left, so they jammed it all in, not giving a flying ♥♥♥♥ how it would end up. Physics engine? Laughable at best. Yes, we needed to see the dead body awkwardly fall down once dying. You guys DO know that a dead body shot by a gun or slapped by a deathclaw would kinda move backwards a bit, not just flop to the ground as if your knees gave out. Oh, the morality system. How about you go to the first location and face your first large morality system. Be nice to this town, or blow it the ♥♥♥♥ up. Blowing up the town would be a good moral choice if, I don't know, the town had a dodgy history like slavery, and actively traded slaves. Then it's ok to put an armed nuclear device in the center of it. Personally I think if you blew Megaton up for the sake of it, you should probably talk to a psychiatrist, because if thats your perception of morality then I think you need help.
Gun play. Yes. Squint down the side of the gun because peering .5x further would increase my aim a bunch.
Story. Let's just watch a bunch of people do the stuff and things and I'll be in the corner being the hired gun yes? You get almost no input in the story until the last part of the game where the enclave just say 'hey we really want you to put the thing in the thing so we can do our thing' instead of trying to wrest control of the things away from you. Have I mentioned the enclave were only here as a weak excuse for the black/white 'bad guys'? Because they are. They just want to slap a Enclave sticker on the water and call it their own.
Open endedness. One good faction and one bad. It is literally shown straight away that Enclave = bad and BoS = good. Not one action so far by the Enclave in Fo3 can be percieved as misguided or in the good. They want to kill. BoS want to protect. Not a lot of freedom there when the 'open-ended game' is actually telling you where to go.
I did like a couple bits of the game. The vaults were fun to explore. I especially liked 112 or whatever it is. Computer simulator vault. Also gary is nice.
If you want a good 3D fallout game, get NV. Not this. Spare yourself.

Storywise i m done, playwise i just started!
The game isnt perfect and the story is average as it can get. If you play a game for FPS or ONLY for an amazing story you can safely drop this one.
If you, however want to try out an incredible combat system, want to experience likable characters and a good soundtrack you should instantly grab it.
Well you are a normal person who can see Seraphs, invisible humans with elemental powers who are worshiped as goddess due to the lack of people that can see them.
You are more or less dragged into to take the burden of the shepherd. A human who can utilize the power of seraphs to defeat the great evil.
Storywise there is not much to it. However its not so much about "i get power and heal/kill all who oppose me" but rather the questions "what will i do if i actually cannot save those who are fallen into evilness" and "What actions will i do and how will it change me".
There are many loose ends and alot isnt well explained (if any information is available at all).
Things supposedly seem very important tp the story but then are not touched again in any way. You mightt get the feeling that the story isnt well presented or written.
It gets the passing mark, but nothing more in this regard.
I dont care. Its 30 FPS locked. I dont care. Some do. It looks amazing in my opinion, but my standards seems to be to low for some guys out there. So i will not drag this out any further.
You have the typical Tales-of action combat system, in which you control one character of your 4-people party in a 3D environment and blast out combo attacks. The other characters are controlled by an AI which can be given general guidelines.
The focus here is similar to Tales of Graces. The main focus is to dodge and wait for opportunities to start combos while the martial artes of humans are layed in a tiered fashion.
There are several types of attacks (calles arte) which cancel each other out the same way as rock, paper, scissors. These types are martial artes, hidden artes and seraphic artes.
Furthermore attacks every arte an elemental or type weakness and may inflict a status alignment.
The bosses usually 1-hits any character, so dodging is a necessity for being successful. Problem arises for AI-controlled which rarlx manage to do so.
Alot micromanagement is necessary in higher difficukties.
Furthermore apart from the already mentioned there is another key mechanic : armetization.
This is a fusion of one of your human characters with a seraph character into a mighty warrior.
This form, despite being powerful, complements the beforementioned rock, paper, scissor mechanic. While humans can do martial artes and hidden artes and seraph can do martial artes and seraphic artes an artetization can do hidden artes and seraphic artes.
Overal there are many things i didnt touch in my explanation. The overal complexity ranges from overly complex to being button smashing depending on difficulty.
The equipment system is rather interesting. Some say its overly complicated. It may be if you restrict yourself to ingame information and dont acknowledge external infos. The really important things are explained but are a bit misleading worded.
Basically each equipment item can only be wield by certain characters. Each equipment has 4 slots of potential skills (attack +4%, +15% against beast enemies and so on). While the first slot is fixed for all items with this name the other 3 are random and can be manipulated.
Each skill represents a slot on a skill-board. Stacking the same skill or chaining skills vertically or horizontally wield special bonusses. Thats basically it. The thing most people dont get is how the 3 changable slots in each equipment can be manipulated.
This can be achieved by fusing same equipments together. These fusions follow strict rules and are by no means random. Yet you can easily get certain gear with specific skills without understanding one specific rule.
This all may sound complicated but its really only a small (unimportant) part which is confusing about this system.
Overall you can compose your equipment supporting your playing style and there is no "best" equipment (and that are not empty words!)
Regarding soundtrack : some think its below Tales average, some think its above Tales average. In my opinion is a below Tales average still an above JRPG average. Especially 2-3 tracks are within of my top 10 list.
Regarding Gradeshop : typical in tales of games is the gradeshop for NewGame+ after defeating the final boss (or continue in post game stuff and then start anew). Depending on the things you did in your playthrough you can purchase bonuses for your next playthrough. Notable things are double/triple experience and double gald (=gold) for fights. There are others too. It only adds to your experience and is overall fun.
Regarding Difficulty : There are initally 4 difficulties. You can unlock 2 harder difficulties by fighting enough battles on the current highest difficulty. The battles are intense on high difficulty and especially regarding boss fights you will get a hard fight. However thats mostly because AI controlled chars are dying to often. But you will die often enough too, so dont worry! ;)
Regarding Minigames and Quest : There are no minigames.
Regarding Skits : Skits are conversations between characters discussion story events or the cooking tips and other (storywise) trivial things. They are fun to watch and you get a good laugh here and there.
Regarding Customization : Characters can change outfits and get attachments greatly changing the visual appearance in combat, field and ingame events (except the drawn anime cutscenes). Its fun even though i avoided it for the first playthrough. The amount is ok, however alot of things are hidden behind DLCs.
Its a game with some sort of bland story and visuals. However the combat and interesting equipment system makes up for it (plenty!).
In my opinion its an immersive game and i will probably play it 300+ hours to get great gear and do every thing. Then i will most likly just start anew to experience to game from scratch on highest difficulty without bonuses.
Its literally a long time ago since i bought a game that is so rewarding for me.
So : thumbs up since first minute! Never regreted buying it.
Hoping to see older Tales games (like Vesperia) and the new ones on steam too in the next years.

I awake near midnight at frigid temperatures. The wind is howling and it's pitch black. The visibility is under 10m and all that can be seen is the ground and blowing snow. I am starting to freeze up.....I need to find shelter immediately. I follow a trail of half-buried train tracks...
An hour later I come upon a depot with log piles and railroad cars. I see a small trailer and run to it. My health is detoriating quickly from the wind; my clothing is nothing against it's powerful strength. I quickly open the door and find myself a much more bearable setting. The air temperature here is -1°C, much better than the unforgiving arctic outside. My clothing makes it feel warmer than it is; allowing me to warm up. Now it's time to search inside and find something helpful.
Wood scraps, a newspaper, one energy bar, and a scarf. Not much to go by sadly. I eat the energy bar and look around the trailer one last time before heading to bed.
I wake up around 9 AM feeling rejuvenated albeit dehyrdated. My thirst has gone up a lot since the previous night. I head back outside after making sure I didn't miss anything. Outside I create a fire from the wood scraps and newspaper. I light it with the matches I had with me. After praying it would light, it luckily worked the first try. Using the fire, I melt snow to boil it after. Finally I relieved my thirst. After one look around the depot I head into the wilderness again....
This has to be one of the best games I had the luck of playing. Everything about it I love. It is detailed with things like weight, temperature, condition, overall health for example. The desolation of being in the Canadian wilderness up north. The reward of searching multiple cabins, corpses, desks, houses, cars just for small items or food. I cannot express how much I love this game. The worst enemy being nature and your health is also realistic. Though they took liberties with the wolves like they say in the disclaimer; I can easily accept that. But even if wolves didn't attack you, living would still be a struggle for a few days. I managed to live almost 5 days till being attacked by a wolf. I even had a gun and couldn't live (Bolt-Actions aren't great for close up attacks by wolves). I highly recommend someone picking up this game. Winter sale is here and 50% for $10 USD is a fantastic deal for this game. This game is worth it's money and shown it's captivating adventure that it offered.

These monsters take the form of your inner childhood fears and stalk the corridors of a derelict pizzeria, eager to, without heistation, force your weak human form into a walking Iron Maiden and kill you in the most horrific way imaginable. One second they're there, the next, gone. But, always watching you.
Simple mechanics. Open a door, close a door. Turn on a light, turn it off again. Open camera view, close camera view. Five Nights (give or take a few, if you play long enough) alone with 4 (5 *wink*) murderous animatronics. The question falls to you.
Are you ready, for when Freddy comes for you?

A Hat in Time plays very well and has extremely fluid movement and satisfying controls, but the gameplay itself suffers. If you're buying this for a collect-a-thon, you should look elsewhere. Lots of misdirection, illusion of freedom and blatantly linear segments. From what I can tell, the beta seemed to be a lot more appealing and open ended. For its price, a Hat in Time isn't worth the amount of content it offers. The game isn't half as open or fun to explore as it makes itself out to be with the first world. Combat is an afterthought, NPC and enemy variety is very slim, and there's only five worlds.
Overall, it just doesn't have a lot of personality beyond being cute and having funny voices. This review may change depending on how the free DLC goes over. As it stands on launch, save your money for something with more personality and soul. If you want a better platformer, play Mario Sunshine. If you want a better collect-a-thon, play Banjo Kazooie. If you've exhausted those and need something new to scratch the old-school 3D platforming itch, this might do something for you. Just don't expect anything standout or genre-defining.
Edit: Eh, some of the custom levels are better than the official ones, but honestly the user created challenges only make the shaky mechanics even more clear. You'll constantly be trying to pull off tricky wall run/jumping manuevers only to fall and not run at all. Lots of frustration with the wall running. This game handles like it's unfinished, but you might not realize that until you play custom levels.

This game is really something special.  There are games that look better graphically, sure.  There are games with bigger budgets, more insane AAA setpieces, and even longer games.  But there are few games out there with the kind of heart that A Hat in Time has.  It isn't just a Mario or Banjo clone (though the DNA of those games is certainly present). It is also its own game, and am I really glad it is.
I have seen many a comparison to Mario Sunshine, but that's just the beginning.  The different levels act as homages to different platform games in some ways, I suppose.  Mafia Town could be a Mario Sunshine stage, but the second level is more like a Psychonauts stage and so on.
I don't want to say too much else, but if you like games with heart and are willing to put up with a few technical problems to enjoy the kind of game that doesn't come along very often, A Hat In Time is something you just need to play.  It won't be a critical success and won't sell millions of copies, but it will be a cult classic and in a few years everyone will be telling you that you should play it, like Psychonauts before it.

Bitesize Review - Unreal Tournament
The Good:
- Great Art Style
- Graphics still look Great
- Runs well on modern systems (sometimes too well, see below)
- Gameplay is still really fun, tons to choose from, and addicting
- Bots, game modes, and modifiers keep the game interesting
- Iconic and varied roster of weapons to choose from
- Tons of maps (like dozens and dozens)
- Music is perfect for the mood of the game and sounds great
The Bad:
- Some modern computers may require a patch or two to slow down the game so it does not play too fast!
- Single player is really just bot matches with some text story, so you might as well just play bot matches
The Verdict:
As you can tell I have a lot of love for this game. In fact I have to think hard just to find some fault with it. It really is one of the highlights of 90s shooters, and I could say that very few games released since then have even come close to providing the same level of quality and quantity of things to do as this game.
The graphics are colourful and still look great, there are so many levels, characters, settings/modifiers for matches, game modes, and guns to play with. Back then game companies really wanted the player to have everything and this is one of the last great games where they thought about the gamer first. The only issue with this game really is that modern system may run it SO fast that you’ll actually have to download a patch or two to slow the game down so your character doesn’t run 100 times faster than they should.
I cannot recommend this game enough, it provides so much content and plays so well. If you enjoy old school shooters this is a must and it will offer you hours and hours of fun.

Outlast has proven to revive the nearly dying genre of horror in the video game universe. It takes cliches of asylums, mad doctors, and German folklore, and turns it into a masterful experience of horror and suspense. I cannot begin to describe the feeling of adrenaline that pumped through my heart as I ran from these mutated genetic lunatics. The plot has taken risks in including the cliches I have mentioned above, but it had not hindered the story. The plot, while at first seems cliche, actually became increasingly interesting as the game went on, and by the end I was craving the answers to what happened with PROJECT WALRIDER and the Murkoff Corporation, and the dead Doctor Rudolph Wernicke. The ideas of science of this game seem to be classic science fiction, bringing back memories of pleasent nostalgia.
As a horror game, Outlast has revived my love for the Horror genre. It takes the aspect of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, that being that one cannot defend one's self from enemies, and tosses the player into a world of uncertainty and hope of escaping the Mount Massive Asylum alive. Never have I been more frightened of figures in the dark. Another interesting aspect of the game is the choice of a camera as opposed to a flashlight. A very interersting way to go, but it makes sense if one looks at the game's basic plot. Eventually, batteries become your goal next to that of escaping the Asylum, and planning an escape route and hiding place if there is an enemy nearby becomes another objective. The Horror genre over the years has suffered greatly, primarily with the major decline of Silent Hill and Resident Evil, and the more shooter route that Dead Space took with its sequels. This game takes aspects from those games in their prime, along with some tactics of Amnesia, and meshes it together, weaving a wonderful and intriguing tale of the Mount Massive Asylum, the Murkoff Corporation, and PROJECT WALRIDER.
Overall, the game is what I claim to be one of the best of the new age of Horror. If they makes sequels, I will most certainly purchase them.

If you're looking for a strategy game that's both challenging and relaxing, go for Banished. The randomly generated environments ensure a different town layout each time you start a new game, and the difficulty is neatly balanced by the reliability of income. As far as I can tell, you won't have a bad crop. You won't have a bad fishing haul.
But your people will die. The winter will come, and they will die. And the more they die, the fewer there are to hunt and forage and farm, and so the stores will run dry again and again, and everybody will die. Everything gets just that little more frantic in those moments and suddenly everything is about surviving that next winter.
But once you make it through, your town expands and your people repopulate, and honestly, I would say the game gets easier the longer you play - provided you do it properly.

My current game has taken a turn for the worse, and I don't think it will recover. Most of my population are too old to reproduce, and there simply aren't enough children to take their place. It's a genuine worry now that my town is going to slowly die off until there's simply nobody left, and I don't think I'm a fan of irreparable saves.
All in all, I recommend Banished. It's realistic (to a point), it's challenging, but you can sit back, and relax and let your villagers work and live on their own whims. If one of your workers wants to hoard a thousand potatoes in his house during a famine, there's not a damn thing you can do about it.
This game it the best of what the total war franchise has to offer and I hope mire similar games are released soon

Its a good game. Its a solid 8/10 probably. Recommend it to anyone who wants a game that combines the civ series with actual rts combat. It scratches that itch without forking over a kitten load of money for a civ game (the new ones anyways).....and I mean lets face it, civ games feel llimited in the combat side of things and they have bad ai always in general. This game seems to have a bit better ai but it still has issues here and there. But it has the rts side of thigns included...its a bargain when its on sale no doubt, 8 dolllars....why not? you kno.
In terms of the theme of the game. I was a huge Napoleon fan growing up. I read books on him from teh library at night for pleasure.....just for the heck of it! It just seems weird to me now that i would spend my teen years doing that of all things. This is the game that woulda made my soooo happpy back then, if i coulda played it. Instead I had rise of nations....which was amazing in its own right. ANd it actually had a Napoleon campaign in Rise of nations i really enjoyed....and would play again.
Here tho THere is no unity or grand story...its just fragments here and there presented in some ill concieved kind of timeline format. They coulda done a much better job creating a sense of progression in this game, as it stands every campaign and battle is a standalone installment....it doesn't feel like ur moving forward when u hit the next campaign...the  process just restarts which is a real pity. Its fairly faithful to the Napoleon I read about though, but like I said its not presented for people new to Napoleon. YOu aren't gonna be able to follow Napoleon's life or his ahcievements in any sense of chronological timeline in this game, which is a pity.
The combat is not like any rts/strat game i've played to date. Its all about positioning rather than firing the most shots or focusing ur fire. And moving ur units is very frustrating at times. for example you have 1 enemy unit left to kill....so u just target ur units and click on the enemy to get them to attack. What happens? Alll kitten breaks looose and you could lose a small army or the entire match depending on what that unit is. however if you move unit by unit and get them in their right positioninig u can clear that unit with hardly any loses.
Moving units is rly hard at times. And getting them to attack or follow orders or face the right direction are things htat can cause alot of grief. They won't turn around or react when some1 is shooting them from behind or from the side or from the far front right..you have to do it for them. Lotta micro management.
My favourite part is the artillery really. you can just wreck havoc from the other side of the map on an eniterly enemy army with enough 12 pound guns. Its really satisfying to mow down a huge force of milita before they even take a single shot at ur army. So I often try to get as many artillery as possible in my army. Problem with that is the artilly dont always listen to my orders....lol. Especially when i clump them, some are prong to not halting fire when i signal. And if anyone friendly units 'move' infront of those cannons while they are firing they get butchered. Very annoying to signal ur troops to move in only to have ur general decide to do  a very wide turn infront of ur arty....then ur general is ded. Then ur troop morale plummets, then the enemy cannon you are charging fires 1 round and ur entire army flees the battle....just plenty of times where I lost a won battle cause of crazy stuff like that.
Ummm problems?
Ai can get predictable after a while. The campaigns are not.....they aren't as scripted as they shoulda been. They all felt the same in how you tackled them. We needed more scripted events like armies appearing and rewards for taking out of the way objectives. And winning a story campaign isnt that fulfilling...its actually the least fulfilling part of the game is winning it. Why? Cause theres no more point conquering the other land u spend so much time trying to conquer. And the victory doesnt mean anyhting. it doesn't lead to anything tangible.
I really woulda liked if it forced you to win a campaign before you could move onto the next.....instead all you have to do to uinlock tthe next campaign is "start" the previous campaign...then it automatically unlocks the next. There is no drive to complete the campaigns, u get a bit of cutscene goodness sure but its not.....its so distant and limited to just that campaign. It doesn't branch into the next campaign.
So major problems:
-ai gets predictable after a bit
-unit pathfinding.....especiallly when fighting in forts is horrible. I can't believe how horrible it is to position units in forts. ANd forts themselves feeel reallly stupid and broken. Like the first fort  is a rectangle thing where you put units ontop and posiitoning them near cannons alllows a really wimply cannon to fire at incoming forced. Forces themselves aren't worth the cost they take to build. They offer next to no combat advantage reallly. Artilly just go to town on these things.....if ur attacking the fort plays to ur advantage when bombing the enemy. Its 9k gold or something for a fort which is HUGEEE and  it takes 8 turns or something to build. ANd once is built you can upgrade it AGAIN to a star fort. THe start fort is a gianttttt fort you won't be able to even man properly.....I don't get it! forts should be there so you can defend with fewer units. You can't defend these forts with fewer units though at all. U still need an army to man the fort to defeat another army. And these star forts which are costing you 8k + 16k gold to make.....are even worse! How can I pay 16k more gold and get something that offers me lesss defense?!?!? Just things like that pop up in the game alot in different forms.
You get alot of moments and amazingly satisfying moments in this game. in the board type thing though you don't get many options. Im sure the expansions add more options to diplomacy and what not. I just found the army and combat options of the ai were limited a bit too much. You basically have to do everyhting it feels like.

This game was a lot of fun when it came out, and I have 154 hours logged, but it has not aged well. The game has a lot of major flaws. I think Fallout New Vegas is an absolute masterpiece, so I will use New Vegas to explain what is wrong with Fallout 3.
Melee and unarmed attacks are completely useless. This is because Fallout 3 armor seems to reduce damage as a percentage rather than reducing damage by a set amount. Suppose your armor in Fallout 3 reduces damage by 30%. How many bullets do you eat before you land a single melee hit on an enemy? That adds up. You take massive damage while closing the gap.
That damage reduction system works in both directions. In Fallout New Vegas, there are a lot of enemies you can't kill within the first hours of the game. Giant radscorpions in New Vegas have a very high damage threshold, so most guns don't do any damage. Attacking them requires a bit of strategy, and you need to think about which gun you are using. High damage with low fire rate is better than low damage at a high fire rate, and shotgun slugs are very effective while shotgun shot is useless. Fallout 3 is nothing like that. Every enemy in the game can be killed with any weapon in the game. It might take a lot of bullets, but you certainly can kill a Deathclaw in Fallout 3 using the SMG.
Grenades are hilariously overpowered in Fallout 3. The VATS aiming thing stays in slow motion until the grenade explodes, and I think you are invincible during VATS. This means you can go nuts and grenade kill everything. The VATS aiming will land the grenade close enough, the enemy can't run away because it's slow motion, and they can't kill you during that time. Some would say this is a positive for Fallout 3 because it gives an easy "i win" button to any problem. Fallout New Vegas did away with all of that. Grenades in New Vegas will aim like the grenades in Fallout 3, but the slow motion ends when the grenade lands, and you can be killed during that time.
I believe Fallout 3 also has a lack of gun options. The first rifle you get is the hunting rifle. It's pretty good, but it doesn't scale well. It has a low fire rate and low damage, so it becomes useless at higher levels. The next long range gun is the sniper rifle. The sniper rifle is a great gun, but it's rare and it breaks very quickly. The game basically forces you to use Chinese assault rifles at the higher levels. How did Fallout New Vegas differ? It has a .357 rifle, a .44 rifle a .45-70 rifle, a 5.56 rifle, a .50 rifle, and each gun has a variety of ammunition types (a .357 can fire .38 special). New Vegas did it right. You are never forced to use one or two guns. There are so many options.
Is Fallout 3 a good game? Yes it is, but I can't play it anymore because I know that Fallout New Vegas is so much better in every possible way.

Beginner's Guide reminded me of the book Pale Fire by Vladimir Nabokov.
Both rely on a narrator telling you a story about someone they admire, with the story becoming unhinged as you proceed through it; and both are framed around an unfinished work (in Pale Fire a poem, in Beginner's Guide series of games).
But the structure of Pale Fire is hypertextual, meaning as you read the story you are encouraged to skip around to different parts of the book. As you do this, you deviate from the main story and pick up on tidbits that provide context to what you have read or will read. So as work through Pale Fire, there's this slow, muddled crescendo of psychological horror that creeps on you until you realize something is very wrong, but you are never explicity told what it is.
In Beginner's Guide, the story is told very linearly. You are told explicitly what is happening as it's happening. There are recurring themes, and some self references, but everything that's happening is presented in a fixed sequence. So the buildup happens quickly (it is an interesting buildup), and dissipates almost immediately.
If Beginner's Guide had some bit of hypertextuality (it has none, which is kind of unforgivable given the medium and the pedigree of the game's creator) it would have been a more meaningful, thrilling, and lasting experience. Beginner's Guide shows promise, but there are already games that tell this kind of story better (like Her Story).
Still recommended, but not enthusiastically.

Below is my review for Super Flippin' Phones as seen on

Score: 7.0
Bottom-line: Fast-paced, satisfying arcade-action that could do with some more content and variety.
Positives:
-Fast, responsive controls
-Intuitive mechanics
-Clean visual aesthetic
-Well-employed risk-reward elements
Negatives:
-Little variety
-All too repetitive music loops
-Weak tutorial
Nobody thinks twice about a one-note joke. Nobody needs to. Super Flippin’ Phones’ meager one-liner about smartphone trends didn’t evoke even a chuckle from me but, luckily, wasn’t loud enough to get in the way of its inviting mechanics and playful nuances. Successor to Blueprint and 3xBlast’s quite similar Flippin’ Phones (2014), Super Flippin’ Phones brings us much-improved and overall great retro-inspired visuals and pure arcadey fun and flare but too little variety in terms of visuals and music.
In case you didn’t notice, everyone at the mall has their eyes glued to their smartphone or at least it seems so. Now imagine if a hobo were to run riot through Macy’s or Neiman Marcus, knocking phones out of everyone’s hands. Haha. What then? That’s about it. Super Flippin’ Phones utilizes this catchy but shallow social commentary to give their game some initial pop and, after some consideration, that’s quite alright by me. Actual gameplay neither reiterates the premise to a point of annoyance nor wholly relies on its meme-ability to move forward like Goat Simulator, Nyan Cat games, and so many others. Taking the joke a step further with an iOS and Android port could bring that extra “meta” to earn a full chuckle. The controls are simple enough and, frankly, the game holds up better played in small bursts than full hours so it could be great, but I digress.
Using only WASD, you must guide your hobo on a rampage as he wildly flails his arms, knocking phones out of the hands of so many unsuspecting smartphone zombies in his path. Doing so “hips them” to his freewheeling lifestyle, inspiring a legion to follow his every step and inciting the wrath of countless mall officers, police dogs, and undercover cops. In addition to flipping phones, our hobo can slap cops and dogs out of his way, given he has enough stamina. Stamina depletes as players leap over or slap cops and replenishes slowly while running and quickly while standing still. Get caught standing still or with low stamina and it’s game over.
Followers must be turned in at the hobo’s cardboard box in exchange for points. The larger your following, the greater the reward per evacuee. Get caught before turning in any followers, however, and you’ll come out empty handed. Whether scoring in the hundreds-of-thousands or zero, this arcadey implementation of risk-reward elements essentially won me over, tempting me to push my luck over and over again. Controls are responsive enough for quick turns and last second getaways and the runner’s pace of gameplay perfectly maintained the excitement.
Gameplay’s mostly intuitive though the game could've used a dedicated tutorial instead of its halting tutorial prompts. Tutorial prompts pause the flow of gameplay whenever players run into something new, taking control away from the player and diminishing the feeling of discovery. It comes off as sloppy and gets annoying, especially since it brings the otherwise fast game to a full stop.
High enough scores unlock additional game modes which feature a greater variety of obstacles. For instance, the League of Extraordinary Police difficulty adds an officer on stilts and one with a riot shield to the mix, both of which have their own simple but complementary solutions: riot shields knock you backward and need to be vaulted over while stilt cops require you to jump to slap them, eating up more stamina than the usual mall cop. Randomly placed giant gift-box drops contain a variety of quirky costumes like underpants only, caped wrestler, and moustache man. They add a good bit of visual variety to gameplay and give players something to work for other than achievements.
I found the overall package to be entertaining but too limited in scope and production to keep longer play sessions feeling fresh. For instance, you spend the entire game in multi-level malls, rioting to the sound of only a few peppy but short tracks. The tracks themselves aren’t so great to begin with and wore out for me after only a few runs. While the enemy variety and core gameplay loop are exciting, the game world begins to feel monotone early on, especially since it can take some time to unlock new levels. In the earliest level for example, the restaurant part of the mall has its own theme and color scheme but the rest of the mall lacks anything remarkable. A few more explicitly detailed shops within the mall, more locations varying in layout and size, and just more of everything could've done a lot to keep the world feeling lively.
The “good,” in a way, is as “good, honest fun” as it gets. Gameplay is addictively challenging and mechanically concise and there’s little if any pretension behind the game’s premise - honestly, knowing nothing about the title before playing, I went in expecting to be bludgeoned over the head with commentary about Generation Z. Although currently lacking in content and variety but considering its $3.00 launch price, Super Flippin’ Phones is well worth its value because it’s straight up fun. Some content support post-launch could help the game become a sure winner though developers have yet to formally announce future plans, if any. I also feel it worth reiterating that I believe the game would excel on mobile platforms: it’s perfect for quick pick-up-and-play and perhaps better suited to thrive in that context than in formal, sit-down desktop sessions. Let’s hope we see a few content updates post-launch and - fingers crossed - a mobile port down the road.

Super Flippin' Phones is a game where you run around a shopping mall knocking people's phones out of their hands, avoiding cops as you do so. The game includes multiple floors, having a unique power-up and class of mall cop, which gives the gameplay some variety. The pixel graphics look great, and suit the game; the music matches the same theme. The controls are simple and easy to learn, and the game also has controller support, which I thought was much easier to use than using a keyboard. The game doesn't really take itself seriously either; the developers gave the game a great sense of humour by adding adding things like cops wearing fairy costumes, and a heart-boxers costume.
I really enjoyed Super Flippin' Phones, and will definitely play it again in future. The game's quirkiness keeps you coming back for more, and the gameplay keeps you hooked in. I'd definitely give this game a play, especially with such a cheap price tag. I also think it's worth mentioning that Super Flippin' Phones is available for Android.

Враждебные воды: Антей Рост это стратегическая игра 2001 года, похожа на оригинал командования и властвуй, где создавать и использовать различные наземные и ПВО, собирать ресурсы, сражаясь с врагом на острове в океане. История ставит вас в середине мира перестроен после войны, что почти уничтожил все. Люди этого нового мира вновь найти себя в конфликт, на этот раз против лидеров старого мира, которые бежали в подполье после поражения в войне.
История довольно хорошо и сделает для интересного перезагрузки с современным дизайном. В качестве стратегии в реальном времени, это на самом деле довольно весело. Озвучкой приличный, и игра выглядит хорошо для выпуска 2001 года, но, безусловно, устарел сегодняшним стандартам. Игра использует 3D-карта, которая является хорошим изменением для RTS игр, выпущенных в то же самое время. Органы управления отличаются, чем я ожидал для РТС. Я обычно на микроуровне мои единиц, но с Враждебные воды: Антей Рост у вас нет этой способности. Есть множество различных блоков, которые можно создать, каждый со своими способностями и недостатками, в отличие от более известный названий, таких как игры командования и властвуй, в Антей Рост у вас есть возможность индивидуально обновления единиц с броней, щитами и т.д. ,
В целом, в то время как это может быть немного устаревшим, это приличный РТС и стоит поднимая если вы в старой школы стратегии в реальном времени игры. Лично я хотел бы, чтобы это в списке перезагрузки в какой-то момент в будущем.

I saw this game was on sale and bought it because of overwhelmingly positive user reviews. Well, thirty minutes later, I can firmly attest that those reviews were not undeserved. This game takes advantage of a of certain aspects of videogames as a medium that other mediums of entertainment can't, such as books or movies. What you get out of this game is entirely up to how you play it. It can be either a fast-paced parkour simulator, or a quick and relaxing way to spend half an hour. The music even reflects this to a certain extent, ranging from peppy beats to soothing synth. Perhaps most importantly is the real sense of progression that this game provides players with in such a short timespan; when the game begins one will most likely be zipping through the game utilizing just the game's most obvious mechanics, however as it progresses players will learn how to move more gracefully and efficiently using more advanced (and at times unexpected) techniques of movement. The best part about this is that the game never blatantly teaches players how to get better; rather it nudges players to teach themselves via its succinct yet subtle level design. All in all, this game is great, and I would reccomend it to anyone who has so much as a passing interest in videogames.
Sidenote: I have to reccomend that in one's first playthrough they collect all the optional cubes before jumping on the yellow button, as the ending is much more satisfying that way IMHO.

I'm not quite sure what, but something awakens from deep within the bowels of the engine.  Something angry.  Something mad as hell.  Something powerful and corrupt.  And something that destroyed my computer.  I'm talking hard reset destroy.  I'm talking can't turn it on because it gives up on life and shuts down destroy.  Eventually, through some miracle after 2-3 months of fiddling, we (me and my dad) got the computer to reactivate in safe mode.  We then deleted my new engine, which I got during a sale and couldn't afford otherwise (This will become important later), but all the while I could only think of all the nicer positive reviews of this engine which claim no such errors happened.  When I deleted the engine, I did so only on my dad's command because he thought the problem would of been a "recently downloaded program that changed the computer."  I then decided, a few months after the incident, to try the engine again and see if it really was it's fault for almost ruining my computer.  I expiremented, reinstalled the program and checked if I could restart my computer, and surely enough it became unstable again.  Through what I can only claim as luck, a few tries restarted the computer in safe mode and I deleted the program again, this time aware that something within it destabilizes my computer.  This REALLY sucks, especially so because I got fairly good at it, and even though I had at the time no way to make custom assets, I do now thanks to another program I've download that works, GIMP 2 (An art program that includes transparent pixels, required to make non-square art assets).  The worst part, although it is a good thing for most, is that somehow the program remembered everything I did even after I uninstalled it, meaning all the game(s) I had made up to that point were still there when I redownloaded it.  I don't know if I am missing something or what, and I'm sure the creators of the engine have no mal-intent, but that doesn't change the terror it caused, or the fact that of all things, this caused the worst break in my computer I've ever faced, more than every virus, and more than every spamware I've ever had (I'm sure there is worse spamware and viruses out there, but I'm not an idiot and avoid them to the best of my ability).  It also doesn't give me a refund, so ouch to my bank account as well ($20 is alot to an 18 year old, what do you want from me?)
If you think you know or can find the solution to the problem, comment with your answer and mark this review as funny.
Here's my specs:
Processor: AMD Athlon(tm) II 170u 2.00 GHz
RAM: 3.00 GB
64 Bit OS
Notice that these are above the supposed minimum requirements for the engine.
If you can't take anything else from this review, at least know that you are using this engine at your own risk and it is NOT worth it.

PROS:
1. No angsty teenage drama. Yes, the story is not particulary captivating but at least it gives you an adult vibe. There are no characters whose only role is to repeat last said words with a puzzled look on their faces when everything is decided by others. Nothing is done blindly because someone said to do it, everything is evaluated and actions taken with consequences in mind.
2. Battle system might seem overcomplicated, especially in the beginning but later you start to appreciate its flexibility. A lot of different monsters require different tactics so there is a necessity to adapt. There is also an easy mode if you only want the story.
3. All girls are best girls.
CONS:
1. Graphics are bad, like very bad. The game looks worse than FF XII, yes, twelve. Giant bland levels which you have to travel across over and over.
2. Speaking of traveling. The game forces upon you an insane amount of backtracking. I lost count how many times I visited more populated central regions. It's common to travel for 15 minutes to see 30 seconds cutscene and then go back the same way. It wouldn't be so bad if the game looked decent but... see 1.
3. Overlocalization and mistranslation. A lot of lines are mistranslated for no apparent reason. The message is delivered but overlocalized. Just a couple of lines from memory: two guards say to each other: "Let's go drink" - "Ah, with pleasure" but it's translated as "Let's go drink" - "Anything to get off this armor". Why? No reason at all. Lailah often compassionly repeats the protagonist name but it always translated differently, like "that is so" or "you do, don't you" etc. The game is full of humour but it's not delivered due to horrible translation job. Puns fall flat because lines make no sense or just simply not funny. Also it's the game in medieval settings, why put so many modern idioms? It breaks the immersion.
Overall I give it 6/10. After all I've said I still like the game, I just wish I knew japanese better to play without the subs, I would have definitely enjoyed it more.

This review assumes you have some familiarity with the Tales of series.
I have mixed feeling about Tales of Zestiria. Did I enjoy it? I'd say yes but no Tales game has such a disparate list what it did well and what it did poorly.
Zestiria's combat is similar to most 3D Tales games. You move either closer to or further from your enemy as you attack them with a diverse range of attacks and spells. Like Tales of Graces, it allows for sidestepping and does away with TP. Instead, all attacks are flashy artes that deplete a stamina meter.
Combat itself is deep and thoughtful. There are several enemy archtypes and each requires a different approach. Each individual playable character controls differently and you can switch between them in combat to adapt a fighting style.
Zestiria features a pair up mechanic similar to Xillia but vastly improved. Rather than one character just following the other's lead, they act independently. Instead, they can fuse through a mechanic called Armatization. It opens a lot of interesting combat options up. Whether it be fusing to exploit a weakness, consolidate into a stronger enemy target, reviving a partner through a fusion, or splitting apart to dodge an attack, it all feels great.
Still, there are a few flaws. New attacks are unlocked and it really makes the variety feel lacking in the early game. Additionally, magic seems more overpowered than in previous iterations. Sometimes an attack will interupt magic, other times it will only speed up the cast.
Most importantly, the friendly AI is probably the worst I've seen it. Your teammates have no sense of spacing despite strategies. They rarely show an inclination to block and get themselves killed frequently. That they can fuse and cause 2 deaths for the price of one makes it all the worse. It can get incredibly frustrating to watch and I ultimately found myself setting them to not blow their combat resources and healing them frequently. It makes me think this game would be far more fun as a co-op game.
Zestiria uses an open world approach that feels amazing. Traversing the world feels good and cutscenes require no transitions. Rather, the camera elegantly shifts and lets the action unfurl from where your characters stand. Entering combat similarly happens by touching an enemy and hopping back into a combat stance. It ends up feeling beautifully cohesive and is something I hope future games keep.
Characters develop in the classic RPG fashion. You gain XP/Levels through fights and equip better equipment as you go. As you level you unlock more moves, making combat more interesting and varied. The big gripe here is the skill system. It's convoluted, grindy, and not the easiest to manipulate. Each piece of equipment comes with skills attached. As you stack skills of the same name, type, or element you gain either bonus stats or a bonus skill. Manipulating these to get what you want requires grinding, use of a item fusion mechanic that doesn't seem to obviate how skills transfer, and finding one time use NPCs that can confer a specific skill on a piece of equipment. It's excessively complex and is probably the worst element of the game.
Dungeons are for the most part right angled ruins. There's occasionally a clever puzzle here and there but there's generally not much to write home about here. Gameplay wise I don't feel like they subtract much save the water dungeon. It's a dungeon built with motion detectors that warp you back to the beginning of the dungeon. The quick save mechanic reduces the pain, but it's still horrendous design.
A fast travel mechanic helps drop the trek time which is appreciated. It's occasionally unavailable, but that's always due to needing to encounter a cutscene on the way to your goal.
Sidequests are easily accessible by simply talking to your party members. You also get the flavor of the world and where other sidequests might be from banter you hear in town as you walk around.
The setting of the plot is probably one of the most novel in a Tales game. The world is comprised of ordinary humans and spirit like creatures known as seraphim that most humans are oblvious to. Sorey, the MC, is a human raised in a village of seraphim and is the rare human who can perceive seraphim. This ultimately leads to him becoming the Shepard. A figure of legend who mediates between the two races and purges the world of malevolance caused by fallen humans and seraphim alike. It's a different player perspective than any other Tales game has provided and it feels fresh.
The character unfortunately mostly underwhelm. Sorey is a competent and sometimes surprisingly mature main but there isn't much of a character arc nor is he terribly interesting. In being the Shephard, his design is that he's a near uncorruptable, pure, and just character. He has some personality which helps, but he's basically shackled from any meaningful change. Other human members are better as while similarly uncorruptable, have interesting spins on why. They're also pretty charismatic.
The seraphim party members on the other hand are all pretty bland. They all experience next to no character development so what you see is what you get. They mostly devolve into trope-like caricatures which hurts. A lot of them had setup or back story to be genuinely interesting but ultimately none of it was capitalized on.
The story itself is about average. It does a good job of taking you through a variety of locales and rationalizes near everything that happens with the plot extremely well. It also presents a lot of epic scenarios that were a joy to play. Still, due to the lack of development in the characters there's no real feeling of gravity for the player behind the events.
Again, it's a competent but not great story. I didn't feel it hurt the game but I also don't think it added much.
The sound direction for this game is outstanding and easily the best in the entire Tales of series. It's strong praise but it's deserving. The orchestration is beautiful and small decisions like not switching to a different combat theme in dungeons goes a long, long way. Several of the dungeons were legitimately more enjoyable due to atmosphere and tension and music underscores them with.
The fire dungeon's energetic theme meshes with the lava filled environment. The water dungoen's piano heavy orchestra fits with the more intellectually based challenge posed in the plot to Sorey. The final dungeon theme leaves the area dripping with a sense of ominous tension.
Zestiria isn't perfect. It has a lot of flaws and some of them are major. The skill system feels bad, friendly AI performs poorly, and plot isn't the best offering of the series. Still for all those things it does so very much right. The open world is beautiful and cohesive. The combat is one of the most varied and legitimately fun entries in recent memory. Not to mention, the soundtrack is the best of the series hands down.
For all the things I disliked, I loved the things it did well enough to brush those issues aside. It honestly gives me a lot of hope for the future of the franchise. If you enjoy the Tales series or are just itching for a JRPG, it's worth playing.

I awake near midnight at frigid temperatures. The wind is howling and it's pitch black. The visibility is under 10m and all that can be seen is the ground and blowing snow. I am starting to freeze up.....I need to find shelter immediately. I follow a trail of half-buried train tracks...
An hour later I come upon a depot with log piles and railroad cars. I see a small trailer and run to it. My health is detoriating quickly from the wind; my clothing is nothing against it's powerful strength. I quickly open the door and find myself a much more bearable setting. The air temperature here is -1°C, much better than the unforgiving arctic outside. My clothing makes it feel warmer than it is; allowing me to warm up. Now it's time to search inside and find something helpful.
Wood scraps, a newspaper, one energy bar, and a scarf. Not much to go by sadly. I eat the energy bar and look around the trailer one last time before heading to bed.
I wake up around 9 AM feeling rejuvenated albeit dehyrdated. My thirst has gone up a lot since the previous night. I head back outside after making sure I didn't miss anything. Outside I create a fire from the wood scraps and newspaper. I light it with the matches I had with me. After praying it would light, it luckily worked the first try. Using the fire, I melt snow to boil it after. Finally I relieved my thirst. After one look around the depot I head into the wilderness again....
This has to be one of the best games I had the luck of playing. Everything about it I love. It is detailed with things like weight, temperature, condition, overall health for example. The desolation of being in the Canadian wilderness up north. The reward of searching multiple cabins, corpses, desks, houses, cars just for small items or food. I cannot express how much I love this game. The worst enemy being nature and your health is also realistic. Though they took liberties with the wolves like they say in the disclaimer; I can easily accept that. But even if wolves didn't attack you, living would still be a struggle for a few days. I managed to live almost 5 days till being attacked by a wolf. I even had a gun and couldn't live (Bolt-Actions aren't great for close up attacks by wolves). I highly recommend someone picking up this game. Winter sale is here and 50% for $10 USD is a fantastic deal for this game. This game is worth it's money and shown it's captivating adventure that it offered.
EDIT: To people freaking out about this being a "cash grab", the story mode is about to be released soon. There's a countdown, stop flipping out folks.

It was a dark and story night aboard the Hindenburg (which has somehow been turned into a multi-level luxury hotel)...
Let's start this right: BLUES AND BULLETS IS AN EPISODIC GAME THAT HAS ONLY HAD 2 EPISODES RELEASED IN TWO YEARS.  DO NOT BUY THE SEASON PASS. DEVS HAVE GONE DARK AT SOCIAL MEDIA. MOST ARE WORKING FULL TIME AT OTHER COMPANIES.
Anyway, you play Elliot Ness a former prohibition era detective. You're hired to find a kidnapped little girl. You don't know what your objective is until 3/5 through the first episode. The problem with the first episode's narrative is that the protagonist's backstory and character are established in two different scenes, slowing down the entire story. An example of how to do introduction and backstory right? The Walking Dead. First 3 minutes Lee is introduced, we know his character, and we know his struggle. Blues and Bullets takes about 40 minutes to introduce the protagonist before getting on with the story.
Aside from the stumbling story of this story oriented game, we also have trouble in the gameplay.
* The dialouge is vauge Fallout 4 style one word choices.
* The gunplay is frankly terrible. It's an on-rail shooter where you can take cover, but there's no reason to.
Luckily, the actual putting together of clues (and the satisying stringing together once its all pieced together) is an awful lot of fun. Unfortunatley, there's only one in the first episode.
Also the voice acting is really hit or miss. The protagonist and the "buddy cop" are pretty consistent, but the side characters range from below average to terrible.
You know, even with its faults, I still want to know the rest of the story. The episode starts and ends with a REALLY strong plot hook, but I guess we'll never find out what happened.

Never.  Again.  Nope.  No.  Done.
This game has one very well designed feature though: upon hitting escape the game immediately shuts down, no questions asked, which is great because in my panic that is what I did, and that is the result I wanted.
Five Nights at Freddy's is terrifying.  I will not be playing it again (maybe), but I give it mad props for being the most innovative, creative, inspired take on survival horror at a time when there are so many games out there just trying to be Amnesia or Slender.  Five Nights at Freddy's is terrifyingly original - and that's a large part of the reason I was completely lacking in any immunity to even the most basic scares this game dropped on me and I had to quit out at 4am on the second day because I was having heart palpitations.
The brilliance of the design here is that unlike every other survival horror game I've ever played, in Five Nights at Freddy's
.  You stay exactly where you are in the one room with minimal ability to change your point of view, monitoring the goings on on the security cameras, listening to noises, flicking on the lights to see if anyone's outside your room and if it's worth spending electricity to close the safety door - and through the whole experience you cannot move, you can't run, you can't hide, you can't do anything at all except stand there and wait, and watch, and listen, and know that eventually they're going to come.   It is a uniquely terrifying; in every other game you can give in to your urge to run (whether that's a good idea or not) but in this game you literally cannot.  That instinctive reaction, that self-preserving power is taken away from you, and that fact makes the game so much more unsettling, just that fact that your natural instinct is gone.  When for the first time I flicked on a light and saw an animatronic standing there, stationary, leering at me, I panicked.  In any other game I would have taken shelter, hidden, prepared to fight, whatever, but here?  I was paralysed because none of my instincts knew to do anything other than
.
I have often said that indie gaming brings creativity and innovation in much the same was as structured poetry does. In Five Nights at Freddy's they took a game with a simple, no-physics point-and-click interface, and handful of static visuals and a whole lot of atmosphere and made the scariest experience I've ever had in front of a computer.

You know what? This is pretty good! It's a hybrid of a simple arcadey vehicle simulator (both aerial and ground), and a real-time strategy. You are tasked with dealing with a bunch of comedically evil villains (like, they have a communist general, and a corrupt corporate executive, among their ranks, and they don't even bicker between one another because they're so concentrated on undermining the utopian society world has become) using one of the last operational carriers capable of creating units on it's own. And it's pretty fun, despite such an uncommon premise and games datedness it not only works fine on my machine, it also has a descent interface, which is lovely. Oh, and, you get to design vehicles on your own - not only do you designate what sort of vehicles you want built, you also get to pick the weapon, and the extra equipment like armor plating, or the "soulcatcher" module if you want to not only directly control the vehicles, but also give them orders. Finally, the RTS aspect also shows itself in the fact you require dedicated resource collector machines to convert scrap metal scattered after battles into resources, while enemies have oil rigs, which means that they have an advantage and you have to think fast and pick your targets before you get overcome. All in all I recommend this game, it's pretty fun.

Jean-Luc Godard was fond of saying that he went from being a film critic to a filmmaker because he perceived actually making films as the ultimate form of criticism. He could say what he wanted to say about the art form by doing, rather than saying.
With The Beginner's Guide, Davey Wreden becomes the first game designer to take up Godard's mantle in this medium. It is a powerful statement about the significance of authorial intent in a gaming context, taking a skeptical look at the idea that you can discern things about a creator's personality and psyche through their work. Saying any more would spoil the experience. Suffice to say that anyone interested in games from an educated, literary perspective will adore The Beginner's Guide. Anyone who isn't should still play The Beginner's Guide, if only to get exposed to some fascinating arguments about the nature of the medium.

THis game is a wonderful look into what it's really like to be insane. I had a great deal of fun simply watching the inmates perform their rituals along with what the game had to really offer, which was a lot of atmospheric scares. But more on that in a moment. I like the objective approach this game took with the inhabitants of Mount Massive, most of them are trapped in their own little world, either too broken to be in touch with reality, or too tortured to realize the reality around them. some even help you in their skewed and twisted ways. especially the main plot point: Father Martin; while he's the main reason you are trapped in the asylum as long as you are, he's also a good chunk of the reason you stay alive. a good chunk of the people want you dead for various reasons, so there's still your danger of getting skewered.
the game is rather atmospheric and relies a lot on opressiveness, capriciousness, and atmospheric and story tension to scare you a lot more than it uses jump scares. I never understood the rejection of jump scares: I know they are cheap, but sometimes the confusion and high intensity is necessary to break you out of the cautious lull you set yourself into. jump scares can be used to enhance an experience without relying on them and this game does a good job of doing that.
the story was a wonderful walk into the dark recesses of the human mind and it's depravity. I was almost convinced the scientists found something they shouldn't have with their deep hypnosis trials. it was a decently profound story with a great deal of necessary unanswered questions for the mind to ponder... untill the last fifteen minutes of the game.
once you decend the elevator into the laboratory, the game quickly changes from a deep psychological horror, to a cheap, clear-cut, action thriller. it's like they hired a different storywriter for the last part who thought any supernatural elements absolutely must be explained in full technicolor detail as to not let anyone believe in the silly ghost stories of the inmates. the game does an absolutely marvelous job of making you believe you just might be an inmate yourself. then strips it way with talk of nanomachines and a cheap as free chase sequence. truly, the last ending of Outlast completely tarnishes what should have been a great story to keep playing again and again.

Some games are so stupid in their concept that they provide enormous amounts of fun to play. That describes the Steam debut of Dutch developer Blauwprint. I honestly thought that I was going to hate this♥♥♥♥♥♥ I thought it was going to be a game that really didn’t need to be on Steam. I thought it was going to be a game that belonged only to mobile devices. I thought I’d play it once for less than half an hour and never return to it again. I don’t know whether to be more shocked about the game or to question my sanity. This game is great.
It doesn’t look like much. It’s actually really simplistic. At $2.99, less than a cup of coffee, it’s getting my vote as one of the biggest bargain of the early year. You may not rack up hour upon hour in the game but I challenge you to play it once and not end up with a huge grin on your face. In a world where we have limited time on our hands cheap quick thrills that we can return to time and again are worth their weight in gold. And that is where Super Flippin’ Phones has few peers.
It’s not going to win many awards. It’s just not that type of game. But it will win your heart. The pixel graphics are superbly illustrated – providing just enough clarity so that you can understand what is happening on the screen despite the frantic pace of the action. Speaking of… It will take you a couple of games to adjust to how crazy the pace is. But that’s the point of the game. It’s supposed to be that fast. In many respects its a twitch game but it lacks the frustrations that typically go along with them. Yes, you will die quickly and often but it’s something that’s too be expected. You’ll learn very quickly and embrace the best ways that you play. You’ll learn and there’s a high likelihood that you will dig it.
It’s not generally my type of game but I really do love it. It has been critically overlooked – Metacritic doesn’t even have a critic or a user score for the game yet. There’s 10 reviews on Steam as of time of writing. Every one of them positive. I am disappointed that the gaming media has overlooked this game. Sure, on the surface it doesn’t seem like much but that’s where you need to dig beneath the surface and actually play a game comes into play. First time developers can and do make fantastic little games. They deserve an opportunity to have their game spotlighted. Yes, that’s where I hope Steamified can come into play and assist developers and show games off. That’s why I’m going to try and move the Steamified Broadcast Network up to an earlier than estimated date and have gameplay videos to show off games such as this one so not only will you read of them but see them being played.
Jump in and buy this game. Don’t wait for it to be bundled – unless that happens sooner rather than later. Buy it. I recommend this game because it’s some of the most fun that I’ve had playing games so far this year.

Outlast... A brilliant game, horror in its purest form.
Amnesia was the only real scary game in existance before this game was released and now there is a game that takes the crown of the king of horror.
In Outlast you play in feet of a journalist called Miles Upshur.  You receive an e-mail from an employee at Mount Massive Asylum which is owned by the company Murkoff Corporation.  Of course you dont find out the source of the tip Miles Upshur received until the DLC content was released where the source of the tip is revealed.
The game progresses through as you are forced further into the asylum by those who reside inside, at first one of the inmates overpowers you and throws you out the window then you're discovered by another inmate who ensures that you do not leave so that you can be his witness.  Throughout the game Miles Upshur sees many things and goes through intense pain while being chased by many other inmates who wish to kill him.
This game is a great horror game, jumpscares are very well done and the ambience is very good.  This game is in the same vein as Amnesia with the fact that you have no weapons and you're only abilities of surviving is running away and hiding from your enemies.
There are not many things to fault about this game but almost all games has faults and one of the problems with this game is that it can get a bit of repetitive with the main threat you face in the game, a man known as Chris L. Walker.  The moments when Chris is pursuing you it's basically just hide and hope that he doesnt check the locker that you hide in.
When it comes down to it all, this game is still a great game and the repetitiveness of the Chris L. Walker moments are not enough to make this game disappointing at all, this game is a must buy for anyone looking for great horror games.

Let me start with the gameplay, the Kid controls fairly well with controls being very responsive and giving you a lot of moves to play with and make your way around the levels. However, certain things get really frustrating because the camera isn't that great, sometimes it's really hard to hell where the Kid is in the middle of a jump because you might not be able to see your shadow and the wall climb/jump is terrible. If you jump towards a wall you'll run up a bit and you have the option to jump off or just slide down the wall. Jumping off the wall leads to a really, really small jump that almost doesn't get you any height and you can't control the direction of it at all, it's always perpendicular off of the wall. You also don't get your double jump back after doing this which you probably should since it'd help.
Most of your moves come in the form of different hats that you knit after finding bundles of yarn, it's pretty interesting but there's no method to this progression. Every yarn bundle looks different, one representing each of the different hats. Once you get a new yarn bundle, you now have a "blueprint" for that hat and any subsequent bundles of the same look just count as a "plus one" on your yarn counter, meaning that any other bundle, no matter what it looks like will contribute to the creation of any hat. It doesn't take long to find every hat bundle and just make all of the hats (if you've been good on finding the bundles). Also, a lot of the hats don't have much of a purpose. One of the first ones you get allows you to run faster, but it's not that much faster and really isn't worth using. The last hat in the game allows you to stop time briefly, but it only has a single use for the entire game and I can't think of any other reason why you'd want to use it. The hat powers are great, but they're not well untilized.
Onto the levels, there's only four and they're not that great. The first level is quite large and sprawling with a lot of visual interest. The second one takes place in a movie studio and has some clever ideas, but nearly every mission is it's own secluded section that's incredibly short. The third is a large forest with a lot of barriers you have to take down but when you do, you're left with a largely empty creepy forest without much in it and it can be confusing to navigate because everything just looks the same. The fourth is an utterly massive level that takes place on the peaks of themed mountain tops but the whole level is "free roam" without any interesting missions or characters to interact with you're left to your own devices to find the various timepieces yourself. It feels pretty lazy. There is a fifth "level" is just the final boss area which is incredibly short, think of the area right before Bowser in Super Mario Sunshine. Other than that there's also several small secluded challenge levels that are all themed exactly the same and really don't have anything to do with the levels they're attached to.
Content: There just isn't enough of it, at 2~ hours of game time I managed to beat the final boss with only optional mopping up to do if I cared to get the 100%. I played for four more hours trying and managed to get to 90% and I won't be going back because I'm already bored of the experience. Also, a lot of the collectibles are pointless, I have all of the hats so all of the extra yarn is pointless to collect and everything else is just cosmetic items that don't even count towards your completion precentage. I believe there's 40 "timepieces" (think Stars in Mario games) and you only need 25 to beat the game.
The good: The music is great (though a lot of it takes heavily from Mario and Zelda), the game has a good art style and stays fresh enough for you to beat it.
I do like the game, don't get me wrong but as someone who spent $15 to get 2 copies I feel like $30 is waaaay too much for what A Hat in Time has to offer and for that I can't recommend it. Definitely get this on sale though if you love 3D platformers.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.
I can't think of a proper review, so here's my favorite soup recipe:
edited:
My favorite soup: Saltibarsciai.
INGREDIENTS:
For the soup:
200 g | 7 oz boiled & cooled beetroot (about 2 medium beets)
100 g | 3.5 oz cucumber (about 2 large pickling cucumbers, either fresh or pickled – see note above)
6 spring onions or 10 green onion leaves
2 hard-boiled eggs
1.5 litres | 3 pints kefir (or 500 ml | 1 pint thick natural yoghurt and 1 litre | 2 pints buttermilk)
Bunch fresh dill
Juice of ½ a lemon (optional)
Salt to taste
For the side dish:
200 g | 7 oz potatoes
METHOD:
Peel the potatoes and chop into bite-sized pieces. Place in a saucepan of boiling water, add a good pinch of salt and boil until a knife can easily pierce the flesh.
While the potatoes are boiling, assemble the soup.
Slice the beetroot & gherkins into fine julienne.
Chop the eggs into small dice.
Chop the scallions or onions leaves into 1 cm (½ inch) pieces.
Finely chop the dill.
Pour the kefir into a large bowl or saucepan and add the chopped ingredients and half of the lemon juice, holding back some of the dill for garnish.
Taste and season salt and additional lemon juice as required.
Ladle the soup into bowls and sprinkle with the remaining dill.
Serve the potatoes on a side plate so that they do not heat the soup.

Im writing this after my first playthrough.I watched the video and  read many reviews before deciding to play the game .i managed to survive for 2 days and 5 hours. I started out in the highway area.There were several wolves far enough away that i could safely travel the raod and access many houses.i got a decent amount of food and  supplies to keep warm for a bit and keep fed .My main problem was  i was finding mostly canned foods which required a tool to open them .I decided to venture onto the lake where the wolves were because i saw several cabins on small islands and i was hoping for a tool that would be useful .I got halfway onto the lake when 2 wolves spotted me .They started chasing me and as luck was on my side a blizzard came on suddenly and i lost them and made it to the first island with  a cabin .No such luck with any tools save for some sewing repair kits. I continued to go from island to island after resting till dawn from the first night .More supplies but no  knives or axes or even a can opener. I went out onto the ice and  started a fire in an ice fishing shack and cooked some fish and brewed some herbal tea.After the fire died down a wolf found me an attacked me.I fought it off but had to use most of my supplies of healing items to stop the bleeding .I made it back to one of the cabins on a small island and  tore up several unneeded  clothing items to repair my damaged  worn clothes  using the sewing kit .Then i rested till day 2 .At this point i went back to the road and follwed it up to some train tracks .I decided to  follow the tracks .They ended up taking me  to the mystery lake which is the other starting point in the game .My fatigue was getting high and i spotted a dam .I decided to duck inside to see what i might find .I found a lantern immediately  on a shelf and picked it up .As soon as i picked it up , my fatigue level was so high it said you are encumbered and then i heard a howl.I turned around and  a wolf inside the damn attacked and killed me . What i like about the game is the  sound effects and the feeling of definate isolation.You actually do feel like your desperate and you have to watch your stats like hunger and thirst plus fatigue or you will be in trouble.I read the disclaimer about the  wolves intentionally  being made to attack humans ,but stepping inside of a building and instantly being attacked was sort of annoying.All in all  the weather,and the feeling of the game that you need to keep moving and finding  neccesary items to survive is fun and keeps you wandering around hoping you find that 1 needed item to get you through till the next day .I  definately reccomend this game.
